  • Classifies the injury as a moderate muscle strain based on findings and sets a realistic range of return-to-play time rather than a promise. critical
  • Sets criteria-based progression rather than date-based, using pain, range, strength and function. critical
  • Includes early phase relative rest, pain-limited loading and gentle movement.
  • Progresses to isometric then eccentric hamstring loading, with sets, repetitions and progression.
  • Includes lumbopelvic control and trunk strengthening in the program.
  • Plans a graded running program leading to sprinting and sport-specific drills including contact only at the end.
  • Names outcome measures such as pain, active knee extension range, strength comparison with the other side and functional tests.
  • Addresses medication use, such as discussing with the physician or pharmacist the use of anti-inflammatories in early healing.
  • Plans return-to-play criteria and a hamstring injury prevention program after return.

Performance scale

4Classifies the injury, sets honest timelines, uses criteria-based phases with dosage, outcome measures and return-to-play criteria, and adds prevention.
3Provides sound phased rehabilitation with criteria but is limited in dosage detail or return-to-play criteria.
2Lists exercises generally with fixed dates and few outcome measures.
1Promises return by the final or uses stretching and heavy loading regardless of pain.

Model spoken answer

From the findings, this looks like a moderate hamstring strain of the biceps femoris, not a mild one. He has bruising, tenderness in the muscle belly, a 15 degree difference in the active knee extension test, weakness with pain on resisted flexion, and pain on sprinting. A moderate strain typically takes a few weeks to return to full sport, and I would tell him that honestly. A final in 10 days is very unlikely to be a safe target for full sprinting and contact, and I would frame the plan around readiness, not the date.

Goals, set with him: within a week, normal pain-free walking and full pain-free isometric contraction; by week three, pain-free jogging and running; by weeks four to six, sprint speed and sport-specific drills, then contact and a return to match play once criteria are met.

Phase one is the next several days. I would use relative rest, avoid stretching to the point of pain and keep him moving with walking in pain-free strides. I would start gentle isometrics at mid-range in prone or bridge position, such as holds of 20 to 30 seconds, five repetitions, and pain-free range exercise. I would also begin trunk and lumbopelvic work that does not load the thigh.

Phase two begins when he has pain-free isometrics. I would progress to bridges with a single leg, then eccentric loading such as slider hamstring curls or Nordic-type work in small ranges, three sets of six to eight, increasing range and load across sessions. I would add a progressive running program, going from jogging at modest speeds to progressive accelerations and then to sprinting at increasing percentages of maximum, with a rest day between loading sessions.

Phase three: change of direction, sport drills, and finally non-contact then contact training.

Progression depends on criteria: no pain at rest, walking and during the task, active knee extension within about 10 degrees of the left side, strength on the right at least 90 percent of the left, and the ability to complete sprint drills without pain or apprehension. I would measure these every visit.

I would ask him to talk to his physician or pharmacist about the ibuprofen, since evidence on anti-inflammatories early in muscle healing is mixed, and I would not tell him to start or stop it myself. After return, a hamstring strengthening program continues because reinjury risk is high.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Jamal mentions the tackle. Explain what you would do about this and how you would handle his request to be taped and returned to play.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes that headaches and light sensitivity since a head knock suggest a possible concussion and takes it as a priority above the thigh. critical
  • Asks about further symptoms: nausea, dizziness, sleep change, concentration problems, mood changes and worsening headache.
  • Advises him not to return to play or training and arranges prompt medical assessment by a physician or nurse practitioner. critical
  • Screens for red flags needing emergency care, such as repeated vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, seizure, weakness or drowsiness. critical
  • Explains that returning with a concussion risks worse injury and a longer recovery, in terms that connect to his goals.
  • Does not clear him for sport or tape him to play. critical
  • Advises that he tell the team doctor and coach and offers to help or, with consent, to do so.
  • Adjusts the thigh program to avoid high exertion until medically cleared.
  • Documents the disclosure, advice and referral.

Performance scale

4Treats the possible concussion as the priority, screens for red flags, refers for medical assessment, refuses to clear or tape him, links advice to his goals and adjusts exertion.
3Identifies concussion and refers him but gives limited red-flag screening or limited response to his request.
2Mentions seeing a doctor about the headaches but still plans to tape or progress him towards play.
1Ignores the head injury or agrees to tape and return him to play.

Model spoken answer

The concussion comes first. It is a bigger risk to him than the thigh, and I would put the hamstring aside for a few minutes to deal with it.

He told me he was tackled and 'got his bell rung,' and since then he has had headaches most days with light sensitivity. That is consistent with a concussion that has not been assessed. I would thank him for telling me, and then ask a set of questions: how the headache has changed, whether there is nausea, dizziness, trouble sleeping or sleeping more, trouble concentrating, irritability or feeling foggy. I would also check for red flags that mean going to the emergency department now: repeated vomiting, a headache that is getting worse, confusion, drowsiness that is hard to rouse, weakness or numbness, slurred speech, a seizure, or unequal pupils. If any of those are present, I would arrange emergency care straight away. If not, I would still tell him that he needs to see a physician or nurse practitioner for a proper concussion assessment in the next day or so, and I would help him book it.

I would also be clear with him that he should not play, train hard or do contact until he has been medically assessed and cleared through a graded return-to-sport process. I would explain this in terms that matter to him. Playing again with a concussion makes another injury more likely, can make symptoms worse and last longer, and can put his studies and long-term health at risk, which would hurt his season far more than missing the final.

On taping him to play, my answer is no, and I would say that kindly. I would not clear him to play, with either the thigh or the head. Tape would not make a moderate hamstring strain safe to sprint on, and I cannot send him out with an unassessed head injury. I would offer what I can do: a plan to get him back as quickly as it is safe, and my help in speaking with the team doctor and coach, if he agrees. It is better if he tells them himself, and I would support him in doing that. I would not tell them without his consent unless there were an immediate safety concern.

In the meantime I would keep his thigh program at low intensity: walking, gentle isometrics, no high-effort running or heavy exertion that could provoke head symptoms. I would document his disclosure, my screening, my advice and the referral.

Question 3: Communication

Jamal is frustrated and says you are costing him his scholarship. Describe what you would say to him and how you would communicate, including how you would handle the coach's messages.

Examiner checklist

  • Acknowledges his frustration and fear about the scholarship before giving information.
  • Uses plain, specific language to explain findings and likely timeline without jargon.
  • Gives a clear, honest message that he is not cleared for the final, framed around his goals. critical
  • Uses open questions and reflective listening to understand what matters to him.
  • Offers options and next steps so that he has some control, such as the plan to return and ways to stay involved with the team.
  • Uses teach-back or checks understanding.
  • Explains that he decides what information is shared with the coach and that you will not share without his consent. critical
  • Suggests ways he can talk to the coach or offers a letter of recommended activity limits with his permission.
  • Stays calm and non-defensive and avoids false reassurance.

Performance scale

4Acknowledges feelings, delivers a clear honest message in plain language, offers choices and checks understanding, and protects his control over what is shared with the coach.
3Communicates clearly and empathically but gives less on choices, teach-back or the coach issue.
2Gives information correctly but in a clinical or defensive way with little acknowledgement of his concerns.
1Argues with him, gives false reassurance, or agrees to contact the coach without consent.

Model spoken answer

I would start by listening, because his frustration makes sense. He has a scholarship, a team that is counting on him and a coach texting him daily. If I jump in with explanations, he will hear it as me taking something away from him. So I would say something like: 'It sounds like this final matters a lot, and that you feel stuck between your health and your season. Tell me what you're most worried about.' Then I would let him talk and reflect back what I hear: 'You're worried that if you miss this game, you lose your place and the scholarship.'

Then I would be clear and kind. 'Here is what I see. Your hamstring has a moderate tear. It's not just a bruise. If you sprint on it in ten days, there's a real chance it tears further and you lose the rest of the season, not just one game. And with the headaches since the tackle, I'm not comfortable with you playing until a doctor has checked your head. I know that's not what you wanted to hear.' I would use plain words, avoid medical jargon and not promise anything I cannot know, such as a particular return date.

Then I would give him control by offering choices. 'I can't clear you for the final, but here is what I can do. We can set up a plan to get you back as soon as it is safe, I can help you get a quick appointment about the headaches, and we can talk about staying involved with the team, for example in film review or training that does not load your leg or head.' I would ask what he thinks would help most, and check he has understood by asking him to tell me, in his own words, what the plan is and what he will do tomorrow.

About the coach: his health information belongs to him. I would explain that I will not share anything with the coach or the team without his permission. He may prefer to tell the coach himself, and I could help him prepare what to say. If he agrees, I can write a short note stating the activity limits without sharing diagnosis details. I would not reply to the coach's messages myself. If he feels pushed by the team, I would also tell him about the team doctor as another route.

I would stay calm if he stays upset, avoid arguing, and leave the door open: 'I'm on your side here, and I want you playing for years, not just this game.'

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is a possible concussion that Jamal has hidden from the coach and team doctor, which outweighs the hamstring problem. A safe candidate screens for red flags, refers for medical assessment, refuses to clear or tape him, and respects his control over disclosure to the coach.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates write a thorough hamstring program and treat the concussion remark as a passing detail, or promise a return by the final. Others offer to phone the coach and share everything without asking Jamal.

Examiner Notes

A pass prioritizes the head injury, gives an honest timeline for the thigh and communicates with empathy while protecting his consent. A fail tapes or clears him, or does not respond to the head injury.

Case 20 (Mock 2, case 10 of 10): Falls at home after stroke in an older man with new medication

Neurological · Client's home, community rehabilitation team

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain what your assessment findings tell you about the reason for Mr. Beaulieu's falls, which factors you consider the most important and what further assessment you would do.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies the drop in standing blood pressure with dizziness as a likely contributor to falls and links it to the recent medication increase. critical
  • Interprets the Berg score and Timed Up and Go time as showing impaired balance and increased fall risk.
  • Links right-sided weakness, reduced balance reactions and use of a walker to fall risk, especially in the dark.
  • Considers the night-time context: urgency to void, poor lighting, fatigue, medication timing, rushing and distance to the bathroom.
  • Distinguishes the contribution of stroke impairments from the medication-related low blood pressure, rather than blaming the stroke only. critical
  • Plans further assessment: lying to standing blood pressure at one and three minutes, heart rate, symptoms, gait observation, transfers and home hazards.
  • Screens for other contributors such as vision, visual field loss, sensation, cognition, mood and continence.
  • Considers fatigue and the effect on caregiver safety.
  • Identifies that medication decisions belong to the physician and plans to report the findings. critical

Performance scale

4Links the orthostatic drop to the medication change and the night pattern, balances this with stroke impairments, uses the test scores correctly and plans specific further assessment and physician reporting.
3Identifies the blood pressure change and balance impairment but gives less on night context, differential factors or further assessment.
2Attributes falls to the stroke and balance scores alone with little comment on the standing blood pressure.
1Misses the blood pressure drop or suggests changing the medication yourself.

Model spoken answer

My impression is that Mr. Beaulieu's falls come from several factors acting together, and the one I would take most seriously is a possible drop in blood pressure on standing, because it is both new and fixable.

Let me go through the findings. His blood pressure sitting is 138 over 80 and one minute after standing is 112 over 66. That is a fall of 26 in the systolic pressure, and he says he feels woozy when he stands. That is a pattern consistent with orthostatic hypotension, and it appeared after his blood pressure medication was increased at discharge. Both falls happened at night on the way to the bathroom, which is exactly when people stand up quickly from bed, often after lying for hours, and are hurrying. Low pressure on standing can cause dizziness and sudden loss of balance even in someone with otherwise reasonable function.

That said, the stroke also contributes. His Berg score of 38 out of 56 and his Timed Up and Go time of 22 seconds are both in the range associated with higher risk of falling. He has right leg and arm weakness, which affects his ability to respond to a loss of balance, and the walker, though helpful, is not always on hand at night. So I see the medication effect and the stroke impairments as working together, and I would not label the falls as just a stroke problem, since that would miss the part that his doctor can change.

For further assessment, I would measure lying and standing blood pressure and heart rate properly: after five minutes of lying, then at one and three minutes standing, noting his symptoms. I would observe his transfers from bed and toilet, how he turns, and how he uses the walker, and look at the route from bedroom to bathroom in the home, including lighting and floor surfaces. I would also screen his vision and visual fields, since stroke can affect these, any changes in sensation, thinking, mood and his need to urinate at night, because urgency leads to rushing.

I also see that Colette is exhausted. I would note that as a factor, because a tired caregiver assisting a transfer is another way someone gets hurt.

I cannot change his medication. What I can do is report my findings with the numbers to his physician promptly and ask for review, while I plan strategies that reduce the risk in the meantime.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Describe what you would put in place to reduce the risk of harm to Mr. Beaulieu and Colette in the next few days, and how you would involve them in the decisions.

Examiner checklist

  • Teaches slow staged position changes at night: sit at the edge of the bed, pause, then stand with support. critical
  • Reduces night-time hazards: lighting, clear path, walker within reach, bedside commode or urinal option. critical
  • Teaches the couple when to stop and sit or lie down, and what to do if he feels woozy.
  • Reviews safe assistance technique for Colette that respects her arthritis and limits lifting. critical
  • Arranges equipment or alternatives for the stairs and bathroom with the occupational therapist, such as sleeping on the main floor.
  • Plans for what to do after a fall: do not rush to lift, check for injury, call for help, and when to call emergency services.
  • Informs them when to contact the physician or emergency services, such as fainting, head strike, chest pain or new stroke symptoms.
  • Explores Mr. Beaulieu's priorities and Colette's capacity and respects their choices after explaining risks.
  • Uses language adapted to his word-finding difficulty and checks understanding.

Performance scale

4Gives specific night-time routines and environmental changes, safe caregiver technique and post-fall plan, and involves both partners in choices while adapting communication to aphasia.
3Provides sound safety measures but with limited caregiver guidance or limited involvement of the couple in decisions.
2Lists generic fall prevention advice without tailoring to the night-time pattern or caregiver capacity.
1Overrides their choices or advises Colette to lift or hold him up.

Model spoken answer

For the next few days I would focus on night time, because that is when both falls happened, and I would do it with both of them, not for them.

The first measure is how he gets up. I would teach and practise with him, in his own bed, a staged routine: sit up, count slowly to ten with feet on the floor, move his ankles up and down, stand with the walker already in place, and wait before walking. I would have him practise it while I watch and keep my hand ready. I would ask him to repeat it back to me or show me, since his word-finding difficulty means a demonstration is better than a long explanation, and I would leave a short picture sheet at the bedside.

The second measure is making the path safe and shorter. A night light between the bed and the bathroom, clear floor with no rugs, walker kept within arm's reach of the bed. The bathroom is downstairs and the bedroom upstairs, which is a risk in itself. With the occupational therapist, I would explore options such as setting up a bed on the main floor, a bedside commode or urinal for the night, a stair-use plan, and grab bars. I would present these as choices and ask what works for them. If he prefers to keep sleeping upstairs, I would explain the risk clearly, respect that it is their home and their decision, and do what I can to make it safer.

For Colette, I would watch how she helps him and teach her a technique that does not need lifting or pulling on his arm: guide at the waist belt, stand slightly behind and to his weaker side, and let him do the standing. Her hands have arthritis, so I would ask what she can safely do, and I would tell her she is not expected to catch him. If he starts to fall, she should guide him down rather than hold him up. After a fall, they should check for pain or injury, not try to lift him alone, and call for help. They should call emergency services for a blow to the head, chest pain, fainting, new weakness, trouble speaking or severe pain.

Throughout, I would ask what they want. He says he is fine, so I would listen to what independence means to him, and I would also ask Colette directly how she is coping.

Question 3: Collaboration

Discuss how you would work with other members of the care team and the family to manage Mr. Beaulieu's situation, including who you would contact, what you would say and when.

Examiner checklist

  • Contacts the family physician promptly with specific findings, including lying and standing blood pressures, symptoms and the timing of the medication change, and asks for medication review. critical
  • Does not alter or advise stopping medication yourself. critical
  • Contacts the occupational therapist about home set-up, bathroom and stairs, equipment and caregiver strategies.
  • Informs the nurse case manager about caregiver strain and requests assessment for respite, home support or other community services.
  • Involves the pharmacist for medication review and timing, if available.
  • Considers the speech-language pathologist for aphasia and communication supports.
  • Obtains consent from Mr. Beaulieu to share information and includes Colette in team communication with his permission.
  • Uses clear structured communication and a fast channel since the physician is distant, and sets a time to follow up.
  • Clarifies roles and who will follow up on each item and documents communication.

Performance scale

4Contacts the physician urgently with a structured, specific message, does not adjust medication, brings in the OT, case manager and others with clear roles, secures consent and follows up.
3Identifies the right team members and communicates well but with limited urgency, roles or follow-up planning.
2Names team members and says they would 'refer' without specifying content, timing or roles.
1Changes the medication, delays contact with the physician or excludes the client and caregiver.

Model spoken answer

The most urgent contact is with his family physician, because the blood pressure finding needs a medical decision that I cannot make. The physician is two hours away, so I would not wait for a routine fax. I would phone the office the same day, ask to speak with the physician or the nurse who can bring it to them, and send the same information in writing. I would be brief and specific: 'Mr. Beaulieu is five weeks after a left MCA stroke and had his blood pressure medication increased at discharge. Since then he has had two night-time falls. Today his sitting pressure is 138 over 80 and one minute after standing it is 112 over 66, with dizziness. I am concerned about orthostatic hypotension contributing to falls. Could you review the medication and timing, and let me know any limits you want on activity in the meantime?' I would ask when to expect a reply and tell them I will call back by the next day if I have not heard. I would not change or advise him to stop any medication myself.

Next, the occupational therapist, today or tomorrow. I would ask them to see the home about the stairs, bathroom, equipment such as a commode and bed set-up, and to work on night-time routines. I would share my transfer teaching so we give the same message. With the nurse case manager, I would raise Colette's exhaustion and arthritis. Her sleep is broken and she is his only caregiver, and that is a safety risk for both of them. I would ask for an assessment for home support, respite and caregiver services. If a pharmacist is accessible, I would ask for a review of the medication timing and interactions. And if his word-finding difficulty is limiting how well he follows instructions, I would suggest a speech-language pathologist assess and advise us on communication strategies.

For the family, I would ask Mr. Beaulieu for permission to share information with the team and with Colette. I would include her in the conversation, because she is the person who sees him at night, and she can give us information on how things really are.

I would set roles: I follow up the physician response and balance work; the OT does the home changes; the case manager does caregiver support. I would document each contact with date, time, the information shared and the plan, and agree on a date for the team to check in again.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is orthostatic hypotension after a recent medication increase, which looks like a stroke-related balance problem. A competent candidate measures it, reports it to the physician with numbers and does not alter medication. The exhausted sole caregiver is a second hidden risk that needs community services and safe assistance technique.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates build a balance and strengthening program and treat the falls as a stroke issue only. Others suggest he stop or delay the blood pressure tablets, or give Colette lifting instructions that her arthritis cannot meet.

Examiner Notes

A pass connects the standing blood pressure drop and night timing to a targeted safety plan and a prompt, specific physician contact without altering medication, and includes the caregiver. A fail misses the blood pressure finding or advises on medication.

Mock 3

Case 21 (Mock 3, case 1 of 10): Neck and arm pain with hand symptoms in an office worker

Musculoskeletal · Private outpatient physiotherapy clinic, first visit

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Based on the history and examination findings, explain your clinical impression and justify how the findings support it. Then describe what further assessment you would complete today and why.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies a left cervical radiculopathy, likely C7 root, using the cluster of Spurling, distraction relief, neurodynamic test, rotation limit and reflex change.
  • Links triceps weakness, reduced triceps reflex and middle finger sensory change to the C7 root level.
  • Explains that a positive cluster of tests raises the likelihood of radiculopathy more than any single test.
  • Recognizes dropping objects as a finding that does not fit a single root problem and raises possible spinal cord involvement. critical
  • Plans an upper motor neuron screen: hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign, clonus, Babinski, gait and tandem walking, hand dexterity. critical
  • Plans a screen for other red flags: night pain, weight loss, fever, bladder or bowel change, history of cancer.
  • Considers differentials such as shoulder pathology, carpal tunnel syndrome and thoracic outlet syndrome and says how to differentiate them.
  • Plans baseline outcome measures and a patient specific functional goal, such as sitting tolerance at work.
  • States that imaging is not needed first for radiculopathy without red flags but that new cord signs change that.

Performance scale

4Names a left C7 radiculopathy with reasoning from the test cluster, spots that dropping objects does not fit, and plans a specific cord screen and red flag questions, with outcome measures.
3Gives a sound radiculopathy impression with good test reasoning but treats the dropping objects as minor or gives only a brief cord screen.
2Lists tests and a diagnosis without explaining why they support it, and misses the dropping objects or the need to screen for cord involvement.
1Gives the wrong impression, ignores the neurological changes, or proposes treatment such as manipulation without further screening.

Model spoken answer

My impression is a left cervical radiculopathy, most likely at the C7 level. I will explain how I got there, and then tell you what I would add before I treat.

First, the pattern. Her arm pain follows a root distribution, with tingling in the middle and index fingers. Her pain is provoked by left rotation and extension, which narrow the foramen on that side. The Spurling test reproduces her arm pain, the distraction test relieves it, and the median nerve neurodynamic test is positive. No one of these is enough alone, but together they make a radiculopathy quite likely. Triceps weakness at 4 out of 5, a reduced triceps reflex and reduced sensation over the middle finger all point to C7 in particular. Her grip is symmetrical, so I am less worried about a C8 or a peripheral median nerve problem like carpal tunnel, although I would still check Phalen and Tinel tests at the wrist to rule it out. I would also screen the shoulder, because shoulder pain can refer into the arm, but rotation of the neck changing her symptoms makes the neck the main source.

Second, the detail that does not fit. She said she has been dropping her coffee cup. A single root problem rarely explains clumsy hands. This could be pain inhibition, but I must also consider that the spinal cord is being compressed, which is cervical myelopathy. So today I would add an upper motor neuron screen: deep tendon reflexes at the biceps, brachioradialis and knee, looking for brisk reflexes, then the Hoffmann sign, ankle clonus and the Babinski response. I would watch her walk, including tandem walking, and ask her to do fine tasks like buttoning or finger tapping. I would ask about balance, any change in walking, and bladder or bowel control.

Third, other red flags. I would ask about night pain unrelated to position, unexplained weight loss, fever, a history of cancer, and recent infection. Her vital signs are normal, which is reassuring.

Fourth, outcome measures. I have a Neck Disability Index of 24 out of 50, and I would add a pain rating and the Patient Specific Functional Scale, with a goal like working ninety minutes at the desk before symptoms rise, since that is what matters to her before her deadline.

If the cord screen is clear, I would not send her for imaging right away, because guidelines support a trial of conservative care for radiculopathy without red flags. If any upper motor neuron sign is present, my plan changes and she needs prompt medical assessment.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Priya's upper motor neuron screen shows brisk knee reflexes and a positive Hoffmann sign on both sides. Describe how you would proceed and how you would speak with her about it.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes bilateral upper motor neuron signs as suggesting possible degenerative cervical myelopathy, needing urgent medical assessment. critical
  • Stops or withholds manual techniques such as thrust manipulation, end range mobilization, and mechanical traction. critical
  • Arranges prompt communication with her family physician or an urgent care pathway, based on local options, the same day. critical
  • Explains findings in plain language without alarming her and without promising or naming a diagnosis as certain.
  • Checks her understanding using teach back and invites questions and concerns.
  • Gives safety netting advice: worsening weakness, falls, loss of bladder or bowel control, or severe new pain needs emergency care. critical
  • Obtains consent to share information with her physician and explains what will be shared.
  • Respects her deadline pressure by offering to provide documentation but not allowing it to shape the safety decision.
  • Documents the findings, the advice given, her response and the communication with the physician.

Performance scale

4Identifies cord involvement, stops loading techniques, arranges same day medical contact with consent, uses clear language and teach back, and gives specific safety netting.
3Refers appropriately and avoids manipulation but gives less detail on communication, consent or safety netting.
2Mentions referral but continues some treatment, delays the referral to the next visit, or uses vague communication.
1Proceeds with manual therapy or traction, or minimizes the findings so that no medical assessment is arranged.

Model spoken answer

These findings change my plan. Bilateral brisk reflexes and a Hoffmann sign on both sides are upper motor neuron signs. With her clumsy hands, this makes me suspect that the spinal cord may be affected, a condition called degenerative cervical myelopathy. That is not something I should treat in the clinic as a simple pinched nerve, so my priority is getting her medical assessment promptly.

Here is what I would do in order. First, I stop any technique that could load the neck. That means no thrust manipulation, no end range mobilization and no mechanical traction, even though the assistant has time this week. I would also avoid sustained end range extension exercises. I would let her sit comfortably and finish the examination gently.

Second, I would talk with Priya before she leaves. I would sit down at her level and say something like, 'Some of your reflexes and hand signs tell me that the nerves in your neck might be under more pressure than I first thought. I cannot tell you the cause from my tests alone, and many people with these findings do well, but I want a doctor to look at this soon and probably arrange imaging.' I would avoid naming a frightening condition as certain. Then I would ask her to repeat back in her own words what we have found and what happens next, and I would ask what worries her most. I expect it may be the tax deadline, and I would tell her honestly that her health comes first and that I can provide a note for work.

Third, I would ask her permission to contact her family physician today, explain what I would share, and call or send a same day message with my findings. If the physician cannot see her within a short time, I would suggest an urgent care clinic or emergency department depending on local options, and I would not wait for her next appointment.

Fourth, safety netting. I would tell her to go to the emergency department right away if she notices new weakness in the arms or legs, trouble walking, falls, numbness in the groin or loss of control of bladder or bowel, or sudden severe neck pain.

Finally, I would document the examination, my reasoning, what I told her, her understanding, the consent for sharing information and who I contacted, and arrange a follow up call in a day or two to confirm that she has been seen.

Question 3: Practice Management

Priya's physician sees her and starts the imaging process. She tells you she wants to keep seeing you. Discuss the practice management issues you must handle regarding visits, billing, documentation and your team.

Examiner checklist

  • Declines to sell or sign her up for the prepaid twelve visit package before the medical findings and plan are known. critical
  • Explains that fees and visit use must match clinical need and her insurance benefit, not clinic sales targets.
  • Tells her openly that her plan pays for ten visits and discusses how to use them, including costs beyond the cap.
  • Does not assign mechanical traction to the physiotherapist assistant, as the plan is on hold and the therapist must assess suitability. critical
  • Describes delegation principles: assessment and plan stay with the physiotherapist, with clear instructions and supervision for any task assigned.
  • Writes accurate, dated records of findings, decisions, communication and consent, kept as the college requires.
  • Provides the insurer report only with her consent and limits content to what the insurer needs.
  • Raises the conflict with the clinic owner if the package pressure continues, and follows the college standards on conflict of interest.
  • Schedules follow up to match the medical timeline, for instance a check after imaging results.

Performance scale

4Declines the package with a client centred reason, is open about benefit limits, refuses to delegate traction with reasons, and covers consent based reporting and documentation.
3Handles most issues correctly but gives thin reasoning on delegation or on reporting consent.
2Mentions billing and documentation in general terms, or agrees to the package or the delegated traction.
1Follows the clinic's sales target over client need or shares information with the employer without consent.

Model spoken answer

There are several practice management issues here, and I will take them in turn.

First, the prepaid package. The clinic owner wants therapists to offer twelve visits up front. I would not offer Priya that package now. Her plan is not clear yet, because she may need surgical or other medical care, and a prepaid package would give her a financial reason to keep coming for treatment that may not be right. Under my college's standards, my duty is to the client, and fees and visits have to follow clinical need. I would tell her, 'Right now we do not know what the next step is, so I would rather book one visit at a time.' If the owner presses, I would explain the conflict of interest concern to the owner respectfully and, if needed, refer to the college's guidance on billing and conflicts.

Second, her insurance. Her plan covers ten visits a year. I would confirm with her and the insurer how many she has already used this year, so we both know how many remain. I would be open about this, including what each visit costs and what she would pay herself after the limit, so that she can choose how to use them. I would also keep a few visits available for after her medical assessment, when rehabilitation may be more clearly useful.

Third, the physiotherapist assistant. The assistant has time for mechanical traction, but I will not assign it. Delegation means I keep responsibility for assessment, diagnosis and the plan. A treatment can only be assigned when I judge that it is safe for this client, the task is within the assistant's training, and I give clear instructions and supervise. For Priya, traction is not safe to assign while cord involvement is unresolved. The assistant could help in other ways later, such as supervising a posture and strengthening program once I have cleared it.

Fourth, documentation. I would write clear, dated notes that cover her history, the upper motor neuron findings, my reasoning, the advice given, her consent to contact her physician, who I spoke with, and the safety advice. I keep the record for the length of time my college requires.

Fifth, reports. For her insurer, I would ask for her written consent and give only the information needed for payment and for work, not every detail of her health. If her employer asks for a note, I would write about function and restrictions, not the diagnosis, unless she agrees.

Finally, scheduling. I would book a short check after her imaging so that we adjust the plan to the results rather than to the clinic's calendar.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is the mention that Priya has been dropping her coffee cup, which hints at hand clumsiness and possible cervical myelopathy. A competent candidate notices it, adds an upper motor neuron screen, withholds traction and manipulation, arranges prompt medical review with her consent, and resists the package sales pressure.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates treat the case as a straightforward C7 radiculopathy and plan traction or manipulation without screening for cord signs. Others recognize the risk but give no plain language explanation, no safety netting, and no plan for consent, billing conflicts or delegation.

Examiner Notes

A passing candidate links the pattern to C7, notices the dropped objects without prompting, and acts on the cord signs with a same day medical referral. A failing candidate continues with traction, or lists tests without reasoning. Practice management answers must refuse the package on ethical grounds, not just describe billing.

Case 22 (Mock 3, case 2 of 10): Freezing of gait and falls in Parkinson disease

Neurological · Hospital based outpatient neurological rehabilitation clinic

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the physiotherapy plan you would develop with Walter, including goals, the main interventions, how you would address freezing, and how you would measure progress.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets patient centred goals with Walter, such as safe household mobility, fewer falls and continued community activity.
  • Schedules sessions and home practice during the on medication period, and notes the wearing off pattern for planning.
  • Includes cueing strategies for freezing: external visual, auditory (metronome) and attentional cues, with practice in doorways and turns. critical
  • Teaches turning strategies using wide arcs and avoiding pivoting, and rehearses dual task walking.
  • Prescribes progressive aerobic and strengthening exercise with intensity, frequency and progression stated.
  • Includes balance training and fall prevention education, and a plan for getting up from the floor. critical
  • Addresses the lightheadedness: orthostatic hypotension screening and referral to the physician and advice on slow position changes. critical
  • Reviews the home, including stairs and bedroom location, and walker use, with an occupational therapy referral if needed.
  • Selects outcome measures: Timed Up and Go, 10 metre walk, Mini BESTest or similar, fall diary, and sets reassessment timing.

Performance scale

4Gives goals set with Walter, on period timing, specific cueing and turning strategies, dosed exercise, orthostatic hypotension action, home review and outcome measures with a reassessment schedule.
3Provides a sound plan with cueing and exercise but misses the blood pressure issue, dosing, or reassessment timing.
2Lists generic exercises without cueing, timing or measures, and does not link choices to the case.
1Proposes unsafe or irrelevant interventions, or ignores freezing and fall risk.

Model spoken answer

My plan is built around three goals that I would set with Walter himself, not only with Grace. I expect they would be to move safely in his house, to fall less, and to stay active enough to keep up his Saturday hockey trips. I would ask him to state in his own words which matters most.

I would start with timing. His freezing is worst when his medication wears off in the mid morning. I would schedule his visits and his home practice in his best on period, about an hour after a dose, and I would ask him to keep a simple diary of doses, freezing and falls for two weeks so that we can see the pattern.

For freezing itself, I would teach cueing. Cues are outside signals that help start movement. Visual cues could be strips of tape on the floor at doorways. Auditory cues could be a metronome app at a comfortable step rate, and attentional cues like thinking 'big step'. We would practise at the real trouble spots, doorways and turns, and we would add a second task such as carrying a cup. For turning, I would teach a wide arc rather than pivoting on the spot.

For exercise, evidence supports progressive training in Parkinson disease. I would start with aerobic work such as treadmill or bike at a moderate level, three times per week for thirty minutes, building slowly, along with lower limb strengthening twice a week, and balance work such as weight shifts, stepping in different directions, and standing up and sitting down. I would progress when he completes the work with good control. I would include a falls plan with him and Grace on how to get up from the floor.

I am concerned about his blood pressure dropping when he stands, from 128 to 104 systolic, with lightheadedness. This can cause falls independently of freezing. I would teach slow position changes and ankle pumps, and I would send a note to his neurologist or family doctor, because medication or hydration may need to be reviewed.

His home matters too. The bedroom is upstairs, and he is not using the walker indoors. I would ask about stairs, bathroom rails and lighting, and I would involve an occupational therapist for a home assessment.

For progress, I would repeat the Timed Up and Go and the 10 metre walk every four to six weeks, add the Mini BESTest, and count falls in his diary. I would reassess sooner if he falls or his medication changes.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Grace asks you to give her all of Walter's results so she can manage him, and Walter stays silent. Explain how you would handle the conversation, including safety concerns and Walter's wishes.

Examiner checklist

  • Speaks directly with Walter and checks that he understands the discussion and wants Grace involved. critical
  • Obtains Walter's consent before sharing his personal health information with Grace, and agrees on what and how much. critical
  • Assesses capacity to consent in a respectful way, recognizing that a MoCA of 24 does not by itself mean incapacity.
  • Explores why Walter does not use the walker indoors, such as pride, space or freezing, using open questions.
  • Acknowledges Grace's stress and invites her view while keeping Walter at the centre of decisions.
  • Offers shared decision making on a fall plan: walker use, night time routes, bathroom set up, medical alert option.
  • Asks about the driving near miss and raises driving safety with Walter in a non judgemental way. critical
  • Provides information on caregiver supports and Parkinson organizations in his region.
  • Avoids labelling Walter as stubborn and describes behaviour in terms of barriers.

Performance scale

4Centres Walter, gets explicit consent before sharing, explores walker barriers, uses shared decision making, supports Grace, and raises the driving near miss with a clear plan.
3Handles consent and the walker well but gives limited attention to the driving issue or to Grace's needs.
2Shares information with Grace without clear consent, or lists safety advice without involving Walter.
1Shares results freely with Grace, dismisses Walter, or ignores the driving near miss.

Model spoken answer

The first thing I would do is turn toward Walter. Grace is asking for his information, but it belongs to him, and he has been quiet. So I would say, 'Walter, I would like to include Grace if you are comfortable. What would you like me to share with her?' If he agrees, I would also ask what level of detail he wants her to have, and I would write down his consent. If he says he wants some things kept private, I respect that. His MoCA of 24 out of 30 shows some mild difficulty, but that alone does not mean he cannot decide. I would assume he has capacity, explain things in short, clear steps, check his understanding, and only raise capacity more formally if I see real doubt about his ability to understand and weigh the information.

Next, I would try to understand the walker. Calling him stubborn does not help us. I would ask him, 'What makes the walker hard to use at home?' It might be narrow hallways, embarrassment, or because freezing happens at doorways where the walker catches. Then I would offer options: moving furniture, a different walker, or practice with cues. We would agree on a plan he chooses, like using it at night and on the stairs, and I would discuss night time routes to the bathroom, lighting, and a medical alert device. This is shared decision making, not a rule I set.

For Grace, I would thank her for her effort. I would tell her, with Walter's permission, what we are working on and how she can help, for instance by cueing rather than rushing him or pulling on him. I would also ask how she is coping and give her information about caregiver support and the regional Parkinson society.

The other safety issue is driving. Walter told me that his legs would not move on the pedal and he almost missed a stop sign. I would not ignore that. I would ask him gently, 'Tell me about that day. How do you feel about driving right now?' Freezing, slower reaction time, medication timing and sleepiness can all affect driving. I would explain my concern, encourage him to talk with his physician about a driving assessment, and ask him whether he can arrange alternatives for a while, like having Grace drive or using ride services. I would document the discussion and his decisions.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Walter declines to stop driving and asks you not to tell anyone about the near miss. Discuss your professional responsibilities, including confidentiality, reporting, scope and documentation.

Examiner checklist

  • States the duty of confidentiality and that disclosure without consent is allowed only where law permits or where serious risk requires it. critical
  • Says the physiotherapist assesses function but does not decide fitness to drive, which is a medical and licensing decision. critical
  • Recommends he speak with his physician and, with his consent, communicates the concern to the physician.
  • Checks the provincial rules on reporting unsafe drivers and what applies to physiotherapists versus physicians. critical
  • Explains the limits of confidentiality to Walter openly rather than acting behind his back.
  • Uses motivational and respectful communication to explore his reasons and offers alternatives to preserve his role with his grandchildren.
  • Documents what was said, advice given, his response and any discussion with others.
  • Seeks advice from the college, a manager or the privacy officer for a difficult decision.
  • Continues to treat him and keeps the relationship rather than discharging him because of the disagreement.

Performance scale

4Balances confidentiality and public safety, states scope limits, checks provincial reporting rules, seeks consent and advice, offers alternatives, documents, and continues care.
3Identifies confidentiality and scope but is vague about provincial reporting rules or about seeking consultation.
2Either breaches confidentiality without a legal basis or ignores the safety concern, with little documentation.
1Reports without any process or consent, or decides Walter's fitness to drive on their own.

Model spoken answer

This is a conflict between two duties: keeping Walter's information confidential, and protecting other people on the road. I would work through it step by step.

First, confidentiality. Walter's health information is protected under provincial health privacy law and my college's standards. I should not share it without his consent, unless the law allows or requires it, or there is a serious and immediate risk of harm. A single near miss that he told me about is not usually an immediate emergency, so I would begin by trying to get his agreement.

Second, scope. Deciding whether a person is fit to drive is not my role. That decision belongs to physicians and the provincial licensing authority, who can order a formal driving assessment. What I can contribute is my observations of function: freezing, slowed movement, and orthostatic changes. I would be honest with Walter that I cannot clear him or ban him from driving, but that I think the near miss matters.

Third, reporting rules. These differ by province. In some provinces, physicians are required to report certain medical conditions that affect driving, while other health professionals may have discretion or no duty at all. I would not guess. I would check my regulator's guidance, and if I am still unsure I would call the college or speak with my manager or the privacy officer before taking any step on my own.

Fourth, how I talk with him. I would not argue. I would say, 'I understand driving the grandchildren means a great deal to you. I am worried about what happened at the stop sign. Can we think together about how to keep you in that role safely?' I would explain that if I think the risk is serious I might need to speak with his doctor, so that nothing happens behind his back. I would ask for his consent to send his physician my observations. I would offer alternatives, such as a formal driving evaluation, driving only at his best medication times for now, or having Grace drive to hockey while he rides along and helps coach.

Fifth, documentation. I would record his statements, my advice, his decision, any consent or refusal, who I consulted, and my reasons.

And finally, I would keep treating him. Discharging him because he disagrees would remove a support and make things less safe.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is the near miss while driving, in the context of freezing, orthostatic drops and mild cognitive change. A competent candidate raises it with Walter respectfully, explains the limits of confidentiality, respects scope, checks the provincial rules, and involves the physician with consent.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates give a generic exercise plan and forget cueing or the on medication timing. They also share information with Grace without asking Walter, or they either ignore the driving risk or decide he is unfit to drive themselves.

Examiner Notes

A pass shows a tailored plan for freezing with on period timing, spots the blood pressure drop, puts Walter's consent first, and handles the driving dilemma within scope. A fail prescribes standard balance exercises only or breaches confidentiality.

Case 23 (Mock 3, case 3 of 10): Heel pain in an elementary school teacher

Musculoskeletal · Outpatient physiotherapy clinic

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the treatment plan you would develop for Mei Ling, including interventions, dosage and progression, outcome measures and how you would decide when to reassess or change the plan.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets goals with Mei Ling such as pain under 3 out of 10 for school days and a return to walking.
  • Educates on load management: reducing aggravating load without complete rest, footwear with support and cushioning, avoiding bare feet on hard floors.
  • Prescribes a calf stretching program with duration and frequency, and plantar fascia specific stretching.
  • Prescribes plantar fascia loading with sets, repetitions and tempo, starting with isometric or low load two leg work and holding added load until the Achilles tenderness settles. critical
  • Considers short term options: taping, a prefabricated insole or heel cup, and manual therapy for the calf, explaining modest evidence.
  • Avoids thrust techniques and added or single leg Achilles loading given tendon tenderness and recent fluoroquinolone use, and contacts the physician promptly if tenderness persists or worsens. critical
  • Selects outcome measures: pain score on first steps, Foot Function Index or FAAM, and functional goal tracking.
  • Sets a reassessment point at about 4 to 6 weeks and defines what would prompt a change of plan. critical
  • Discusses a plan for weight and activity changes that she can sustain, without blame.

Performance scale

4Gives a dosed, progressive plan with load management, calf and fascia work, notes the Achilles and antibiotic caution, includes measures and a defined reassessment trigger.
3Provides appropriate interventions with dosage but misses the Achilles and antibiotic link or the criteria for changing the plan.
2Lists treatments without dosage, progression or measures, or relies on passive modalities.
1Proposes unsafe or irrelevant treatment, or ignores load and the recent antibiotic use.

Model spoken answer

My working impression is plantar heel pain, commonly called plantar fasciitis, driven by a lot of standing on hard floors, restricted ankle dorsiflexion, a tight calf and a mildly pronated foot. The plan has to work in a classroom, so I would build it with Mei Ling and begin by asking what a good result looks like. I would suggest goals such as pain no worse than 3 out of 10 during the school day, steady first steps in the morning, and a return to her walks within eight weeks.

First, education and load. I would explain that the tissue needs gradual loading, not complete rest. We would reduce the extra load, for instance by wearing supportive shoes with cushioning, not walking barefoot on hard floors at home, and using a gel heel cup at school. I would also ask her to keep her activity at a level that leaves her pain no more than mild and settled within a day.

Second, stretching. I would teach calf stretching in two positions for the gastrocnemius and soleus, held thirty seconds, three repetitions, twice daily, and the plantar fascia stretch with the toes pulled back, ten seconds held ten times before getting out of bed and before standing after sitting.

Third, strengthening, which has good evidence. I would start with isometric holds, such as a plantar fascia loading hold with a rolled towel under her toes, and slow two leg heel raises with no added weight, three sets of ten, every second day. I would not add a backpack or single leg work until the Achilles tenderness has settled or her physician has reviewed it. Once the tendon is quiet, we would progress the tempo, then add load.

Fourth, short term pain relief. I might use rigid taping to unload the fascia for the first weeks, and soft tissue work for the calf. Evidence for these is modest, so I would not rely on them.

Fifth, a caution. She had ciprofloxacin five weeks ago, and she has tenderness at the Achilles insertion. Fluoroquinolones are linked with tendon problems that can show up weeks later. So I would keep Achilles loading low for now, avoid any thrust or forceful technique, and monitor the tendon. I would tell her to report sudden sharp pain, swelling or weakness. If the tendon tenderness persists or worsens, I would contact her physician now rather than wait for reassessment.

For measurement, I would record her first step pain rating and the Foot Function Index at baseline and every four weeks. I would reassess in four to six weeks. If she has less than a third improvement, if the Achilles tenderness persists or worsens, or if new features appear, I would change the plan and discuss the next medical steps with her physician.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Mei Ling mentions she may accept the corticosteroid injection because she wants quick relief. Explain how you would discuss this with her and what safety concerns you would raise.

Examiner checklist

  • Respects her right to choose and explores her reasons, hopes and fears about the injection. critical
  • Tells her what the injection may do, a short term effect on pain, and that long term benefit is limited.
  • Explains risks including plantar fascia rupture, fat pad atrophy and infection.
  • Raises the recent ciprofloxacin course and Achilles tenderness as a combined risk factor for tendon rupture and asks her to tell the physician. critical
  • Does not tell her to refuse the injection but encourages an informed decision with her physician. critical
  • Checks her understanding with teach back.
  • Describes safety netting if she gets injected: rest advice, signs of rupture or infection.
  • Offers choices and a timeline, for example a four week trial of the plan first.
  • Documents the discussion and her decision.

Performance scale

4Respects her choice, explains benefits and risks clearly, links the antibiotic and Achilles findings to tendon risk, gets her physician informed with consent, and checks understanding.
3Gives balanced information and respects autonomy but does not connect the antibiotic history or neglects safety netting.
2Lists risks generally, or tells her not to have the injection without discussing the reasons.
1Ignores her wishes, gives inaccurate information, or misses the injection risks entirely.

Model spoken answer

I would start with a question rather than advice: 'Tell me what you are hoping the injection will do for you.' She wants quick relief because of work, and that is a reasonable concern. The decision is hers, and my job is to make sure she has the facts and that her physician has the whole picture.

I would explain what the evidence says in plain terms. A corticosteroid injection can reduce heel pain for a few weeks, but studies show the benefit often fades by around three months and may not be better than exercise alone over the long run. There are also risks. The injection can weaken the plantar fascia, and in some people it leads to a rupture. It can thin the fat pad under the heel, which then makes walking on hard floors more painful. There is a small chance of infection and some pain from the needle itself.

Then I would raise the point that I think matters most for her. She took ciprofloxacin five weeks ago, and she has some tenderness at the Achilles insertion. Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are associated with tendon damage, and that risk can appear weeks after the course ends. Corticosteroids also weaken tendon tissue, and the combination is thought to raise the risk further. I cannot say whether her physician knew about the antibiotic when mentioning the injection, so I would ask for her permission to send a note or ask her to share this herself. I would say, 'This is not me saying no. It is information I think your doctor needs to weigh.'

I would then check she has understood by asking her to tell me in her own words what the main benefits and risks are. I would offer a middle path: try the exercise program and loading plan for four weeks, and if she is not improving we revisit the injection with her physician. I would not pressure her either way.

If she goes ahead, I would tell her about rest after the injection, ask her to avoid strong loading for a short period as her physician advises, and tell her to call if she hears or feels a pop, has sudden worse pain, swelling, or signs of infection such as heat, redness or fever.

Finally, I would record the discussion, the information I gave, her decision, and whether she gave consent for me to contact her physician.

Question 3: Collaboration

Describe how you would collaborate with others involved in Mei Ling's care, including who you would contact, what you would share and how you would manage her work situation.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies her family physician as a key partner and communicates the findings, the ciprofloxacin timing and the Achilles tenderness with her consent. critical
  • Specifies what to ask the physician: review of the injection decision and need for further investigation if the tendon worsens.
  • Obtains consent and limits what is shared with the school to functional needs and not the full medical details. critical
  • Proposes practical workplace accommodations: a stool for short breaks, a cushioned mat, supportive shoes, shared recess duty.
  • Provides a brief functional letter for the principal that she approves before it is sent.
  • Considers referral to a chiropodist or orthotist for orthotics only if she does not improve, and explains the funding rule.
  • Uses clear, timely communication, such as a short written note with a specific question.
  • Agrees on roles and a follow up schedule with Mei Ling as the central team member.
  • Documents all contacts and consents.

Performance scale

4Names the physician as a key partner with a specific question including the antibiotic and Achilles information, limits school disclosure with consent, proposes workable accommodations and documents.
3Describes appropriate partners and accommodations but with less specific communication, or does not limit disclosure to the school.
2Lists people to contact without a purpose, content or consent.
1Shares full medical information with the employer without consent or fails to involve the physician.

Model spoken answer

I would think of this as a small team with Mei Ling in the centre, and I would ask her who she is comfortable having me contact.

The most important person is her family physician. She is considering an injection, and the physician may be prescribing and deciding on orthotics. I would ask Mei Ling's written or recorded consent, and then send a short letter. It would say that I have assessed her for plantar heel pain over ten weeks, that I started a loading and stretching program, and that she completed a course of ciprofloxacin five weeks ago and now has some tenderness at the right Achilles insertion. I would state my specific question: 'Given the recent fluoroquinolone and the Achilles findings, do you still consider an injection appropriate, and would you like her tendon reviewed first?' I would ask for a reply within a week and mention that I plan to reassess her in four to six weeks. If she gets worse before then, I would call rather than write.

Second, the school. The principal does not need her diagnosis or her medical history. With Mei Ling's permission I would write a functional letter that says she has a foot condition that is being treated, that she is able to work, and that short seated breaks, a cushioned mat in the classroom, supportive footwear and, if possible, a limit on supervising uneven ground for a few weeks would help her recovery. I would ask her to read it and approve it before it goes out. I would also suggest that she talk with a union or health and safety representative if the school does not respond.

Third, orthotics. Her insurance covers them only with a prescription from a physician or chiropodist. I would not push this now, since prefabricated insoles are a reasonable first step and the evidence for custom devices is limited. If she is not improving at the reassessment, I would raise referral to a chiropodist or an orthotist with her physician.

Fourth, roles and follow up. I would give Mei Ling a simple one page summary of who is doing what: me for exercise and monitoring, her doctor for medication and injection decisions, and the school for the accommodations. I would check back in with her physician after reassessing.

Finally, I would document each contact, what was shared, consent, and the replies.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is the ciprofloxacin course finished five weeks ago, combined with Achilles insertion tenderness and a planned corticosteroid injection, which together raise tendon rupture risk. A competent candidate recognizes this, adjusts loading, informs the physician with consent, and supports an informed choice.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates give a standard plantar fasciitis program and never notice the antibiotic in the medication history. They also send full medical details to the employer, or tell the client not to have the injection instead of supporting an informed decision.

Examiner Notes

A pass offers a dosed loading program, links the antibiotic and Achilles findings to the injection risk, and collaborates with the physician and school with consent. A fail gives generic advice and misses the medication history.

Case 24 (Mock 3, case 4 of 10): Sudden low back and leg symptoms with urinary change

Musculoskeletal · Community physiotherapy clinic, about 50 minutes by road from the nearest hospital

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the plan you would put in place for Daniel today, including your decision about treatment, the urgency of that decision and the steps you would take in the clinic.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes the combination of bilateral leg symptoms, bilateral weakness and reflex change, and urinary hesitancy as suggestive of cauda equina syndrome. critical
  • Decides that physiotherapy treatment is not appropriate today and that emergency assessment with urgent MRI is needed. critical
  • Asks about saddle numbness, bowel function, sexual function and bladder sensation to complete the screen without delaying the referral. critical
  • Performs a brief focused neurological check: saddle sensation, anal tone is not examined by the physiotherapist unless trained, and strength and reflexes.
  • Explains that outcome depends on time to decompression and that waiting for a morning appointment is not acceptable.
  • Chooses transport: ambulance or accompanied transport, not driving himself, given weakness and possible deterioration. critical
  • Monitors vital signs and symptoms while arranging transfer and does not leave him alone.
  • Does not apply manual techniques, traction or loaded exercise.
  • Contacts the hospital emergency department or on call physician to alert them before arrival.

Performance scale

4Names cauda equina syndrome from the cluster, withholds treatment, completes a quick targeted screen, arranges ambulance or accompanied transport, and phones ahead and monitors him.
3Recognizes the emergency and refers urgently but is unclear about transport, monitoring or the pre-arrival call.
2Sends him for a routine physician visit or offers some treatment first.
1Treats the back with manual therapy or traction, or fails to recognize the urinary and bilateral symptoms.

Model spoken answer

My plan today is not to treat his back. Daniel has a pattern that I have to take very seriously: symptoms in both legs, weakness in both ankles, reduced ankle reflexes on both sides, reduced sensation, and, most important, a weak stream and difficulty starting to urinate over the last two days. Together these suggest cauda equina syndrome, which is compression of the nerve roots at the end of the spinal canal. It is a surgical emergency, because the chance of recovering bladder, bowel and sexual function depends on how quickly the pressure is relieved. The back pain from lifting makes a disc herniation the likely cause, but I do not need to prove that. I need to act on the risk.

Here is what I would do, in order.

First, I would quickly finish the screening that does not delay anything. I would ask about numbness around the groin or inner thighs, which is the saddle area, and test light touch there. I would ask about bowel control and any change in sensation when passing urine or stool, and about sexual function. I would not perform a rectal examination, since that is outside my training and is done by physicians. If saddle numbness is present, the case is clear. If it is absent, I still refer, because urinary retention can come before numbness.

Second, I would tell him clearly that he needs an emergency assessment and probably an urgent MRI today. Physiotherapy treatment, manual therapy, traction or exercise would be unsafe and a waste of time. I would not let the tests I have done become a reason for delay.

Third, transport. He drove here, but I would not let him drive back or to the hospital. His legs are weak and his condition could worsen. Given the 50 minute distance, I would call an ambulance, and I would stay with him, checking his symptoms and basic vital signs while we wait. If I cannot reach an ambulance, I would arrange for another adult to drive him, with me calling the hospital to say he is coming.

Fourth, I would phone the emergency department or the regional on call physician line, give a clear handover, and ask them to expect him. I would write down the time of each call.

I would also ask if he has any pain medication or allergies to pass along, and document everything I found and did.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Daniel refuses to go to the hospital because of his jobs tomorrow and his children. Explain how you would respond, including how you would handle consent and his concerns.

Examiner checklist

  • Listens to and acknowledges his work and childcare concerns without dismissing them.
  • Explains in plain language the specific risk of delay: permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction and leg weakness. critical
  • Recognizes that he has the right to refuse but only a decision based on understanding the risks is informed. critical
  • Checks understanding by asking him to restate the risks in his own words.
  • Works with him to solve barriers: calling his wife, a neighbour, relative or his clients, childcare options, clinic staff support.
  • Involves a physician by phone if he continues to refuse and offers the clinician to speak to him directly.
  • If he still refuses, documents the refusal, information given and his understanding, and gives written and verbal safety netting: not to drive himself, to have someone with him, and to call 911 at once if current symptoms persist or progress. critical
  • Does not use pressure, threats or guilt.
  • Asks permission to contact a support person and keeps the door open for him to change his mind.

Performance scale

4Acknowledges his concerns, explains specific risks clearly, checks understanding, solves barriers, involves a physician, and if he refuses documents informed refusal with safety netting.
3Explains the risk and respects autonomy but offers fewer practical solutions or limited documentation.
2Repeats that he must go without addressing his concerns, or accepts his refusal without explaining risks.
1Coerces him, dismisses his concerns, or lets him leave without any safety advice or documentation.

Model spoken answer

I would begin by showing Daniel that I have heard him. I would say, 'You have two jobs tomorrow and no one to look after the children tonight. That is a real problem, and I want to help you solve it.' He is not being difficult. He is a father who is worried about money and about his kids.

Then I would explain, in plain words, why I am so concerned, without frightening him more than the facts justify. I might say, 'The nerves at the bottom of your spine control your bladder, your bowel and your legs. The trouble you are having starting to pass urine, together with the weakness in both legs, tells me those nerves may be squeezed. If that is true and it is not relieved within hours, the damage can be permanent. That could mean problems with your bladder and bowel, your sexual function, and walking. The only way to find out is an MRI scan today.' I would not say that I am certain of the diagnosis, but I would be clear that the risk is serious and time sensitive.

He has the right to refuse, and I will respect that, but a refusal is only valid when he understands what is at stake. So I would ask him, 'Can you tell me in your own words what could happen if you wait until after work tomorrow?' If his answer shows he has missed the point, I would explain again in a different way.

Next, I would try to remove the barriers together. We could call his wife to see if she can leave work or arrange a relative or a neighbour to take the children. I could ask the clinic staff whether someone can make a call. I could offer to speak with the on call physician by phone with him, as some people accept the same advice more readily from a doctor.

If he still refuses after all that, I would not force or shame him. I would document that I explained the risks, that he showed understanding in his own words, and that he chose to decline. I would give him written and spoken instructions. I would tell him he must not drive himself, because of the weakness in his foot and the pain, and that someone should stay with him. I would also say that his symptoms already meet the threshold for urgent care, so if they continue or progress, or if he notices numbness in the groin or any loss of bladder or bowel control, he should call 911 immediately. The offer stands, and I will call the ambulance whenever he changes his mind. With his permission, I would call his wife so that someone else knows the situation.

Question 3: Collaboration

Daniel agrees to go to hospital by ambulance. Describe how you would collaborate with the other people and services involved, including what you would communicate and when.

Examiner checklist

  • Calls emergency services with a clear request and the reason for urgency.
  • Gives a structured verbal handover to the emergency department, such as SBAR, with key findings, timing of urinary symptoms and neurological signs. critical
  • Sends a written summary with him including the examination findings, times, medication taken and contact details.
  • Asks for his consent to contact his wife and arranges childcare support.
  • Uses plain, respectful communication that avoids giving a firm diagnosis to Daniel, and leaves interpretation to the medical team.
  • Coordinates with clinic staff to cover the clinic while the therapist stays with him.
  • Plans follow up with the hospital team and the family physician after discharge and says when physiotherapy might resume.
  • Respects confidentiality and shares only information needed for care. critical
  • Documents the calls, handover, times and people spoken to.

Performance scale

4Calls emergency services, gives a structured handover with specific findings and times, sends a written summary, involves family with consent, covers the clinic, plans follow up and documents.
3Describes the right contacts and a reasonable handover but with limited detail on content, consent or documentation.
2States that they would call but gives no structure or content, or omits the receiving team or family.
1Fails to communicate with the receiving team or shares information without consent.

Model spoken answer

I would organize the communication around who needs to know what, and by when. Most of it happens in the next fifteen minutes.

First, the ambulance. I would call emergency services from the clinic phone while Daniel is with another staff member or with me within sight. I would say that I am a physiotherapist with a 38 year old man with suspected cauda equina syndrome, bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention symptoms, and that I need urgent transfer to a hospital with MRI and spine surgery access. If I do not know which hospital has those services, I would ask the dispatcher or the regional on call line. Giving the reason for urgency matters because it affects how the call is prioritized. With Daniel I would explain that the team needs to scan his back urgently, without naming a firm diagnosis, and leave interpretation to the doctors.

Second, the receiving team. As soon as the ambulance is on its way I would phone the emergency department and give a handover with SBAR. Situation: possible cauda equina syndrome, arriving by ambulance. Background: 38 year old plumber, back pain after lifting three days ago, no known history of surgery, no regular medication. Assessment: bilateral leg symptoms, ankle weakness of 3 out of 5 on the right and 4 out of 5 on the left, reduced ankle reflexes, reduced sensation on the right lateral foot, difficulty initiating urination and weak stream for two days, and vitals. Recommendation: urgent MRI and neurosurgical or spine review. I would say what I have not done, which is a rectal examination or bladder scan, because that is outside my scope. I would note the time of the call.

Third, a written summary to go with him, with these findings, the times of onset and any medications he took, such as the ibuprofen and acetaminophen, and my contact details so that the team can reach me.

Fourth, his family. With his permission I would call his wife, tell her where he is going, and ask whether someone can care for the children. I would only share what he agrees to share.

Fifth, my own clinic. I would ask a colleague or the front desk to look after other clients and to reschedule appointments while I stay with him.

Finally, after he has been seen, I would ask for his permission to follow up with the hospital team and his family physician, to learn the diagnosis and plan. If surgery happens, I would offer to plan rehabilitation when the surgeon allows. I would document each call with the time, the person, what was said and his consent.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case
