The buried issue is the urinary hesitancy and weak stream, mentioned briefly at the end of the profile, which together with bilateral leg signs indicates cauda equina syndrome. A competent candidate notices it, refuses to treat, arranges emergency transport rather than self driving, and handles the refusal with informed consent.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates focus on the back pain and straight leg raise and begin manual therapy or schedule a follow up. Others send him to his family doctor tomorrow, allow him to drive himself, or accept his refusal without confirming that he understood the risks.

Examiner Notes

A pass recognizes cauda equina syndrome, acts the same day, arranges transport and gives a structured handover. A fail treats or delays. Candidates must show respect for his concerns while still communicating the urgency clearly.

Case 25 (Mock 3, case 5 of 10): Breathlessness during training in a teenage athlete

Cardiovascular-Respiratory · High school gym, physiotherapist working with the school's sports teams

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the plan you would put in place for Amara over the next two weeks, including what you would do in your role, what you would recommend and how you would monitor her.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes the pattern as suggestive of exercise induced bronchoconstriction but states that diagnosis needs medical assessment. critical
  • Recommends prompt physician assessment, with possible spirometry and an exercise challenge, before the meet. critical
  • Advises that she does not use a friend's inhaler and explains why. critical
  • Adapts training: a gradual warm up with intervals, scarf or mask in cold air, and warm down, with symptom monitoring.
  • Sets a clear stop rule: she stops activity if she has wheeze, chest tightness or breathlessness, and rests.
  • Establishes an action plan with school staff for a flare up, including who to call and when to call emergency services.
  • Uses simple monitoring such as symptom diary, peak flow if available, and performance and tolerance log.
  • Screens for other causes: cardiac symptoms, vocal cord dysfunction, deconditioning, and pollen triggers.
  • Explains that running at the meet depends on medical review and symptom control, not on the date.

Performance scale

4Recognizes the likely pattern but defers diagnosis, arranges prompt medical review, addresses the borrowed inhaler, adjusts training safely, creates a school action plan and monitors symptoms.
3Recommends medical review and safe training changes but omits the borrowed inhaler, school action plan or monitoring.
2Gives general exercise advice without medical referral or safety rules.
1Diagnoses and treats asthma on their own, advises more use of the borrowed inhaler or tells her to push through symptoms.

Model spoken answer

My role is to support safe training and get her to the right medical assessment, not to diagnose or prescribe. From what Amara describes, her symptoms start five to ten minutes into hard exercise, include cough, chest tightness and wheeze, and settle within thirty minutes of rest. They are worse in cold air and pollen season, and she has eczema and a father with asthma. That pattern fits exercise induced bronchoconstriction, where the airways narrow during or after exercise, but I cannot confirm it. A physician has to diagnose it, often with spirometry and sometimes an exercise challenge test.

So my first step is to recommend a prompt appointment with her family doctor or a sports medicine physician, and I would help by writing a short note describing what I saw and what she reports. I would not want her to wait until after the meet.

The second step is safety in the meantime. I would explain that she should not use her friend's inhaler. It is medication prescribed for someone else, the dose may not be right for her, and it may be hiding a problem that needs a different treatment. That is a point I would raise with her kindly.

Third, training changes that are safe and reasonable. I would plan a longer warm up of ten to fifteen minutes with a few short, hard efforts, since this can reduce symptoms for some athletes. In cold air I would have her cover her mouth and nose with a scarf. I would keep her sessions at an intensity where she can speak in short sentences until she is seen, and include a cool down. The rule is simple: if she gets chest tightness, wheeze or breathlessness, she stops, sits, and rests, and she tells me or the coach right away.

Fourth, an action plan with the school. The coach, the teacher on duty and I would agree on what to do if she has a bad episode: stop activity, sit upright, call me or the first aid person, and call emergency services if she is struggling to speak, her lips look blue, or she is not improving with rest.

Fifth, monitoring. I would ask her to keep a diary of symptoms, timing, weather and how far she ran. If a peak flow meter is available, I would record readings before and after exercise.

I would also ask about fainting, palpitations, chest pain at rest and family history of sudden cardiac death, to screen for other causes, and I would mention that other conditions, such as vocal cord problems, can look similar. Whether she runs the 1500 metres will depend on the medical review and how well her symptoms are controlled.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Amara asks you not to tell her parents about the inhaler. Explain how you would respond, including consent, confidentiality and her safety.

Examiner checklist

  • Responds without judgement and thanks her for telling you.
  • Assesses her maturity and understanding and considers the role of a mature minor in consent under provincial rules.
  • Explains the limits of confidentiality: serious risk to health may require involving her parents. critical
  • Strongly encourages parental involvement in her care and notes the school form needs a parent signature, without making it a precondition of her consent. critical
  • Explores her fear of her parents' reaction and offers to support her in the conversation.
  • Gives her a choice about how and when to tell, such as her telling them with you present.
  • Does not promise secrecy that cannot be kept. critical
  • Explains the risks of using someone else's medication in language she understands.
  • Documents the discussion and her decisions.

Performance scale

4Responds without judgement, explains limits of confidentiality before promising anything, addresses parental involvement and school forms, explores her fears, offers choices and documents.
3Handles confidentiality and parental involvement reasonably but offers fewer supportive options or does not explain the risk of borrowed medication.
2Either promises secrecy or contacts parents immediately without explanation or without assessing her capacity to consent.
1Agrees to keep it secret indefinitely, shames her, or ignores the safety implications.

Model spoken answer

I would start by thanking her. I would say, 'It took courage to tell me about the inhaler. You are not in trouble with me.' A teenager who feels judged will stop telling us things, and that makes her less safe.

Then I would be honest about what I can and cannot promise. I would not agree to keep this secret, because I might not be able to keep it. I would say, 'I will respect your privacy as much as I can. But if something puts your health at risk, I might need to involve your parents or a doctor, and if so I would tell you first.' That way she is not surprised.

Next, I would talk about why her parents matter here. She is 15. Under provincial rules a capable young person can consent to her own care, so I would first check her understanding of what is going on and what she is asking. I would still strongly encourage involving her parents, because a diagnosis, ongoing treatment and the school form all work best with them, and the school form needs a parent signature before she can carry a medication at school. I would also say that her symptoms on running are real, and that her parents can help her get the right treatment.

I would ask about her fear. 'What do you think your parents will say?' She may worry that they will be angry about the borrowed inhaler or that they cannot afford the medication. Understanding that lets me offer something practical. I could say, 'Would it help if you told them with me in the room, or if I called them first to explain that this is common in athletes and treatable?' I would give her the choice, and a day or two to decide, as long as she agrees to stop using the friend's inhaler right away.

I would explain why the borrowed medication is a problem in terms she understands: it is prescribed for someone else, she does not know the right dose or whether she needs a different medicine, and if it makes her feel better she may think she is fine when there is something that needs to be checked.

I would record the conversation, her understanding, the plan we made and the date by which she will tell her parents. If she did not do so, I would follow up with her first. I would contact her parents without her agreement only if a serious risk to her health required it, and I would tell her before I did.

Question 3: Communication

Describe how you would communicate with Amara, her coach and her parents about her condition and plan, giving the specific approach and wording you would use with each.

Examiner checklist

  • Uses plain, age appropriate language with Amara and checks understanding with open questions.
  • Talks with the coach about needs without disclosing medical details beyond what Amara agrees, and corrects the lazy label. critical
  • Gives the coach practical information about warm up, stop rules and the emergency plan.
  • Explains to parents, with Amara's involvement, what was seen, why medical assessment is recommended and what the school needs signed. critical
  • Adapts to parents' work schedules and uses a call, text or written note, and an interpreter if needed.
  • Uses a non-blaming tone and acknowledges concerns about cost and time.
  • Provides a short written summary or action plan to each party as appropriate.
  • Invites questions from each party and confirms next steps.
  • Documents the communication and consent.

Performance scale

4Tailors plain language and wording for Amara, coach and parents, protects confidentiality, corrects the lazy label, adapts for parents' schedule or language, and confirms next steps.
3Describes appropriate messages for each person but with limited attention to consent, language needs or written follow up.
2Uses the same message for everyone, or shares details without Amara's agreement.
1Uses jargon, blames Amara or her parents, or discloses private information without consent.

Model spoken answer

I would use a different approach with each person, but the same message: Amara's symptoms are real, they need a medical check, and a safe plan is in place.

With Amara, I would speak plainly and warmly, and let her talk first. I would ask, 'What do you notice in your chest and breathing when you run, and what worries you the most?' Then I would explain in simple terms: 'When some athletes exercise, the tubes that carry air into the lungs tighten, which causes the cough and wheeze. It is common, and it is treatable. A doctor can test for it.' I would ask her to repeat the plan back, the stop rule and the doctor visit, in her own words. And I would tell her that being slower this term is not about laziness, so she does not carry that label.

With the coach, I need Amara's permission about what I share. I would ask her what she is comfortable with, and with her agreement I would say, 'Amara has breathing symptoms during hard running that need a medical check. She is not lazy. Pushing through them can be dangerous. Until she has seen a doctor, please give her a longer warm up, let her stop when she needs to without penalty, and call me if she struggles. I will send you a one page plan.' I would not share the details of the borrowed inhaler. About the meet, I would say that her participation will depend on the medical review, and I would be willing to talk through the decision with him.

With her parents, I would ideally contact them with Amara beside me or after she agrees. Because they work long shifts, I would offer a phone call at a time that suits them, or a short text asking when to call, followed by a written note. If English is not their first language, I would use an interpreter. I would start with what they are likely to care about: 'Amara has been having chest tightness and wheeze when she runs. This is common in young athletes and usually treatable, but she needs a doctor to check her breathing. The school also needs a form signed before she can use any medication at school.' I would acknowledge possible cost or time worries and mention the options for assessment. I would not blame anyone, and I would invite questions.

For all three, I would give a short written summary suitable for each, check understanding, confirm who does what by when, and document what was said and what consent I had.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is that Amara has used a friend's inhaler without a diagnosis, parental knowledge or a school medication form. A competent candidate addresses the medication safety issue, explains the limits of confidentiality honestly, involves her parents with her input, and avoids diagnosing or prescribing.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates diagnose asthma and recommend medication use, or promise to keep the inhaler secret. Others agree with the coach's view that she should push through, or share her health information with the coach and parents without discussing it with her.

Examiner Notes

A pass defers diagnosis, refers promptly, deals with the borrowed inhaler, and handles confidentiality for a minor with honesty and support. A fail diagnoses and treats within the clinic, ignores the inhaler, or communicates poorly with the three parties.

Case 26 (Mock 3, case 6 of 10): Deep groin pain in a competitive hockey player

Musculoskeletal · Sport medicine clinic attached to a junior-A to semi-professional hockey organization

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Describe how you would interpret these findings to form your clinical impression, which other sources of groin pain you would still need to consider, and what further assessment you would do today.

Examiner checklist

  • Links reduced flexion and internal rotation with pinching pain and positive FADIR to an intra-articular hip source. critical
  • Recognizes the radiographic cam morphology as supportive but not diagnostic on its own, since it is common in asymptomatic hockey players.
  • Considers labral pathology as a likely associated problem given clicking and pinching.
  • Differentiates adductor-related groin pain using the painless, strong adductor squeeze.
  • Considers inguinal-related or core muscle pain and lumbar or sacroiliac referral and states why each is less likely.
  • Screens for femoral neck stress fracture and other serious causes, using history of night or rest pain and loading tolerance. critical
  • Proposes further tests such as scour, FABER, log roll, hip flexor strength, fulcrum test, single leg stance tolerance, and movement screening.
  • Identifies the need for clinical-imaging correlation and possible referral for MR arthrography if conservative care fails.
  • Selects a patient-reported outcome measure to baseline and track change.

Performance scale

4Names FAI syndrome with labral involvement, reasons from history, motion loss and tests, explains why imaging alone is not diagnostic, rules adductor, core, lumbar and stress fracture in or out with findings, and plans next tests and referral thresholds.
3Reaches the correct impression and mentions some alternatives, but weak on stress fracture screening or on why the radiograph is only supportive.
2Lists tests or labels FAI from the X-ray alone without reasoning, with little differential.
1Misses the hip as the source, treats as an adductor strain, or ignores a serious cause such as stress fracture.

Model spoken answer

My clinical impression is femoroacetabular impingement syndrome of the right hip, probably cam type, with a possible labral component. I reason from three groups of findings. First, his history fits: deep groin pain, aggravated by flexion based positions like sitting low and skating crossovers, with clicking. Second, the examination: flexion is 20 degrees less than the left, internal rotation at 90 degrees of flexion is 15 degrees against 35, end range is pinching, and the flexion, adduction, internal rotation test reproduces his pain. That test is sensitive but not specific, so I treat it as pointing to the hip joint, not proving the exact structure. Third, the radiograph shows a cam bump with an alpha angle of 68 degrees. Cam morphology is common in elite hockey players with no symptoms, so the picture only matters because it matches his symptoms and his motion loss.

I would keep other sources of groin pain in mind. Adductor related pain is the classic competitor in hockey, but his adductor squeeze is strong and painless, which makes it less likely. Inguinal related or core muscle pain usually hurts with sit-ups, coughing and sprinting, and palpation of the inguinal canal, so I would palpate there and check resisted sit-up. Lumbar or sacroiliac referral is less likely because lumbar movement is full and pain free, but I would add a slump test and a sacroiliac cluster. A femoral neck stress fracture must be ruled out. He says pain occasionally wakes him when he rolls over, which is a rest symptom, and he carries high training loads, so I would ask exactly how often and how long it lasts, and avoid heavy loading and defer hop testing until a stress fracture is reasonably excluded. If pain is reproduced by the fulcrum test, or he cannot tolerate single leg stance, I would stop and refer for urgent imaging. Testicular and hernia sources also need a basic screen, and I would ask about urinary or systemic symptoms.

For further assessment today I would do the scour and FABER, log roll for the joint capsule, hip flexor and abductor strength with a handheld dynamometer, single leg squat and step-down quality, and thoracolumbar and pelvic motion, since lost hip motion is often borrowed from the spine and the pubic symphysis. I would record the Hip Outcome Score sport subscale of 62 percent as the baseline and agree on one sport-specific functional test.

My plan is to try a structured conservative program first, with a clear time frame. If he has a poor response after about 3 months, or if he needs the labrum assessed, I would discuss referral to an orthopedic surgeon experienced in hip preservation, who may order MR arthrography. I would explain that the picture is a joint that is mechanically limited, not damaged beyond repair, and invite his questions.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Dmitri wants to keep skating through the playoffs. Explain how you would build a rehabilitation plan that keeps him safe while respecting his goals, including what you would tell him about the injection.

Examiner checklist

  • Avoids provocative end-range flexion with adduction and internal rotation during early loading and uses a pain monitoring rule. critical
  • Exercises start in a pain-tolerable range and progress by load, with a clear stop or modify rule for sharp or locking pain.
  • Explains benefits and limits of conservative care versus surgery, including realistic time frames.
  • Explains that an injection may mask pain and does not change bony shape, so risk of more labral damage should be discussed with the physician. critical
  • Respects Dmitri's right to decide about playing, using shared decision-making and documented informed choice. critical
  • Plans graded return to skating drills with objective criteria, not only the calendar of playoffs.
  • Addresses limiting anti-inflammatory use before games and advises discussion with the physician.
  • Re-screens for red flags on each visit, including night pain and loss of weight bearing.
  • Confirms with the physician that a femoral neck stress fracture has been reasonably excluded before progressing load or return to skating.

Performance scale

4Gives specific movement and load precautions with a pain rule, explains injection benefits and limits accurately, frames decisions as the client's, sets objective return criteria and red-flag monitoring.
3Safe plan with precautions and shared decision-making but vague on objective criteria or on the injection.
2Generic rehabilitation list without precautions, or tells the client what to do without exploring his goals.
1Encourages playing through pain without limits, gives advice on the injection beyond scope, or dismisses the client's goal.

Model spoken answer

I want Dmitri to leave knowing that this is his decision, and that my job is to give him a plan that protects the hip as far as I can while he chases the playoffs. So I would start with an honest conversation. I would explain in plain words that the hip bone is shaped so that, in deep flexion with the knee turning in, the ball pinches the socket rim. We cannot change the bone with exercise, but we can change how much of his skating happens in the painful zone and how well the muscles around the hip control it.

Before I progress load or return him to skating, I would confirm with the physician that a femoral neck stress fracture has been reasonably excluded, with imaging if the night pain or fulcrum test findings persist. The first stage is load management. I would avoid the pinching range, which is deep hip flexion combined with adduction and internal rotation, in the gym and on the bench. For example, I would use box squats to a pain-free depth instead of deep squats, and hip hinge patterns rather than deep lunges. I would give him a simple pain rule: mild discomfort up to about 3 out of 10 that settles within 24 hours is acceptable, but sharp pain, catching or locking, or pain that lingers into the next day means we scale back. I would add gluteal, deep hip rotator and trunk strengthening, hip flexor tendon loading in a comfortable range, and movement practice for crossovers and skating starts to cut down on pelvic tilt and valgus.

Second, return to skating. I would build steps: straight skating at a controlled intensity, then curves and crossovers, then contact drills, with objective criteria for each step such as a symmetric single leg squat, pain at or below 3 out of 10, and no next-day flare. If he is not meeting them, I would say so plainly.

About the injection, I would be clear that it is a medical decision for the physician and him. An injection may reduce pain for a time, which may let him tolerate more skating, but it does not change the cam shape, and numbing pain can hide the signal that tells him to stop, so there may be risk of more damage to the labrum or cartilage. I would encourage him to ask the physician those questions. He also takes ibuprofen before games, which can mask pain; I would ask him to discuss that with the physician and pharmacist, since medication advice is theirs, and not use it to push through warning pain.

I would also tell him that surgery is a real option. The best time to decide is when we know whether the conservative program is working. Throughout, I would ask him to tell me right away about night pain, groin pain when walking, or any inability to bear weight, because those would change my plan to urgent medical review. At the end, I would check his understanding, document what he chooses and why, and book a reassessment within a week.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Later that week the head coach texts you asking for Dmitri's diagnosis and expected return date. Dmitri has asked you not to share details. Explain how you would respond and how you would document this.

Examiner checklist

  • Does not release health information to the coach without Dmitri's informed consent. critical
  • Recognizes that the organization paying for the clinic does not change the duty of confidentiality owed to the patient. critical
  • Speaks with Dmitri first about what he is willing to share, and offers a limited, agreed summary such as availability or restrictions.
  • Identifies the dual role and conflict of interest and explains how to manage it, including telling the organization the terms in writing.
  • Responds to the coach professionally without confirming or denying treatment details.
  • Documents the request, Dmitri's consent decisions and what was shared in the record.
  • Knows the file must reflect the full clinical findings, including night pain, regardless of who can see it. critical
  • Considers obtaining written consent and reviewing provincial privacy legislation and regulator standards.

Performance scale

4Protects consent and confidentiality, handles the dual role and contract conflict, offers a limited agreed disclosure, and documents complete findings while controlling access.
3Refuses disclosure and documents, but does not address the dual role or does not discuss options with the client.
2Gives partial details to the coach or says only that the employer can decide.
1Releases information without consent, omits findings from the record, or yields to team pressure.

Model spoken answer

My first duty is to Dmitri. Even though the team pays for the clinic, he is my patient, and the information about his hip belongs to him. I cannot give the coach his diagnosis, his findings or an expected return date unless Dmitri gives informed consent. So I would not answer the question as asked, and I would not ignore the coach either.

Here is what I would do. First, I would speak to Dmitri before replying. I would tell him that the coach has asked, and ask what he is comfortable with. Many athletes are happy to share something limited, like playing availability or restrictions, because it helps them. I would explain what the coach would learn from each option and what could happen if the coach hears nothing. Dmitri may decide that he wants me to say he is being treated and is following a rehabilitation plan, and that is his choice. If he wants nothing shared, I respect that. I would also tell him honestly that I cannot promise the team will not draw conclusions from silence, but that is separate from what I can disclose.

Second, I would reply to the coach politely and briefly, something like: I understand you need to plan. I am not able to discuss any player's health information without his permission, and I will pass your request to him. That neither confirms a diagnosis nor lets the coach guess. If Dmitri consents to share a limited summary, I would keep it to what the coach actually needs, for example the activities he can do, and I would write down exactly what was agreed. Ideally the consent is written.

Third, the dual role. I work under a contract with the organization, which creates a possible conflict between the team's interest in winning and my duty to the player. I would raise it with my employer in the clinic, ask for the information sharing terms to be set in writing, and make sure that medical decisions about return to play remain with the athlete, the physician and me, based on clinical criteria. If I ever felt pressure to release information or to clear him early, I would speak to my regulator for guidance and my professional liability provider.

Fourth, documentation. I would record the coach's request, my conversation with Dmitri, his decisions and anything shared and to whom. I would also make sure the clinical file contains complete and honest findings, including the night pain, even though he asked me to keep it out of the file the coach can see. I should not leave out findings because the record might be seen by others. The right fix is to protect access to the record under our privacy policy and provincial health privacy law, not to alter its contents. I would tell Dmitri who has access to his file and review that if needed.

Finally, I would continue to review the practices of the clinic, such as separate records for medical information and a short availability form.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

Two buried issues. Night pain that wakes him is a possible red flag for stress fracture or another serious cause and must be explored and recorded. Also, the team contract creates a conflict of interest: the coach and the team doctor want a fast return, and the client asks for findings to be left out of the record. A competent candidate protects consent, never alters the record, and manages the dual role in writing.

Common Candidate Errors

Diagnosing FAI from the radiograph alone and not ruling out adductor, core or stress fracture causes. Telling the coach a general return date because the employer pays, or promising the client that some findings can be left off the chart.

Examiner Notes

Passing candidates reason from motion loss and tests to a hip source while ruling out alternatives, give specific movement precautions, and hold firm on consent and honest documentation despite employer pressure. Failing candidates default to a list of exercises or give the coach information.

Case 27 (Mock 3, case 7 of 10): Exercise guidance in pregnancy with elevated blood pressure

Other Systems · Pelvic and women's health physiotherapy clinic in a community health centre

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Describe how you would organize your assessment today, and explain how you would interpret her findings before deciding about exercise.

Examiner checklist

  • Interprets blood pressure of about 148/96 on repeated readings as elevated and above the threshold used to define hypertension in pregnancy. critical
  • Asks specifically about headache characteristics, visual disturbances, right upper abdominal or epigastric pain, nausea and sudden swelling. critical
  • Recognizes that gestational hypertension can progress to preeclampsia and that symptoms change the urgency. critical
  • Checks fetal movement and asks about vaginal bleeding, fluid loss and contractions.
  • Repeats and records blood pressure with correct cuff size and position.
  • Notes that mild ankle edema is common in pregnancy and does not alone indicate disease, but sudden or facial and hand edema matters.
  • Separates musculoskeletal findings, including the pelvic girdle pain, from medical issues and does not let them distract from the priority.
  • Asks about current medication, prenatal monitoring and who last reviewed her blood pressure.

Performance scale

4Prioritizes the blood pressure and headache over the musculoskeletal findings, names preeclampsia and its symptoms, plans accurate repeat measures and fetal screen, and ties interpretation to urgency.
3Recognizes elevated pressure and asks about symptoms but weak on preeclampsia links or on prioritizing over back pain.
2Begins with a musculoskeletal exam and mentions blood pressure briefly, or lists generic tests.
1Dismisses the headache and edema, or treats pelvic girdle pain as the main problem.

Model spoken answer

I would start by treating today's blood pressure as the main finding, not the back pain. Her two readings, about 148/96 and 146/94 after rest, are above the 140/90 level used to define hypertension in pregnancy. She already has a diagnosis of gestational hypertension, so I need to know whether it is stable or moving toward preeclampsia, and I cannot tell that from blood pressure alone.

My assessment would be organized in this order. First, a focused history about symptoms. The afternoon headaches she mentioned in passing matter. I would ask about how severe they are, whether they are new or worse over the last week, whether paracetamol helps, and whether they come with blurred or flashing vision, spots, pain under the right ribs or in the upper stomach, nausea or vomiting, shortness of breath, or sudden swelling of her face and hands. These are the typical warning signs of preeclampsia. I would also ask about fetal movement, which she reports as normal, bleeding, fluid leaking and contractions, and when her blood pressure was last checked by her midwife and what she was told to do if it rose.

Second, repeat the vital signs with a correctly sized cuff, seated, with her arm supported at heart level. I would repeat the measurement and record both arms if the reading is surprising. I would check heart rate, respiratory rate and SpO2, and look at her face and hands for edema. Ankle edema on its own is common at 32 weeks, so I would not interpret it by itself, but swelling that is sudden or involves her face or hands raises concern. I would also ask whether the urine dipstick result from the nurse is available, since protein would matter to the medical team, although I would not interpret it myself.

Third, a limited musculoskeletal assessment. Her lumbar movement is full and the posterior pelvic pain provocation test is positive on the right, which supports pelvic girdle pain, a common and manageable condition. But it is a distractor today because it does not decide whether she can safely exercise.

So my clinical reasoning is that she has gestational hypertension, with a blood pressure that is above the diagnostic threshold, plus a new symptom, headache, that I cannot attribute to marking and screens until a medical provider has excluded preeclampsia. That puts her at risk of progressing to a condition that can endanger her and the baby. If her history reveals visual changes, right upper abdominal pain, or her blood pressure rises to the severe range of 160 systolic or 110 diastolic, I would treat it as urgent. Even if none of these is present, the combination of elevated pressure and headache means exercise guidance is secondary, and I need her prenatal care provider to assess her today or within a very short time, not in 10 days.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Priya says she feels fine and wants to do her exercises today as planned. Explain what you would do and say, including how you would involve her in decisions.

Examiner checklist

  • Does not start exercise today and explains why in plain language. critical
  • Contacts her prenatal provider or arranges same-day medical assessment through the appropriate route, with her consent. critical
  • Explains warning signs that mean going to the emergency department immediately, such as severe headache, vision changes, severe upper abdominal pain, decreased fetal movement or breathing difficulty. critical
  • Supports her to choose how to get there safely, considering the long drive and that her partner works nights.
  • Uses teach-back to confirm understanding.
  • Explains that exercise can be safe and helpful in pregnancy in general, and that today's decision is about her current risk.
  • Offers safe, low-risk information such as relaxed breathing or positioning for pelvic girdle pain that does not raise blood pressure, if medically acceptable.
  • Acknowledges her goals and plans, such as the baby shower and her work leave.

Performance scale

4Declines exercise with clear reasoning, arranges same-day medical assessment with consent, gives specific emergency warning signs with teach-back, and addresses practical barriers while respecting autonomy.
3Holds exercise and refers but warning signs, consent or practical planning are incomplete.
2Modifies exercise intensity or suggests monitoring at home without arranging assessment.
1Proceeds with exercise, reassures falsely, or makes a medical diagnosis.

Model spoken answer

I would not start exercise today, and I would say that early and kindly. I would acknowledge that she has been looking forward to getting active and that she feels well, then explain why I want to pause. I might say: Your blood pressure is higher than it should be, and you have mentioned headaches. In pregnancy, that combination can sometimes mean a condition called preeclampsia, which can develop quickly and can affect you and your baby. Exercise raises blood pressure further, so I do not think it is safe for you to exercise until your doctor or midwife has checked you. This is not because you did something wrong, and I expect to help you get back to exercise.

Next, I would ask her permission to contact her midwife or the on-call provider for the practice today. With her consent, I would call, give the readings and the headache, and ask for same-day assessment, which usually means an obstetric triage unit or a hospital assessment, depending on the local pathway. If I could not reach anyone within a short time, I would recommend that she go to the nearest obstetrical assessment unit rather than wait for the appointment in 10 days. I would not diagnose or tell her she has preeclampsia, because that is for the medical team.

She has practical barriers I should consider. The family doctor is 90 minutes away and her partner works nights. I would ask how she can get to the unit, and suggest she not drive herself if she has any visual changes or a severe headache. I would also tell her that the baby shower is her decision, but that I would want her to have been assessed first, and that it would help if she knew the warning signs when away from home.

I would give her those warning signs clearly and in writing: a severe or persistent headache that does not settle with rest or paracetamol, blurred vision or flashing lights, pain in the upper right abdomen or under the ribs, sudden swelling of the face or hands, nausea and vomiting, trouble breathing, or fewer baby movements. If any of those happen she goes to the emergency department or calls 911, and she does not wait. I would use teach-back by asking her to tell me in her own words what she will do.

Before she leaves, I would give her something helpful for the pelvic girdle pain that does not raise her blood pressure, for example lying on her left side with a pillow between her knees, only if her provider agrees it is fine in the meantime. I would reassure her that we will plan her exercise once she has been cleared, and ask what worries her about the plan. If she declines to be assessed, I would respect that she is an adult who can decide, explain the risks again honestly, document her decision and what I told her, and still encourage her to call her midwife that evening.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Priya declines to go in today and asks you not to contact anyone, saying her midwife will be annoyed and her employer must not hear about it. Discuss your professional responsibilities in this situation.

Examiner checklist

  • Respects the competent adult's right to refuse and documents informed refusal and the information given. critical
  • Weighs the duty to act for patient safety, and explains that seeking an urgent same-day plan remains the aim, using persuasion not coercion. critical
  • Explores her reasons for declining and addresses fears about the midwife and the employer.
  • Confirms that her health information is confidential and will not go to her employer without consent. critical
  • Explains what limited disclosure, if any, might be made without consent under privacy law only if there is serious imminent risk, and knows to seek regulator guidance.
  • Stays within scope: does not diagnose preeclampsia or advise medication.
  • Documents blood pressure readings, symptoms, advice, her decision and follow-up plan.
  • Arranges a safety-net follow-up such as a phone call that evening, with her agreement.

Performance scale

4Balances autonomy with duty to promote safety, addresses her fears, explains confidentiality accurately including the narrow limits, stays in scope, offers alternatives and a safety net, and documents.
3Respects refusal and documents but weak on exploring reasons, confidentiality limits or alternatives.
2Accepts refusal without further information or breaches confidentiality too readily.
1Contacts the employer or others without consent, coerces her, or leaves without documentation.

Model spoken answer

She is a competent adult, and she has the right to refuse. My responsibility is to make sure that refusal is informed, to respect it, to protect her privacy, and to keep trying, in a respectful way, to get her the care she needs. So I would not contact anyone against her wishes unless there were a very serious and immediate risk, and I would explain this to her openly.

First, I would explore why she is saying no. She said her midwife will be annoyed and that her employer must not hear. About the midwife, I would tell her that midwives expect this kind of call and would much rather hear about a high reading and a headache than not. About the employer, I would tell her that her health information is confidential. I would not share it with her employer. The clinic needs her consent to share information with her midwife or anyone else, and nothing about today goes to her workplace unless she asks me to provide a note.

Second, I would make sure she understands the risk, in plain words, without frightening her or pressuring her. I would repeat what I found, what could be going on, why I cannot rule it out myself, and the symptoms that mean she must go immediately. I would ask her to tell me back what she understands. If she still declines, I would offer middle options: calling the midwife herself from here with me present, calling the provincial prenatal telephone line if there is one, or agreeing to a same-day phone assessment with her midwife or a provincial prenatal health line, with a firm plan to attend an obstetrical assessment unit that day if any warning sign appears, though I would be honest that I would prefer same-day in-person assessment.

Third, I stay within my scope. I would not tell her she has preeclampsia, advise any medication, or tell her it is safe to wait. I can only describe my findings and recommend assessment.

If she continues to refuse, I would respect that. I would not breach confidentiality on my own. Privacy legislation allows disclosure without consent only in narrow situations of serious imminent risk, and I do not believe the threshold is met by a person who is currently well and understands the warning signs, but if her condition changed, for example in the clinic, I would call emergency services. If I were unsure, I would call my regulator or the clinic's privacy officer for guidance.

Fourth, documentation. I would write the readings, the symptoms she reported, my advice, the warning signs I gave her, her decision and the reasons, and that I offered other options. Finally, with her agreement, I would arrange a safety net, such as a phone call that evening to check on her and a written note to bring to her next appointment. I would tell her she can change her mind at any time and I will help her go straight in.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is that new headaches plus blood pressure above 140/90 in a woman with gestational hypertension may signal preeclampsia, so exercise must be held and same-day medical assessment arranged. The professional layer is a competent adult's refusal and the confidentiality of her information against her employer.

Common Candidate Errors

Starting a pregnancy exercise program because she feels well and the back pain is the referral reason, and treating the headache as unrelated. Overstepping scope by naming preeclampsia as a diagnosis or calling the employer.

Examiner Notes

A pass requires recognizing that the blood pressure and headache override the referral question, holding exercise, arranging prompt medical assessment, giving clear warning signs and handling the refusal with respect and documentation. Candidates who focus on pelvic girdle pain fail.

Case 28 (Mock 3, case 8 of 10): Two weeks after a first shoulder dislocation

Musculoskeletal · Hospital outpatient physiotherapy department

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Describe how you would interpret Mateo's findings today, including what further assessment you would do and what you would conclude about his current status.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies reduced sensation over the lateral upper arm with poor deltoid activation as a possible axillary nerve injury. critical
  • Notes this finding was not documented at discharge, so it is new or was missed, and requires communication to the physician. critical
  • Performs a thorough neurovascular screen including sensation by dermatome and peripheral nerve, motor testing of the C5 to T1 myotomes and pulses.
  • Recognizes his age under 25 and contact sport as high risk for recurrent instability.
  • Considers associated injuries such as Bankart lesion, Hill-Sachs lesion, rotator cuff and fracture, and notes that they are suspected but not confirmed by exam alone.
  • Defers provocative tests such as apprehension and relocation, or performs them gently, at this early stage.
  • Uses WOSI score as a baseline for tracking.
  • Reasons that pain and motion limits are expected at 2 weeks and are not the priority.

Performance scale

4Identifies probable axillary nerve injury as the priority, explains its newness, performs a full neurovascular screen, links age and sport to recurrence risk, avoids provocative tests, and plans to communicate.
3Notes the sensory change and plans referral but incomplete screening or weak risk reasoning.
2Focuses on motion loss and instability tests, mentions nerve only in passing.
1Misses the neurological deficit or performs aggressive stress tests.

Model spoken answer

The most important finding today is not the range of motion. It is the combination of reduced light touch over the lateral upper arm and a deltoid that I cannot feel contracting. Together they suggest an axillary nerve injury, and the discharge note said there was no neurovascular problem, so this was either missed or developed afterwards. Axillary nerve injury is a recognized complication of anterior shoulder dislocation, especially in younger patients. Many recover, but I need the physician to know now, because the plan, timing of imaging and nerve studies, and return to sport all depend on it.

So I would build my assessment around confirming and describing that finding. I would test light touch and pinprick over the regimental badge area and compare with the right side, and map the extent so I can track it. I would test deltoid in all three parts as best I can: anterior with flexion, middle with abduction, posterior with extension, in a pain-limited position, and I would palpate the muscle belly during attempted contraction. I would also check teres minor with external rotation, since the nerve supplies both. I would screen the rest of the neurovascular status: musculocutaneous, radial, median and ulnar function with sensation and myotomes, along with radial pulse, capillary refill, colour and temperature of the hand, and compare the limbs. His elbow and hand strength are normal, so this seems isolated, but I should confirm that.

Other findings I would interpret carefully. Active motion of 80 degrees of flexion and 60 of abduction at 2 weeks is not unusual after a dislocation and sling use, and partly reflects pain and guarding. But with a weak deltoid, it may also reflect the nerve. I would not do the apprehension test, relocation test or load and shift today. They can provoke a re-dislocation and add little right now. I would, however, note his age. Under 25 and contact sport is the strongest group for recurrence, with some studies reporting a high rate. His first dislocation, a possible Bankart or Hill-Sachs lesion, or a rotator cuff injury are all possible, but I cannot confirm those clinically, and I would ask the physician about further imaging.

My conclusion is that he is in an early subacute stage after a first traumatic anterior dislocation, with a probable axillary nerve deficit that needs prompt medical review, and a high risk of recurrence. I would record his baseline WOSI score of 41 percent, measure the sensory area and any visible deltoid wasting, and communicate my findings by phone to the orthopedic team today. In the meantime I would continue gentle, safe care and avoid loading the shoulder in ways that need the deltoid.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Explain how you would manage the next few weeks of his care to protect the shoulder and the nerve while addressing what matters to Mateo.

Examiner checklist

  • Communicates the neurological finding to the orthopedic team or physician promptly, with consent. critical
  • Avoids positions that stress the anterior capsule, such as combined abduction and external rotation, and avoids forced stretching. critical
  • Uses gentle pain-limited motion and isometrics within safe ranges, and protects a weak deltoid from overload.
  • Provides sling use guidance suited to his stage and not prolonged immobilization beyond what the physician advises.
  • Gives clear advice not to return to rugby in four weeks and explains why. critical
  • Discusses early referral to an orthopedic shoulder surgeon given his age and sport, framed as a choice.
  • Teaches him to monitor numbness, pulses, colour and warning signs of re-dislocation, and what to do if one occurs.
  • Elicits his goals and uses shared decision-making about activity and school.

Performance scale

4Communicates the nerve finding, specifies positions and loads to avoid, gives staged safe rehabilitation, gives a clear no on rugby with reasons, discusses surgical referral as a choice, and teaches warning signs.
3Safe plan with precautions and rugby advice, but incomplete on communication, nerve implications or shared decisions.
2Generic shoulder exercises without precautions or timeline.
1Clears rugby, applies aggressive stretching or strengthening, or ignores the neurological finding.

Model spoken answer

My first step is to let the orthopedic team know about the sensory change and deltoid weakness today. I would phone, explain what I found and ask whether they want him seen sooner, or want nerve studies or imaging arranged. I would explain what I found and ask Mateo for his agreement to share it with the orthopedic team today, then phone. This does not change how kindly I treat him, but it does change what I can safely ask the shoulder to do.

For protection of the shoulder, I would avoid the position that puts the anterior capsule at risk, which is abduction combined with external rotation, like throwing or reaching behind the head. I would avoid forced stretching and passive pushing into end range. For the first weeks I would stay with gentle, pain-limited movement: pendulums only if tolerated, elbow, wrist and hand movement every day to prevent stiffness and swelling, scapular setting, and isometric rotator cuff work in neutral with the arm by his side. I would keep deltoid loading very light until I know the state of the nerve, because pushing a weak deltoid into big efforts leads to poor movement patterns and compensation. If the deltoid shows signs of recovery, I would progress to assisted elevation in the scapular plane, for example table slides, and later to light resisted work. For the sling, I would follow the physician's instruction, but in general a sling is for comfort and early protection, and I would encourage him to take it off to move his elbow and hand several times daily and when seated at his desk.

I need to be honest about rugby. He will not be ready in four weeks. A joint that recently dislocated, with a possible nerve injury and no strength or control yet, would be at high risk of dislocating again and of damaging the nerve or other structures. I would say that directly, and also explain what I can do: get him moving, keep his fitness up with lower body and cardio work that does not stress the shoulder, and let him help set the criteria for return, such as full motion, symmetrical strength, confidence, and a decision from the surgeon.

I would raise the idea of seeing an orthopedic shoulder surgeon early. In young contact athletes, surgical stabilization is often discussed after a first dislocation because recurrence is common. I would not decide for him. I would explain the choices, which are rehabilitation first or early surgery, with the risks and benefits of each, and encourage him to ask the surgeon about them.

As a safety net, I would teach him to tell me or the clinic promptly if numbness spreads, his hand becomes cold, pale or weak, he feels the shoulder slip, or pain worsens suddenly. I would ask what matters most to him, maybe school, work or sport, and make the plan around that.

Question 3: Communication

Mateo asks you to explain what his friend called the surgery thing, and his father keeps answering for him. Describe how you would communicate with them.

Examiner checklist

  • Speaks directly to Mateo as the patient and invites his own understanding and preferences. critical
  • Asks Mateo privately or openly whether he wants an interpreter or his father to translate, and offers a professional interpreter. critical
  • Uses plain language and avoids jargon such as Bankart, labrum or capsule without simple explanation.
  • Explains recurrence risk and surgical stabilization in balanced terms, covering benefits and risks.
  • Uses teach-back and checks understanding rather than accepting yes. critical
  • Uses visuals or a model and gives written information in a language he prefers.
  • Acknowledges his anxiety and responds to emotion with empathy.
  • Includes his father respectfully while maintaining Mateo's privacy and consent.

Performance scale

4Centres Mateo, offers interpreter and explores language preference, explains surgery and recurrence in plain balanced terms with visuals, uses teach-back, handles anxiety and the father's role respectfully.
3Plain language and teach-back present but interpreter or role of the father not addressed.
2Explains with jargon, talks mostly to the father, or gives one-sided information.
1Pressures toward surgery or rehabilitation, ignores language barrier, or dismisses concerns.

Model spoken answer

I would begin by setting up the conversation so that Mateo is at its center. I would greet both of them and then turn to Mateo, and say that I want to hear things from him, and that his father is welcome to help. I would ask him in a warm, non-pressuring way: Which language would you like to use for the health parts of today? Would you like a professional interpreter, or are you comfortable with me and your father helping? Many people are fluent in everyday English but find medical terms hard, and saying yes to a clinician does not always mean they understood. I would make clear that using an interpreter is normal, free and confidential, and it would let his father be a father instead of an interpreter. If Mateo prefers his father to help, I would respect that, and I would still check his understanding directly.

For the explanation, I would start by asking what he already knows from his friend and what worries him, because that tells me where to start. Then I would use plain words and a shoulder model or a simple drawing. I might say: The shoulder is like a golf ball sitting on a tee. When it came out the front, the soft rim of the socket, the tee, can tear, and the ball can get a small dent. After a first dislocation, especially in young men who play contact sports, the shoulder pops out again often, and each time there is more damage. Surgery is an operation to repair the rim and tighten the front so it is less likely to come out. Some people do very well with physiotherapy only, others have repeat dislocations and then choose surgery. Nobody can know ahead of time which way it will go, and I would not pressure him either way. I would describe benefits and risks of both options at a level he can follow: surgery lowers the chance of re-dislocation but involves anesthesia, recovery of several months and small risks of stiffness or infection, while rehabilitation alone avoids surgery but has a higher chance of the shoulder coming out again. I would tell him a surgeon is the right person to advise, and I can help with the referral.

I would use teach-back: Just so I know I explained it clearly, can you tell me in your own words what the choices are? If he repeats only yes, I would try again with a different explanation, not repeat the same one louder. I would give him a short written summary in Spanish if he wants it, and a diagram.

I would acknowledge his worry about the final games: it sounds like rugby matters a lot to you, and I want to help you get back to it safely. I would also include his father: I would ask him whether he has questions, and thank him for his support, while pointing out gently that Mateo decides about his own care. I would also tell them they can call the clinic with questions at any time.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

A new lateral upper arm sensory loss with a weak deltoid suggests an axillary nerve injury not noted at discharge. The candidate must find it, tell the physician, and avoid loading it. A communication layer is the risk of the father answering for the patient and Mateo's yes not meaning understanding.

Common Candidate Errors

Concentrating on range of motion and instability tests and missing the nerve deficit, or allowing rugby return on a calendar. Using the father as interpreter without asking Mateo and accepting yes as understanding.

Examiner Notes

Passes find and escalate the axillary nerve finding, give specific position precautions, say no to rugby with reasons, and communicate in plain language with an interpreter option. Failures treat this as a routine post-dislocation protocol.

Case 29 (Mock 3, case 9 of 10): Exercise rehabilitation for chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

Cardiovascular-Respiratory · Hospital outpatient cardiac rehabilitation program

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the goals and the plan of care you would propose for Walter over the 12 week program, including how you would choose exercise intensity and measure progress.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets person-centred goals such as walking tolerance, ability to attend family events, symptom control, and self-management.
  • Includes baseline and repeat outcome measures such as six minute walk test, symptom scale, and NYHA class.
  • Chooses low to moderate intensity using RPE (about 11 to 13 on the Borg 6 to 20 scale) and talk test, not a heart rate target alone, as beta blockade limits heart rate. critical
  • Plans a longer warm-up and cool-down and gradual progression from short intervals with rest to continuous exercise.
  • Adds light resistance training and balance work as tolerated.
  • Specifies monitoring: weight, blood pressure, symptoms, SpO2, and rhythm if available, at each session. critical
  • Includes education on daily weights, symptom diary, fluid and sodium advice per team, and medication adherence.
  • States reassessment triggers for holding or modifying exercise, such as weight gain or worsening symptoms. critical
  • Confirms the ICD detection rate with the device clinic and keeps exercise heart rate at least 10 to 20 beats per minute below it.

Performance scale

4Person-centred measurable goals, outcome measures, intensity by RPE with beta-blocker rationale, progression, monitoring, education and clear modification triggers.
3Sound exercise plan and measures but intensity rationale or monitoring and triggers are incomplete.
2Generic exercise prescription based on age-predicted heart rate or without monitoring.
1Prescribes high intensity or ignores heart failure specific safety.

Model spoken answer

My goals would come from Walter, so I would begin by asking what he most wants to do. It sounds like attending family events without rushing, and walking farther. I would turn those into measurable goals over 12 weeks: for example to walk 400 metres on level ground without stopping, to climb one flight of stairs, to improve his six minute walk distance from 240 by a clinically meaningful amount such as 30 metres or more, to reduce symptoms, and to be able to manage his weights and medications himself.

For outcome measures, I would use the six minute walk test, repeated at 6 and 12 weeks if he is stable, a symptom scale such as a Borg dyspnea rating, a heart failure quality of life questionnaire, and a functional test like the sit to stand. I would track NYHA class by history.

Intensity is the key decision. Because he takes bisoprolol, his heart rate response is blunted, so I would not prescribe by a percentage of maximum heart rate. I would prescribe by perceived exertion, aiming for about 11 to 13 on the Borg 6 to 20 scale, which is fairly light to somewhat hard, and use the talk test, where he can speak in short sentences. I would begin with short bouts of 3 to 5 minutes of walking or stationary cycling with equal or longer rests, accumulating 10 to 15 minutes in total, with a longer warm-up and cool-down of 5 to 10 minutes each to avoid sudden changes in blood pressure, especially given his drop on standing. Over several weeks I would increase duration first and then intensity, aiming for 20 to 30 minutes of continuous activity three times a week, along with daily walking at home. Once he is stable I would add light resistance exercise, for example sit to stand and light weights, with breathing throughout and no breath holding, and balance training, since he is dizzy and at risk of falls.

Because Walter has an ICD, I would confirm its detection rate with the device clinic and keep his exercise heart rate at least 10 to 20 beats per minute below it. At each visit I would check weight against his dry weight, blood pressure sitting and standing, heart rate, SpO2, symptoms such as breathlessness, orthopnea and swelling, and rhythm if monitoring is available. I would compare it to rules about when to hold exercise, such as a weight gain of more than about 2 kg over 3 days, worsening swelling or breathlessness, a drop in blood pressure with symptoms, or new chest pain or palpitations.

Education is part of the plan: daily morning weights on the same scale, a diary of symptoms and weights, the medications he takes and why, what the team has advised for sodium and fluids, and how to pace activity. I would use teach-back with Walter and his wife. I would reassess every few weeks and adjust, and I would talk with the heart failure team about any changes.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Walter wants to start the first session today. Explain your decision and how you would involve Walter and his wife in the plan for today.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes the weight gain of about 2 kg in 3 days, extra pillow and stopped diuretic as signs of possible decompensation.
  • Holds the exercise session today and explains why in plain words. critical
  • Contacts the heart failure clinic or responsible physician the same day for review, with consent. critical
  • Checks the clinic scale against the home scale and does not dismiss his concern, and does not assume the clinic scale is wrong.
  • Addresses orthostatic drop and dizziness, including fall prevention advice.
  • Gives warning signs requiring emergency care, such as chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting, two or more ICD shocks or a shock with symptoms, and a same-day clinic call for a single shock when well. critical
  • Explores his reasons for skipping the diuretic and plans practical strategies with the team.
  • Offers a safe alternative today such as education, and rebooks promptly.

Performance scale

4Recognizes decompensation signs, holds exercise, contacts team same day, gives clear emergency and call-the-clinic signs, respects his scale concern and explores the missed diuretic without judgement.
3Holds exercise and refers but warning signs, orthostatic issue or collaboration are incomplete.
2Modifies to light exercise or continues with monitoring only.
1Proceeds with the full session, tells him to restart or stop medications, or dismisses weight gain.

Model spoken answer

I would not run an exercise session today, and I would explain it carefully so that Walter does not feel turned away. What I see together is a weight about 2 kilograms above his dry weight in three days, a second pillow at night, a bit more swelling, less energy, and he stopped his water pill over the weekend. In heart failure, those are the classic signs that fluid may be building up and the heart is not coping. A rise of around 2 kilograms in three days is the usual trigger for heart failure patients to call their team. Exercise now could worsen his breathlessness, and with an ejection fraction of 30 percent and an ICD, I would rather he be reviewed first. I would say that this is a pause to protect him, not a refusal to help.

He thinks our scale is wrong. I would take that seriously. I would recheck his weight on a second scale, with light clothing and no shoes, and I would ask him to tell me what his home reading was, when he weighs and what he wears. If the numbers differ, I would still contact the team, because the swelling, pillows and missed medication tell the same story. I would not dismiss him.

I would then call the heart failure clinic or his cardiologist the same day, with Walter's permission, give them the readings, the symptoms and the missed diuretic, and ask whether he should be seen today. If I cannot reach anyone, I would advise him to go to the emergency department or call his family doctor urgently, depending on his symptoms. I would pass on that he had dizziness on standing as well, since his pressure fell by only 8 over 4 on standing, below the usual 20 over 10 criterion for orthostatic hypotension, yet he is symptomatic, which may relate to his heart failure medications and is another reason for a physician to review. I would not tell him what to do about his medications, because that is the prescriber's decision. For the dizziness, I would suggest rising slowly, sitting at the edge first and holding a support.

I would give Walter and his wife clear warning signs. Call 911 for chest pain, severe breathlessness at rest, fainting, two or more ICD shocks, or a shock with symptoms such as feeling unwell or a fast irregular heartbeat. Call the clinic the same day for a single shock when he feels well, increased swelling, needing more pillows, or further weight gain. I would ask them to repeat these back.

I would also ask about the diuretic. It is common to skip it before an outing because of the urgency. Rather than judging, I would ask what makes it hard, and tell the team so they can adjust timing, which may solve it. His wife can help with a simple chart for weights and medications. Today I can use the visit for teaching, such as how to take daily weights, and for planning, and I would rebook for as soon as the team says it is safe, ideally within days.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Walter asks whether you can tell him to stop the medication that makes him dizzy, and his wife asks to see his chart. Discuss your professional responsibilities.

Examiner checklist

  • States that advising on starting, stopping or changing medication is outside physiotherapy scope and belongs to the prescriber. critical
  • Communicates the dizziness and orthostatic readings to the physician or pharmacist in writing or by phone.
  • Tells Walter not to stop medications on his own and why, and gives a plan to reach the team quickly. critical
  • Requires Walter's consent before sharing chart information with his wife, and asks what he wants her to know. critical
  • Explains how to access records through the proper process and respects his right of access.
  • Documents findings, advice, referral and conversations accurately and promptly.
  • Recognizes his wife's role as a support and involves her with his permission in education.
  • Keeps communication within the interprofessional team clear about who is responsible for follow-up.

Performance scale

4States medication scope boundary, advises against self-stopping, escalates findings to prescriber, handles wife's request through consent and record access rules, and documents.
3Recognizes scope and consent but does not communicate with the team or explain access to records.
2Gives general advice on medications or shares chart details with the wife without consent.
1Tells him to stop the medication, shares records freely, or fails to document.

Model spoken answer

Two requests, two different professional issues. I will deal with the medication first. Deciding whether Walter should stop a medication is a prescribing decision, outside the scope of physiotherapy. I can observe and measure the effects, such as his dizziness on standing and the fall in blood pressure from 104 over 64 to 96 over 60, and I should report those, but I cannot tell him to stop or change anything. I would say that clearly and kindly: I know the dizziness is annoying and scary, and I take it seriously. I am not the right person to decide about the medications, but I will make sure the right person hears about it today. I would also tell him not to stop any heart medication on his own. Stopping drugs such as the beta blocker or ramipril suddenly can make heart failure worse, and the doctor may be able to adjust the dose or timing. I would link this to what he already did with the water pill, without blaming him, and say that this is exactly the kind of thing the team wants to hear about.

Then I would act. I would call or send a written message to his cardiologist or heart failure nurse, or his family doctor or pharmacist, whoever is responsible, with the readings, when the dizziness occurs, the missed diuretic, the weight gain and the swelling. I would write down who I spoke to and what they said, and I would tell Walter what to expect. If the response is delayed, I would follow up rather than assume it is dealt with. A pharmacist review of his medications could also help, and I could suggest that to him.

Now his wife's request. His health information belongs to him. His wife is clearly an important support, and she is welcome in sessions, but I need Walter's permission before showing her his chart or discussing details outside the room. So I would ask him privately or in front of her, depending on his preference: How much would you like your wife to know and see? Some people are happy to share everything. If he agrees, I would document his consent and what is covered. If he prefers that I share only certain things, I would respect that. A patient also has the right to see his own record, so I would explain how to request a copy from the hospital's health records department under the privacy rules, and I would not simply hand over my notes to someone else.

I would document everything accurately and promptly, including the objective findings, my education about warning signs, the advice that he should not stop his medications, the communication with the team, and his consent decisions. Finally, I would be clear with the team about who is following up, so that Walter is not left waiting.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is early decompensated heart failure: weight gain of about 2 kg in 3 days, an extra pillow, edema and a skipped diuretic. Exercise must be held and the team contacted the same day. The professional layer is medication advice being outside scope and consent before sharing information with the wife.

Common Candidate Errors

Starting the exercise session at low intensity because he wants to, or using an age-predicted heart rate target despite a beta blocker. Telling him to stop the dizziness-causing medication, or showing the chart to his wife.

Examiner Notes

A pass sets person-centred goals with RPE-based intensity, recognizes the decompensation signs, holds the session and escalates the same day, and respects scope and consent. Candidates who give a generic cardiac rehabilitation prescription fail.

Case 30 (Mock 3, case 10 of 10): Early mobilization after a left hemisphere stroke in inpatient rehabilitation

Neurological · Inpatient stroke rehabilitation unit in a regional hospital

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Describe how you would approach your assessment today, including which findings you would prioritize and how you would interpret them for planning rehabilitation.

Examiner checklist

  • Examines the right calf for swelling, warmth, tenderness, redness, and compares circumference, because of the wife's report. critical
  • Recognizes immobility, stroke and age as risk factors for deep vein thrombosis and that anticoagulation does not exclude it. critical
  • Checks vital signs and asks about chest pain, breathlessness, or cough as screening for pulmonary embolism. critical
  • Interprets motor findings: distal weakness greater than proximal (ankle dorsiflexion and distal arm 1 out of 5), mild spasticity, foot drop, and expected recovery patterns.
  • Interprets Berg score of 18 as high fall risk and need for assisted transfers and walking.
  • Identifies the glenohumeral subluxation and its implications for handling and pain.
  • Chooses communication methods for aphasia such as short instructions, gestures and yes/no questions, and checks comprehension.
  • Plans additional measures such as 10 metre walk, sit to stand, cognitive and neglect screening, and orthostatic blood pressure.

Performance scale

4Prioritizes DVT and PE screening before mobilization, interprets motor, balance and shoulder findings, adapts for aphasia, and plans appropriate measures.
3Notes the calf concern but screening incomplete, or interprets findings without plan implications.
2Focuses on motor and balance without addressing the calf report.
1Ignores the calf or proposes massage or standing before assessment.

Model spoken answer

My first priority is the report from his wife about the right leg, because it might change everything else I do today. Harold has several strong risk factors for a deep vein thrombosis: a recent stroke, a paralysed leg, reduced mobility, and age. His anticoagulant lowers the risk, but it does not remove it, and the wife's observations of a bigger leg and wincing on touch are exactly what I need to take seriously. So before any standing practice I would look at the leg. I would compare both calves and thighs for swelling, warmth, redness, visible veins, and tenderness along the calf, and measure circumference 10 centimetres below the tibial tuberosity on both sides. I would not massage the calf or do any vigorous passive stretching. Physical examination alone cannot rule a DVT in or out, so a positive or even equivocal finding would be sent for a medical assessment rather than interpreted by me. I would also ask about chest pain, shortness of breath, cough or a fast heart rate, and check his heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. His atrial fibrillation makes a pulse irregular, so I would pay attention to rate and symptoms.

If the leg looks normal, I would continue the rest of the assessment but with caution. For motor findings, he has right distal weakness greater than proximal: the arm is 2 out of 5 proximally and 1 out of 5 distally, and ankle dorsiflexion is 1 out of 5 against 3 out of 5 at the hip and knee, with increased tone in the elbow flexors. The fair hip and knee strength is helpful for standing and walking, but the foot drop needs an ankle foot orthosis or similar to manage the foot drop. A Berg score of 18 out of 56 puts him at high risk of falls, so I would plan for hands-on assistance with transfers and walking, and good footwear and a gait belt. The palpable gap at the shoulder suggests glenohumeral subluxation, which is common with a flaccid arm. I would avoid pulling on the arm during transfers, support the arm on a table or tray when sitting, and educate the nursing team and his wife.

Communication matters because of his aphasia. I would use short, clear sentences, gestures and demonstration, check that he has understood with yes or no questions or by asking him to show me, and allow time for his responses. I would screen for neglect and cognition as well, because they affect safety.

Additional measures include sit to stand tests, a 10 metre walk test when it is safe, orthostatic blood pressure, and the Berg for tracking. My plan would be that if the calf examination is positive or I am uncertain, no standing or walking happens until a physician has reviewed him, otherwise I proceed with a graded, assisted program.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

On examination, the right calf is 3 cm larger than the left, warm and tender. Harold wants to keep practising standing because he is determined to go home. Explain what you would do and how you would involve him.

Examiner checklist

  • Stops standing, walking and vigorous leg exercise and keeps him at rest in a safe position pending medical review. critical
  • Notifies the physician or nurse in charge immediately, using clear information such as SBAR. critical
  • Does not massage or rub the calf.
  • Monitors for pulmonary embolism signs and tells nursing staff what to watch for. critical
  • Explains the situation to Harold and his wife using aphasia-friendly communication and obtains his understanding and assent.
  • Acknowledges his motivation and describes what can continue safely, such as upper body, trunk and seated activities as medically allowed.
  • Gives instructions for the team about positioning, arm support and fall prevention in the meantime.
  • Documents the findings, communication and the activity plan.

Performance scale

4Stops mobilization, escalates with a structured handoff, tells staff PE warning signs, uses aphasia-friendly explanation, offers safe alternatives and documents.
3Stops mobilization and informs physician but incomplete on PE monitoring, communication or alternatives.
2Reduces activity or continues light leg exercise while waiting.
1Proceeds with standing or massage, delays reporting, or leaves without explanation.

Model spoken answer

Now that the right calf is 3 centimetres bigger than the left, warm and tender, with his risk factors, I would treat this as a possible deep vein thrombosis until a physician says otherwise. A clot can break loose and travel to the lungs, and exercise like standing and walking could make that more likely. So I would stop any standing, walking and vigorous leg exercise now. I would keep Harold resting in a comfortable position in bed or chair, with the leg supported, and I would not massage or rub the calf.

I would tell the physician and the nurse in charge right away, in person or by phone, not by leaving a note. I would use a clear structure. Situation: Mr. Beaulieu has a swollen, warm, tender right calf, 3 centimetres larger than the left. Background: three weeks post left MCA stroke, atrial fibrillation on an anticoagulant, reduced mobility, catheter removed two days ago. Assessment: I am concerned about a possible DVT, and I have stopped mobilization. Request: please review him today and consider a diagnostic ultrasound and decide on the activity plan. I would ask for clear instructions about activity until they decide.

I would also tell the nurse what to look for, so that the whole team is watching for a pulmonary embolism: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, a fast heart rate, coughing blood, low oxygen saturation, or a sudden change in his condition. If any of those happen, the team should activate the emergency response right away.
