For Harold, I would explain what I found and why we are pausing. Because he has aphasia, I would use short sentences, a calm voice, a drawing of a leg and a vein, and gestures. I would say something like: Your leg is swollen and sore. It may be a blood clot. We stop walking for now. The doctor will check. Then I would check that he understands by asking him to point to the leg that is the concern, and asking yes or no questions. I would include his wife, who noticed the swelling, and thank her, since it was her observation that mattered.

I know how determined he is to go home, so I would not leave him with only a no. I would tell him that his goal is still the goal, and that this pause is to keep him safe. I would offer what is safe, with the physician's agreement: seated trunk exercises, work on the left arm, positioning, and arm support for the right shoulder, plus ankle pumps on the left. I would not do ankle pumps on the right until a clot is excluded. Meanwhile I would ask the team to protect his shoulder and prevent falls, with a bed alarm if needed.

I would document my findings, who I contacted and when, what the physician ordered, my advice to staff, and my talk with Harold and his wife. I would ask when the result is expected, and plan to reassess as soon as he is cleared.

Question 3: Practice Management

The assistant asks to take Harold for standing and walking at 10 o'clock because your afternoon is full. Discuss how you would manage delegation, your caseload and your documentation.

Examiner checklist

  • Does not delegate standing and walking to the assistant until Harold's medical status is cleared and his condition is stable and predictable. critical
  • Explains that delegation depends on the patient's complexity, the assistant's training, and supervision, and that the physiotherapist remains accountable. critical
  • Gives the assistant a clear, specific plan for the day and tasks she can safely do, such as positioning, upper body or seated activity if cleared.
  • Ensures the assistant knows what to watch for and when to stop and call.
  • Reprioritizes the caseload by acuity, and asks the unit lead for help or redistribution when workload is unsafe.
  • Communicates the change in plan to nursing, the team and the wife, and updates the care plan visible at the bedside.
  • Documents the clinical reasoning, delegation decisions and communications accurately and on time. critical
  • Addresses the equipment and infection control needs such as gait belt, orthosis cleaning and shared equipment.

Performance scale

4Declines delegation with clear reasoning on accountability, gives assistant specific safe tasks and stop criteria, re-prioritizes caseload and escalates workload, updates team and documents fully.
3Declines delegation and documents but weak on caseload management or assistant instructions.
2Delegates with general instructions or ignores workload constraints.
1Delegates walking while the leg is unresolved or fails to document.

Model spoken answer

I would not ask the assistant to take Harold for standing and walking this morning. Delegation is a decision I make as the physiotherapist, and it depends on three things: how stable and predictable the patient is, what the assistant has been trained to do, and what supervision is available. Harold is currently not stable and predictable. He may have a deep vein thrombosis, the physician has not reviewed him, and he has a high fall risk and a fragile right shoulder. Sending an assistant to walk him would put both of them at risk. The fact that another assistant did it with him last week does not change this, because his condition has changed. And although I am busy, I remain accountable for the plan even when I delegate, so I cannot hand over a decision I have not made.

I would explain this to her respectfully, because she is trying to help. I would thank her for asking, and say: Mr. Beaulieu has a new concern in his leg, so he is on hold for standing and walking until the physician reviews him. I would tell her what she can do. If the physician agrees, she could help with positioning, seated upper body exercises with the left arm, supported sitting practice, or ankle pumps on the left, using written instructions. I would tell her exactly what to watch for and when to stop and call me or the nurse, including sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, a change in alertness, or pain in the leg. I would make sure the plan is in his chart and at the bedside, so everyone gives the same message, and I would check in with her at an agreed time.

About my caseload: I have 14 patients and this change means I must re-prioritize. I would rank by acuity and risk. Harold needs the urgent handoff and a reassessment as soon as he is cleared. I would also see patients who are new, unstable or due for discharge decisions, and cluster stable patients' tasks for the assistant within her role. If I cannot safely cover my afternoon, I would tell the unit lead or my manager early, and ask for help from the other physiotherapist or to adjust the schedule, instead of cutting corners. I would not allow workload to pressure me into delegating tasks I should do myself.

Communication with the team: I would let nursing and the other staff know that Harold is not for standing practice, and ask them to keep the same restrictions. I would also update his wife, and explain that her observation helped.

Documentation: I would write the assessment findings, the circumference, my reasoning for stopping mobilization, who I notified and their response, the delegation decision and instructions to the assistant, and my reassessment plan. I would also note equipment needs when he restarts, such as a gait belt, a properly fitted ankle foot orthosis, and cleaning of shared equipment between patients according to infection prevention policy.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The wife's report of a larger, tender right leg in a stroke patient with immobility is a possible DVT that must be examined and escalated before any standing practice. A second issue is delegating walking to an assistant while the patient's status is unresolved and workload pressure is high; the physiotherapist stays accountable.

Common Candidate Errors

Starting the planned standing program without examining the calf, or massaging the leg. Delegating to the assistant because the schedule is full and a colleague did it before.

Examiner Notes

Passing candidates act on the wife's observation, examine the calf, stop mobilization, escalate with clear communication and monitor for pulmonary embolism, then apply delegation principles correctly. Failing candidates treat the case as routine stroke rehabilitation.

Mock 4

Case 31 (Mock 4, case 1 of 10): Lateral ankle sprain in a rotating-shift nurse

Musculoskeletal · Walk-in physiotherapy clinic in a mid-sized Ontario city, late afternoon

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the physiotherapy plan of care you would develop with Amara for the next six weeks. Include your goals, the main interventions and how you would progress them, how you would measure change, and what would prompt you to modify the plan.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets a functional goal tied to her work: safely tolerating a full 12-hour shift of standing and walking, with a stated timeframe.
  • Starts with early protected weight bearing as tolerated, weaning from crutches and boot as pain and gait allow.
  • Addresses swelling with elevation, then compression and active ankle pumping once the calf is cleared, rather than prolonged rest.
  • Restores dorsiflexion range early with pain-limited mobilization and calf and ankle movement.
  • Progresses strengthening of peroneals and the whole lower limb from isometric to resisted to functional loading, only after the calf is medically cleared.
  • Includes balance and proprioceptive training with progression from stable to unstable surfaces and eyes closed. critical
  • Names outcome measures such as the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure, pain scale, dorsiflexion range, girth and gait quality, with reassessment points.
  • Proposes a graded return to shift work, such as shorter or lighter duties first, with supportive footwear or a lace-up brace or taping.
  • Gives self-management and home exercise dosage (sets, repetitions, frequency) and a plan for the eight covered visits.
  • States triggers to modify the plan: stalled range or strength, recurrent giving way, escalating swelling or pain, or new findings requiring other care. critical

Performance scale

4Gives phased goals tied to a 12-hour shift, with early loading, range, strength, balance, dosage, outcome measures, graded return and clear triggers to modify, all justified for a grade 2 sprain.
3Covers most phases and a work goal with reasonable interventions but lacks dosage, progression criteria or modification triggers.
2Lists generic ankle exercises or rest and ice with little progression, measurement or link to her job.
1Recommends prolonged immobilization or full duty at once, or ignores function and measurement entirely.

Model spoken answer

My plan has one aim: get Amara through a full 12-hour shift on her feet, confidently and without re-injury, in about six weeks, with a first check at two weeks. I will agree those goals with her, because her own priority is work.

First, the early phase, roughly the first two weeks. This is a grade 2 sprain, so the ligament is partly torn and needs load that is protective but not absent. The whole plan is conditional on one thing: her right calf must be medically assessed and a deep vein clot excluded first, which I explain in my next answer. Until then I offer only elevation and protected walking, and I wean her off the crutches and boot as gait allows, aiming for a normal heel-to-toe pattern in the clinic first. Once the calf is cleared, I add a compression sleeve and active ankle pumps, since movement drives fluid out better than rest does. After clearance I will start pain-limited dorsiflexion work and gentle joint mobilization, because her five degrees of dorsiflexion will otherwise distort her gait. Calf stretching, strengthening and progression all wait for that medical clearance.

Second, the strengthening phase, roughly weeks two to four, starting only once the calf is cleared. I will start with isometric peroneal and ankle strength, move to resisted eversion with a band, then heel raises and single-leg work. I will include hip and knee strength too, since nurses lose general conditioning quickly when off their feet.

Third, balance and control, which is the part that most reduces repeat sprains. We start with single-leg stance on a firm floor, add eyes closed, then foam, then reaching and hopping tasks. I will give her a home program of about ten to fifteen minutes, once or twice daily, written with sets and repetitions.

Fourth, return to work. I will suggest a graded plan: shorter shifts or lighter duties first if her employer can accommodate that, supportive footwear, and a lace-up brace or taping for the first weeks back. I will rehearse her actual tasks, such as walking fast, turning, and standing for long periods.

I will measure progress with the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure, starting at 54 percent, plus pain, dorsiflexion range, figure-of-eight girth and single-leg balance time, and I will repeat them at visits two, four and six. I have eight funded visits, so I will front-load them in the first two weeks, then space them out.

I will change the plan if range or strength stalls, if she reports the ankle giving way, if swelling or pain rises as load rises, or if any new finding changes my impression. In those cases I will reassess, adjust load, or refer to her physician for further assessment.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss the safety considerations you would address with Amara before she leaves the clinic today, and explain how you would involve her in the decisions that follow.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes the calf tenderness and 2 cm girth difference as a possible deep vein thrombosis rather than part of the ankle sprain. critical
  • Links risk factors: recent reduced mobility, immobilization in a boot, and the combined oral contraceptive.
  • Stops or defers calf stretching, massage and vigorous exercise until the possibility is excluded. critical
  • Arranges same-day medical assessment, such as an emergency department or urgent care visit, rather than waiting for the next appointment.
  • Explains in plain language why she is being sent and what the physician is likely to do, such as a clinical risk score and ultrasound.
  • Gives warning signs of pulmonary embolism: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing blood, racing heart, and says to call 911. critical
  • Seeks Amara's consent to the plan and to any communication of her findings to the physician.
  • Discusses transport so she does not drive herself if unwell or without a plan, and offers a phone call to the facility.
  • Documents findings, the advice given, her response and who was informed.
  • Addresses her work guilt and respects her decision-making, offering choices about how to get assessed rather than imposing them.

Performance scale

4Identifies the calf findings and risk factors as a possible clot, stops calf loading, arranges same-day medical care, gives red-flag advice and shares decisions respectfully with her.
3Refers appropriately and gives advice but is vague about risk factors, urgency or warning signs.
2Mentions seeing a doctor eventually or monitoring the calf, with no urgency, no loading restriction or no explanation.
1Dismisses the calf as part of the sprain, continues calf stretching or massage, or lets her leave without advice.

Model spoken answer

Before Amara leaves, my main safety concern is her right calf, not the ankle. She has tenderness over the posterior-medial belly of the calf and it measures 2 cm larger than the other side. She has also spent four days mostly sitting with the leg up, she wears a walking boot, and she takes a combined oral contraceptive. Together, those are risk factors for a blood clot in a deep vein. I cannot call it a clot, and I should not call it a stretched muscle either. The ankle sprain can explain swelling near the joint, but not tenderness in the calf belly, so I will treat this as needing medical assessment today.

I would stop what I was planning to do in the calf. No stretching, no massage and no strong calf exercise until a physician has had a look, because those could dislodge a clot if one is present.

Next I talk to her. I will say it plainly: your ankle sprain looks like it is healing, but I am concerned about your calf, and the safest thing is to have a doctor check it today. I will explain that the usual approach is a short clinical assessment and often an ultrasound of the leg veins, and that most people sent for this turn out to be fine. That helps her avoid panic and also avoid dismissing it.

I will give her options and let her choose among them: the closest emergency department, an urgent care that offers same-day ultrasound, or a call to her family doctor for a same-day slot. I will ask what works with her transportation, since she should not be left to decide that alone if she feels unwell. I will offer to phone ahead, with her permission, and to send a short written note describing my findings.

I also give her warning signs. If she develops sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing, coughing up blood, a racing heart or fainting, she should call 911 instead of driving. I will make sure she can repeat these back to me.

Finally, she is worried about missing work. I will acknowledge that, say that her health comes first, and tell her I will help with documentation so she does not feel she has failed her unit. I will record my findings, what I advised, her decision and who I contacted, and I will follow up by phone tomorrow with her consent.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Later that day, the manager of Amara's hospital unit telephones the clinic and asks whether Amara can work her scheduled 12-hour shift on Thursday. Describe how you will respond and which professional responsibilities arise.

Examiner checklist

  • Does not release any health information to the manager without Amara's informed consent. critical
  • Explains that being a friend or colleague of the client does not change confidentiality obligations.
  • Offers to contact Amara and ask whether she wants any information shared, and what exactly.
  • If she consents, limits disclosure to functional information, such as restrictions, not diagnosis or investigation results. critical
  • Declines to write a fit-for-full-duty note while the calf concern is unresolved and the ankle is not yet at work-level function. critical
  • Suggests that fitness for duty be based on objective findings and a graded plan, possibly with occupational health.
  • Documents the call, what was said and the client's decision.
  • Respects the regulator's standards on honest, accurate reporting and avoiding pressure from employers or friends.
  • Acknowledges the staffing pressure empathically while keeping the decision with Amara and her physician.

Performance scale

4Protects confidentiality, seeks consent and limits disclosure to function, refuses an unsupported fitness note, explains the reasoning and documents.
3Protects confidentiality and declines the note but is thin on consent scope, documentation or regulator standards.
2Is vague about confidentiality or gives partial information without consent, or declines without reasoning.
1Discloses diagnosis or attendance to the manager without consent or signs a full-duty note.

Model spoken answer

My first duty on that phone call is confidentiality. Amara has not told me I may speak to her manager. The fact that the manager is a friend of hers, or a colleague of other health professionals, does not matter. Under provincial health privacy legislation and my regulator's standards, information about a client's attendance, diagnosis or ability to work belongs to her unless she gives informed consent for me to share it. So I would say something like: I understand you are short-staffed and I appreciate your call, but I am not able to confirm whether she is a client here or share anything without her permission. I would then offer to pass on the request to her.

I would phone Amara and ask whether she wants me to share anything, and if so what and with whom. If she agrees, I would share only what is needed for the work decision, which is her functional restrictions and the expected time frame, not her diagnosis, her test results or the medical concern from today. I would document the consent, what she agreed to and what I said.

The second responsibility is honesty about fitness for work. Amara asked me for a note saying she is fit for regular duties. I cannot sign that. Her dorsiflexion is five degrees, her anterior drawer is positive, she still has swelling and pain of 5 out of 10 on walking, and the calf concern is unresolved. A twelve-hour shift on her feet is a heavy load for an ankle at this stage and, if there were a clot, the risk would be more serious. My regulator expects me to base statements on objective findings and to resist pressure from friends or employers. I would instead offer a note describing temporary restrictions only, if she consents, and suggest that her physician or occupational health decide on a return date once the calf is cleared.

Third, I should be sensitive to the system pressure. I would acknowledge the staffing strain to Amara without letting it direct her decision, and I would give her a graded return-to-work plan to take to her manager if she chooses.

Last, I document the call, the consent discussion and the note I did or did not issue, and I let the clinic's administrator know in case further calls arrive, so the same answer is given every time.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is a possible deep vein thrombosis: calf tenderness and girth difference with immobility, a boot and a combined oral contraceptive, hidden among ordinary sprain findings. A competent candidate recognizes it before any calf loading, arranges same-day medical assessment and gives red-flag advice. A second issue is the friend-manager call and the request for a fit-for-duty note, which tests confidentiality and honest reporting.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates describe an excellent ankle rehabilitation plan and never mention the calf, or they dismiss the calf as a bruise. In question 3 many answer the manager's question informally because the manager is a friend, or agree to write a full-duty note to be helpful.

Examiner Notes

A pass requires the calf to be acted on the same day with clear reasoning and red-flag advice, plus consent before any contact with the employer. A candidate with a perfect rehabilitation plan who misses the calf should not pass this case.

Case 32 (Mock 4, case 2 of 10): Week 6 after ACL reconstruction in a teenage soccer player

Musculoskeletal · Private physiotherapy clinic in a suburb, after-school appointment

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the plan of care you would put in place for Mateo over the next six weeks, including your goals, how you will progress his rehabilitation, how you will measure change, and your criteria for advancing to the next stage.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets goals for full active knee extension, quadriceps strength and normal gait within the next phase, with measurable targets.
  • Prioritizes restoring terminal extension and eliminating the extension lag before adding higher loads. critical
  • Uses quadriceps strengthening progressing from isometric and neuromuscular electrical stimulation to closed-chain and open-chain exercise within the graft-protection limits of the surgeon's protocol.
  • Notes hamstring autograft implications: gradual hamstring loading, avoiding aggressive resisted knee flexion early.
  • Includes gait retraining, hip and trunk strength, and balance work.
  • States that running and jumping are not started on a calendar date but on criteria such as effusion, range, strength symmetry and movement quality. critical
  • Names outcome measures: quadriceps limb symmetry index, hop tests later, International Knee Documentation Committee score, and a psychological readiness measure.
  • Gives dosage for the home program (sets, repetitions, frequency) and rules for pain and swelling response.
  • Plans collaboration with the surgeon's protocol and restrictions and schedules reassessment points.
  • Addresses his fear of re-injury and goals for school and sport as part of the plan.

Performance scale

4Criterion-based phased plan with extension first, quadriceps and hamstring-graft-aware strengthening, dosage, outcome measures, criteria to advance and links to the surgeon's protocol.
3Sound phases and measures but weak on criteria, dosage or the graft site.
2Generic knee rehabilitation list or a time-based plan with little measurement.
1Advances to running, cutting or jumping by calendar date to meet the tournament, or omits strength and range goals.

Model spoken answer

At six weeks Mateo is in the strength and control phase, so I would set my plan around criteria, not dates. My goals with him, which I would confirm together, are full active extension with no lag within two weeks, a quadriceps symmetry moving toward 80 percent by week twelve, normal walking with a full heel strike, and a safe return to jogging only when he meets criteria, not simply because a tournament is coming.

First priority: extension. A five-degree lag with a trace effusion tells me the quadriceps is not yet driving the knee fully straight, and the loss of extension, if it persists, will alter his gait and load the patellofemoral joint. So I will start with heel props, quad sets with neuromuscular electrical stimulation, and straight leg raises until the lag is gone, together with effusion control.

Second, strength. Once the lag is gone I will add mini squats, leg press in a limited range, step-ups, and open-chain knee extension through the range allowed by his surgeon's protocol. His quadriceps are at 45 percent of the other side, so this is the main deficit. I will dose at three sets of eight to twelve repetitions, two or three times weekly in clinic and a lighter set daily at home, and increase the load when he completes the sets without pain above 3 out of 10, loss of form or more swelling the next morning.

Third, because the hamstring was the graft source, I will introduce hamstring loading gradually: bridges, then light curls, and I will avoid heavy resisted flexion early.

Fourth, movement and control: gait retraining in front of a mirror, hip abductor and trunk strengthening, and balance tasks progressing from firm to unstable surfaces.

I will measure change every two weeks with handheld dynamometry for the quadriceps symmetry index, active range and lag, effusion, the International Knee Documentation Committee score, and a readiness-to-return measure, because fear is a real barrier in teenagers. Later, once he meets strength and effusion criteria, I will add hop testing.

Criteria to advance: no effusion increase, full extension without lag, flexion near the other side, a symmetric walking pattern, and a quadriceps symmetry of at least about 80 percent, with no effusion and full extension, for light jogging, as agreed with his surgeon. Running and jumping come after, and return to sport later again.

Before I start the loading plan I need the surgeon to clear the wound, which I raise in the next answer. I will review his surgeon's protocol, send a short progress update, and revise the plan if he flares, plateaus, or has any concerns about the wound or his health.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss the safety considerations you would address in today's session, and explain how you would make sure Mateo takes part in decisions about his care.

Examiner checklist

  • Notices the combination of a warm, red, draining harvest incision, low-grade fever and malaise as a possible surgical site infection. critical
  • Takes his temperature, inspects and palpates the wound and checks the dressing before exercising.
  • Defers the exercise session or stops loading the knee and hamstring until the wound is assessed by a physician. critical
  • Arranges same-day contact with the surgeon's office or urgent medical assessment and does not wait until week 12. critical
  • Gives warning signs: increasing redness, pus, fever, severe pain, calf swelling and shortness of breath.
  • Advises Mateo and his parents to stop the home band and jumping drills until cleared.
  • Explains findings to Mateo directly in plain language and asks what he understands and wants.
  • Obtains informed consent from Mateo, a mature 17-year-old, and invites but does not require his parents' involvement.
  • Documents findings, advice and who was contacted, and arranges follow-up despite the paper booking system.

Performance scale

4Links wound, temperature and malaise to possible infection, holds loading, arranges same-day medical review, gives warning signs and engages Mateo as the decision-maker.
3Identifies the wound concern and refers but is vague on urgency, hold on loading or his role in decisions.
2Notes the wound and suggests monitoring, or talks mainly to the parent, or carries on the session.
1Ignores the signs, progresses the program as planned or defers all decisions to the father.

Model spoken answer

Before I start any exercise today, I want to look at his wound and his temperature, because several small things together worry me. Mateo said he felt achy and tired yesterday and skipped dinner. The harvest incision on his proximal shin is red and warm over a few centimetres and there was some drainage on the dressing. His temperature is 37.9. Any one of these could be ordinary, but together they are consistent with an early infection at the surgical site, and an infection near a new graft is serious. I will not progress his program or load the hamstring today.

So my plan is this. First, I take a full set of vitals, examine the wound without contaminating it, note its size and the drainage, and compare with my last record. Second, I stop any loading exercise that involves the hamstring and knee. I keep him comfortable, I might do gentle range and swelling control only if I am confident it will not worsen anything, but I would hold the session otherwise.

Third, I contact the surgeon's office the same day, not week 12. I describe what I found, ask for an urgent review, and if the office cannot see him that day, I advise urgent care or the emergency department. I would telephone ahead with his permission.

Fourth, I give clear warning signs: spreading redness, pus, fever above 38, worsening pain, a hot swollen joint, a swollen painful calf, or shortness of breath. Any of these means going straight to the emergency department.

Now, how Mateo takes part. He is 17. I would speak to him first, in plain words, and ask what he has noticed and what he thinks is going on. I would explain what I found and why I am worried, and let him say what he wants, including who should be in the room. Consent for assessment and sharing information rests on his capacity, which is expected at his age, so I would ask whether he is happy for his father to hear this, and I would encourage it, but the decision is his. I would also tell him that the band work and jumping drills his father has been doing need to stop until the wound is cleared, and explain why, so that this does not feel like blame.

Finally, because the electronic system is down, I document on paper, note the time of the call, and file it later in the record. I would also telephone him tomorrow to check on progress.

Question 3: Communication

Mateo's father then tells you he is frustrated and that Mateo should be jogging by now because he knows what pro players do. Describe how you will communicate with Mateo and his father, including the specific words and strategies you would use.

Examiner checklist

  • Acknowledges the father's concern and investment before responding.
  • Explains in plain language that return to running depends on criteria such as swelling, strength and movement quality, not on the calendar. critical
  • Uses concrete numbers from today, such as the 45 percent quadriceps strength and the extension lag, to show where Mateo is.
  • Directs the main conversation to Mateo and asks for his own goals and worries. critical
  • Uses teach-back or open questions to check understanding by both.
  • Offers a clear role for the father, such as supporting the home program, driving, and encouragement.
  • Addresses the wrong home drills gently and without blame.
  • Handles the scholarship pressure and tournament honestly without promising an outcome. critical
  • Offers a written summary and agrees on how updates will be shared, respecting Mateo's preferences.

Performance scale

4Acknowledges the father, centres Mateo, explains criteria with today's findings, checks understanding, gives the father a role and is honest about outcomes.
3Respectful and clear but lacks teach-back, concrete numbers or a defined role for the father.
2Defensive or technical language, or responds mainly to the father without checking Mateo.
1Promises a return date, dismisses the father or gives in to the pressure to start running.

Model spoken answer

I would start by listening. I would say to Luis: I can hear how much you want Mateo back on the field, and I can see how much time you give him. That is a real strength. That small acknowledgement lowers the temperature before I explain anything.

Then I would speak to both of them, but I would look at Mateo when I speak about his knee. I would say: Mateo, I would like to show you and your dad where things are, and then ask what you think. I would use today's numbers. Your thigh muscle is working at about half the strength of the other leg, and your knee still lags about five degrees when you try to straighten it. Running with that gap puts more load through the new ligament and the joint, and that is when setbacks happen. I would put it as a map, not a no: we do not jog on a date, we jog when we reach these markers, and here they are in writing.

I would avoid jargon and keep sentences short. I would then ask each of them to say back what they understood: so, what would you tell your mom about when running starts? That is teach-back, and it shows me whether the message got through.

Next I would ask Mateo about his own goals. What matters most to you this spring: the tournament, the scholarship tryout, or being sure the knee is safe? A teenager is often more worried than he says. I would ask about fear of re-injury and tell him that this is common and can be worked on.

I would be honest about the schedule. I cannot promise a return for the tournament in ten weeks, and I will not guess a date, but I can promise a plan that gets him as far as safely possible and that we will review every two weeks together, and I will update the surgeon at key points. I would say the same about the scholarship tryout and suggest that, if he wants, we write a letter describing his progress.

About the home drills, I would say without blame: I know you did these to help. Right now, until his wound has been checked, the band work and jumping should wait, and I will give you a short home list that is safe, so you have something useful to do together.

Finally, I would offer a one-page written summary and ask Mateo how he would like updates shared, with his father in the room, by text, or after sessions.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is a possible surgical site infection: a warm, red, draining hamstring-harvest incision with low-grade fever and malaise, with no surgeon visit until week 12. A competent candidate examines the wound, holds loading, arranges same-day medical review and gives warning signs. A second thread is that a 17-year-old may be capable of consenting to his own care, so he is the person to inform and ask.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates produce a strong rehabilitation plan and never notice the wound, or note it and still plan to continue the exercises. In the communication question, candidates argue with the father about running or speak only to the parent and forget Mateo.

Examiner Notes

The pass line is identifying the wound and fever as urgent, stopping loading and getting a medical review the same day, while keeping Mateo at the centre. Good rehabilitation reasoning cannot compensate for missing the infection.

Case 33 (Mock 4, case 3 of 10): Starting exercise with type 2 diabetes and hypoglycemia risk

Other Systems · Hospital outpatient physiotherapy department, mid-morning appointment

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain how you interpret Gurpreet's history and findings, which of them most influence how you will start an exercise program, and what further information or assessment you would gather today.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes the exercise-related shakiness and sweating as probable hypoglycemia in a person taking gliclazide and insulin. critical
  • Links hypoglycemia risk to medication timing, meal timing and exercise duration and intensity, and asks for his glucose log.
  • Interprets reduced monofilament and vibration sensation as peripheral neuropathy that raises foot injury risk. critical
  • Identifies the callus, erythema and blister as a pre-ulcer foot lesion needing protection and medical or foot-care follow-up. critical
  • Screens for cardiovascular red flags and notes that blood pressure 148/88 is elevated but not by itself a reason to withhold light to moderate exercise.
  • Considers autonomic neuropathy, retinopathy and kidney disease as factors that alter exercise precautions and asks about them.
  • Checks hypoglycemia awareness and what he carries to treat a low.
  • Uses the six-minute walk and perceived exertion to estimate fitness and set starting intensity.
  • Explores his work schedule, meals, preferences and barriers to adherence.

Performance scale

4Interprets the pattern as hypoglycemia, the foot findings as a pre-ulcer neuropathic lesion, weighs cardiovascular and other risks and states what to gather and how it changes the start.
3Identifies hypoglycemia and neuropathy but misses the foot lesion, the cardiovascular screen or the link to medication timing.
2Lists diabetes exercise facts with little linkage to his findings or no further assessment.
1Treats the findings as unremarkable or proceeds to an unrestricted program.

Model spoken answer

I will reason from what could harm him first, then from what will help him.

The finding that most changes my plan is the pattern of shakiness and sweating after about 40 minutes of walking that settled with a banana. In a man taking gliclazide and bedtime insulin, that picture fits exercise-related hypoglycemia. Both drugs lower glucose, exercise increases glucose uptake in the muscles for hours afterwards, and his clinic reading today of 5.1 mmol/L is low-normal for starting exercise on these medications. So I need his glucose log, when he takes the gliclazide, what he ate today, how long and how hard the walks were, and whether he notices lows before they become severe. I also ask what he carries to treat a low, and I would plan for fast-acting carbohydrate within reach every session.

The second finding is the feet. Reduced monofilament and vibration sensation mean peripheral neuropathy. The callus with redness and a blister under the first metatarsal head is a pre-ulcer lesion he cannot feel, in worn shoes that offer no cushioning, and he is about to walk daily. Until it has been looked at by his physician or a foot-care clinic, I will not give a program that loads that foot repeatedly. I will check temperature, pulses and the skin between the toes, and consider non-weight-bearing options such as cycling or seated resistance work in the meantime.

Third, cardiovascular risk. He is 57, with long-standing diabetes, obesity and blood pressure of 148/88. He denies symptoms, which is reassuring, but diabetes can mask them. I would ask about exertional chest or arm discomfort, breathlessness, palpitations, and check whether his heart rate responds normally to the six-minute walk, since a blunted response could suggest autonomic neuropathy. The blood pressure alone is not a reason to withhold light to moderate activity, but I will tell his physician. I would also ask about eye disease and kidney problems because they affect how hard he should strain.

Fourth, his function and context. Six minutes of walking at 360 metres is below expected for his age and tells me to start low, around light to moderate effort on a perceived exertion scale, and build time gradually. I need to know what he can realistically do on the road: truck stops, parking lots, motel stairs and resistance bands.

So my impression is a man with type 2 diabetes at risk of exercise-related hypoglycemia and foot injury, with likely neuropathy and unclear cardiac status, who is ready and motivated to be active.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss the safety measures you will put in place today and over the coming weeks, and describe how you will plan them with Gurpreet so they fit his life.

Examiner checklist

  • Protects the left forefoot lesion: no repeated loading until assessed, and arranges a same-week medical or foot-care review. critical
  • Advises proper footwear, daily foot inspection and what to report, such as a new blister, redness or drainage.
  • Sets a hypoglycemia plan: check glucose before and after, carry fast-acting carbohydrate, and know symptoms and the treatment rule. critical
  • Explains the risk of delayed lows after exercise, including overnight, because he takes bedtime insulin.
  • Starts at a low to moderate intensity and short duration with gradual progression and a stop rule for symptoms.
  • States when to stop and seek help: chest discomfort, severe dyspnea, confusion, or a glucose that does not recover. critical
  • Shares information with his physician about the lows, the foot and the blood pressure with his consent.
  • Builds options that fit trucking life, such as walking breaks, resistance bands and stair work, with his input.
  • Uses shared decision-making and checks his understanding with teach-back.

Performance scale

4Protects the foot, builds a specific hypoglycemia plan including delayed lows, sets stop rules, coordinates with the physician and designs the plan with Gurpreet.
3Covers hypoglycemia and foot protection in general terms with some personalization.
2General diabetes exercise advice with little prioritization or without his input.
1Ignores the foot or the glucose risk, or imposes a fixed program.

Model spoken answer

I want to set safety in three layers: today, the first few weeks, and his life on the road, and I want Gurpreet to choose the details.

Today. The first thing I protect is his left forefoot. A callus with redness and a blister that he cannot feel will turn into an ulcer if he walks on it daily in flat shoes. I will explain this by saying: you cannot feel this, so your eyes have to do the job your nerves are not doing. I would contact his family physician today, with his consent, to arrange a foot check within the week, and in the meantime I would choose exercise that spares that foot: cycling on a stationary bike with cushioned shoes, seated upper body work or leg work with bands. I would show him how to inspect his feet each evening with a mirror or his phone camera, and I would tell him to report any new redness, warmth, drainage, or blister.

Hypoglycemia. I would teach him that low glucose is the main exercise risk on gliclazide and insulin. Before sessions he checks his glucose; I would use the target his physician or diabetes educator gives, and ask them to confirm it. He carries fast-acting carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or juice at every session, and we practise the rule: treat, wait, recheck. I would also explain that lows can appear hours later or overnight, because exercise keeps sensitizing muscle to insulin and he takes insulin at bedtime. So after a session he checks again before sleep, and any pattern gets reported.

Intensity. We start with light to moderate effort, about ten minutes of walking or cycling and build slowly, with a stop rule: chest pain, severe shortness of breath, dizziness, confusion or glucose he cannot bring up means stop and call for help.

His life. I would ask him: what could you realistically do in a motel parking lot at 10 pm? Together we might pick a ten-minute walk after each driving block, a set of band exercises he keeps in the cab, and stairs at truck stops. He writes the plan in his own words, and I ask him to say it back to me, so that I know it is workable.

Finally, with his permission I send a short note to his physician about the lows, the foot, the blood pressure and what we agreed, and ask for guidance on medication adjustments, since that is not my decision to make.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Gurpreet asks you to leave any mention of his low-sugar episodes out of correspondence, and also asks how much he should cut back his insulin before walking. His wife's earlier call raises a further issue. Describe how you will respond and which professional responsibilities apply.

Examiner checklist

  • Declines to advise a specific insulin or gliclazide dose change and explains that this is outside physiotherapy scope and belongs to his prescriber or diabetes educator. critical
  • Offers to help him get a timely adjustment by contacting the prescriber with his consent.
  • Explains that the lows are clinically relevant and should go to his physician, and discusses what that means for his consent. critical
  • Does not share information with his employer without his consent, and does not fabricate or omit when reporting to the physician.
  • Discusses honestly the safety issue of hypoglycemia while driving a commercial vehicle and encourages him to talk to his physician about driving requirements. critical
  • Addresses the wife's call: no disclosure to family without his express consent and corrects the receptionist's assumption.
  • Reviews clinic practice on verifying consent before sharing and documents the incident.
  • Documents the discussion, advice and the client's decisions.

Performance scale

4Stays within scope, refers the insulin question, insists on physician communication, addresses driving risk and consent properly, handles the wife's call and documents.
3Handles scope and consent adequately but misses the driving issue, the clinic privacy process or documentation.
2Partially addresses scope or confidentiality, vague about the physician or the wife.
1Gives an insulin dose, agrees to hide the lows from the physician, or shares details with the wife.

Model spoken answer

There are three separate issues in what Gurpreet and his wife have asked, and I will deal with each.

First, the insulin question. He asks how much he should cut back before walking. That is a prescribing decision. Adjusting insulin or gliclazide is outside physiotherapy scope, and a wrong number could cause a severe low or a very high glucose. So I tell him kindly: I cannot give you a number, and I would not want to guess. What I can do is make it easy to get one. With his permission I will contact his physician or diabetes educator today, tell them about the two lows during walking, and ask for a written plan on his medication timing and pre-exercise carbohydrate for the exercise we are planning. I can help him write down the questions to ask.

Second, his request to keep the lows out of correspondence. I would respect that he decides what is shared with his employer, and I will not write to his employer without his consent. But the lows are clinically important, and the person who needs to know is his prescriber, because it changes his treatment. I would explain that omitting them from my report to his physician would be unsafe and not something I can do. I would also have an honest conversation about driving: a low blood sugar behind the wheel of a truck is dangerous to him and to others. I am not his driving authority, and I will not make a report on my own, but I would encourage him to discuss fitness to drive and any requirements with his physician, and I would document that I raised it. If I thought he was at imminent risk, my regulator's standards and provincial rules would guide me on whether disclosure without consent was justified, and I would seek advice from the college.

Third, his wife's call. Health information belongs to Gurpreet. Nobody told her he agreed. I would ask him whether he wants her to have information, and what kind, and I would record his answer. Until I know, no information is released. I would then speak to the receptionist and my manager so that we confirm consent before releasing any details, and I would note the incident in the record and follow the clinic's privacy procedure, including whether a breach report is needed.

Finally, I would record the conversation, my advice, his decisions and every contact I made.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

Two buried issues: a pre-ulcer neuropathic foot lesion he cannot feel, and exercise-related hypoglycemia in a commercial driver on a sulfonylurea and insulin, plus an unauthorized family disclosure assumption at reception. A competent candidate protects the foot, builds a hypoglycemia plan, keeps medication decisions with the prescriber and secures consent before any disclosure.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates design a generic aerobic program with no foot lesion management, or tell him how to adjust insulin. They also tend to overlook the receptionist-wife disclosure and the driving hazard when they answer the professional question.

Examiner Notes

Passing responses connect the lows to medications, protect the foot, stay in scope and handle consent cleanly. A response that adjusts medication doses, or ignores the foot, is a fail on this case.

Case 34 (Mock 4, case 4 of 10): Hip pain in a retired farmer with long travel to care

Musculoskeletal · Rural community health centre with a physiotherapist on site one day a week

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the plan of care you would develop with Walter for the coming weeks, including goals, interventions, and how you would deliver and follow up care given where he lives. Include how you would measure change and when you would alter the plan.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets goals that Walter values, such as sleeping through the night and doing farm tasks, with measurable targets and a timeframe.
  • Makes loading, strengthening and walking progression conditional on medical clearance of the night pain and weight loss, keeping interim care protective. critical
  • Limits interim care to pain-limited non-resisted range, protected weight bearing with a cane in the opposite hand, and falls avoidance, deferring strengthening and walking targets until medical review.
  • Gives activity modification advice for farm work, such as limiting lifting, climbing in and out of equipment and prolonged driving.
  • Offers a short written or illustrated home program with dosage that needs no equipment and no broadband.
  • Plans follow-up by telephone or in-person clustered visits, and arranges contact points before the next weekly clinic day.
  • Names outcome measures such as hip pain score, the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, walking tolerance and night pain frequency.
  • States triggers to change the plan: pain not easing, night pain persisting, new findings, falls, or imaging and investigations that alter the diagnosis. critical
  • Considers weight, nutrition and general fitness within the context of unexplained weight loss, without recommending weight loss as a goal.

Performance scale

4Builds a plan around his goals with conservative interim care, conditional progression, dosage, remote follow-up, outcome measures and clear triggers to change the plan in light of the red flags.
3Sound plan with some personalization but progression is not tied to the unexplained findings or follow-up is not realistic.
2Standard hip osteoarthritis exercises with no regard to his location, goals or measurement.
1Prescribes heavy loading and impact or a plan he cannot access, with no follow-up.

Model spoken answer

My plan has to work for a man who lives 160 km away, who will not make a fuss, and who has a clear deadline: seeding in three weeks. It also has to respect that his night pain and weight loss are not what I would expect from simple osteoarthritis, so my plan is a safe, simple bridge while that question is answered.

Goals. I would ask Walter what he wants and write it down. Likely: sleep through the night, walk to the barn and back without stopping, climb into the tractor, and get through seeding with a plan. I would set targets like pain at night no more than 2 out of 10, with walking and strength goals set only after the bone is cleared, and review them in one and in three weeks.

Interventions. Because I want medical clarification before any real loading progress, I would start low-risk and unaggravating. First, positions and pacing: breaks every hour in the tractor cab, a footstool or cushion, getting out and moving, and avoiding long lifting and twisting. Second, protected weight bearing: a cane in the left hand, the side opposite the sore hip, which I would fit today, and care to avoid falls. Third, a short program of about ten minutes of pain-limited, non-resisted hip range that he can do lying or seated, with a simple rule that pain should settle within an hour and should not be worse the next morning. I would hold off on strengthening, bridging, sit-to-stand loading, walking-duration targets, impact and resisted hip movements until imaging and medical review show the bone is safe.

Delivery. Because he will not come back often, I would give him a printed, picture-based program with large type, and put dosage in plain words: one set of ten slow movements, once a day. I would book a telephone check in one week, because he has a telephone even if he has no broadband, ask Irene to be part of the call with his permission, and offer a slot on the next clinic day, grouped with other visits to cut the driving.

Weight and nutrition. His loss of 6 kg in three months is unexplained, so I would not treat it as a goal to encourage and I would not advise him to lose weight. I would ask his physician to review it, and suggest a dietitian if the physician agrees.

Measurement. I would record numeric pain at night and walking, the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, and his own report of how far he can walk, and repeat at each contact.

Modification. I would change the plan if night pain continues or worsens, if he falls, if the leg feels weak, or if the physician's investigations give a different explanation for his hip. If the answer is osteoarthritis alone, once cleared I would progress to strengthening, a walking program and a work-conditioning plan. If not, the plan follows the diagnosis.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss the safety considerations in Walter's case, including what you would do today and what you would tell him, and explain how you will involve Walter in deciding what happens next.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes night pain unrelieved by rest, unintentional weight loss, fatigue and a cancer history as red flags that make a serious cause, such as a bone metastasis, possible. critical
  • Does not attribute everything to the radiographic osteoarthritis and recognizes that the old x-ray does not explain the new pattern. critical
  • Recommends urgent medical assessment and investigations, such as bloodwork including prostate-specific antigen and updated imaging, and contacts his physician promptly. critical
  • Considers pathological fracture risk and gives advice on protected loading, such as avoiding falls, heavy lifting and impact.
  • Gives clear warning signs: sudden severe pain, inability to bear weight, a new deformity, leg shortening, neurological symptoms or bladder changes.
  • Explains this honestly without causing alarm, in plain language and at a pace Walter can follow.
  • Asks what Walter understands and what matters to him, including seeding, and explores his fear and barriers to attending.
  • Obtains consent for referral, and for involving Irene, and respects his decision, including a decision to wait.
  • Documents the findings, advice and plan to ensure follow-up is not left to chance.

Performance scale

4Identifies the cluster of red flags and cancer history, arranges prompt medical investigation, protects the bone, gives warning signs and engages Walter with tailored communication and respect for his choice.
3Recognizes red flags and refers but is vague about urgency, fracture precautions or his participation.
2Mentions seeing a physician at some point but treats the case as osteoarthritis and carries on.
1Attributes all findings to the osteoarthritis, with no referral, or pressures him without explanation.

Model spoken answer

The safety question here is whether Walter's hip pain is osteoarthritis only, and my answer is that I cannot be sure. Some of what he describes fits osteoarthritis: the groin pain, the morning stiffness of twenty minutes, the limited internal rotation and the old x-ray. But several things do not: pain that wakes him most nights even when he lies still, a loss of 6 kg in three months without trying, new tiredness, and pain on gentle heel strike that suggests the bone itself may be irritated. He also had prostate cancer five years ago, and prostate cancer commonly spreads to bone, including the upper femur and pelvis. A year-old x-ray cannot tell me what is happening now. So I treat this as possible serious pathology until a physician has ruled it out.

What I do today. I contact his family physician by phone today, explain what I found and why I am worried, and ask for urgent assessment, including blood tests such as a prostate-specific antigen and an updated hip and pelvis image. If the physician cannot see him within days, I would ask for a plan for urgent imaging. I would give him a letter to carry.

I protect the bone in the meantime. I would advise him to avoid heavy lifting, jumping, climbing on and off equipment where he could fall, and to use a cane. I give warning signs: sudden severe pain, inability to put weight on the leg, a leg that looks shorter or turned, new numbness or weakness in the legs, or trouble passing urine. These mean going straight to the nearest emergency department.

Now how I involve him. He is stoic and might nod without understanding, so I would speak slowly, face him, make sure his hearing aids are in, and use short sentences. I would say: Walter, I think your hip arthritis is real, but some things you told me are not typical for arthritis alone, and I want a doctor to check, because it is better to find out now. Then I would ask what he thinks and what worries him. I expect he will say seeding. I would not dismiss that. I would explain that if there is a problem in the bone, working through seeding could lead to a break that would cost him far more time, and ask what help his son could give.

I ask his permission to speak to Irene and to send information to his physician. If he chooses to wait, I respect that, document it, repeat the warning signs and book a call in a few days. I record all of it in the chart.

Question 3: Communication

Describe the specific communication strategies and words you would use with Walter and Irene to explain your concerns and the next steps, given his hearing, his stoicism and the distance he lives from care.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets up the conversation for hearing: face-to-face, good lighting, hearing aids on, reduced background noise, slow clear speech.
  • Uses plain language and short sentences, avoiding words such as metastasis or pathology unless explained. critical
  • Uses teach-back and asks Walter to say in his own words what happens next. critical
  • Gives key points in writing in large print, including who will call him, and when.
  • Asks permission before involving Irene and checks what he wants her to know.
  • Responds to stoicism by normalizing concerns and inviting questions without pushing him.
  • Acknowledges his farm responsibilities and links the plan to what he values.
  • Addresses travel barriers with telephone follow-up, a named contact person and clustering of only non-urgent visits, without delaying the urgent physician assessment.
  • Shows cultural humility by asking about his preferences, transport and finances rather than assuming rural life, means or capacity.

Performance scale

4Adapts to hearing and stoicism, uses plain language and teach-back, includes Irene with consent, gives written information and solves distance with specific follow-up.
3Clear and respectful but misses hearing adaptation, teach-back or a concrete remote follow-up plan.
2Generic communication advice without specific words or adaptation to Walter.
1Uses jargon, relies on a yes from Walter, or dismisses his concerns about seeding.

Model spoken answer

Three things shape how I speak to Walter: he is hard of hearing and tends to say yes quickly, he does not like to make a fuss, and he lives 160 km from the centre. I plan for each.

First, hearing. I would ask him to put his hearing aids in, sit facing me in good light, and move to a quieter room. I would speak slowly, in short sentences, and look at him, not at the chart or at Irene. I would not rely on him saying yes. I would ask him instead to tell me what he heard.

Second, words. I would say: Walter, your hip has some arthritis, and that is real. But you also told me about night pain and about losing weight without trying, and with your history of prostate cancer, I want your doctor to look at the bone in your leg. I will not use the words metastasis or pathology unless he asks, and if he asks I will answer honestly and simply. I would use plain pictures of the hip and femur to show where I am concerned. I would stop after each point and ask: does that make sense? What questions do you have?

Third, his stoicism. I would say that many people put up with pain and hope it passes, and that it is not a fuss to ask for a test, it is how we find the right treatment. I would name his seeding season out loud, because I expect it is his main worry: I know seeding matters. If there is a problem in the bone, finding it now protects your ability to work this spring. I would ask what his son could do to help.

For Irene, I would ask Walter first whether he is happy for me to include her, then speak to both. She books his appointments, so I would ask her to help with the plan, such as who will drive him and how they will reach me.

For distance, I would write a one-page summary in large print: what I found, what the doctor will do, what to do if the pain suddenly worsens, and my clinic phone number. I would say, I will call you on Thursday at 10, is that a good time? The physician assessment cannot wait for a combined trip, so I would arrange it as soon as possible, locally or by phone referral, and only cluster non-urgent follow-up with it. I would ask what he prefers and what transport he has, rather than assuming how far he can travel or what he can afford.

To close, I would ask: to be sure I explained well, can you tell me what will happen next, and what would make you call 911? If anything is missing, I explain again in different words.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is a red-flag cluster: night pain at rest, unintentional weight loss, fatigue and a prior prostate cancer in a man whose hip radiograph shows osteoarthritis. A competent candidate does not anchor on the x-ray, arranges prompt medical investigation, protects against fracture and explains this in a way Walter can understand.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates anchor on the visible osteoarthritis and write a strengthening program without raising the red flags. Others raise the concern but leave the plan vague on timing, or use jargon with a patient who has hearing loss and says yes automatically.

Examiner Notes

A pass identifies the red-flag cluster and acts on it with urgency while still giving Walter a workable interim plan. Failing to recognize the cancer history and night pain is a fail on this case.

Case 35 (Mock 4, case 5 of 10): Fatigue in relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis

Neurological · Hospital-based outpatient neurology rehabilitation clinic

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain your clinical impression of what is contributing to Esi's presentation, which findings from today most influence your thinking, and what further assessment you would carry out or arrange.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies several contributors to fatigue: primary multiple sclerosis fatigue, heat sensitivity, possible sleep disorder (snoring, unrefreshing sleep), deconditioning, mood, medication effects.
  • Notes the new right foot catching, mild right dorsiflexion weakness, brisker right reflex and eye pain with movement as findings that may represent new neurological deficits rather than fatigue. critical
  • Recognizes that new symptoms lasting more than 24 hours may indicate a relapse and asks about onset, duration, heat or infection triggers and progression. critical
  • Considers the lapse in disease-modifying therapy as increasing the risk of new disease activity.
  • Explains why heat-related transient worsening (Uhthoff phenomenon) does not fit symptoms lasting days.
  • Plans screening for sleep apnea, depression, anemia or thyroid problems by arranging medical follow-up rather than diagnosing them.
  • Uses and interprets standardized measures: fatigue scale, six-minute walk, timed walk, Timed Up and Go, with a view to a baseline.
  • Describes further neurological examination: tone, sensation, coordination, gait and visual screening.
  • Identifies the unmet need for a neurology follow-up.

Performance scale

4Gives a multifactorial view of fatigue and identifies the new unilateral deficits and visual symptoms as a possible relapse, explaining why heat sensitivity does not fit, with specific further assessment and referral.
3Identifies multiple fatigue contributors and flags some new findings but is unclear on relapse or urgency.
2Attributes all findings to MS fatigue and heat with standard measures only.
1Misses the new deficits or advises that symptoms are expected and will pass.

Model spoken answer

Esi came because of fatigue, and fatigue is very common in multiple sclerosis, so I will take it seriously. But my impression is that fatigue is probably not the only thing happening, and the findings that most influence my thinking are not the fatigue score.

First, the fatigue. Her Modified Fatigue Impact Scale is 52 out of 84, worse in the afternoon and when it is hot, which fits primary multiple sclerosis fatigue and heat sensitivity. But other things add to it. She snores, wakes unrefreshed and sleeps six hours, which makes me think of a sleep disorder such as sleep apnea. She is also anxious and under financial strain, so mood could contribute. Deconditioning from avoiding activity, the night baclofen, and medical problems like low iron or thyroid disease can also play a part. I cannot diagnose these, but I can ask about them and ask her physician to test.

Second, the findings that matter more. For four days her right toes have been catching on stairs, her right ankle dorsiflexion is 4 out of 5 and the right knee reflex is brisker than the left. For five days her right eye has been blurry and sore when she looks sideways. These are new neurological symptoms on one side, lasting days. Heat-related worsening of old symptoms usually fades within an hour of cooling and does not last four or five days. New or worsening deficits lasting over 24 hours, without fever or infection, raise the possibility of a relapse, and pain with eye movement and blurred vision could be optic neuritis. Her disease-modifying therapy lapsed three months ago, which raises the chance of new activity. I will not call it a relapse, but I will treat it as a possible one.

Further assessment today. I would ask when each symptom started, whether they come and go with heat, any recent infection, fever, or a new urinary or bowel problem, and any other new numbness or imbalance. I would examine tone, sensation, coordination, gait, and do a basic visual screen including acuity with her glasses and eye movements, without going beyond my scope. I would record the six-minute walk, 25-foot walk and Timed Up and Go as baselines.

And I would arrange what I cannot do myself: contact her neurologist or family physician the same day about possible new activity, and ask about sleep and blood testing, since both matter for her fatigue.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss the safety considerations in this case, including Esi's wish to start a gym program and hot yoga, and explain how you will involve her in decisions.

Examiner checklist

  • Advises same-day contact with her neurologist or physician for the possible relapse, and not waiting for a routine appointment. critical
  • Explains that vision symptoms or worsening weakness should lead to urgent care and gives clear warning signs. critical
  • Holds new intense exercise until medical assessment but advises against complete inactivity and supports safe movement.
  • Advises against hot yoga because heat can worsen symptoms and fatigue, and offers cooling strategies and cooler options. critical
  • Addresses fall risk with the right foot catching and offers gait aid or footwear advice and stair safety.
  • Explains that exercise is beneficial in multiple sclerosis when dosed carefully and fatigue pacing is used.
  • Addresses driving safety if vision is affected and discusses with her physician.
  • Uses shared decision-making, explores her fears about cost and work, and checks understanding.
  • Obtains consent before contacting the physician and documents the plan.

Performance scale

4Arranges prompt medical review of possible relapse, gives warning signs, holds intense exercise, advises against heat exposure, addresses falls and driving and shares decisions with Esi.
3Makes a medical referral and advises on heat and exercise but lacks urgency, fall or driving safety or shared decision-making.
2Gives general MS exercise and heat advice with only a routine neurology referral.
1Approves hot yoga or a vigorous program, or does not address the new deficits.

Model spoken answer

My first safety concern is that Esi may be having a relapse and may be treating it as tiredness. She told me about new right foot catching and eye pain and blurring, and I found mild weakness and a brisker reflex on the right. Because relapses can be treated, and early assessment can protect vision and function, I want her seen by a physician quickly. So I would say to Esi: I am glad you told me about your foot and eye. I do not think this is just fatigue, and I would like your neurologist or a doctor to look at it today or tomorrow. I would offer to call with her permission from the clinic while she is here, and give her a short written summary to take along. I would give her warning signs: if her vision gets worse, if she loses vision in either eye, if the weakness spreads or she cannot walk safely, if she develops new numbness, a loss of bladder or bowel control, or severe dizziness, she should go to the emergency department.

Second, her wish to start a gym program and hot yoga. I would explain that exercise is good for multiple sclerosis and is not the cause of her fatigue, and that I want to help her become active. But I would hold new intense exercise for a few days until a doctor has looked at her, because if she is relapsing, a strenuous program could worsen things and fatigue could make her fall. Meanwhile, light activity such as short walks in a cool place is fine. Hot yoga I would advise against, and I would say why: heat raises body temperature, and in multiple sclerosis a small rise can temporarily worsen vision, weakness and fatigue. I would suggest alternatives such as cooler pools, fans, cooling vests or neck wraps, and exercise in the morning when she is freshest.

Third, falls. Her right toes are catching, and she uses stairs at school every day. I would check her footwear, teach her to use the handrail, discuss an ankle-foot orthosis if the foot drop persists, and ask her to tell me about any near-falls.

If her vision is blurry, driving may be unsafe. I would ask her to discuss this with her physician and not drive if it is hard to see.

How she takes part. I would ask her what worries her most. I suspect money and work. I would ask what she understands, offer choices on how to reach her doctor, such as phoning now or going to a walk-in clinic, and check that she can repeat the plan. I would document it all, with her consent for every contact.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Esi asks you to complete her insurer's long-term disability form and says she has not told her employer she stopped treatment. Describe how you will respond and which professional responsibilities apply.

Examiner checklist

  • Obtains explicit written consent before releasing any information to the insurer, and limits it to what the form requires. critical
  • Completes only the parts within physiotherapy scope, such as observed function and measures, and defers diagnosis and prognosis to the physician. critical
  • Reports accurately and objectively, without exaggerating or omitting findings, including the date of assessment.
  • Does not disclose to the employer that she stopped treatment and does not pressure her either way.
  • Discusses without judgment the lapse in therapy and encourages her to resolve it with her neurologist, including coverage options and social work. critical
  • Offers to refer to social work or patient navigation for drug coverage and benefits.
  • Discloses fees for form completion according to clinic policy and the regulator's standards.
  • Documents the request, consent, what was completed and what was deferred.

Performance scale

4Secures consent, stays within scope, reports objectively, respects her control of employer information, addresses the treatment lapse supportively and documents.
3Handles consent and scope but is thin on accuracy, the treatment lapse or documentation.
2Completes the form with little concern for scope or consent, or refuses without helping.
1Provides diagnosis and prognosis, shares information with the employer or inflates findings.

Model spoken answer

The disability form raises scope, honesty and consent, and the treatment lapse raises advocacy.

Consent first. The form asks for diagnosis, prognosis and functional abilities, and it goes to her insurer. I will not send anything until Esi has read what I plan to include and signed consent that names the insurer, the purpose and the information to be shared. If the form asks for more than it needs, I would share only what is relevant and explain why. This follows provincial health privacy legislation and my regulator's standards.

Scope. I can describe what I assessed: her walking measures, balance, strength, fatigue scores and what she can do in a session, and I can describe those observations with dates. I cannot provide a diagnosis or a prognosis, since those belong to her neurologist or physician. I would say: I can fill in the functional parts based on what I observed, and I will ask your neurologist to complete the diagnosis and outlook. Because her symptoms may be changing, I would mark my findings as of today's date and say that they may change after medical review. I will write only what I measured. I will not exaggerate to help her claim, and I will not leave out findings that she may not want mentioned. Accuracy protects her and me, and fraud or misleading statements would breach professional standards.

Employer. She has not told her employer she stopped treatment. That is her information. I would not contact the employer, and I would not push her to disclose. I would explain what the insurer form will and will not tell the employer, and I would suggest she think about how to talk to her workplace about accommodations such as scheduling and cooling.

The treatment lapse is the more important issue. I would not judge her. I would say that I understand money is tight and that stopping her disease-modifying therapy raises the chance of new disease activity, especially with the new symptoms we found today. I would encourage her to talk with her neurologist about restarting and offer to refer her to social work or a patient navigator who can look at public drug programs and manufacturer assistance. With her permission I would include the lapse in my communication to her physician.

Finally, I would disclose any fee for completing forms before I do the work, according to clinic policy, and document the request, her consent, what I completed and what I deferred.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is a possible multiple sclerosis relapse: new right foot catching, dorsiflexion weakness, brisker reflex and eye pain with movement for days, in a woman who has been off disease-modifying therapy for three months and who attributes it all to fatigue. A competent candidate flags it, arranges same-day medical review, advises against heat exposure and respects consent and scope on the insurer form.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates design a fatigue-management program (pacing, exercise, cooling) and never question the new neurological signs. In question 3 they complete the diagnosis and prognosis parts of the insurer form themselves or share details without written consent.

Examiner Notes

A pass notices that the new unilateral deficits and visual symptoms are not just fatigue and acts the same day, while keeping scope and consent sound. A fatigue-only answer is a fail on this case.

Case 36 (Mock 4, case 6 of 10): Widespread pain and fatigue in a retail worker in a pain program

Musculoskeletal · Hospital-based interdisciplinary chronic pain program, outpatient physiotherapy clinic room

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the physiotherapy care plan you would develop with this client over the first eight weeks. Include goals, the main interventions, how you would set the exercise dosage and progress it, and how you would measure change.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets collaborative, functional goals tied to her work and caregiving roles, such as walking duration and shift tolerance
  • Provides pain neuroscience and condition education to explain that hurt does not always mean harm critical
  • Prescribes low-intensity aerobic exercise starting well below the current flare threshold, for example 5 to 10 minutes critical
  • Teaches pacing with planned rest and a fixed baseline rather than boom and bust activity
  • Progresses gradually, about 10 percent or 1 to 2 minutes per week, with a flare plan that avoids full rest critical
  • Adds light resistance and flexibility work after tolerance to aerobic exercise is established
  • Includes sleep hygiene and links with the psychologist and occupational therapist on shared goals
  • Uses outcome measures such as the Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire, 6-minute walk and pain scale and sets reassessment points
  • Plans a graded return to work discussion rather than an immediate full schedule

Performance scale

4Gives a collaborative plan with functional goals, education, a low starting dose below the flare threshold, specific progression and flare rules, pacing, and named outcome measures with reassessment, linked to her case.
3Sound plan with education, exercise and pacing, but dosage, flare management or measurement is vague.
2Lists interventions such as exercise and modalities without a dose, progression or reasoning tied to the flare pattern.
1Prescribes vigorous exercise or passive treatment only, ignores the boom and bust pattern, or imposes goals without her input.

Model spoken answer

Thank you. My plan is built around what Priya wants to be able to do, so first I would agree on goals with her. She told me she wants to get through a shift, keep helping her mother, and stop crashing after good days. I would set a goal such as walking 15 minutes at an easy pace within eight weeks, building toward 30 minutes over the following months, and tolerating a four hour shift without a multi-day flare. Second, education. I would explain in plain words that fibromyalgia involves a sensitive pain system, that her tests are normal because her joints and muscles are not being damaged, and that carefully dosed movement calms the system over time. That reduces fear, and fear of movement is a major reason people stop. Third, aerobic exercise, which has the best evidence in this condition. Because she flares after 10 minutes, I would start at about half of that, five minutes of easy walking or stationary cycling, at an effort she can talk through, roughly 3 out of 10 on a perceived exertion scale.
