I would have her do it most days, and add one or two minutes per week only if she has no worse than a mild increase in pain the next day. If she flares, she drops back one step rather than stopping. Fourth, pacing. We would find her baseline, the amount she can do on a bad day, and have her do that amount every day, so good days no longer trigger crashes. Fifth, from about week three or four I would add light resistance exercises for large muscle groups, such as sit to stand and band rows, two sets of eight to ten at low load, and gentle stretching. Sixth, sleep and stress. I would give basic sleep routines, coordinate with the psychologist on cognitive behavioural strategies, and with the occupational therapist on how she organizes her evenings with her mother and her workstation. Seventh, measurement. I would repeat the Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire and the 6-minute walk at week four and week eight, and track her daily walking minutes and pain in a simple diary. A change of about 14 percent on the questionnaire or a clear gain in walking distance would tell us the plan is working. If there is no change by week four, I would review dosage, adherence, mood and sleep, rather than just pushing harder. Finally, I would use her private visits to supervise progression between group sessions and help her prepare a graded return to work letter for her physician and employer.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

As the client is leaving, she makes a comment that concerns you. Describe how you would respond right then and what steps you would take afterward, while keeping her at the centre of decisions.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes the comment as possible suicidal ideation and does not let her leave without a response critical
  • Pauses the exit, sits down with her, and asks directly and calmly whether she is thinking of ending her life
  • Asks about plan, means, intent, timing, past attempts and protective factors in a non-judgmental way critical
  • Acknowledges her exhaustion and thanks her for telling you before offering any solutions
  • Knows the clinic procedure and involves the program psychologist or physician the same day when risk is present
  • Provides crisis resources such as 9-8-8 and the local emergency department and does not leave an at-risk client alone critical
  • Seeks her consent to share information and explains the limits of confidentiality if safety is at risk
  • Documents her words, your questions, her answers, actions and follow-up objectively
  • Arranges a specific follow-up contact rather than waiting for next week's session

Performance scale

4Responds immediately and directly, assesses risk with specific questions, involves the right team members with consent, provides crisis resources, plans follow-up and documents, all in a warm client-centred way.
3Recognizes the risk and refers appropriately but misses direct questioning of plan or means, or follow-up detail.
2Notes concern and suggests she see her physician later without assessing risk or acting the same day.
1Ignores the comment, treats it as a joke, or reassures without assessing safety.

Model spoken answer

I would not let that comment pass. Even though she laughed it off, saying some nights it would be easier not to wake up can mean passive or active thoughts of suicide, and asking about it does not plant the idea. So I would put down my notes, ask her to sit with me for a few minutes, and say something like: I heard what you said at the door and I am glad you told me. You sound exhausted. Are you having thoughts of ending your life? I would ask it directly, in plain words, and then listen. Next I would find out how serious it is. Does she have a plan, access to means such as stored medication, a sense of when, any past attempts, and what keeps her going, such as her mother, her family, her work? I would also ask about her sleep, her mood, and whether she has told her physician. If she says the thoughts are fleeting, with no plan or intent and strong reasons to live, I would still involve the team. I would tell her what I am going to do and why, and ask permission to bring in the program psychologist today, who is already part of her care, and to let her family physician know. I would explain that confidentiality has limits, and that if I believed she was in immediate danger I would have to get help even without her agreement. If she tells me she has a plan or intent, I would not leave her alone, I would call the program psychologist or physician or the emergency department and follow our clinic crisis procedure, and I would help her get there safely. In either case I would give her the 9-8-8 Suicide Crisis Helpline number, which is available by call or text at any hour, and write it down for her, and encourage her to include a trusted person. I would collaborate with her on a safety plan rather than imposing one: what she will do on a bad night, who she will call, and how her medication is stored. Afterward I would document her exact words, my questions, her answers, who I contacted and what we agreed, and I would arrange a call or visit within a day or two rather than waiting a week. Her exercise plan would be paused or reduced until she is supported, because her wellbeing comes first.

Question 3: Practice Management

Discuss how you would organize her physiotherapy services across the group program and her insurance-funded visits, including scheduling, documentation, and what you would delegate or not delegate.

Examiner checklist

  • Coordinates group sessions and individual visits so they complement rather than duplicate each other
  • Uses the ten individual visits strategically, such as early dosing, week four review and transition to self-management
  • Bills only for services actually delivered and does not extend visits or add unnecessary treatments to use up coverage critical
  • Documents assessments, goals, dosage, progression, consent, outcome measures and safety discussions in the shared record
  • Delegates supervised exercise practice to a physiotherapist assistant with clear written instructions and keeps assessment and plan changes critical
  • Keeps risk-related decisions and the progression of the plan with the physiotherapist
  • Books longer sessions or flexible times around her shifts and caregiving, with reminders and a cancellation plan
  • Uses an interpreted or written home program and tracks adherence with a simple diary

Performance scale

4Describes coordinated scheduling around her life, deliberate use of limited visits, honest billing, safe delegation with retained clinical decisions, and thorough documentation and privacy.
3Covers scheduling, documentation and delegation but with limited detail on billing ethics or how the visits are used.
2Lists administrative tasks without reasoning or without separating what can and cannot be delegated.
1Delegates assessment or safety decisions, bills for unneeded services, or ignores coordination.

Model spoken answer

There are two streams of care, the publicly funded group program and her ten private visits, and my job is to make them work as one plan. First, scheduling. Her group sessions are weekly and fixed, so I would schedule her individual visits around her shifts and her evenings with her mother. I would offer early morning or late afternoon times, send a reminder, and discuss a clear cancellation approach, because missed visits are common when someone has unpredictable pain and caregiving duties. Second, I would plan the use of the ten visits rather than spending them evenly. I would use the first for individual assessment and to set her exercise dose, since group classes cannot be dosed to one person, then visits in weeks two, four and six to progress her program and review her flare plan. I would reserve the last few for the transition to independent exercise and a return to work letter. Third, billing. Her insurer covers ten visits, but I would only bill for care I actually deliver and that she needs. I would not add passive treatments or extend the program because coverage remains, and if she needs fewer visits I would say so. If a service is delivered by an assistant, it should be billed accurately as such. Fourth, delegation. A physiotherapist assistant could supervise her walking and strengthening practice in the gym once I have set the dose and written clear instructions with stop and flare rules. The assessment, interpretation of her response, decisions about progression, and the safety follow-up from today all remain with me, because those require clinical judgement. I would check in with the assistant after the first sessions and review her notes. Fifth, documentation. I would record the assessment, goals agreed with her, dosage, outcome measures, education, consent, and the safety discussion and actions, in the shared program record following the privacy rules, and share only what the team needs, with her consent. Finally, I would give her a written home program and a simple diary so progress between visits is visible to her and to the team, and I would review caseload so I have time for brief phone follow-ups when she flares.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is her remark that some nights it would be easier not to wake up, said as she leaves. A competent candidate catches it, asks directly about suicide, assesses plan and means, uses crisis resources, involves the team with consent, and documents. Treating it as a joke or deferring it to next week is unsafe.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates spend all their time on exercise detail and never mention her comment, or note it and only advise seeing her doctor without direct questions. Others prescribe an aerobic dose that matches her good day, which triggers flares.

Examiner Notes

A pass shows a low starting dose with pacing and measurement, plus a clear, direct, same-day response to the suicide comment. Missing the comment is a fail on Question 2 even with a strong care plan.

Case 37 (Mock 4, case 7 of 10): Airway clearance and exercise planning in a young adult with a chronic lung condition

Cardiovascular-Respiratory · Outpatient specialty clinic, shared waiting area and physiotherapy room

Question 1: Care Planning

Outline the airway clearance and exercise plan you would develop with Jasmine. Include techniques, schedule, how you would set and progress exercise, and how you would support her adherence and monitor her response.

Examiner checklist

  • Reinforces twice daily airway clearance and extra sessions during exacerbations, timed around her lecture schedule
  • Reviews her technique with the oscillating device and active cycle of breathing, checking pressure, huff and cough effectiveness
  • Sequences inhaled therapy before airway clearance, as already prescribed, and coordinates timing with the team
  • Prescribes regular aerobic exercise, with strength training, using a graded program based on her tolerance and a measured baseline, started once the team has cleared the sputum bleeding critical
  • Sets oxygen saturation monitoring during exercise and a stop threshold agreed with the respiratory team critical
  • Addresses hydration, enzyme timing and fuelling around exercise, linked to the dietitian
  • Uses motivational strategies and shared goals, such as playing intramurals, to support adherence
  • Sets outcome measures and review points such as sputum volume, FEV1 trend, exercise test and adherence log
  • Teaches cleaning and drying of equipment per manufacturer and clinic guidance

Performance scale

4Gives a specific, client-centred plan covering twice daily airway clearance with technique check, graded exercise with SpO2 limits, adherence strategies, equipment care and monitoring tied to her findings.
3Covers airway clearance and exercise reasonably but dose, saturation limits or adherence strategy is thin.
2Lists techniques and exercise in general terms without schedule, progression or monitoring.
1Recommends unmonitored vigorous exercise, drops airway clearance, or ignores her desaturation and goals.

Model spoken answer

I would plan this with Jasmine, because she is an adult who manages her own care and has her own priorities. Her main goal is to play intramurals and go to the gym, so I would use that as the thread. First, airway clearance. She is doing it once a day and her lung function has fallen from 71 to 62 percent over a year, with a recent exacerbation, so I would aim for twice daily, morning and evening, each lasting about 20 to 30 minutes once her team has advised on the bleeding, and until then I would use only gentle techniques, relaxed breathing control and gentle huffing, as in my safety answer, with extra sessions if she has more sputum or feels unwell. Together we would look at her calendar and choose fixed times that fit lectures, such as a session on waking before class and one before bed, and discuss a private space in residence. I would watch her do a session with her oscillating device and active cycle of breathing, checking her breathing control, thoracic expansion, and a forced expiration technique that produces sputum rather than just noise, and correct anything that needs correcting. She would take her hypertonic saline first, as prescribed, then clear her airway. Second, exercise. Exercise supports airway clearance and fitness. I would test her baseline, such as a 6-minute walk or the step test, with SpO2 monitoring. Her saturation fell from 94 to 90 percent, so I would agree with her respiratory physician on a threshold, and teach her to use a pulse oximeter and stop and rest if she drops below it, or has more than the usual breathlessness. Because she told me about pink streaks in her sputum, which I address in my safety answer, I would keep clearance gentle and hold high-intensity exercise until her cystic fibrosis team has assessed it. Once they have cleared her, I would start with 20 minutes of aerobic exercise three times a week at a moderate effort, around 3 to 4 out of 10 on a dyspnea scale at first, add two sessions of strength work, and progress duration by about 5 minutes every week or two. She can join intramurals as her tolerance improves, with a plan for hydration, salt and enzymes around sessions. Third, adherence. I would use motivational interviewing, explore what makes the second session hard, and agree a small written plan with specific times. A simple log or phone reminder would help. Fourth, equipment. I would teach her to wash the device after each use, air dry it, and follow the manufacturer's disinfection steps, because her chronic Pseudomonas makes contamination matter. Finally, I would monitor her response with her sputum volume, FEV1 at clinic visits, exercise tolerance, and her own log, and review in four weeks.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

What safety concerns do you have with this client at this visit and what would you do about each of them, including how you would speak with her about them?

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes pink streaks in sputum as possible hemoptysis and asks about amount, frequency, pain, fever and trend critical
  • Withholds or modifies vigorous airway clearance and intensive exercise until the respirologist assesses the bleeding critical
  • Contacts the cystic fibrosis team the same day and explains the urgency, with a plan for large bleeds and emergency services critical
  • Recognizes cross-infection risk from close contact with another person with cystic fibrosis and applies masking and separation
  • Explains that people with cystic fibrosis should keep distance, avoid shared spaces and equipment, and corrects this without blame
  • Reviews desaturation on exertion and sets monitoring and stopping rules
  • Addresses hand hygiene, equipment cleaning and clinic cleaning between patients
  • Uses plain language, thanks her for mentioning the blood and respects her autonomy while explaining the reasons

Performance scale

4Identifies hemoptysis as the priority, modifies treatment, contacts the team the same day and sets emergency criteria, also addresses cross-infection and exertional desaturation, with respectful plain communication.
3Identifies hemoptysis and cross-infection and acts reasonably but with gaps in urgency, specifics or communication.
2Notes one concern, or mentions several without a clear action or explanation to the client.
1Misses the bleeding or continues vigorous clearance and exercise without assessment.

Model spoken answer

I have three safety concerns, and the first one is the most urgent. First, the pink streaks in her sputum. She mentioned it almost in passing, but blood in the sputum can be a sign of airway bleeding in cystic fibrosis, and vigorous airway clearance, forceful coughing, or intense exercise could worsen it. I would thank her for telling me, then ask specific questions: how much, a streak or a teaspoon or more, how many days, whether it is increasing, any chest pain, fever, or more breathlessness. For small streaks with no distress I would hold the more forceful elements of clearance and any high-intensity exercise for now, and call her cystic fibrosis team, the respirologist or nurse coordinator, the same day to report it and ask whether she needs to be seen sooner. I would explain this to her plainly: this is not a punishment, I am trying to keep her safe, and the decision about how to continue treatment will be made together with her team. If the bleeding were larger or increasing, I would hold airway clearance completely and arrange urgent assessment the same day. If it were heavy, meaning large amounts of fresh red blood, or she were dizzy, very breathless or unstable, I would call 911 and not wait for a clinic call. Second, cross-infection. She sat close to another person with cystic fibrosis and they chatted. People with cystic fibrosis can pass resistant organisms such as Pseudomonas to each other, so current practice is to keep them apart, usually at least two metres, with masks, and without shared rooms. I would gently explain this to her, not blame her, and tell her I will arrange separate times or waiting areas, and make sure my room is cleaned between patients. I would also review hand hygiene and discuss with her how this applies in residence and at the gym. Third, her desaturation from 94 to 90 percent on a step test. That is mild, but I would set clear rules: use a pulse oximeter during exercise, stop and rest if below the threshold the team agrees, and report persistent changes. Last, I would remind her to clean and dry her devices after each use. Throughout, I would check she understands and agrees with the plan, and document the discussion and who I contacted.

Question 3: Collaboration

Explain how you would collaborate with the team and others to support Jasmine over the next few months. Include who you would involve, what you would share, and how you would keep the communication clear.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies the cystic fibrosis multidisciplinary team members and their roles, including respirologist, nurse, dietitian, respiratory therapist, social worker and pharmacist
  • Obtains Jasmine's consent about what is shared with whom, including the university critical
  • Communicates the bleeding report and findings clearly to the respirologist with a structured summary critical
  • Coordinates exercise limits and oxygen saturation thresholds with the medical team
  • Involves the dietitian about low body mass index, enzymes and exercise fuelling
  • Suggests contacting university accessibility or health services for scheduling and space for treatments, with her permission
  • Considers social work for psychosocial support, adherence barriers and transition from pediatric care
  • Plans how and when team members will follow up and share updates, including with Jasmine herself

Performance scale

4Names the right team members with their roles, obtains consent first, gives a structured urgent report on the bleeding, coordinates exercise limits, nutrition and psychosocial support, and sets clear follow-up with Jasmine included.
3Names the team and shares appropriate information but with limited consent discussion, structure or follow-up.
2Lists professionals without explaining what is shared, why or how.
1Shares information without consent, omits the medical team, or does not communicate the bleeding concern.

Model spoken answer

Jasmine's care depends on a team, and my role is to be one clear part of it. First, I would ask her consent: who she is happy for me to talk to and what can be shared. She is an adult managing her own care, and she may not want her university to know details of her health, so I would explain what I would like to share and why, and respect her decisions. Second, the cystic fibrosis clinic team. The respirologist needs to know about the pink-streaked sputum today, so I would phone and give a short structured report: who she is, what I found, what I did, and what I am asking. That would be that she is 19 with cystic fibrosis and chronic Pseudomonas, finished intravenous antibiotics two weeks ago, FEV1 is 62 percent and down from 71 percent, saturation drops from 94 to 90 percent on a step test, she reports several days of pink streaks, and I have held vigorous clearance and exercise until I hear back. I would ask for advice on her exercise limits and saturation threshold. The clinic nurse coordinator is a good first contact for follow-up. Third, the dietitian. Her body mass index is 19.5, and exercise increases energy needs, so I would ask for advice on calories, salt, hydration, and enzyme timing around exercise. Fourth, the social worker or psychologist on the team, because she lives away from her mother in residence, is skipping treatments, and may be struggling with the burden of daily care. Fifth, with her permission, the university accessibility or health services could help with a private space for treatments, flexible lecture schedules, and a plan for exacerbations. Sixth, her pharmacist and the respiratory therapist on devices and inhaled therapy timing. For clear communication, I would send written notes after each visit, agree who contacts Jasmine about what so she is not given conflicting messages, and set a review date in four weeks. I would also tell Jasmine what I report back, so she is part of the conversation, and ask her which method of contact she prefers, such as text or email.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

Two issues are buried. Pink streaks in the sputum are possible hemoptysis and need same-day team contact and modified treatment. Her chat with another person with cystic fibrosis is a cross-infection risk. A competent candidate asks questions, holds vigorous clearance, calls the team, and corrects the contact kindly.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates focus on airway clearance technique and exercise and never pick up the pink streaks, or they note it but continue the planned program. Others lecture her about the waiting room contact in a way that shames her.

Examiner Notes

A pass identifies the blood and the infection risk, modifies treatment and communicates with the team and consent. The candidate who writes an excellent exercise plan but ignores the sputum fails the safety question.

Case 38 (Mock 4, case 8 of 10): Profound weakness after prolonged critical illness on an acute care ward

Other Systems · Medical-surgical acute care ward, bedside, day 3 after transfer from the intensive care unit

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain your clinical impression of Gordon's weakness and describe the further assessment you would do to support or refine it, including how you would interpret the findings you have so far.

Examiner checklist

  • Interprets a sum score of 38 out of 60 as significant weakness, below the threshold of 48 used to identify acquired weakness critical
  • States an impression of ICU-acquired weakness and distinguishes likely polyneuropathy, myopathy or both
  • Identifies risk factors in his history such as sepsis, ventilation, sedation, steroids, hyperglycemia and immobility
  • Considers differentials such as stroke, spinal cord, Guillain-Barre syndrome, electrolyte problems, medication effect and deconditioning
  • Notes symmetric, proximal and distal weakness with preserved cranial nerves and sensation as consistent with the impression
  • Plans standardized measures such as repeat sum score, grip dynamometry, sit-to-stand and functional mobility scales, and tracks change
  • Examines the right calf: circumference, tenderness, warmth, swelling, and considers deep vein thrombosis risk with anticoagulation on hold critical
  • Checks respiratory muscle function, orthostatic response, delirium, nutrition and skin
  • Recommends discussion with the team about electrophysiology or other testing if the picture is unclear

Performance scale

4Gives a clear impression of ICU-acquired weakness with reasons from history and findings, interprets the sum score and grip, names differentials, plans specific measures and recognizes the calf finding as needing assessment.
3Reaches the correct impression with some support but limited differentials, measures or attention to the calf.
2Names the condition or lists tests without interpreting the findings.
1Misattributes the weakness, ignores the findings or overlooks the calf.

Model spoken answer

Based on what I have, my working impression is intensive care unit acquired weakness, most likely critical illness polyneuropathy, myopathy, or a combination of the two, on top of deconditioning. I will explain why. First, his history carries the classic risk factors: sepsis, 9 days of mechanical ventilation, sedation, a course of corticosteroids, diabetes, and 16 days in intensive care with limited movement. Second, the pattern fits. His weakness is symmetrical and affects both arms and legs, his cranial nerves and eye movements are normal, his sensation is intact, his reflexes are reduced rather than absent or brisk, and he is alert, so this is not a central problem. His Medical Research Council sum score is 38 out of 60. A score below 48 is the usual threshold for clinically significant acquired weakness, so he is well into that range, and a score at this level predicts a longer recovery and higher risk of complications. His grip, 8 and 10 kilograms, supports this because values under about 11 kilograms in men also indicate weakness. I would keep other possibilities in mind: a stroke or spinal cord problem, though symmetrical weakness with normal cranial nerves argues against them, Guillain-Barre syndrome, which would usually show absent reflexes and progress, electrolyte disturbances such as low potassium or phosphate, medication effects, and simple deconditioning, which does not usually produce this degree of weakness. Next steps in assessment. I would repeat the sum score and grip at consistent times, assess sitting balance, sit to stand with assistance, and use a functional scale suited to the ward, such as the Physical Function in ICU Test or the Functional Status Score for the ICU, so I can track change. I would check his breathing pattern and cough for respiratory muscle weakness, his blood pressure and heart rate when moving from lying to sitting, his cognition for delirium, his nutrition and skin. I would ask the physician whether electrophysiological testing or review of his electrolytes and creatine kinase would help. I would also examine his right calf now. It looks fuller than the left and he reports cramping. Pain in both legs can be from weakness, but with his anticoagulation on hold because of low platelets, I need to measure the calf, check warmth and tenderness, and talk to the nurse and physician today, before any mobilizing, about whether he needs imaging.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Describe the precautions you would take and the decisions you would make about whether and how to mobilize Gordon today, and how you would involve him and his wife in these decisions.

Examiner checklist

  • Holds mobilization of the legs until the calf has been assessed and a possible deep vein thrombosis has been discussed with the physician critical
  • Communicates the concern to the nurse and physician the same day and requests imaging and an anticoagulation decision critical
  • Continues safe bed-level activity that does not stress the right leg, such as upper limb and left leg active exercise, with clinician agreement
  • Uses contact precautions with correct personal protective equipment and equipment cleaning
  • Monitors heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2 and fatigue and sets stop criteria critical
  • Plans safe handling with a mechanical lift or sufficient staff once cleared, to avoid falls and injury to the shoulders
  • Explains risks and options to Gordon and his wife in plain language and respects his preferences
  • Addresses his wife's question honestly about recovery without false promises

Performance scale

4Withholds leg mobilization pending assessment of a possible clot, escalates same day, offers safe alternatives, sets monitoring and stop criteria, applies infection and handling precautions, and communicates honestly with Gordon and his wife.
3Recognizes the calf risk and takes appropriate precautions but is vague on escalation, monitoring or communication.
2Mentions precautions in general without addressing the calf or setting criteria.
1Mobilizes him on the legs without addressing the calf, or promises full recovery.

Model spoken answer

My main decision today is that I will not mobilize his legs until his right calf has been assessed, and I will not wait to raise it. His right calf is fuller than the left, he reports cramping, he has been immobile for weeks, he has sepsis and diabetes, and his preventive anticoagulation is on hold because of low platelets. That makes a deep vein thrombosis a real possibility, and walking, standing or vigorous leg exercise could dislodge a clot and cause a pulmonary embolism. So first I would examine the calf quickly and gently, measuring circumference at a marked point, checking warmth, tenderness and swelling. Whatever I find, I would tell his nurse and the physician today and ask for a decision about imaging and about whether anticoagulation can be restarted. Until I hear back, I would avoid active or passive exercise of the right leg and no standing, tilt table or transfers to chair. I can still do useful things safely: active and assisted exercises for his arms, deep breathing, positioning, and gentle active movement of the left leg, as the team agrees. Once there is no clot or it is treated, I would start sitting at the edge of the bed and progress. Second, his vital signs. I would check heart rate, blood pressure and SpO2 before, during and after activity, and stop if heart rate rises above an agreed limit, blood pressure drops, SpO2 falls below 90 percent, or he feels dizzy or very fatigued. His resting heart rate of 98 is a little high and I would watch it. Third, infection control. He is on contact precautions, so I would put on gown and gloves before entering and clean equipment such as the lift sling and any dynamometer afterward. Fourth, safe handling. When he is cleared, I would use the mechanical lift or enough staff, because with his weak shoulder girdle, pulling on his arms could injure him, and a fall would be serious. Finally, I would speak with Gordon and his wife in simple words. I would tell them I noticed something in the leg that needs checking first, that this delay is about keeping him safe, and ask what matters to him. About walking again, I would say that most people improve, but it can take weeks to months, and I would not promise a timeline.

Question 3: Practice Management

Discuss how you would manage your workload and the resources available today, including prioritization of patients, delegation to the physiotherapist assistant, equipment, infection control and documentation.

Examiner checklist

  • Prioritizes patients by acuity and risk, with those at risk of deterioration or needing urgent decisions seen first critical
  • Sees Gordon's calf concern early and communicates it before routine caseload critical
  • Delegates only stable, predictable tasks to the assistant with clear instructions, limits and a way to report concerns critical
  • Keeps assessment, clinical decision making and any patient with unclear status with the physiotherapist
  • Books shared equipment such as the lift and tilt table and cleans it between patients
  • Applies contact precautions, hand hygiene and equipment cleaning, including for the assistant
  • Documents findings, escalations, who was informed, treatment given and plan, in a timely manner
  • Communicates with nursing about the schedule and informs the manager if safe coverage is not possible

Performance scale

4Prioritizes by risk, acts early on the calf, delegates appropriate tasks with explicit limits and retains judgement tasks, plans shared equipment and infection control, documents promptly and escalates workload limits.
3Describes sound prioritization and delegation but is less detailed on equipment, infection control or documentation.
2Lists management tasks generally without linking to this workload or showing reasoning.
1Delegates unsafe tasks, ignores priority, or leaves Gordon's concern unaddressed.

Model spoken answer

With 14 patients and one assistant, I cannot give everyone equal time, so I would prioritize by risk and urgency. First, I would take two minutes at the start of the shift to review my list with the charge nurse, ask who is unstable, who has new orders, and who is going home. Patients who are deteriorating, who have new respiratory problems, or who need a discharge decision come first. Gordon would be near the top, not because he needs long treatment, but because of his calf and the decision about imaging and anticoagulation. I would assess and report his calf early so that the team can act while I see others, instead of discovering it at the end of the day. Second, delegation. The assistant can safely supervise stable patients with clear programs, for example a patient who is already walking with a cane and has an established exercise routine, or provide upper-limb range of motion for Gordon if I have specified exactly what is permitted. For each task I would give written, specific instructions, name the limits, such as heart rate, saturation, and pain, tell the assistant to stop and call me if anything changes, and tell them I will be reachable. I would not delegate the assessment of Gordon's calf, his first mobilizations after clearance, or any patient whose status is uncertain, because those need clinical judgement. Third, equipment. The lift and tilt table are shared across two floors, so I would book them in advance with the other ward, plan Gordon's use for when he is cleared, and clean them between patients. Fourth, infection control. For Gordon I would use gown and gloves under contact precautions, and I would tell the assistant the same rules and check that they clean shared equipment. Hand hygiene before and after every patient. Fifth, documentation. I would write my assessment, the calf measurements, who I informed and when, what the physician decided, what treatment I gave or held, and the plan, as soon as possible after each visit, not at the end of the day. Finally, if I cannot safely see everyone, I would tell the manager and the nurses which patients will not be seen today and why, so that nobody is unaware.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is the fuller, cramping right calf in a bedbound patient whose anticoagulation is on hold for low platelets. It may be a deep vein thrombosis. A competent candidate examines the calf, holds leg mobilization, escalates the same day and prioritizes Gordon early.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates give a good account of weakness and an exercise program but start standing or leg exercises without looking at the calf. Others delegate Gordon's first mobilization to the assistant.

Examiner Notes

A pass links the calf to the held anticoagulation and acts before mobilizing. Naming ICU-acquired weakness with the sum score of 38 is expected. Missing the calf is a fail on safety even with a strong assessment answer.

Case 39 (Mock 4, case 9 of 10): Hot, swollen knee with fever in a restaurant owner at a community clinic

Musculoskeletal · Private community physiotherapy clinic, direct access, late Thursday afternoon

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain your clinical reasoning about the cause of this knee presentation. Include what findings are most important, what other conditions you considered, and what you would conclude from the assessment.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies acute monoarthritis with fever, warmth, large effusion and severe pain on any motion as consistent with joint infection until proven otherwise critical
  • Lists risk factors: diabetes, recent intra-articular injection, possible skin break, age and existing joint disease critical
  • Notes that ibuprofen can mask fever and symptoms and that the temperature may understate the problem
  • Considers differentials such as gout, pseudogout, inflammatory arthritis, hemarthrosis, cellulitis and osteoarthritis flare
  • Explains why the old X-ray finding of wear and tear does not explain this presentation
  • Explains that infection cannot be excluded by physical examination and needs joint fluid analysis, blood tests and urgent medical assessment critical
  • Notes systemic signs such as heart rate 102 and fever suggesting possible sepsis
  • Avoids further provocative testing and limits examination to what is needed

Performance scale

4Concludes joint infection must be assumed, reasons from fever, severe pain on movement, effusion, diabetes, recent injection and masked fever, considers differentials but explains why they cannot be excluded, and states the need for same-day fluid analysis.
3Identifies infection as the leading concern and urgency but reasoning on risk factors or differentials is thin.
2Lists possible diagnoses without prioritizing infection or explaining the urgency.
1Concludes osteoarthritis flare or strain, or proposes treatment.

Model spoken answer

My conclusion is that Rashid has a hot, swollen joint with fever that must be treated as a joint infection until a physician proves otherwise, and that this is a medical emergency, not something I can treat or wait on. I will explain how I got there. First, the pattern. He has an acute single joint problem over two days with a large effusion, warmth and redness, and he holds the knee semi-flexed and resists passive motion because even small movement is very painful. That severe pain with any movement is what raises my concern most. Second, he has a temperature of 38.4 and a heart rate of 102, which suggest the body is reacting to something systemic. And he is taking ibuprofen three times a day, which lowers fever, so his real temperature may be higher and his picture may be worse than it looks. Third, his risk factors. He is 55 with diabetes, which lowers resistance to infection, he had a corticosteroid injection into this knee ten days ago, which is a recognized route for bacteria to enter the joint, and there is a small scab near the joint line, a possible skin entry point. Fourth, what else it could be. Gout or pseudogout can look the same, with a hot red joint and sometimes fever. An inflammatory arthritis, bleeding into the joint, cellulitis over the knee, or a flare of his osteoarthritis are possible, and a reaction to the injection can occur. But these cannot be separated from infection by looking at the knee or by the old X-ray, which only shows that he has osteoarthritis, not what is happening now. In fact, someone can have gout and infection together. Only joint fluid analysis, with cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals, along with blood tests such as white cell count and inflammatory markers and blood cultures, can tell. A delay of even a day or two can destroy cartilage and lead to bone infection or sepsis. So my conclusion is that he needs urgent same-day medical assessment at an emergency department, where the joint can be aspirated. I would not push on the joint further, I would not do any special tests that move it, and I would not try to treat it with manual therapy, heat or exercise.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Rashid says he wants to be treated now and will see his doctor on Monday. Describe what you would say and do in response, including how you would handle the situation and support his decision making.

Examiner checklist

  • Declines to provide treatment such as manual therapy, heat, exercise or taping and explains that it could cause harm critical
  • Explains in plain language the risk of joint destruction, spread of infection and sepsis if care is delayed critical
  • Recommends same-day emergency assessment and does not suggest waiting until Monday critical
  • Assesses decision-making capacity and confirms understanding using teach-back
  • Explores his reasons, such as the banquet and staff, and works on solutions such as asking a manager or a friend to take over
  • Offers to arrange transport or ambulance, and advises not to drive himself given pain and possible sepsis
  • If he still refuses, respects the informed refusal, explains return warning signs, gives written information and plans follow-up
  • Asks about someone who can be with him because he lives alone and his wife is away

Performance scale

4Respectfully explains the risk in plain words, recommends same-day emergency care, declines treatment, assesses capacity with teach-back, problem-solves his barriers, and if he refuses documents informed refusal with return precautions.
3Recommends urgent care and explains the risk but is less thorough on capacity, barriers or informed refusal.
2Suggests seeing the doctor soon or monitoring without urgency, or lectures without exploring his concerns.
1Provides treatment, agrees to wait until Monday, or overrides his choice without information.

Model spoken answer

I would begin by acknowledging his situation, the banquet, the pressure, being the only one who can run the kitchen, because he is more likely to listen if he feels heard. Then I would be direct and clear. I would say: Rashid, I am worried about your knee. Your knee is hot and swollen, you have a fever, and you have diabetes and had an injection in this joint ten days ago. These together can mean the joint is infected. That is serious. An infected joint can be damaged permanently within days, and the infection can spread to your blood. I cannot treat this in my clinic, and treatments like massage, heat or exercises could make it worse. I recommend that you go to the emergency department today, so a doctor can drain a sample of fluid and decide on antibiotics. Waiting until Monday is not safe. I would ask him to tell me in his own words what he understands, which is the teach-back, and ask what worries him most about going. If the worry is the banquet, we could problem-solve together: could a sous chef, a friend, a family member, or a caterer cover? Could the restaurant postpone? I would also ask who can take him and whether a friend or family member can stay with him tonight, since he lives alone and his wife is away, and I would check his emergency contact. He should not drive himself in severe pain with a fever. If he is unsteady or looks unwell, I would call an ambulance. He is alert and understands what I say, so I think he has capacity to decide, and it is his right to decide even if I disagree. If he still refuses after clear explanation, I would not argue or pressure him further, and I would still not provide treatment. I would document that he was informed of the risks, including permanent joint damage, sepsis, and death, and that he chose to decline. I would give him a written summary, tell him exactly what signs mean he must go immediately, such as shaking chills, a rising fever or heart rate, confusion, faintness or spreading redness, which means he must call 911 at once, and I would keep urging the emergency department tonight, not a walk-in clinic and not Monday, and ask him to let me phone him this evening to check. I would also ask permission to speak to his physician or the emergency doctor, since that is the safest thing for him.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Rashid asks you not to contact anyone. Discuss your professional responsibilities in this situation regarding consent, confidentiality, communication with other clinicians, documentation and your follow-up plan.

Examiner checklist

  • Seeks consent before sharing information and explains why contacting the emergency department or physician protects him critical
  • Recognizes that confidentiality has limits when there is serious risk and acts proportionately if he lacks capacity or is in imminent danger critical
  • Shares only the information needed with the receiving clinicians, such as findings, risk factors and timing
  • Reassures him that his staff will not be told and respects his privacy wishes where possible
  • Records his presentation, findings, advice, his decision, capacity, and the discussion in a timely and objective way critical
  • Acts within scope: does not diagnose definitively, aspirate or prescribe, and refers to the appropriate service
  • Arranges follow-up contact and confirms what happened, within what he agrees to
  • Reflects on whether the earlier injection or other events require reporting through the clinic or provider channels

Performance scale

4Seeks consent and explains the benefit, states limits of confidentiality accurately, shares minimum information, stays within scope, documents capacity and decisions, and arranges follow-up.
3Covers consent, confidentiality and documentation correctly but with limited detail on disclosure limits or follow-up.
2Names responsibilities in general terms without applying them to his request.
1Breaches his privacy without justification, agrees to do nothing, or oversteps scope.

Model spoken answer

My professional responsibilities here begin with respect for Rashid's autonomy and privacy and end with his safety, and I would work to meet both. First, consent. His information is his, so I would ask permission before I contact anyone. I would explain what I would like to do and why: phone the emergency department or his physician so that they know he is coming with a possibly infected joint and can see him quickly. I would explain that this helps him get care sooner, and ask if that is acceptable. I would be honest about what I will share, and I would tell him I will share only what is needed, such as his symptoms, temperature and heart rate, my findings, his diabetes and the recent injection, and nothing about his business or other personal details. I would assure him that I will not contact his staff or anyone he does not name, and that my clinic keeps his information private under provincial health privacy legislation. Second, the limits of confidentiality. If he declines but has capacity, I respect that wherever possible and keep urging urgent care, because adults have the right to refuse. I would only consider the minimum necessary disclosure if provincial privacy law and my regulator's standards allow it for a significant risk of serious harm, and I would tell him first. But if his condition worsened, if he became confused, faint, or could not decide, I would call emergency services, because disclosure to protect a person from serious harm is permitted when he cannot consent, and I would share the minimum needed. Third, scope. I am not able to diagnose an infection definitively, aspirate the knee or prescribe antibiotics, so my responsibility is to recognize the red flag, avoid harm, and refer to the right service promptly. Fourth, documentation. I would record the time, his history, vital signs, examination, my reasoning, my advice, his understanding and decision, capacity, who I contacted with consent, any written information I gave, and the follow-up plan, in clear objective language, and sign it. Fifth, follow-up. I would ask him to tell me where he is going, call him that evening with his permission, and if I cannot reach him I would follow my clinic's procedure. Finally, because he had an injection at another clinic, I would suggest he tell the treating doctor about it, and with his consent the treating physician and the clinic that gave the injection should be informed, so a possible post-injection infection can be reviewed and reported through their incident process. I would also reflect on whether anything in my own clinic process could help clients like him get seen faster.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issues are ibuprofen masking fever and the recent steroid injection with a possible skin entry point, together with his plan to wait three days. A competent candidate recognizes probable septic arthritis, declines treatment, urges same-day emergency care, respects capacity and consent, and documents.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates treat it as an osteoarthritis flare and offer gentle mobilization, or recommend a doctor visit on Monday. Others override his confidentiality request and phone his staff without thought.

Examiner Notes

A pass names infection as the working concern, refuses to treat, recommends the emergency department today, and handles consent and refusal properly. Offering any physical treatment or accepting a delay until Monday is a fail.

Case 40 (Mock 4, case 10 of 10): Recovery from a rapidly progressive nerve condition at transfer to rehabilitation

Neurological · Inpatient rehabilitation unit, first assessment on admission from acute care

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain how you would interpret Ana's current findings and what additional assessment you would carry out, including what the main problems are, which findings are expected and which concern you.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies the pattern as consistent with recovery from an acute demyelinating polyneuropathy with distal predominance, absent ankle reflexes and sensory loss
  • Recognizes the heart rate of 112 and the blood pressure fall from 134/82 to 92/58 on sitting as autonomic dysfunction with orthostatic hypotension critical
  • Notes symptoms of presyncope and pallor and treats them as a safety finding rather than deconditioning critical
  • Plans repeat orthostatic vital signs at stages of lying, sitting and standing, with timing, and identifies other autonomic signs such as sweating, bowel and bladder changes
  • Interprets the forced vital capacity of 2.1 L as reduced and plans monitoring of respiratory function
  • Plans standardized measures such as sum score, grip, Berg Balance Scale, 10-metre walk when possible, and a fatigue scale
  • Assesses neuropathic pain, joint range, skin, and foot drop impacts on gait and sets orthotic needs
  • Considers other causes of tachycardia and hypotension such as dehydration, infection, pulmonary embolism, medication and pain

Performance scale

4Separates expected neuropathy findings from the autonomic instability, quantifies orthostatic hypotension, recognizes it as a safety problem, plans staged assessment and measures, and considers other causes.
3Interprets the neuropathy well and recognizes blood pressure change but is thin on plan or differentials.
2Describes weakness and balance only, with limited mention of the blood pressure and heart rate change.
1Attributes dizziness to deconditioning or ignores the vital sign findings.

Model spoken answer

Let me separate what I expect from what worries me. What I expect: Ana's findings fit someone recovering from Guillain-Barre syndrome. Her weakness is symmetrical and more distal, her ankle reflexes are absent, her knee reflexes are reduced, her sensation is reduced in the feet, and she has foot drop. A sum score of 46 out of 60, grip of 12 kilograms, and a Berg of 24 out of 56 tell me she has moderate weakness and a high fall risk. She stands only with a walker and two helpers. Her burning foot pain at night is common, as is severe fatigue after small amounts of activity. Her forced vital capacity of 2.1 litres, about 65 percent of predicted, shows some residual respiratory muscle weakness after ventilation, so I would measure it regularly. What worries me most is not her strength. It is that her resting heart rate is 112 and that when I sat her up, her blood pressure fell from 134/82 to 92/58, and she turned pale and felt faint. That is a drop of 42 systolic, well over the 20 systolic or 10 diastolic that defines orthostatic hypotension. In this condition it points to autonomic dysfunction, which can cause both fast heart rates and unstable blood pressure, and the discharge summary has hints that this was seen before. It is a safety problem, because it can lead to fainting, falls and, in severe cases, dangerous arrhythmias. I would not call it deconditioning. I also have to rule out other contributors that could produce the same picture: dehydration, infection, a blood clot in the lung, pain, medication such as pain medication or blood pressure drugs, and bleeding. I would report to the physician today. For my assessment, I would repeat blood pressure and heart rate lying and then in staged head-up positions or on the tilt table at one and three minutes, progressing to standing only after the physician has advised and readings are stable, and ask about sweating, bowel and bladder function, and vision changes. I would also complete the rest of my examination in a staged way: repeat the sum score and grip, monitor fatigue with a scale, check her ankle and knee range, skin on her heels, and test sensation. I would use the Berg Balance Scale and, when she can, a 10-metre walk and sit to stand. And I would assess her foot drop and decide with the orthotist whether ankle-foot orthoses are needed. I would document the baseline so that we can show change.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Describe the safety precautions and decisions you would make for Ana's therapy this week, and how you would discuss her wish to push through the tiredness.

Examiner checklist

  • Reports the autonomic findings to the physician the same day and obtains guidance before progressing upright activity critical
  • Monitors blood pressure and heart rate lying, sitting and standing before and during therapy, with stop criteria critical
  • Uses gradual position changes, a tilt table or supported sitting, compression garments if the team agrees, and fluids as directed
  • Prescribes low-intensity, short, frequent sessions with rest, avoiding exhaustive or high-resistance exercise that can cause overwork weakness critical
  • Explains why pushing through fatigue can set back recovery and teaches energy conservation
  • Prevents falls: assistance, walker, gait belt, bed alarm and safe footwear or orthoses
  • Protects insensate feet and skin and positions joints to prevent contractures
  • Involves Ana in setting goals and uses motivational language to respect her drive

Performance scale

4Reports and responds to autonomic instability before upright progression, sets monitoring and stop criteria, prescribes low-intensity paced exercise, prevents falls and skin injury, and discusses her determination respectfully.
3Covers monitoring and pacing with reasonable safety measures but less detail on stop criteria, reporting or communication.
2Mentions general safety, falls and energy conservation without addressing blood pressure instability.
1Progresses standing and exercise despite hypotension or encourages pushing through fatigue.

Model spoken answer

My priorities this week are to keep her safe from her blood pressure changes and from overdoing it, and to do that together with Ana. First, the blood pressure. I would call the rehabilitation physician today, describe the numbers, 134/82 lying and 92/58 sitting with pallor and faintness, along with her resting heart rate of 112, and ask for guidance on monitoring, fluids, whether to use compression stockings or an abdominal binder, and any medication review. Until I hear back I would lay her flat, check her vital signs again, and not stand her up. After that, I would use gradual changes in position, for example raising the head of the bed in stages or using a tilt table, and check blood pressure and heart rate lying, then one and three minutes after each change. I would stop and lay her flat if the systolic falls by more than about 20 mmHg with symptoms, if she is pale, sweaty or dizzy, if her heart rate rises abnormally, or if she reports chest pain. I would keep a nurse informed so that nobody sits her up quickly on the ward. Second, the exercise dose. In this condition, too much exercise too soon can cause overwork weakness and a longer recovery. So I would plan short sessions of 10 to 15 minutes, several times a day, at light effort, no more than moderate on a perceived exertion scale, with rests, and avoid training to exhaustion or heavy resistance. I would stop when she is tired, not when she is exhausted, and monitor for a drop in strength or more pain the next day. I would talk to Ana directly about her wish to push through. I would say that I can see how determined she is, that this will help her recovery, but that her nerves are healing and tired nerves and muscles recover best with pacing, and that the tiredness she feels is a signal. We would set goals together, for example sitting in a chair for her meals, and I would show her how to track her fatigue. Third, falls and skin. I would use two assistants, a gait belt, and a walker when she stands, and a good-fitting ankle support for the foot drop. I would check her feet and heels for pressure because her sensation is reduced, and position her joints to prevent stiffness.

Question 3: Collaboration

Explain how you would collaborate with the rehabilitation team, Ana's family and her workplace, including who would be involved, what information would be shared, and how you would organize communication.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies rehabilitation team members and roles: physician, nursing, occupational therapist, speech-language pathologist, psychologist, dietitian, orthotist and social worker
  • Gives a structured report of the autonomic findings to physician and nursing and agrees shared monitoring rules critical
  • Obtains Ana's consent about what is shared with her husband, sister and employer critical
  • Holds a family meeting or teaching session with Ana's agreement, explaining expected recovery and pacing in plain language
  • Communicates with the school board only through what Ana authorizes, such as a general update from her physician rather than detailed health information
  • Agrees with occupational therapy on fatigue, self-care, and return to work planning, and with the psychologist on coping
  • Sets regular team goals review and a shared goals board or note
  • Plans for discharge and community follow-up, including home assessment and outpatient therapy

Performance scale

4Names team roles, gives a structured urgent report, obtains consent before sharing with family or employer, plans family education and a limited workplace update, coordinates with occupational therapy and others and includes discharge planning.
3Covers team and family communication with consent but with limited detail on structure, workplace or discharge.
2Lists professionals without describing communication, roles or consent.
1Shares details with the sister or employer without consent or omits the physician report.

Model spoken answer

Ana's recovery involves many people, so I would be clear about who does what and what each person needs from me. First, consent. She is an adult, awake and able to decide, so I would ask her what she would like me to share and with whom. Her husband is here and her sister is a nurse who is asking questions, but I would not give health details to her sister or her employer without Ana's agreement. I would ask Ana if she wants a family meeting, who she wants there, and what she wants discussed. Second, the rehabilitation team. The physician is the first person I need today, to report the blood pressure drop and the heart rate. I would give a short structured message: Ana, 42, Guillain-Barre syndrome five weeks ago, transferred today, heart rate 112 at rest, blood pressure 134/82 lying and 92/58 sitting with pallor and faintness, I have returned her to lying and I am holding upright activity, and I would like advice on monitoring and treatment. I would agree with nursing on shared rules: how often to check vital signs, how to change her position, and who to call. The occupational therapist and I would plan together so that fatigue, energy conservation, self-care and positioning are consistent and we are not both asking her to do the same tiring task on the same day. The psychologist can support her adjustment, since she is a mother and teacher facing a long recovery. The speech-language pathologist may be needed if she has swallowing or voice difficulty after ventilation. The dietitian can help with intake and weight. The orthotist can assess her foot drop for ankle-foot orthoses. A social worker can help with family needs and funding. Third, her family. With her agreement, I would run a session to explain the likely course: recovery can take months, may be incomplete, fatigue and pain are common, and pacing is important. I would use plain language, invite questions, and avoid promising a date. Fourth, work. The school board needs to know when she might return, but not the details. With her consent, her physician can provide a general update, and the occupational therapist can plan a graded return later. Finally, I would suggest a weekly team meeting with shared goals written in one place that Ana can see, and begin early discharge planning, including a home assessment and outpatient follow-up.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is autonomic dysfunction: resting heart rate 112 and a blood pressure fall from 134/82 to 92/58 with pallor and faintness on sitting. A competent candidate recognizes it, returns her to lying, reports to the physician, monitors with stop criteria, and does not mistake it for deconditioning.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates concentrate on strength, balance and gait training and never address the blood pressure, or they plan vigorous strengthening to match her drive. Others share information with the sister and school board freely.

Examiner Notes

A pass recognizes the autonomic instability, acts and reports it, and prescribes paced, low-intensity exercise. Planning upright and strengthening work without addressing the hypotension is a fail on safety.

Mock 5

Case 41 (Mock 5, case 1 of 10): Adolescent with a spinal curve found at school screening

Musculoskeletal · Pediatric outpatient physiotherapy clinic in a regional children's centre

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Using the findings provided, explain what you conclude about Amara's spinal presentation, what you would still need to rule out, and how you would decide on your next steps.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies a right thoracic curve of 28 degrees with Risser 1 as consistent with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis with significant growth remaining.
  • Recognizes idiopathic scoliosis is a diagnosis of exclusion and that atypical features need further workup. critical
  • Flags the asymmetric abdominal skin reflexes as an atypical neurological finding that does not fit idiopathic scoliosis. critical
  • Links recent menarche and rapid growth to a higher risk of curve progression.
  • Explains that a 28 degree curve in a skeletally immature adolescent sits in the range where bracing is usually considered.
  • Proposes further questions about headache, back pain at night, sensory changes, bladder or bowel changes and gait.
  • Plans a full neurological exam including cranial nerves, tone, clonus, plantar responses and gait.
  • States that a neurological abnormality leads to prompt communication with the physician for referral rather than starting treatment. critical
  • Mentions the scoliometer is a screening tool and does not replace the radiograph for measuring the curve.
  • Treats the volleyball ache and backpack use as minor contributors rather than causes of the curve.

Performance scale

4Names probable adolescent idiopathic scoliosis with progression risk factors, identifies the asymmetric abdominal reflex as atypical, outlines a targeted neurological screen, and commits to physician communication before treatment.
3Recognizes the curve and progression risk and mentions the reflex, but is vague about the action or the reasoning behind it.
2Describes scoliosis and treatment options but treats the reflex finding as minor or does not plan further screening.
1Proceeds to treatment without addressing the neurological finding, or blames sport or posture for the curve.

Model spoken answer

First, my impression. The right thoracic rib hump, the shoulder asymmetry and a Cobb angle of 28 degrees fit adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Her Risser grade of 1 means she has a lot of growth left, and she has just had her first period and grown 6 centimetres this year. Those are the factors that make a curve more likely to progress, so I treat this as a curve that needs active management, not simple watching. The scoliometer reading of 9 degrees is only a screen; the radiograph Cobb angle of 28 degrees is what measures the curve.

Second, and this is what I would not let slide, idiopathic scoliosis is what we call it only after other causes are excluded. One finding does not fit. The abdominal skin reflexes are present on the right and absent on the left. A one sided loss of these reflexes can point to a problem in the spinal cord or brainstem, such as a syrinx or a Chiari type malformation, and such conditions can come with a curve. It is not a diagnosis, but it is enough to stop me from simply starting an exercise program.

Third, I would extend my screening. I would ask about headaches, especially with coughing, neck pain, numbness, hand clumsiness, changes in how she walks, and any bladder or bowel changes. I would examine cranial nerves, tone, deep tendon reflexes, clonus, plantar responses, sensation, and look for a foot deformity such as a high arch. I would watch her walk and do a tandem walk.

Fourth, the decision. If I find any other neurological sign, or if the reflex finding holds up, I contact the family physician the same day, explain exactly what I found, and ask for further assessment, which may include MRI and a pediatric spine referral. I would not delay that referral to run a trial of exercise. If the exam is otherwise completely normal, I would still tell the physician about the reflex asymmetry, because the decision about imaging belongs with them, and I would ask for a pediatric spine opinion because a curve of 28 degrees at Risser 1 is in the range where bracing is usually considered.

Finally, I would be honest with Amara and her father, in plain words, that the shape of her back is a spinal curve, that this is common, that it is not caused by volleyball or her backpack, and that I want one more check before we plan treatment. That keeps them informed and avoids frightening them.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Amara says she is afraid of a brace and wants to stop volleyball. Discuss how you would respond, including the safety considerations and how you would involve Amara in the decisions.

Examiner checklist

  • Acknowledges Amara's fear and body image concerns before giving information.
  • Speaks to Amara directly as the person affected, while including her father. critical
  • Explains that bracing aims to stop progression, not to correct the curve, and is worn for set hours.
  • Clarifies that the brace decision belongs to the spine specialist team and the family, not to the physiotherapist alone.
  • States that volleyball does not cause or worsen scoliosis and that sport is generally encouraged.
  • Explains why any activity limit is temporary and minimal, advises stopping and reporting new symptoms, and gives clear return criteria. critical
  • Asks what matters most to Amara and what she is most worried about being seen.
  • Offers options to ease brace concerns such as clothing advice, peer support or talking with other teens who wear a brace.
  • Screens for low mood or anxiety linked to appearance and plans to share concerns with the physician if present.
  • Checks understanding using teach back, assesses Amara's capacity to consent, and involves her father with her agreement. critical

Performance scale

4Centres Amara's voice, explains brace aims accurately, corrects the sport myth while keeping any activity limit minimal, temporary and explained, and checks understanding and consent.
3Handles the emotional side and sport advice well but is vague about the specialist decision or consent.
2Gives information on bracing and sport but speaks mainly to the father or ignores the reason for the pending medical review.
1Dismisses her fear, says she must quit sport indefinitely, or promises a brace outcome.

Model spoken answer

I would start with Amara, not with the curve. I would turn to her, since she is the one who will live with this, and say that it makes sense to be worried about a brace, and ask her to tell me what she imagines. Often a teen has a picture of an old metal device, and today's braces are different. I would ask what matters most to her. If it is volleyball and her friends, that tells me what a good plan has to protect.

On the volleyball question, I would be direct. Volleyball did not cause her curve, and nothing she does in practice will make it worse. Staying active is good for her, so she can keep doing light, pain-free activity, and her usual volleyball if my full examination finds nothing new, while the physician reviews one finding I want checked. The only limit is to stop and tell me if anything new appears, such as numbness, weakness, new back pain or a change in how she moves. I would tell her what the check is for, in simple terms, so it does not sound like a punishment, and I would say that any restriction would be temporary and minimal, with a clear point at which she is cleared.

On bracing, I would explain what I know and the limits of my role. A brace is meant to hold the curve where it is while she finishes growing, not to straighten it. Whether she needs one is decided with the spine specialist team, using her X-ray and how much growing she has left. I am not the one deciding this alone, and I would not promise that she will or will not need one. What I can do is make sure she understands the options so that she can take part in the conversation.

I would offer practical help. Many teens wear a brace under loose clothing, and worn hours can often be set around school and sport. I could connect her with a peer support group or another teen who has worn one, if she wants that.

I would watch for how she is coping. Body image worries in adolescents with scoliosis are real, and if I notice withdrawal, low mood or persistent anxiety, I would tell her father and the family physician so they can help.

Finally, I would ask her and her father to explain back to me what we agreed, so I know my words made sense. I would assess Amara's capacity to consent, which in Canada depends on understanding rather than a set age. If she is capable, her consent is what counts, and I would still involve her father with her agreement. I would write down what each of them decided.

Question 3: Practice Management

Your clinic has a long waiting list, limited insurance coverage and a physiotherapist assistant. Describe how you would organize Amara's care and documentation, including what you would and would not delegate.

Examiner checklist

  • Prioritizes Amara's visit and follow up based on clinical risk rather than the order of the waiting list.
  • Documents the abdominal reflex asymmetry, the examination findings and the communication with the physician with dates and times. critical
  • Does not delegate assessment, interpretation of neurological findings or changes to the plan to the assistant. critical
  • Identifies tasks suitable for delegation once the plan is set, such as supervised exercise practice with a written program.
  • Describes supervising and checking in with the assistant, and clear criteria for the assistant to stop and call the physiotherapist.
  • Plans scheduling around the father's Thursday availability and makes the best use of ten insured visits.
  • Requests clarification of the vague referral and sends a clear written summary to the physician.
  • Records a baseline outcome measure such as a scoliosis quality of life questionnaire and asks the physician to set the plan for repeat curve monitoring.
  • Avoids ordering or arranging repeated radiographs herself and defers imaging decisions to the physician.
  • Explains fees and coverage honestly and avoids proposing unneeded visits to use up insurance.

Performance scale

4Prioritizes by clinical risk, documents the flagged finding and the physician contact, delegates only after a plan with explicit boundaries and supervision, and handles funding honestly.
3Covers scheduling, documentation and delegation sensibly but with thin boundaries or no stop rules.
2Lists generic administrative tasks without linking them to Amara's risk or the assistant's limits.
1Delegates the assessment or neurological findings to the assistant, or books visits to use coverage.

Model spoken answer

I would organize this in three parts: what happens first, what is documented, and who does what.

First, scheduling. Amara has a finding that needs action, so she does not wait her turn on the list. I would complete the full neurological exam at this visit and contact the family physician promptly, then book her next visit soon, on a Thursday so her father can come. I would not tuck this into a routine slot. The referral just says to treat scoliosis, so I would write back to the physician with a clear summary: the curve, the Cobb angle and Risser grade, the absent left abdominal reflex, what I tested, and my request for further assessment and a pediatric spine opinion. I would ask them to confirm they received it.

Second, documentation. I would record the history, the scoliometer reading, the full neurological findings including the reflex asymmetry, the advice I gave Amara and her father about activity, their questions, their agreement, and the time I contacted the physician and what was said. If the physician does not reply in the time I expect, I would follow up and note it. Good notes protect Amara, because another clinician reading them will see at once that something was flagged.

Third, delegation. I would not delegate the assessment, the interpretation of any neurological finding, or any decision to change the plan. Those need my judgment and are mine to answer for. Once the physician has weighed in and the plan is set, my assistant can supervise Amara practicing a written exercise program that I design and teach first. I would show the assistant exactly what to watch for and give clear stop rules: new pain, numbness, weakness, dizziness, or anything the assistant is unsure about means stop and get me. I would watch the first session, then check in regularly and review notes.

I would record a baseline outcome measure such as the SRS-22 questionnaire and ask the physician to set the plan for repeat radiographs to monitor the curve. On funding, the ten insured visits are limited, so I would be upfront with the family about how I plan to use them, spacing visits with a home program rather than filling the calendar. I would not book extra visits just because coverage exists. Repeat X-rays are the physician's decision, so I would not arrange them myself.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The absent left abdominal skin reflex is an atypical neurological sign that can accompany a syrinx or Chiari malformation. A candidate who treats this as classic idiopathic scoliosis and starts exercise has missed the buried issue. The competent path is a full neurological exam, same day communication with the physician and a request for imaging and specialist review before treatment.

Common Candidate Errors

Starting a scoliosis specific exercise program straight away without addressing the reflex finding, and promising the family that exercise will correct the curve. A second error is delegating the follow up screening to the assistant or saying volleyball must stop without a clear reason.

Examiner Notes

A pass identifies the reflex asymmetry as a reason to escalate before treating, speaks to Amara directly, and sets firm limits on delegation. A fail treats this as straightforward idiopathic scoliosis or gives a brace or cure promise.

Case 42 (Mock 5, case 2 of 10): Positional spinning after a neck adjustment

Neurological · Outpatient physiotherapy clinic in a community health centre

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Based on the history and screening findings, explain your working impression, what must be considered before you perform positional testing, and how you would proceed.

Examiner checklist

  • States that the brief positional spinning with no hearing symptoms fits benign paroxysmal positional vertigo as a probable cause.
  • Recognizes the recent rapid cervical rotation with new occipital headache and neck pain as a possible sign of cervical artery injury. critical
  • Explains that vertebral artery dissection can present with vertigo and headache and can cause stroke. critical
  • Decides not to proceed with provocative neck extension and rotation testing until the vascular concern is addressed. critical
  • Plans to ask about neck pain, visual changes, double vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, facial numbness and drop attacks.
  • Notes that blood pressure is elevated and checks both arms or repeats the measurement.
  • Recommends same-day emergency assessment with vascular imaging and communicates with the emergency department and physician.
  • Distinguishes peripheral from central causes using nystagmus pattern, persistence and associated neurological signs.
  • Mentions that BPPV can be confirmed later with positional testing and supine roll tests once safe.

Performance scale

4Names BPPV as probable, identifies the manipulation plus headache as a possible vertebral artery injury, withholds provocative testing, and acts on urgent medical communication.
3Recognizes both BPPV and the vascular concern but is hesitant about withholding the test or about urgency.
2Focuses on BPPV and mentions the neck adjustment without letting it change the plan.
1Performs positioning tests or the manoeuvre without addressing the vascular risk.

Model spoken answer

My working impression has two layers, and the second one drives what I do.

The first layer is what her symptoms look like. Short spells of spinning, 20 to 30 seconds, brought on by rolling over or looking up, with nausea and no hearing loss or ear fullness, fit benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, most likely the posterior canal. That is the most common cause of this story in her age group, and it is very treatable.
