The second layer is what the history also contains. Five days ago she had a rapid neck rotation adjustment, and since then she has a dull occipital headache. The spinning began the day after, and the headache has been there since. Neck manipulation is a recognized risk factor for injury to the vertebral artery, and a dissection can present with vertigo, neck pain and a back of the head headache, sometimes before any other sign. She also has hypertension that is not well controlled today. Her neurological screen is normal, which is reassuring, but a normal screen does not rule out a dissection, and the main danger is a stroke in the days that follow.

So before I do anything that puts her neck in extension and rotation, as a Dix-Hallpike does, I want to question and screen further. I would ask about neck pain, visual disturbance, double vision, trouble speaking or swallowing, facial numbness, limb weakness, and any episode of near fainting. I would check blood pressure again, and in both arms. I would look for nystagmus at rest, since persistent or vertical nystagmus would point to a central cause.

I would not do the positional test today. Even a test that is usually safe is not worth the risk until a vascular cause has been considered. Given a new headache and neck pain after a manipulation, I suspect a cervical artery dissection, so I would recommend same-day emergency assessment with vascular imaging, and I would phone ahead to the emergency department with my findings and let her physician know. If she has any neurological symptom, she goes by ambulance, and in every case not by her own driving.

Once a dissection has been properly excluded by the medical team, I would come back and confirm BPPV with positional testing and treat it.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Marguerite asks you to perform the manoeuvre her friend had and says she needs to keep driving. Explain how you would respond, including her safety and her involvement in the decision.

Examiner checklist

  • Acknowledges her wish for quick relief and her work worries without dismissing them.
  • Explains in plain language why you are not doing the manoeuvre today and what you are concerned about. critical
  • Avoids frightening language while being clear about the possible seriousness of her symptoms.
  • Advises her not to drive until medically cleared and explains why. critical
  • Gives red flag symptoms and exactly what to do if they occur, including calling emergency services. critical
  • Arranges safe transport home or to the emergency department and does not leave her unsupported.
  • Gives fall prevention advice for the interim such as rising slowly and avoiding heights.
  • Recommends emergency assessment today and involves her in how she gets there and who accompanies her.
  • Checks her understanding with teach back and obtains her consent to share information with her physician. critical

Performance scale

4Responds with empathy, explains the reason for withholding the manoeuvre truthfully, stops driving, gives clear red flags and emergency instructions, and confirms consent and understanding.
3Explains and advises on driving and red flags but with limited shared decision making or no teach back.
2Declines the manoeuvre with little explanation or gives incomplete safety advice.
1Agrees to do the manoeuvre, permits driving, or alarms her without a clear plan.

Model spoken answer

I would begin by telling her I understand. Spinning is frightening, her job depends on driving, and her friend got better quickly. Wanting the same thing is reasonable and I would say so.

Then I would explain, in plain words, why I am not doing it today. I would say something like: your symptoms are very likely from a small problem in the inner ear that I can treat, and I expect to be able to help you. But you also had a quick twist of the neck five days ago and you now have a headache at the back of your head. Sometimes that kind of neck movement can injure a blood vessel in the neck. It is uncommon, but it matters because it can lead to a stroke. The manoeuvre puts the neck in a position I do not want to use until a doctor has checked that. I would not hide the reason, and I would not say she has a serious problem, because I do not know that.

On driving, I would be clear. Until a physician has assessed her, she should not drive. Sudden spinning at the wheel is a danger to her and to others. I would offer to help with practical steps, such as arranging a ride, and I would explain that I can provide a note stating she needs medical assessment, which may also help her workplace plan.

I would give her the warning signs: sudden severe headache, worsening neck pain, double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, numbness of the face or limbs, weakness, loss of balance, or fainting. If any of these happens she calls 911 and does not drive herself.

I would let her take part in the decision. I recommend emergency assessment today. I would explain my reasoning and ask her how she would like to get there and who can go with her. For the days until she is seen, I would suggest rising slowly, sitting to dress, and avoiding ladders or reaching overhead.

I would ask her to repeat back the plan and warning signs, and ask her permission to phone her physician and share my findings.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Marguerite's workplace plan wants a note saying she can return to driving next week, and she asks you not to tell her physician about the neck adjustment. Describe how you would handle your professional responsibilities in this situation.

Examiner checklist

  • States that you cannot certify fitness to drive or make a return to driving decision that is outside your scope in this situation. critical
  • Explains that withholding the neck adjustment history from the physician could harm her and that you will share it with her knowledge. critical
  • Describes seeking her informed consent for disclosure and what to do if she refuses, within provincial privacy law.
  • Recognizes duty of care to act on an urgent safety concern even if the client is reluctant, using the least disclosure needed.
  • Documents the history, the findings, the advice given, the driving advice and her response.
  • Offers a factual note describing what you found and recommended, without stating she is fit to drive.
  • Notes that the provincial driver licensing authority and medical reporting rules are a matter for the physician.
  • Avoids criticizing the practitioner who did the adjustment and, if appropriate, advises on how she can raise concerns through the proper regulator.
  • Keeps follow up and treatment planning dependent on medical clearance.

Performance scale

4Declines to certify driving, offers an accurate factual note, secures consent for disclosure with a reasoned approach to refusal, documents fully and avoids blaming.
3Handles the note and disclosure appropriately but is vague on privacy law, refusal or documentation.
2Raises scope or confidentiality but gives an incomplete or inconsistent resolution.
1Writes the return to drive note, or agrees to conceal a safety relevant history.

Model spoken answer

There are two requests here, and I would treat them separately.

The first is the note saying she can drive next week. I cannot write that. Deciding whether someone is fit to drive is a medical judgment that depends on a diagnosis I do not yet have, and in my province it sits with her physician and the licensing authority, not with me. If I wrote it and she had an episode on the road, I would have put her and others at risk and stepped outside my scope. What I can do is write a factual letter for her workplace plan stating that she was seen on this date, that she has symptoms requiring medical assessment, and that she has been advised not to drive until a physician has assessed her. That is true and it supports her claim without overstating anything.

The second is her request that I not tell her physician about the neck adjustment. This is her information, and I would respect her right to control it, but I would not simply agree. I would explain why it matters: her physician needs that detail to decide what tests she needs, and without it she could be missed or delayed. I would ask for her consent to share, and ask what her worry is. Sometimes people fear being blamed or embarrassed. I would reassure her that nobody is blaming her. If she agrees, I phone and also send a written summary, sharing what is needed for the assessment and nothing more.

If she still refuses, I would not act behind her back as a first step. I would explain again, keep my advice clear, and document her decision and my explanation. However, if I judged there was a serious and imminent risk to her life, such as new neurological signs, I would follow my regulator's standards and provincial privacy legislation, which allow limited disclosure to prevent serious harm, disclosing only what is necessary, and I would tell her what I was doing. I would consult my regulator or my employer's privacy officer if I was unsure.

I would document everything: the history, the findings, my reasoning for not testing, the driving advice, her consent decisions, and who I contacted and when. I would not criticize the other practitioner. If she has concerns about that care, I would tell her how a complaint can be made to the relevant regulator, and leave the choice to her.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

A rapid neck rotation adjustment followed by new occipital headache and vertigo raises the possibility of cervical artery dissection. The candidate must find this, withhold provocative neck positioning, advise against driving and involve medical care urgently. The distractor is the classic BPPV story that invites an immediate Epley manoeuvre.

Common Candidate Errors

Performing a Dix-Hallpike and Epley manoeuvre because the story sounds like BPPV, and agreeing to the return to drive note. A second error is accepting the client's request to keep the neck adjustment from the physician.

Examiner Notes

A pass holds two diagnoses in mind, withholds the test, advises against driving and handles disclosure and the note within scope. A fail treats the case as routine BPPV.

Case 43 (Mock 5, case 3 of 10): Young adult with epilepsy starting a fitness program

Neurological · Outpatient neurology rehabilitation clinic in a university hospital

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain what you would conclude from Tomas's history and examination about his readiness to exercise, and which findings you would explore further before finalizing a plan.

Examiner checklist

  • States that regular exercise is generally recommended for people with epilepsy and that Tomas has no neuromotor limitations on testing.
  • Identifies the possible rash after a recent lamotrigine dose increase as needing medical review before exercise begins. critical
  • Explains that rash with lamotrigine can signal a serious hypersensitivity reaction, so the itchy skin is not assumed to be laundry soap. critical
  • Plans to inspect the skin and ask about fever, mouth sores, swollen glands, sore throat or blistering.
  • Recognizes missed doses, short sleep and alcohol as seizure triggers affecting risk.
  • Asks about seizure triggers, auras, warning time, injuries and seizure types, and whether exercise has ever triggered one.
  • Notes that 7 months seizure free is not long enough to treat him as low risk for water activities without precautions.
  • Uses vital signs and a submaximal walk test to set a baseline exercise intensity.
  • Identifies the need to communicate with the neurologist about the rash and about clearance for the specific activities. critical

Performance scale

4Finds him physically ready, treats the rash after the lamotrigine increase as a medical priority, explores triggers and seizure risk, and plans neurologist contact.
3Identifies rash and triggers but is slow to prioritize the rash or lacks reasoning on its seriousness.
2Assesses fitness and seizure triggers but accepts the soap explanation or does not escalate.
1Clears him to begin training without addressing the rash.

Model spoken answer

My conclusion has two parts: he is physically ready, and he is not yet ready to start because of something in the history.

Physically, Tomas has a normal examination. His strength, balance, coordination and gait are fine, blood pressure and heart rate are normal, and he walked 640 metres in six minutes, which is a good base for a young adult. Exercise is generally recommended in epilepsy. It supports mood, sleep and fitness, and it does not usually raise seizure frequency. So I support the goal.

The finding I would pursue first is the itchy skin on his chest and back. He thinks it is laundry soap, but the timing matters. His lamotrigine was raised three weeks ago, and rash is a known effect of this drug, usually in the first weeks after starting or increasing it. Most rashes are mild, but a small number are the start of a serious hypersensitivity reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and that can get worse fast. I cannot tell the difference by looking, and it is not my role to decide. So I would look at the skin today with his permission, and ask about fever, sore throat, mouth or eye sores, blistering, swollen glands, and feeling unwell. If he has any of those, he needs same day emergency care. Even if he does not, I would contact his neurologist or physician today and say what I saw. I would hold the start of exercise until the rash is reviewed.

Second, I want to understand his seizure risk. Seven months without a seizure is encouraging but not long, and I would ask about auras, how much warning he gets, whether he has ever injured himself, and whether exercise or overheating has ever set one off. Sleeping five hours, missing two doses this month and drinking on weekends are all recognized triggers, so these raise his risk more than the exercise itself.

Third, I would use his resting vitals and walk test to choose a starting intensity, using the talk test and perceived effort.

Finally, I would ask his neurologist to confirm clearance for the specific activities, especially swimming.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Tomas wants to swim alone at 6 a.m. and does not want anyone at the gym to know about his epilepsy. Discuss how you would advise him on safe activity and respect his preferences.

Examiner checklist

  • Advises against swimming alone and explains that a seizure in water can lead to drowning. critical
  • Recommends a supervised setting with a lifeguard present, or a swim buddy who knows what to do. critical
  • Respects his right to decide who is told about his epilepsy and explores options for limited disclosure. critical
  • Explores the reasons for his fear of stigma without judgment.
  • Offers safer alternatives while swimming is not cleared, such as walking, stationary cycling or running on a track with company.
  • Gives precautions for cycling and running such as avoiding unsupervised heights, traffic and extreme heat and dehydration.
  • Addresses sleep, medication adherence and alcohol as part of safe participation.
  • Describes a basic seizure first aid plan and suggests he carry medical identification.
  • Confirms understanding and agreement and records his choices.

Performance scale

4Clearly advises against swimming alone with reasons, offers safer options, respects confidentiality while explaining the value of limited disclosure, and addresses triggers.
3Gives sound safety advice but is thin on respecting disclosure choices or alternatives.
2Lists generic precautions without firm advice on the swimming risk.
1Allows solo swimming or discloses his condition without his consent.

Model spoken answer

I would begin by saying that I want him to be active, and that my goal is a plan he will actually follow. That keeps the conversation about what he can do.

On swimming alone at 6 a.m., I would be firm and honest. Of all the activities he mentioned, water is the one where a seizure can be fatal, because a person who loses awareness can go under and not be noticed, and with only a lifeguard at peak hours nobody would be watching at that time. Seven months without a seizure does not remove the risk. So I would advise him not to swim alone, and not to swim at that hour unless a lifeguard is on duty. I would explain the choices that would let him swim: swimming at staffed times, or with a buddy who knows what to do and stays close, and a conversation with his neurologist about clearance. Until that is sorted, I would suggest he begin with land activities.

For the land activities, I would give specific precautions. For the spin class, a stationary bike is reasonable, as long as he is not riding to the point of dehydration or overheating. For running, I would suggest a track or a familiar route with a running partner, away from traffic, ravines and water, and I would suggest avoiding heat and keeping up fluids. I would add that sleep, taking his medication every day and limiting alcohol matter as much as the exercise plan.

On disclosure, I would respect that it is his information and his choice. I would ask what worries him. Many people fear being treated differently. I would not tell the gym. I would explain that telling one trusted person, like a swim partner or class instructor, can make a big difference in an emergency, and he decides who and how much to say. I could help him word a short statement such as, 'I have epilepsy that is controlled. If I have a seizure, I need time and space, and I should not be restrained.'

I would also review basic seizure first aid, suggest a medical alert bracelet, and ask him to repeat back the plan. I would note his decisions in the chart.

Question 3: Collaboration

Describe how you would collaborate with the other people involved in Tomas's care, including what you would communicate, to whom, and how you would manage his privacy.

Examiner checklist

  • Obtains Tomas's consent before contacting anyone and specifies what will be shared. critical
  • Contacts his neurologist or prescribing physician promptly about the rash and the missed doses. critical
  • Gives the neurologist objective information such as the timing of the dose increase, skin findings and symptoms.
  • Asks the neurologist for specific clearance and limits for swimming, cycling and running.
  • Involves the family physician or student health service as appropriate and clarifies who is the lead for follow up.
  • Considers a pharmacist for medication adherence strategies such as reminders or blister packs.
  • Describes how to work with the campus recreation staff without revealing diagnosis unless Tomas agrees.
  • Offers a referral to a social worker or counsellor for stress, sleep and stigma concerns.
  • Agrees on a feedback loop with a time frame and documents the communication.

Performance scale

4Seeks consent, contacts the neurologist promptly with factual information and specific questions, clarifies the lead, uses allied professionals sensibly, and protects privacy at the gym.
3Includes the right people and consent but is vague on content, timing or the lead.
2Names team members without a clear purpose or ignores his privacy preferences.
1Shares his diagnosis with the gym without consent or does not involve the prescriber about the rash.

Model spoken answer

I would begin with Tomas. Before I speak to anyone, I would ask his permission and tell him what I want to share and with whom. He is worried about being treated differently, so how I handle his privacy will decide whether he trusts the plan.

The first call is to his neurologist, today, because of the rash. I would say clearly what I saw and when: that his lamotrigine went from 150 to 200 milligrams three weeks ago, that he now has an itchy rash on the chest and back, whether or not he has fever or mouth sores, that he has missed two doses and is sleeping five hours. I would give facts and not guess at the cause. I would ask whether he needs to be seen the same day, and I would ask what instructions I should give him in the meantime. I would also ask for specific guidance on exercise: whether he is cleared for swimming and under what conditions, and any limits on intensity or heat.

Then I would ask who leads his care. If the neurologist is the lead for his epilepsy, I update them, and I let his family physician or student health clinic know if he is also followed there, so that nobody assumes someone else is watching the rash. I would agree on when I will hear back and what I will do if I do not.

I would suggest to Tomas that a pharmacist can help with missed doses, with reminders, a pill organizer or blister packs, and can advise on drug interactions and alcohol. A counsellor or social worker at student health could support his stress, sleep and worry about stigma, and I would offer that as an option, not a requirement.

With campus recreation, I would only share what he agrees to. If he is comfortable, I could ask staff to arrange for a lifeguard at a time he can swim, without naming his diagnosis, or he might choose to tell one instructor. His choice stands.

I would document what I shared, with whom, his consent, and the replies, and I would review progress with him at the next visit.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The itchy rash three weeks after a lamotrigine dose increase is the buried issue: it may be an early serious hypersensitivity reaction and must be reviewed medically before exercise starts. The second issue is the unsupervised early morning swim. A competent candidate finds both and respects the client's control over disclosure.

Common Candidate Errors

Accepting the laundry soap explanation and writing a training program, and forbidding all exercise on the basis of epilepsy alone. A second error is telling the gym about his diagnosis without consent.

Examiner Notes

A pass escalates the rash, forbids solo swimming with reasons, and keeps Tomas in charge of disclosure. A fail clears him for exercise without raising the rash or breaches his privacy.

Case 44 (Mock 5, case 4 of 10): Calf swelling nine days after hip replacement

Cardiovascular-Respiratory · Outpatient physiotherapy clinic attached to a community hospital

Question 1: Care Planning

Outline your plan of care for today's visit and the next 48 hours, and explain the reasoning behind your priorities.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes calf swelling, pitting edema, tenderness and recent surgery as making deep vein thrombosis likely, using a clinical prediction rule.
  • Holds all exercise, manual therapy, massage and compression of the leg today. critical
  • Recognizes shortness of breath, a heart rate of 102 and saturation of 94 percent as possible signs of pulmonary embolism. critical
  • Explains that same day diagnostic imaging and medical assessment are required and she should not wait until Monday. critical
  • Notes that stopping the anticoagulant without telling the surgeon increases the risk of clot formation.
  • Plans repeat vital signs and monitoring of symptoms while arranging transfer.
  • Sets goals for the next 48 hours focused on safety and assessment rather than hip rehabilitation.
  • Plans to resume the hip rehabilitation program only after medical clearance, with reassessment triggers.
  • Describes the information to give the receiving team: timeline, surgery, medication change, findings and vitals.
  • Arranges ambulance transport rather than a private vehicle and keeps her at rest and monitored until paramedics arrive.

Performance scale

4Identifies a likely DVT with possible PE, stops treatment, arranges ambulance transfer for emergency assessment, plans monitoring and a clear handover, and defers rehabilitation until cleared.
3Recognizes the DVT and urgency but is slower to link the breathlessness or the medication lapse, or has a thin handover.
2Suspects a clot but proposes to continue modified treatment or to wait for the surgeon on Monday.
1Continues rehabilitation, massages the leg or treats it as routine post operative swelling.

Model spoken answer

My plan has one main priority for today, which is to get Priya assessed for a blood clot, and everything else waits.

Here is my reasoning. Nine days after hip surgery, she has a right calf that is 3.5 centimetres bigger than the left, pitting edema, tenderness over the deep calf, warmth, and she has had these for three days. Using a prediction rule such as the Wells criteria, surgery in the last 12 weeks, calf swelling over 3 centimetres, pitting edema and localized tenderness already add up to a score that makes a deep vein thrombosis likely. On top of that, she stopped her anticoagulant four days ago. I cannot confirm or exclude a clot in the clinic. That needs imaging, usually an ultrasound, and that is a medical decision.

The breathlessness changes things further. Shortness of breath on stairs since yesterday, a heart rate of 102 and an oxygen saturation of 94 percent could mean a clot has reached the lungs. I would not wait for the surgeon's office to open on Monday.

So today, I stop the session. No exercise, no manual therapy, no massage and no compression wrap or stocking over that leg, because these could move a clot. I keep her sitting or lying comfortably, recheck her vital signs, and ask about chest pain, cough, blood in the sputum, light-headedness or fainting. With a likely clot and possible pulmonary embolism, I call 911 now for ambulance transfer, and she does not drive or go by private vehicle. I keep her at rest and monitored until the paramedics arrive, and if she is worse I tell the dispatcher right away. She has the right to decide, so I explain the risk plainly and ask what worries her about going, but I make a clear recommendation.

In the next 48 hours, my goals are safety, a diagnosis and restarting the anticoagulant, if the medical team decides that. I would hand over the history clearly: date of surgery, the drug and the date she stopped it, the findings, the vital signs and the breathing symptoms.

Only after medical clearance would I restart the hip program. I would then check with the treating team on what activity is permitted, and reassess if the leg swells again or breathlessness returns.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Priya says she does not want to go to the hospital because she must care for her grandson. Describe how you would respond, including the precautions you would take while she is in your care.

Examiner checklist

  • Acknowledges her caregiving obligations and offers practical help to arrange cover.
  • Explains in plain language the possibility of a clot in the leg and the lung and the danger of delay. critical
  • Checks her understanding of the risks and her capacity to make the decision. critical
  • Respects her right to make her own decision while making a clear recommendation for same day care. critical
  • Keeps her at rest, monitors vital signs and breathing and does not leave her alone.
  • Recognizes the symptoms that mean call 911 now, such as chest pain, worsening breathlessness, fainting or coughing blood.
  • Recommends she not drive herself and arranges safe transport.
  • Helps contact her daughter or another person to care for the child.
  • Documents an informed refusal if she still declines, with advice given and a safety net.

Performance scale

4Combines empathy and practical problem solving with a clear recommendation, checks understanding and capacity, monitors her, and handles refusal respectfully with safety netting.
3Explains the risk and recommends care but has gaps in capacity, monitoring or practical help.
2Gives a general warning but accepts her refusal quickly or neglects monitoring.
1Agrees to treat her or lets her leave without warning signs or transport.

Model spoken answer

I would start by recognizing that her worry is genuine. She looks after her grandson, and nobody else is available this afternoon. I would say that and ask her to tell me about the arrangements, because if I can solve the child care problem, the hospital stops being the barrier.

Then I would explain what I think, calmly and in everyday words. I would say that her leg and her breathing have me concerned that she may have a blood clot in her leg, and that a piece of a clot can travel to the lungs, which can be life threatening. I would say I cannot tell for sure in the clinic, and the only way to find out is a scan and blood work at the hospital today. I would explain that waiting until Monday risks the clot moving, and that treatment, if she needs it, works well when started early.

I would make a clear recommendation: go to the emergency department now. I would check that she understands, by asking her to say in her own words what could happen. I want to know she can weigh this decision, and I would be satisfied that she understands the risk, the options and the consequences. If she can, the choice is hers.

While she is with me, I would keep her resting, not walking around, and stay with her. I would recheck pulse, saturation and breathing every few minutes and ask about chest pain or light-headedness. If any red flag appears, I call 911 immediately. I would not allow her to drive herself.

Then I would help with the practical side. I would offer to phone her daughter or a neighbour, or the school, to arrange care for her grandson, and ask whether a family member could take her.

If she still refuses, I would not argue or threaten. I would tell her she can change her mind at any time, give her the warning signs in writing, ask her to have someone stay with her, and offer a call back this evening. I would document her refusal, the information I gave, her understanding and her decision, and inform her physician.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Describe your professional responsibilities after Priya leaves your clinic, including communication, documentation and any follow up related to her medication and your own practice.

Examiner checklist

  • Communicates findings directly to the receiving emergency team and to the surgeon or responsible physician. critical
  • Documents the history, objective findings, vital signs, advice given, the time she left and the mode of transport. critical
  • Reports that the anticoagulant was stopped by the client and does not advise her to restart it herself. critical
  • Stays within scope by not changing, restarting or advising on dose of the medication.
  • Follows up with the client or the hospital to confirm she was assessed.
  • Respects confidentiality by sharing information only with those involved in her care.
  • Considers whether a post operative adverse event should be reported through the clinic's incident or patient safety process.
  • Reflects on whether earlier screening at the first visit could have been better and what practice changes might follow.
  • Updates the rehabilitation plan only after receiving medical instructions.

Performance scale

4Handles urgent direct communication with receiving and responsible clinicians, stays within scope on medication, documents thoroughly, follows up, and reflects on practice.
3Covers communication and documentation but is vague about scope on medication or follow up.
2Describes routine documentation without direct handover or without addressing the medication.
1Advises restarting or changing the medication, or relies on the client to pass on the information.

Model spoken answer

My responsibilities continue after she leaves, and I would organize them in order of urgency.

First, communication. Before she goes, or as soon as she is on her way, I would phone the emergency department and speak to the nurse or physician who will receive her. I would not rely on her to explain it. I would give a short, clear handover: she is 9 days after a right total hip replacement, has a swollen, tender right calf 3.5 centimetres larger than the left with pitting edema, she has had shortness of breath on stairs since yesterday, heart rate 102 and saturation 94 percent, and she stopped her anticoagulant four days ago without telling the surgeon. I would also contact the surgeon's service, using the on call number since it is after hours on a Friday, so the person responsible for her operation knows. Sharing this information is justified because it is needed for her care, and I would tell her I was doing it.

Second, the medication. She stopped the drug herself. I do not advise her to restart it, change the dose or choose another drug. That belongs to the physician or pharmacist. My role is to report that she stopped it and why, because she said it caused bruising and stomach upset, and let the team decide.

Third, documentation. I would write the history, my findings with measurements and times, the vital signs, the reasoning for holding treatment, the advice I gave, her response and decision, who accompanied her and how she travelled, and every call I made with names and times. I would record that I held treatment and why.

Fourth, follow up. I would phone the hospital or Priya in the evening or next morning to confirm that she was seen, and I would hold any further bookings until I receive instructions on activity.

Fifth, my own practice. I would follow the clinic's process for a significant safety event, and reflect on whether the leg and her symptoms could have been screened for at her first visit, for example by routinely checking calf swelling, medication adherence and breathlessness at every post operative visit. I would share my learning with colleagues.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The likely deep vein thrombosis with signs suggesting pulmonary embolism, plus an anticoagulant stopped without the surgeon's knowledge, requires stopping treatment and arranging same day emergency care. The breathlessness is mentioned in passing and is the buried issue. The competent candidate also respects her right to decide while making a clear recommendation.

Common Candidate Errors

Continuing gentle hip exercises or applying compression to the leg, and waiting for the surgeon on Monday. A second error is advising the client to restart her anticoagulant, which is outside physiotherapy scope.

Examiner Notes

A pass picks up the breathlessness, stops all treatment and arranges same day assessment with direct handover. A fail treats the swelling as routine post operative edema or modifies the exercise program.

Case 45 (Mock 5, case 5 of 10): Severe hand pain and swelling after wrist fracture

Musculoskeletal · Outpatient hand and upper limb physiotherapy clinic

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain what you conclude from Dolores's presentation, the findings that support your conclusion, and what you would do next with respect to assessment.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies the presentation as consistent with complex regional pain syndrome type 1 using the clinical diagnostic criteria.
  • Links continuing pain out of proportion to the injury and allodynia to the sensory category.
  • Identifies temperature asymmetry and skin colour change as vasomotor signs.
  • Identifies edema and sweating asymmetry as sudomotor signs.
  • Identifies reduced range, weakness, tremor and hair and nail changes as motor and trophic signs.
  • States that the diagnosis is clinical, that other causes must be excluded, and that the diagnosis is confirmed by the physician. critical
  • Differentiates from expected post fracture stiffness, infection, a missed injury, nerve injury or a vascular problem.
  • Recognizes the statement about her family being better off without her as a possible suicide risk requiring direct inquiry. critical
  • Plans baseline measures such as pain scores, edema volume or circumference, range of motion, grip and a function questionnaire.

Performance scale

4Applies the diagnostic criteria across all four categories, frames the diagnosis as clinical and physician confirmed, considers alternatives, plans repeatable measures, and picks up the suicide risk statement.
3Identifies complex regional pain syndrome and supporting findings but is thin on alternatives or misses the risk statement in the assessment.
2Lists findings and names the syndrome without linking categories or with overconfident diagnosis.
1Treats as ordinary post cast stiffness or does not address the risk statement.

Model spoken answer

My conclusion is that Dolores has the pattern of complex regional pain syndrome after her wrist fracture, most likely type 1 since there is no known nerve injury. I base this on the recognized clinical criteria, which look for pain that continues and is out of proportion to the original injury, along with symptoms in several categories and signs in at least two.

Her sensory category is clear: burning pain at 8 out of 10, and allodynia, where light touch from a sleeve and cold air hurt. The vasomotor category fits too: the left hand is blotchy red and warmer by 2.5 degrees. For the sudomotor category, she has swelling and sweating on the left hand only. The motor and trophic category includes reduced finger and wrist range, weak grip, a fine tremor, and increased hair and nail growth. That is signs in all four categories, which is a strong picture. The patchy bone loss on the X-ray fits as well.

I would be careful about how I frame this. The diagnosis is clinical and made by excluding other causes, and the confirming diagnosis belongs to her physician. Ordinary stiffness after cast removal would not explain the colour change, the temperature difference or the allodynia. I would still consider infection, a missed fracture or tendon problem, nerve entrapment, a vascular problem such as arterial or venous obstruction, and a lymphedema picture, and I would ask about fever, wound problems and any numbness in a nerve distribution.

My next steps in assessment are baseline measures that I can repeat: pain scores at rest and with movement, allodynia mapping, skin temperature and colour, hand circumference or volume, range of motion, grip strength, and a functional questionnaire such as the QuickDASH. I would observe how she holds and uses the hand.

Separately, something she said matters more than any measure. She said her family would be better off if she were not here. I would not let that pass. I would ask her directly and kindly whether she is thinking of ending her life, because asking does not plant the idea and it is the only way to know. I would let that guide the rest of the visit.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Dolores has just told you her family would be better off without her and asks you not to tell her husband. Describe how you would respond right now, including safety and her involvement in decisions.

Examiner checklist

  • Responds with calm, empathy and attention, and gives her time to talk.
  • Asks directly about thoughts of suicide, including whether she has a plan, means and intent. critical
  • Explains the limits of confidentiality in a safety situation in a respectful way. critical
  • Does not leave her alone if she is at risk and does not promise secrecy. critical
  • Involves her in deciding who will be contacted and how, while prioritizing her safety.
  • Describes a next step according to risk such as contacting a crisis line, her physician, or emergency services for imminent risk.
  • Asks about supports, protective factors and access to medications or other means.
  • Acknowledges her pain, sleep loss and money worries as real stressors without minimizing them.
  • Documents the discussion and the actions taken.

Performance scale

4Asks directly about suicide, explores plan and means, explains limits of confidentiality without promising secrecy, scales response to risk, and keeps her involved.
3Takes the statement seriously and gets help but is indirect in questioning or unclear about confidentiality.
2Expresses concern and suggests counselling without assessing risk or setting up a same day plan.
1Agrees to keep it secret, ignores the statement, or continues the physical assessment.

Model spoken answer

I would stop the physical assessment and turn my attention to her. I would say something like, 'Thank you for telling me that. It sounds like things have been very heavy.' I would sit, lower my voice and give her time.

Then I would ask directly: 'Are you having thoughts of ending your life?' I would not soften it so much that it is unclear. If she says yes, I would ask whether she has thought about how, whether she has the means, such as medications at home, whether she has a time in mind, and whether she has ever tried before. I would also ask what has kept her going, such as her family or her work, because her protective factors matter. I would listen without arguing or lecturing and without saying that things will be fine.

On her request not to tell her husband, I would be honest. I would tell her that I care about her privacy and that most of what she tells me stays with me, but that if I think her life is at risk I cannot keep that secret. I would not promise silence. I would say it kindly: 'I want to keep you safe, and I do not want to do that behind your back.' Then I would invite her to help decide. She might prefer to tell her husband herself with me beside her, or I might offer to do it with her consent.

What I do depends on what she says. If she has a plan, the means and intent, or I cannot be confident she is safe, I stay with her, and I arrange emergency help, either calling 911 or taking her to the nearest emergency department with someone accompanying her. If the risk is lower, I would still arrange same day contact with her family physician or a mental health crisis service, give her the crisis line number, and agree on a safety plan with her, including limiting access to medications at home. I would involve her husband with her permission, or without it if the risk is imminent.

I would acknowledge that her pain, her lack of sleep and her loss of income are real and heavy, and that treatment exists for all three. I would document her words, my questions, her answers, my actions and who I contacted.

Question 3: Collaboration

Describe how you would work with other professionals and people in Dolores's life to coordinate her care, explaining who, why, and how you would communicate.

Examiner checklist

  • Contacts the family physician promptly to confirm the diagnosis, address mental health risk and review pain management. critical
  • Obtains Dolores's consent for each communication and explains what will be shared. critical
  • Proposes referral to a pain clinic or physician experienced with complex regional pain syndrome.
  • Includes an occupational therapist for desensitization, hand function and work adaptation.
  • Includes a psychologist or counsellor for mood, sleep and pain coping.
  • Describes how physiotherapy will fit with graded activity, mirror therapy or graded motor imagery and desensitization, as the team agrees.
  • Suggests a social worker or financial support resources for her income loss.
  • Engages her husband as a support with her agreement and gives him clear information.
  • Sets shared goals, roles and a communication schedule among providers.

Performance scale

4Seeks consent, prioritizes the physician for diagnosis and risk, names appropriate team roles with reasons, and sets shared goals and communication.
3Names suitable team members and reasons but with limited detail on roles, consent or communication.
2Lists professionals with little explanation of purpose or no consent process.
1Proceeds alone, shares information without consent, or omits mental health follow up.

Model spoken answer

Coordinating this well matters because complex regional pain syndrome responds best to a team that works to a common plan, and because Dolores has more than a hand problem. She is in pain, not sleeping, low in mood and short of money.

I would start with her family physician, today. I want them to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other causes, and I want them to know about her statement about her family and the safety steps we have taken, so mental health follow up is not lost. I would ask them to review her pain medication, since acetaminophen and ibuprofen are probably not enough, and to decide on a referral. I would ask for consent from Dolores first and tell her exactly what I will share.

I would suggest a referral to a pain clinic or a physician with experience in this condition, since medical options, such as medications or nerve blocks, are decided there and not by me. I would send a clear summary with measurements.

An occupational therapist would be a key partner for desensitization, safe use of the hand in daily tasks, splinting advice, and adapting her work as a stylist. A psychologist or counsellor can help with mood, sleep and pain coping, which has been shown to matter in this condition. I would present it as part of treatment for pain and not as a sign that her pain is imagined.

Within physiotherapy, I would agree with the team on a graded plan: desensitization, mirror therapy or graded motor imagery, gentle active movement within tolerable limits, and edema control, progressing as pain allows, and I would say that I will adjust based on her responses. I would ask her to stop using the sling all day, with the team's agreement.

A social worker could help with income supports and benefits, since stress from money is feeding her pain.

With her permission, I would speak to her husband so he understands the condition and how to support her. Finally, I would write down who does what, share goals, and agree on how often we update one another, for example a brief message after each key visit.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The statement that her family would be better off if she were not here is a possible suicide risk, tucked into a visit about a hand. A competent candidate asks directly, explains the limits of confidentiality, does not promise secrecy and arranges help matched to risk. The classic complex regional pain syndrome picture is the distractor.

Common Candidate Errors

Concentrating on the diagnostic criteria and exercise progression while moving past her remark, and promising not to tell her husband. A second error is recommending aggressive stretching or forced range of motion.

Examiner Notes

A pass asks directly about suicide and sets up appropriate help, and frames the diagnosis as clinical with team care. A fail treats the remark as background or promises secrecy.

Case 46 (Mock 5, case 6 of 10): Walking limited by leg heaviness in a retired man

Musculoskeletal · Community outpatient physiotherapy clinic

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the physiotherapy plan you would develop with Mr. Gill for the first six weeks, including the main interventions, how you would progress them, and the outcome measures you would use to judge change.

Examiner checklist

  • States goals linked to the client: longer walking tolerance, dog walking, stairs, and independence with self-management.
  • Selects flexion-biased positions and strategies such as forward-leaning walking, cycling or stationary bike, and pacing between rests.
  • Prescribes a graded walking or body-weight-supported treadmill program using time or distance targets that extend gradually.
  • Includes hip mobility and lower limb and trunk strengthening, with dosage such as sets, repetitions and frequency.
  • Includes balance and falls-prevention work given the reduced reflexes and the stairs complaint.
  • Names repeatable outcome measures such as walking distance or time to symptoms, two-minute or six-minute walk, Timed Up and Go, and a patient-reported scale.
  • Defines reassessment triggers and a plan to refer or reconsider if function does not improve or neurological signs worsen. critical
  • Recognizes that the new urinary hesitancy and rubbery legs change the plan and must be acted on before progressive loading. critical
  • Includes education on self-management, activity pacing and realistic expectations about natural course.

Performance scale

4Gives a prioritized, individualized plan with flexion-based strategies, walking intervals, strengthening and balance dosage, named outcome measures, and clear reassessment triggers, while linking the new urinary and leg symptoms to the plan.
3Sound plan with appropriate interventions and measures but weak on dosage, progression, or the link to the new symptoms.
2Lists generic exercises or modalities without tying them to stenosis, progression or measurement.
1Prescribes extension-based or high-load work, ignores the new symptoms, or suggests a plan that would be unsafe.

Model spoken answer

I would build the plan around what Mr. Gill wants, which is to walk the dog with his wife and manage stairs safely. Before I describe the exercise, I want to say that the new urinary hesitancy and the rubbery legs he mentioned are not part of a routine stenosis plan, so I would address that first and treat everything I describe as the plan once those are looked at by a physician. I will explain that reasoning in the next question.

First, goals. In six weeks I would aim for a two-minute walk test that has improved by a meaningful margin from 88 m, walking 400 m with pacing, and managing a flight of stairs with a rail without legs giving way. We would agree these together.

Second, interventions. His symptoms ease in flexion, so I would teach him to use that. He can lean on a cart, use a pole or walker temporarily, and rest in a forward-leaning posture rather than just sitting. I would use a stationary bicycle or recumbent bike, because it keeps the spine flexed and lets him build aerobic capacity without provoking symptoms. For walking I would use intervals: for example, walk until symptoms reach a mild level, rest in flexion until they settle, then repeat, three to four times a week. Over weeks I would lengthen the walking intervals rather than the rest, and consider body-weight-supported treadmill walking if the clinic has it.

Third, strengthening and mobility. I would work on hip flexor and hamstring flexibility, glute and core strength in neutral or slightly flexed positions, and sit to stand practice, two or three sets of eight to twelve, two to three days a week, increasing load when he can finish the set with good control. I would add balance work, such as tandem stance and single leg stance near a counter, because of his reduced reflexes and stair complaint.

Fourth, education. I would explain that stenosis changes slowly, that exercise helps function even when imaging stays the same, and how to pace activity. I would give a written plan with large print, as he has hearing difficulty.

Fifth, measurement. At each visit I would record distance or time to first symptoms, the two-minute walk, Timed Up and Go, and a patient-reported scale. I would reassess at three weeks. If there is no improvement by six weeks, or if neurological signs progress, I would refer back to his physician about a surgical opinion rather than continue the same plan.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Mr. Gill has just told you about changes in his urine and his legs. Explain what you would do next in this visit, how you would involve him in the decision, and what precautions you would apply to his activity.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes the combination of new urinary hesitancy and worsening leg heaviness as a possible serious neurological compromise needing urgent medical assessment. critical
  • Performs or arranges a focused neurological screen: perianal or saddle sensation, lower limb myotomes and dermatomes, reflexes, gait, and asks about bowel function and sexual function. critical
  • Asks specific questions about retention, incontinence, onset, progression, and falls.
  • Explains the concern in plain words and asks permission to contact his physician or arrange same-day assessment. critical
  • Decides who to contact and how, such as phoning the family physician, clinic physician or sending him to emergency, based on findings, rather than waiting for the three month appointment.
  • Holds off on progressive loading or high-intensity exercise until medical clearance, offering safe activity such as walking with rests.
  • Involves his wife with his consent and checks his understanding with teach-back.
  • Gives red flag advice about going to emergency if retention, incontinence, saddle numbness or sudden weakness occurs.
  • Documents findings, advice given, and the communication with the physician.

Performance scale

4Identifies the pairing of urinary and leg change as a red flag, screens neurologically, acts the same day with the physician or emergency, respects his consent, and sets clear activity limits and return precautions.
3Recognizes the concern and refers but misses part of the screen, the consent process, or specific activity precautions.
2Notes the issue but advises waiting for the scheduled appointment or only gives general advice.
1Dismisses the symptoms as age related or continues progressive exercise without assessment.

Model spoken answer

I would stop the end of the visit from becoming a casual goodbye, because what he said matters. New difficulty starting urine over two weeks, together with legs that feel rubbery, could mean more serious compression of the nerves in his canal. I should not assume it is age or the prostate, and I should not wait for a three month appointment.

Here is what I would do. I would sit him back down, face him so he can see my lips, speak slowly, and tell him that I would like to ask a few more questions and do a short check, and ask if that is acceptable. I would ask about the stream: hesitancy, dribbling, feeling that the bladder is not empty, any leaking, and any change in bowel control, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, or sexual function. I would ask if his legs have given way or if he has fallen.

Then I would do a focused neurological screen: sensation around the saddle area if he agrees and a chaperone is offered, lower limb strength by myotome including ankle dorsiflexion, great toe extension, and knee extension, sensation by dermatome, reflexes, and his gait including heel and toe walking. I would compare with the baseline I already recorded today, where strength was normal.

If the screen is abnormal, or if he describes retention, incontinence or saddle numbness, I would explain that he needs to be seen today and I would help him go to the emergency department, phoning ahead with my findings. If the screen is normal and symptoms are mild, I would still contact his physician the same day by phone, explain the new urinary change and leg change together, ask for an expedited assessment, and agree a timeframe with Mr. Gill. I would tell him in plain words why, and ask his permission to share the information. I would use teach-back: 'Tell me what you will do if the passing of urine gets harder.'

With his consent, I would include Mrs. Gill so that she can reinforce the plan, but I would speak to him directly.

For activity, I would not progress him to harder exercise or loaded treadmill work until a physician has reviewed him. He can keep gentle walking with rests, as that is low risk, and I would ask him to stop and call if he notices any new weakness, tripping, or numbness. I would give him written advice in large print about going straight to the emergency department if he cannot pass urine, loses control of bladder or bowel, or notices numbness in the groin.

Finally, I would document my questions, findings, who I contacted, the advice given, and his decisions.

Question 3: Communication

Mr. Gill has hearing loss, his wife often answers for him, and he is asking whether surgery is the answer. Describe how you would communicate with him in your next conversation so that he understands his options and can make his own decision.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets up the environment to support hearing: quiet room, face to face, good lighting, reduced background noise.
  • Speaks clearly and at a measured pace, avoids shouting, and checks whether he uses hearing aids or an amplifier.
  • Addresses Mr. Gill directly and invites his wife to add information only with his agreement. critical
  • Uses plain language and avoids jargon such as stenosis without explaining it.
  • Provides written or pictorial information in large print.
  • Presents options neutrally: exercise program, medical review, injections and surgery as decisions for the physician or surgeon, with general benefits and risks. critical
  • Stays within scope by not promising a surgical result or advising for or against surgery. critical
  • Uses teach-back and open questions to confirm understanding.
  • Explores his values, goals and fears and responds to emotion.

Performance scale

4Adapts the environment and style to hearing loss, speaks directly to the client with his wife included by consent, gives neutral information within scope, and confirms understanding with teach-back.
3Uses good communication strategies but misses one of consent for his wife's role, scope limits, or understanding checks.
2General statements about being clear with little tailoring to hearing loss or autonomy.
1Speaks mainly to the wife, advises for or against surgery, or uses jargon throughout.

Model spoken answer

My aim is that Mr. Gill leaves this conversation understanding his options in his own words and feeling that the decision is his.

I would start with the setting. I would use a quiet room, close the door, sit at his level about one metre away so he can see my face, and have good light on me. I would ask him what helps him hear best, whether he has hearing aids that he is not wearing, and whether there is a pocket amplifier I could use. I would speak at a steady, slightly slower pace and a normal volume, not shout, and I would pause between ideas.

Next, his role. I would greet him first, and look at him when I ask questions. I would say, 'Mr. Gill, I'd like to hear from you first, and then your wife can add anything you would like her to.' I would ask him privately, at the start of the visit, whether he is happy for his wife to speak for him or to stay in the room, because I want to respect his choice rather than assume. If she answers for him, I would gently redirect: 'Thank you, I would like to hear how that is for Mr. Gill.'

Then the content. I would explain the problem in everyday words: 'The channel the nerves run through in your lower back has become narrow, which is why your legs get heavy when you stand and ease when you bend forward.' I would draw a simple picture and give him a one page summary in large print. On surgery, I would explain that I am a physiotherapist, so the decision about surgery belongs to him and a surgeon. I can describe in general that some people choose surgery when walking stays very limited despite exercise and that others improve with exercise, and that a physician can explain risks and likely results for him. I would not promise an outcome or tell him what to choose. I would also tell him I want his physician to see him about the urinary change before we plan further, and that this may affect which options are suitable.

I would ask open questions: 'What matters most to you about walking again?' and 'What worries you about surgery?' If he seems anxious or says he fears becoming dependent, I would acknowledge that.

Finally, I would use teach-back: 'So that I explained it clearly, can you tell me what the next steps will be?' I would write the next steps on the page and invite him to bring questions to the appointment with his physician or surgeon.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is the new urinary hesitancy for two weeks and rubbery legs, mentioned casually at the end. Together with severe multilevel stenosis they may signal progressive neural compression, so the candidate should recognize it, screen, contact the physician or send him to emergency the same day, and pause progressive loading. The imaging report is the distractor.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates write a complete exercise plan and treat the urinary comment as a footnote, or they say they will 'monitor' it. Others answer the communication question with generic advice and forget hearing loss, his autonomy and scope.

Examiner Notes

A pass requires a safe, reasoned stenosis plan and clear recognition of the red flag with same-day action. Strong candidates connect the urinary change to the exercise plan and communicate within scope and with his consent.

Case 47 (Mock 5, case 7 of 10): Lateral elbow pain in a carpenter with a workplace claim

Musculoskeletal · Private clinic accepting workplace compensation board claims

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the treatment plan you would set for Mr. Kowalczuk over the next eight weeks, including the interventions, how you would dose and progress them, and how you would know if the plan is working.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets function and work-based goals, such as pain-free tool grip and return to full duties.
  • Advises load management and temporary modification of aggravating tasks rather than complete rest. critical
  • Prescribes progressive tendon loading, beginning with isometric holds and moving to isotonic and eccentric or heavy slow resistance work, with dosage. critical
  • Includes grip, forearm and shoulder or scapular strengthening and addresses kinetic chain contributors.
  • Mentions work technique and tool adjustments such as handle size, neutral wrist posture or counterforce bracing as options.
  • Uses pain as a guide with an acceptable threshold during and after loading and a 24 hour response rule.
  • Names outcome measures: PRTEE, pain-free grip, grip dynamometry, and work tasks.
  • Explains the natural course and sets a timeframe for reassessment and escalation if not improving.

Performance scale

4Gives a staged loading program with dosage, load management, work modification, outcome measures, and a clear review point, tied to the client's trade.
3Appropriate interventions but incomplete dosage, progression or measurement.
2Mostly modalities, rest or stretching with little progressive loading.
1Recommends complete rest, repeated injections as the plan, or an unsafe approach.

Model spoken answer

I would organize the plan around getting his tendon able to take the loads of his trade again, not just settling pain. His goals are likely to be gripping tools without pain and working a full day, and I would confirm that with him.

First, load management. Complete rest would weaken the tendon, so I would not take him off everything. I would identify the tasks that provoke most symptoms, such as repetitive hammering and power driving with a tight grip, and reduce the volume of these while keeping other work. I would discuss tool changes with him: a larger diameter handle, a lighter driver, keeping the wrist in neutral, and trying a forearm counterforce strap for work tasks as an option for short term relief, not a cure.

Second, progressive loading, which is the core of treatment. In weeks one to two I would begin isometric wrist extension holds, for example five holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice a day, at an effort that gives pain no more than 3 or 4 out of 10 and that is settled by the next morning. Once holds are comfortable and grip is improving, I would move in weeks three to six to slow isotonic loading: wrist extension with a dumbbell or resistance band, about three sets of 10 to 15 with three seconds up and three seconds down, three to four days a week, adding load when he completes all sets with pain at or below the agreed threshold. In the last phase I would add heavy, slow resistance work, grip work with a dynamometer or putty, and functional tasks like holding a hammer at different grips and weights, then work-specific simulations.

Third, other regions. I would include shoulder and scapular strengthening, because poor proximal control raises load on the forearm, and I would look at his neck and wrist as contributors.

Fourth, I would explain the course. This condition usually improves over months, not weeks, and the injection gave brief relief but is not a long term solution, so I would not rely on repeat injections.

Fifth, measurement. I would repeat the PRTEE, pain-free grip and grip strength every two weeks, and use a task test such as hammering a set number of times at a given weight. I would expect a clear change by six weeks. If there is no improvement at six to eight weeks, or if he develops neurological signs, I would discuss imaging or referral to a physician for other options.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss what you would do about the safety concerns that arise from Mr. Kowalczuk's current work, and how you would make decisions with him about what he does at work this week.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies that dropping a tool while working on a ladder is a risk to him and others. critical
  • Asks specific questions about the dropping: frequency, weakness versus pain inhibition, other neurological symptoms, and tasks at height. critical
  • Re-examines for neurological or other causes of the 'letting go', such as cervical or radial nerve involvement.
  • Advises to avoid ladder and overhead power tool work or use alternatives until grip is reliable, explaining why. critical
  • Respects his autonomy and finances by discussing options such as modified duties and the likelihood of income effects.
  • Explains the workplace modification in a way he can take to his employer, with his consent.
  • Discusses medication safety, including the injection history and analgesic use.
  • Documents the safety discussion and decisions.

Performance scale

4Identifies the ladder and tool risk, screens for the cause, gives clear advice to modify work, supports his decision-making, and documents.
3Recognizes the risk and advises modification but with limited exploration or limited shared decision-making.
2Mentions safety in general terms or only passes on a work note.
1Ignores the dropped tool or tells him to continue full duties.

Model spoken answer

The safety concern is that his hand let go of a nail gun while he was working on a ladder. That is a risk of a fall and of the tool striking someone, and it needs to be handled before the plan. I would raise it directly and calmly with him.

I would begin by asking him to tell me about it in his own words. How often has his grip let go? Is it sudden weakness, or is the pain making him drop things? What was he doing, how high was he, and who was nearby? Any numbness, tingling, neck pain or weakness elsewhere? I have already done a neurological screen today, which was normal, but I would repeat a quick check of the radial nerve and C6 to C8 myotomes, and test grip and wrist extension for a true loss of strength, so that I am not assuming this is only tendon pain. If the drop was a pain-related reflex, the risk is still real, because it could happen again at height.

Then I would give him my professional advice. I would say that until his grip is reliable and he can hold his tools without his hand giving out, I recommend that he avoids ladder work and overhead use of heavy power tools, or works with another person to hold or use a tool lanyard and a lighter tool. I would explain why in practical terms: a fall from a ladder could be far more harmful to him than a few days of reduced hours.

Then I would involve him in the decision. He knows his worksite and his financial pressures. I would ask what tasks he could do at ground level, whether the employer has other work, and what he is worried about. I would explain that the board and employer have processes for modified duties, and that I can provide a functional abilities note listing what he can and cannot do, with no diagnosis, if he agrees. The final decision about whether to follow the advice is his, but I would make sure he understands the risk and document that.

I would also check on analgesics: how much ibuprofen he takes, because of stomach and kidney effects, and I would remind him that I cannot advise on further injections but his physician can discuss them.

At the end, I would summarize the agreement in his words, ask him to repeat the safety plan, and book a short follow-up within one week to review his grip and work.

Question 3: Practice Management

The board and the employer are both asking for information, and you have an assistant available. Discuss how you would manage reporting, documentation, privacy, delegation and billing for this claim.

Examiner checklist

  • Provides the board with the required progress report by the deadline using accurate, objective information.
  • Obtains and documents consent before sharing health information and limits what is shared with the employer to functional abilities and restrictions, not diagnosis or treatment detail. critical
  • Redirects the employer's request for diagnosis to the proper channel and explains why. critical
  • Documents each visit contemporaneously: findings, plan, response, advice, communications.
  • Delegates appropriately to the assistant, such as supervised exercise instruction and measurement of grip, while retaining assessment, plan and progression. critical
  • Ensures the assistant is trained, supervised and the client agrees to the assistant's involvement.
  • Bills only for services provided at the board's agreed rates and codes, without charging the worker for covered services or inflating items.
  • Retains records and stores them securely according to regulator and provincial privacy requirements.

Performance scale

4Separates board, employer and client information needs, protects privacy and consent, delegates within scope with supervision, documents and bills ethically.
3Covers most elements but is vague on consent, delegation limits or billing ethics.
2Mentions reporting and documentation in general terms without handling the employer request or delegation.
1Shares diagnosis with the employer without consent, delegates assessment, or bills inappropriately.

Model spoken answer

There are three audiences here: the board, the employer and Mr. Kowalczuk himself, and each has a different right to information. I would manage them separately.

First, the board. They are funding the claim and have asked for a progress report in seven days. I would put that date in my schedule today. The report would be objective and brief: findings at the initial assessment, measures such as grip strength and PRTEE, the plan, response so far, restrictions, and expected timeline. I would stick to what I measured and avoid speculation, and I would sign it with my name and registration number. I would send it by the board's secure method.

Second, the employer. The supervisor has no automatic right to the diagnosis or the plan. I would not give details by phone. Questions about the diagnosis or claim status should go through Mr. Kowalczuk himself or the board's case manager. I would tell the supervisor, politely, that I need the worker's consent to release information and that I can provide, with his consent, a functional abilities form, with his written consent, that lists what he can do, such as no ladder work and limited gripping with power tools, and the expected review date. For the question about full duty on Monday, I would say that return to full duty depends on reassessment and I would not commit on a date. I would tell Mr. Kowalczuk what was asked and what I shared, and note that in the record.

Third, documentation. I would write notes at the time of each visit, including the history, findings, safety discussion, advice, his decisions and every communication with the board and employer. Notes should be clear enough that another therapist could continue care.

Fourth, delegation. The assistant can supervise his exercises, teach technique, record grip measures, and apply tools like a strap under my direction. I would remain responsible for the assessment, diagnosis, plan and progression, and I would tell Mr. Kowalczuk who the assistant is and obtain his agreement. I would not delegate the reassessment, the decision about safety or the report.

Fifth, billing. I would bill the board only for sessions and items that took place, using the codes in the board's fee schedule, and I would not bill the worker for covered services or add charges for items the board does not approve. If he needs a larger sleeve or strap that the board does not cover, I would discuss that cost with him before purchase.

Finally, I would keep the record secure and kept for the length of time my regulator requires.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is that Mr. Kowalczuk dropped a nail gun while on a ladder because his hand let go. The candidate should recognize the fall and tool hazard, screen for a neurological cause, advise work modification, and respect his decision. The employer's request for diagnosis is a related privacy issue.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates give a long exercise plan and treat the dropped tool as background, or they send the diagnosis to the employer to be helpful. Others delegate assessment to the assistant or forget billing ethics.

Examiner Notes

A pass needs evidence-based loading with dosage, a clear safety response to the ladder risk, and firm privacy boundaries with the employer. Strong answers keep roles for the assistant specific.

Case 48 (Mock 5, case 8 of 10): Thigh contusion in a university hockey player

Musculoskeletal · University varsity athletics clinic

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the phases of your management plan for Mr. Okoye over the coming weeks, including what you would do now, how you would progress, and the criteria you would use for return to play.

Examiner checklist

  • Grades the injury as moderate based on knee flexion range and swelling and explains why this guides the plan.
  • Initial phase: relative rest, protection, light non-constricting compression only after a same-day recheck shows no increasing tightness, cold in short applications, avoiding heat and massage. critical
  • Advises to avoid deep massage, heat, and aggressive stretching early because of the risk of heterotopic ossification. critical
  • Uses pain-free progression: active range of motion within tolerance, isometrics, then strengthening, then sport-specific work.
  • Gives criteria for progressing between phases, such as pain-free flexion range, symmetrical strength, and swelling reduced.
  • Gives return to play criteria: full pain-free range, near symmetrical strength, sport-specific drills and contact tolerance with padding. critical
  • Names a reassessment schedule and measures, such as thigh circumference, knee flexion range, hop and strength tests.
  • States that return before day five is unrealistic for this grade, with an expected timeline range.

Performance scale

4Gives phased plan with specific precautions against heterotopic ossification, objective progression and return to play criteria, and a realistic timeline.
3Appropriate phases and avoids harmful treatments but with limited criteria or dosage.
2Generic RICE or exercise list without phases, criteria or the myositis ossificans link.
1Recommends heat, massage, aggressive stretching or early return to sport.

Model spoken answer

From what I found today this is a moderate quadriceps contusion. I base that on knee flexion limited to 55 degrees, the 3.5 cm increase in thigh circumference, and a limp. This grade usually needs about three to six weeks in an athlete, not five days. The main thing I want to protect against is a bad complication called myositis ossificans, where bone forms inside the muscle. So the plan is staged, and what we avoid early matters as much as what we do.

Phase one, the first 48 to 72 hours, is the acute phase and we are in it. The aim is to limit bleeding and swelling. He should rest from sport, walk with crutches if he cannot walk without a limp, and, once the same-day recheck I describe next shows no increase in tightness, I would apply a light compression wrap that is snug but never tight, with the knee resting in as much flexion as is comfortable. I would take the wrap off and send him to emergency if the thigh gets tighter or more painful, or if he notices numbness or colour change. I would use ice for ten to fifteen minutes with a barrier at a time, several times a day. I would stop the heat and the massage, and ask him to check with the team physician or a pharmacist about the ibuprofen, and avoid aggressive or forced passive stretching early, and explain why: heat and deep massage can increase bleeding and are linked to bone forming in the muscle, and forced stretching raises that risk too, and anti-inflammatory drugs early on are a question for his physician or the team doctor.

Phase two begins once swelling is settling and he can move without strong pain, usually after several days. I would begin gentle active knee flexion and extension within comfort, pain-free quadriceps isometrics, stationary bicycle with a high seat, and gradual weight-bearing. Progress when flexion is at least 90 degrees, he walks without a limp, and pain at rest is low.

Phase three is strengthening: closed chain exercise such as leg press and squats, eccentric work, hip and core strength, and then straight line running when he has near full pain-free range and strength about 80 to 90 percent of the other leg. Phase four is sport-specific: skating, cutting, shooting, and drills, then non-contact and contact practice with a thigh pad.

Return to play criteria are full pain-free flexion, no tenderness or palpable firmness, strength and hop tests close to symmetrical, and tolerance of full practice. I would reassess every few days, measuring thigh circumference, flexion range and function, and if the firm area is not softening by week three, or range stalls, I would arrange medical review and possible imaging. I would tell the coach, with his permission, that he will not be ready by Saturday, and give the three to six week range.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss the safety precautions you would take with Mr. Okoye today, and how you would make decisions with him, given what he has told you about the last two days.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes that increasing tightness and tension in the thigh at 48 hours requires screening for compartment syndrome. critical
  • Checks for the signs: severe pain out of proportion, tense swelling, pain on passive stretch, paresthesia, weakness, pulses and capillary refill. critical
  • Gives clear instructions to go to emergency immediately if these signs appear or worsen, and defers compression until a same-day recheck shows no increase. critical
  • Advises to stop heat and massage and explains the reason.
  • Raises the use of ibuprofen and advises him to speak to the team physician or pharmacist.
  • Screens for other injuries such as head injury or knee injury from the hit.
  • Respects his autonomy and addresses his fear of losing his spot with open questions and shared decision-making.
  • Arranges a same-day recheck and a check on him tonight, involves the team physician, and documents the discussion.

Performance scale

4Identifies the worsening tightness as a possible compartment syndrome, screens with specific findings, gives clear escalation criteria, stops harmful treatments and supports his choices.
