3Notes the concern and advises monitoring but with limited screening or escalation detail.
2Gives general RICE safety advice without considering compartment syndrome.
1Does not recognize the warning sign or advises continued heat or massage.

Model spoken answer

The thing that stands out is that his thigh felt tighter this morning than last night. After two days I would expect a bruise to be stabilizing, not tightening. That is a warning sign that bleeding may be continuing inside the muscle, and a rare but serious complication is compartment syndrome, where pressure inside the thigh compartment cuts off blood supply to nerves and muscle. I will not treat that as a minor detail.

So first I would check. I would ask him about the pain: is it worsening, is it out of proportion to what I see, does it wake him at night, and does he have numbness, tingling, or weakness in the leg or foot? On examination I would feel for a tense, hard or tight compartment compared with the other side, I would repeat the thigh circumference and compare it with my earlier number, I would check how much pain is provoked by passively bending the knee, test sensation in the thigh and foot, look at the colour and temperature of the foot, and check the dorsalis pedis pulse and capillary refill. Today those were normal, which is reassuring, but findings can change over hours.

If I find a very tense thigh, rapidly increasing swelling, disproportionate pain, or any numbness or weakness, I would send him to the emergency department right now rather than wait, and call ahead. If findings remain reassuring, I would not apply compression yet, because compression over a tightening thigh could make pressure worse. I would keep the leg rested and supported at about heart level, not raised high, and avoid compression and heat, recheck tightness and circumference in a few hours the same day, and apply only light compression if nothing has increased. I would give him the warning signs in plain language: rising tightness, pain out of proportion, numbness, weakness or a cold, pale foot. If any occur he goes to emergency immediately. I would ask the team physician to see him today, and arrange for a friend or the team athletic therapist to check on him tonight, since he lives in residence away from family.

Second, I would explain that heat and deep massage should stop, because heat can increase bleeding and massage can damage the injured muscle and raise the chance of bone forming in it. On the ibuprofen, I would ask how much he has taken and tell him that it is best to speak to the team doctor or a pharmacist about whether to continue, since that is a medication decision. I would also ask whether he hit his head or injured his knee in the collision.

Third, his choice. I would ask him how he feels about being out. I would say, 'It sounds like you are worried about your place on the team. Tell me more.' I would give him options and let him decide how to communicate with his coach, supporting him with a note.

Question 3: Communication

The coach wants him back on Saturday and Mr. Okoye is anxious about his place on the team. Describe how you would communicate with each of them, and what you would say.

Examiner checklist

  • Speaks with Mr. Okoye first, privately, listening to his concerns before explaining the plan.
  • Obtains his consent to share information with the coach and agrees what will be shared. critical
  • Explains the injury and the reason for the timeline in plain language, with a clear message that Saturday is not safe. critical
  • Uses an empathetic response to his fear and focuses on what he can still contribute and control.
  • Gives the coach functional information such as expected timeline and phases, not unnecessary detail, and holds the position if pressured. critical
  • Offers alternatives, such as training upper body, bike, team meetings, and a defined reassessment date.
  • Uses teach-back or asks him to restate the plan.
  • Documents the communication and follows up.

Performance scale

4Listens to the athlete first, gets consent, gives a clear and consistent no-play message, supports him emotionally, and communicates limited, appropriate information to the coach.
3Communicates the message clearly but with limited emotional response or consent process.
2Focuses on informing the coach with little attention to the athlete's fear or consent.
1Yields to the coach's pressure, shares excessive information, or uses blaming language.

Model spoken answer

I would talk to Mr. Okoye before anyone else. I would find a private room and start with listening: 'You mentioned that you are worried about your spot. What is on your mind?' He is nineteen, away from home, and he may fear that being hurt makes him replaceable. I would acknowledge that: 'That sounds stressful, and it makes sense that you want to be out there.'

Then I would explain the injury with plain words and a drawing if helpful. 'You have a deep bruise in the big muscle at the front of your thigh. The muscle has bled inside, and that is why it is tight and why bending your knee is limited. If we push too early, the bleeding can continue, you can get a scar or even bone growing in the muscle, and a short injury can become a season ending one.' I would be clear: 'I cannot clear you for Saturday, and I would not want you to play.' I would say it kindly and without hedging, because mixed messages invite pressure.

Next, I would give him things he can control. He can keep training upper body, use the bike once I clear it, attend video sessions and team meetings, and follow a phased plan that has clear steps toward being back. I would tell him the usual range of weeks for this grade and that I would reassess in a few days so he can see progress.

I would then ask permission to speak with the coach, and agree what I will share: that he is out for Saturday, a general timeline in phases, what he can do in practice, and the date of the next review. I would not share more than that without his consent.

For the coach, I would speak calmly and directly, and say, 'He has a moderate thigh injury, and playing on Saturday would put him at real risk of a longer absence. I can give you a plan and a date when we will reassess.' If the coach pushes, I would repeat the same message and refer to the team physician for the final medical decision, rather than negotiate on the safety issue. I would offer to put the information in writing.

Finally, I would check Mr. Okoye's understanding with, 'So that I explained it well, tell me how you will describe this to your coach.' I would document both conversations and follow up.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is the thigh feeling tighter this morning two days after the injury, along with heat and massage use. The candidate should screen for compartment syndrome with specific signs, set escalation criteria, and stop heat and massage because of myositis ossificans risk. The coach's pressure is related but secondary.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates give a standard sprain-style RICE plan and neglect the worsening tightness, or agree to a return date to please the coach. Others forget the myositis ossificans precautions.

Examiner Notes

A pass requires a phased plan with the precautions, recognition of the compartment syndrome risk, and firm, empathetic communication that protects the athlete's consent.

Case 49 (Mock 5, case 9 of 10): Arm swelling and fatigue after breast cancer treatment

Other Systems · Hospital-based oncology rehabilitation clinic

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Based on what Ms. Ferreira has told you and your findings, explain your clinical impression, the further assessment you would perform, and how you would sort out the contributors to her symptoms.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies probable secondary upper limb lymphedema, early stage, based on swelling, risk factors (node dissection, radiation) and circumference difference.
  • Notes that circumference difference and minimal pitting suggest an early or mild stage and plans further staging.
  • Uses additional measures: bilateral arm circumferences at standard points or volumetry, skin and tissue assessment, and function.
  • Identifies the night-time, non-mechanical mid back pain with unexplained weight loss as a red flag for possible metastatic disease or other serious pathology. critical
  • Recognizes that the lymphedema is not the explanation for the back pain and the weight loss. critical
  • Proposes a screen of the thoracic spine and neurological status and other systemic symptoms.
  • Considers fatigue contributors: treatment effects, sleep, anxiety, deconditioning, medications, anemia, and thyroid, and the need for medical input.
  • Considers other causes of swelling such as infection, venous thrombosis, and recurrence, and the findings that would distinguish them.

Performance scale

4Separates the probable lymphedema from the red flag cluster, names specific assessments, and explains why the back pain and weight loss need prompt medical review.
3Identifies lymphedema and red flags but with limited differential reasoning or assessment detail.
2Focuses on lymphedema and fatigue with minimal attention to the back pain.
1Attributes the back pain to posture or the school bag, or misses the red flags.

Model spoken answer

My clinical impression has two parts, and I want to keep them separate. The first part is that she most likely has mild secondary lymphedema in the left arm. She had a 12 node axillary dissection and radiation to the axilla, which are two of the biggest risk factors, the swelling has been present for four months, the arm is 3 cm bigger above the elbow and 2 cm bigger in the forearm, and there is only minimal pitting, no redness and no warmth. That fits an early stage, where swelling comes and goes and the tissue is still soft. The shoulder flexion loss may reflect scar and radiation changes in the chest wall and fascia.

To stage the lymphedema I would measure both arms at the same landmarks every 4 cm or use volume measurement if available, record the skin, the presence of fibrosis, and the effect on her hand function and daily activity. I would also check for signs that would point away from lymphedema: redness, heat and pain would suggest cellulitis; a sudden swelling with a tender cord would suggest a clot; and a hard or fixed supraclavicular or axillary mass or arm swelling that increases quickly could mean recurrence or compression.

The second part is more important. A new mid back ache that wakes her at night, does not change with position, and comes with 4 kg unintentional weight loss in someone who has had breast cancer is a red flag combination for possible bone metastasis or other serious disease. That is not explained by lymphedema or by carrying a school bag. I would ask more: when it started, how severe, whether it is constant, any other pain, cough or breathlessness, appetite, fever, abdominal symptoms, headaches, or weakness or numbness. I would examine her thoracic spine for tenderness, percuss gently, screen her neurology for strength, sensation, reflexes and gait, and ask about bladder and bowel function. I would not try to diagnose it, but I would conclude that this needs medical assessment soon.

Fatigue has many contributors: effects of chemotherapy and radiation, aromatase inhibitor, poor sleep, anxiety, low activity and sometimes anemia or thyroid problems. I would use a fatigue scale, and ask about sleep, mood, and activity, and ask her physician to check for medical causes. But I would not attribute the fatigue to treatment effects until the red flag is dealt with.

So my working impression is mild lymphedema plus a possibly serious unexplained symptom cluster that needs prompt medical review.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Explain the precautions and advice you would give Ms. Ferreira about her arm, her activity and her upcoming flight, and how you would involve her in decisions.

Examiner checklist

  • Gives skin care and infection precautions and instructs on signs of cellulitis that require urgent medical care. critical
  • Discusses compression: fitting by a qualified person, sleeve and glove options, and wearing for flights as a reasonable measure to discuss with the clinician.
  • Advises on safe exercise: gradual progression, monitoring arm response, and avoiding overloading, rather than avoiding exercise entirely. critical
  • Advises on holding off on loading the thoracic spine or strenuous strengthening until the back pain is assessed. critical
  • Provides red flags to seek urgent care: back pain with weakness or numbness, bladder or bowel change, sudden swelling, fever, or breathlessness.
  • Addresses travel: hydration, movement, and a plan for the flight, and carrying advice for swelling.
  • Elicits her fears and preferences and uses shared decision-making.
  • Explains the limits of what physiotherapy can do and checks understanding.

Performance scale

4Gives specific infection, compression, exercise and travel advice, defers loading of the spine pending assessment, lists red flags, and involves her in decisions.
3Gives sound lymphedema advice but weak on the back pain precaution or shared decisions.
2General lymphedema precautions with little tailoring.
1Gives unsafe advice such as heavy loading or ignoring the back pain.

Model spoken answer

My safety advice would cover her arm, her activity and her back, and I would start by asking what matters to her about the flight and about staying active, so that my advice fits her life.

For the arm, the main risk is infection. An arm with lymphedema has slower fluid drainage and a higher chance of cellulitis, which can progress quickly. I would teach her to keep the skin clean and moisturized, treat small cuts and insect bites right away, use gloves for gardening, avoid very hot baths and saunas on that arm, and to call her physician or go to emergency the same day if she sees redness, warmth, pain, fever or sudden increase in swelling. I would not tell her never to have blood pressure taken on that arm as an absolute rule, but I would mention that she can ask staff to use the other arm.

For compression, a well-fitted sleeve and glove can control swelling, and many people wear one on flights because of pressure changes. I would explain that she should be measured and fitted by a certified fitter so that it is the right size and class, and I would discuss with her whether to wear one on the flight, with her lymphedema therapist or physician. I would also suggest hydration, moving about the cabin, simple arm movements, and not carrying a heavy bag on the left arm.

For exercise, I would encourage regular aerobic activity and gradual strengthening, because both are safe with lymphedema when progressed slowly. I would say to watch for increases in heaviness or swelling for 24 hours after, and adjust. But today I would hold off on any thoracic loading, resisted work or manual techniques to her back until her physician has assessed the new back pain, because I do not yet know the cause. Walking is fine.

I would explain the red flags: back pain that gets worse, numbness or weakness in the legs, trouble with bladder or bowel, new breathlessness, or fever. If any occur, she should go to emergency.

Throughout, I would ask her for her thoughts, give her choices about compression and activity, and have her tell me back the plan in her own words. I would tell her honestly what I can and cannot do: I can help with swelling, movement and activity, but I cannot determine why her back hurts, and that is why I want her doctors to check it.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Ms. Ferreira has asked you not to tell anyone about her back pain. Discuss your professional responsibilities in this situation and what you would do.

Examiner checklist

  • Acknowledges her right to autonomy and confidentiality and explores her reasons and fears.
  • Explains the clinical concern honestly and the reason that prompt medical assessment matters. critical
  • Attempts to obtain her informed consent to communicate with her physician or oncologist, offering options such as her calling or a joint call. critical
  • Does not diagnose or tell her it is a recurrence and stays within scope.
  • Recognizes that if she refuses, she has the capacity to decide, and the physiotherapist must respect it, document the discussion and the advice, and keep the door open, unless a legal exception applies. critical
  • Does not disclose without consent unless required by law or there is serious risk to her or others that meets the legal threshold.
  • Documents the history, red flags, advice, her decision and follow-up plan.
  • Plans follow-up, including a time-limited recheck and offers to help with the appointment.

Performance scale

4Balances autonomy and duty, seeks consent with options, explains the concern honestly within scope, respects capacity if she refuses, documents, and plans follow-up.
3Seeks consent and documents but explores her fears or legal limits less fully.
2Either simply accepts her request or says she will contact the oncologist without consent.
1Breaches confidentiality without justification or ignores the issue.

Model spoken answer

This is a conflict between respecting her wishes and my duty to act on a possible serious problem. I would handle it by working with her, not around her.

First I would listen. I would say, 'I hear that you do not want this to be shared. Can you tell me what worries you most?' She is probably frightened of hearing the word recurrence, and she may feel she cannot go through more treatment. I would acknowledge that, and I would not hurry. I would remind her that what she tells me is confidential and that I will not share her information without her permission, except in the rare situations the law requires.

Then I would be honest and clear about my concern, in plain words and without alarming her or giving a diagnosis. 'A back pain that wakes you at night and does not ease with position, together with the weight loss, is not something I can explain from physiotherapy. Most of the time causes are manageable, but because of your history, it is important that your doctor looks at it soon, not in four months.' I would tell her that I cannot treat or assess the cause of this, and that continuing physiotherapy on the back without knowing could be unsafe.

Next I would ask for her consent. I would offer choices: she could call her family physician or oncology nurse line from my office with me present, I could call with her permission, or I could write a note she brings. I would offer to help her book it and to go over what to say. I would ask what would make this easier.

If she still refuses, I would respect that, since she is an adult with capacity and the decision is hers. I would not contact her oncologist behind her back, because the situation does not meet the threshold for disclosure without consent. I would make sure that she understands the possible consequences of waiting, give her the red flags that mean emergency, and tell her that she can change her mind at any time. I would document the history, my findings, my advice, her understanding, her refusal and the reasons she gave. I would hold off on any treatment to the spine and book a short follow-up within a week to revisit.

I would also check with my regulator's guidance or a senior colleague if I was unsure about disclosure requirements.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is the new night-time mid back pain with 4 kg unintentional weight loss in a breast cancer survivor, with a request for secrecy. The candidate should treat it as a red flag for possible metastasis, separate it from the lymphedema, seek consent for medical referral, and respect capacity if she refuses while documenting. The arm circumference is the distractor.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates focus on lymphedema staging and compression and treat the back pain as a minor comment, or they promise secrecy or breach confidentiality. Some tell her it is probably a recurrence.

Examiner Notes

A pass requires recognizing the red flag cluster, separating it from lymphedema, and handling the confidentiality conflict with consent seeking, honesty and documentation. Strong answers do not diagnose.

Case 50 (Mock 5, case 10 of 10): Calf pain on walking in a man with type 2 diabetes

Cardiovascular-Respiratory · Community outpatient physiotherapy clinic

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the exercise-based plan you would develop for Mr. Nakamura, including the type, dosage and progression of the exercise, the other strategies you would include, and how you would measure change.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets goals linked to the client such as walking with grandchildren and increasing pain-free walking distance.
  • Prescribes a structured walking program to moderate claudication pain with rest between bouts, for example 30 to 60 minutes total, at least three times a week, for 12 weeks or more. critical
  • Describes progression by increasing time or distance or intensity as pain-free or moderate-pain walking improves.
  • Includes lower limb strengthening and optionally cycling or arm ergometry if walking is limited.
  • Includes risk factor education: smoking cessation support, foot care, glucose and blood pressure management with his health care team. critical
  • Names outcome measures: treadmill or six-minute walk, pain-free and maximum walking distance, a claudication scale, ABI by appropriate provider, and a function questionnaire.
  • Plans reassessment and criteria for modifying or stopping, including signs of limb threat. critical
  • Acknowledges limits of 10 visits and plans home program and community exercise support.

Performance scale

4Gives an exercise plan with intervals to moderate pain, dosage and progression, risk factor and foot education, named outcome measures and referral triggers, and notes the visit limit.
3Sound exercise plan but with limited dosage, progression or measurement.
2Generic exercise advice without claudication-specific dosing or risk factor management.
1Prescribes unsafe or unrelated treatment such as lumbar traction or high-intensity exercise through limb threat signs.

Model spoken answer

I would plan around the goal of walking with his grandchildren, and I would be upfront that this plan is for exercise therapy for claudication, and that I would set it up only after the foot concerns are dealt with, which I describe in the next question. Assuming that is done, this is the plan.

The central intervention is supervised or structured walking. The best-supported approach for claudication is walking to a moderate level of calf discomfort, resting until it settles, and repeating. I would start with intervals: walk until the pain reaches about 3 out of 4 on a claudication scale, rest standing or sitting for a few minutes, and repeat, building up to 30 minutes of total walking time at the start and progressing toward 45 to 60 minutes, three or more times a week, for at least 12 weeks. Because he can manage about 120 m, I would begin with a time target, perhaps 20 to 30 minutes of walking plus rests, then progress by adding about five minutes every one to two weeks as the walking time to pain improves, and then raise speed or add a slight incline. With only 10 insured visits, I would use them to teach, supervise the first sessions, monitor and adjust, and I would build a home program with a log, and look for a community program or a track for the rest.

Second, I would add leg strengthening twice a week: calf raises, sit to stand, step ups, two sets of 10 to 12, progressing as tolerated. If walking is limited by pain, he can do stationary cycling or arm cranking as a complement.

Third, the risk factors. I would explain that walking helps the legs but that smoking, glucose and blood pressure drive the disease. I would offer support for quitting, with the recommendation that he talk to a physician or pharmacist about cessation aids, and encourage him to establish a family physician. I would teach daily foot checks, proper shoes, and never walking barefoot, given his reduced sensation and diabetes.

Fourth, measurement. At the start, at four weeks, at 12 weeks, I would record the six-minute walk, time to first pain and to maximal pain, a claudication rating, and a function questionnaire. The ABI would be repeated by the appropriate provider if needed. I expect the walking time to improve over the first weeks.

Fifth, I would set triggers to stop and refer: any new wound, color change, rest pain, or a drop in walking tolerance. If there is no improvement at 12 weeks, I would discuss with his physician about further vascular assessment.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Explain how you would respond to what you noticed on his toe and what he told you about night pain, including your precautions with exercise and how you would involve him in the decision.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes the combination of a non-healing dark toe lesion and rest pain with low ABI as suggesting chronic limb-threatening ischemia needing urgent vascular assessment. critical
  • Examines the foot further: lesion size, colour, temperature, signs of infection, pulses, capillary refill and sensation.
  • Explains to Mr. Nakamura in plain language why this is not just a claudication problem and may risk the toe or foot.
  • Holds exercise program and walking to tolerance until medically cleared, and avoids anything that could injure or load the foot. critical
  • Gives wound and foot protection advice and the signs of infection or worsening that need emergency care.
  • Arranges same-day urgent assessment (emergency department or urgent vascular or wound clinic), by phone with him present or by sending him directly, because rest pain with tissue loss threatens the limb. critical
  • Addresses his minimization and fear, uses shared decision-making, and checks understanding.
  • Documents findings and advice.

Performance scale

4Identifies chronic limb-threatening ischemia features, examines further, arranges urgent assessment despite no physician, pauses exercise, gives protection advice, and engages his fear and choices.
3Recognizes the problem and refers but with limited examination, safety advice or engagement of his minimization.
2Notes the toe but continues exercise or advises routine follow-up.
1Ignores the lesion and night pain or applies heat or debridement.

Model spoken answer

What I noticed changes the visit. A dark, dry area on the tip of the toe that has not healed in three weeks, in a man with diabetes, reduced sensation, weak pulses and an ankle brachial index of 0.62, together with an ache in the foot at night that he relieves by hanging the foot down, is a pattern that suggests the blood supply is no longer enough to keep the tissue healthy at rest. That is different from claudication, and it can progress to infection, gangrene and loss of the toe or foot. I would not begin an exercise program until a physician has assessed it.

I would begin by examining the foot more fully, with his permission. I would look at the lesion: size, depth, colour, edges, any drainage, odour, or redness spreading up the foot. I would compare skin temperature, colour on elevation and dependency, capillary refill, and pulses, and I would check sensation again. The night pain and the posture he uses to relieve it help me understand how severe it is.

Then I would talk to him. 'Mr. Nakamura, I am glad you showed me this. The mark on your toe and the night ache tell me your foot is not getting enough blood, and that needs to be looked at by a doctor soon, not just treated with walking. I know you wanted exercise, and I will help with that, but I want to make sure your foot is safe first.' I would ask what worries him. People often minimize this because they fear amputation, and I would acknowledge that fear honestly, and explain that early treatment gives the best chance of keeping the foot.

Because he has no family physician, I would not just tell him to book something. I would phone a walk-in clinic or a vascular referral line with him present if possible, or send him to the emergency department or an urgent vascular or wound clinic the same day. Rest pain with a dark toe lesion threatens the limb even if the foot looks stable, and it is more urgent still with infection, spreading redness, a wet or painful wound, or a cold, pale foot. I would give him a letter with my findings.

For exercise, I would pause the walking program. He can still do gentle, non-weight-bearing movement if comfortable. I would ask him to protect the foot, wear closed shoes with clean socks, not walk barefoot, avoid heat packs, not cut the lesion or use corn remedies, and go to emergency if he sees pus, redness, or increasing pain. I would ask him to repeat the plan, and document everything.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Mr. Nakamura has no family physician and says he will not go anywhere. Discuss your professional responsibilities and what you would do to see that he gets the assessment he needs.

Examiner checklist

  • Acknowledges his right to make decisions and explores barriers such as cost, transport, past experiences and fear.
  • Takes reasonable active steps to connect him to care, such as calling a clinic, providing a written referral letter, or arranging transport, and does not just advise. critical
  • Stays within scope by describing findings and concerns without diagnosing or prescribing.
  • Obtains his consent before sharing information with other providers and explains what will be shared. critical
  • If he declines, confirms capacity and informed refusal, explains the risks, documents the discussion, and keeps follow-up open. critical
  • Considers cultural safety and respectful communication and avoids blame or judgment about smoking.
  • Documents findings, advice, actions taken, his decisions and the plan.
  • Follows up within a defined period to check whether he was seen.

Performance scale

4Takes active steps to connect him to care with consent, stays within scope, explores barriers, respects capacity if he declines, documents, and follows up.
3Refers and documents but is passive about connecting him or limited on consent and scope.
2Simply advises him to see a doctor and notes it in the chart.
1Discharges him, treats the wound beyond scope, or shares information without consent.

Model spoken answer

My responsibility here is greater than giving advice. I have found something that could threaten his foot, and he has no physician to hand it to. As a physiotherapist I cannot diagnose or treat it, so I have a duty to take reasonable steps to see that someone who can does, while respecting his choices.

First I would understand why he says he will not go anywhere. I would ask, 'Help me understand what makes it hard to see a doctor.' It might be cost, a bad experience, difficulty with transport, long waits, or fear of what he will hear about his foot. Understanding the barrier lets me address it. I would avoid blame about his smoking, because judgment will make him close up, and I would use respectful language and ask what he understands about his own health.

Then I would take active steps. I would offer to phone a walk-in clinic or an after-hours vascular or wound clinic from our office while he is here, explain the situation briefly, and arrange a time. If there is a regional nurse navigator or a primary care attachment program, I could help him register. I would write a short referral letter with my findings: the toe lesion, duration, ankle brachial index, pulses, rest pain, and diabetes, and ask for assessment for peripheral arterial disease. Before I share any of this I would ask for his permission, tell him what I will include, and who will see it. If he wants, I could help with transport, such as asking a family member, a taxi voucher, or a community service.

I would stay in my scope. I would say what I observed and what it could mean, but I would not tell him he has gangrene or that he will lose the toe, and I would not prescribe or treat the wound beyond protective advice.

If he still refuses, he is an adult with capacity and it is his decision. I would make sure he truly understands the risks of waiting, in plain words, and tell him that the door stays open. I would give him written red flags and a number to call, document what I observed, what I advised, what I offered, his reasons and decision, and I would pause exercise. I would call him within two or three days to ask whether he went, and to offer help again. Using more of his insured visits for that follow up is reasonable.

I would also consider talking with my clinical lead or regulator guidance if I was unsure about what more I should do.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is a three week non-healing dark toe lesion with night rest pain in a man with diabetes, neuropathy and an ABI of 0.62, which suggests chronic limb-threatening ischemia. The candidate should pause exercise, examine, arrange urgent assessment despite no physician, and respect his consent. The low back MRI is the distractor.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates write a full claudication walking program and mention the toe in passing, or tell him to see a doctor without taking steps to connect him. Some treat the wound beyond scope.

Examiner Notes

A pass needs a correct claudication exercise plan, recognition of limb threat with urgent action, and a professional response to the lack of a physician that goes beyond advice. Strong answers keep his consent and capacity central.

Mock 6

Case 51 (Mock 6, case 1 of 10): Dupuytren fasciectomy, hand therapy, retired welder

Musculoskeletal · Outpatient hand therapy clinic in a community hospital

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the treatment plan you would set up for Mr. Medeiros over the next six weeks, including your goals, the interventions you would choose, how you would progress them and how you would measure progress.

Examiner checklist

  • States goals tied to the case: maintain finger extension, restore PIP flexion, control swelling and scar, return to woodworking.
  • Plans a custom thermoplastic extension splint for night wear with a schedule and a plan to check fit and skin.
  • Addresses edema and scar with elevation, light compression, gentle massage once the wound is closed.
  • Prescribes active, pain limited range of motion exercises several times daily, avoiding forceful passive stretching of the fresh wound. critical
  • Sets progression by wound healing and symptoms, with strengthening delayed until the wound is closed and pain settles. critical
  • Names outcome measures such as total active motion, extension lag, grip strength and a patient reported hand function scale.
  • Plans reassessment at set visits and states triggers to modify the plan, such as rising pain, swelling or worsening lag. critical
  • Links work and hobby demands to a graded return, including lifting limits until cleared by the surgeon.

Performance scale

4Gives case-specific goals, splint, edema and scar care, graded exercise, progression tied to wound healing, named outcome measures and clear triggers to modify, all linked to his woodworking and family role.
3A sound plan covering most elements with reasoning, but lacking named outcome measures, triggers to modify, or a clear link between progression and the state of the wound.
2Lists generic hand therapy items such as a splint and exercises without dose, progression logic or links to the case, or overlooks the open wound and the high pain level.
1Plans forceful stretching or early heavy strengthening, or leaves out splinting and reassessment, so the plan could damage the surgical result or ignore the findings.

Model spoken answer

My goals for the next six weeks are to protect the surgical result, keep the fingers straight, get the bent range back, settle swelling and scar, and get Mr. Medeiros safely back to woodworking. First, the splint. I would make a custom thermoplastic night splint that holds the ring and small fingers in extension, and I would check the fit and the skin at every visit because he already finds it uncomfortable. I would ask what exactly bothers him, and adjust edges or padding, because a splint he does not wear gives him no benefit. The plan would usually continue for several months, and I would explain that this is the usual course and not a punishment. Second, swelling and scar. I would teach elevation, light compression with a sleeve if the surgeon agrees, and gentle scar massage with silicone once the open area is closed. Third, exercise. I would prescribe active range of motion several times a day in short sets, working PIP and DIP flexion, then full extension against the splint plate. I would avoid forceful passive stretching right now, because the wound is still partly open and his pain is high for ten days after surgery. Fourth, progression. I would progress by tissue healing and symptoms, not by a calendar. Once the wound is closed and pain is settling, I would add tendon gliding, then light putty, then grip work, and finally lifting and tool use in steps. Heavy lifting stays off the table until the surgeon clears it, and I would say that plainly about the workbench. Fifth, outcome measures. I would record extension lag at the PIP joints, total active motion, grip strength compared with his left side, and a patient reported measure of hand function so we can see change that matters to him. I would also set a goal in his own words, such as using his chisels comfortably. Sixth, reassessment. I would see him two or three times a week at first, then weekly. If pain stays high, if swelling or lag increases, or if the wound changes, I would slow down, stop loading and contact the surgeon. If lag stays stable and motion improves, I would progress and space visits out. Finally, I would answer his question about stopping therapy honestly. Straight fingers at six weeks do not mean finished, because contracture can return, so we would agree on a splint and review schedule and a plan for what to do if the fingers start to curl again.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

While you work, Mr. Medeiros asks how his hand compares with other patients and whether the pain and sensitivity you noticed are normal. Discuss how you would respond and what safety steps you would take before he leaves.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes that pain at rest that is high for this stage plus light touch pain, shiny skin and swelling are not typical.
  • Considers early complex regional pain syndrome and also infection from the open wound drainage as possible explanations. critical
  • Takes a focused history of pain pattern, temperature and colour change, sweating, nights, fever, drainage and medication use.
  • Examines wound, colour, temperature, swelling and sensation, and compares with the opposite hand.
  • Avoids aggressive stretching or modalities that provoke pain while symptoms are unexplained. critical
  • Contacts the surgeon the same day to report findings and seeks medical assessment, with his permission. critical
  • Asks about acetaminophen dose and discusses safe daily limits without prescribing or changing medication.
  • Gives clear return precautions about fever, spreading redness, pus and sudden worsening pain.
  • Respects autonomy by explaining findings, checking understanding and agreeing next steps with him.

Performance scale

4Identifies the abnormal pain and skin pattern, names infection and early pain syndrome as concerns, stops provocative treatment, contacts the surgeon and gives precautions while respecting his autonomy.
3Recognizes the problem and refers, but leaves out one of the infection or pain syndrome reasoning, medication safety advice, or clear return precautions for him to follow.
2Treats the findings as normal post-operative stiffness or only reassures him, with a thin history, no same day contact with the surgeon or no change to the treatment.
1Continues stretching or treats through the pain, or fails to inform the surgeon, leaving a possible infection or pain syndrome unaddressed and the client at risk.

Model spoken answer

I would answer him honestly and not just reassure him. I would say that stiff fingers and some soreness are expected after this operation, but pain this strong at rest and a hand that hurts from a light touch is more than I would expect at ten days, so I want to look more closely and get the surgeon involved. First, I would take a focused history. When did the pain change, is it burning or throbbing, does it keep him awake, has the colour or temperature of the fingers changed, is there more sweating, any fever or chills, and what has the drainage looked like. I would ask how many acetaminophen he is taking and how often, because he said he is taking extra, and I would remind him of the daily maximum on the label and ask him to check with his pharmacist or doctor. I would not change his medication myself. Second, I would examine. I would look at the wound for redness, warmth, swelling, smell and the type of drainage, compare skin colour, temperature and swelling with the left hand, and test light touch and sensation. I am thinking about two possibilities. One is an early wound infection, because there is drainage from the open area. The other is an early pain syndrome such as complex regional pain syndrome, because the pain is out of proportion, the skin is shiny and light touch hurts. I cannot diagnose either, and both need a physician. Third, I would change what I do today. I would stop any forceful stretching, deep massage or heat, and keep to gentle active movement within comfort, plus elevation. If I push into pain, I could make an inflamed or sensitized hand worse. Fourth, communication. With his permission, which he has given, I would call the surgeon's office before he leaves and ask for a same day or next day assessment, giving my findings in short, clear terms. I would write down what I told him. Fifth, return precautions. I would tell him in plain words to go to emergency or call the surgeon immediately if he gets a fever, redness spreading up the hand, pus, a bad smell, or pain that suddenly gets much worse. I would ask him to say it back to me. Finally, I would check that he feels heard. He is proud of his hands, so I would invite his questions and tell him that checking early is the best way to protect the result he had surgery for.

Question 3: Communication

Mr. Medeiros becomes irritated and says he has used his hands for 40 years and does not need to be told what to do. Explain how you would communicate with him to reach agreement on splint wear, home exercises and activity limits.

Examiner checklist

  • Acknowledges his expertise and frustration without defensiveness before giving any advice.
  • Uses open questions to explore why the splint is uncomfortable and what matters most to him.
  • Uses plain language, short sentences and avoids jargon, checking reading comfort in English. critical
  • Offers an interpreter or Portuguese materials and the option to include his daughter by phone or video.
  • Uses teach back to confirm he understands exercises, splint schedule and lifting limits. critical
  • Frames advice around his goals, such as woodworking and helping his son, using shared decision making.
  • Gives demonstrations and written or pictorial home program with large print instead of a dense pamphlet.
  • Explains the reason for each limit, including why the workbench lift must wait, and negotiates alternatives. critical
  • Sets a follow up plan and invites him to call with concerns.

Performance scale

4Acknowledges his expertise, explores barriers, adapts language and format to his needs, uses teach back, explains the reasons for limits and negotiates alternatives tied to his own goals.
3Communicates respectfully and checks understanding, but misses his language or literacy needs, or does not negotiate the lifting limit and splint plan with him. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
2Mostly instructs or repeats advice with little exploration of his concerns, uses jargon, or does not check that he has understood the plan before he leaves.
1Dismisses or argues with him, talks down to him, or lets him leave with unclear instructions and no agreement on the splint, exercises or lifting limits.

Model spoken answer

I would start by slowing down and listening. He is irritated because he feels talked down to, and he is right that he knows his hands. So I would say something like, you know your hands better than anyone, and I want to use that. I would not defend my pamphlet. Then I would ask open questions. What has made the splint hard to wear? What does a good week look like for you? What are you hoping to be doing with your hands in two months? His answers tell me what to build the plan around, probably woodworking and helping his son. Second, language and literacy. He reads English slowly, so I would ask in a respectful way which language he prefers for instructions, and offer a professional interpreter or Portuguese materials. I would also offer to phone his daughter or have her join by video so the plan is shared at home. I would use short sentences and plain words, such as straighten, bend and rest, not terms like extension lag. Third, I would show instead of tell. I would do the exercises with him, hand over hand if he agrees, and give a large print sheet with photos of his own hand in the positions, with three or four exercises, not a long pamphlet. Fourth, teach back. I would say, I want to be sure I explained this well, can you show me how you will do your exercises and tell me when you will wear the splint? If something is missing, I would take responsibility for the explanation and try again. Fifth, the splint. Because it is uncomfortable, I would look at the fit with him and adjust it, then agree on a realistic schedule, for example every night and only a short trial for the days. We would agree on what to do if he cannot tolerate it. Sixth, the workbench. I would not simply say no. I would explain that the palm wound and the fascia are still healing, that a heavy pull can open the wound or bring back swelling and pain, and that the surgeon will tell us when lifting is safe. Then I would offer ways he can still help, such as directing the move, carrying light items with the other hand, or doing it in a few weeks. Finally, I would ask him what is still unclear and agree on when we meet next, so he knows the decisions remain his.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

Pain at rest of 6 out of 10, allodynia, shiny skin, swelling and wound drainage at ten days may signal early infection or complex regional pain syndrome. A competent candidate notices the cluster, stops provocative treatment, contacts the surgeon the same day and gives return precautions. The extra acetaminophen use also needs a safe-dose conversation.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates treat the case as routine post-fasciectomy stiffness and push stretching or strengthening. They also list a generic plan without tying progression to wound healing, and respond to his irritation with more instructions instead of exploring his goals.

Examiner Notes

A pass notices the abnormal pain and skin signs without being told, changes treatment and escalates the same day. Strong responses also adapt communication to a proud, first-language Portuguese speaker. Failing responses stretch through pain or miss the escalation.

Case 52 (Mock 6, case 2 of 10): Transtibial amputation, prosthetic training, diabetes

Musculoskeletal · Inpatient and day program at a regional rehabilitation centre

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain how you would interpret these assessment findings for Mr. Kowalchuk and decide what further assessments you would complete today to guide prosthetic training and discharge planning.

Examiner checklist

  • Interprets the knee flexion contracture as a barrier to prosthetic alignment and gait, and plans management.
  • Notes mild edema and limb shape as appropriate for the temporary prosthesis and monitors volume change and socket fit.
  • Identifies the pink, warm distal area as a possible early pressure injury needing monitoring and socket review. critical
  • Recognizes the right foot callus and reduced sensation as high risk for ulceration of the remaining limb. critical
  • Interprets the Berg score as a fall risk and plans additional balance and mobility testing.
  • Plans a functional mobility measure such as the Amputee Mobility Predictor or a timed walk test, and pre-prosthetic strength testing.
  • Reviews glycemic control, cardiovascular status and exercise tolerance with the team.
  • Considers home environment, steps, support and driving requirements in the assessment.
  • Plans to inspect both limbs fully, including skin, temperature and pulses. critical

Performance scale

4Interprets skin, remaining foot, contracture, strength and balance with clear reasoning, chooses specific further measures and links the findings to prosthetic training and the discharge plan.
3Interprets most findings and selects relevant tests, but gives the remaining foot or the distal skin area too little weight, or offers limited reasoning for the tests.
2Lists tests and findings without interpretation, misses the foot or distal skin concern, or treats the findings only as a strength and gait training problem.
1Dismisses the skin and foot findings, or proceeds with full prosthetic loading without further assessment, creating a risk of harm to the limb and the other foot.

Model spoken answer

I would interpret the findings in order of what could harm him, then what limits his walking. First, skin. The pink, warm, blanching area at the end of the residual limb tells me the tissue is under load. Blanching is reassuring because it is not a deep tissue injury yet, but warmth and redness after 5 hours of wear could be early pressure from the socket. I would remove the prosthesis, look at the whole limb, mark the area, take a photo if the centre policy allows, and check socket fit and liner with the prosthetist. The right foot worries me just as much. He has diabetes, reduced sensation and a callus under the first metatarsal head, and now he puts more weight through that foot. Those are the conditions in which an ulcer forms, and he told me it is sore in the evenings. Today I would do a full foot inspection, check skin temperature, pulses and sensation, and look at his footwear. Second, the contracture. Eight degrees of knee flexion limits terminal extension, which changes alignment and increases load on the end of the limb. I would measure it again, look at hamstring and soft tissue tightness and at how he sits, and plan stretching and positioning. Third, strength and balance. Hip extension at 4 minus and knee extension at 4 out of 5 are fair, but his Berg of 38 puts him at risk of falls, especially on stairs. I would add a validated mobility measure such as the Amputee Mobility Predictor to help predict his prosthetic mobility level, a timed walk and a single leg stance on the right. I would also test his transfers and how he manages the six entry steps. Fourth, general health. His HbA1c of 8.4 percent suggests healing and infection risk, so I would check blood glucose records and ask about hypoglycemia during exercise, and talk to the team about his cardiovascular fitness. Fifth, function and goals. I would ask about the truck, the bed height, the pedals and the hours he sits. Driving a commercial vehicle will have medical and licensing steps that depend on his province, so I would flag that early to him and his physician. Together, I would say his current status is a safe walker with a temporary prosthesis, a limb that needs close monitoring, and a high risk remaining foot, and that these findings should shape the discharge plan, not just the walking program.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss how you would manage safety during today's prosthetic training session and how you would respond to what Mr. Kowalchuk has asked you to do about his symptoms.

Examiner checklist

  • Does not agree to keep the foot and skin findings secret and explains why in a respectful, non-judgemental way. critical
  • Explores his fear that discharge will be delayed and explains that early care prevents a bigger setback.
  • Modifies training: shortens wear time, offloads the distal limb and reduces weight bearing on the sore areas until reviewed. critical
  • Arranges review of the remaining foot and residual limb by the nurse or physician and a footwear check. critical
  • Protects against falls with guarding, a gait belt, appropriate walking aid and environmental setup.
  • Monitors blood glucose, hypoglycemia symptoms and vital signs before and during exercise.
  • Teaches daily skin checks of both limbs with a mirror and what to do when a spot looks wrong.
  • Respects autonomy by sharing decisions about the walking aid and goals, while explaining safety limits.

Performance scale

4Declines secrecy with empathy, modifies the session, arranges review, covers glucose, falls and skin teaching, and keeps him involved in decisions about his walking aid and goals.
3Reports the findings and modifies the session appropriately, but omits glucose monitoring, fall precautions, or the explanation of why the information cannot be kept private.
2Reports or modifies the plan in part, but gives generic safety statements, does not address his request directly, or fails to offload the foot and the residual limb.
1Agrees to hide the findings or continues full training on a threatened foot and limb, creating a clear risk of harm and breaking professional duties.

Model spoken answer

I would begin with what he asked, because it shapes everything. I would tell him kindly that I cannot keep this from his team. I would say that I understand he is worried about being sent home late, and that I want him walking at home too. But a sore spot on the foot he now depends on can turn into an ulcer quickly, and an ulcer on the right foot is the thing that would really delay his plans and could threaten the other leg. Telling the nurse and physician is how we protect his discharge date, not how we lose it. I would ask if he would like to be in the room when I tell them, so he stays part of the decision. Second, the session itself. Before we start I would check his blood glucose, because he is on insulin and exercise can drop it, and I would have juice and a snack at hand. I would take a baseline blood pressure and heart rate. I would inspect the residual limb and his right foot first. Because the distal limb is pink and warm, I would shorten wear time to what the skin allows, check the socket and liner with the prosthetist, and remove the prosthesis if the area reddens more or does not blanch within a few minutes after doffing. For the right foot, I would reduce time on it, check his shoe for room and a good insole, and avoid barefoot standing in the parallel bars. Third, falls. He walked 20 m with close supervision in the bars and his Berg is 38. I would keep the gait belt on, stand on the side of the prosthesis, use the parallel bars or a walker rather than a cane for now, and set the room so a chair is behind him for rest. I would explain why the walker comes first and set criteria to progress to a cane, for example when his balance, step length and walking speed meet targets, because the cane is his goal and that gives him something to work toward. Fourth, teaching. I would show him how to inspect both limbs each day with a mirror, how to wash and dry, how to manage sock ply, and I would tell him to stop wearing the prosthesis and call us if a spot stays red, opens, drains or hurts. I would ask him to repeat the plan back. Finally, I would document my findings and communicate them the same day.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

The team leader asks you to support the planned discharge date and to have the assistant continue the hallway walking program unchanged. Discuss your professional responsibilities in this situation.

Examiner checklist

  • States that the clinical findings, not bed pressure, determine safe discharge and advocates for the client. critical
  • Communicates concerns to the team leader and physician clearly, objectively and in a timely way. critical
  • Reassesses the delegation to the physiotherapist assistant and provides updated written instructions. critical
  • Explains that accountability for the plan remains with the physiotherapist and that tasks require competence and supervision.
  • Documents findings, communication, the client's wishes and the changes made.
  • Considers shared information with the client's consent and respects privacy within the team.
  • Uses an escalation route, such as the manager or professional practice lead, if the concern is not addressed.
  • Offers solutions such as a short delay, enhanced home care, outpatient follow up and prosthetist visits.

Performance scale

4Puts client safety ahead of discharge pressure, communicates objectively, updates delegation and supervision, documents, escalates appropriately and offers workable alternatives to the team. The answer is organized, prioritizes safety and explains the reasoning clearly.
3Advocates for the client and addresses delegation, but lacks clear escalation steps, documentation of the discussion, or constructive solutions to offer the team leader. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
2Mentions advocacy or delegation only in general terms, or complies with the date while noting a concern but taking no action to change the plan.
1Agrees to the discharge date and the unchanged delegation despite known risks, or breaches confidentiality or scope of practice in handling the request. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

Model spoken answer

My first responsibility is to the client, and my professional standards require me to act on what I have found even when the system is under pressure. I would tell the team leader that I understand bed pressure is real and that I want to help find a safe route, but I cannot support the date until the distal limb area and the right foot are reviewed. I would not present it as a complaint. I would give clear facts: a warm, pink, blanching area at the end of the residual limb after 5 hours of wear, a callus and reduced sensation on his right foot with evening soreness, a Berg of 38, and no one at home during the day. I would ask for a physician or nurse review of both limbs today and a prosthetist visit to check the socket. Second, the assistant. I can delegate gait practice, but I remain accountable for the plan, so delegation has to match the client's current condition. Since my assessment changed today, I would update the assistant in person and in writing: shorter sessions, check both limbs before and after every walk, use the walker, gait belt always, and report any redness, pain, drainage or change in glucose to me at once. I would confirm the assistant understands, and I would increase my supervision. If I judged the assistant could not manage the new risk safely, I would do the walking myself for now. Third, I would be honest and open with the client. I would tell him what I am sharing and why, and ask what he wants the team to know about his goals, including the truck. Information is shared within the care team for his care, but I would keep it to what the team needs. Fourth, documentation. I would record my findings, who I contacted and when, the plan changes, his concerns and what he was told. Fifth, if the leader still pressed discharge without review, I would escalate to the clinical manager or the professional practice lead, and I would recognize my regulator's standards say I must advocate for safe care. Finally, I would offer solutions: a few extra days, home care nursing for foot checks, outpatient prosthetic follow up with transport, and a clear plan for what to do if a spot opens. That shows I am solving the same problem as the team, safely.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The client asks the therapist to hide a sore remaining foot and a warm distal limb area to protect his discharge date. The therapist must decline secrecy, explain why, offload the areas, arrange medical review and update the assistant's delegated tasks. Safe care and honest advocacy outrank discharge pressure.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates focus only on strength and gait training and overlook the remaining foot and the distal skin area. Others agree to the client's request for secrecy or accept the team leader's plan without reassessing the assistant's delegation.

Examiner Notes

A pass finds the two skin risks without being told, declines secrecy with empathy and links delegation to the changed risk. A fail trains toward the cane and the driving goal while missing the foot, or defers entirely to discharge pressure.

Case 53 (Mock 6, case 3 of 10): Crohn disease with fatigue and low bone density, young adult

Other Systems · Outpatient physiotherapy clinic in a community health centre

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the exercise program you would design for Ms. Okafor, including your goals, the types of exercise, how you would dose and progress them, and how you would monitor her response.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets goals for bone health, fatigue, strength and function that match her priorities and condition.
  • Plans progressive resistance training and gradual weight bearing impact, with spinal loading patterns added only after medical clearance.
  • Starts at a lower load and volume, with a defined frequency and progression by symptoms and tolerance. critical
  • Limits the program to walking and spine-sparing work, with no spinal loading or impact until the back pain is medically reviewed and imaged. critical
  • Adds low to moderate aerobic work and flexibility with pacing based on fatigue and hemoglobin.
  • Plans for bathroom access, hydration, fuelling and flare days when exercise is reduced.
  • Names monitoring tools such as rate of perceived exertion, sit to stand time, grip strength, fatigue scale and pain.
  • Sets triggers to pause exercise and asks her physician to review the orthostatic heart rate rise, dizziness and anemia. critical
  • Educates on protein and calcium adequacy through the dietitian and gastroenterology team.

Performance scale

4Gives a specific, individualized program with dose, progression, back precautions, monitoring and triggers, linking choices to steroids, low bone density, anemia and Crohn symptoms. The answer is organized, prioritizes safety and explains the reasoning clearly.
3Provides a sound program with dose and progression, but with limited individualization to her condition, thin monitoring, or few triggers to reduce or pause exercise.
2Lists general exercise ideas such as weights and walking, without dose, progression logic or case-specific precautions related to steroids, bone density and her recent back pain.
1Prescribes heavy lifting, running or spinal flexion loading despite low bone density, steroid use and new back pain, placing the client at risk of fracture.

Model spoken answer

My goals are to build strength and bone loading safely, reduce fatigue, and keep her active through flares. I would set them with her, for example lifting at work without back pain and feeling less wiped out by afternoon. First, I would start lower than she expects. She is on prednisone, her bone density is low for her age, her hemoglobin is 98 and her standing heart rate rises to 112. So I would begin with two or three sessions a week of about 30 to 40 minutes. Second, resistance training, in stages. Until her back pain is medically reviewed and imaged, I would limit this to sit to stand, supported leg work and gentle pain free movement that does not load the spine. Once she is cleared, I would add hip hinge, row and press patterns with machines or light free weights, at a load she can lift for 10 to 12 repetitions with good form, two sets, and progress about 5 percent every week or two if there is no pain increase the next day. These patterns are bone loading and useful for work. I would not ask for heavy lifting yet. Third, impact. I would add brisk walking, stairs and small step ups first, then low-level hopping or jumping in small doses later in the plan, if the back and her blood count allow. I would not begin running now. Fourth, the back and her blood work. She has a sharp mid back pain after a heavy lift, so until a physician has reviewed it, I would avoid loaded forward bending, twisting, sit ups and impact, and use pain free movements only. I would also ask her physician to review her standing heart rate rise and dizziness along with her hemoglobin of 98 before I progress anything. Fifth, aerobic and flexibility work. Easy walking or cycling at a conversational pace, building toward 150 minutes a week over several weeks, and gentle mobility work. Sixth, practical details. I would plan sessions after meals when she is least urgent, near a washroom, bring water, and avoid exercise during a flare, replacing it with short gentle walks. Seventh, monitoring. I would track rate of perceived exertion, a fatigue scale, five repetition sit to stand time, grip strength and pain at each visit. I would ask her to check her heart rate and dizziness when she stands. I would reduce or pause if she has worsening back pain, cramping or diarrhea that interferes, dizziness, or a heart rate that stays high. I would share my plan with her gastroenterologist and a dietitian, because protein, calcium, vitamin D and iron are outside what I should prescribe, but are part of the same goal. I would reassess every four weeks and review the plan if she progresses or her medication changes.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Ms. Okafor mentions what happened at work last week. Discuss how you would respond to this information today, including what you would assess, what you would do with her exercise plans and what you would tell her.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes that new focal back pain after lifting a 25 kg load in a person on prednisone with a lumbar Z-score of minus 2.3 needs fracture to be considered. critical
  • Takes a pain history including onset, location, night pain, neurological symptoms, bowel or bladder change and fever.
  • Examines posture, palpation for focal midline tenderness, neurological screen and movement tolerance gently. critical
  • Avoids spinal loading, manual pressure over the tender area and provocative testing until imaging or medical review.
  • Arranges prompt medical assessment and imaging by the physician, communicating findings with her consent.
  • Explains findings in plain language without giving a diagnosis, and without causing alarm.
  • Provides interim advice on activity modification, pain strategies within scope and signs needing emergency care.
  • Addresses the online advice about stopping prednisone, explaining that medication decisions belong to her physician. critical
  • Respects her choices and invites her questions about work and exercise.

Performance scale

4Identifies possible vertebral fracture, assesses safely without provocative loading, holds spinal loading, arranges prompt medical review and addresses the steroid advice within scope of practice.
3Recognizes the concern and refers, but omits some assessment detail, interim safety advice, or the discussion about the online advice to stop the medication. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
2Treats the pain as a simple muscle strain, continues the exercise plan, or refers without clear reasoning or safety precautions for her spine. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
1Applies manual pressure, loads the spine, or advises stopping or changing the medication, creating a risk of harm and operating outside scope. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

Model spoken answer

I would treat this seriously but calmly. A sharp mid back pain after lifting a 25 kg load, in a 26 year old on prednisone with a lumbar Z-score of minus 2.3, could be a muscle strain, but it could also be a vertebral compression fracture. I cannot tell the difference by feel, so my job is to look for features that push me toward fracture, protect her spine, and get her to the right assessment quickly. First, I would take a focused history. When exactly did it start, what was she doing, where is the pain, does it wake her at night, does it catch with twisting, does it spread around the ribs or into her legs, and has she had any numbness, weakness, trouble passing urine or stool changes beyond her Crohn symptoms, fever or unexplained weight loss. Second, I would examine gently. I would look at posture and any new rounding, ask her to point to the spot with one finger, and palpate lightly for focal tenderness over a vertebra, which would raise my concern. I would do a neurological screen for strength, sensation and reflexes in the legs, and observe movement only within comfort. I would not push on the spine, do repeated end range movements, test for spinal loading or give manual therapy there. Third, the plan. I would hold all spinal loading, twisting and impact today, which means no lifting program or running, and keep her to walking and gentle movements that do not hurt. I would explain that we are pausing because her bones are more vulnerable while on steroids, and that this is temporary. Fourth, referral. With her permission, I would contact her gastroenterologist or family physician today to describe the findings and ask for assessment and imaging. If she had leg weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control, or severe uncontrolled pain, I would send her to emergency now. Fifth, communication. I would say that I do not know yet what this is, that most back pain after lifting is not serious, but with her medication and bone scan we check early. Sixth, the prednisone. I would tell her I understand the worry, because steroids do affect bone. But stopping prednisone suddenly can be dangerous and could trigger a flare, and I am not the person who can change it. I would encourage her to ask her gastroenterologist about bone protection options and offer to help her write her questions. Finally I would let her decide what she shares and when.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Ms. Okafor asks you to write a note for her manager about her work limits and to help her keep her diagnosis private. Discuss your professional responsibilities in responding to her requests.

Examiner checklist

  • Obtains informed, documented consent before releasing any information and explains what will be shared. critical
  • Shares only minimum necessary information, such as functional limits, not her diagnosis or medications. critical
  • Bases work restrictions on objective findings and notes that they are temporary pending medical review.
  • Stays within scope: does not diagnose, set medical restrictions beyond physiotherapy findings or comment on drug dosing. critical
  • Supports her in making disclosure decisions and informs her about workplace accommodation processes.
  • Documents the request, consent, content of the note and communication with other providers.
  • Considers coordination with her physician for formal medical documentation and fitness to work forms.
  • Avoids discrimination, and acts with cultural safety and respect for her wishes.

Performance scale

4Obtains consent, limits the note to function, stays within scope, supports her disclosure choices, coordinates with the physician and documents the whole process. The answer is organized, prioritizes safety and explains the reasoning clearly.
3Addresses consent and minimal sharing, but is weaker on scope boundaries, coordination with the physician, or documentation of what was released. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
2Writes a note without clear consent or minimum necessary content, or gives general privacy statements without applying them to her request. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
1Discloses the diagnosis or medications to the employer without consent, or oversteps scope with long-term medical restrictions or drug advice. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

Model spoken answer

I want to respect her privacy, help her with a real workplace need, and stay within what I am qualified to say. First, consent and purpose. Her health information belongs to her. Before I write anything for her employer, I would ask what she wants the manager to know and what she wants to keep private, then explain what I am proposing to share and why, and get her consent in writing. She can say no, change her mind, or limit it. I would also tell her that once I give a note to her, she controls who sees it. Second, the content. A work note should describe function, not diagnosis. I would write about what she can safely do for a defined time, for example, avoid lifting over a stated weight, avoid repetitive twisting and heavy carrying, allow short breaks and washroom access, with a review date. I would not include Crohn disease, her medications or her bone density results. The manager does not need them to arrange lighter duties. Third, basis and scope. My limits must come from my assessment and be honest about what they are. Because we are still waiting on a medical review for her back, I would call them temporary physiotherapy recommendations. I would not set long-term medical restrictions, declare her unfit to work, or comment on whether she should stay on prednisone. Those are decisions for her physician. If her employer needs a formal fitness-to-work or accommodation form, I would suggest her physician complete it and offer to send my functional findings to the physician with her consent. Fourth, supporting her choice. I would explain what disclosure can do and not do. Many workplaces provide accommodations based on functional needs alone, and she might talk with a human resources contact or union representative, and in Canada there are human rights protections against discrimination due to disability. I would not give legal advice, but I would let her know where she can get it. If she decides to disclose more, that would be her decision. Fifth, documentation. I would record her request, my explanation, her consent, what the note says, and the date. I would keep a copy of exactly what was released. Sixth, respect. She is young and anxious about her job, so I would make sure she does not feel her condition is something to hide in shame, only something she gets to manage on her terms.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

New focal mid back pain after a heavy lift in a young person on steroids with a low lumbar Z-score may be a vertebral compression fracture. A competent candidate withholds spinal loading and manual pressure, screens neurology, arranges prompt medical review, and declines to advise on stopping prednisone while respecting privacy.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates build a full lifting and running program without addressing the back pain, or focus on the fatigue and anemia and forget the injury. Others disclose the diagnosis in the employer note or give an opinion about the prednisone.

Examiner Notes

A pass notices the new back pain as the priority and changes the plan before referring. Strong responses explain the consent and minimum necessary points in concrete terms. A fail prescribes impact or heavy spinal loading or gives medication advice.

Case 54 (Mock 6, case 4 of 10): Postpartum urinary leakage, pelvic health clinic

Musculoskeletal · Women's health physiotherapy clinic in a hospital outpatient department

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain how you would organize your assessment and what clinical impression you would form from the information so far, including what else you would want to find out.

Examiner checklist

  • Forms an impression of stress urinary incontinence related to weak pelvic floor muscle function after vaginal delivery.
  • Screens for urgency, urge incontinence and mixed symptoms, voiding difficulty, bowel and prolapse symptoms using history.
  • Screens for red flags: infection, blood in urine, fistula, severe pain, fever, retention and neurological signs. critical
  • Explains the pelvic floor palpation, with consent, including strength, endurance, coordination and relaxation.
  • Considers contributors such as perineal tear, birth trauma, breastfeeding hormones, constipation, cough, lifting load and fatigue.
  • Notes the diastasis and decides whether it is a priority or a distractor in this context.
  • Uses an outcome measure and a bladder diary to quantify symptoms and plan reassessment.
  • Screens psychosocial factors and mood, including the low mood statements, and considers a validated screening tool. critical
  • Explains the findings and impression in plain language and agrees next steps with her.

Performance scale

4Forms a justified impression of stress incontinence, screens red flags and mixed symptoms, plans a consented examination, treats the diastasis as secondary and screens her mood.
3Forms the impression and plans a sound assessment, but misses mood screening, a full red flag screen, or the detail of consent for the examination.
2Lists assessment items without linking them to an impression, or over-focuses on the diastasis and exercise while skipping mood and red flags. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
1Misses red flags and the mood concern entirely, or proceeds with an internal examination without informed and ongoing consent. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

Model spoken answer

I would begin with a clear impression, then show how I would test it. From what I have, the most likely picture is stress urinary incontinence after vaginal birth, with pelvic floor muscles that are weak and tire quickly. The pattern fits: leakage with cough, sneeze and lifting, no burning or blood, and a palpated grade 2 with a short hold. But I would not stop there, because other conditions can look similar. First, history. I would ask about urgency and urge leaks, because a mixed pattern changes the plan. I would ask how often she voids, whether she feels she empties, how the stream is, and whether she feels heaviness or a bulge, which would suggest prolapse. I would ask about bowel leakage and constipation, pain with the scar, and a bladder diary over three days would show her volume and fluid pattern. Second, red flags. I would ask about fever, pain on voiding, blood in the urine, constant dribbling that suggests a fistula, retention, severe perineal pain, foul discharge from the scar, and numbness or weakness in the legs. Any of these means medical review, not exercise. She has none now, but I would document that I asked. Third, the examination.
