With her clear consent, and an explanation of each step, and the option of a chaperone, to stop at any time, and a trauma-informed approach, I would palpate the pelvic floor externally or internally, whichever she prefers, and assess strength, endurance, repeated contractions, coordination with a cough and the ability to relax. The 100 Kegels a day her friend suggested could overwork the muscles, so I would assess for overactivity as well. I would also check the scar. Fourth, the diastasis. A three finger gap at 14 weeks is common and I would treat it as a secondary finding. Its function matters, so I would check whether she can control tension through the midline during a lift, but it is not the reason she leaks, and I would tell her that. Fifth, her wellbeing. She said she is just getting through the days and cries in the car. I would not skip over this. I would ask her directly and kindly about mood, sleep, support and any thoughts of harm. A validated screening tool such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, would help, and I would talk to her about it. Finally I would explain my impression in plain words, use the questionnaire score as a baseline, and agree what we do first.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss how you would approach the next part of this visit so that it is safe and respectful for Ms. Venkataraman, including how you would respond to the things she has told you outside of her bladder symptoms.

Examiner checklist

  • Obtains informed, ongoing consent for any examination, offers choices, a chaperone and the right to stop. critical
  • Uses trauma-informed communication, privacy, and explains each step before touching.
  • Asks directly about her mood and any thoughts of self harm or harm to the baby, calmly and without judgement. critical
  • Responds to a positive screen or risk with same day contact to her physician or crisis resources as appropriate. critical
  • Provides information on supports such as the public health nurse, perinatal mental health services and crisis lines.
  • Adjusts the visit for the baby, time and fatigue, and uses short feasible home exercises.
  • Advises against overdoing 100 daily contractions and teaches a dosed program with rest.
  • Documents the discussion, the consent obtained and any referrals made, with the date and who was contacted.

Performance scale

4Provides trauma-informed, consent-centred care, adapts to her time and baby, asks directly about mood and risk, acts on risk the same day and gives a realistic, dosed exercise plan.
3Handles consent and the mood discussion well, but lacks a clear same day action pathway, or practical adaptations to her time and fatigue. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
2Mentions consent and referral in general terms, or notes the mood comment without exploring it or planning a response to it. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
1Examines without clear consent, or ignores the mood disclosure and possible risk, leaving the client unsupported. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

Model spoken answer

My first priority is that she feels in control of what happens. I would pause before any examination and say, you decide what we do today, and you can stop me at any time. I would explain what the examination involves in plain words, offer a choice of external or internal assessment or doing it another day, offer a chaperone, and give her privacy to change. I would ask whether anything about the delivery would make this hard, and I would not ask her to describe the trauma unless she wants to. Her consent is not a one-time yes. I would check in during the exam, and if she hesitates, I would stop. Second, the baby. Her neighbour is watching the baby, and she is worried about time. I would ask her whether she would like a shorter visit today, or the baby in the room. We can do the history and teaching now and the examination at the next visit if she prefers. That is part of client-centred care. Third, what she told us about her mood. She said she is just getting through the days and cries in the car, and she has not told her family doctor. I would not wait for a later visit. I would say gently that many new mothers feel this way, that it is common and treatable, and that I would like to ask a few questions. I would ask about sleep when the baby sleeps, appetite, enjoyment, worry, and whether she has had thoughts of harming herself or the baby. If she says yes, or if the screening tool shows risk, I would stay with her, make sure she is not left alone, contact her physician or the local crisis service the same day, and ask her to agree to a plan, using a warm handoff. If she has no thoughts of harm but scores high, I would encourage her to see her family doctor within days, offer to help book it, and give her phone numbers for perinatal support lines, her public health nurse and the crisis line. I would ask permission before sharing anything with her husband or physician. Fourth, her exercise. The 100 Kegels a day idea could tire her muscles and does not suit a fatigued new mother, so I would teach a simple dose, such as 8 to 10 contractions of a few seconds, three times a day, linked to feeding, plus a brace with cough. Finally, I would document her consent, the mood discussion and my actions, and tell her what will happen next.

Question 3: Collaboration

Describe how you would work with other professionals and people in her life to support Ms. Venkataraman, including who you would involve, what you would share and how.

Examiner checklist

  • Gets her consent before sharing information with anyone and agrees on what is shared. critical
  • Contacts her family physician about mood symptoms, with a clear summary, and arranges follow up timing. critical
  • Identifies the midwife or obstetric provider and public health nurse as contacts for postpartum care.
  • Considers referral for medical assessment if red flags, prolapse or persistent leaks occur.
  • Involves her husband or support person only if she agrees, with practical roles such as night feeds.
  • Considers other supports: lactation consultant, community parent groups, a psychologist, a dietitian if relevant.
  • Communicates clearly who is responsible for what and the timelines for follow up.
  • Plans to monitor progress and reassess, including communicating changes to the team.

Performance scale

4Specifies who, what, when and how, grounds all sharing in her consent, urgently links the mood concern to her physician, and sets clear roles, timelines and monitoring.
3Identifies relevant team members and addresses consent, but lacks timelines, defined roles, or a plan for urgent contact about her mood. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
2Names professionals in general terms without consent, content or timing, or focuses only on other physiotherapists and exercise. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
1Shares information without her consent, or fails to involve any physician about the mood concern, leaving her at possible risk. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

Model spoken answer

I would start with who, what, when and how, and I would start with her permission. I would ask Ms. Venkataraman who she wants involved and what she is comfortable with me sharing, and I would write her answer in the chart. First, her family doctor. She has low mood and has not told them. With her consent I would phone the clinic and then send a short written summary. I would state what she said, any screening score, that there are no thoughts of harm if that is the case, and the date I suggest she be seen, within the week. I would ask the doctor to confirm they received it. If she showed any risk to herself or the baby, the call would be urgent, the same day. Second, her birth team. The midwife or obstetric provider who delivered her knows about the tear and can check the healing, and the public health nurse often does postpartum home visits and screening. With consent, I would let them know that I am treating her urinary leakage and ask them to tell me about anything unusual they see. Third, if red flags appear, such as blood in the urine, fever, pain, a bulge or constant dribbling, I would stop exercise and ask her physician or a urogynecologist to assess her promptly. If she still leaks after a trial of well-dosed training, say six to twelve weeks, I would discuss with her whether to refer for further evaluation. Fourth, her partner and family. Her husband travels three weeks per month, so I would ask if she would like him to know about the plan, for example sharing night feeds so she can sleep. I would not tell him anything without her permission. I would ask about neighbours, friends or a parent group, and give her information on local supports. A lactation consultant could help if breastfeeding adds stress. Fifth, roles and timelines. I would tell her, and write in my letter, that I am responsible for the pelvic floor program and the review in two weeks, her family doctor for mood and medical care, and the public health nurse for baby and family support. I would also ask her to tell me what she hopes to get from each person. Finally, I would send brief updates after each major change, and I would check at the next visit whether she saw her doctor.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The client describes crying in the car and just getting through the days, and has not told her doctor. This may signal postpartum depression. A competent candidate asks directly about mood and safety, screens with a validated tool, acts the same day if there is risk, and obtains consent before sharing information.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates focus on pelvic floor training and the diastasis and never return to the mood statement, or they share information with her husband or doctor without asking. Another common error is an internal examination without clear, ongoing consent.

Examiner Notes

A pass catches the mood clue unprompted and handles it as a priority with consent and a clear pathway. Strong responses stay trauma-informed. A fail treats the case as a pure incontinence exercise prescription.

Case 55 (Mock 6, case 5 of 10): Cerebral palsy GMFCS III, school-based physiotherapy

Neurological · Elementary school, resource room and gym, community school physiotherapy service

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Explain how you would interpret Kaito's current findings and history, and describe what further information or assessment you would seek before you change any part of his school program.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes reduced left hip abduction with pain and prior migration percentage of 32 percent as a concern for progressive hip displacement. critical
  • Notes that surveillance is overdue since the last radiograph was 18 months ago in a child at GMFCS III risk. critical
  • Considers other sources of night pain such as spasticity, positioning, hip subluxation, fracture and constipation.
  • Interprets contractures and tightness as limiting standing, gait and positioning, and prioritizes them.
  • Notes that an unchanged GMFM-66 is within expectation for GMFCS III at age 8, and that migration over 30 percent warrants orthopedic referral through the physician.
  • Plans to take a pain history from Kaito using an age appropriate scale and to ask parents about sleep and behaviour.
  • Plans a focused exam: hip range, palpation, observation of pelvic obliquity, scoliosis screen and skin check.
  • Plans to request updated hip imaging and medical review through the responsible physician. critical
  • Considers goals from Kaito and family, such as school participation and mobility.

Performance scale

4Identifies possible left hip displacement from the findings and overdue surveillance, considers other causes of pain, plans a focused assessment and requests imaging and review before changing the program.
3Recognizes the hip concern and requests imaging, but gives limited reasoning about other causes of pain or about what his unchanged function score means. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
2Focuses on contractures and function without connecting the hip findings and pain to displacement risk or the need for updated imaging. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
1Dismisses the hip pain as behaviour or ordinary spasticity and proceeds to increase standing and stretching, placing the hip at risk. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

Model spoken answer

I would interpret Kaito's findings through the lens of his hips first, because that is the part with the highest stakes. Children with bilateral spastic cerebral palsy at GMFCS III are at real risk of hip displacement, and the risk rises with higher migration percentage and limited abduction. His left migration percentage was 32 percent 18 months ago, and the right 18. A migration over 30 percent is the usual point to ask the physician for an orthopedic referral, and he was already past it. Now his left hip abducts only 25 degrees against 40 on the right, it hurts to move into abduction, and he has night pain. That pattern makes me worry that the left hip may have progressed. I cannot tell from my hands, because only a radiograph can measure migration, so the key missing piece is a current hip X-ray and medical review. Surveillance is meant to be regular, so 18 months without it is overdue. Second, other causes of night pain. It could be spasticity, difficult positioning in bed, constipation, a growth related muscle problem, or a fracture. His bone density may be lower because of limited weight bearing. I would ask Kaito, using a faces scale or a body drawing, where and when it hurts and what helps, and ask his parents about sleep, mood, bowel habits, any fall, and what has changed in the last few months. Third, the other findings. Hip flexion contractures of 15 degrees, tight hamstrings and 10 degrees of lacking dorsiflexion explain the crouched stance and fatigue with walking, and they are important for standing and gait. But they are less urgent than the hip. His GMFM-66 score of 52 has not changed in a year, which is within what I would expect at this age for GMFCS III, so I would not read it as a failure of his effort or as a plateau to fix. Pain could still limit his participation, so I would ask what he wants to do at school and recess. Fourth, my examination. I would observe sitting and standing alignment for pelvic obliquity and windswept posture, screen the spine for scoliosis, check skin over the hips, and measure range gently, stopping at the first resistance or pain. I would not stretch the hip to its end range. I would also record a pain score and sleep pattern as a baseline. Fifth, communication. I would contact his parents and the child's pediatric rehabilitation clinic or physician for updated hip imaging. Until then, I would hold any change to the program that adds load or stretch around the left hip. In short, my interpretation is possible progressive left hip displacement until proven otherwise, with the other findings as contributors, and I would act on that before extending standing time.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Discuss how you would respond to the teacher's request and what you would put in place to keep Kaito safe while the questions about his program are answered.

Examiner checklist

  • Holds or reduces the extended standing and aggressive stretching until the hip has been reviewed. critical
  • Explains the reason to the teacher in plain language without breaching Kaito's privacy.
  • Changes the educational assistant's instructions: no forced stretching, stop if pain or resistance, use comfort based positioning. critical
  • Provides alternative active ways to stay mobile and participate, such as short supported standing and seating options.
  • Asks for Kaito's views, uses assent and listens to his refusal and pain as important information. critical
  • Teaches the assistant and family signs needing prompt review such as increasing pain, new refusal to bear weight, swelling or fever.
  • Plans night positioning and pain management discussion with parents and physician, within scope.
  • Documents instructions given, who received them and the date for review.

Performance scale

4Holds the standing and stretching plan, retrains the assistant in writing, gains Kaito's assent, offers alternatives, and gives clear warning signs and a review date.
3Modifies the plan and informs the assistant, but lacks child assent, written instructions, or specific warning signs for the school staff. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
2Agrees to a reduced program in general terms without explaining the reasons, retraining the assistant or involving Kaito in the decision. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
1Proceeds with the teacher's request or allows forceful stretching to continue despite his pain, risking harm to the hip. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

Model spoken answer

I would tell the teacher that I am glad she is thinking about how to help Kaito get more standing, and that I need to pause the plan for a short time because of what I found in his hip. I would not share details beyond what the school needs. I would say, Kaito's left hip is sore and I need his doctor to look at it before I ask him to stand longer or stretch more, so for now we should keep things comfortable. Second, the standing. Supported standing is useful for bone health and hip development when the hips are healthy, but if the hip is migrating or painful, long periods in an unsuitable position could add pressure. So until the hip is reviewed, I would reduce standing to short, comfortable periods, perhaps 20 to 30 minutes with his hips in a position that does not push the left into adduction, or I would pause it, depending on what I find. I would not push through pain. He has been avoiding the frame because his leg hurts, and I take that as information. Third, the educational assistant. She has been told to stretch his hips as far as they go. I would meet with her today, show her what is safe, and replace that instruction in writing: no stretching to end range, no forcing, stop at the first resistance or sign of pain on his face, and use slow, active movements and comfortable positions instead. I would tell her to report anything that worries her and who to call. Fourth, Kaito. He has started to say he does not want to do physio. I would sit with him, at his level, and ask what is hard and what he would like to be able to do. I would explain, in words an 8 year old understands, that we are going to look at his leg so it can feel better, and that he has a say in what we do. His assent matters, and if he says no or shows pain, we stop. Fifth, alternatives. I would suggest ways he can still take part, such as supported sitting in a good chair, short walks in his walker with a rest option, and recess games that do not stress the hip. Sixth, warning signs. I would give the teacher and parents a short list: new or worse pain, crying at night, refusing to bear weight, a swollen or hot hip, fever, or a fall. Any of these leads to a call to the parents and a same day medical visit. Finally I would document all instructions and set a review date for the week after the hip result.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Discuss your professional responsibilities in this situation, considering the school board's proposal, Kaito's parents, and how you would handle information and decisions about his care.

Examiner checklist

  • Obtains informed consent from the parents, includes Kaito's assent, and explains the plan to change and referral for imaging. critical
  • Shares only the necessary information with school staff, with parental consent, and keeps records confidential. critical
  • Advocates for Kaito's clinical needs when the board proposes consult-only service, and escalates through the proper channels. critical
  • Contacts the pediatric clinic or physician for follow up, handles the unsigned annual form and clarifies responsibility for surveillance.
  • Practises within scope by not ordering imaging or prescribing, and by referring to the responsible physician.
  • Provides supervision and clear written delegation to the educational assistant, who is not a regulated provider.
  • Communicates in an accessible, culturally safe way with parents who have limited availability, such as phone or flexible times.
  • Documents findings, communication, consent, and decisions about caseload and service level.

Performance scale

4Addresses parent consent and child assent, privacy, scope, delegation to the assistant, advocacy against service reduction with objective escalation, and documentation of each step. The answer is organized, prioritizes safety and explains the reasoning clearly.
3Covers consent, referral and delegation adequately, but is weak on advocacy, the limits of privacy sharing, or documentation of decisions. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
2Mentions consent and communication in general terms without applying them to the board proposal, the assistant or the surveillance gap. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
1Accepts discharge or a change of service without raising the clinical risk, or shares information with the school without consent. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

Model spoken answer

My first responsibility is to Kaito and his family, and that begins with consent and open communication. His parents make decisions for him and Kaito should be included at a level he understands. I would phone them or meet at a time that suits their shifts, and explain in plain words that I found a painful, stiff left hip, that his last hip X-ray was a year and a half ago, and that I recommend a new one through his doctor. I would ask for permission to contact the pediatric rehabilitation clinic and to share my findings with the teacher and educational assistant, and I would tell them what I would share. I would ask if they want an interpreter or written notes, and offer a call or a message if they cannot come in. I would also ask about the unsigned annual form, whether they have been told why it matters, and offer to help them complete and return it. Second, scope. Imaging and medical decisions are outside what I can decide. So I would contact the physician or clinic with a short, clear message of the findings and ask for a prompt hip X-ray and review, and I would tell them what I changed in the school program. Third, the educational assistant. She is not a regulated provider, so I stay accountable for what she does. I would give written, specific instructions and train her, check her competence, review how she follows them, and tell her who to call. Fourth, information and privacy. The teacher and assistant need to know what to do and what to avoid, but not his full history. With consent, I would share function and precautions, not diagnosis details or imaging numbers. Fifth, the board's proposal. Moving to consult-only may reduce my direct contact exactly when his hip needs monitoring. I would write to my supervisor with objective facts: possible hip displacement, a pain complaint, overdue hip surveillance, a need for assistant training, and a need for follow up. I would explain the clinical risk of a change at this time and ask that the decision wait until his hip is reviewed. I would not make the decision on my own or hide my concern, and if the concern is not addressed, I would use the board's escalation process and my regulator's standards on advocacy. Sixth, documentation. I would record the findings, consent and assent, who was contacted and when, instructions given to the assistant, and the service decision. Finally I would follow up with the parents after the X-ray and make sure someone owns the surveillance plan going forward.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

A 32 percent left migration percentage 18 months ago, now reduced and painful left hip abduction and night pain suggest possible progressive hip displacement with overdue surveillance. The candidate must hold forceful stretching and extended standing, seek updated imaging and review, retrain the assistant and advocate against reduced service.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates extend the standing and stretching program as the teacher asked, or concentrate on contractures and GMFM scores without noticing the hip. Others delegate stretching to the assistant without limits or accept the board's consult-only model.

Examiner Notes

A pass connects the migration percentage, abduction loss and night pain to displacement risk, holds the plan and escalates. Strong responses respect Kaito's assent. A fail follows the school's request or misses the overdue imaging.

Case 56 (Mock 6, case 6 of 10): Phase II cardiac rehabilitation after bypass surgery with postoperative atrial fibrillation

Cardiovascular-Respiratory · Hospital-affiliated outpatient cardiac rehabilitation program, first visit

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the exercise plan you would set up for Mr. Kowalczyk over the first four weeks of the program, including how you would prescribe intensity, what you would monitor, and how you would decide when to progress him.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets intensity using perceived exertion and talk test rather than relying on heart rate alone because of atrial fibrillation and beta-blocker.
  • Starts with low to moderate aerobic work such as walking or stationary cycling, with a warm-up and cool-down.
  • Targets a rating of perceived exertion of about 11 to 13 on the 6 to 20 scale initially.
  • Applies sternal precautions, avoiding pushing, pulling and heavy lifting through the arms during healing. critical
  • Monitors resting and exercise heart rate, rhythm, blood pressure and symptoms at each session, with defined stop criteria. critical
  • Plans gradual increases in duration before intensity, using a stated progression rule.
  • Adds lower limb range of motion and gentle strengthening, respecting the saphenous harvest site.
  • Includes a home walking program with a written log and warning symptoms.
  • Sets outcome measures such as repeated six minute walk, and patient-stated goals for golf and driving.
  • Starts exercise only after the team reviews the weight gain, ankle swelling and sternal drainage, and holds if fluid overload or wound infection is suspected. critical

Performance scale

4Prescribes intensity by perceived exertion because of atrial fibrillation and beta-blocker, applies sternal precautions, states stop criteria and a clear progression rule, and links the plan to his goals with reasons.
3Gives a sound aerobic plan with monitoring and sternal precautions but explains the intensity method or progression rule only briefly.
2Lists generic exercise advice and heart rate targets without adjusting for rhythm or medication, or omits stop criteria.
1Uses heart rate targets as the sole guide, ignores sternal precautions, or proposes unsafe progression.

Model spoken answer

I would build the plan around three things: a safe starting dose, close monitoring because of his rhythm and medications, and a clear rule for moving forward.

First, intensity. Mr. Kowalczyk is in atrial fibrillation with a rate control medication, so his heart rate is irregular and blunted. A target heart rate range would be unreliable for him. I would prescribe by perceived exertion on the 6 to 20 scale, aiming for 11 to 13, which feels fairly light to somewhat hard, and I would confirm with the talk test, meaning he can speak in full sentences. His six minute walk peak rating of 13 at 118 beats per minute tells me that is a reasonable place to begin. I would still record heart rate as a safety measure, with an agreed upper limit set together with the cardiac rehabilitation physician.

Second, the starting condition. His weight is up 2.5 kg in four days, his ankles are puffy and his incision is weeping. Those could mean fluid overload or a wound infection, so before I start aerobic work I would contact the cardiac rehabilitation physician or surgical team to review them. I would begin at low intensity only after that review, and hold exercise if either concern is confirmed.

Third, the mode and structure. Weeks one and two would be five minutes of warm-up, then 10 to 15 minutes of continuous or interval walking or recumbent cycling, then a cool-down. I would increase duration by about two to five minutes per session before I raise speed or resistance. I would add gentle range of motion and light lower limb strengthening, such as sit to stand and heel raises, working around the tender saphenous site. For the upper body I would keep to sternal precautions: no pushing up from chairs with the arms, no lifting beyond what the surgeon allows, and active range of motion within comfort. Resistance work would be introduced only after surgical clearance.

Fourth, monitoring. At every session I would check resting heart rate and rhythm, blood pressure, symptoms, weight and the incision and ankles by simple observation. During exercise I would watch for chest discomfort, dizziness, unusual breathlessness, palpitations that feel different from his baseline, or a systolic pressure fall with effort. Those would be stop criteria, and I would have a plan for who I contact.

Fifth, progression. I would progress him when he completes a session at a rating of 11 to 13 with a stable rhythm, appropriate blood pressure response and no symptoms for two consecutive sessions. If he exceeds that rating, I hold or drop back.

Finally, I would link to his goals. For golf I would later add trunk rotation and then light swing practice with surgical approval, and for driving I would confirm the surgeon's clearance. I would repeat the six minute walk at week four, and give him a home walking plan with a log and a card listing symptoms that mean stop and call.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

During his third session, Mr. Kowalczyk becomes light-headed on the bike and says his heart is 'fluttering'. Explain how you would respond in the moment and what you would do before he leaves the building.

Examiner checklist

  • Stops the exercise immediately, keeps him seated and supported, and does not allow him to stand abruptly. critical
  • Checks pulse rate and regularity, blood pressure, SpO2 and symptoms and compares with baseline. critical
  • Calls for help from the program nurse or physician according to the emergency protocol. critical
  • Activates emergency response if chest pain, syncope, severe breathlessness or marked hypotension develops.
  • Stays with him, reassures him, and monitors until symptoms settle.
  • Does not discharge him until a physician or nurse has reviewed him. critical
  • Documents the event, vital signs, actions and who was informed.
  • Explains what happened and obtains his consent about informing his surgeon and family physician.
  • Reviews medication timing and whether he took his metoprolol and apixaban.

Performance scale

4Stops exercise, assesses vital signs, involves the team, holds discharge until reviewed, documents, and communicates honestly with him about the reason, including his fear of readmission.
3Responds safely and calls for help but is less specific about escalation criteria or about communicating with him.
2Stops exercise but handles the event alone, lets him leave after he feels better, or gives limited documentation.
1Allows him to continue, to stand abruptly, or to leave without clinical review.

Model spoken answer

My first move is to stop the bike and keep him sitting. Light-headedness with a fluttering heart in someone with known atrial fibrillation could be a fast ventricular rate or a drop in blood pressure, and standing him up could make that worse. So I lower the resistance, stop pedalling, have him sit upright with his feet supported, and stay beside him.

Next I assess. I take his pulse at the wrist and note the rate and whether it is more irregular than usual, then I measure blood pressure and SpO2 and ask him about chest discomfort, breathlessness, vision changes and whether he feels faint. I compare these with his baseline numbers from the start of the session. At the same time I signal the program nurse, because in our program the supervising team is part of the response. I do not manage a rate and rhythm problem alone.

If at any point he develops chest pain, loses consciousness, is very short of breath, his systolic pressure drops markedly, or he does not improve, I activate the emergency response and follow the facility protocol, including positioning and having the defibrillator brought over.

If he settles, I still do not send him home. He needs to be reviewed by the nurse or physician before leaving, who may take a rhythm strip or arrange an assessment. I would also ask whether he took his metoprolol and apixaban today and whether he had caffeine, skipped a meal or was dehydrated, because those details help the team.

I would document the time, symptoms, vital signs, my actions, who I called and the outcome.

Then the client-centred part. I would tell him calmly what I saw, that I took it seriously and why the team needs to look at it. He has already shown that he fears being sent back to hospital, so I would acknowledge that worry and explain that reporting changes protects his recovery. I would ask his permission to contact his surgeon and family physician, and I would give him a clear plan for the rest of the day with symptoms that mean calling 911. I would also ask his wife to stay with him until he is reviewed, with his consent.

Question 3: Professional Responsibilities

Mr. Kowalczyk asks you not to tell anyone about the weeping incision and his weight gain, saying he will 'sort it out himself'. Discuss how you would handle this request and your professional obligations.

Examiner checklist

  • Explores his reasons and fears respectfully and listens before advising.
  • Recognizes weight gain, ankle swelling and incision drainage as findings needing prompt medical assessment. critical
  • Explains the clinical reasons and the possible consequences of delay in plain language.
  • Seeks his consent to share the information with the surgeon or physician, and encourages him to call himself. critical
  • Explains that information relevant to his care is shared within the care team under privacy legislation.
  • Acknowledges that a competent adult may refuse, and documents the discussion and his decision. critical
  • Escalates within the program team even if he declines, based on duty to act on safety concerns.
  • Does not diagnose infection or heart failure but communicates the observations accurately.
  • Arranges follow-up and gives clear written advice on warning signs.

Performance scale

4Explores his fear, explains the clinical significance, seeks consent, respects capacity while escalating within the care team, documents and gives safety-net advice.
3Seeks consent and escalates appropriately but offers less exploration of his reasons or less detail on documentation and privacy.
2Either complies with secrecy or overrides him without discussion, with limited explanation.
1Keeps the findings hidden from the team, or breaches his privacy outside the care team without justification.

Model spoken answer

I would start by listening. He has asked for secrecy, and I do not think this is stubbornness. He told us he does not want to be readmitted, so there is fear underneath. I would say something like, 'It sounds like going back to hospital worries you a lot. Tell me what you are most afraid of.' That respects him and often changes the conversation.

Then I would be clear about what I have seen. A weight gain of 2.5 kg in four days, evening ankle swelling and drainage from a sternal incision are not things I can interpret on my own, but they are the kinds of findings a surgeon or physician needs to know about soon. Fluid gain after bypass surgery can mean the heart or kidneys are not coping, and drainage from a sternal wound can be an early sign of a wound problem. Both are easier to treat when caught early. I would explain that in plain words without scaring him, and I would stress that telling the team does not automatically mean admission. Often it means a phone call, an examination or a medication change.

My aim is his consent. I would offer to sit with him while he phones the surgeon's office or the cardiac nurse, or I can make the call with him present. I would explain that information relevant to his care can be shared with the team looking after him, under the provincial health privacy rules, and that I would prefer he agrees to it.

He is a competent adult, so he has the right to decide how his information is shared and to decline advice. If he still refuses, I would not argue or threaten. I would document his decision and my explanation, give him written warning signs such as increasing breathlessness, rapid weight gain, fever, spreading redness or pus, and advise when to call 911. I would also inform the supervising physician or nurse in our program because they are part of his current care team and these findings affect whether it is safe to continue exercise. I would stay honest with him about that step. His wife already knows about the weight and swelling, but I would not share anything further with her beyond what he agrees to, and I would ask his permission before discussing the incision with her.

Finally, I would hold intensity at a low level for now, check the incision and weight at each visit and follow up next session.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is weight gain of 2.5 kg in four days, evening ankle swelling and a weeping sternal incision that the client has not told the surgeon about. A competent candidate recognizes possible fluid overload or wound complication, seeks his consent to report, respects his autonomy, escalates within the care team, and documents. The saphenous harvest tightness is a distractor.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates focus on a heart rate target and skip rhythm-specific monitoring, or they promise confidentiality and keep the findings to themselves. Others report behind his back without exploring his fear or documenting the conversation.

Examiner Notes

A pass shows rhythm-aware exercise prescription, a calm and safe response to arrhythmia symptoms, and a respectful handling of the consent conflict that still gets the findings to the team. Failing candidates either collude in secrecy or override him without communication.

Case 57 (Mock 6, case 7 of 10): Distal radius fracture after cast removal in an older woman with osteoporosis

Musculoskeletal · Private outpatient physiotherapy clinic, initial assessment

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Based on this presentation, explain your clinical impression and the priority issues you would identify. Describe what further examination you would complete today and how it would shape your decisions.

Examiner checklist

  • Identifies that pain, swelling, skin changes and burning with light touch out of proportion to the time since fracture raise concern for complex regional pain syndrome. critical
  • Notes stiffness of wrist, forearm and fingers as expected after immobilization but distinguishes it from the disproportionate features.
  • Plans a sensory and autonomic exam including temperature, colour, sweating, allodynia and hair or nail changes, and compares with the left side. critical
  • Screens for median nerve involvement or carpal tunnel signs after distal radius fracture.
  • Assesses circulation and neurological status of the hand and fingers. critical
  • Recognizes the fragility fracture and untreated osteoporosis as a need for medical follow-up.
  • Checks tendon function and signs of extensor tendon irritation or rupture risk.
  • Uses measures such as goniometry, volumetric or circumferential swelling, and PRWE to establish baseline.
  • Asks about function, goals and falls history.

Performance scale

4Distinguishes expected stiffness from features disproportionate for time since injury, plans a systematic CRPS and neurovascular examination, links findings to referral decisions, and recognizes the fragility fracture.
3Identifies stiffness and raises CRPS or nerve concern with a reasonable examination but with limited reasoning about how results change decisions.
2Lists tests without interpreting the findings or concentrates only on range of motion and strength.
1Treats as simple stiffness, ignores neurovascular and pain features, or plans aggressive stretching.

Model spoken answer

My overall impression is a distal radius fracture, healed enough to remove the cast, with the expected stiffness of wrist, forearm and fingers. But two things do not fit a straightforward stiff wrist. She describes burning pain on light touch, and I see shiny skin and swelling across the back of the hand six weeks out. Pain of 8 out of 10 with gentle movement and a burning quality that seems greater than the injury would explain makes me think about complex regional pain syndrome, which is a recognized complication after distal radius fracture. I cannot confirm it from this alone, so my job is to look for the pattern and decide whether to refer.

The first priority is a neurovascular check. I would check capillary refill, radial pulse, colour and temperature of both hands. I would test sensation in the median, ulnar and radial nerve distributions, because median nerve compression at the wrist is common after this fracture and could also cause burning. I would ask about night pain and numbness in the thumb to middle finger and perform Phalen and Tinel tests as findings allow.

Second, I would look for the features of complex regional pain syndrome systematically. That means asking about sensory changes such as allodynia, vasomotor changes such as colour and temperature asymmetry, sudomotor change such as sweating and swelling, and motor or trophic changes such as weakness, tremor or changes to hair and nails. I would compare each with the left hand. If several of these categories are present, I would contact her physician promptly, because early treatment matters.

Third, I would examine tendon function, since extensor pollicis longus can be affected after distal radius fracture, and observe finger flexion and extension. I would measure range with a goniometer, swelling by figure of eight circumference, and repeat the PRWE as a baseline.

Fourth, I would not neglect the bigger picture. A fall onto an outstretched hand at 68 with known osteoporosis, a stopped medication and no medical follow-up is a fragility fracture. That needs communication with her physician about bone health and falls.

How this shapes my decisions: if signs point toward complex regional pain syndrome, I would keep treatment gentle, graded and pain-guided and refer; if not, I would proceed with progressive mobility.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Ms. Okonkwo says she wants her hand 'back to normal' quickly and asks you to stretch her wrist as hard as needed. Describe how you would respond and how you would adapt treatment to keep her safe while still supporting her goals.

Examiner checklist

  • Explains why forceful passive stretching is avoided and the risk of increasing pain and swelling. critical
  • Uses graded, pain-guided active and active-assisted movement within tolerance. critical
  • Addresses swelling with elevation, active finger and shoulder movement, and gentle compression if appropriate.
  • Considers desensitization, graded motor activity and education about pain.
  • Checks understanding of her goals, such as caring for the child and daily tasks, and sets shared goals.
  • Reviews fall risk and home safety, including winter footwear and ice. critical
  • Educates on osteoporosis and encourages medical follow-up, including discussing stomach upset with her physician.
  • Obtains informed consent for each technique and encourages her to stop movements that sharply raise pain. critical
  • Advises on safe lifting and avoiding weight bearing through the wrist until cleared.

Performance scale

4Validates her goal, explains why forceful stretching is avoided, builds a graded and pain-guided plan with swelling and sensitivity management, addresses falls and bone health, and uses consent and shared goals.
3Provides a safe, gentle plan with explanation but is limited in addressing falls, bone health or collaborative goal setting.
2Agrees to stretch within tolerance without explaining risk, or gives generic exercises only.
1Uses forceful passive stretching or dismisses her pain and sensitivity.

Model spoken answer

I would begin by acknowledging her goal. She is alone, she looks after a child, and she wants function back. That is a perfectly reasonable wish, and I would tell her I want to help her get there as fast as is safe.

Then I would explain why I will not stretch hard. Her wrist is stiff, but her hand is also swollen, sensitive and very painful. Pushing hard into a painful, sensitive hand can raise pain, increase swelling and, if there is an early nerve or pain system problem, set her back. So the plan is to work with her pain level, not against it. I would agree on a signal: movements that bring a brief ache that settles within a few minutes are acceptable, and anything that sharply increases pain or leaves it worse an hour later means we ease off.

The treatment would include active and active-assisted range of motion of the wrist, forearm and especially the fingers, thumb and shoulder, to reduce stiffness and swelling. I would use elevation and gentle compression with a sleeve if it is comfortable, and a short hand program, five minutes every hour, rather than one long session. If sensitivity to touch is prominent I would introduce graded desensitization with textures, and graded use in light tasks such as holding a cup. I would explain what we know about pain after injury so that she understands that sensitive does not mean damaged. I would avoid passive stretching and weight bearing through her wrist until she is cleared.

Safety goes beyond the wrist. She fell on ice, has osteoporosis, and lives alone. I would ask about footwear, ice cleats, walking aids, lighting and what she does when the sidewalks are slippery, and discuss a balance and strength program for later. I would also say plainly that the bone problem needs attention from her doctor, and that stopping the bisphosphonate because of stomach upset is something to discuss with him because there are other options.

I would get her agreement before each hands-on technique, show her what I will do, and ask her to tell me to stop. We would write down two or three goals together, such as being able to lift the child's cup and turn a door handle, and review in two weeks.

Question 3: Practice Management

The clinic owner wants Ms. Okonkwo to purchase the twelve-session package, but her insurance covers six visits. Explain how you would manage scheduling, delegation and billing for her care, and what you would document.

Examiner checklist

  • Bases the number and frequency of visits on her clinical needs and not on a package target. critical
  • Informs Ms. Okonkwo of her coverage limit and fees clearly before treatment and obtains informed financial consent. critical
  • Does not pressure her into prepaying and offers pay-per-visit or a refund policy for unused sessions. critical
  • Plans visits with a front-loaded schedule and a review point to decide on continued care.
  • Uses a home program and group or assistant-supervised sessions to extend value within her coverage.
  • Delegates only suitable tasks to the physiotherapist assistant, such as exercise supervision, with clear instructions and ongoing reassessment by the physiotherapist. critical
  • Documents assessment, consent, plan, outcome measures, communication with the physician, and fee discussion.
  • Raises the concern about the package policy with the clinic owner in line with ethical billing standards.
  • Applies infection prevention measures for shared equipment such as hand therapy tools.

Performance scale

4Bases visits on need, discloses coverage and fees for informed financial consent, rejects pressure to prepay, delegates appropriately with oversight, documents thoroughly and addresses the owner's policy.
3Handles scheduling, billing disclosure and delegation sensibly but with less attention to ethics of the package or documentation detail.
2Describes scheduling or billing in general terms and does not challenge the package or specify delegation limits.
1Pushes the package regardless of need, hides cost information, or delegates assessment to the assistant.

Model spoken answer

My first principle is that the number of visits comes from what Ms. Okonkwo needs, not from what a package requires. If the clinic's policy conflicts with that, I have to raise it. I would also keep her informed about money before we start, not after.

For scheduling, I would plan more frequent visits early, perhaps twice a week for the first two to three weeks, because we need to monitor her pain and sensory signs and teach her the home program. Then I would taper to once every one or two weeks as she gains independence. With six covered visits, that front-loaded approach makes the most of her coverage. I would set a formal review at visit four to decide whether she needs more care, and if so, what and why.

On billing, I would tell her plainly that her plan covers six visits a year, state our fee per visit, and explain what she would pay out of pocket beyond that. I would ask whether she wants to proceed on a pay-per-visit basis. I would not present the twelve-session package as the only option, and I would not encourage her to prepay for sessions we may not need. If the clinic does offer a package, she must understand what happens if she needs fewer sessions, including a refund policy in writing. Charging for care that is not clinically indicated would be a breach of ethical billing standards from my provincial regulator.

I would talk with the clinic owner respectfully, explain that I am obliged to base recommendations on need and informed consent, and ask for a pay-per-visit option for her.

Delegation: the physiotherapist assistant can supervise her exercise sessions once I have assessed her, written the program and explained the limits, such as no forceful stretching and what to do if pain flares. I remain responsible for reassessment and for adjusting the plan, so I would see her myself at set intervals and ask the assistant to report any changes in swelling, colour or pain.

Documentation would include my assessment findings, outcome measures, my reasoning, her consent to treatment and to the fee discussion, the plan, the delegation instructions, and my communication with her physician. I would also follow infection prevention practices for shared equipment such as putty and exercise tools, cleaning between clients.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issues are the possibility of complex regional pain syndrome (burning pain on light touch, shiny swollen skin, pain out of proportion) and an untreated fragility fracture with no physician follow-up. The package policy creates an ethical billing conflict. A competent candidate screens, refers, avoids aggressive stretching and protects her financial consent.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates treat the case as simple post-cast stiffness and plan strong passive stretching. Others accept the package as written or delegate reassessment to the assistant.

Examiner Notes

A pass shows recognition of out-of-proportion pain and sensory change with a cautious, referring plan, and a billing answer driven by need and consent. A fail ignores the red flags or goes along with the prepaid package.

Case 58 (Mock 6, case 8 of 10): Community falls prevention screening event for older adults

Other Systems · Seniors' community centre multipurpose room, group screening morning

Question 1: Assessment and Diagnosis

Interpret Mr. Rahimi's screening results and describe what they indicate. Explain what additional questions or tests you would add in the time available, and how you would decide on next steps.

Examiner checklist

  • Interprets TUG of 14.8 seconds as above the commonly used threshold of 12 seconds and indicative of increased fall risk.
  • Interprets chair stand of 8 and tandem stance of 4 seconds as below age-expected norms indicating reduced lower limb strength and balance.
  • Identifies a systolic drop of 26 mmHg with symptoms as orthostatic hypotension. critical
  • Links the timing of new antihypertensive and alpha-blocker with near-falls at getting out of bed. critical
  • Asks about number and circumstances of falls, injuries, fear of falling, vision, feet, alcohol, nocturia and cognitive concerns.
  • Recognizes that a medication review by a physician or pharmacist is a priority and that the physiotherapist does not change medications. critical
  • Decides on next steps combining medical referral and a balance and strength program.
  • Considers a quick visual screen and footwear or home hazard questions.
  • Recognizes screening limits and avoids diagnosing.

Performance scale

4Interprets each test against norms, prioritizes the orthostatic drop and its link to new medications, stays within scope by referring for medication review, and chooses focused questions and next steps.
3Interprets most findings and identifies orthostatic hypotension and referral, with less rationale for added questions.
2Reports test results as abnormal without linking them or notices the blood pressure only in passing.
1Ignores the blood pressure drop, or advises him to change or stop medication.

Model spoken answer

When I look at the full picture, Mr. Rahimi screens as high risk for falls, and the most important finding is not the balance test but the blood pressure.

I will take the performance tests first. A Timed Up and Go of 14.8 seconds is slower than 12 seconds, which is the cutoff commonly used to flag increased fall risk in community-dwelling older adults. Eight chair stands in 30 seconds is below what we would expect for a man in his mid seventies, so his leg strength is reduced. Holding tandem stance for only four seconds, when about ten is expected, shows limited static balance. Together these suggest that he has real strength and balance impairments that exercise can improve.

But his blood pressure dropped from 138 over 80 lying to 112 over 68 after three minutes of standing, a systolic fall of 26 mmHg, and he was light-headed. A fall of 20 mmHg systolic or more is generally treated as orthostatic hypotension. The history lines up: his near-falls happened on getting out of bed, and he started two blood pressure lowering medications six weeks ago. That suggests a medication-related cause that may be contributing, though I cannot determine that. It is outside my scope to change medication, so my priority is to get this reviewed by his physician or pharmacist promptly.

With five minutes per person, I would add only a few focused questions. How many falls or near-falls in the past year, any injuries, any fear of falling that limits his activity, night-time trips to the toilet because of the prostate, vision and last eye exam, foot problems, alcohol use and any memory worries. I would take a quick look at his footwear, since he is wearing lace-up shoes, and ask about hazards at home, stairs and lighting.

Next steps: first, a written note for his physician describing the orthostatic findings and timing with the medication change, and advice to see them this week. Second, give him safety advice to rise slowly in stages: sit at the edge of the bed, move ankles, then stand. Third, refer him to a community balance and strength program, or to physiotherapy for a fuller assessment. Screening results show risk, not a cause, so I would explain that clearly.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Explain how you would run the stations safely for this group, including the sit-to-stand and balance tests, and how you would involve participants in decisions about their own results and next steps.

Examiner checklist

  • Screens for contraindications to testing, such as acute illness, recent fall injury, uncontrolled symptoms or severe dizziness, before performance tests. critical
  • Uses a sturdy armless-compatible chair against a wall and guards or spots participants during balance and walking tests. critical
  • Stops testing if symptoms such as light-headedness occur and seats the participant safely. critical
  • Obtains informed consent for screening and for sharing results with the centre and family physician. critical
  • Explains results privately and in plain language, checking understanding.
  • Respects choices, including declining a test or referral.
  • Provides written results and an action plan the participant can keep.
  • Adapts for language, hearing, vision or mobility needs.
  • Has an emergency plan and first aid equipment in the room.

Performance scale

4Screens before testing, sets up chair and guarding safely, defines stopping rules, obtains consent including sharing, delivers results privately and supports choice with adapted communication.
3Describes sound safety measures and respectful communication but with less detail on stop criteria or consent.
2Mentions safety and consent in general terms without specific measures for the tests.
1Omits guarding or screening, or pressures participants to complete tests.

Model spoken answer

Safety begins before anyone stands up. At the sign-in I would use a short health check: have they felt unwell today, fallen recently with injury, had chest pain, uncontrolled dizziness, or been told by a doctor not to exercise. Anyone with a yes would be offered a conversation with me and, if needed, a medical check before doing performance tests. For people like Mr. Rahimi who feel dizzy on standing, I would stop and seat him after the blood pressure test rather than continue to the walking tests until he feels settled.

Next, equipment. The chair for sit-to-stand must not slide. This one is light and has no arms, which is the correct style for the test, but I would place it against a wall or have the assistant hold it from behind. For tandem stance and Timed Up and Go, I would stand close, within arm's reach, and use a gait belt if there is concern. I would clear a walkway and a landing space. The volunteer would be trained to guard and not to give results. I would keep a chair behind participants for balance tests and have first aid supplies and a phone nearby, with a clear plan to call 911.

I would stop any test if there is dizziness, chest pain, breathlessness or unsafe movement, and sit them down.

Now the client-centred side. Before the screening, I would explain what each test is for, what it involves and who will see the results, and ask for consent to participate and to share results with their physician. People can decline any part. After testing, I would give results privately, not at the table. I would use plain language: 'Your leg strength and balance are lower than we would like, and there are things that help.' I would ask what matters to them, offer choices such as a class, a home program or a clinic visit, and check that they understood by asking them to tell me back the plan. Each person gets a written summary and a contact name.

For people with hearing, vision or language needs, I would use large print, a quiet corner or an interpreter, and give them time. Some may feel embarrassed, so I would frame results as information they can act on, not a judgment.

Question 3: Practice Management

Describe how you would improve the organization of this screening event, including privacy, records, use of volunteers and the assistant, equipment, and the summary the manager wants for funding.

Examiner checklist

  • Stops public display of names and results and changes the sign-in system to protect privacy. critical
  • Corrects the volunteer who is disclosing results and defines volunteer tasks that do not include interpreting results. critical
  • Provides the funding report as de-identified, aggregate data only unless participants consent otherwise. critical
  • Delegates measuring tasks to the assistant with training and supervision, while the physiotherapist interprets results and counsels.
  • Plans scheduling and station flow for 40 registrants, including more cuffs, time per person and appointment slots.
  • Uses standard protocols and calibrated equipment, and cleans cuffs, chairs and stopwatches between participants.
  • Documents results, consent and referrals in a secure record and gives participants copies.
  • Establishes referral pathways to physicians and community programs and follow-up for high-risk participants.
  • Reviews liability, insurance and incident reporting for community events.

Performance scale

4Corrects privacy breach and volunteer role, delegates measurement with oversight, redesigns flow and infection control, protects records, and gives aggregate de-identified reporting with referral pathways.
3Addresses privacy, delegation and reporting but with less detail on flow, equipment or records.
2Mentions general organization points but leaves the public results and volunteer disclosure unaddressed.
1Shares identifiable results with the manager, or lets volunteers continue giving interpretations.

Model spoken answer

I see several problems, and the first one is privacy, so I would fix that immediately. A sign-in sheet that shows names and results to everyone breaks the confidentiality of personal health information. I would replace it with a sign-in that collects only a name and a participant number, and place any results on a separate private form kept face down or in a folder. I would also speak with the volunteer, politely and right away. Telling participants their results in front of others is a privacy breach and also risky, because a volunteer is not trained to interpret findings. I would clarify roles: volunteers greet, guide, time flow, carry water and hold chairs steady where trained, but do not give or discuss results.

For the assistant, I would delegate the measurement tasks, such as taking blood pressure, timing standard tests and recording values, after confirming their training with a demonstration. I remain responsible for the screening protocol, for interpreting results and for counselling. I would be present and check any abnormal reading, such as the orthostatic drop we found.

On scheduling, forty people at five minutes each is over three hours of testing if done one at a time with two cuffs. I would add stations in parallel, such as one for blood pressure, one for strength and balance and one for questions and education, and use appointment times so that people do not queue. I would borrow more cuffs or set up a second blood pressure station, and keep orthostatic readings for everyone with falls, near-falls or relevant medication, since a person can have a large drop without feeling dizzy. All equipment would be checked and calibrated and the same test protocols used for every participant. I would wipe the cuffs, stopwatch and chairs between participants and provide hand sanitizer.

For records, each participant gets a written summary and I keep a consent-based record in a secure, locked place or password-protected file. High-risk results get a referral letter to the family physician and a list of local balance programs.

For the manager's funding report, I would provide aggregate figures only: number screened, proportion above the risk cutoff, and number referred. No names or identifying details. If the centre wants stories or quotes, I would ask participants for consent first.

Finally, I would confirm that insurance covers the event and have an incident report process.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issues are an orthostatic drop of 26 mmHg temporally linked to new antihypertensive and alpha-blocker medication, and a privacy breach from a public sign-in sheet and a volunteer disclosing results. A competent candidate prioritizes the orthostatic finding for physician review, stays within scope, and corrects the privacy practices without blaming anyone.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates give a list of balance exercises and miss the blood pressure drop and its link to medications. In the management question they often forget to correct the privacy breach or share named results for funding.

Examiner Notes

A pass interprets screening results with norms, flags the orthostatic hypotension and refers, runs a safe consented screening and fixes privacy and role problems. A fail ignores the medication link or accepts public disclosure.

Case 59 (Mock 6, case 9 of 10): Inpatient rehabilitation after moderate traumatic brain injury

Neurological · Inpatient neurological rehabilitation unit, week 3 after injury

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the physiotherapy plan you would set for Mr. Sandhu for the next two weeks, including goals, how you would structure sessions at this level of recovery, and how you would measure and reassess progress.

Examiner checklist

  • Sets goals appropriate to Rancho level V such as safe mobility with assistance, sitting and standing tolerance, and prevention of secondary complications.
  • Structures sessions with short duration, a quiet environment, simple one-step commands and repetition. critical
  • Uses functional, familiar tasks rather than complex tasks that overload attention and increase restlessness.
  • Provides positioning, range of motion and tone management for the plantar flexors, including splinting or stretching.
  • Progresses standing and gait practice with appropriate assistance and supervision, observing weight bearing orders. critical
  • Plans for safety measures including fall precautions and monitoring for restlessness. critical
  • Selects measures suited to this level such as Orientation Log, Rancho level, Modified Ashworth and a mobility scale, and reassesses at defined intervals.
  • Coordinates sessions with the interdisciplinary team and times therapy for best arousal.
  • Includes family education and a role for the family in graded activity.

Performance scale

4Matches goals and session structure to Rancho level V and post-traumatic amnesia, combines tone, mobility and safety planning, uses suitable measures with set reassessment and engages family.
3Provides appropriate mobility goals and structure but is thin on cognitive-behavioural adaptation or measures.
2Offers a generic neuro rehabilitation plan without adjusting to confusion and restlessness.
1Proposes high-intensity or complex tasks that ignore cognition, or omits safety.

Model spoken answer

At Rancho level V, Mr. Sandhu is confused, easily overstimulated and still in post-traumatic amnesia. That shapes everything: what I ask of him, how I deliver it, and what I expect.

Goals first. Over two weeks, I would aim for him to sit unsupported for longer, perhaps 15 minutes, and to stand and take steps with one person assisting and a walker, with fewer cues, while remaining safe. I would also aim to prevent contractures, skin problems and loss of conditioning. These are modest goals, because at this stage the priorities are safe, repeated movement experience and preventing complications, not high-level skill.

Structure of sessions. I would keep them in short blocks, perhaps two sessions of 20 to 30 minutes in the day, scheduled when he is most alert, usually mornings, and spaced from other therapies. I would work in a quiet area with one person talking, using short, single-step commands, consistent words and demonstration. I would give him a lot of repetition of the same few tasks, such as sit to stand, standing at the parallel bars or walker, and stepping, because he will learn through doing rather than through instruction. I would give a break when restlessness builds, rather than pushing through, and redirect rather than correct him. Familiar activities like reaching for a tool, a cup or his phone could keep him engaged.

Physical management. For the left ankle plantar flexor tone, I would do daily stretching and positioning, consider a resting splint, and use weight bearing through the leg in standing, within his tibial fracture orders. I would also do active range of motion and cycling or supported exercise to maintain strength and aerobic fitness.

Safety. I would use a gait belt, two people for early standing, a low bed and a sensor alarm if the unit has one, and ask nursing to follow the same approach.

Measuring. I would record the Rancho level, the Galveston Orientation and Amnesia Test or the unit's Orientation Log, Modified Ashworth, time sitting and standing, assistance level and distance walked. I would reassess weekly and when behaviour changes.

Finally, I would invite his family to join sessions and show them how to cue him, so that practice carries over.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Explain how you would respond to your observations of the right calf and what you would do about it in today's session, including how you would keep him safe and manage his restlessness.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes swelling and tenderness of the calf as a possible deep vein thrombosis despite prophylaxis. critical
  • Holds standing, walking and any vigorous exercise of the right leg until medical assessment. critical
  • Informs the physician or nurse immediately and requests assessment such as ultrasound. critical
  • Avoids massage, forceful stretching or squeezing the calf. critical
  • Observes for signs of pulmonary embolism such as sudden breathlessness, chest pain or increased heart rate, and responds if present.
  • Measures and records calf circumference on both sides and notes colour, warmth and pain.
  • Keeps him comfortable and calm, using redirection and a low-stimulation approach.
  • Uses safe, simple bed-level activity that does not compromise the leg, as allowed by medical advice.
  • Documents findings, communication and decisions.

Performance scale

4Identifies possible DVT despite prophylaxis, withholds mobilization and massage, escalates immediately with objective findings, watches for embolism, and manages restlessness calmly while documenting.
3Recognizes the concern and escalates and holds activity but gives less detail on monitoring or behavioural management.
2Notes the calf but proceeds with modified exercise or delays reporting.
1Ignores the calf finding, massages it or continues mobilization.

Model spoken answer

What I noticed is a right calf that looks fuller than the left and that makes him wince when squeezed. After a tibial fracture, immobility, head injury and a recent period of limited movement, he is at higher risk of a deep vein thrombosis, and the fact that he is on enoxaparin does not rule it out. Note that the fracture is on the left, which means the right leg would not normally be explained by fracture swelling. So I treat this as a possible clot until someone proves otherwise.

What I do today. I stop and do not start standing or walking. If there is a clot, activity could dislodge it, and a clot reaching the lungs can be fatal. I do not massage the calf, squeeze it again or stretch it. I make him comfortable in bed or a chair with the leg supported, and I find the nurse or physician immediately. I tell them clearly what I saw: right calf larger than left, tender, with timing and prophylaxis details, and I ask for an assessment, likely a Doppler ultrasound. While waiting, I measure the circumference 10 centimetres below the knee on both sides, and record colour, warmth and tenderness, so there is objective information.

I watch for signs of a pulmonary embolism: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, a fast heart rate, falling oxygen saturation or coughing blood. If any of those appear, I call for emergency help and stay with him.

Because of his restlessness and confusion, I have to manage him gently. He may not understand why I stopped or why he must stay still. I would use a calm voice, simple words and a familiar activity such as holding something he likes or listening to music, in a quiet space. I would keep the call button within reach, have another staff member or family nearby, and avoid restraint or arguing. If he gets restless, I redirect him rather than correct him.

If the physician rules out a clot, I resume the plan. If it is confirmed, I follow medical direction about activity before moving him again.

I document the findings, measurements, time, who I informed, their response and my decision to hold mobilization.

Question 3: Communication

His mother, through his sister, says the team is not listening and wants him pushed harder. Describe how you would communicate with her, including the language and strategies you would use, and what you would say about his progress and the plan.

Examiner checklist

  • Arranges a qualified interpreter rather than relying on the sister, at least for important discussions. critical
  • Acknowledges her concern and listens to her goals and worries without defensiveness. critical
  • Explains post-traumatic amnesia and why short, calm sessions are more effective than pushing harder, in plain language. critical
  • Gives concrete, honest information about progress and expected course without making firm promises about return to work.
  • Mentions the calf concern as appropriate, shared with his substitute decision-maker (confirm who this is under provincial law) in keeping with team communication.
  • Respects cultural and family values and asks about her preferences for how information is shared.
  • Gives her a meaningful role, such as helping with cueing, familiar objects and orientation.
  • Uses teach-back and short written or pictorial materials in her language if available.
  • Offers a regular update time and a point of contact in the team.

Performance scale

4Uses a professional interpreter, listens first, explains post-traumatic amnesia and plan in plain language, is honest about prognosis, gives the mother a role and uses teach-back with a contact point.
3Communicates respectfully with an interpreter and clear explanation but offers less on prognosis honesty or family involvement.
2Relies on the sister, or explains in technical terms without addressing her concern.
1Dismisses her concern, argues, or promises recovery timelines.

Model spoken answer

The first thing I would do is arrange a professional interpreter for Punjabi. Her daughter's help is welcome and comforting, but the daughter may soften or filter difficult news, may feel pressured and should not carry the role of translating medical information about her brother. So I would book an interpreter for a proper meeting with the team, and use a telephone or video interpreter if one is not in person.

I would begin by listening. 'You come every day, and you want to see him get better. Tell me what worries you most and what you hope to see.' I would summarize what I hear to show I have listened, and thank her. If she feels the team has not listened, I would acknowledge it: 'I am sorry you have felt that way. I want to hear you now.'

Then I would explain, in simple language and short sentences, what is happening. His brain is healing, and right now he is confused and does not remember new things, which is called post-traumatic amnesia. Because of this, long or hard sessions confuse him and can make him upset and slow his recovery. Short, calm sessions with plenty of repetition help his brain more. So 'pushing harder' would feel to him like more noise, not more learning. I would use an analogy, such as a tired muscle that needs rest between lifts. I would show her what he can do now, such as sitting and standing with help, and what we are working toward.

I would be honest about uncertainty. Brain injury recovery is slow and varies, and I cannot promise when he will return to work, but I can tell her what we will review and when.

I would offer her a role: bringing familiar items like his own clothes and photos, speaking in Punjabi, and learning the cues we use so she can practise with him. I would ask what her family wants us to know about him. I would use teach-back by asking her, through the interpreter, to tell me in her own words what we agreed. I would give her a time each week when she can meet the team and a name to contact.

Because Mr. Sandhu is likely not capable of making complex care decisions at this stage of post-traumatic amnesia, and the team determines capacity for each decision, I would confirm with the team who his substitute decision-maker is under provincial law, which may be his mother or may be someone else. If the calf concern is being investigated, I would make sure the team shares it with that person, and that his mother hears it from them with the interpreter.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issue is a fuller, tender right calf in a patient with traumatic brain injury and recent immobility, raising possible deep vein thrombosis despite enoxaparin prophylaxis. A competent candidate withholds mobilization, avoids massage, escalates at once, watches for embolism and manages restlessness gently. Reliance on a family member as interpreter is a second communication risk.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates continue with standing practice or massage the calf, or they use a high-intensity plan unsuited to post-traumatic amnesia. In communication they accept the sister as interpreter or promise a return-to-work date.

Examiner Notes

A pass matches rehabilitation to Rancho level V, recognizes and escalates the possible clot, and communicates with the mother through a professional interpreter. A fail mobilizes the leg or overlooks the language barrier.

Case 60 (Mock 6, case 10 of 10): Congenital muscular torticollis in a 3 month old infant

Musculoskeletal · Pediatric outpatient clinic in a regional hospital

Question 1: Care Planning

Describe the treatment program you would set up for Noor and her parents, including the techniques, how often and how long, and how you would monitor progress and decide on further steps.

Examiner checklist

  • Teaches gentle, parent-performed passive stretching of the right sternocleidomastoid into left lateral flexion and right rotation, with the infant calm. critical
  • Gives a specified frequency, such as several short stretches at each diaper change throughout the day.
  • Promotes active head control and strengthening in tummy time, side-lying and supported sitting, with positioning to encourage turning toward the right.
  • Advises environmental changes such as toys, feeding and carrying positions that encourage turning to the restricted side.
  • Gives positioning advice for the flat skull, including supervised tummy time and varied head position while awake.
