  • Uses measures such as range of motion with goniometer or photographs, and a severity classification, at planned intervals.
  • Sets criteria for reassessment and escalation if there is no improvement, for example specialist referral. critical
  • Uses teach-back and a written or video home program.
  • Plans frequent follow-up in the first weeks and describes expected outcomes honestly.

Performance scale

4Provides a specific, gentle parent-led stretching dose, active and positioning strategies, head shape advice, measurable monitoring and clear escalation criteria with teach-back.
3Describes appropriate stretching and positioning with some measurement but with less specifics on dose or escalation.
2Gives general advice about exercises without dosage, monitoring or escalation.
1Recommends forceful stretching or unsafe equipment, or omits parent teaching.

Model spoken answer

Noor has the typical picture of congenital muscular torticollis: a right head tilt with the face turned left, a palpable mass in the right sternocleidomastoid, limited passive rotation to the right, and some flattening of the skull on the left. The good news is that early, parent-led treatment usually works well, so my plan relies on teaching her parents.

The core of treatment is a home program. I would teach them to stretch the right sternocleidomastoid gently by tilting her head toward the left ear and rotating her chin toward the right shoulder. The stretch should be slow and sustained for about 20 to 30 seconds, repeated a few times, with Noor calm and relaxed, with one hand stabilizing her shoulder, so that the stretch comes from the neck and not from the whole body. I would aim for this at most diaper changes, around six to eight times a day. It should never be forced or done while she is crying hard. I would have the parents practise on a doll first, then on Noor with me watching, and finish when I am satisfied that the technique is gentle and correct.

Second, active work. Tummy time should be built up from one minute in several short sessions, using a rolled towel under her chest, or lying on a parent's chest, so she gets used to it. I would encourage her to turn her head to the right by placing toys, light and voices on that side, by changing the direction she lies in the crib, and by feeding or carrying her so that her right side faces the room. Side-lying and supported sitting help her to work against gravity and strengthen the left neck muscles.

Third, the head shape. Positioning when awake, supervised tummy time and carrying upright will reduce pressure on the flattened area.

To monitor, I would measure passive rotation and lateral flexion with a goniometer, photograph head posture, record the sternocleidomastoid mass and grade severity, and repeat every two to four weeks. I expect improvement within a few weeks. If there is no meaningful change after about four to six weeks, or if she worsens, I would refer to the pediatrician or pediatric specialist for further assessment.

I would give a written and video home plan and check understanding with teach-back.

Question 2: Client Safety and Client-Centred Care

Describe how you would respond to what the parents are doing at home and to the pillow they are considering. Explain what you would advise about positioning, sleep and handling, and how you would support the parents' wishes and worries.

Examiner checklist

  • Advises against forceful stretching and holding a crying infant, and demonstrates a gentle technique. critical
  • Advises that positioning wedges or pillows in the crib are unsafe because of suffocation risk and sudden infant death risk. critical
  • Recommends that she sleeps on her back on a firm, flat surface with nothing else in the crib. critical
  • Explains that supervised tummy time is done only while awake and watched.
  • Acknowledges the parents' anxiety and effort, avoids blame and validates their wish to help.
  • Uses shared decision-making and respects family values and preferences, including the relative's advice, in a non-confrontational manner.
  • Teaches safe handling and carrying of the infant, with head support.
  • Gives signs that mean seek urgent help such as feeding difficulty, vomiting, lethargy, fever or limb weakness. critical
  • Offers written guidance and a contact for questions.

Performance scale

4Validates the parents, corrects forceful stretching with demonstration, firmly rejects the wedge pillow with safe sleep guidance, teaches handling, gives red-flag signs and uses a respectful, shared approach.
3Corrects stretching and the pillow with explanation but gives limited safe sleep detail or warning signs.
2Mentions gentle technique or safe sleep briefly with little explanation or empathy.
1Endorses the pillow or forceful stretching, or leaves the parents' worry unaddressed.

Model spoken answer

I would start with what is right. Samira is stretching Noor every day before feeds because she wants to help, and that shows love and commitment. I would say so. Then I would explain, kindly, what needs to change.

First, the stretching. Holding Noor's head firmly while she cries is not safe or helpful. A baby's neck muscles tighten up when she is upset, which makes stretching less effective, and forceful stretching may injure the muscle or cause more scarring. The stretch that works is gentle, slow and done when she is calm. I would demonstrate on a doll, then guide Samira's hands with Noor, and ask her to show me back. I would suggest short stretches at diaper changes rather than several minutes before feeds, which could also upset the feeding. I would tell her that if Noor is crying hard, stop, comfort her and try again later.

Second, the wedge pillow. I would advise firmly against it. Anything soft, wedge-shaped or placed in the crib to hold the head can block her breathing, and raises the risk of suffocation and sudden infant death. Safe sleep guidance is that she sleeps on her back on a firm, flat mattress with nothing else in the crib. We can address the head tilt with daytime strategies instead. Tummy time is only when she is awake and watched. For the flat spot, we use varied positions during the day, and, at night, we position the crib so she has to turn to the right to see the room or the door, and her toys and light come from the right.

I would also teach safe handling: always support her head, carry her so that her right side faces outward, and avoid pulling her up by the arms.

Finally, I would ask about the relative's advice. Rather than argue, I could invite the relative to a session or give Samira a sentence to use: 'The physiotherapist showed us a gentle way.' I would ask what worries her most, and respect her choices once she has the information.

I would give a written list of warning signs: trouble feeding, repeated vomiting, unusual sleepiness, fever, a new lump, weakness in an arm or leg, or her eyes not tracking. Any of these mean see a doctor the same day.

Question 3: Collaboration

You also note asymmetry of the left thigh creases and reduced left hip abduction. Describe who you would involve, what you would communicate to them, how and when, and how you would coordinate care with the family.

Examiner checklist

  • Recognizes that hip asymmetry and reduced abduction in an infant with torticollis require screening for developmental dysplasia of the hip. critical
  • Contacts the pediatrician or family physician promptly, the same day, to request hip assessment and imaging such as ultrasound. critical
  • Uses a clear structured message stating the findings, her age and sex, and any relevant risk factors, with a specific request, and follows up in writing.
  • Explains the finding and referral to the parents honestly, calmly and with their consent to share information. critical
  • Does not diagnose the hip condition or delay the referral until the next visit.
  • Coordinates with the public health nurse for monitoring, feeding support and parent reinforcement.
  • Considers referral to a pediatric specialist or orthopedics for torticollis if there is no improvement.
  • Clarifies each professional's role and who is the primary contact for the family.
  • Plans follow-up of the outcome and adjusts the home program as advised, such as avoiding certain hip positions if a brace is used.

Performance scale

4Links torticollis and hip asymmetry, contacts the physician the same day with a structured request, informs parents with consent, involves the public health nurse, clarifies roles and follows up.
3Refers promptly and informs parents, with less detail on message content or role coordination.
2Plans to mention the hip at the next visit or refers vaguely without urgency.
1Ignores the hip finding or tries to manage it alone.

Model spoken answer

The hip finding changes the picture. Asymmetrical thigh creases and less abduction on the left are signs that can go with developmental dysplasia of the hip, and it has been reported to occur more often in infants with torticollis, and female sex is itself a risk factor. I cannot diagnose it, but I also should not wait for the next appointment in six weeks. The earlier a hip problem is found, the simpler the treatment, so I would act today.

Who I involve first is Noor's physician, either the pediatrician or the family doctor who referred her. I would phone the same day, not just send a note. I would give a short structured message: who she is, that I am seeing her for torticollis, that I found asymmetrical thigh creases and reduced left hip abduction, that she is a three month old girl with torticollis, and that I am concerned about the hip and request an assessment and likely hip ultrasound. I would ask what they want me to do in the meantime and confirm that in writing, with a copy of my findings.

Next, the parents. I would explain what I saw and why I am asking the doctor to check, in plain words, without alarming them: 'The way her hip moves is a little different on the left. Sometimes that is nothing, but it is easy to check and better to check early.' I would explain that this is common with torticollis, and not their fault. I would ask for their consent to share information and to book the test, and give them a time frame for when they will hear back.

Third, the public health nurse, with the parents' permission. She sees the family monthly and can reinforce feeding and sleep advice, and notice if the hip plan changes. If the doctor confirms the hip concern, the orthopedic or pediatric hip service will lead that care, and I would adjust my program to avoid positions that conflict with their advice, for example hip positioning if a harness is used.

I would clarify who the main contact is for the family, probably me for the neck and the physician for the hip, and share each other's numbers. I would review progress in two weeks and refer on for torticollis if she is not improving.

Safety or Professional Point Built Into the Case

The buried issues are the unsafe forceful stretching and the planned crib wedge pillow (suffocation risk), and the asymmetrical thigh creases with reduced left hip abduction needing screening for developmental hip dysplasia. A competent candidate corrects the handling gently, rejects the wedge, contacts the physician the same day and communicates honestly with the parents.

Common Candidate Errors

Candidates describe stretching and positioning well but do not notice the hip finding, or they mention it without a same-day call. Some approve the pillow or stretching 'as hard as it takes'.

Examiner Notes

A pass gives a specific gentle parent-led program, rejects unsafe practices with respect, and escalates the hip finding promptly with clear communication. A fail misses the hip or accepts unsafe home practices.

PART 3: Supplementary Questions

Question 1

Musculoskeletal

A 62-year-old retired carpenter from Regina reports four months of aching in both thighs and calves after walking about two blocks. Symptoms settle within minutes of sitting, and he can cycle thirty minutes without trouble. Foot pulses are strong and symmetrical. Standing extension reproduces the discomfort. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

  • A. Neurogenic claudication from narrowing of the central spinal canal, eased by lumbar flexion
  • B. Vascular claudication from peripheral arterial disease of the iliac arteries
  • C. Unilateral S1 radiculopathy from a posterolateral intervertebral disc herniation
  • D. Bilateral hip osteoarthritis producing referred pain into the thighs and calves

The correct answer is A (Neurogenic claudication from narrowing of the central spinal canal, eased by lumbar flexion): Relief with sitting or flexion and reproduction with extension is the classic posture pattern of canal narrowing. Strong pulses and good cycling tolerance make an arterial cause unlikely, since arterial pain follows effort rather than posture. A single-root disc syndrome would not give symmetrical symptoms, and hip disease would show restricted hip motion.

Question 2

Musculoskeletal

A 41-year-old warehouse worker in Moncton has two days of severe low back pain with new numbness around the genitals and difficulty starting urination. Both legs feel heavy and the weakness is worsening over hours. Straight leg raise is positive on the right. Which action is most appropriate at this visit?

  • A. Arrange an outpatient lumbar MRI within the week and continue exercise therapy in the meantime
  • B. Teach neural sliders for the right leg and reassess neurological signs in clinic tomorrow morning
  • C. Ask the family physician for a same-week review of bladder function and leg strength
  • D. Send the patient to emergency now for urgent imaging and surgical review

The correct answer is D (Send the patient to emergency now for urgent imaging and surgical review): New saddle numbness, bladder disturbance and worsening bilateral leg weakness suggest cauda equina compression, where outcome depends on how quickly decompression happens. An outpatient scan within the week is the right test at the wrong speed, and a same-week physician review is tempting but still too slow. Nerve sliders cannot relieve a compressive lesion and would only delay surgical care.

Question 3

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist in Halifax suspects an acute anterior cruciate ligament rupture in a 19-year-old hockey player who felt a pop after a sudden pivot and developed a large effusion within hours. Hamstring guarding limits testing. Among stability tests of the knee, which one has the highest sensitivity for detecting this injury?

  • A. Anterior drawer test performed with the knee at ninety degrees
  • B. Lachman test performed with the knee in twenty to thirty degrees of flexion
  • C. Pivot shift test performed with a valgus and rotational load
  • D. Posterior drawer test performed with the knee at ninety degrees

The correct answer is B (Lachman test performed with the knee in twenty to thirty degrees of flexion): The Lachman test is the most sensitive clinical test for an acute tear because the hamstrings relax and the knee sits near the position of greatest anterior translation. The anterior drawer is tempting but loses reliability with effusion and hamstring guarding. The pivot shift is highly specific yet is often limited in the acute painful knee. The posterior drawer tests the other cruciate ligament.

Question 4

Musculoskeletal

A 34-year-old woman from Kelowna inverts her ankle stepping off a curb. She cannot take four steps in the clinic. Palpation shows tenderness along the back edge of the lateral malleolus, six centimetres upward from its tip. Swelling is moderate. What is the best next step according to the Ottawa ankle rules?

  • A. Refer for ankle radiographs to exclude a malleolar fracture before any weight bearing is attempted
  • B. Treat as a grade two ligament sprain with a brace and start rehabilitation immediately
  • C. Refer for foot radiographs to exclude a fifth metatarsal base fracture before any loading
  • D. Order an ultrasound of the lateral ligaments to grade the injury before imaging

The correct answer is A (Refer for ankle radiographs to exclude a malleolar fracture before any weight bearing is attempted): Inability to take four steps combined with bone tenderness at the posterior edge of the malleolus meets the criteria for ankle radiographs. Foot films are tempting because the foot zone is part of the rule, but no midfoot tenderness is described. Treating as a sprain or grading ligaments first would risk missing a fracture that rehabilitation could displace.

Question 5

Musculoskeletal

A 55-year-old painter from Winnipeg has six weeks of right shoulder pain after lifting a ladder. He has pain during active elevation between 60 and 120 degrees, weakness when resisting external rotation, and a positive drop arm test. Passive elevation is full. Which diagnosis best fits?

  • A. Adhesive capsulitis in the early freezing stage of the glenohumeral joint
  • B. Full-thickness tear of supraspinatus extending into infraspinatus tendon fibres
  • C. Isolated subacromial bursitis irritation without any rotator cuff tendon disruption present
  • D. Acromioclavicular joint sprain after a direct fall on the point of the shoulder

The correct answer is B (Full-thickness tear of supraspinatus extending into infraspinatus tendon fibres): Weak resisted external rotation with a positive drop arm test points to loss of tendon continuity rather than irritation alone. Full passive range rules out a capsular restriction. Bursitis alone does not usually cause measurable weakness, and the history gives no direct fall on the shoulder.

Question 6

Musculoskeletal

On the first day after a cemented total knee arthroplasty in Calgary, a 68-year-old man is alert and has a pain score of 4 out of 10 with regional analgesia. The surgeon has ordered weight bearing as tolerated. Which goal is most appropriate for the first session?

  • A. Stand at the bedside and walk short distances using a walker with staff supervision
  • B. Begin gentle knee flexion in bed and delay standing until the second day
  • C. Start stair climbing practice with a handrail to prepare early for discharge
  • D. Progress straight to walking without an aid to restore a normal gait pattern

The correct answer is A (Stand at the bedside and walk short distances using a walker with staff supervision): Early mobilization lowers the risk of venous thromboembolism, pneumonia and stiffness, and the surgeon has allowed loading. Short supervised walking with a walker also begins gait retraining. Bed-based flexion work is tempting for range, but it delays function, and stairs or walking without an aid are goals for later sessions.

Question 7

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist in Ottawa is reviewing instructions with a patient who had a total hip arthroplasty through a posterior approach and has not yet been cleared by the surgeon to stop precautions. Which combination of movements puts the new joint at greatest risk of dislocation?

  • A. Hip extension beyond neutral combined with abduction and external rotation while lying
  • B. Hip abduction to thirty degrees with the knee extended and the foot supported
  • C. Hip flexion to sixty degrees with neutral rotation while sitting on a raised seat
  • D. Hip flexion beyond ninety degrees with adduction and internal rotation

The correct answer is D (Hip flexion beyond ninety degrees with adduction and internal rotation): After a posterior approach the posterior capsule and short rotators are repaired or weakened, so a position that combines deep flexion, crossing the midline and inward rotation pushes the head backward. Extension with external rotation is the risky pattern after an anterior approach instead.

Question 8

Musculoskeletal

A 46-year-old recreational runner from Victoria has eight weeks of morning stiffness and pain two to six centimetres above the heel, with a thickened, tender midportion of the tendon. There is no history of rupture. Which exercise approach has the best support for management?

  • A. Full rest from all walking and running activity for three months
  • B. Progressive heavy slow calf loading with an eccentric emphasis, continued over twelve weeks
  • C. Static calf stretching held for sixty seconds several times every day
  • D. Deep friction massage applied to the tendon before each training session

The correct answer is B (Progressive heavy slow calf loading with an eccentric emphasis, continued over twelve weeks): Midportion tendinopathy responds to progressive loading that increases tendon capacity, and eccentric or heavy slow resistance programs are both well supported. Rest leaves the tendon deconditioned. Stretching and massage can ease symptoms briefly but do not rebuild load tolerance.

Question 9

Musculoskeletal

A 39-year-old electrician from Thunder Bay has lateral elbow pain for ten weeks that worsens when he grips a hammer or lifts a kettle with the forearm pronated. Pressure just distal to the lateral epicondyle is tender. Resisted wrist extension with the elbow straight reproduces pain, and neck movements do not. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  • A. Cervical radiculopathy at the C6 nerve root level
  • B. Radial tunnel syndrome from compression of the posterior interosseous nerve
  • C. Common extensor tendinopathy at the origin on the humerus
  • D. Medial collateral ligament sprain of the elbow joint

The correct answer is C (Common extensor tendinopathy at the origin on the humerus): Gripping pain with resisted wrist extension and focal tenderness at the lateral origin is the usual picture of extensor tendon overload. Radial tunnel pain is deeper and more distal and is not reproduced by local palpation at the origin. A neck source would respond to cervical movement.

Question 10

Musculoskeletal

A 71-year-old woman in Edmonton is in a cast after a distal radius fracture sustained on ice. Two days later she reports pins and needles in the thumb, index and middle fingertips that worsen overnight. Pain is mild, passive finger stretch is comfortable and the fingers are warm. Which complication is most likely?

  • A. Early forearm compartment syndrome from swelling beneath the tight cast
  • B. Acute median nerve compression within the carpal tunnel caused by swelling beneath the tight cast
  • C. Superficial radial nerve neuritis from pressure of the cast edge over the wrist
  • D. Cervical radiculopathy aggravated by the sling position during sleep at night

The correct answer is B (Acute median nerve compression within the carpal tunnel caused by swelling beneath the tight cast): Swelling inside a cast can raise pressure in the carpal tunnel and compress the median nerve, which supplies the thumb, index and middle fingers. The cast should be assessed urgently by the medical team. Compartment syndrome is tempting, but it causes severe pain with painful passive stretch, which are absent here. A cervical root or the superficial radial nerve would not produce this fingertip pattern.

Question 11

Musculoskeletal

A 70-year-old woman from Fredericton has a recent bone density result with a T-score of minus 3.1 at the lumbar spine and no fractures. She asks which exercises are appropriate in her class. Which instruction is safest and most useful?

  • A. Perform full sit-ups and toe touches daily to improve trunk flexibility
  • B. Stop all weight-bearing activity until osteoporosis medication has taken full effect
  • C. Do high-impact jumping drills daily to stimulate rapid bone gain in the spine
  • D. Do balance and back extensor strengthening, avoiding loaded spinal flexion

The correct answer is D (Do balance and back extensor strengthening, avoiding loaded spinal flexion): Loaded flexion concentrates stress on the anterior vertebral body and raises fracture risk. Weight bearing and back extensor strengthening support bone and posture, and balance work lowers fall risk. Unsupervised high-impact drills are not appropriate at this level of risk.

Question 12

Musculoskeletal

A 66-year-old man in Quebec City reports groin pain and stiffness after sitting for long periods, with difficulty putting on his socks. A physiotherapist examines both hips for a capsular pattern consistent with early osteoarthritis and notes reduced motion. Which movement is typically restricted first and most?

  • A. External rotation first, then extension, then adduction, as the capsule gradually tightens
  • B. Adduction first, then internal rotation, then extension, as the capsule gradually tightens
  • C. Extension first, then external rotation, then flexion, as the capsule gradually tightens
  • D. Internal rotation first, then flexion, then abduction, as the capsule tightens

The correct answer is D (Internal rotation first, then flexion, then abduction, as the capsule tightens): Hip osteoarthritis generally limits internal rotation earliest, then flexion and abduction. Loss of internal rotation also helps to separate hip disease from lumbar referral. Knowing the usual order guides the screening of the groin and thigh.

Question 13

Musculoskeletal

A 27-year-old man from Surrey has had low back and buttock pain for eight months. It wakes him at 4 a.m., lasts over an hour on rising, and improves with a jog but not with rest. Anti-inflammatory tablets help. Examination shows reduced chest expansion. Which condition should be suspected?

  • A. Axial spondyloarthritis presenting with an inflammatory pattern of spinal pain
  • B. Mechanical low back pain with a sacroiliac component from asymmetric running load
  • C. Fibromyalgia with widespread pain, morning stiffness and disturbed sleep in a young adult
  • D. Spondylolysis from repetitive extension loading, which commonly affects young active men

The correct answer is A (Axial spondyloarthritis presenting with an inflammatory pattern of spinal pain): Onset before 40, night waking, prolonged morning stiffness and improvement with activity rather than rest describe inflammatory back pain, and reduced chest expansion supports axial involvement. Mechanical and stress-related causes are tempting in a runner, but they worsen with activity and ease with rest. Fibromyalgia does not reduce chest expansion. Referral to rheumatology is appropriate.

Question 14

Musculoskeletal

A 24-year-old netball player from Hamilton has anterior knee pain around the kneecap that worsens on stairs and after prolonged sitting. Single-leg squat shows hip drop and knee collapse inward. Imaging was not required. Which program has the strongest support for her condition?

  • A. Patellar taping with temporary activity modification and avoidance of stairs
  • B. Foot orthoses with a gradual walking program over twelve weeks
  • C. Quadriceps-focused strengthening using open-chain knee extension through full range
  • D. Combined hip and quadriceps strengthening with movement retraining

The correct answer is D (Combined hip and quadriceps strengthening with movement retraining): Evidence supports combined hip and knee strengthening with movement retraining for patellofemoral pain, and her single-leg squat shows a hip control deficit that the program can correct. Foot orthoses and taping can give short-term relief but do not address that deficit. Quadriceps-focused work in open chain addresses only part of the problem and can load the painful joint. Surgery is not indicated.

Question 15

Musculoskeletal

A 22-year-old skateboarder from Saint John falls on an outstretched hand. Initial wrist radiographs are read as normal, yet he has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial loading of the thumb. What is the most appropriate management at this point?

  • A. Provide a removable wrist splint for comfort and reassess in six weeks without imaging
  • B. Order an ultrasound of the thumb ulnar collateral ligament for a skier's thumb injury
  • C. Prescribe anti-inflammatory medication and early motion exercises for a wrist sprain
  • D. Immobilize the wrist and thumb in a spica splint and arrange repeat radiographs in two weeks

The correct answer is D (Immobilize the wrist and thumb in a spica splint and arrange repeat radiographs in two weeks): Snuffbox tenderness and pain on axial thumb loading after such a fall suggest a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise, and early films can miss it. The bone has a precarious blood supply, so delayed treatment risks avascular necrosis. A removable splint with no repeat imaging is tempting but leaves the question open, and a thumb ligament injury would be tender elsewhere.

Question 16

Musculoskeletal

A 28-year-old soccer player in Montreal is three weeks after a grade 2 biceps femoris strain. He walks without pain and has full passive straight leg raise. Isometric hamstring strength is within 10 percent of the other side. Which criterion should be met next before full match play?

  • A. Complete absence of any tightness during a long static hamstring stretch
  • B. Normal findings on a repeat ultrasound scan of the injured muscle
  • C. A fixed calendar date six weeks after injury without further testing
  • D. Pain-free sport-specific sprinting and high-speed eccentric strength testing

The correct answer is D (Pain-free sport-specific sprinting and high-speed eccentric strength testing): Hamstring injuries most often happen at high speed, so return should depend on demonstrating tolerance to sprinting and eccentric loading. Time since injury and imaging do not reflect function. Flexibility is a weak predictor of reinjury compared with strength and sprint capacity.

Question 17

Musculoskeletal

A 49-year-old teacher from London, Ontario has neck pain with right arm pain extending into the middle finger. Resting the right hand on the head eases the arm pain. Triceps strength is reduced, and the triceps reflex is diminished. Spurling test reproduces arm symptoms. Which nerve root is most likely involved?

  • A. The C7 nerve root, which supplies the central hand
  • B. The C5 nerve root, which supplies the shoulder and lateral upper arm
  • C. The C6 nerve root, which supplies the thumb and radial forearm
  • D. The C8 nerve root, which supplies the small finger and hand muscles

The correct answer is A (The C7 nerve root, which supplies the central hand): Middle finger sensation, triceps weakness and a reduced triceps reflex all map to C7. Relief when the hand rests on the head is the shoulder abduction sign, which supports root compression. C6 would give thumb symptoms with biceps changes, and C8 would affect the small finger and hand intrinsics.

Question 18

Musculoskeletal

A 53-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes in Charlottetown has progressive shoulder pain and stiffness over five months. Active and passive movement are equally limited. A physiotherapist applies the usual capsular pattern for the glenohumeral joint. Which order of restriction is typical?

  • A. Greatest loss of external rotation, then internal rotation, with abduction least affected overall
  • B. Greatest loss of abduction, then external rotation, then internal rotation, with flexion spared
  • C. Greatest loss of internal rotation, then abduction, then external rotation, as in posterior capsule tightness
  • D. Greatest loss of external rotation, then abduction, then internal rotation

The correct answer is D (Greatest loss of external rotation, then abduction, then internal rotation): The glenohumeral capsular pattern is greatest loss of external rotation, then abduction, then internal rotation. Diabetes is a recognized risk factor. The other orders are tempting because they use the same three movements, but only this sequence matches the capsular pattern. Equal loss of active and passive range separates a capsular restriction from a tendon problem.

Question 19

Musculoskeletal

A 45-year-old plumber from Barrie felt a pop while squatting and now has medial joint line pain, intermittent catching, and difficulty fully straightening the knee. Palpation of the medial joint line is tender, and a rotational compression test with the knee flexed reproduces a click. Valgus stress at 30 degrees is stable. What is the most likely injury?

  • A. Grade 2 sprain of the medial collateral ligament
  • B. Rupture of the posterior cruciate ligament after a fall onto the flexed knee
  • C. Meniscal tear with a displaced fragment blocking terminal knee extension
  • D. Iliotibial band friction syndrome at the lateral femoral condyle in a runner

The correct answer is C (Meniscal tear with a displaced fragment blocking terminal knee extension): Catching, loss of terminal extension, joint line tenderness and a provoked click suggest a meniscal tear with a fragment interfering with motion. A stable valgus stress argues against a collateral ligament injury. The pain location also excludes lateral band friction.

Question 20

Musculoskeletal

A 52-year-old nurse in Sudbury has sharp pain in the heel with her first steps each morning that eases after several minutes. Pressing the medial calcaneal tubercle is tender. Passive big toe extension while standing reproduces her pain. Sensation is normal and there is no night pain. Which diagnosis fits best?

  • A. Tarsal tunnel syndrome from compression of the tibial nerve at the ankle
  • B. Plantar fasciopathy from overloaded tissue under the arch of the foot
  • C. Stress fracture of the heel bone from repetitive impact during standing work
  • D. Retrocalcaneal bursitis at the Achilles tendon insertion behind the heel bone

The correct answer is B (Plantar fasciopathy from overloaded tissue under the arch of the foot): Pain on the first steps after rest, focal tenderness at the medial calcaneal origin and a positive windlass test describe plantar fasciopathy. Nerve entrapment produces burning or numbness. A stress fracture typically hurts on squeezing the heel and gets worse through the day.

Question 21

Musculoskeletal

A 15-year-old gymnast from Red Deer has had low back pain for three months that worsens with back extension and landing, despite two weeks off training. Standing on one leg while extending the spine is painful on the same side. There are no neurological signs. Which diagnosis should be considered first?

  • A. Sacroiliac joint dysfunction from repeated single-leg landings on the mat during floor routines
  • B. Vertebral endplate injury causing pain mostly with flexion and prolonged sitting in adolescents
  • C. Lumbar erector spinae strain from overuse during floor routines that settles with rest
  • D. Stress injury of the pars interarticularis in the lumbar spine

The correct answer is D (Stress injury of the pars interarticularis in the lumbar spine): Repeated extension and loading in a young athlete stresses the pars, and a one-leg extension test that reproduces unilateral pain supports this. Muscle strain is tempting in a gymnast, but it settles with rest rather than lasting three months. A sacroiliac or endplate source would not be provoked by this extension test. Referral for imaging and activity modification is the usual next step.

Question 22

Musculoskeletal

A 24-year-old basketball player in Brampton is four weeks after anterior cruciate reconstruction using a hamstring autograft. Swelling is mild, she has full knee extension and the donor site is still tender. Which exercise needs caution at this stage to protect the harvest site and graft?

  • A. Heavy resisted hamstring curls performed through full range of motion against a cuff weight
  • B. Closed-chain mini squats performed within a comfortable range of knee motion
  • C. Prone knee hangs to encourage passive extension with a light ankle weight
  • D. Stationary cycling at low resistance with the seat set high

The correct answer is A (Heavy resisted hamstring curls performed through full range of motion against a cuff weight): The harvested hamstring tendons are still healing and the donor site is tender, so strong resisted curls through full range place unsuitable load on it. Mini squats, gentle extension work and low-resistance cycling can look risky for a fresh graft, yet they keep shear on the graft low and support recovery. The surgeon's protocol sets the timeline for adding hamstring loading.

Question 23

Musculoskeletal

A 31-year-old accountant from Windsor sprained her ankle two days ago and has an isolated grade 2 lateral ligament injury. Radiographs are negative and she walks with a limp, with moderate swelling and bruising. She works at a desk and plays recreational badminton. Which plan reflects current best practice for the first two weeks?

  • A. Lace-up brace for six weeks with walking restricted to essential household tasks
  • B. Protect briefly then begin graded loading and balance exercises early
  • C. Ice, compression and rest for the first week, then begin range exercises
  • D. Walking boot for two weeks, then start strengthening and balance

The correct answer is B (Protect briefly then begin graded loading and balance exercises early): Early graded loading with support and balance training leads to faster recovery and fewer recurrences after a stable grade 2 sprain. A brace, a boot or a week of rest each feels protective, but they postpone active rehabilitation that this ankle can already tolerate. Proprioceptive exercise also reduces the chance of chronic instability.

Question 24

Musculoskeletal

A 34-year-old new mother in Gatineau has radial-sided wrist pain from repeatedly lifting her baby, with tenderness over the radial styloid and pain on gripping. A therapist wants a provocative test for tendinopathy of the first dorsal compartment. Which test is most appropriate?

  • A. Phalen test, compressing the median nerve with sustained wrist flexion
  • B. Finkelstein test, stressing the tendons that move the thumb
  • C. Grind test, compressing the first carpometacarpal joint with axial thumb loading
  • D. Watson test, assessing instability between the scaphoid and lunate bones

The correct answer is B (Finkelstein test, stressing the tendons that move the thumb): The Finkelstein test stresses abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the first dorsal compartment and reproduces pain when those tendons are inflamed. The grind test is tempting because it also provokes radial-sided thumb pain, but it targets the carpometacarpal joint. Phalen testing looks for median nerve compression, and the Watson test looks for scapholunate instability.

Question 25

Musculoskeletal

A 58-year-old woman from Brandon has lateral hip pain that wakes her when lying on the painful side. Single-leg stance for thirty seconds reproduces it. Palpation over the greater trochanter is tender, and resisted hip abduction is painful. Hip internal rotation is full and painless. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  • A. Femoral neck stress fracture from repetitive loading in a runner
  • B. Early osteoarthritis of the hip joint with capsular pattern loss
  • C. Lumbar radiculopathy at the L5 level producing referred lateral pain
  • D. Gluteal tendinopathy from overload of the hip abductor tendons

The correct answer is D (Gluteal tendinopathy from overload of the hip abductor tendons): Lateral pain at night on that side, pain in single-leg stance and tenderness over the trochanter point to gluteal tendinopathy. Full pain-free internal rotation makes hip joint disease unlikely. Management centres on load management, avoiding compressive postures and progressive abductor strengthening.

Question 26

Musculoskeletal

A 20-year-old distance runner from Kingston has had groin pain for three weeks that worsens with running and now appears during walking. Hopping on the right leg causes deep groin pain, and passive hip internal rotation at the end of range is painful. Her training volume recently doubled. What is the most appropriate response?

  • A. Request hip radiographs at the next routine visit and allow running on softer surfaces
  • B. Reduce running to alternate days and add hip abductor strengthening, then review in one month
  • C. Stop weight bearing and arrange urgent imaging and medical review
  • D. Refer for ultrasound of the adductor origin and begin graded loading of the groin

The correct answer is C (Stop weight bearing and arrange urgent imaging and medical review): Groin pain provoked by hopping and end-range rotation after a sudden rise in load is a red flag for a femoral neck stress fracture. This injury can displace and cause avascular necrosis, so loading must stop. Reduced running or adductor imaging is tempting because tendon and muscle causes are common in runners, but each keeps load going through a bone at risk.

Question 27

Musculoskeletal

A 26-year-old man in Saint-Jerome is eight hours after a tibial shaft fracture treated with a cast. He now reports escalating calf pain not eased by analgesics, and the therapist notes tense swelling. Passive toe extension causes intense pain. Pedal pulses are still palpable. Which condition is most likely developing?

  • A. Expected pain after fracture that is gradually improving with limb elevation
  • B. Acute compartment syndrome developing in the lower leg muscles
  • C. Deep vein thrombosis within the veins of the calf after immobilization
  • D. Complex regional pain syndrome type 1 following the fracture and cast

The correct answer is B (Acute compartment syndrome developing in the lower leg muscles): Increasing pain unrelieved by analgesia, tense swelling and pain on passive stretch are early signs of rising compartment pressure. Palpable pulses do not exclude it, because pulses are lost late. This is a surgical emergency that needs immediate medical attention and release of the cast.

Question 28

Musculoskeletal

A 63-year-old man in Lethbridge is on day three after hip arthroplasty. During physiotherapy he shows new unilateral calf swelling, warmth and tenderness, and a difference of three centimetres in calf circumference. He has no chest symptoms. What is the most appropriate action?

  • A. Stop the session, keep the patient resting and contact the medical team urgently
  • B. Elevate the leg and apply intermittent compression before notifying anyone
  • C. Perform a Homans sign test and notify the team if positive
  • D. Measure the calf again tomorrow and continue gait training if unchanged

The correct answer is A (Stop the session, keep the patient resting and contact the medical team urgently): Recent surgery together with unilateral swelling, warmth, tenderness and a three centimetre calf difference gives a high pretest likelihood of deep vein thrombosis. Homans sign is tempting but cannot exclude a clot, so waiting on it delays care. Activity, compression or waiting a day could move a clot toward the lungs. Prompt medical assessment with imaging and anticoagulation is required.

Question 29

Musculoskeletal

A 36-year-old courier from Moose Jaw has acute low back pain with right buttock and thigh symptoms. Repeated lumbar extension in lying moves the pain from the thigh to the buttock, and pain is worse after repeated flexion. There are no neurological deficits. How should this finding be interpreted?

  • A. Peripheralization suggesting a flexion bias for exercise prescription
  • B. Centralization indicating a favourable response to extension-based exercise
  • C. Nerve root irritation indicating a neural mobilization program
  • D. Probable disc involvement, indicating traction as the preferred care

The correct answer is B (Centralization indicating a favourable response to extension-based exercise): Pain moving from the leg toward the spine during repeated movement is called centralization and predicts a good outcome with the matching direction of exercise. Her pain moved away from the thigh with extension and worsened with flexion, which supports an extension bias rather than a flexion bias. Disc involvement may be present, but the finding guides exercise direction, not traction. It is not a red flag and does not require imaging without neurological loss.

Question 30

Musculoskeletal

A 64-year-old woman in Truro with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis and a body mass index of 33 asks what care is most effective to begin with. She walks independently, works part time and has no inflammatory signs or locking. Based on Canadian and international guidelines, which combination should be offered initially?

  • A. Education, oral anti-inflammatory medication and rest from impact activity until symptoms settle
  • B. Glucosamine supplements and a home walking program without supervised progression
  • C. Education, a knee brace and walking aid use to offload the joint
  • D. Education, supervised exercise and a weight management plan

The correct answer is D (Education, supervised exercise and a weight management plan): Core treatment for knee osteoarthritis is education, exercise and weight loss where appropriate, since these reduce pain and improve function. Medication, a brace or a supplement can look reasonable, but they are adjuncts at best and rest weakens the joint. Unsupervised walking without progression misses the supervised exercise that the guidelines support.

Question 31

Musculoskeletal

A 57-year-old woman from Sherbrooke is two weeks after an arthroscopic repair of a medium supraspinatus tear. Her surgeon's protocol states a sling for six weeks and no active elevation. She reports mild pain at night and wants to begin exercises. Which activity is appropriate at this stage?

  • A. Active-assisted overhead pulley exercises performed for twenty minutes each day
  • B. Gentle pendulum swings and supported passive arm raising within protocol limits
  • C. Resisted external rotation using a light elastic band in the sling position
  • D. Lifting a two kilogram shopping bag with the operated arm at home

The correct answer is B (Gentle pendulum swings and supported passive arm raising within protocol limits): The repaired tendon needs protection from active contraction while it attaches to bone. Gentle passive motion maintains range and limits stiffness without loading the repair. Resistance and lifting belong to much later phases after tendon healing.

Question 32

Musculoskeletal

A 13-year-old soccer player from Whitehorse has pain and a firm, tender prominence at the tibial tuberosity during a growth spurt. Pain follows kicking and jumping, and radiographs are not needed. Strength is full and the knee is stable. Which plan is most appropriate?

  • A. Rest from sport for two to four weeks, then resume full training
  • B. Apply a patellar tendon strap during sport and add hamstring stretching
  • C. Modify load to a tolerable level while building quadriceps strength and flexibility
  • D. Immobilize the knee in a hinged brace for six weeks

The correct answer is C (Modify load to a tolerable level while building quadriceps strength and flexibility): This traction apophysitis settles with growth, so management keeps activity within a tolerable level while maintaining quadriceps strength and flexibility. A short rest, a strap or a brace can ease pain, but none builds capacity and a brace adds deconditioning. Surgery and corticosteroid injection are not part of routine care here.

Question 33

Musculoskeletal

A 12-year-old afebrile boy in Surrey with a body mass index above the 95th percentile reports a limp and vague knee pain for three weeks. Hip examination shows limited internal rotation, and the hip rotates outward when it is flexed. He cannot run. What is the most appropriate step?

  • A. Order inflammatory markers and arrange hip aspiration today to exclude septic arthritis
  • B. Refer for knee radiographs and an orthopedic opinion about possible patellar instability
  • C. Arrange a hip ultrasound for an irritable hip effusion and allow gentle weight bearing
  • D. Refer urgently for hip radiographs and avoid weight bearing

The correct answer is D (Refer urgently for hip radiographs and avoid weight bearing): Knee pain with limited hip internal rotation and obligate external rotation on flexion in an overweight adolescent suggests slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Continued weight bearing can cause further slip and avascular necrosis. Transient synovitis and infection are tempting causes of an irritable hip, but this age, build and afebrile state favour a slip. Urgent imaging and orthopedic review are required.

Question 34

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist in Burlington assesses a 35-year-old patient with buttock pain below the L5 level after a fall onto the buttocks. Lumbar movements do not change the pain. The therapist wants to improve diagnostic confidence that the sacroiliac joint is the source. Which approach is best supported in the literature?

  • A. A single positive thigh thrust test performed with the hip flexed to ninety degrees
  • B. A cluster of at least three positive provocation tests
  • C. Patient pointing with one finger to the posterior superior iliac spine
  • D. Palpation of pelvic landmark symmetry combined with a standing flexion test

The correct answer is B (A cluster of at least three positive provocation tests): Individual sacroiliac tests have poor accuracy, but when three or more provocation tests reproduce the patient's pain the cluster becomes useful. A single thrust test, palpation of landmarks and finger pointing are tempting because they are quick, yet each is found in people without sacroiliac pain or lacks confirmation. The cluster is the best supported approach.

Question 35

Musculoskeletal

A 44-year-old hairdresser from Peterborough has numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers waking her at night for two months. Phalen test reproduces symptoms and there is no thenar wasting. Which initial management is best supported for mild to moderate symptoms?

  • A. Carpal tunnel release surgery scheduled once night symptoms persist for three months
  • B. A wrist splint worn in thirty degrees of extension during sleep and work
  • C. A neutral wrist night splint with activity modification
  • D. Median nerve gliding exercises performed with sustained end-range wrist extension

The correct answer is C (A neutral wrist night splint with activity modification): A splint holding the wrist in neutral keeps the carpal canal at its widest and relieves night symptoms. Without thenar wasting or severe sensory loss, conservative care comes first, which makes early surgery premature. A splint in extension still narrows the canal, and a sustained end-range extension stretch compresses the median nerve instead of unloading it.

Question 36

Musculoskeletal

A 48-year-old woman from Saskatoon has bilateral swelling of the knuckles and middle finger joints for three months. Morning stiffness lasts ninety minutes, and squeezing across the metacarpal heads is painful. Distal finger joints are spared. Which condition best explains this presentation?

  • A. Primary hand osteoarthritis causing degenerative change in the distal joints
  • B. Rheumatoid arthritis, an inflammatory condition affecting the synovial lining
  • C. Gouty arthritis producing episodic attacks from urate crystal deposition in the joints
  • D. Psoriatic arthritis presenting with sausage-shaped digits and scaly skin plaques

The correct answer is B (Rheumatoid arthritis, an inflammatory condition affecting the synovial lining): Symmetrical swelling of metacarpophalangeal and proximal joints with prolonged morning stiffness and a positive metacarpal squeeze is typical of rheumatoid arthritis. Hand osteoarthritis favours distal joints and stiffens briefly. Early referral is important because disease-modifying treatment limits joint damage.

Question 37

Musculoskeletal

A 67-year-old woman is seen in a Winnipeg clinic after a low-speed rear-end collision on an icy road. She has neck pain, is alert, and can rotate her neck 45 degrees to each side. She has no numbness or weakness. A clinician applies the Canadian C-spine rule to decide on radiography. Which finding alone makes imaging necessary?

  • A. Ability to walk at any time since the collision, including at the scene
  • B. Pain onset arriving several hours after the collision rather than immediately
  • C. Being at or above the age of sixty-five years
  • D. Absence of midline cervical tenderness on palpation by the examining clinician

The correct answer is C (Being at or above the age of sixty-five years): Age 65 or older is a high-risk factor in the Canadian C-spine rule and calls for radiography whatever the other findings. Delayed onset, ambulation and absent midline tenderness are low-risk features that allow safe assessment of rotation, so they are tempting but do not require films alone. A simple low-speed rear-end collision is also a low-risk feature.

Question 38

Musculoskeletal

A 59-year-old man from Moncton has a hot, red, swollen knee since yesterday. His temperature is 38.6 degrees Celsius, and he cannot bear weight or move the joint passively in any direction. He has no recent injury. What is the most appropriate action?

  • A. Send for same-day medical assessment for possible septic arthritis
  • B. Provide a walking aid and advise a follow-up visit early next week
  • C. Begin gentle range of motion exercises with ice and compression this afternoon
  • D. Treat as acute gout and provide a dietary advice sheet for home

The correct answer is A (Send for same-day medical assessment for possible septic arthritis): A hot swollen joint with fever and pain on any passive movement is septic arthritis until proven otherwise, because infection destroys cartilage within days. Gout can look similar, but fever and inability to move the joint call for urgent aspiration and antibiotics. Exercise and delay are unsafe.

Question 39

Musculoskeletal

An 82-year-old woman in Charlottetown had a hemiarthroplasty for a femoral neck fracture yesterday. The surgeon allows weight bearing as tolerated. She lives alone, is cognitively intact and medically stable, and her pain is controlled. Which approach to physiotherapy is most appropriate?

  • A. Begin bedside sitting and standing on day one, with walking started on day three
  • B. Delay mobilization until the second day to complete a falls risk assessment
  • C. Use a tilt table or hoist-assisted sit-to-stand practice for the first three days
  • D. Begin standing and walking with an aid on the first day

The correct answer is D (Begin standing and walking with an aid on the first day): Early mobilization after hip fracture surgery improves survival, function and discharge outcomes, and it reduces pneumonia and pressure injury. Her orders permit loading and she is medically stable, so standing and walking with an aid should begin on day one. Staged progressions, a delayed start or equipment-based practice are tempting cautious options, but each postpones benefit without a clinical reason.

Question 40

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist in Mississauga records manual muscle test results for knee extension after a nerve injury. The patient lifts the leg through the whole available range while seated, working against its own weight, but the limb gives way at once under any pressure from the examiner's hand. Which grade on the 0 to 5 scale should be recorded?

  • A. Grade 5, which is normal strength with the limb holding against maximal manual resistance
  • B. Grade 2, which is complete movement when the effect of gravity is removed
  • C. Grade 4, which is movement against gravity and a moderate level of manual resistance
  • D. Grade 3, which is movement against gravity without tolerance of resistance

The correct answer is D (Grade 3, which is movement against gravity without tolerance of resistance): Grade 3 means full range against gravity with no resistance tolerated. Grade 2 is full range with gravity eliminated, grade 4 holds against moderate resistance, and grade 5 is normal strength. The distinction depends on whether gravity and then resistance can be overcome.

Question 41

Musculoskeletal

A 29-year-old volleyball player from Oshawa has repeated giving way of the ankle after three sprains in two years, mainly when landing from a block. Radiographs and ligament testing show only mild laxity, and she has full strength and normal dorsiflexion. Which component should be central to her rehabilitation program?

  • A. Lace-up bracing during sport with a gradual return to jumping
  • B. Neuromuscular training that includes balance and dynamic control tasks
  • C. Peroneal strengthening with resistance bands progressed through all planes of motion
  • D. Ankle joint mobilization to restore dorsiflexion before returning to jumping tasks

The correct answer is B (Neuromuscular training that includes balance and dynamic control tasks): Repeated sprains leave deficits in neuromuscular control that balance and perturbation training can improve, reducing recurrence. Bracing, peroneal strengthening and joint mobilization are tempting because each is a true part of ankle care, but her strength and dorsiflexion are already normal. Gradual return to jumping is needed for sport.

Question 42

Musculoskeletal

A 21-year-old rugby player from Langley takes a knee to the anterior thigh and develops pain, swelling and limited knee flexion to 60 degrees one hour later. Which advice during the first 48 hours best reduces the risk of myositis ossificans?

  • A. Apply ice and compression for forty-eight hours with the knee held in extension
  • B. Avoid massage and heat while keeping the knee positioned in flexion
  • C. Begin resisted quadriceps strengthening on day one with ice applied afterwards
  • D. Begin passive stretching into end-range flexion and apply ultrasound from day one

The correct answer is B (Avoid massage and heat while keeping the knee positioned in flexion): Early heat, massage and forceful stretching can increase bleeding and the likelihood of heterotopic bone forming in a deep contusion. Holding the knee in flexion keeps the quadriceps lengthened and preserves range. Ice in extension, early passive stretch with ultrasound, or early resisted work each sounds active, but they either shorten the muscle or provoke more bleeding.

Question 43

Musculoskeletal

A 50-year-old man from Orillia has burning and numbness over the outer thigh that began after he gained weight and started wearing a tight tool belt. Strength and reflexes are normal. Symptoms increase with standing and ease with sitting. Which diagnosis is most likely?

  • A. L4 radiculopathy caused by a disc herniation compressing the exiting nerve root
  • B. Femoral nerve palsy caused by a pelvic hematoma in the iliacus compartment
  • C. Compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the inguinal ligament
  • D. Greater trochanteric pain syndrome with irritation of the gluteal tendons and bursa

The correct answer is C (Compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the inguinal ligament): Burning sensory change over the lateral thigh with preserved strength and reflexes matches entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the inguinal ligament. Belt pressure and abdominal weight are classic contributors. A root lesion would affect strength or reflexes, and trochanteric pain presents with tenderness.

Question 44

Musculoskeletal

A 38-year-old office worker in Fredericton has right-sided headaches starting in the neck and spreading to the forehead. Headaches are triggered by sustained neck postures. There is no aura or nausea. Neck rotation is reduced on the right in full flexion. Which finding best confirms a cervicogenic source?

  • A. Suboccipital muscle tenderness and neck stiffness at the end of long working days
  • B. Upper cervical segmental restriction that reproduces the usual head pain
  • C. Partial pain relief after simple analgesic medication taken at the onset of an attack
  • D. Aggravation of the headaches by stress and tiredness during busy periods at work

The correct answer is B (Upper cervical segmental restriction that reproduces the usual head pain): Upper cervical segmental restriction that reproduces the usual head pain links the headache to the neck, which is what defines a cervicogenic source. Muscle tenderness, stress aggravation and analgesic response are tempting because they occur in many neck-related headaches, but they also occur in tension-type headache and do not confirm the source.

Question 45

Musculoskeletal

A 25-year-old volleyball player in Victoria has pain at the lower tip of the kneecap that builds during jump-heavy weeks. Pain is reproduced with a single-leg decline squat, and palpation of the inferior pole is tender. Knee swelling is absent. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  • A. Complete rupture of the quadriceps tendon just above the upper pole
  • B. Patellar tendinopathy caused by repeated jump-related overload of the tendon
  • C. Prepatellar bursitis from repeated kneeling on hard floors with visible swelling
  • D. Medial plica syndrome causing catching and snapping along the inner knee border

The correct answer is B (Patellar tendinopathy caused by repeated jump-related overload of the tendon): Load-related pain localized to the lower pole of the patella and provoked by decline squatting is characteristic of patellar tendinopathy. A tendon rupture would block active extension. Bursitis shows anterior swelling, and plica irritation is felt medially.

Question 46

Musculoskeletal

A patient in Regina is three days after open reduction and internal fixation of an ankle fracture. The surgeon's order reads touch-down weight bearing on the operated leg. The patient has been issued crutches and asks what this means for walking at home. How should the physiotherapist interpret this instruction when teaching gait?

  • A. Up to half of body weight may be placed through the foot when walking
  • B. Full body weight is permitted through the foot while using crutches
  • C. The leg should be held clear of the floor throughout every step taken
  • D. The foot may rest lightly on the ground for balance but must carry no load

The correct answer is D (The foot may rest lightly on the ground for balance but must carry no load): Touch-down means the toes or foot contact the ground for balance only, with no meaningful load transmitted. Partial weight bearing allows a stated percentage, and non-weight bearing means no contact. Clear terms protect the fixation while fracture union begins.

Question 47

Musculoskeletal

A 19-year-old cross-country runner from Halifax has had two metatarsal stress fractures in a year. She reports irregular periods, low energy and a recent weight loss of 5 kilograms. What is the most appropriate recommendation beyond managing the current fracture?

  • A. Recommend the combined oral contraceptive pill to regulate her periods and protect her bones
  • B. Refer for medical and dietitian review of her energy intake
  • C. Refer for a bone density scan and start calcium supplements before any change in training
  • D. Plan a graded return to running with cross-training and gait analysis to correct overload

The correct answer is B (Refer for medical and dietitian review of her energy intake): Recurrent stress fractures with menstrual change and weight loss suggest relative energy deficiency in sport, which impairs bone health. Treatment needs medical and nutritional assessment as well as load management. The contraceptive pill and a bone scan are tempting but treat signs rather than the energy deficit, and a gait or footwear approach misses the cause.

Question 48

Musculoskeletal

A 40-year-old cyclist from Calgary has deep buttock pain radiating to the back of the thigh, worse with prolonged sitting. Slump testing is negative and lumbar movements do not change symptoms. Resisted hip external rotation in flexion is painful with muscle tenderness, while resisted knee flexion and palpation of the ischial tuberosity are pain-free. Which diagnosis is most likely?

  • A. L5 disc herniation causing compression of the exiting nerve root at the foramen
  • B. Proximal hamstring origin tendinopathy from repeated heavy cycling load on the bike
  • C. Deep gluteal syndrome from piriformis irritation of the sciatic nerve
  • D. Lumbar facet joint pain referred into the buttock

The correct answer is C (Deep gluteal syndrome from piriformis irritation of the sciatic nerve): A negative slump with symptoms that do not respond to lumbar movement points away from a root lesion. Pain with resisted external rotation and local muscle tenderness suggest irritation of the sciatic nerve in the deep gluteal space. Proximal hamstring tendinopathy is tempting in a cyclist, but it hurts with resisted knee flexion and palpation of the ischial tuberosity, and both are pain-free here.

Question 49

Musculoskeletal

A 23-year-old hockey defenceman from Sault Ste. Marie twisted his ankle with the foot planted and rotated outward. He has pain above the ankle joint and cannot push off. Squeezing the calf at mid-shin causes pain at the ankle, and external rotation stress reproduces it. Which injury is most likely?

  • A. Avulsion fracture of the medial malleolus with bony tenderness over the tip
  • B. Lateral ligament complex sprain from a typical inversion mechanism of injury
  • C. Partial rupture of the Achilles tendon during a forceful push off
  • D. Syndesmotic sprain involving the ligaments between the tibia and fibula

The correct answer is D (Syndesmotic sprain involving the ligaments between the tibia and fibula): An outward rotation mechanism with pain above the joint and a positive squeeze and external rotation test indicates syndesmotic injury. These ankles recover more slowly than lateral sprains and may require imaging and longer protection. A lateral ligament sprain is more common but follows inversion.

Question 50

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist in Vancouver is explaining recovery from a muscle strain to a patient and describes the phases of soft tissue repair. One phase is characterized by fibroblasts laying down collagen and by new capillary growth, beginning roughly three to five days after the injury. Which phase is being described?

  • A. The inflammatory phase, when bleeding is controlled and debris is cleared
  • B. The remodelling phase, when collagen is realigned and strengthened over months
  • C. The proliferative phase, which builds granulation tissue and new matrix
  • D. The hemostasis phase, when a platelet plug forms within minutes

The correct answer is C (The proliferative phase, which builds granulation tissue and new matrix): The proliferative phase starts around day three to five and involves fibroblast activity, collagen production and angiogenesis. The inflammatory phase precedes it, and remodelling follows over weeks to months. Loading should be graded to match the phase.

Question 51

Musculoskeletal

A 44-year-old finish carpenter in Saskatoon reports six weeks of outer elbow pain that is worse when gripping a hammer. Resisted wrist extension reproduces his pain, and tenderness lies over the lateral epicondyle. Neck screening is clear. He asks what will give the best result over the coming year.

  • A. Graded loading of the wrist extensors, with temporary reduction of provocative gripping tasks
  • B. A repeat corticosteroid injection at the tendon origin to settle pain so he can keep working
  • C. Complete rest in a rigid wrist splint for six weeks to let the tendon calm
  • D. Therapeutic ultrasound to the extensor origin plus a counterforce strap, leaving out any loading exercise

The correct answer is A (Graded loading of the wrist extensors, with temporary reduction of provocative gripping tasks): Progressive tendon loading, with activity modification so pain stays tolerable, gives better medium and long-term outcomes than injection or rest. Corticosteroid injection often brings short-term relief but is followed by higher recurrence. Rigid immobilization reduces tendon capacity, and passive ultrasound does not build load tolerance.

Question 52

Musculoskeletal

A 28-year-old recreational soccer player inverted her ankle yesterday in Halifax. She could take only two steps at the time and cannot take four steps in the clinic. Swelling is marked, and there is tenderness along the posterior edge of the distal fibula. The anterior drawer test is positive but guarded.

  • A. Refer for ankle radiographs before loading, since bone tenderness and failed weight-bearing meet the criteria
  • B. Apply protective taping and reassess in two weeks, ordering imaging if swelling persists beyond then
  • C. Use the squeeze test result alone to decide whether imaging is needed
  • D. Begin weight-bearing exercises today, since a positive drawer test shows a ligament sprain rather than fracture

The correct answer is A (Refer for ankle radiographs before loading, since bone tenderness and failed weight-bearing meet the criteria): Bone tenderness at the posterior edge of the distal fibula, and inability to take four weight-bearing steps, each meet the Ottawa criteria for imaging. A positive drawer test describes ligament laxity and does not exclude a fracture. Waiting two weeks delays a diagnosis that changes loading, and the squeeze test addresses a different question.

Question 53

Musculoskeletal

A 52-year-old nurse reports sharp heel pain with her first steps each morning that eases after several minutes and returns after long shifts. Pressure on the anteromedial calcaneus reproduces it, and passive great toe extension in standing reproduces the pain. A calcaneal squeeze test is negative. Pain is not worse at rest at night.

  • A. Tarsal tunnel syndrome, because the pain is located on the medial side of the foot
  • B. Calcaneal stress fracture, because heel pain begins after prolonged standing and builds with repeated weight-bearing
  • C. Heel fat pad syndrome, because heel pain follows prolonged standing on hard floors
  • D. Plantar fasciopathy, supported by first-step pain, medial calcaneal tenderness and a positive windlass test

The correct answer is D (Plantar fasciopathy, supported by first-step pain, medial calcaneal tenderness and a positive windlass test): First-step pain, tenderness at the medial calcaneal origin and a reproduced windlass response point to the plantar fascia. A stress fracture would give a positive squeeze test and pain that builds with activity or at night. Fat pad pain is central and bruise-like, and tarsal tunnel syndrome gives burning or numbness rather than start-up pain.

Question 54

Musculoskeletal

A 31-year-old has had a grade II calf muscle strain for ten days. A physiotherapist in Winnipeg explains the repair process to her. Considering where she is in the typical healing timeline, which cellular events would be expected to predominate at this point in the course of her injury?

  • A. Macrophage clearance of debris with ongoing release of cytokines and growth factors at the injury site
  • B. Collagen cross-linking with realignment along lines of mechanical stress
  • C. Myofibroblast contraction of the wound edges with early replacement of type III by type I collagen
  • D. Fibroblast proliferation, new capillary growth and early deposition of weak collagen

The correct answer is D (Fibroblast proliferation, new capillary growth and early deposition of weak collagen): Around day ten the proliferative phase predominates, with fibroblasts, angiogenesis and early type III collagen that is weak and disorganized. Macrophage clearance and cytokine release are tempting because they begin the repair, but they peak in the first few days, not at ten days. Cross-linking and realignment, or contraction with collagen conversion, belong to remodelling from about three weeks, when tensile strength is still well below normal at this stage.

Question 55

Musculoskeletal

A 24-year-old sprinter in Calgary strained his biceps femoris during a race three days ago. He walks with a short stride, has mild bruising, and pain of 3/10 on resisted knee flexion at 90 degrees. There are no signs of avulsion. He wants to know how to approach the next two weeks.

  • A. Start aggressive static hamstring stretching into pain twice daily to prevent scar shortening
  • B. Rest fully for two weeks, then start strengthening once the bruising has resolved
  • C. Begin early pain-limited loading with isometrics, then progress to eccentric hamstring work
  • D. Wait for painless sprinting before beginning any resisted hamstring exercise

The correct answer is C (Begin early pain-limited loading with isometrics, then progress to eccentric hamstring work): Early, pain-limited loading is safe after a mild to moderate strain and supports orderly collagen alignment and faster return. Prolonged rest produces weaker, stiffer repair tissue. Aggressive stretching early can disrupt the healing fibres, and sprinting is a late-stage goal rather than a prerequisite for strengthening.

Question 56

Musculoskeletal

A 63-year-old retired teacher in Moncton has moderate knee osteoarthritis and a BMI of 31. She wants to start strengthening and walking but fears that any pain means damage. During your first session she rates knee pain 4/10 during squats, and it returns to her usual 2/10 within an hour.

  • A. Stop the program and switch to non-weight-bearing work, since exercise pain signals cartilage injury
  • B. Continue, since moderate pain that settles within about a day is acceptable and not joint damage
  • C. Replace exercise with hot packs until the baseline pain falls below the level she reports
  • D. Reduce the load until the exercise causes no discomfort, then progress very slowly

The correct answer is B (Continue, since moderate pain that settles within about a day is acceptable and not joint damage): In knee osteoarthritis, moderate pain during exercise that settles within roughly 24 hours is acceptable and exercise is a core treatment. Insisting on pain-free training or avoiding load reinforces fear and loses benefit. Heat can ease symptoms, but it does not improve strength or function.

Question 57

Musculoskeletal

A 66-year-old man in Regina reports groin pain for eight months and difficulty putting on socks. Passive hip internal rotation is limited and painful at end range, and flexion reproduces his groin pain. Lumbar extension and repeated movements do not change his symptoms, and the straight leg raise is negative.

  • A. Lumbar radiculopathy at L2, because groin pain commonly arises from an upper lumbar nerve root
  • B. Hip osteoarthritis, since hip movements reproduce the groin pain while lumbar testing is unchanged
  • C. Adductor tendinopathy, because groin pain with limited flexion suggests a muscle origin
  • D. Inguinal hernia, because groin pain with sock difficulty indicates a soft tissue bulge

The correct answer is B (Hip osteoarthritis, since hip movements reproduce the groin pain while lumbar testing is unchanged): Pain and loss of internal rotation with reproduction of groin pain on hip flexion indicate an intra-articular hip source, and normal lumbar testing argues against referral. An upper lumbar root would usually give neurological signs. Adductor tendinopathy would be provoked by resisted adduction, and a hernia would not alter with hip range.

Question 58

Musculoskeletal

A 48-year-old accountant in Mississauga has rheumatoid arthritis. This week both wrists and several metacarpophalangeal joints are warm, swollen and stiff for over an hour in the morning. She has been prescribed a flare plan by her rheumatologist and asks how to adjust her usual strengthening and aerobic routine.

  • A. Continue her full resistance program through the flare to keep the joints strong
  • B. Immobilize both wrists in rigid splints for several weeks until swelling and stiffness disappear
  • C. Stop all movement for the whole flare and restart once blood tests normalize
  • D. Keep gentle pain-limited joint movement and low-impact aerobic work, resuming hand loading as flare settles

The correct answer is D (Keep gentle pain-limited joint movement and low-impact aerobic work, resuming hand loading as flare settles): During a flare, gentle movement keeps range and function while avoiding heavy resisted loading of hot, swollen joints. Pushing through the flare risks joint stress, while prolonged splinting or complete rest causes stiffness and weakness. Loading is rebuilt gradually as inflammation settles.

Question 59

Musculoskeletal

A 27-year-old man in Edmonton has had low back and alternating buttock pain for five months. It began gradually, wakes him at 4 am, and eases with a run but not with rest. Morning stiffness lasts 60 minutes. He asks you for help with exercise and wants to know the next step in his care.

  • A. Start mobility and extension exercises while arranging medical assessment for possible spondyloarthritis
  • B. Manage as mechanical low back pain with rest and a lumbar roll for comfortable sitting
  • C. Treat with high-velocity lumbar thrust manipulation and reassess the pain pattern after three treatment visits
  • D. Order a lumbar spine MRI yourself and withhold exercise until the imaging report has been received

The correct answer is A (Start mobility and extension exercises while arranging medical assessment for possible spondyloarthritis): Insidious onset under 40, night waking, relief with exercise but not rest and prolonged morning stiffness form an inflammatory back pain pattern, so rheumatology assessment through his physician is needed. Exercise is helpful meanwhile. Rest suits mechanical pain, and thrust manipulation does not address the underlying cause.

Question 60

Musculoskeletal

A 61-year-old man in Ottawa arrives with a hot, swollen right knee that began yesterday without trauma. He has a temperature of 38.6 degrees Celsius, cannot move the knee and has chills. He had a knee replacement on the other side years ago. A friend recommended gentle motion and ice.

  • A. Start gentle active-assisted motion to limit stiffness and reassess his fever after the first two sessions
  • B. Refer him for a physician visit within the week for blood tests and a knee X-ray
  • C. Send him for same-day emergency assessment, since a hot swollen joint with fever may be septic
  • D. Apply compression wrap and refer him within the week for a gout assessment

The correct answer is C (Send him for same-day emergency assessment, since a hot swollen joint with fever may be septic): A hot, swollen joint with fever and severe movement loss needs same-day aspiration and treatment because septic arthritis can destroy cartilage within days. Early motion is tempting because stiffness is a real concern, but it loads a possibly infected joint. Booking tests within the week or assuming gout both accept a delay that fever and sudden onset do not allow.

Question 61

Musculoskeletal

A 41-year-old woman in Thunder Bay has widespread pain and fatigue lasting more than three months, poor sleep and low exercise tolerance. A physician has diagnosed fibromyalgia. She has been inactive for a year and expects a flare after any exercise. You are designing her starting program.

  • A. Begin with low-intensity aerobic activity in short bouts a few times weekly, increasing duration gradually
  • B. Delay exercise until her pain scores have fallen below 2/10 on most days
  • C. Prescribe heavy resistance training, since aerobic work aggravates central pain and fatigue
  • D. Start high-intensity interval training three times weekly to overcome her deconditioning as quickly as possible
