The correct answer is A (Begin with low-intensity aerobic activity in short bouts a few times weekly, increasing duration gradually): Graded low-intensity aerobic activity, increased slowly, improves pain, function and sleep in fibromyalgia without provoking big flares. Starting too hard commonly causes setbacks that confirm fear. Waiting for pain to resolve means she may never start, and aerobic exercise is recommended rather than avoided.

Question 62

Musculoskeletal

A 39-year-old warehouse worker in Surrey has had low back pain for 14 months. Imaging showed mild degeneration only. He avoids bending, scores high on a fear-avoidance questionnaire and says his back is damaged. Neurological examination is normal. You plan how to combine education with activity.

  • A. Explain the imaging findings as the main cause and advise him to avoid bending
  • B. Prescribe passive modalities for six weeks before discussing any movement or activity goals with him
  • C. Explain how pain can persist without tissue damage, and add graded activity toward feared tasks
  • D. Give detailed anatomy teaching on the discs and leave exercise choices entirely to him

The correct answer is C (Explain how pain can persist without tissue damage, and add graded activity toward feared tasks): Education that reframes persistent pain as an oversensitive protective system, paired with graded activity, reduces fear and disability. Blaming mild degeneration and advising avoidance feeds the belief. Passive care or anatomy teaching alone does not change behaviour.

Question 63

Musculoskeletal

A 45-year-old paramedic in Kelowna has had low back pain for nine months. She scores very high on fear-avoidance beliefs about lifting, describes pain as unpredictable, and has stopped lifting at home and work. Examination reveals no neurological deficit. Which approach best targets the main barrier to her recovery?

  • A. A general strengthening program for the trunk muscles, avoiding any lifting until she is stronger
  • B. Graded exposure to the specific lifts she fears, paced by her confidence rather than pain
  • C. Lumbar mobilization sessions to restore mobility so the fear subsides on its own
  • D. Time-limited bed rest on flare days, resuming lifting after full pain relief

The correct answer is B (Graded exposure to the specific lifts she fears, paced by her confidence rather than pain): When avoidance driven by fear is the main barrier, graded exposure to the specific feared activity, paced by confidence, reduces threat and restores function. Strengthening alone leaves the avoidance intact, and passive mobilization does not address beliefs. Resting until pain is gone reinforces the pain contingent pattern.

Question 64

Musculoskeletal

A 58-year-old retired electrician in Victoria has had four months of lateral shoulder pain with overhead reaching. He has a painful arc between 70 and 120 degrees and pain with resisted external rotation, but no weakness greater than pain explains, and passive range is full. Plain films are normal.

  • A. A progressive shoulder strengthening program with load and pain guidance over at least twelve weeks
  • B. Repeated subacromial corticosteroid injections to settle pain before any exercise is considered
  • C. Passive capsular stretching of all planes without resistance work, three times per week
  • D. Referral for subacromial decompression surgery, since conservative care rarely helps after four months

The correct answer is A (A progressive shoulder strengthening program with load and pain guidance over at least twelve weeks): Supervised, progressive loading is first-line for rotator cuff related shoulder pain and often matches surgical results at one year. Decompression surgery is reserved for failed conservative care, and repeated injections carry tendon risk. Passive stretching does not suit a shoulder with full passive range.

Question 65

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist in Brandon is examining a 54-year-old woman who has had shoulder pain and stiffness for three months. Passive movements are limited with a firm end feel. Which pattern of passive restriction is classically described as the capsular pattern of the glenohumeral joint?

  • A. External rotation most limited, then abduction, then internal rotation
  • B. Internal rotation most limited, then abduction, then external rotation
  • C. Abduction most limited, then flexion, with external rotation relatively preserved
  • D. Flexion most limited, then internal rotation, with abduction nearly full

The correct answer is A (External rotation most limited, then abduction, then internal rotation): The glenohumeral capsular pattern is loss of external rotation first, abduction second and internal rotation third. Reversing the order or preserving external rotation does not match this pattern. It supports adhesive capsulitis when seen with a firm end feel.

Question 66

Musculoskeletal

A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes in Windsor has had severe shoulder pain at night for six weeks, and external rotation is now half the other side. Pain is easily provoked, and her last session of vigorous stretching left her sleepless for two days. She wants to know how to proceed.

  • A. Increase stretching to the end of range so the capsule lengthens quickly, repeating twice daily
  • B. Use gentle pain-limited movement and education, avoiding aggressive stretching in the irritable stage
  • C. Apply strong end-range mobilization three times weekly to break through the restriction and regain range
  • D. Stop all shoulder movement until the pain subsides, then begin range exercises with a physiotherapist

The correct answer is B (Use gentle pain-limited movement and education, avoiding aggressive stretching in the irritable stage): In the painful freezing stage the capsule is inflamed, so gentle movement within comfortable range and reassurance are best, and aggressive stretching or forceful mobilization tends to flare symptoms. Complete rest leads to more stiffness, and the stage typically evolves over many months.

Question 67

Musculoskeletal

A 19-year-old runner in Hamilton has had anterior knee pain for ten weeks that is worse on stairs and after sitting. Palpation of the patellar facets is tender, there is no effusion, and ligament testing is normal. Single-leg squat shows hip adduction and knee valgus. Which program has the strongest support?

  • A. Combined hip and knee strengthening with temporary adjustment of aggravating running volume
  • B. Complete avoidance of running and stairs for twelve weeks, with ice after any activity
  • C. Knee extension in terminal range with heavy weights to target the vastus medialis and nothing else
  • D. Long-term patellar taping alone worn daily, with no strengthening component added

The correct answer is A (Combined hip and knee strengthening with temporary adjustment of aggravating running volume): Combining hip and knee strengthening gives better pain and function than knee exercise alone in patellofemoral pain, and load management keeps activity possible. Prolonged avoidance loses fitness, while taping may help symptoms short term but does not build capacity. Selective vastus medialis activation is not supported.

Question 68

Musculoskeletal

A 22-year-old basketball player in London, Ontario is seven months after ACL reconstruction. Her quadriceps strength is 92 percent of the other leg, hop tests are 94 percent, and she feels ready. She wants to return to full games this week. Her surgeon is open to your opinion on timing.

  • A. Delay full return, since returning before about nine months carries higher reinjury risk
  • B. Clear her now, because self-reported readiness is the most reliable predictor of graft safety and reinjury
  • C. Delay return until the quadriceps reach one hundred and twenty percent of the other leg's strength
  • D. Clear her now, since symmetry scores above ninety percent show the graft is ready

The correct answer is A (Delay full return, since returning before about nine months carries higher reinjury risk): Return to pivoting sport before roughly nine months after ACL reconstruction is linked to much higher reinjury, even with good symmetry scores, so time and criteria both count. Strength symmetry alone and confidence are incomplete. A target well over symmetry is not an established criterion.

Question 69

Musculoskeletal

A 47-year-old walker in Montreal has pain at the back of the heel where the Achilles inserts, worse on hills and when stepping off kerbs. Your plan is a heavy loading program, and she asks about heel drops from the edge of a step. Calcaneal bursitis and a Haglund deformity are not suspected.

  • A. Use full-range heel drops below the step edge, as in the program for mid-portion pain
  • B. Prescribe prolonged calf stretching on a slant board into deep dorsiflexion before starting any loading
  • C. Load the tendon but avoid dorsiflexion past neutral, using floor heel raises or a wedge
  • D. Avoid all calf loading until the pain disappears, then start gentle heel raises

The correct answer is C (Load the tendon but avoid dorsiflexion past neutral, using floor heel raises or a wedge): Insertional tendinopathy is aggravated by compression against the calcaneus at end-range dorsiflexion, so loading is done in a limited range. The mid-portion step-edge program and deep stretching add compression. Complete avoidance reduces tendon capacity.

Question 70

Musculoskeletal

A 46-year-old hairdresser in Gatineau has tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night and eases by shaking her hand. Phalen's test reproduces symptoms in 40 seconds, and thenar strength is preserved. Symptoms began three months ago, and there is no wasting.

  • A. Surgical release as the first step because persistent night symptoms predict failure of non-operative care
  • B. Neutral-position night splinting with activity modification, reviewing if numbness or weakness progresses
  • C. A rigid wrist extension splint worn at all times, including during work tasks
  • D. Cervical traction for several weeks, since symptoms in the median distribution arise at the neck level

The correct answer is B (Neutral-position night splinting with activity modification, reviewing if numbness or weakness progresses): For mild to moderate carpal tunnel syndrome without wasting, a neutral night splint with modification of provoking tasks is first-line, with escalation if weakness or constant numbness appears. Surgery is reserved for failure or advanced signs. Extension raises carpal tunnel pressure, and the findings do not point to the neck.

Question 71

Musculoskeletal

A 43-year-old man in Quebec City has neck pain radiating into his right arm for two weeks. He has numbness in the middle finger, weak elbow extension, and a reduced triceps reflex. Spurling's test reproduces arm symptoms, and shoulder abduction relieves them. Which nerve root level is most likely involved?

  • A. C6, because thumb and index finger numbness with biceps and brachioradialis weakness defines it
  • B. C5, because deltoid weakness and lateral upper arm numbness define the lesion
  • C. C7, matching middle finger numbness, triceps weakness and a reduced triceps reflex
  • D. C8, because ring and little finger numbness with finger flexor weakness defines it

The correct answer is C (C7, matching middle finger numbness, triceps weakness and a reduced triceps reflex): Triceps weakness and reflex loss with middle finger numbness map to C7. C6 gives thumb numbness and a reduced brachioradialis or biceps response, C5 affects the deltoid, and C8 produces little finger numbness with finger flexor weakness. Relief on shoulder abduction supports root irritation.

Question 72

Musculoskeletal

A 71-year-old woman in Sudbury has bilateral thigh and calf pain after walking 200 metres. She finds relief by leaning on a shopping cart or sitting, and she can cycle for 30 minutes comfortably. Foot pulses are normal. Which finding makes lumbar spinal stenosis more likely than vascular claudication?

  • A. Relief by flexed postures, and tolerance of stationary cycling despite poor walking tolerance
  • B. Pain that stops within a minute of standing still without any need to sit
  • C. Cool, pale feet with absent pedal pulses when pain develops during walking
  • D. Pain that reproducibly worsens with walking uphill compared with walking on level ground

The correct answer is A (Relief by flexed postures, and tolerance of stationary cycling despite poor walking tolerance): Neurogenic claudication eases with lumbar flexion, such as leaning forward or sitting, and cycling is tolerated because the spine is flexed. Quick relief on standing still, reduced pulses and uphill-provoked pain suggest vascular disease. Her normal pulses also point away from an arterial cause.

Question 73

Musculoskeletal

A 68-year-old woman in Fredericton has a bone density T-score of minus 2.8 at the lumbar spine and no previous fracture. She asks which exercises are suitable. She is otherwise healthy, walks daily and wants a plan that reduces her risk of fracture and falls.

  • A. Progressive resistance, balance and weight-bearing work, avoiding loaded spinal flexion and twisting
  • B. Brisk walking daily, since high-load exercise is unsafe and bone responds mostly to light activity
  • C. Swimming as the main exercise, because water supports the spine and protects against vertebral fractures
  • D. Sit-ups and loaded forward bending to strengthen the abdominals and spinal flexors

The correct answer is A (Progressive resistance, balance and weight-bearing work, avoiding loaded spinal flexion and twisting): Bone responds to progressive resistance and weight-bearing exercise, and balance training reduces fall risk, while loaded spinal flexion and twisting raise vertebral fracture risk. Walking alone provides limited stimulus, and swimming is excellent for fitness but is not weight-bearing.

Question 74

Musculoskeletal

A 35-year-old begins a new eccentric-heavy leg workout in a Toronto gym. She feels no soreness afterwards and no sudden sharp pain, but two days later she has marked thigh stiffness and tenderness that makes stairs difficult. Which statement best describes this experience and the usual advice?

  • A. Soreness typically peaks around one to three days, and light activity usually eases it
  • B. Soreness usually peaks at about one week, and rest from all training is advised
  • C. Soreness typically reflects lactic acid build-up, and stretching is the usual remedy
  • D. Soreness usually signals a mild strain, so ice and a week off exercise are advised

The correct answer is A (Soreness typically peaks around one to three days, and light activity usually eases it): Delayed onset soreness follows unaccustomed, often eccentric, exercise, typically peaks between 24 and 72 hours and settles within days with light activity. A mild strain is the tempting alternative, but a strain produces sharp pain at the moment of loading, not stiffness that appears two days later. Lactate clears within hours and does not cause this soreness, and prolonged rest delays adaptation.

Question 75

Musculoskeletal

A 24-year-old volleyball player in Burnaby suddenly increased jump training from twice to six times weekly. She now has diffuse patellar tendon swelling and pain on loading, with no prior history. Which management step best fits a reactive tendon that has been overloaded within the past two weeks?

  • A. Add heavy eccentric decline squats daily to stimulate collagen production as soon as possible
  • B. Use deep friction massage and static stretching of the quadriceps to remodel the tendon
  • C. Continue the same jump volume and add a corticosteroid injection to reduce the swelling
  • D. Reduce the jumping load and use isometric holds, avoiding stretching and compression

The correct answer is D (Reduce the jumping load and use isometric holds, avoiding stretching and compression): A reactive tendon is responding to a sudden spike in load, so the answer is to reduce that load and use isometrics for pain relief. Heavy eccentrics, stretching and compression add stress, and continuing the same volume leaves the cause intact.

Question 76

Musculoskeletal

A 57-year-old woman in Lethbridge had a wrist fracture treated in a cast. Five weeks later she has burning pain out of proportion to the injury, a swollen, shiny, warmer hand, and pain from light touch. The fracture has united on films. What is the best next action?

  • A. Arrange medical review for suspected complex regional pain syndrome, with gentle graded movement
  • B. Perform firm stretching into the stiff wrist to restore range before stiffness worsens
  • C. Discharge her with advice that the symptoms are normal healing and will pass
  • D. Immobilize the hand again until the colour, swelling and warmth have returned to normal

The correct answer is A (Arrange medical review for suspected complex regional pain syndrome, with gentle graded movement): Pain out of proportion, allodynia, swelling and temperature and skin changes after a fracture fit complex regional pain syndrome, and early medical review plus graded movement gives the best chance of recovery. Immobilization and forceful stretching typically worsen it, and dismissal delays care.

Question 77

Musculoskeletal

A 31-year-old runner in Winnipeg has lateral knee pain starting after 20 minutes of running that disappears when she stops. Tenderness is over the lateral femoral epicondyle at 30 degrees of knee flexion, and hip abductor strength is reduced on the painful side. Which program is most appropriate?

  • A. Corticosteroid injection at the lateral epicondyle followed by an immediate return to full training
  • B. Daily foam rolling and stretching of the band to lengthen it, with unchanged running volume
  • C. Complete rest from all exercise for three months before any rehabilitation work begins
  • D. Hip abductor and lateral chain strengthening with temporary reduction in running volume

The correct answer is D (Hip abductor and lateral chain strengthening with temporary reduction in running volume): Lateral knee pain from compression of tissue under the band is managed by reducing aggravating volume and building hip and lateral chain strength. The band cannot be meaningfully lengthened, rest alone does not restore capacity, and injection with full return ignores the underlying load problem.

Question 78

Musculoskeletal

A 20-year-old cross-country runner in Moncton has had shin pain for three weeks that is now present when walking and at night. There is focal bony tenderness over a four-centimetre segment of the tibia, and single-leg hopping reproduces sharp pain. She wants to run in a meet this weekend.

  • A. Treat as medial tibial stress syndrome with calf stretching and continue running at a reduced pace
  • B. Prescribe shock-absorbing insoles and allow the meet if she can hop without limping
  • C. Stop running, protect weight-bearing and arrange imaging for a suspected tibial stress fracture
  • D. Begin heavy calf strengthening immediately to improve the bone's ability to absorb load

The correct answer is C (Stop running, protect weight-bearing and arrange imaging for a suspected tibial stress fracture): Focal bony tenderness, night pain and pain on hopping point to a tibial stress fracture, which needs relative rest and imaging. Medial tibial stress syndrome gives a diffuse band of tenderness and eases with warm-up. Insoles and heavy loading do not protect an injured bone.

Question 79

Musculoskeletal

A 26-year-old rugby player in Halifax suffered a quadriceps contusion three weeks ago. Despite deep massage and heat sessions, knee flexion has fallen from 90 to 50 degrees and a firm, tender mass is palpable in the muscle. Which action is most appropriate?

  • A. Increase deep massage frequency to break down the mass and restore knee flexion much faster
  • B. Stop deep massage and heat, avoid forceful stretching, and arrange imaging for myositis ossificans
  • C. Apply more heat before activity and expect the mass to dissolve gradually over several weeks
  • D. Begin aggressive passive knee flexion stretching to regain range before the mass hardens and blocks motion

The correct answer is B (Stop deep massage and heat, avoid forceful stretching, and arrange imaging for myositis ossificans): A worsening range, a firm mass and a history of contusion treated with massage and heat suggest heterotopic ossification, which can be aggravated by vigorous techniques. Imaging and medical input are needed while loading is protected, and heat and forceful stretching are avoided.

Question 80

Musculoskeletal

A 33-year-old man in Red Deer has had a tibial shaft fracture fixed with a nail eight hours ago. In recovery he has increasing leg pain despite analgesia, a tense swollen calf, and severe pain when his toes are passively stretched. Pulses are present. What is the correct response?

  • A. Reassure that present pulses exclude compartment syndrome and elevate the leg for swelling
  • B. Apply a tight compression bandage over the calf to limit swelling and reduce pain
  • C. Continue routine post-operative mobilization and reassess pain when analgesia is increased
  • D. Alert the surgical team now for suspected compartment syndrome, since pulses often stay present

The correct answer is D (Alert the surgical team now for suspected compartment syndrome, since pulses often stay present): Disproportionate pain, a tense compartment and pain on passive stretch are the key signs, and pulses are usually present until late. It is a surgical emergency requiring immediate escalation. Compression, elevation alone or routine mobilization all delay fasciotomy.

Question 81

Musculoskeletal

A 72-year-old woman in St. John's reports two weeks of morning stiffness in both shoulders and hips lasting over an hour, with difficulty rising from a chair. She also mentions a new headache, scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, and jaw ache when chewing. What is your priority?

  • A. Begin a shoulder and hip stretching program and reassess the stiffness again in two weeks' time
  • B. Advise heat packs for the girdle stiffness and a routine appointment next month
  • C. Treat the headache as cervicogenic and start cervical mobilization at the next visit
  • D. Arrange urgent same-day medical assessment, as headache and jaw pain raise concern for arteritis

The correct answer is D (Arrange urgent same-day medical assessment, as headache and jaw pain raise concern for arteritis): Girdle stiffness suggests polymyalgia rheumatica, but new headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication in a person over 50 point to giant cell arteritis, which risks vision loss and needs same-day medical assessment. Exercise, neck treatment or a routine appointment would delay that care.

Question 82

Musculoskeletal

A 57-year-old woman in Charlottetown has lateral hip pain that is worst when lying on that side and climbing stairs. Single-leg stance for 30 seconds reproduces the pain, and the greater trochanter is tender. Hip range is full. She asks what to do at night and during the day.

  • A. Sleep on the painful side with a firm pillow and wait for the tendon to settle
  • B. Stretch the hip adductors deeply in crossed-leg positions several times daily to relieve the tension
  • C. Avoid side-lying on the painful side and adduction postures, with progressive gluteal strengthening
  • D. Stop walking and use a cane on the painful side until the night pain has resolved

The correct answer is C (Avoid side-lying on the painful side and adduction postures, with progressive gluteal strengthening): Lateral hip pain that is worse with side-lying and single-leg stance is typically gluteal tendinopathy, which is aggravated by compression against the trochanter in adduction. Relieving that compression and building gluteal strength is the evidence-based approach, while crossed-leg stretches and side-lying add compression.

Question 83

Musculoskeletal

A 13-year-old soccer player in Calgary has pain and a bony prominence at the tibial tubercle in both knees, worse with kicking and jumping. Examination shows tenderness at the tubercle and normal knee range with no effusion. His parents worry that he will have to stop the sport permanently.

  • A. Place both knees in a rigid cast for six weeks to allow the apophysis to heal
  • B. Refer for surgical removal of the prominent bone fragment as the standard treatment in most adolescents
  • C. Reassure that it is self-limiting, modify activity to tolerance and add quadriceps strengthening
  • D. Stop all sport for the whole growth period and avoid any quadriceps exercise

The correct answer is C (Reassure that it is self-limiting, modify activity to tolerance and add quadriceps strengthening): Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis that resolves as growth finishes. Education, pain-guided activity modification and strengthening allow sport to continue. Casting, surgery and prolonged rest are not routine, and quadriceps work helps rather than harms.

Question 84

Musculoskeletal

A 25-year-old hockey player in Ottawa sustained a grade II medial collateral ligament sprain two days ago with a firm end feel on valgus stress at 30 degrees. There is no cruciate laxity. He wants the safest approach that does not cost him months of fitness.

  • A. Rigid immobilization in a straight-leg cast for six weeks before any knee movement is attempted
  • B. Immediate return to full contact practice with a compression sleeve for support
  • C. Protected early motion in a hinged brace, with progressive weight-bearing and strengthening
  • D. Surgical repair of the ligament in the first week to restore stability reliably

The correct answer is C (Protected early motion in a hinged brace, with progressive weight-bearing and strengthening): Grade II medial collateral injuries heal well with protected early motion, bracing and progressive loading, which supports organized collagen and avoids stiffness. Prolonged casting causes weakness and stiffness, a sleeve does not protect against valgus load, and surgery is not routine.

Question 85

Musculoskeletal

A 29-year-old nurse in Saskatoon has recently had three ankle sprains in two years and feels the ankle giving way on uneven ground. Examination shows mild laxity but good strength. She asks what will best reduce recurrence and restore confidence.

  • A. A neuromuscular program of balance and perturbation training, with evertor strengthening
  • B. Permanent rigid ankle bracing without any exercise, worn for all activities of daily living
  • C. Passive stretching of the calf and peroneals to lengthen the tissues surrounding the ankle joint
  • D. Rest from running for six months until the ligaments have fully tightened again

The correct answer is A (A neuromuscular program of balance and perturbation training, with evertor strengthening): Balance, perturbation and strength training improve sensorimotor control and reduce recurrent sprains. Permanent bracing alone does not improve control, stretching does not treat instability, and rest will not tighten stretched ligaments.

Question 86

Musculoskeletal

A 38-year-old woman in Winnipeg has had sudden severe neck pain and headache for two days after hanging wallpaper. During the interview she reports dizziness, slurred speech and double vision that comes and goes. You were planning cervical mobilization at this visit.

  • A. Perform a vertebrobasilar screen with position testing before deciding whether to mobilize her neck today
  • B. Withhold treatment and send her for emergency assessment for possible vertebral artery dissection
  • C. Refer her for a physician visit within 24 hours for blood pressure and neurological review
  • D. Switch to non-thrust soft tissue work and thoracic mobilization, then recheck next visit

The correct answer is B (Withhold treatment and send her for emergency assessment for possible vertebral artery dissection): Sudden severe neck pain with dizziness, dysarthria and diplopia are warning signs of possible vertebral artery dissection, so manual therapy is withheld and emergency care is arranged. Position testing is tempting as a routine screen, but it cannot exclude dissection and may provoke harm. A next-day physician visit or gentler technique still leaves a possible stroke in progress without emergency imaging.

Question 87

Musculoskeletal

A 34-year-old new mother in Victoria has pain at the radial wrist when lifting her baby. Finkelstein's test reproduces sharp pain, and there is thickening over the first dorsal compartment. No neurological findings are present. She wants conservative care that allows her to keep caring for the baby.

  • A. A rigid forearm cast for eight weeks to ensure complete tendon rest
  • B. A thumb spica splint with load modification, then graded tendon loading as symptoms settle
  • C. Immediate referral for sheath release surgery as the first-line option
  • D. Strong friction massage and thumb stretching several times daily to loosen the tendon sheath

The correct answer is B (A thumb spica splint with load modification, then graded tendon loading as symptoms settle): A splint and modified handling reduce irritation of the first dorsal compartment, and gradual tendon loading restores capacity. Prolonged casting and vigorous friction are unnecessary or irritating, and surgery is reserved for cases that do not respond to conservative care.

Question 88

Musculoskeletal

A 50-year-old teacher in Charlottetown has had non-specific chronic low back pain for a year, with no red flags. She has tried walking and yoga but disliked both, and enjoys swimming and cycling. She asks which exercise type is scientifically best and what you advise.

  • A. Motor control exercise of the deep trunk muscles is clearly better than every other type
  • B. No type is clearly superior, so choose one she enjoys and can sustain as it progresses
  • C. Yoga alone has shown benefit, so she should return to it despite disliking it
  • D. Exercise is unhelpful for chronic pain, so passive treatment is the recommended core approach

The correct answer is B (No type is clearly superior, so choose one she enjoys and can sustain as it progresses): Trials show similar benefits across exercise types in chronic low back pain, so adherence and preference should guide selection. No form has proved clearly superior, and passive treatment alone does not match the benefit of active care.

Question 89

Musculoskeletal

A 29-year-old man in Toronto did an intense unaccustomed spin class yesterday. Today both thighs are very swollen and painful, he cannot lift his legs, and his urine is dark brown. He feels weak and nauseated. He asks you to massage his thighs before his next class.

  • A. Advise oral hydration, light walking and gentle thigh soft tissue work, then recheck in three days
  • B. Refer him to his family physician for a routine appointment this week
  • C. Arrange urgent medical assessment, since swollen thighs and dark urine suggest rhabdomyolysis
  • D. Treat as bilateral quadriceps strains with relative rest, compression and graded return

The correct answer is C (Arrange urgent medical assessment, since swollen thighs and dark urine suggest rhabdomyolysis): Dark urine with marked swelling and weakness after unaccustomed intense exercise suggests muscle breakdown, with a risk of kidney injury, so urgent testing and fluids are needed. Hydration advice is tempting because fluids do matter, but it cannot replace blood tests and monitoring. A routine appointment or strain protocol misses that dark urine and weakness point to a systemic problem.

Question 90

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist in Moose Jaw is teaching students about age-related change in muscle. Compared with a younger adult, an older person with no disease is expected to show a loss of strength. Which change in muscle structure is most characteristic of this age-related decline?

  • A. Preferential loss of slow-twitch type I fibres, with preservation of fast-twitch fibres
  • B. An increase in the number of motor units with unchanged fibre size in all muscles
  • C. Preferential atrophy and loss of fast-twitch type II fibres, with fewer motor units
  • D. Increased tendon stiffness alone, without any meaningful change in the muscle fibres

The correct answer is C (Preferential atrophy and loss of fast-twitch type II fibres, with fewer motor units): Ageing muscle loses fast-twitch type II fibres and motor units preferentially, reducing power, and this is why power training is useful in older adults. The loss of type I fibres is less marked, and motor unit number falls rather than rises.

Question 91

Musculoskeletal

A student physiotherapist is asked to explain why high-impact and resistance exercise are suggested for bone health. The explanation centres on a principle that relates mechanical loading to changes in the structure of bone over time. Which principle is that?

  • A. Davis's law, that bone remodels toward the direction of tensile stress after fracture
  • B. Wolff's law, that bone adapts its density and architecture to the loads placed on it
  • C. Hilton's law, that bone density follows the nerve supply of the overlying joint
  • D. The Arndt-Schulz principle, that stronger stimuli produce proportionally greater bone gain

The correct answer is B (Wolff's law, that bone adapts its density and architecture to the loads placed on it): Wolff's law states that bone adapts to mechanical load, increasing density where load is applied and losing it when unloaded. Davis's law concerns soft tissue, and other named principles do not describe bone adaptation to load.

Question 92

Musculoskeletal

A 15-year-old gymnast in Vancouver has had unilateral low back pain for six weeks. It is worse with back extension and landing, and eases with rest. The single-leg hyperextension test is painful on the right and neurological screening is normal. What is the most appropriate plan?

  • A. Stop the aggravating extension activities and refer for imaging of a possible pars stress injury
  • B. Treat as a muscle strain with deep tissue massage and return to full gymnastics next week
  • C. Continue training and add lumbar extension exercises to strengthen the painful segment
  • D. Begin lumbar traction and manual therapy to open the painful segment and reduce symptoms

The correct answer is A (Stop the aggravating extension activities and refer for imaging of a possible pars stress injury): Unilateral extension-provoked back pain in a young athlete with a painful single-leg hyperextension test suggests a pars stress injury, so extension activities are stopped and imaging is arranged. Extension loading, massage and traction do not protect the bone.

Question 93

Musculoskeletal

A 55-year-old gardener in Nanaimo has had medial knee pain for four months with occasional catching. MRI reports a degenerative medial meniscal tear and mild osteoarthritis. There is no true locking, and the knee extends fully. He asks if arthroscopic surgery is the best first step.

  • A. Complete rest from squatting and gardening for six months to allow the tear to heal
  • B. Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy first, because imaging confirms a tear that will not heal
  • C. Supervised exercise therapy first, since outcomes match arthroscopic meniscectomy in these cases
  • D. A series of knee corticosteroid injections to treat the tear before any exercise begins

The correct answer is C (Supervised exercise therapy first, since outcomes match arthroscopic meniscectomy in these cases): For degenerative tears without true locking, trials show exercise therapy gives results similar to partial meniscectomy, so it is tried first. Imaging tears are common in people without symptoms, and prolonged rest or repeated injection does not rebuild capacity.

Question 94

Musculoskeletal

A 63-year-old woman in Kingston has had rheumatoid arthritis for 25 years and now reports neck pain, tingling in both hands and recent unsteadiness walking. She asks for cervical manipulation because it helped her years ago. Examination shows brisk reflexes in the legs.

  • A. Perform gentle cervical manipulation, since it helped before and pain is her main complaint
  • B. Reassure her that hand tingling is common in rheumatoid arthritis and begin hand exercises
  • C. Start cervical traction and deep neck flexor training, and review progress in a month
  • D. Withhold manual therapy and arrange urgent medical review for possible upper cervical instability

The correct answer is D (Withhold manual therapy and arrange urgent medical review for possible upper cervical instability): Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis can destabilize the upper cervical spine, and gait changes, hand paraesthesia and brisk reflexes suggest possible cord compromise. Manipulation and traction are unsafe, and the findings need urgent medical review rather than reassurance.

Question 95

Musculoskeletal

A 70-year-old man in Peterborough has severe osteoarthritis of the left hip and is waiting for surgery. His pain limits walking, and you prescribe a cane to reduce load on the joint. Which instruction on use of the cane is correct?

  • A. Hold the cane in the left hand and advance it with the left leg
  • B. Hold the cane in the right hand and advance it with the right leg
  • C. Hold the cane in the right hand and advance it forward with the left leg
  • D. Hold the cane in the left hand and advance it with the right leg

The correct answer is C (Hold the cane in the right hand and advance it forward with the left leg): The cane goes in the hand opposite the affected hip and moves with the affected leg, which widens the base and reduces the abductor force needed. Using it on the painful side or moving it with the other leg loses that benefit.

Question 96

Musculoskeletal

A 36-year-old office worker in Red Deer has had one-sided headaches for four months, starting in the neck and spreading over the eye. They are provoked by prolonged computer work and neck movement, with no aura or nausea. The flexion-rotation test is limited to the left. What is the best approach?

  • A. Treat as migraine with a daily headache diary and no neck treatment at all
  • B. Treat as tension-type headache with relaxation alone and discontinue neck exercises
  • C. Arrange urgent brain imaging because headaches that begin in the neck are sinister until proven otherwise
  • D. Treat as cervicogenic headache with cervical mobility, motor control exercise and posture advice

The correct answer is D (Treat as cervicogenic headache with cervical mobility, motor control exercise and posture advice): Unilateral, neck-provoked headache with a limited flexion-rotation test indicates a cervical source, and cervical exercise, mobility work and posture advice are effective. Migraine lacks neck provocation and nausea, and urgent imaging is not required without red flags.

Question 97

Musculoskeletal

A 46-year-old gardener in Abbotsford has chronic widespread pain. On good days she gardens for four hours and then spends the next two days in bed. She asks how to break this cycle without giving up the garden she loves.

  • A. Plan timed activity blocks with scheduled breaks, and add small increments each week
  • B. Stop gardening until she is pain-free, then resume at her previous four-hour level of activity
  • C. Garden as long as she feels able on good days, then rest fully on bad days
  • D. Limit gardening permanently to ten minutes weekly to prevent any further flare-ups

The correct answer is A (Plan timed activity blocks with scheduled breaks, and add small increments each week): A boom and bust pattern keeps pain and disability high. Pacing uses planned, time-contingent activity with breaks, and gradual increases build tolerance. Pain-guided exertion or permanent restriction reproduces the problem or narrows her life.

Question 98

Musculoskeletal

A 52-year-old man in Winnipeg with chronic knee osteoarthritis is otherwise healthy and asks what weekly amount of physical activity Canadian guidelines recommend for adults. A physiotherapist explains the general adult recommendation for aerobic and strengthening activity. Which statement is accurate?

  • A. At least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity daily, plus two strengthening days
  • B. At least 75 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly, plus strengthening on one day
  • C. At least 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly, plus two balance training days
  • D. At least 150 minutes of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity weekly, plus two strengthening days

The correct answer is D (At least 150 minutes of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity weekly, plus two strengthening days): Canadian guidance for adults is at least 150 minutes of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity each week and muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days. The 60 minutes daily figure is the child and youth target and is the most tempting wrong option because the activity type matches. The 75 minute figure only applies to vigorous activity, and 300 minutes with balance training is a higher benefit target that omits strengthening.

Question 99

Musculoskeletal

A 22-year-old recreational runner in Ottawa has pain along the posteromedial border of the tibia over a 10-centimetre stretch. It begins at the start of runs, eases once warm and returns afterward. There is no focal bony tenderness, no night pain, and hopping is painless. What is the likely diagnosis?

  • A. Tibial stress fracture, because pain along the tibia on running indicates bone injury
  • B. Acute compartment syndrome, because exercise pain along the lower leg indicates raised pressure
  • C. Medial tibial stress syndrome, shown by diffuse tibial tenderness without focal bone signs
  • D. Popliteal artery entrapment, because pain during running in the lower leg suggests vascular cause

The correct answer is C (Medial tibial stress syndrome, shown by diffuse tibial tenderness without focal bone signs): Diffuse tenderness along the posteromedial tibial border, pain that eases with warm-up, no focal bony tenderness and a painless hop test fit medial tibial stress syndrome. Stress fractures give focal tenderness, night pain and hop pain, while compartment syndrome and entrapment have distinct features.

Question 100

Musculoskeletal

A 38-year-old plumber in Brampton has had sharp low back pain for ten days with pain down the back of the left leg to the ankle. Straight leg raise reproduces leg pain at 40 degrees, and ankle reflex is reduced. There is no bladder change or saddle numbness. What is the best plan now?

  • A. Strict bed rest for two weeks to let the irritated nerve root recover before moving much
  • B. Aggressive lumbar flexion stretching into leg pain to desensitize the nerve root over several weeks
  • C. Immediate referral for spinal surgery because the straight leg raise is positive at forty degrees
  • D. Education, staying active as tolerated and monitoring neurology, referring if deficits progress

The correct answer is D (Education, staying active as tolerated and monitoring neurology, referring if deficits progress): Most lumbar radiculopathies improve with time, education and staying active, and surgery is reserved for progressive deficit or failure over weeks. Bed rest delays recovery, and forcing the nerve into provocative positions flares symptoms. Cauda equina signs are absent here.

Question 101

Musculoskeletal

A 67-year-old retired farmer is three weeks after a transtibial amputation for diabetic vascular disease. Sutures are out, and the residual limb is swollen and cylindrical in shape. The team wants to reduce the swelling and shape the limb for a first prosthesis. Which approach should the physiotherapist choose for his daily care?

  • A. Rest the limb on a pillow under the knee between sessions to let the swelling drain
  • B. Apply a tubular stockinette sock without compression so the healed skin is not stressed
  • C. Use a rigid dressing or shrinker with graded compression, tightest at the distal end
  • D. Massage the swollen limb and tap the distal end daily to desensitize it before fitting

The correct answer is C (Use a rigid dressing or shrinker with graded compression, tightest at the distal end): Graded compression that is highest distally and lower proximally pushes fluid toward the trunk and moulds a conical limb ready for a socket. A rigid or semi-rigid system also protects against knee flexion and trauma. Resting the limb on a pillow under the knee is tempting for swelling, but it encourages a flexion contracture that would later block prosthetic alignment. An uncompressed sock or massage does not control the edema or shape the limb.

Question 102

Musculoskeletal

A 34-year-old cyclist lost his left forearm in a farm accident six weeks ago. He reports burning and cramping sensations in the missing hand that wake him at night. The residual limb skin is intact and wound healing is normal. Which physiotherapy intervention has the best support for reducing this particular symptom?

  • A. Desensitization of the residual limb with progressive textures and light tapping
  • B. Compression shrinker wear to reduce residual limb edema and swelling
  • C. Mirror therapy using movements of the intact hand while watching its reflection in a mirror
  • D. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation over the residual limb scar at sensory level

The correct answer is C (Mirror therapy using movements of the intact hand while watching its reflection in a mirror): Mirror therapy gives the brain visual feedback of a moving missing hand and can reduce phantom sensations through cortical reorganization effects. It is low risk and can be taught for home use. Desensitization is tempting because it is a standard residual limb program, but it addresses skin hypersensitivity, and his skin is intact and healing normally. Shrinker wear controls swelling, and electrical stimulation has weaker support for this symptom.

Question 103

Musculoskeletal

A 52-year-old woman with a transfemoral prosthesis walks with her trunk leaning sharply toward the prosthetic side during stance on that leg. The socket fits well and is not painful. Her residual hip abductors are weak after surgery, and her prosthesis length was checked as correct last month. Which cause most likely explains this gait deviation?

  • A. Hip flexion contracture, creating excess lumbar lordosis in stance
  • B. Weak hip stabilizers on the amputated side, so the trunk shifts toward the hip
  • C. A prosthetic knee set with too little alignment stability, so it buckles in early stance
  • D. Reduced hip extension strength on the amputated side, causing a forward trunk lean at heel strike

The correct answer is B (Weak hip stabilizers on the amputated side, so the trunk shifts toward the hip): A lateral trunk lean over the prosthesis in stance is the classic compensation for abductor weakness, because moving the centre of mass closer to the hip joint reduces the muscle force needed. Hip flexion contracture and weak extensors are tempting hip-related causes, but they change lordosis or forward trunk position rather than lateral lean. Knee instability would show buckling. Strengthening the abductors is the targeted fix.

Question 104

Musculoskeletal

A 45-year-old man wears a transtibial prosthesis daily for work as a delivery driver. After long shifts he has noticed a persistent red area over the distal tibia. The skin is intact, blanches with pressure and fades within twenty minutes of removing the prosthesis. What advice is most appropriate at this stage?

  • A. Apply a silicone gel liner and continue full wear while monitoring the area
  • B. Reduce wearing time briefly and have the prosthetist assess the socket fit and sock ply
  • C. Add one extra sock ply and continue the full work shift as usual
  • D. Apply a protective foam pad over the distal tibia inside the socket liner

The correct answer is B (Reduce wearing time briefly and have the prosthetist assess the socket fit and sock ply): Redness that blanches and resolves within twenty minutes is a sign of pressure that has not yet damaged tissue, but it signals a fit problem. Reducing wear and involving the prosthetist lets the socket and sock ply be adjusted before breakdown occurs. Adding a sock ply or a pad is a common response to pressure, but changing fit without assessment can shift the load to a new site, and a liner does not correct the fit.

Question 105

Musculoskeletal

A rehabilitation team is explaining to a patient's family why the surgeon prefers to preserve the knee joint in a patient scheduled for lower limb amputation. The family asks how the amputation level affects the effort of walking afterwards. Which statement best describes the effect of level on energy expenditure during walking?

  • A. Energy cost is higher after vascular amputation than after traumatic loss at the same level
  • B. Loss of more proximal limb segments raises the metabolic cost of gait compared with distal losses
  • C. Component weight is the main driver of walking energy cost, more than level
  • D. Patient-chosen walking speed explains most of the energy cost difference between levels

The correct answer is B (Loss of more proximal limb segments raises the metabolic cost of gait compared with distal losses): Walking energy use rises as more joints and muscle are lost, so a transfemoral amputation costs more than a transtibial one, and a bilateral loss costs more again. Preserving the knee improves gait efficiency and the chance of functional prosthetic use. The cause of amputation is tempting because vascular causes do raise cost, but the question asks about level. Component weight and walking speed matter, yet level remains a major driver.

Question 106

Musculoskeletal

A 71-year-old woman recovering from a transfemoral amputation spends most of the day in a wheelchair with the residual limb resting on a cushion. She is two weeks postoperative and has no wound complications. Which positioning and exercise advice best prevents a deformity that would later limit prosthetic use?

  • A. Support the residual limb on a pillow in bed and a cushion in the chair
  • B. Position the residual limb abducted on a wheelchair side support while sitting
  • C. Practise active hip abduction and flexion in sitting to keep the muscles strong
  • D. Lie prone for periods each day and practise active hip extension and adduction exercises

The correct answer is D (Lie prone for periods each day and practise active hip extension and adduction exercises): Prolonged sitting encourages hip flexion and abduction contractures in a transfemoral amputee. Prone lying and active hip extension and adduction work counter these positions. Flexion and abduction exercises feel productive because they keep the muscles active, but they train the muscles already prone to shortening. Pillow support and supported abduction both reinforce the same shortened positions.

Question 107

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist is preparing a patient for the stages of care after a lower limb amputation. The patient asks what happens between wound closure and receiving the definitive prosthesis. The residual limb is still changing size from week to week. Which step usually occurs in that interval?

  • A. Immediate fitting of the definitive socket once the incision has closed and sutures are out
  • B. Full rest from weight bearing until the limb volume has stabilized, then first prosthesis fitting
  • C. Fitting of a rigid dressing prosthesis in the operating room during the first postoperative week
  • D. A preparatory prosthesis worn while limb volume settles and gait training starts

The correct answer is D (A preparatory prosthesis worn while limb volume settles and gait training starts): A preparatory or temporary prosthesis is used because the residual limb continues to shrink for months. It allows early gait training while volume changes are managed and the definitive socket is delayed. A definitive socket is tempting once sutures are out, but it would fit poorly as swelling resolves. An immediate postoperative prosthesis belongs to the surgical period, and prolonged rest causes deconditioning.

Question 108

Musculoskeletal

A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is learning to walk with a transtibial prosthesis. His remaining foot has reduced protective sensation, and it now carries more load than before. Which instruction is most important for protecting the remaining limb during daily activity at home and in the community?

  • A. Wear cushioned supportive shoes and have a family member check the foot weekly at bedtime
  • B. Inspect the sole daily and wear well-fitted closed footwear whenever standing
  • C. Limit standing time on the remaining foot and keep it elevated after each outing
  • D. Apply moisturizing cream between the toes daily and wear open-toed sandals at home

The correct answer is B (Inspect the sole daily and wear well-fitted closed footwear whenever standing): The remaining foot bears more load and is at higher risk of ulceration in a person with neuropathy. Daily inspection and well-fitted closed footwear detect and prevent injury early. Cushioned shoes with a weekly check feel sensible, but a weekly check misses early breakdown in skin that cannot feel pain. Resting the foot or wearing sandals does not protect numb skin during activity.

Question 109

Musculoskeletal

A newborn is referred with a rigid congenital talipes equinovarus deformity of the right foot. The parents ask about treatment during the first weeks of life, and the pediatric team wants the physiotherapist to explain the established approach. Which option describes the accepted first-line management for this condition?

  • A. Posteromedial surgical release in the first three months, followed by casting to hold the correction
  • B. Serial manipulation and casting, followed by bracing to hold the correction
  • C. Daily parent-performed stretching and taping program, with casting added if the foot relapses
  • D. Foot abduction brace with boots and bar started at birth, adding casting if correction stalls

The correct answer is B (Serial manipulation and casting, followed by bracing to hold the correction): Serial casting using the Ponseti method starts in the first weeks and corrects the foot gradually, usually with a small tenotomy of the Achilles tendon, then bracing prevents relapse. Bracing from birth is tempting because it is part of the program, but it holds a correction that casting has already achieved. Surgical release is reserved for resistant cases. Stretching and taping cannot correct a rigid deformity.

Question 110

Musculoskeletal

A 3-week-old girl born breech is brought in for review. Her left hip abducts less than the right, and the thigh skin folds look asymmetric. The family doctor noted a hip click earlier. Which finding on examination would most strongly suggest a dislocated hip rather than a stable hip?

  • A. Asymmetric thigh skin folds noted on the same side as the earlier hip click
  • B. A positive Barlow or Ortolani test with a palpable clunk as the femoral head moves
  • C. Breech birth and female sex, both known risk factors for hip dysplasia
  • D. A soft click without a clunk felt at the hip during abduction and adduction

The correct answer is B (A positive Barlow or Ortolani test with a palpable clunk as the femoral head moves): An Ortolani clunk as a dislocated head is reduced into the acetabulum, or a Barlow clunk as it is dislocated, is the hallmark of instability in the first weeks of life. Skin fold asymmetry is tempting because it sits on the affected side, but it also occurs in stable hips. Soft clicks without a clunk are common and benign. Breech birth and female sex raise risk but are not examination findings.

Question 111

Musculoskeletal

A 6-week-old boy has been diagnosed with a reducible dislocated right hip. The pediatric orthopedic team prescribes a Pavlik harness, and his mother asks the physiotherapist what position the straps are designed to hold his legs in. Which description of the harness position is correct for this treatment?

  • A. Hips flexed near ninety degrees with strapped, forced abduction to the limit of motion
  • B. Hips held in extension and moderate abduction, as a spica cast would position them
  • C. Hips flexed well past ninety degrees with gentle supported abduction in a natural frog position
  • D. Hips flexed about ninety degrees with the thighs held together in adduction

The correct answer is C (Hips flexed well past ninety degrees with gentle supported abduction in a natural frog position): The harness holds the hips in flexion with comfortable abduction, a position that centres the femoral head in the acetabulum and lets the socket mould. Forced abduction is tempting because more abduction seems to seat the head better, but it risks avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Extension with abduction describes a cast, and adduction promotes redislocation.

Question 112

Musculoskeletal

A 5-year-old with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy, classified at a mid-level of gross motor function, has increasing adductor tightness and reduced hip abduction range. Her family reports no pain yet. The physiotherapist wants to monitor for the complication that adductor tightness most directly threatens. Which should be monitored?

  • A. Progressive migration of the femoral head out of the socket on pelvic radiographs
  • B. Fixed knee flexion contracture from hamstring shortening, which limits standing and walking efficiency
  • C. Scoliosis developing from asymmetric trunk tone, followed with serial clinical and radiographic spine measures
  • D. Equinus ankle deformity from calf spasticity, tracked by serial measures of ankle dorsiflexion range

The correct answer is A (Progressive migration of the femoral head out of the socket on pelvic radiographs): Spastic adductors and hip flexors pull the femoral head laterally and upward, so hip migration or dislocation is the complication most directly threatened, and surveillance radiographs are advised. Detecting migration early allows soft tissue or bony intervention before pain and deformity develop. Knee, spine and ankle deformities are also common in cerebral palsy, which makes them tempting, but each follows from a different muscle pattern than the adductor tightness described.

Question 113

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapy clinic is preparing to treat a 9-year-old with myelomeningocele for the first time. A colleague asks about a precaution tied to the child's repeated exposure to medical materials since birth, and how it affects the gloves and equipment used during assessments and exercise sessions. Which precaution is recommended?

  • A. Avoid weight bearing because of the high risk of spontaneous fractures during exercise sessions
  • B. Use latex-free gloves, exercise bands and equipment because sensitization risk is high
  • C. Pad splints and positioning wedges with foam, since insensate skin breaks down under prolonged pressure
  • D. Use sterile single-use exercise equipment for every session because shunt infection risk is high

The correct answer is B (Use latex-free gloves, exercise bands and equipment because sensitization risk is high): Children with myelomeningocele have repeated early exposure to latex through surgery and catheters and are at elevated risk of latex allergy, so latex-free materials are standard. Padding insensate skin is a good habit, which makes it tempting, but it is a pressure precaution and not the one tied to repeated exposure. Weight bearing is encouraged within tolerance, and sterile equipment does not address shunt risk.

Question 114

Musculoskeletal

An 8-week-old infant has a head tilt to the right with the chin turned to the left. A firm, non-tender swelling is palpable in the right neck muscle. The pregnancy was uncomplicated apart from a long second stage of labour. Which first-line physiotherapy plan is most appropriate for this infant?

  • A. A custom-fitted molding helmet worn day and night to correct the skull shape and neck tilt
  • B. Botulinum toxin injection into the shortened neck muscle arranged through the pediatric orthopedic team
  • C. Positioning changes, tummy time and gentle stretching of the shortened neck muscle
  • D. Referral for surgical release of the shortened neck muscle once the swelling has settled

The correct answer is C (Positioning changes, tummy time and gentle stretching of the shortened neck muscle): Congenital muscular torticollis is treated first with gentle stretching of the shortened sternocleidomastoid, repositioning to encourage active turning, and tummy time to strengthen the neck. Most infants improve with early conservative care. A helmet is tempting because it is used for head shape problems, but it does not lengthen the muscle. Botulinum toxin and surgical release are reserved for infants who do not respond.

Question 115

Musculoskeletal

A 38-year-old teacher, six months after her second vaginal delivery, leaks urine when she coughs or jumps. She is unsure how to find the correct muscles. During a consented assessment, which instruction is most useful to help her contract the pelvic floor effectively during practice at home?

  • A. Draw the muscles up and in as if holding back gas, while breathing normally
  • B. Contract the lower abdominals strongly and flatten the back while holding the breath for ten seconds
  • C. Squeeze the inner thighs and buttocks together tightly
  • D. Stop the urine stream midflow once a week to check the muscles

The correct answer is A (Draw the muscles up and in as if holding back gas, while breathing normally): A gentle lift and squeeze around the vagina and anus, as if holding in gas, targets the pelvic floor while normal breathing prevents bearing down. Abdominal and thigh contractions are tempting because they feel like effort, but they signal substitution. Stopping the urine stream is used as a brief check of the muscles, but repeated practice can interfere with normal voiding.

Question 116

Musculoskeletal

A 55-year-old woman describes sudden, intense urges to void followed by large leaks before she reaches the toilet. She has no leakage with coughing, sneezing or lifting. She gets up three times each night to void, and her urine test is clear. Which type of incontinence does this history most strongly indicate?

  • A. Stress incontinence from reduced urethral support when abdominal pressure rises
  • B. Urgency incontinence related to an overactive bladder muscle
  • C. Overflow incontinence related to an obstructed or poorly emptying bladder outlet
  • D. Mixed incontinence with both stress and urge components present in the history

The correct answer is B (Urgency incontinence related to an overactive bladder muscle): Sudden strong urges with large-volume leakage and nocturia point to detrusor overactivity, which responds to bladder training and urge suppression strategies. Mixed incontinence is tempting because urge symptoms are common in it, but she denies any leakage with effort. Stress incontinence involves leakage with effort. Overflow typically presents with dribbling and incomplete emptying.

Question 117

Musculoskeletal

A 68-year-old woman reports a dragging sensation and a bulge at the vaginal opening that worsens by evening and after standing. She has no bowel symptoms. On examination, the anterior vaginal wall descends to the introitus on straining. Which condition does this finding most likely describe?

  • A. Cystocele, a descent of the bladder into the front vaginal wall
  • B. Rectocele, a bulge of the rectum into the lower posterior vaginal wall
  • C. Enterocele, a herniation of small bowel into the upper posterior vaginal wall
  • D. Uterine prolapse, with the cervix descending toward the vaginal opening on straining

The correct answer is A (Cystocele, a descent of the bladder into the front vaginal wall): A bulge on the anterior wall points to the bladder, called a cystocele. Symptoms worsen with gravity and prolonged standing, and improve when lying down. Uterine prolapse is tempting because it also causes a dragging sensation, but the examination describes the anterior wall descending. A rectocele involves the posterior wall near the perineum, and an enterocele sits at the apex.

Question 118

Musculoskeletal

A 60-year-old woman with a mild symptomatic prolapse works in a nursing home and lifts residents several times daily. She also has chronic constipation from a low fibre diet and strains at the toilet. Which advice is most likely to reduce progression of her pelvic organ support problem?

  • A. Perform pelvic floor contractions before and during each resident lift using a quick brace
  • B. Wear a firm abdominal binder during lifting shifts to lessen pressure on the pelvic floor
  • C. Increase dietary fibre and fluids to keep stools soft and avoid straining during bowel movements
  • D. Change duties to mostly standing work, which reduces the repeated lifting loads on the pelvis

The correct answer is C (Increase dietary fibre and fluids to keep stools soft and avoid straining during bowel movements): Repeated straining raises intra-abdominal pressure over a weakened support system, so bowel management is central. Pelvic floor bracing during lifts is tempting and helpful, but her daily toilet straining keeps loading the same tissues. Proper lifting technique with an exhale on effort also helps. A binder can push pressure downward, and prolonged standing worsens symptoms.

Question 119

Musculoskeletal

A 29-year-old woman is eight weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal birth with a second degree tear that has healed well. She asks when and how she can safely begin pelvic floor exercises and what she should expect from them. Which guidance is most appropriate for her at this point?

  • A. Wait until she has stopped breastfeeding and periods return before any pelvic floor training
  • B. Begin with maximal contractions held ten seconds, repeated fifteen times, twice daily
  • C. Begin core stabilization with planks and sit-ups, adding pelvic floor work once symptom free
  • D. Begin gentle contractions and progress gradually as comfort, healing and perineal tissue tolerance allow

The correct answer is D (Begin gentle contractions and progress gradually as comfort, healing and perineal tissue tolerance allow): Gentle early activation promotes circulation and recovery, and training is progressed as healing and comfort permit. Delaying until breastfeeding ends is tempting because it sounds cautious, but it has no basis. High-volume maximal contractions fatigue the muscles and are not where training starts. Planks and sit-ups raise intra-abdominal pressure and do not train the pelvic floor.

Question 120

Musculoskeletal

A 33-year-old woman has had three months of deep pelvic ache, painful intercourse and tender pelvic floor muscles. At today's visit she reports a new fever, malodorous vaginal discharge and sharp lower abdominal pain, and she guards when her abdomen is touched. What is the most appropriate action?

  • A. Refer her urgently for medical assessment of a possible pelvic infection before any hands-on treatment
  • B. Start a graded relaxation and breathing program and review her again in a few days
  • C. Book a family doctor pelvic exam within the next week and hold treatment
  • D. Complete a full lumbopelvic orthopedic screen today and decide on referral from the results

The correct answer is A (Refer her urgently for medical assessment of a possible pelvic infection before any hands-on treatment): Fever, odorous discharge and guarding suggest a possible pelvic inflammatory process that needs same-day medical evaluation. Booking a doctor visit within the week is tempting because referral is the right idea, but it is too slow for possible infection. Further screening or relaxation work treats a muscular problem and delays care. Physiotherapy for myofascial pain resumes once infection is excluded.

Question 121

Musculoskeletal

A 9-year-old boy has had four days of limp, a temperature of 38.9 C and focal tenderness over the distal femur after a minor scrape on his leg. He refuses to bear weight, and range of motion is limited by pain. What should the physiotherapist do first?

  • A. Arrange urgent medical assessment because bone infection is suspected
  • B. Arrange a same-week pediatric appointment and advise rest from running in the meantime
  • C. Begin gentle hip and knee mobility work to relieve guarding and review his progress tomorrow
  • D. Treat it as a soft tissue injury with rest, ice and compression, reviewing in three days

The correct answer is A (Arrange urgent medical assessment because bone infection is suspected): Fever, focal bone tenderness and refusal to weight bear in a child suggest acute osteomyelitis, which needs urgent investigation and antibiotics to protect bone and growth. A same-week appointment is tempting because medical referral is correct, but a delay of days risks spread and permanent damage. Treating the problem as a soft tissue injury misses the infection. Referral comes before any rehabilitation plan.

Question 122

Musculoskeletal

A 72-year-old man with a knee replacement from last month presents with a hot, red, swollen knee, chills and severe pain on any movement. The wound has some drainage, and his pulse is 102 beats per minute. What is the most appropriate response from the treating physiotherapist?

  • A. Advise him to see his family doctor within the week and hold exercise until then
  • B. Phone the surgeon's office for advice later today and continue a gentle ankle pump program
  • C. Reduce weight bearing, apply ice and elevation and review him again in two days
  • D. Stop treatment and send him urgently to hospital to assess for a postoperative joint infection

The correct answer is D (Stop treatment and send him urgently to hospital to assess for a postoperative joint infection): A hot swollen joint with chills, drainage and a fast pulse after surgery is septic arthritis or prosthetic infection until proved otherwise. This is an emergency because joint destruction and sepsis can follow. Contacting the surgeon later today or seeing a family doctor within the week is tempting because both involve medical input, but each delays care by hours or days. Ice and elevation treat swelling and miss the infection.

Question 123

Musculoskeletal

A 48-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has morning stiffness lasting ninety minutes and swollen metacarpophalangeal joints. During a flare she asks how she should use her hands for housework and cooking. Which advice best matches the principles of joint protection for her hands?

  • A. Use a firm grip on thick-handled tools to maintain hand and finger strength during flares
  • B. Use larger joints and spread the load, such as carrying items on the forearms
  • C. Carry items in the hands with the fingers flexed to keep the finger joints moving
  • D. Wear rigid resting splints all day during a flare and avoid active finger movement

The correct answer is B (Use larger joints and spread the load, such as carrying items on the forearms): Joint protection means using the strongest joints, avoiding sustained grips and distributing load to reduce deforming forces on inflamed finger joints. Thick handles and firm grips seem protective, but sustained gripping still stresses the finger joints and encourages ulnar drift. Splinting all day stiffens joints, while carrying with the fingers flexed adds load. Pacing and adaptive equipment complete the approach.

Question 124

Musculoskeletal

A 24-year-old man reports three months of lower back stiffness that is worst in the early morning, eases with activity and improves little with rest. He wakes in the second half of the night with the pain. There was no injury. Which condition does this pattern most suggest?

  • A. A lumbar muscle strain from recent heavy lifting that settles with relative rest
  • B. Axial spondyloarthritis, an inflammatory condition of the spine and pelvis
  • C. A lumbar disc herniation with leg pain that worsens on sitting
  • D. Early facet joint osteoarthritis causing stiffness after inactivity

The correct answer is B (Axial spondyloarthritis, an inflammatory condition of the spine and pelvis): Inflammatory back pain begins before age 40, comes on gradually, improves with exercise but not rest, and wakes people in the second half of the night. This pattern prompts referral for further testing. Facet joint osteoarthritis also causes stiffness after inactivity, which makes it tempting, but it is unusual at his age and does not wake him at night. Mechanical strain and disc problems usually worsen with activity and ease with rest.

Question 125

Musculoskeletal

A 58-year-old man wakes with an intensely painful, red, warm and swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. He drank heavily the night before, takes a diuretic for blood pressure and has no fever. Even a bedsheet touching the toe is painful. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  • A. Septic arthritis of the great toe following a skin infection
  • B. Acute gout caused by urate crystals in the joint
  • C. Cellulitis of the forefoot spreading beyond the joint margins
  • D. Pseudogout from calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the first toe joint

The correct answer is B (Acute gout caused by urate crystals in the joint): Sudden, severe monoarticular pain at the first MTP joint after alcohol or rich food, with diuretic use as a risk factor, is the classic picture of gout. Pseudogout and infection are tempting because they also produce a hot red joint, but the absence of fever, the toe location and the triggers favour gout. Infection must still be considered if fever or systemic illness appears.

Question 126

Musculoskeletal

A 74-year-old woman on long-term oral steroids develops sudden mid-back pain after bending to pick up a bag. There was no fall. She has marked point tenderness over T11 and cannot lie flat. Which condition should the physiotherapist suspect before choosing any treatment?

  • A. Thoracic disc herniation with band-like trunk pain after sudden bending and loading
  • B. Thoracic muscle strain from lifting the bag with an awkward twist
  • C. Costovertebral joint dysfunction with referred rib pain after sudden flexion under load
  • D. Vertebral compression fracture caused by weakened bone under only a minor load

The correct answer is D (Vertebral compression fracture caused by weakened bone under only a minor load): Long-term steroid use, age and sudden pain with focal spinal tenderness after a minor load suggest an osteoporotic compression fracture, and she needs medical imaging before any manual therapy or loading. A muscle strain, costovertebral problem or disc herniation is tempting after a bending injury, but none of them explains marked point tenderness over one vertebra and inability to lie flat in a steroid-treated patient.

Question 127

Musculoskeletal

A 22-year-old basketball player falls on an outstretched hand. Wrist radiographs at the emergency department appear normal, but he has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain with axial loading of the thumb. He wants to return to play this weekend. What is the best next step?

  • A. Treat it as a wrist sprain with a compression wrap and graded strengthening
  • B. Arrange repeat radiographs in one month and allow non-contact activities in the meantime
  • C. Immobilize the wrist in a cast and allow return to play when he can grip comfortably
  • D. Immobilize the wrist and thumb and arrange repeat or advanced imaging

The correct answer is D (Immobilize the wrist and thumb and arrange repeat or advanced imaging): Snuffbox tenderness and pain on axial thumb loading after a fall suggest a scaphoid fracture, which can be invisible on initial films and carries a risk of nonunion and avascular necrosis. Immobilization plus repeat or advanced imaging is standard. Casting is tempting because it protects the wrist, but clearing him to play without imaging misses the diagnosis. Repeat films in a month leave the wrist unprotected, and a sprain plan loads a possible fracture.

Question 128

Musculoskeletal

A 46-year-old man with long-standing low back pain reports new numbness around the groin and inner thighs, difficulty starting urination and weakness in both legs that began yesterday. He walks with a wide, unsteady gait and says the symptoms are getting worse each hour. Which action should the physiotherapist take at this visit?

  • A. Refer him to a spine surgery clinic for a routine assessment within the next week
  • B. Arrange an urgent outpatient MRI and advise him to avoid bending until the results return
  • C. Arrange emergency transfer to hospital for urgent imaging and surgical review
  • D. Send him to a family doctor for a same-day neurological examination before deciding on transfer

The correct answer is C (Arrange emergency transfer to hospital for urgent imaging and surgical review): Saddle sensory loss, urinary difficulty and bilateral weakness that worsen by the hour are red flags for cauda equina compression, a surgical emergency in which delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction. An outpatient MRI, a family doctor visit or a clinic appointment is tempting because each moves toward diagnosis, but each adds delay. Treatment should not be started in the clinic.

Question 129

Musculoskeletal

A 63-year-old man with a past history of prostate cancer reports constant mid-back pain that is worse at night, unrelated to movement, and has not eased with rest. He has lost 6 kg over two months without trying. What is the most appropriate response?

  • A. Refer for prompt medical investigation for possible metastatic disease given his night pain
  • B. Arrange a routine physician review within about a month and continue his home exercises
  • C. Teach a thoracic extension and mobility program and reassess his night pain in two weeks
  • D. Complete lower limb neurological testing and refer if any deficit is found

The correct answer is A (Refer for prompt medical investigation for possible metastatic disease given his night pain): Cancer history, unexplained weight loss and constant night pain unrelated to movement are strong red flags for spinal metastasis. Prompt medical work-up is needed before any mechanical treatment. A neurological screen is part of the assessment, which makes that option tempting, but normal findings do not remove the red flags. A routine review in a month or a trial of exercise could delay diagnosis or lead to a pathological fracture.

Question 130

Musculoskeletal

A 19-year-old rugby player has a tibial fracture treated with a cast six hours ago. He now has severe pain out of proportion to the injury, a tense calf, and pain when the toes are passively extended. His foot pulses are still present. What should be done?

  • A. Call for emergency medical review of possible compartment syndrome
  • B. Elevate the leg to heart level and monitor his pain over the next two hours
  • C. Apply ice over the cast and recheck him in one hour
  • D. Give the prescribed analgesia and recheck the leg after one hour for any change
