The correct answer is A (Call for emergency medical review of possible compartment syndrome): Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome, and pulses can remain present until tissue damage is advanced. Urgent decompression can save the limb. Elevation and analgesia are common first measures and feel reasonable, but waiting an hour or two masks the evolving problem. Ice over the cast does not relieve pressure.

Question 131

Musculoskeletal

A 59-year-old woman is five days after a total hip replacement. She develops a swollen, warm, tender left calf and mild shortness of breath, with a pulse of 98 beats per minute. A gait training session is booked for this morning. Which action is most appropriate before continuing with that planned session?

  • A. Fit a compression stocking and begin gait practice, rechecking the calf at the next visit
  • B. Measure calf girth and proceed if the difference is under 2 cm
  • C. Hold treatment and seek urgent medical assessment for possible thrombosis
  • D. Check pulse oximetry first and proceed with treatment if oxygen saturation is normal

The correct answer is C (Hold treatment and seek urgent medical assessment for possible thrombosis): Calf swelling, warmth and tenderness after major surgery suggest deep vein thrombosis, and new breathlessness with a fast pulse raises concern about pulmonary embolism. Checking girth or oxygen saturation is tempting because both are objective measures, but neither can exclude a clot. A compression stocking with gait practice could dislodge a clot. Urgent medical evaluation is required.

Question 132

Musculoskeletal

A 41-year-old woman has sudden severe neck pain with a new headache unlike any she has had. She also reports dizziness, difficulty swallowing and a drooping right eyelid. A colleague suggests high-velocity cervical manipulation to relieve the pain. What is the best course of action?

  • A. Use gentle low-grade mobilization of the upper cervical segments and monitor symptoms
  • B. Perform a vertebral artery screen with sustained rotation before choosing a treatment
  • C. Avoid manipulation and arrange emergency assessment for possible cervical arterial injury
  • D. Arrange a same-week medical review and give cervical soft tissue care meanwhile

The correct answer is C (Avoid manipulation and arrange emergency assessment for possible cervical arterial injury): Severe new neck pain and an unusual headache with dizziness, difficulty swallowing and ptosis are warning signs of a cervical artery dissection. A same-week review is tempting because referral is correct, but this needs emergency care. Manipulation, gentle mobilization or provocative testing could worsen the injury or cause stroke.

Question 133

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist plans joint mobilization for a 66-year-old patient with shoulder pain. The patient mentions that he takes an anticoagulant and has an unexplained bruise over the upper arm. Which consideration should guide the approach to manual treatment for this patient?

  • A. Use standard techniques and add a note about the bruise to the chart
  • B. Ask the patient to stop the anticoagulant for two days before manual treatment starts
  • C. Check clotting results and use gentler techniques with close skin monitoring
  • D. Proceed with low-grade joint mobilization after applying ice to the bruised upper arm

The correct answer is C (Check clotting results and use gentler techniques with close skin monitoring): Anticoagulants increase bleeding and bruising risk, so techniques are modified and the medical record or physician is consulted if the result is out of range. Low-grade mobilization is tempting because it is gentler, but ice does not change the bleeding risk. Forceful work or friction over a bruise may cause hematoma. Skin monitoring catches problems early.

Question 134

Musculoskeletal

A 27-year-old dancer with generalized joint laxity and a Beighton score of 8 has shoulder pain with a feeling of instability. A colleague suggests end-range joint mobilization to improve her movement. What is the most appropriate approach for this dancer?

  • A. Prioritize stabilizing exercises and avoid end-range stretching of the joint to protect lax tissues
  • B. Use grade IV end-range mobilization to restore the full shoulder motion the dancer lacks
  • C. Stretch the posterior shoulder capsule and add scapular taping to relieve her tightness
  • D. Prescribe a rigid brace for dance and training and defer strengthening until pain settles

The correct answer is A (Prioritize stabilizing exercises and avoid end-range stretching of the joint to protect lax tissues): A hypermobile joint lacks passive stability, so treatment builds dynamic control through muscle strengthening and motor control. Capsular stretching and end-range mobilization are tempting because they treat tightness, but the feeling of tightness in a hypermobile dancer is protective muscle guarding and not true capsular shortening. They increase laxity. A rigid brace with deferred exercise weakens the muscles she needs.

Question 135

Musculoskeletal

A 76-year-old woman with severe osteoporosis has a stiff thoracic spine and mild kyphosis. She wants help with her posture and has asked about hands-on treatment because she finds it relaxing. Which technique is safest for the thoracic region of this particular patient?

  • A. Moderate-grade mobilization of thoracic segments combined with deep breathing and rib springing
  • B. Thoracic extension over a firm foam roller with body weight pressing on the kyphotic segments
  • C. Strong rib springing in side-lying to improve chest wall mobility and breathing capacity
  • D. Low-grade, pain-free mobilization combined with active extension exercises

The correct answer is D (Low-grade, pain-free mobilization combined with active extension exercises): Low-grade gentle techniques and active exercises lower fracture risk while improving mobility. Moderate-grade mobilization or a roller feels like a mild step up, but any concentrated pressure on osteoporotic vertebrae and ribs can cause a fracture, as can thrusts. Education on safe loading supports the program.

Question 136

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist plans therapeutic ultrasound for a 35-year-old man with chronic tendinopathy at the elbow. He mentions that he is receiving treatment for a malignant tumour in the muscle a few centimetres above the elbow, and he asks to continue his usual elbow program today. Which decision is correct for this treatment session?

  • A. Avoid ultrasound over or near the malignancy site and nearby tissue
  • B. Use pulsed ultrasound at low intensity over the elbow tendon
  • C. Treat the tendon but keep the sound head moving and avoid the tumour itself
  • D. Use continuous ultrasound at a lower intensity to limit heating of the nearby tumour

The correct answer is A (Avoid ultrasound over or near the malignancy site and nearby tissue): Ultrasound is avoided over and near active malignancy because heating and cavitation may stimulate cell growth or spread, and a tumour a few centimetres from the planned field means nearby tissue would be treated. Lower intensity, pulsed mode or avoiding just the tumour itself are tempting adjustments, but none removes the exposure. Alternative treatments are chosen.

Question 137

Musculoskeletal

A 44-year-old woman has patellar tendon pain and a metal plate in her distal femur from an old fracture. Her physiotherapist wants to use pulsed therapeutic ultrasound near the knee. Which statement best guides safe use of the modality in this situation?

  • A. Treat the tendon but keep the sound head at least ten centimetres from the metal plate
  • B. Metal alone is not a contraindication, but keep the head moving throughout
  • C. Reduce the intensity by half whenever the beam is over the plate
  • D. Apply a thicker layer of gel and hold the head still over the knee

The correct answer is B (Metal alone is not a contraindication, but keep the head moving throughout): Metal implants are generally not a contraindication for ultrasound because it does not heat metal significantly, but a stationary head can cause local overheating, so the head should keep moving and the patient reports any discomfort. Avoiding the limb or keeping a set distance from the plate is tempting because it sounds cautious, but it is unnecessary. Pulsed mode is acceptable.

Question 138

Musculoskeletal

A clinic is preparing to use TENS for a 57-year-old man with chronic low back pain. He has a demand cardiac pacemaker and asks to start treatment this week. Which instruction best reflects safe practice for this patient when planning electrical stimulation?

  • A. Use interferential current rather than TENS to avoid the chest region
  • B. Place electrodes on the low back and treat at usual settings today
  • C. Keep electrodes away from the chest and the device, and seek medical clearance
  • D. Use a low frequency setting with the electrodes close to the device

The correct answer is C (Keep electrodes away from the chest and the device, and seek medical clearance): TENS can interfere with a demand pacemaker, so electrodes are kept away from the chest and the device, and many clinicians seek clearance from the cardiology team. Treating the back at usual settings is tempting because the back is far from the chest, but it skips the clearance step. Switching to interferential current does not remove the interference risk.

Question 139

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist is choosing sites for transcutaneous electrical stimulation for a 50-year-old patient with neck pain. A student asks which placement the clinician should avoid for safety reasons, since the neck contains several sensitive structures. Which placement should be avoided during treatment of the neck?

  • A. Across the back of the neck over the spinous processes at midline
  • B. Over a healed posterior neck scar where sensation is normal after earlier surgery
  • C. Over the upper trapezius muscles on both sides of the neck base
  • D. Across the front of the neck over the carotid sinus

The correct answer is D (Across the front of the neck over the carotid sinus): Stimulation over the carotid sinus can trigger a sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure, so the anterior neck is avoided. Posterior sites, including midline and healed scars with normal sensation, are acceptable when skin is intact. The scar option is tempting because scars sometimes need caution, but normal sensation makes it acceptable. Posterior and shoulder sites are suitable for neck pain.

Question 140

Musculoskeletal

A 69-year-old woman with diabetic neuropathy and reduced foot sensation asks to use a hot pack at home for ankle stiffness. She lives alone and often falls asleep in her chair. What is the safest advice about heat use for her?

  • A. Apply a heated wheat bag wrapped in a towel while she sits
  • B. Use an electric heating pad on its lowest setting through the evening while she reads
  • C. Use a paraffin wax bath at home because wax heat is gentle and surrounds the joint
  • D. Avoid heat over numb skin, or use mild warmth with frequent skin checks

The correct answer is D (Avoid heat over numb skin, or use mild warmth with frequent skin checks): Reduced sensation means she cannot sense a burn, so heat is avoided or kept mild with a barrier and frequent checks by sight. A towel-wrapped pack, wax or a low setting feels safer, but each still relies on feeling that she lacks, and long exposure or dozing off adds risk. Active movement may be a safer first choice.

Question 141

Musculoskeletal

A clinic uses continuous shortwave diathermy on a 38-year-old woman for hip pain. The physiotherapist must screen the patient before starting the treatment, and she has several pieces of jewellery on. Which screening step is correct before applying this modality?

  • A. Leave small metal jewellery in place and cover it with a dry towel layer
  • B. Confirm no pregnancy or implanted device, then treat with the jewellery taped flat to skin
  • C. Remove jewellery and check for pregnancy, then treat over a plastic-backed dressing
  • D. Remove metal jewellery and confirm no pregnancy or implanted device

The correct answer is D (Remove metal jewellery and confirm no pregnancy or implanted device): Shortwave diathermy heats tissues and can heat metal, affect fetuses and disturb implanted devices, so screening is required. Confirming pregnancy and device status is half the task, which makes the taped jewellery option tempting, but metal still heats. Plastic-backed dressings trap heat and risk burns, and towels do not insulate metal from the field.

Question 142

Musculoskeletal

A physiotherapist is about to use low-level laser therapy on a patient's shoulder. A student observing asks about safety measures in the treatment room. Which safety measure is required for the therapist, the patient and any observer present during the treatment?

  • A. Wear tinted safety glasses rated for ultraviolet light, as used with other modalities
  • B. Wear protective eyewear rated for the wavelength of the laser
  • C. Require eyewear for the therapist, who holds the probe, while the patient looks away
  • D. Close the door, post a warning sign and keep the beam pointed away from other people

The correct answer is B (Wear protective eyewear rated for the wavelength of the laser): Laser light can damage the retina, so the patient, therapist and others wear eyewear rated for the specific wavelength. Warning signs and beam control are tempting because they are part of laser safety, but they do not protect eyes from reflections. Ultraviolet or ordinary tinted glasses are not rated for the laser, and protecting just the therapist leaves others exposed.

Question 143

Musculoskeletal

A 31-year-old man has quadriceps weakness after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. His physiotherapist adds neuromuscular electrical stimulation to his strengthening program and wants the sessions to build force in the muscle. Which setting approach best supports strengthening of the muscle during these sessions?

  • A. Set the intensity at a visible twitch with a long rest between contractions
  • B. Use sensory-level conventional current tuned for comfort and pain relief during exercise
  • C. Use pulsed current for a strong, tolerable contraction with rest between bursts
  • D. Use a very low pulse rate of two pulses per second to build tetanic force

The correct answer is C (Use pulsed current for a strong, tolerable contraction with rest between bursts): Strengthening needs a strong, comfortable contraction with duty cycles that allow rest and avoid fatigue. A twitch-level intensity or a comfort-level current is tempting because it is gentle and well tolerated, but it does not produce enough force to train the muscle. Very low pulse rates give twitches rather than a fused contraction.

Question 144

Musculoskeletal

Before applying electrical stimulation to a patient's lower leg, the physiotherapist notices a scabbed, weeping area directly under the planned electrode site. The patient is keen for the treatment to go ahead today and says the area is not painful. What is the appropriate action?

  • A. Cover the wound with an occlusive dressing and place the electrode on top of the dressing
  • B. Place the electrode over the scab after cleaning with saline and use the lowest intensity
  • C. Halve the usual current and place the electrode at the edge of the scab
  • D. Move the electrode to intact skin away from the broken area

The correct answer is D (Move the electrode to intact skin away from the broken area): Broken skin has low resistance and concentrates current, which can cause burns. Electrodes are placed on healthy skin with normal sensation. Covering the wound, cleaning it or lowering the current feels cautious, but the electrode still sits on or beside compromised skin.

Question 145

Musculoskeletal

A 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks of pregnancy has pain over the pubic symphysis and sacroiliac joints with walking, turning in bed and climbing stairs. Neurological screening is normal, and she wants to stay active at her job as a cashier. Which advice best fits current physiotherapy care for her?

  • A. Rely on a lumbar brace at work and avoid stairs until delivery
  • B. Use a pelvic support belt, pace activities and avoid asymmetric loading
  • C. Add wide-stance squats and deep hip abduction stretches to loosen the stiff pelvic joints
  • D. Stop weight-bearing activity at work and use crutches for the remainder of the pregnancy

The correct answer is B (Use a pelvic support belt, pace activities and avoid asymmetric loading): Pelvic girdle pain responds to stabilizing exercise, supports, pacing and avoiding asymmetric loads such as single-leg standing. A lumbar brace and stair avoidance sound protective, but they limit activity without addressing the pelvic joints. Wide stretches add shear to lax joints, and prolonged activity restriction leads to deconditioning.

Question 146

Musculoskeletal

A 34-year-old woman is four months postpartum with a 3 cm midline gap above the umbilicus that domes when she sits up from lying. She has no pain and wants to return to running soon. Which exercise approach is most appropriate to start with at this stage of her recovery?

  • A. Train deep abdominal activation and avoid exercises that dome the midline
  • B. Begin with heavy double leg lowering to load the abdominal wall
  • C. Wear a compression binder during exercise and begin with graded planks
  • D. Begin planks and crunch exercises to close the gap between the abdominal muscles quickly

The correct answer is A (Train deep abdominal activation and avoid exercises that dome the midline): Doming indicates too much pressure on the linea alba, so exercise starts with deep transversus abdominis control and breath coordination. Planks, crunches and heavy leg work are tempting because they strengthen the core, but they raise pressure and dome the midline. A binder gives support but does not retrain the muscles. Progressing loads while keeping the midline flat is the goal.

Question 147

Musculoskeletal

A 43-year-old woman has had widespread pain for eight months, along with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and poor concentration. Blood tests and imaging are normal, and she asks what treatment has the best evidence for long-term improvement. Which approach should the physiotherapist recommend?

  • A. Heavy resistance training progressed rapidly over the first month
  • B. Rest breaks and avoidance of exertion on painful days
  • C. Graded aerobic exercise with education and activity pacing
  • D. Heat, massage and passive joint work each week

The correct answer is C (Graded aerobic exercise with education and activity pacing): Graded aerobic activity, education and pacing improve pain and function in fibromyalgia. Rest breaks are tempting because pacing is part of the plan, but avoiding exertion leads to deconditioning. Rapid heavy resistance work provokes flares. Passive care gives short-term relief.

Question 148

Musculoskeletal

A 20-year-old female distance runner has rapidly increased her weekly mileage over the past month. She reports focal pain over the shin that worsens with running and is now present at night. Hopping on the leg reproduces the pain, and she has irregular menstrual cycles. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  • A. Tibial stress fracture from repetitive loading of the shin bone
  • B. Medial tibial stress syndrome with a diffuse band of pain
  • C. Tibialis posterior tendinopathy with pain behind the ankle
  • D. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome with burning tightness that settles within minutes of stopping

The correct answer is A (Tibial stress fracture from repetitive loading of the shin bone): Focal bone tenderness, night pain and pain with hopping after a training increase point to a stress fracture. Medial tibial stress syndrome is tempting because it is the common shin pain in runners, but it tends to be diffuse and does not wake the patient. Compartment syndrome settles with rest. Female athlete triad should be considered.

Question 149

Musculoskeletal

A 58-year-old woman, eight months after a transradial amputation, has sharp, electric pain at the end of the residual limb when the socket presses on it. Tapping the distal scar reproduces a shooting sensation. Which problem does this most likely indicate?

  • A. Phantom limb pain from central reorganization in the nervous system
  • B. A symptomatic neuroma forming at the cut end of a divided nerve
  • C. Heterotopic bone forming within the muscle of the stump
  • D. Socket pressure injury at the distal end causing deep tissue damage

The correct answer is B (A symptomatic neuroma forming at the cut end of a divided nerve): Pain provoked by pressure with a positive Tinel-type response at the distal scar points to a neuroma, a tangle of regenerating nerve fibres. Socket pressure injury is tempting because the socket presses the area, but tapping the scar would not produce a shooting sensation. Phantom pain is felt in the missing part, not triggered by local tapping. Socket modification and desensitization can help.

Question 150

Musculoskeletal

A 4-year-old girl has a limp, a fever of 39.2 C and refuses to move her right hip, which she holds flexed and slightly abducted. Any attempt at passive rotation causes crying. She was well three days ago. What is the most urgent concern?

  • A. Transient synovitis, usually managed with rest at home
  • B. Perthes disease needing orthopedic follow-up within the next few weeks
  • C. Septic arthritis of the hip needing emergency referral to hospital
  • D. Juvenile arthritis presenting in a single hip joint

The correct answer is C (Septic arthritis of the hip needing emergency referral to hospital): A feverish child who will not bear weight and guards the hip against all rotation has septic arthritis until proven otherwise, because delay can destroy the joint. Transient synovitis is tempting because it is the common cause of a limping child, but it is a diagnosis made after infection is excluded. Referral to emergency care takes priority.

Question 151

Musculoskeletal

A 24-year-old soccer player in Halifax rolled her ankle two hours ago. She can take four steps in the clinic, has no bony tenderness at the malleoli or base of the fifth metatarsal, but has marked lateral swelling and bruising. What is the most appropriate decision about radiography?

  • A. No radiograph is needed because the Ottawa ankle rules are negative, as she walked four steps
  • B. Order an ankle series if swelling has not settled after about five days of rest
  • C. Order a foot series to look for an avulsion fracture at the fifth metatarsal base
  • D. Arrange ultrasound of the lateral ligaments to grade the sprain before deciding on films

The correct answer is A (No radiograph is needed because the Ottawa ankle rules are negative, as she walked four steps): The Ottawa ankle rules call for films only with bony tenderness at the malleoli or the midfoot bases, or inability to take four steps. She meets neither criterion, so a clinically important fracture is very unlikely. Waiting five days to image applies the rule at the wrong time, and a foot series targets a site with no tenderness. Ligament ultrasound does not change fracture management, and swelling and bruising do not predict fracture.

Question 152

Musculoskeletal

A 19-year-old hockey player felt a pop and immediate knee swelling after a pivot. At 48 hours the physiotherapist wants the most sensitive test for an anterior cruciate ligament tear. The knee is moderately effused and hamstring guarding is mild. Which test should be performed first?

  • A. Pivot shift test moving the knee from extension into flexion with valgus and internal rotation applied
  • B. Lachman test with the knee in about 20 to 30 degrees of flexion
  • C. Anterior drawer test with the knee flexed to 90 degrees and the foot stabilized
  • D. Posterior drawer test with the knee flexed to 90 degrees to compare tibial position

The correct answer is B (Lachman test with the knee in about 20 to 30 degrees of flexion): The Lachman test is the most sensitive clinical test for acute ACL rupture because it is performed near extension, where effusion and hamstring guarding interfere least. The anterior drawer at 90 degrees is tempting but is less sensitive in an effused knee. The pivot shift is highly specific but is usually limited by guarding and pain in the acute phase, and the posterior drawer tests a different ligament.

Question 153

Musculoskeletal

A 52-year-old electrician reports pain lifting his right arm overhead. Passive elevation is full and painless. Active abduction is painful between 60 and 120 degrees, resisted external rotation is weak and painful, and the drop arm test is negative. Which structure is most likely involved?

  • A. Rotator cuff tendinopathy affecting the infraspinatus and supraspinatus tendons
  • B. C5 radiculopathy with weakness of shoulder abduction and external rotation
  • C. Acromioclavicular joint sprain with focal joint tenderness and a painful arc on elevation
  • D. Subscapularis tendinopathy with pain on resisted internal rotation

The correct answer is A (Rotator cuff tendinopathy affecting the infraspinatus and supraspinatus tendons): Painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees with weak, painful resisted external rotation and full passive motion points to rotator cuff tendinopathy. An acromioclavicular sprain is tempting because it also causes an arc, but it brings focal joint tenderness and no external rotation weakness. Radiculopathy would bring neck or dermatomal findings, and subscapularis tendinopathy shows up on resisted internal rotation. A frozen shoulder or complete tear does not fit full passive range and a negative drop arm test.

Question 154

Musculoskeletal

A 68-year-old retired teacher has groin pain and stiffness after sitting. Examination of her left hip shows a loss of range in a typical capsular pattern. Which sequence of motion loss describes the hip capsular pattern? She has no other joint symptoms and has not tried any treatment yet.

  • A. External rotation, then abduction, then internal rotation, with external rotation lost first
  • B. Flexion, then abduction, then internal rotation, with internal rotation most limited
  • C. Abduction and external rotation, with full flexion and internal rotation preserved
  • D. Flexion lost more than extension, with rotation and abduction relatively preserved

The correct answer is B (Flexion, then abduction, then internal rotation, with internal rotation most limited): The hip capsular pattern is gross limitation of flexion, abduction and internal rotation, with internal rotation usually the most restricted early, and it supports osteoarthritis in this presentation. The shoulder pattern is tempting because it also lists rotation and abduction, but it belongs to the glenohumeral joint. The knee pattern concerns flexion and extension, and preserved flexion with internal rotation would not suggest a hip capsular problem.

Question 155

Musculoskeletal

A 45-year-old warehouse worker in Winnipeg has severe low back pain with bilateral leg pain for three days. Today he notes numbness around his buttocks and difficulty starting urination. Ankle reflexes are reduced bilaterally. What is the most appropriate action?

  • A. Arrange an urgent same-day MRI through the family physician and review the result tomorrow
  • B. Arrange emergency department transfer for urgent imaging and surgical assessment
  • C. Refer to a spine surgeon for a non-urgent consultation after a trial of rest and analgesics
  • D. Begin a McKenzie extension program and recheck his bladder symptoms at the next visit

The correct answer is B (Arrange emergency department transfer for urgent imaging and surgical assessment): Saddle numbness, new difficulty starting urination and reduced ankle reflexes on both sides suggest cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency in which outcome depends on rapid decompression. An urgent MRI is tempting because it is the right test, but sending it through the family physician and waiting a day loses critical time. A non-urgent surgical referral and an exercise trial also delay decompression while the compression continues.

Question 156

Musculoskeletal

A 41-year-old recreational runner has two months of morning stiffness and pain two to six centimetres above the heel insertion. Ultrasound shows mid-portion thickening without a tear. Which management is best supported to start the rehabilitation program? He has had no previous back problems.

  • A. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy as the first-line treatment before any loading program is started
  • B. Progressive heavy slow calf raise loading, with pain kept tolerable
  • C. Therapeutic ultrasound with deep transverse friction massage three times weekly for four weeks
  • D. Walking boot with heel lifts for six weeks, then a gradual return to calf strengthening

The correct answer is B (Progressive heavy slow calf raise loading, with pain kept tolerable): Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy responds best to progressive tendon loading such as heavy slow resistance calf work, with pain kept at a tolerable level. Shockwave therapy is tempting because it has some support, but it is used as an adjunct to a loading program rather than before one. Passive modalities do little to rebuild tendon capacity, and a boot reduces load and lets the tendon weaken further.

Question 157

Musculoskeletal

On postoperative day one after a cemented total knee arthroplasty, a 70-year-old man has pain 5 out of 10, knee flexion of 40 degrees and a lag of 10 degrees on straight leg raise. The surgeon allowed weight bearing as tolerated. What is the best priority?

  • A. Continuous passive motion machine for several hours daily, with walking added once flexion reaches ninety degrees
  • B. Manipulation under anesthesia within the first week to restore knee flexion before scar tissue forms firmly
  • C. Isometric quadriceps sets in bed, with walking held until the straight leg raise lag has resolved
  • D. Early mobilization with gait training, quadriceps activation and gradual knee motion

The correct answer is D (Early mobilization with gait training, quadriceps activation and gradual knee motion): Early mobilization, quadriceps activation and gradual range gains are standard after total knee arthroplasty and lower the risk of stiffness, weakness and complications. A continuous passive motion machine is tempting as an early range tool, but it does not replace active exercise and walking, which he is cleared to do. Manipulation under anesthesia is reserved for stiffness that persists for weeks, and holding walking until the lag resolves lets deconditioning set in.

Question 158

Musculoskeletal

A 38-year-old dental hygienist has lateral elbow pain provoked by gripping and wrist extension against resistance. There is no neck pain or sensory change. She wants to keep working. Which first-line advice best matches current evidence? She is otherwise healthy and wants to keep working.

  • A. Counterforce brace worn during gripping tasks, with exercise added once the pain has settled
  • B. Graded wrist extensor loading with activity modification, keeping pain tolerable
  • C. Wrist extensor stretching and ice after shifts, with gripping continued
  • D. Corticosteroid injection now for faster short-term relief, followed by a gradual return to gripping

The correct answer is B (Graded wrist extensor loading with activity modification, keeping pain tolerable): Lateral epicondylalgia is a tendinopathy, so graded loading of the wrist extensors with workload adjustment is first line. A counterforce brace is tempting because it eases symptoms during gripping, but waiting to start exercise delays the treatment that restores tendon capacity. Steroid injection gives brief relief but is linked to worse outcomes later, and stretching with ice leaves the aggravating load unchanged.

Question 159

Musculoskeletal

A 56-year-old cashier has night waking with numb thumb, index and middle fingers. Tinel's sign at the wrist is positive, thenar bulk is normal, and neck movements do not reproduce symptoms. Sensation over the thenar eminence is preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  • A. Median nerve compression at the wrist within the carpal tunnel itself
  • B. C6 radiculopathy with sensory loss in the thumb and index finger and a reduced biceps reflex
  • C. Median nerve entrapment in the forearm, known as pronator syndrome
  • D. C7 radiculopathy with middle finger numbness and weak triceps

The correct answer is A (Median nerve compression at the wrist within the carpal tunnel itself): Median distribution numbness with sparing of the thenar eminence, nocturnal symptoms and a positive Tinel's sign at the wrist fit carpal tunnel syndrome. The palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel, which explains preserved thenar sensation. C6 radiculopathy is tempting because it also involves the thumb, but it would be provoked by neck movement. Proximal forearm entrapment would reduce thenar sensation, and a C7 root problem would weaken the triceps.

Question 160

Musculoskeletal

A 22-year-old runner in Calgary has anterior knee pain on stairs and after prolonged sitting, with no effusion or instability. Squatting reproduces the pain. Which exercise program is best supported for this presentation? Consider both the evidence and the runner's goal of returning to training soon.

  • A. Combined hip and knee strengthening at tolerable load, with gradual return to running
  • B. Patellar taping and a knee brace for twelve weeks, with exercise added later
  • C. Iliotibial band stretching and foam rolling daily, with a graded return to running
  • D. Deep-range quadriceps strengthening with a return to running within two weeks

The correct answer is A (Combined hip and knee strengthening at tolerable load, with gradual return to running): Evidence supports combined hip and knee exercise for patellofemoral pain, introduced at a tolerable load with a gradual return to running. Deep-range quadriceps work is tempting because the quadriceps matter, but deep flexion often irritates the joint and a two-week return is rushed. Taping and bracing can ease pain but do not replace exercise, and stretching and rolling lack the strengthening that has the best support.

Question 161

Musculoskeletal

A 30-year-old nurse has a grade II lateral ankle sprain three days ago. Swelling is reducing and she can bear weight with pain 3 out of 10. She works twelve-hour shifts and wants to return quickly. Which approach best promotes recovery in this stage?

  • A. Walking boot for two weeks, then range of motion and strengthening in a fixed sequence
  • B. Early protected weight bearing with supervised movement and balance training
  • C. Compression and elevation with rest from weight bearing until swelling and pain have settled fully
  • D. Ice and ankle pumps, with balance work delayed until week six

The correct answer is B (Early protected weight bearing with supervised movement and balance training): A functional approach with protected weight bearing, early motion and balance training gives better results than immobilization for most grade II sprains. A short boot period is tempting because it protects the ligament, but she already bears weight comfortably and early movement speeds recovery. Resting until swelling clears prolongs disability, and holding balance work until week six leaves the ankle at risk of re-injury.

Question 162

Musculoskeletal

A 72-year-old woman with a recent bone density T-score of minus 3.0 and no fractures asks about exercise. She walks daily and has good balance. She enjoys swimming and abdominal crunches. Which prescription is most appropriate? She takes no medications and has no history of fractures.

  • A. Loaded forward trunk flexion exercises to strengthen the abdominal muscles and the trunk
  • B. Swimming as the main form of exercise to avoid loading the skeleton
  • C. Progressive resistance and balance training, avoiding loaded spinal flexion
  • D. Avoidance of resistance work because of her fracture risk

The correct answer is C (Progressive resistance and balance training, avoiding loaded spinal flexion): Resistance and balance training with weight bearing is advised, while loaded spinal flexion and twisting are avoided because they raise vertebral fracture risk. Swimming does not load the skeleton enough. Avoiding resistance work removes a key bone stimulus.

Question 163

Musculoskeletal

Six weeks after a wrist fracture treated in a cast, a 48-year-old man has burning pain out of proportion, swelling, colour change and sweating in the hand, spreading beyond any single nerve territory. Light touch causes pain. Radiographs show healed bone. Which condition is most consistent?

  • A. Complex regional pain syndrome type 1 affecting the hand and wrist
  • B. Low-grade infection under the cast causing swelling, colour change and pain in the hand
  • C. Acute carpal tunnel syndrome from cast pressure on the median nerve at the wrist
  • D. Post-immobilization stiffness with capsular tightness in the wrist and finger joints

The correct answer is A (Complex regional pain syndrome type 1 affecting the hand and wrist): Burning pain out of proportion with allodynia, swelling, colour change and sweating after a fracture indicates complex regional pain syndrome type 1, especially when the signs spread beyond one nerve territory. Carpal tunnel from cast pressure is tempting after cast treatment, but it follows the median nerve and does not cause hand-wide autonomic change. Infection would usually bring fever or raised inflammatory markers, and disuse stiffness lacks allodynia and sweating.

Question 164

Musculoskeletal

A 27-year-old right-handed snowboarder fell on an outstretched hand. Initial wrist radiographs are read as normal, yet there is tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain with axial loading of the thumb. Swelling is mild and grip is slightly reduced. What is the most appropriate management?

  • A. Apply a compression wrap and arrange repeat radiographs at six weeks if pain persists
  • B. Splint the wrist for two weeks and then restart graded strengthening if pain settles
  • C. Immobilize in a thumb spica splint and arrange repeat or advanced imaging in about ten days
  • D. Order thumb ligament stress testing and begin gentle thumb range of motion exercises

The correct answer is C (Immobilize in a thumb spica splint and arrange repeat or advanced imaging in about ten days): Snuffbox tenderness and pain on axial thumb loading after a fall on an outstretched hand suggest a scaphoid fracture even when initial films are normal, because these fractures can be occult. A compression wrap is tempting when pain is tolerable, but waiting six weeks leaves a possible fracture unprotected. A brief wrist splint without imaging does not confirm the diagnosis, and ligament testing with early movement risks displacement, nonunion and avascular necrosis.

Question 165

Musculoskeletal

A 44-year-old carpenter twisted his knee while squatting and now reports catching and locking. Joint line tenderness is present medially, and pain occurs with a rotational compressive test. The knee has a fixed extension block of 15 degrees that does not improve with gentle effort. What is the best next step?

  • A. Refer to orthopedics, as a displaced torn meniscal fragment is the likely obstruction
  • B. Start a progressive strengthening program first, as most meniscal tears settle with conservative care
  • C. Apply a compression bandage and allow normal walking while the extension block gradually settles
  • D. Order a non-urgent MRI and continue squatting and lifting at work in the meantime

The correct answer is A (Refer to orthopedics, as a displaced torn meniscal fragment is the likely obstruction): A true extension block with catching and medial joint line tenderness points to a displaced meniscal fragment, which needs orthopedic assessment. Conservative strengthening is tempting because many meniscal tears do well without surgery, but that applies when the knee moves freely. Waiting with a bandage or imaging at leisure while squatting and lifting continue risks further cartilage damage, so a mechanical obstruction needs specialist review.

Question 166

Musculoskeletal

A 50-year-old office worker has neck pain radiating into the right thumb and index finger. Spurling's test reproduces the arm pain, shoulder abduction relieves it, and the biceps reflex is reduced. He has no weakness in the hand. Which level is most likely affected?

  • A. C6 nerve root, with a reduced biceps reflex and thumb and index finger sensory change
  • B. C5 nerve root, with a reduced biceps reflex also fitting this level
  • C. C7 nerve root, whose middle finger sensation and triceps reflex would change
  • D. C8 nerve root, whose ring and little finger sensation and grip would change

The correct answer is A (C6 nerve root, with a reduced biceps reflex and thumb and index finger sensory change): Thumb and index finger paraesthesia with a reduced biceps reflex corresponds to the C6 root, and the positive Spurling's test with relief on shoulder abduction supports radiculopathy. C5 is tempting because it also shares the biceps reflex, but it supplies the lateral upper arm rather than the thumb. C7 and C8 involve the middle finger and the ulnar side of the hand.

Question 167

Musculoskeletal

A 55-year-old with diabetes has insidious shoulder pain and progressive stiffness over four months. Passive and active motion are equally limited. Which pattern of movement loss is characteristic of this condition? There is no history of shoulder trauma, and her neck movements are pain free.

  • A. Greatest loss of internal rotation, then flexion, then external rotation
  • B. External rotation lost most, then abduction, then internal rotation
  • C. Full passive range, with pain and weakness on resisted external rotation and abduction
  • D. A painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction, with near full passive range

The correct answer is B (External rotation lost most, then abduction, then internal rotation): Adhesive capsulitis produces a capsular pattern at the glenohumeral joint, with external rotation lost most, then abduction, then internal rotation. Equal active and passive limitation points to a joint cause. A rotator cuff problem is tempting in a shoulder with pain, but it keeps passive range and shows weakness on resisted testing, and a painful arc suggests subacromial pain rather than global stiffness.

Question 168

Musculoskeletal

A 58-year-old woman has lateral hip pain at night when lying on the affected side and with single-leg stance. Palpation over the greater trochanter reproduces the pain. Which advice is most helpful early on? Her pain eases when she is out of bed during the day.

  • A. Strengthen the hip abductors with side-lying leg raises on the painful side each night
  • B. Corticosteroid injection at the trochanter now, followed by a gradual return to side lying
  • C. Daily iliotibial band stretching over the trochanter, with side lying continued as tolerated
  • D. Limit side lying and crossing legs while gradually loading the hip abductors over several weeks

The correct answer is D (Limit side lying and crossing legs while gradually loading the hip abductors over several weeks): Gluteal tendinopathy is aggravated by compression against the trochanter, so avoiding side lying on the painful side and crossed-leg postures while gradually loading the abductors is recommended. Abductor exercises are the right target, but performing them lying on the painful side adds the compression that irritates the tendon. An injection may relieve pain briefly without addressing load, and iliotibial band stretching across the trochanter adds compression.

Question 169

Musculoskeletal

A 36-year-old teacher in Regina has had back pain for four days after gardening. There are no red flags, neurological deficits, or leg symptoms. She asks whether she should stay in bed. What is the best advice? She has no neurological symptoms in her legs.

  • A. Limit activity for one week, then restart gradually
  • B. Bed rest for two days, then return to normal activity using a lumbar support belt
  • C. Begin spinal manipulation twice weekly for three weeks
  • D. Stay active within comfort and return gradually to normal activity

The correct answer is D (Stay active within comfort and return gradually to normal activity): Nonspecific low back pain without red flags is managed with reassurance and staying active within comfort. Short bed rest with a belt is tempting because it is milder than a week in bed, but any rest slows recovery. Manipulation can offer short-term relief, yet it does not answer her question about rest, and limiting activity for a week still delays recovery and builds fear of movement.

Question 170

Musculoskeletal

An 82-year-old woman had a hip hemiarthroplasty after a fall at home in Moncton. The surgeon orders weight bearing as tolerated. What is a main aim of the early rehabilitation after hip fracture surgery? She is otherwise healthy and lives alone in a two-storey house.

  • A. Chair transfers and bed exercises for one week, with standing practice added after discharge
  • B. Strict hip precautions and bed-level strengthening for ten days before standing is attempted
  • C. Early mobilization within a day or two, with supervised standing, to reduce complications and decline
  • D. Sitting out of bed for meals and short supervised walks beginning on the third postoperative day

The correct answer is C (Early mobilization within a day or two, with supervised standing, to reduce complications and decline): Early mobilization within the first one to two days after hip fracture surgery lowers the risk of pneumonia, pressure injury, delirium and functional decline. Sitting out of bed with walks from day three is tempting because it is progressive, but it starts later than the benefit window. Delaying standing until after discharge or for ten days adds deconditioning and complications when weight bearing is already permitted.

Question 171

Neurological

A 29-year-old cyclist struck by a car has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7 on arrival at a Toronto trauma centre. How is the severity of his traumatic brain injury classified using this scale at the time of the first assessment?

  • A. Moderate on arrival, with classification based on the best motor response rather than the total score
  • B. Provisionally severe, with final classification set by the score at 24 hours after injury
  • C. Severe, because a score of 8 or less indicates severe injury
  • D. Mild to moderate, because sedation and intoxication commonly lower scores at the first assessment

The correct answer is C (Severe, because a score of 8 or less indicates severe injury): The Glasgow Coma Scale classifies 13 to 15 as mild, 9 to 12 as moderate and 3 to 8 as severe, so a score of 7 on arrival is severe. Using only the motor response is tempting because it predicts outcome, but the classification uses the total score. Later scores guide prognosis and sedation can confound the reading, but the initial classification is made from the first assessment.

Question 172

Neurological

Four days after a motor vehicle crash a 34-year-old woman is oriented to place but not date, cannot recall what she ate at lunch, and is conversational. A nurse asks the physiotherapist whether formal exercise testing is appropriate. What is the best decision?

  • A. Test balance and mobility with a brief standardized battery and use results to plan therapy
  • B. Use short, repetitive, simple sessions and defer formal testing
  • C. Provide a written exercise program and have a family member supervise it at home each day
  • D. Hold treatment until she is oriented to date, then begin the usual progressive program

The correct answer is B (Use short, repetitive, simple sessions and defer formal testing): Continuing post-traumatic amnesia limits learning and carryover, so sessions should be brief, familiar and repetitive, with orientation support, and formal testing should wait. A brief balance and mobility battery is tempting because early data are useful, but results are unreliable while new information is not retained. A home program depends on memory and judgment, and holding treatment removes structured practice that helps.

Question 173

Neurological

A 16-year-old basketball player in Ottawa sustained a concussion six days ago. She has completed 24 hours of relative rest. Symptoms are mild, but light walking still provokes a slight headache. According to the graded return to activity, what is the best next step?

  • A. Sport-specific drills such as dribbling and passing without any contact
  • B. Non-contact training drills combined with progressive resistance training
  • C. Light aerobic exercise below the level that provokes symptoms
  • D. Continued strict rest at home until every symptom has resolved, then restart activity

The correct answer is C (Light aerobic exercise below the level that provokes symptoms): Current Canadian guidance supports a short period of relative rest and then symptom-limited light aerobic activity, progressing step by step only when symptoms stay stable. Sport-specific drills are tempting because she is mildly symptomatic, but they belong to a later step that requires tolerating light aerobic work first. Prolonged strict rest is no longer recommended, and resistance and contact work come much later.

Question 174

Neurological

A 40-year-old man with a recent severe brain injury is disoriented, shouting and pulling at his lines during a morning physiotherapy session. He becomes calmer in a quiet room. Which strategy is the best response? Nursing notes describe poor sleep overnight and a busy ward corridor outside his room.

  • A. Continue the session at full length with two staff to keep him safe from the lines
  • B. Reorient him to date and place with a whiteboard and family photographs
  • C. Reduce stimulation, use one calm voice, keep instructions simple and shorten the session
  • D. Postpone the session until the afternoon and ask nursing to review his sedation

The correct answer is C (Reduce stimulation, use one calm voice, keep instructions simple and shorten the session): Agitation in early recovery from brain injury often reflects overstimulation, so quieting the setting, using one calm voice, simple instructions and a shorter session works best. Reorientation with a whiteboard is tempting because he is confused, but it adds demands. Adding staff keeps him safe but does not reduce the stimulation, and postponing for a sedation review gives up a session he can already tolerate in a quiet room.

Question 175

Neurological

Three months after a severe brain injury, a 35-year-old man has a warm, swollen right hip with progressively reduced range of motion and low-grade fever. Deep vein thrombosis has been excluded, and he has no wound or distant source of infection. Which complication should be suspected?

  • A. Septic arthritis of the hip from low-grade bacteremia, needing joint aspiration
  • B. Reactive arthritis of the hip following a recent genitourinary infection
  • C. Hip stress fracture from prolonged immobility and bone loss, needing non-weight-bearing
  • D. Heterotopic ossification forming around the hip joint after injury

The correct answer is D (Heterotopic ossification forming around the hip joint after injury): Warmth, swelling, falling range and low-grade fever around a large joint after neurological injury suggest heterotopic ossification, a common complication in this population. Septic arthritis is tempting because of the warmth and fever, but without a wound or distant source and with a gradual course, ossification is more likely. Stress fracture and reactive arthritis do not fit the picture, and imaging and medical review are indicated.

Question 176

Neurological

A 52-year-old woman with a stroke has increased plantarflexor tone that interferes with gait but has no fixed contracture. Which combination of measures is most appropriate to improve her walking over the next few weeks of outpatient therapy? She walks with a cane and has no pain at rest.

  • A. Serial casting of the ankle into dorsiflexion, with walking practice paused until the tone settles
  • B. Botulinum toxin injection to the calf, with gait training deferred until the tone has fallen
  • C. Prolonged calf stretching for thirty minutes daily with a night resting splint
  • D. Task-specific gait training with positioning, stretching and an orthosis as needed

The correct answer is D (Task-specific gait training with positioning, stretching and an orthosis as needed): Spasticity management combines active task practice with stretching, positioning and orthoses where useful, and walking practice drives improvement. Botulinum toxin is tempting because the tone is the visible problem, but it is an adjunct to training rather than a reason to defer it. Passive stretching with a splint does not train gait, and casting is for fixed shortening, which she does not have.

Question 177

Neurological

A 67-year-old woman arrives at a Vancouver emergency department 90 minutes after sudden right arm weakness and slurred speech. A computed tomography scan shows no bleeding. Within what general time window is intravenous thrombolysis considered for ischemic stroke? She lives in Burnaby and arrived by ambulance.

  • A. Within about 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients
  • B. Within 3 hours of symptom onset, the original window
  • C. Within about 6 hours of symptom onset, the window used for endovascular thrombectomy
  • D. Within 60 minutes of arrival, the door-to-needle target

The correct answer is A (Within about 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients): Intravenous thrombolysis is considered for eligible ischemic stroke patients within roughly 4.5 hours of onset, and sooner treatment gives better outcomes. A 6-hour window is tempting because it belongs to endovascular thrombectomy, which is a different treatment. Three hours was the original window and has been extended, and the 60-minute figure is a door-to-needle quality target, not the eligibility limit. Eligibility also depends on imaging and other criteria.

Question 178

Neurological

A 71-year-old man has right-sided weakness greater in the face and arm than the leg, with difficulty producing speech but good comprehension. Which vascular territory is most likely affected? He also has a right facial droop. His hearing and vision are normal, and he has had no earlier strokes.

  • A. Left internal capsule lacunar infarct from small vessel disease causing pure motor weakness
  • B. Left middle cerebral artery, affecting the inferior division
  • C. Right middle cerebral artery territory affecting the lateral cortex
  • D. Left middle cerebral artery territory, affecting the superior division

The correct answer is D (Left middle cerebral artery territory, affecting the superior division): Face and arm weakness greater than the leg with expressive aphasia and good comprehension suggests the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery. The inferior division is tempting because it is the same artery, but it causes fluent speech with poor comprehension. A lacunar infarct produces weakness without aphasia, and a right-sided lesion would weaken the left side.

Question 179

Neurological

A 63-year-old woman has left leg weakness greater than arm weakness, reduced initiation and urinary incontinence after a sudden event. Her face and speech are relatively spared. Which artery is most likely involved? She has no visual complaints, and her sensation is mildly reduced in the leg.

  • A. Right middle cerebral artery territory affecting the lateral frontal and parietal cortex
  • B. Left anterior cerebral artery supplying the medial cortex
  • C. A small right lacunar infarct in the internal capsule
  • D. Right anterior cerebral artery territory affecting the medial cortex

The correct answer is D (Right anterior cerebral artery territory affecting the medial cortex): Contralateral leg weakness, reduced initiation and incontinence are typical of anterior cerebral artery infarction, since the medial cortex represents the leg. The left anterior cerebral artery is tempting because it is the same artery, but a right-sided lesion causes left leg weakness. A middle cerebral lesion affects the face and arm more, and a capsular lesion weakens face, arm and leg together.

Question 180

Neurological

A 74-year-old man bumps into objects on his left side after a stroke. His strength is normal and he is alert. Confrontation testing of each eye separately shows the same left half of the visual field missing in both eyes. Which finding is present?

  • A. Left homonymous hemianopia from a right occipital lobe infarct
  • B. Left hemispatial neglect from a right parietal stroke, with intact visual fields
  • C. Right homonymous hemianopia from a left occipital infarct
  • D. Left superior quadrantanopia from a right temporal lesion involving Meyer's loop

The correct answer is A (Left homonymous hemianopia from a right occipital lobe infarct): Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes is homonymous hemianopia, and a left-sided loss arises from the right occipital lobe in the posterior cerebral territory. Neglect is tempting because he bumps into objects on the left, but it is an attention problem with intact fields, whereas the missing half-field is present in each eye separately. A quadrantanopia loses only a quarter of the field, and a right-sided loss would implicate the left hemisphere.

Question 181

Neurological

A 60-year-old man with a flaccid right arm after a stroke is being positioned in bed. A one-finger-width gap is palpable below the acromion. Which handling approach best protects the shoulder? He is cooperative, has no pain at rest, and is transferred with two staff.

  • A. Pull firmly on the hand to help lift him up the bed with the staff
  • B. Support the arm on a pillow, avoid pulling it, and protract the scapula
  • C. Allow the arm to hang unsupported at his side when he sits upright
  • D. Use overhead pulleys to exercise the shoulder early in the rehabilitation program

The correct answer is B (Support the arm on a pillow, avoid pulling it, and protract the scapula): A flaccid shoulder is vulnerable to subluxation, so the arm should be supported and not pulled. Unsupported hanging stretches the capsule, and overhead pulleys encourage unsafe elevation.

Question 182

Neurological

A 69-year-old woman with a right hemisphere stroke eats from the right side of her plate and neglects her left arm. What is the most useful strategy to improve her awareness during therapy? Her husband reports she ignores people who speak from the left.

  • A. Practise left-sided tasks in a quiet room with distractions removed and no cues
  • B. Keep belongings on her right within reach, with verbal reminders about the left
  • C. Place items and cues on the left, and guide attention to that side
  • D. Approach and speak from the right to keep her calm and make each session predictable

The correct answer is C (Place items and cues on the left, and guide attention to that side): Neglect training encourages scanning and attention toward the neglected side, using cues, placed items and approach from the affected side. Keeping everything on the right is tempting because it makes tasks easier today, but it avoids the deficit and does not improve awareness. A quiet room without scanning cues or approaching from the right leaves attention drawn to the intact side.

Question 183

Neurological

A 66-year-old man after a stroke sits leaning strongly toward his weak side, pushes with his stronger arm and leg, and resists correction toward midline. Which condition does this describe? Before the stroke he was a left-handed carpenter. He is cooperative and motivated, and he has no vision problems.

  • A. Contraversive pushing, with upright perceived as tilted toward the weak side
  • B. Unilateral neglect, with attention drawn away from the weak side and a lean toward it
  • C. Cerebellar ataxia with truncal instability, causing a wide base and a lean toward one side
  • D. Poor trunk control from weakness, with a lean that corrects when he is cued upright

The correct answer is A (Contraversive pushing, with upright perceived as tilted toward the weak side): In pusher syndrome the person pushes toward the weak side and resists correction because they perceive upright as tilted toward that side, so training uses visual feedback and midline orientation. Neglect is tempting because it also follows a hemisphere stroke and involves the weak side, but it does not produce active pushing against correction. Ataxia and simple trunk weakness both allow the person to accept correction toward midline.

Question 184

Neurological

A 58-year-old woman three months after a stroke has some wrist and finger extension in her affected hand and avoids using it. Which approach is designed to overcome learned non-use? She is motivated and follows two-step commands. Her sensation is intact and she has no pain.

  • A. Constraint of the stronger hand with intensive practice of the affected hand
  • B. Electrical stimulation of the wrist extensors during task practice
  • C. Mirror therapy using the reflection of the stronger hand to stimulate the affected side
  • D. Bilateral arm training with both hands moving together in the same tasks

The correct answer is A (Constraint of the stronger hand with intensive practice of the affected hand): Constraint-induced movement therapy restricts the stronger hand and requires intensive practice with the affected hand to reverse learned non-use, and it suits people who already have some active wrist and finger extension. Mirror therapy, electrical stimulation and bilateral training are tempting because they are recognized post-stroke arm approaches, but none is designed to overcome learned non-use by forcing use of the affected hand.

Question 185

Neurological

A 75-year-old woman two days after a stroke coughs after sips of water and her voice sounds wet. She is alert and hungry. What is the most appropriate action? Her vital signs are stable, and the nurse asks whether to give her lunch.

  • A. Hold oral intake and request a speech language pathologist swallowing assessment
  • B. Allow thickened fluids by teaspoon with a chin tuck while watching for further coughing
  • C. Offer a pureed diet under supervision, since pureed textures carry a lower aspiration risk
  • D. Repeat the water sip test in an hour and resume her diet if the cough settles

The correct answer is A (Hold oral intake and request a speech language pathologist swallowing assessment): Coughing and a wet voice after swallowing signal possible aspiration, so oral intake should be held until a speech language pathologist completes a formal swallow assessment. Thickened fluids and a chin tuck are tempting because they are real strategies, but they are chosen after assessment shows which one helps. Alertness and hunger do not guarantee a safe swallow, and repeating a failed screen delays the right pathway.

Question 186

Neurological

A 58-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension develops a sudden severe headache, vomiting and decreasing consciousness while gardening. What is the most likely cause and the most urgent step? His blood pressure is 210/120 and his wife called an ambulance after he collapsed in the garden.

  • A. Seizure with postictal drowsiness, needing recovery position and monitoring until he wakes
  • B. Ischemic stroke, needing emergency transfer so thrombolysis can begin on arrival
  • C. Hypertensive emergency without stroke, needing emergency transfer for blood pressure lowering
  • D. Intracerebral hemorrhage, needing emergency transfer for brain imaging

The correct answer is D (Intracerebral hemorrhage, needing emergency transfer for brain imaging): Sudden severe headache with vomiting and falling consciousness in a hypertensive person suggests intracerebral hemorrhage, an emergency that needs urgent brain imaging. Ischemic stroke is tempting because it also needs emergency transfer, but the headache, vomiting and very high pressure point to bleeding, and clot-dissolving medication is not given before imaging excludes hemorrhage. A hypertensive emergency without a brain cause or a seizure at the roadside would delay brain imaging.

Question 187

Neurological

A 62-year-old woman six weeks after a minor stroke has stable blood pressure and wants to return to exercise. Which aerobic prescription is most appropriate? She has hypertension controlled by medication and a resting heart rate of 72. She was independent before the stroke and walks with a cane.

  • A. Light walking at home for three months, with structured aerobic training added after that
  • B. Vigorous interval training at 90 percent of maximum heart rate three times each week
  • C. Moderate aerobic training started now, with progression to vigorous intensity within two weeks
  • D. Moderate aerobic training several times weekly with medical clearance, monitoring and gradual progression

The correct answer is D (Moderate aerobic training several times weekly with medical clearance, monitoring and gradual progression): Moderate-intensity aerobic exercise several times weekly, with medical clearance and monitoring, improves fitness and lowers the risk of recurrence after stroke. Light walking for three months is tempting as a cautious choice, but it prolongs deconditioning. Vigorous intervals are not an appropriate start, and a fast jump to vigorous intensity within two weeks outpaces what monitoring and gradual progression allow.

Question 188

Neurological

A 64-year-old man after a stroke understands instructions but speaks in short, effortful phrases and cannot repeat sentences back accurately. He is oriented, speaks slowly with many pauses, and follows two-step commands. His right arm is weak and he is frustrated by his speech. Which type of aphasia best describes this?

  • A. Broca's aphasia with nonfluent effortful speech and good comprehension
  • B. Transcortical motor aphasia with nonfluent speech and well-preserved repetition
  • C. Conduction aphasia with fluent speech, good comprehension and poor repetition
  • D. Apraxia of speech with effortful articulation and intact language comprehension

The correct answer is A (Broca's aphasia with nonfluent effortful speech and good comprehension): Nonfluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension and impaired repetition is Broca's aphasia. Transcortical motor aphasia is tempting because speech is also nonfluent and comprehension is good, but repetition is preserved there, and this man cannot repeat sentences. Conduction aphasia has fluent speech, and apraxia of speech is a motor planning disorder rather than a type of aphasia.

Question 189

Neurological

A 31-year-old woman has a spinal cord injury with some preserved sensory and motor function below the neurological level, including sacral segments. Muscle grades below the level are mostly less than 3. How is this injury classified? Light touch is preserved in some sacral dermatomes.

  • A. Incomplete injury, ASIA B, as sensation is preserved but motor function is absent
  • B. Incomplete injury, ASIA C, as most key muscles below are under grade 3
  • C. Incomplete injury, ASIA D, as most key muscles are grade 3 or above
  • D. Complete injury, ASIA A, with partial preservation below the level

The correct answer is B (Incomplete injury, ASIA C, as most key muscles below are under grade 3): Sacral sparing makes the injury incomplete. Motor function with most key muscles under grade 3 is C. Grade B is tempting because sensation is preserved, but B has no motor function below the level, and grade D requires at least half of key muscles at grade 3 or more. A complete ASIA A injury has no sacral sparing, whatever is preserved above.

Question 190

Neurological

A 28-year-old man with a T4 spinal cord injury develops a pounding headache, flushing above the injury and a blood pressure of 190/110 while seated. His pulse is 52. What should be done first? He is sitting in a wheelchair in the gym when it begins.

  • A. Sit him upright, loosen tight clothing and check bladder and bowel for triggers
  • B. Give his prescribed fast-acting antihypertensive immediately, then search for the trigger afterward
  • C. Stop activity, move him to a quiet room and monitor his vital signs every five minutes
  • D. Lay him flat with the legs raised and call for help

The correct answer is A (Sit him upright, loosen tight clothing and check bladder and bowel for triggers): This is autonomic dysreflexia, an emergency in injuries at T6 or above, and the first step is to sit him upright, loosen tight clothing and look for the noxious trigger, usually bladder or bowel. Giving medication first is tempting because the pressure is dangerously high, but removing the trigger often resolves it and sitting up lowers pressure. Moving to a quiet room to monitor leaves the cause in place, and lying flat raises the pressure further.

Question 191

Neurological

A 22-year-old man injured in a diving accident has a complete C6 spinal cord injury with intact elbow flexion and shoulder movement. He is beginning inpatient rehabilitation and asks what hand function and independence he can realistically expect. Which functional outcome is typically expected with rehabilitation?

  • A. Independent breathing and cough from active intercostal and abdominal muscle contraction
  • B. Active finger flexion for grasp, catheter use and self-feeding
  • C. Triceps function giving unaided push-ups for level transfers and manual propulsion on all surfaces
  • D. Wrist extension gives tenodesis grasp, and transfers may be independent

The correct answer is D (Wrist extension gives tenodesis grasp, and transfers may be independent): At C6 the wrist extensors are present, which allows a tenodesis grasp and some independence in transfers. Triceps-based push-ups are tempting because they sound like the next functional step, but they depend on C7 function. Finger flexors are also not active at C6, and the intercostal and abdominal muscles are paralyzed, which weakens cough.

Question 192

Neurological

A 35-year-old woman with a T5 spinal cord injury feels faint and pale when raised to sitting for the first time. Blood pressure has dropped. What is the best immediate action? She was transferred by two staff and is accompanied by her mother.

  • A. Tilt her back, raise the legs, then use abdominal binding and graded progression
  • B. Lay her flat, give a large oral fluid load, and attempt sitting her upright immediately
  • C. Keep her seated upright with slow deep breathing while waiting for her pressure to recover
  • D. Return her to bed and postpone sitting until her pressure has been stable for a week

The correct answer is A (Tilt her back, raise the legs, then use abdominal binding and graded progression): Orthostatic hypotension after spinal cord injury is managed by returning to a reclined position, raising the legs, then using abdominal binding and compression with gradual progression to upright. Fluids are tempting because low pressure suggests low volume, but they do not address pooling of blood. Staying upright with breathing exercises ignores the faint, and waiting a week removes the graded exposure that builds tolerance.

Question 193

Neurological

A 26-year-old man has a stab wound to the left side of the spine at T8. Examination shows left leg weakness with loss of proprioception, and right leg loss of pain and temperature sensation. Which syndrome is present? He is alert and has no breathing difficulty.

  • A. Anterior cord syndrome, with bilateral weakness, pain loss and preserved proprioception
  • B. Posterior cord syndrome, with loss of proprioception and vibration but preserved strength
  • C. Brown-Sequard syndrome, with same-side motor and proprioception loss and opposite-side pain loss
  • D. Central cord syndrome, with arm-predominant weakness and variable sensory loss

The correct answer is C (Brown-Sequard syndrome, with same-side motor and proprioception loss and opposite-side pain loss): A hemisection of the cord produces Brown-Sequard syndrome, with ipsilateral weakness and proprioception loss and contralateral loss of pain and temperature. Anterior cord syndrome is tempting because it also affects motor function and pain sensation, but it is bilateral and spares proprioception. Posterior cord syndrome spares strength, and central cord syndrome causes arm-predominant weakness without a crossed pattern.

Question 194

Neurological

A 66-year-old woman with known cervical spondylosis falls forward and hyperextends her neck. She has weakness greater in the hands and arms than the legs, variable sensory loss below the level and urinary retention since the fall. Which pattern of injury is likely?

  • A. Anterior cord syndrome, with loss of motor function and pain sensation below the level
  • B. Central cord syndrome from a hyperextension injury with spondylosis and arm-predominant weakness
  • C. Posterior cord syndrome, with loss of proprioception and vibration but intact strength
  • D. Brown-Sequard syndrome, with one-sided weakness and opposite loss of pain and temperature

The correct answer is B (Central cord syndrome from a hyperextension injury with spondylosis and arm-predominant weakness): Hyperextension in an older person with cervical spondylosis typically causes central cord syndrome, with the arms weaker than the legs, variable sensory loss and often urinary retention. Brown-Sequard syndrome is tempting because it is also a partial cord injury, but it gives one-sided weakness with crossed sensory loss. Anterior and posterior cord syndromes affect different tracts and do not fit this arm-predominant pattern.

Question 195

Neurological

A 33-year-old man with a complete T10 spinal cord injury has recently started using a wheelchair. Which instruction best lowers the risk of a pressure injury over his sitting bones? He reports no pain, uses a standard cushion and has had no skin breakdown so far.

  • A. Perform weight shifts at set intervals and check the skin each day
  • B. Use a donut-shaped ring cushion to relieve the sitting bones
  • C. Shift his weight whenever he notices discomfort or spasms
  • D. Use a pressure-redistributing cushion and check his skin once each week at home

The correct answer is A (Perform weight shifts at set intervals and check the skin each day): Without sensation, scheduled weight shifts and daily skin checks are essential. A good cushion is tempting because it lowers pressure, but a weekly skin check allows damage to progress. Ring cushions concentrate pressure at their edges, and shifting weight only when discomfort is noticed depends on sensation he lacks.

Question 196

Neurological

A 24-year-old man injured in a motor vehicle crash has a complete C4 spinal cord injury and is two weeks into inpatient rehabilitation. The team is reviewing his respiratory status and planning cough assistance and ventilator weaning. Which statement best describes his breathing?

  • A. The diaphragm is intact and the intercostals are weak, so ventilation reaches a normal capacity
  • B. The diaphragm is fully denervated, so he depends on a ventilator and weaning is not possible
  • C. The diaphragm is partly spared, but reduced capacity often needs ventilatory support
  • D. The intercostals are spared and carry ventilation, so his cough remains strong

The correct answer is C (The diaphragm is partly spared, but reduced capacity often needs ventilatory support): The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5, so a C4 injury may leave partial diaphragm function but with reduced capacity, and ventilatory support is often needed. Total diaphragm paralysis is tempting because C4 is high, but part of the nerve supply arises at and above this level. Weak intercostals and abdominals reduce capacity and cough, so normal ventilation or a strong cough cannot be expected.

Question 197

Neurological

Two days after a T6 spinal cord injury, a 40-year-old man has flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes and no sensation or movement in his legs. His resident asks what the absent reflexes mean and when they should return. Which description explains the absent reflexes at this early stage?

  • A. Neurogenic shock, with low blood pressure and a slow heart rate from lost sympathetic tone
  • B. Lower motor neuron injury at the root level, so reflexes stay absent
  • C. Spinal shock, with temporary loss of reflexes that later return as spasticity
  • D. An established upper motor neuron lesion, with hyperreflexia and spasticity below the injury

The correct answer is C (Spinal shock, with temporary loss of reflexes that later return as spasticity): Spinal shock is a temporary state after acute injury with flaccidity and absent reflexes below the lesion, and reflexes later return as spasticity may develop. Neurogenic shock is tempting because low blood pressure and a slow heart rate can occur with a high injury, but it explains the circulation and not the absent reflexes. A root-level lower motor neuron picture would be permanent, and an established upper motor neuron lesion does not appear at two days.

Question 198

Neurological

A 57-year-old man with a stroke has a foot drop but good calf strength and no ankle instability. Which device is most appropriate to improve toe clearance in swing? He walks 40 metres with a cane, has no sensory loss, and his knee is stable in stance.

  • A. Posterior leaf spring orthosis that assists dorsiflexion during swing
  • B. Solid ankle foot orthosis set in neutral to control the ankle during stance and swing
  • C. Posterior shell orthosis set in slight plantarflexion to encourage knee extension
  • D. Rocker-bottom shoe modification with a heel wedge to ease push-off and loading

The correct answer is A (Posterior leaf spring orthosis that assists dorsiflexion during swing): A flexible posterior leaf spring orthosis lifts the foot in swing while allowing ankle motion, which suits a person with good calf strength, a stable knee and a mild foot drop. A solid orthosis is tempting because it controls the foot reliably, but it blocks useful ankle motion. A plantarflexed shell targets knee control, which he does not need, and a shoe change does not improve toe clearance.

Question 199

Neurological

A 27-year-old man with a concussion three weeks ago has brief spinning vertigo when rolling onto his right side in bed. The Dix-Hallpike test on the right reproduces vertigo lasting under a minute, with torsional upbeat nystagmus that fades on repeat. He has no hearing loss. What is the likely cause and management?

  • A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, treated with repositioning manoeuvres
  • B. Cervicogenic dizziness from the neck injury, treated with manual therapy and neck retraining
  • C. Central vertigo from a posterior circulation stroke needing imaging
  • D. Unilateral vestibular hypofunction after the concussion, treated with gaze stabilization exercises
