The correct answer is A (Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, treated with repositioning manoeuvres): Brief positional vertigo with torsional upbeat nystagmus that fatigues on repeat testing after head injury suggests benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, treated with a repositioning manoeuvre. Vestibular hypofunction is tempting after concussion and is managed with exercises, but it does not cause brief positional episodes. A central cause would not typically fatigue, and neck-related dizziness is not reproduced by a positional test of the canals.

Question 200

Neurological

A 69-year-old man 10 weeks after a stroke walks with a cane and has had two near falls at home. His Berg Balance Scale score is 40 out of 56. What is the best addition to his program? He lives with his wife in a bungalow.

  • A. Lower limb strengthening on machines with a home hazard review
  • B. Seated trunk and balance exercises with a home hazard review, with standing practice added later
  • C. Task-specific balance training with progression and a home hazard review
  • D. A walker for all outdoor walking, with a home hazard review

The correct answer is C (Task-specific balance training with progression and a home hazard review): A Berg score of 40 out of 56 suggests elevated fall risk. Task-specific balance training with progression and a home hazard review address risk while preserving mobility. Seated balance work is tempting because it is safe, but it delays the standing practice he needs. Machine strengthening does not train balance, and a walker for all outdoor walking tilts toward restriction rather than training.

Question 201

Neurological

A 38-year-old data entry clerk in Winnipeg reports night waking with tingling in her right hand. Examination must separate median nerve compression at the wrist from a C6 nerve root problem. Which finding best supports carpal tunnel syndrome as the source of her symptoms?

  • A. Reduced biceps reflex with arm pain that increases on neck extension
  • B. Numbness of the little finger and ulnar ring finger with weak finger abduction
  • C. Numbness of the thumb to radial ring finger with normal sensation over the thenar eminence
  • D. Weak wrist extension with numbness over the dorsal first web space of the hand

The correct answer is C (Numbness of the thumb to radial ring finger with normal sensation over the thenar eminence): The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves before the carpal tunnel, so thenar skin sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome. A reduced biceps reflex with neck movement provoking arm pain points to the C6 root. Ulnar and radial patterns involve different skin territories and muscles.

Question 202

Neurological

A 29-year-old man wakes after falling asleep with his arm over a park bench following a Saturday evening in Halifax. He cannot extend his wrist or fingers, and sensation is reduced over the dorsal first web space. Triceps strength is normal. Which initial physiotherapy intervention is most appropriate?

  • A. Referral for surgical nerve exploration, since recovery from this type of compression is unlikely
  • B. Neural tensioning exercises held at end range to free the radial nerve from the spiral groove
  • C. A wrist extension splint holding the hand neutral while the extensors recover
  • D. A neutral wrist splint combined with heavy resisted extension loading from the first week

The correct answer is C (A wrist extension splint holding the hand neutral while the extensors recover): Compression at the spiral groove spares the triceps because its branches leave higher. Neurapraxia usually recovers on its own, so the goal is to protect overstretched extensors and keep joints supple. Heavy resistance on weakened muscle risks harm without speeding recovery, tensioning an irritated nerve adds strain, and surgery is considered only if no recovery appears over several months.

Question 203

Neurological

A 62-year-old woman develops foot slap and catches her toes on stairs two days after a long leg cast was removed. She has weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, and numbness over the lateral shin and dorsum of the foot. Plantarflexion and inversion are strong. Which site of nerve compression is most likely?

  • A. The common fibular nerve as it wraps around the fibular neck
  • B. The tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus within the tarsal tunnel
  • C. The L5 nerve root at the lumbar intervertebral foramen on the same side
  • D. The sciatic nerve at the greater sciatic notch beneath the piriformis muscle

The correct answer is A (The common fibular nerve as it wraps around the fibular neck): Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with preserved plantarflexion and inversion fit a common fibular nerve lesion at the fibular neck, a superficial site vulnerable to casts and crossed legs. An L5 root or sciatic lesion would usually affect tibialis posterior and the plantarflexors, which are strong here.

Question 204

Neurological

A 45-year-old man in Saskatoon presents two weeks after a gastrointestinal illness with symmetrical leg weakness that has climbed to his hips over three days. Deep tendon reflexes are absent and he reports mild distal tingling. Which additional finding would most urgently require escalation to the medical team?

  • A. Pain in the low back and thighs that wakes him at night despite resting
  • B. Falling vital capacity with a weak cough and trouble speaking in full sentences
  • C. Persistent distal numbness and tingling spreading to the fingertips without any new weakness there
  • D. Marked fatigue with light exertion and a drop in walking tolerance since his last visit

The correct answer is B (Falling vital capacity with a weak cough and trouble speaking in full sentences): Ascending weakness with areflexia after an infection suggests Guillain-Barre syndrome, in which respiratory muscle weakness can develop quickly. Falling vital capacity with a weak cough means the breathing muscles are failing and needs immediate medical action. Night pain, fatigue and sensory spread are common in this condition and are monitored, but they do not threaten life the way respiratory decline does.

Question 205

Neurological

A 34-year-old teacher in Regina wakes with right facial weakness: she cannot close the right eye, her forehead does not wrinkle on that side, and her mouth droops. Taste is altered. Her doctor diagnoses Bell palsy. Which advice should the physiotherapist give about eye care during recovery?

  • A. Wear a firm eye patch over the weak eye all day to rest the cornea
  • B. Use lubricating drops at bedtime alone, since daytime blinking by the weak lid protects the cornea
  • C. Use lubricating drops and tape the eyelid closed at night to prevent corneal drying
  • D. Wear sunglasses outdoors and leave the eye uncovered overnight so that air can keep it moist

The correct answer is C (Use lubricating drops and tape the eyelid closed at night to prevent corneal drying): When the orbicularis oculi cannot close the eyelid, the cornea is at risk, so lubrication through the day and night taping are priorities. A patch worn all day can scratch the cornea, and protection only at night leaves the eye dry while awake. Gentle, symmetrical facial exercise is favoured over strong resisted work because overactivity can contribute to unwanted co-movement during reinnervation.

Question 206

Neurological

A 51-year-old cyclist in Victoria reports tingling in the ring and little fingers that worsens when she rests her elbows on the handlebar drops and when her elbows are held flexed. Ulnar nerve compression at the elbow is suspected. Which self-management advice is most appropriate?

  • A. Keep the elbows bent past ninety degrees at night with a pillow to rest the nerve
  • B. Wear a neutral wrist splint overnight and keep the riding position on the handlebars unchanged
  • C. Perform repeated ulnar nerve tensioning glides into full elbow flexion to desensitize the nerve
  • D. Avoid sustained elbow flexion, pad the elbow and consider a night extension splint

The correct answer is D (Avoid sustained elbow flexion, pad the elbow and consider a night extension splint): Elbow flexion stretches the ulnar nerve around the medial epicondyle and raises pressure within the cubital tunnel. Reducing sustained flexion, padding the elbow and using night extension splinting reduce irritation. Wrist splinting treats a different site, and sleeping bent or repeated tensioning adds strain to an already irritated nerve.

Question 207

Neurological

A newborn delivered after shoulder dystocia holds the right arm adducted, internally rotated and extended at the elbow, with the forearm pronated. The grasp reflex is present. Moro response is asymmetrical. Which parent teaching point is most appropriate during the first weeks?

  • A. Firm stretching of the shoulder into end range to prevent contracture formation early
  • B. Gentle passive shoulder range of motion with positioning that avoids pulling on the arm
  • C. Immobilization of the whole arm in a sling until the first clinic review in several weeks
  • D. Lifting the infant by the affected arm to encourage active shoulder activity

The correct answer is B (Gentle passive shoulder range of motion with positioning that avoids pulling on the arm): The posture describes an upper trunk (Erb) palsy, with a preserved grasp suggesting lower roots are spared. Early care protects the plexus while keeping joints mobile, using gentle range of motion and careful handling. Traction on the arm or forceful end range stretching can cause harm.

Question 208

Neurological

After a closed forearm contusion, a clinician explains nerve injury grades. The physiotherapist needs to describe the grade in which the axon is intact but conduction is temporarily blocked, with full recovery expected within weeks to a few months. Which term describes this injury?

  • A. Axonotmesis, with axon disruption but a preserved connective tissue framework
  • B. Neurotmesis, with complete disruption of the axon and surrounding sheath structures
  • C. Wallerian degeneration, with distal axon breakdown following a complete nerve transection
  • D. Neurapraxia, with a focal conduction block and intact axon continuity

The correct answer is D (Neurapraxia, with a focal conduction block and intact axon continuity): Neurapraxia is a reversible conduction block with no axonal loss, and recovery is usually complete without regeneration. Axonotmesis involves axon loss, with regrowth at roughly one millimetre a day. Neurotmesis needs surgical repair. Wallerian degeneration is a process that follows axonal injury, not a grade.

Question 209

Neurological

During follow-up of a patient with a repaired median nerve at the wrist, the physiotherapist taps along the course of the nerve from distal to proximal. Paresthesia is reproduced progressively higher up the forearm over several visits. What does this advancing finding most likely indicate?

  • A. Scar tissue tethering the nerve to surrounding tissue as the wound matures
  • B. Return of protective sensation at the fingertip pad, a late recovery milestone
  • C. Axonal regeneration advancing along the nerve at its growing tip, usually about 1 mm per day
  • D. Reinnervation of the target muscles, confirmed by visible voluntary contraction

The correct answer is C (Axonal regeneration advancing along the nerve at its growing tip, usually about 1 mm per day): An advancing Tinel sign marks the leading edge of regenerating sensory axons and supports ongoing recovery. Return of fingertip sensation is a later milestone and does not move up the forearm over visits. Scar tethering gives a fixed tender point that does not migrate, and muscle reinnervation lags well behind the advancing front, so visible contraction would not yet be expected.

Question 210

Neurological

A 71-year-old retired farmer in Alberta with Parkinson disease takes short shuffling steps and his feet stop at doorways. He walks well when following lines on the floor. Which strategy should the physiotherapist teach to improve his gait in the home?

  • A. Counting each step aloud and concentrating on heel strike
  • B. Talking with family while walking to build automatic gait through dual task practice at home
  • C. External cues such as floor markers or a metronome to lengthen each step
  • D. Leaning forward and walking quickly through doorways to keep momentum and avoid stopping

The correct answer is C (External cues such as floor markers or a metronome to lengthen each step): Basal ganglia dysfunction impairs automatic movement, so external cues such as floor markers or a metronome route movement through more conscious pathways and help with freezing and short steps. Focusing on each movement is usually less effective, extra attention demands such as conversation tend to provoke freezing, and rushing forward increases festinating steps.

Question 211

Neurological

A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease freezes when turning in his narrow kitchen and when approaching the front door, but has no trouble walking a long hallway. He has recently had medication changes. Which finding best distinguishes freezing that is related to wearing off of levodopa from other causes?

  • A. Freezing that clusters before the next dose and eases soon after taking it
  • B. Freezing that appears suddenly together with new weakness on one side of the body
  • C. Freezing that occurs equally across the day with no link to medication timing
  • D. Freezing that is provoked by dizziness on standing with low blood pressure

The correct answer is A (Freezing that clusters before the next dose and eases soon after taking it): Freezing that follows the medication cycle suggests an off period due to wearing off, which the medical team may address with dosing changes. Physiotherapy then teaches cues and turning strategies. Sudden unilateral weakness suggests another problem, and dizziness on standing suggests orthostatic hypotension.

Question 212

Neurological

A physiotherapist performs a pull test on a patient with Parkinson disease by giving a quick backward tug at the shoulders. The patient takes several steps backward and would fall if not caught. What does this result most strongly indicate?

  • A. Normal postural reflexes, with one or two recovery steps being expected
  • B. Impaired postural reflexes, which predict a high risk of falls in later disease
  • C. Orthostatic hypotension from impaired blood pressure control causing brief loss of balance on rapid change
  • D. Cerebellar ataxia with a wide-based gait and overshooting corrections when balance is disturbed

The correct answer is B (Impaired postural reflexes, which predict a high risk of falls in later disease): A response of several steps backward, or no recovery without being caught, reflects loss of postural reflexes, which typically appears in later Parkinson disease and predicts falls. One or two recovery steps would be the normal response, which is why the closest alternative is tempting, but this patient took several. Blood pressure change and cerebellar disease do not explain this response to a shoulder tug. Guard the patient closely during testing.

Question 213

Neurological

A 66-year-old woman with early Parkinson disease has small handwriting and reduced arm swing. Her physiotherapist considers an amplitude based exercise program that uses large, high effort whole body movements in intensive daily sessions. Which principle underlies this approach? She is otherwise independent.

  • A. Rhythmic external cueing, since an auditory beat can compensate for faulty internal movement timing
  • B. Retraining the sense of movement size, since normal effort feels too large to patients
  • C. Lower limb strengthening, since leg weakness contributes to reduced walking speed
  • D. Aerobic conditioning, since improved fitness supports walking and general health

The correct answer is B (Retraining the sense of movement size, since normal effort feels too large to patients): Amplitude focused training works on the sensory miscalibration in Parkinson disease, where patients feel that normal sized movements are too large while producing movements that are too small. Intensive, high effort practice with large movements aims to reset that perception and carry over into daily activity. External cueing helps timing and strengthening or aerobic work help fitness, but none targets the perception of movement size.

Question 214

Neurological

A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease becomes lightheaded each time he rises from his chair at the Calgary day program. Lying blood pressure is 138 over 80 and standing is 108 over 66 after three minutes. Which intervention is most appropriate for the physiotherapist to teach?

  • A. Eating one large meal at midday and walking right after it while his pressure feels stable
  • B. Rising slowly in stages with ankle pumps, and extra fluids if his physician agrees
  • C. Taking a long hot shower first thing in the morning before getting out of bed
  • D. Drinking a large volume of water in one sitting just as he rises to stand

The correct answer is B (Rising slowly in stages with ankle pumps, and extra fluids if his physician agrees): A fall in systolic pressure of at least 20 mmHg on standing confirms orthostatic hypotension, which is common in Parkinson disease. Gradual position changes, muscle pumping and adequate hydration support venous return. Large meals and heat widen blood vessels and lower pressure further, and a single large drink on rising has no time to help.

Question 215

Neurological

A 33-year-old woman in Vancouver with multiple sclerosis notices blurred vision and heavier leg weakness during hot yoga and after a hot shower. Symptoms settle within an hour of cooling down. What should the physiotherapist advise? Her last neurology visit showed stable disease without new lesions.

  • A. Continue hot yoga with longer breaks and rely on hydration to keep the symptoms away
  • B. Arrange urgent neurology review because transient vision loss with heat signals a relapse needing steroids
  • C. Exercise in a cool room with cooling garments, since the symptoms reflect heat sensitivity
  • D. Take a hot bath after exercise to relax tight muscles and shorten the recovery time

The correct answer is C (Exercise in a cool room with cooling garments, since the symptoms reflect heat sensitivity): Uhthoff phenomenon is a temporary worsening of symptoms with raised core temperature, because demyelinated axons conduct poorly when warm. It is not a new relapse, particularly when symptoms settle with cooling and her disease is stable. Cooling strategies and cooler environments let the person remain active, whereas more heat, even after exercise, brings the symptoms back.

Question 216

Neurological

A neurologist reports an Expanded Disability Status Scale score of 6.0 for a client with multiple sclerosis. What does this score most closely indicate about walking? His neurologist has asked the physiotherapist to describe his mobility status for the care plan and for equipment planning.

  • A. Unrestricted walking without aid for more than 500 metres at a normal pace
  • B. Confinement to a wheelchair with inability to take any steps
  • C. Unilateral support such as a cane is needed to walk about 100 metres
  • D. Walking without aid but with limited endurance of about 300 metres

The correct answer is C (Unilateral support such as a cane is needed to walk about 100 metres): An EDSS of 6.0 means a cane or crutch, or unilateral support, is needed to walk about 100 metres with or without resting. Scores near 4 involve unaided walking of roughly 300 to 500 metres, and scores of 7 and above involve wheelchair use as the main means of mobility.

Question 217

Neurological

A 29-year-old man with a history of unexplained vision loss last year feels an electric shock that runs down his spine and into his limbs whenever he flexes his neck during testing. Strength and reflexes are otherwise normal. Which interpretation fits best? Cranial nerve testing is normal.

  • A. Irritation of a cervical nerve root from foraminal narrowing causing arm pain on neck extension
  • B. Irritation of demyelinated dorsal column pathways in the cervical cord
  • C. Vertebral artery insufficiency causing brainstem symptoms during sustained neck rotation at end range
  • D. Increased dural tension from neck flexion, consistent with a positive slump test in the lumbar spine

The correct answer is B (Irritation of demyelinated dorsal column pathways in the cervical cord): Lhermitte sign is an electric sensation down the spine on neck flexion that suggests cervical cord pathology, classically demyelination in multiple sclerosis, though it can occur with other cord lesions. Nerve root irritation produces arm pain in a dermatomal pattern, slump testing provokes leg symptoms, and vertebral artery problems cause brainstem symptoms with rotation rather than a shock with flexion.

Question 218

Neurological

A 47-year-old man with progressive multiple sclerosis has increased calf tone that causes plantarflexor clonus and a toe drag during swing. Which combination is most appropriate within physiotherapy? He lives in Kingston, works part time from home, and wants to keep walking in his neighbourhood.

  • A. Calf stretching and a night resting splint, with walking practice deferred until clonus settles
  • B. Cold application to the calf with calf stretching and gait practice, without an orthosis
  • C. Daily calf stretching, positioning, gait practice and an ankle foot orthosis for weak dorsiflexion
  • D. High intensity resisted calf strengthening with gait practice and a heel raise in the shoe

The correct answer is C (Daily calf stretching, positioning, gait practice and an ankle foot orthosis for weak dorsiflexion): Spasticity management combines sustained stretching, positioning, active movement and orthoses where needed, with medical review of medications. Stretching with a night splint is useful, but deferring walking removes the practice he needs to keep his function. Cold can briefly lower tone but does not address the toe drag, and resisted calf work with a heel raise adds to plantarflexor overactivity.

Question 219

Neurological

A 36-year-old woman reports new leg numbness that began three days ago and has persisted. She had a viral illness last week and no fever now. Which feature is required to consider this a relapse of multiple sclerosis rather than a pseudo relapse?

  • A. Symptoms lasting a few minutes and settling quickly with cooling the body
  • B. Symptoms occurring mainly after exercise and ending within thirty minutes of rest
  • C. Symptoms that coincide with a urinary infection and fever above 38 degrees
  • D. New or worsening neurological symptoms lasting 24 hours or more without fever or infection

The correct answer is D (New or worsening neurological symptoms lasting 24 hours or more without fever or infection): A relapse is generally defined as new or worsening neurological symptoms lasting at least 24 hours, in the absence of fever or infection and separated from a prior attack by at least 30 days. Transient heat or exercise related changes and symptoms with infection are pseudo relapses.

Question 220

Neurological

A 55-year-old woman has a wide based, lurching gait. She overshoots when reaching for a cup, and her finger to nose test shows a tremor that worsens as she nears the target. Her eyes closed do not worsen her balance. Which lesion site best explains the findings?

  • A. The dorsal columns, causing loss of position sense in the legs
  • B. The vestibular nerve, causing positional vertigo when turning the head
  • C. The basal ganglia, causing a resting tremor and bradykinesia
  • D. The cerebellum, causing ataxia and an intention tremor

The correct answer is D (The cerebellum, causing ataxia and an intention tremor): Wide based gait, dysmetria and an intention tremor that grows near the target point to cerebellar disease. Sensory ataxia from dorsal column loss worsens markedly with eyes closed, and parkinsonian tremor is present at rest rather than with purposeful movement.

Question 221

Neurological

A 60-year-old man sways mildly with eyes open but falls sideways within seconds when he closes his eyes with feet together. He also has reduced vibration sense at both ankles. Which interpretation of the Romberg test is most appropriate? He denies dizziness.

  • A. A positive result, suggesting lost proprioceptive input when vision stops compensating
  • B. A positive result suggesting vestibular loss, usually with dizziness
  • C. A result that indicates a cerebellar lesion, since balance is lost when visual input is removed
  • D. A positive result suggesting upper motor neuron weakness in both legs

The correct answer is A (A positive result, suggesting lost proprioceptive input when vision stops compensating): The Romberg test is positive when balance is lost on eye closure, showing reliance on vision to cover for proprioceptive or vestibular loss. With reduced vibration sense at both ankles, a dorsal column or peripheral sensory problem is likely. Cerebellar ataxia typically persists with eyes open as well. Vestibular loss usually brings dizziness, which he denies, and his findings are sensory rather than weakness.

Question 222

Neurological

A physiotherapist asks a patient to rapidly pat one hand on the other palm, turning it over each time. The movement is irregular and clumsy with uneven timing, but its size does not shrink. What is this finding called, and which structure does it suggest? Her strength and sensation are normal.

  • A. Bradykinesia, suggesting basal ganglia loss with a decrement in amplitude
  • B. Dysdiadochokinesia, which suggests cerebellar dysfunction on the affected side of the body
  • C. Dysmetria, suggesting cerebellar dysfunction in the ipsilateral limb on reaching tasks
  • D. Rigidity with cogwheeling, suggesting basal ganglia involvement and loss of dopamine

The correct answer is B (Dysdiadochokinesia, which suggests cerebellar dysfunction on the affected side of the body): Impaired rapid alternating movements are called dysdiadochokinesia and indicate ipsilateral cerebellar dysfunction. Bradykinesia is the closest alternative, but it shows a progressive decline in amplitude and speed in Parkinson disease, which is not described here. Dysmetria is overshoot on reaching, and cogwheel rigidity is a tone finding found on passive movement.

Question 223

Neurological

A 63-year-old woman experiences brief spinning for about 30 seconds when she lies back in bed or looks up. During the Dix-Hallpike maneuver to the right, upbeating torsional nystagmus appears after a short delay and fades within a minute. Which diagnosis is most likely?

  • A. Vestibular neuritis affecting the right inferior branch of the vestibular nerve
  • B. Right posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of the inner ear
  • C. Meniere disease with fluctuating hearing and aural fullness
  • D. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency with brainstem signs and sustained vertigo

The correct answer is B (Right posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of the inner ear): Brief positional vertigo with delayed, fatigable upbeating torsional nystagmus toward the lower ear is typical of posterior canal BPPV. Vestibular neuritis causes continuous vertigo lasting days, Meniere disease causes attacks lasting longer than 20 minutes with hearing symptoms, and brainstem ischemia shows other neurological signs.

Question 224

Neurological

A 63-year-old woman in Hamilton has had three weeks of brief spinning when she rolls over in bed. Her physiotherapist confirms right posterior canal BPPV with a positive Dix-Hallpike test. She has no neck restrictions or vascular symptoms. Which treatment is most appropriate to reposition the displaced otoconia?

  • A. Repeated head shaking with the neck flexed to loosen debris within the canal
  • B. The Brandt-Daroff habituation exercise, performed once in the clinic as the sole treatment
  • C. The log roll maneuver performed toward the unaffected side while lying supine
  • D. The Epley maneuver, moving the head through staged positions to reposition the otoconia

The correct answer is D (The Epley maneuver, moving the head through staged positions to reposition the otoconia): The Epley maneuver uses sequenced head positions to move otoconia from the posterior canal back to the vestibule. The log roll is used for horizontal canal BPPV, and Brandt-Daroff is a home habituation exercise rather than a single clinic repositioning treatment.

Question 225

Neurological

During a supine roll test, a patient develops intense spinning with horizontal nystagmus beating toward the lower ear on rolling to either side, stronger when the head is turned to the right. The Dix-Hallpike test is negative. Which diagnosis fits best?

  • A. Posterior canal BPPV on the right with upbeating nystagmus
  • B. Central positional vertigo with direction changing nystagmus unrelated to head position
  • C. Anterior canal BPPV with downbeating nystagmus on supine positioning
  • D. Horizontal canal BPPV, geotropic form, affecting the right side

The correct answer is D (Horizontal canal BPPV, geotropic form, affecting the right side): Bidirectional horizontal nystagmus beating toward the undermost ear with a negative Dix-Hallpike indicates geotropic horizontal canal BPPV, with the stronger response marking the affected side. Posterior canal BPPV produces torsional upbeating nystagmus in the Dix-Hallpike position.

Question 226

Neurological

A 44-year-old man develops sudden severe spinning vertigo with nausea lasting two days. There is no hearing loss, tinnitus or neurological deficit. Spontaneous horizontal nystagmus beats to the left and worsens when he looks left, and the head impulse test is abnormal when the head is turned to the right. Which diagnosis is most likely?

  • A. Meniere disease with hearing loss and fluctuating aural fullness
  • B. Right vestibular neuritis with reduced peripheral function of the affected inner ear
  • C. Posterior canal BPPV with brief vertigo on lying back
  • D. Cerebellar stroke with severe truncal ataxia and normal head impulse test

The correct answer is B (Right vestibular neuritis with reduced peripheral function of the affected inner ear): Acute prolonged vertigo with spontaneous horizontal nystagmus, an abnormal head impulse test toward the lesion side and no auditory or central signs fits vestibular neuritis. A normal head impulse test in this setting would raise concern for a central cause such as cerebellar stroke.

Question 227

Neurological

A 58-year-old woman recovering from unilateral vestibular hypofunction reports blurred vision when walking and moving her head quickly. Which exercise is most specific to improve this symptom? She has no hearing loss and no positional vertigo, and her neck movements are pain free.

  • A. Brandt-Daroff habituation exercises moving from sitting to side lying repeatedly twice each day
  • B. Gaze stabilization drills holding a visual target while turning the head
  • C. Balance training on foam with the eyes closed to retrain vestibular and somatosensory input
  • D. Smooth pursuit tracking of a slowly moving target while keeping the head held still

The correct answer is B (Gaze stabilization drills holding a visual target while turning the head): Gaze stabilization drills challenge the vestibulo-ocular reflex and promote adaptation, which reduces blurred vision during head movement. Habituation exercises treat positional vertigo, which she does not have, and foam balance work trains postural control rather than the reflex. Pursuit tracking with the head still does not load the vestibulo-ocular reflex at all.

Question 228

Neurological

A physiotherapist screens a 50-year-old man who reports recurrent episodes of spinning lasting about three hours, with a roaring sound in one ear, muffled hearing and fullness on the same side. Which condition is most consistent with this triad? He has no history of head injury.

  • A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo with otoconia in a semicircular canal
  • B. Vestibular migraine with headache and sensitivity to light
  • C. Acoustic neuroma with slowly progressive hearing loss and no episodic vertigo
  • D. Meniere disease, from endolymphatic fluid pressure change in the inner ear

The correct answer is D (Meniere disease, from endolymphatic fluid pressure change in the inner ear): Episodic vertigo lasting from twenty minutes to hours, with tinnitus, fluctuating hearing loss and aural fullness, characterizes Meniere disease. BPPV attacks last under a minute and have no hearing loss. Acoustic neuroma causes steady progressive hearing loss.

Question 229

Neurological

During an outpatient session in Moncton, a 27-year-old man with epilepsy suddenly falls and has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting about two minutes. Which action should the physiotherapist take? The clinic is quiet, and a colleague is nearby. He has no history of recent head injury.

  • A. Restrain his limbs gently to prevent injury and speak loudly to bring back awareness quickly
  • B. Lower him gently, call an ambulance immediately and keep him flat until paramedics arrive on scene
  • C. Hold his jaw open and place a padded bite block between his teeth to protect airways
  • D. Protect the head, loosen tight clothing, turn him onto his side afterward and note the time

The correct answer is D (Protect the head, loosen tight clothing, turn him onto his side afterward and note the time): Safe seizure care protects the head, clears the area, times the event and places the person in a recovery position once movements stop. Nothing is placed in the mouth and limbs are not restrained, because both can cause injury. Lying flat risks airway compromise, and an ambulance is called when a seizure lasts five minutes or longer, recurs, or follows injury.

Question 230

Neurological

A patient tells a physiotherapist that before some of her seizures she smells burning rubber and feels a rising sensation in her stomach. The experience is identical each time and lasts under a minute. What do these experiences represent? She works as a nurse in Fredericton and has been seizure free for several months on medication.

  • A. A migraine aura caused by cortical spreading depression in the occipital lobe
  • B. A transient ischemic attack with brief sensory disturbance
  • C. A focal aware seizure, which may precede progression to a larger seizure
  • D. A psychogenic non-epileptic event, triggered by stress or anxiety

The correct answer is C (A focal aware seizure, which may precede progression to a larger seizure): An aura is itself a focal aware seizure, commonly arising in the temporal lobe with olfactory or epigastric sensations. The stereotyped, brief and identical pattern before each seizure supports an epileptic origin, whereas a migraine aura is usually visual and builds over minutes. A transient ischemic attack is not stereotyped, and a stress related event does not fit her seizure history. Recognizing the aura gives time to move to a safe position.

Question 231

Neurological

A 19-year-old swimmer with well controlled epilepsy asks whether she can continue to train at her local pool in Kelowna. What advice is most appropriate? She takes her medication regularly, sleeps well, and has had no seizure for two years. Her neurologist has cleared her to swim.

  • A. Swimming should stop until another two years pass without a seizure, since water carries high risk
  • B. Swimming without supervision is fine if she takes an extra medication dose before each session
  • C. Training alone in a quiet lane is acceptable because her seizures are controlled and sleep good
  • D. Exercise is encouraged with a buddy and a lifeguard who knows about her condition

The correct answer is D (Exercise is encouraged with a buddy and a lifeguard who knows about her condition): Exercise generally does not provoke seizures and offers health benefits, so a well controlled swimmer cleared by her neurologist can continue. Water activities carry a drowning risk if a seizure occurs, so a buddy and an informed lifeguard matter. Good control and good sleep do not remove that risk, and extra medication is never a substitute for supervision.

Question 232

Neurological

A 82-year-old woman admitted after a hip fracture is usually oriented, but over one day becomes drowsy, then agitated and confused, with fluctuating attention. Her family reports that her memory was normal. Which condition best explains these changes? She has no fever.

  • A. Dementia with Lewy bodies, which can fluctuate in attention and alertness over days to weeks
  • B. Vascular dementia, which progresses in step-wise declines after each small stroke over months
  • C. Delirium, an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention that often has a medical cause
  • D. Depression with withdrawal and slowed responses that develops gradually over several weeks

The correct answer is C (Delirium, an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention that often has a medical cause): Rapid onset over one day, fluctuating attention, drowsiness and agitation, with normal memory beforehand, define delirium, a medical issue needing prompt assessment for infection, medication effects, pain or metabolic causes. Dementia with Lewy bodies can fluctuate, but it develops over months and years. Vascular dementia and depression also evolve over weeks to months rather than a single day.

Question 233

Neurological

A physiotherapist screens a 70-year-old client using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and records a total of 22 out of 30 after adding a point for low education. How should this score be interpreted? He lives alone and manages his own medications and finances.

  • A. Normal for his age, because the education point lifts the score into range
  • B. Below the usual cutoff of 26, suggesting possible impairment needing further assessment
  • C. Moderate dementia, because scores under 24 correspond to a defined severity stage
  • D. Borderline, so screening should be repeated in a year with no referral

The correct answer is B (Below the usual cutoff of 26, suggesting possible impairment needing further assessment): A MoCA score under 26 suggests possible impairment, but it is a screening tool and does not provide a diagnosis or a stage of severity. The education point is already included in his total of 22, so the result is still below the cutoff. A fuller assessment by the medical team is required rather than waiting a year. Physiotherapists use results to tailor instruction, safety planning and communication.

Question 234

Neurological

A daughter in Charlottetown asks the physiotherapist about her 76-year-old father, who was recently diagnosed with mild Alzheimer disease and still walks daily. She wonders whether supervised exercise could help him or whether it is unsafe now. Which statement reflects current evidence best?

  • A. Regular supervised physical activity supports mobility, mood, sleep and falls prevention in dementia
  • B. Regular exercise improves mobility and mood, but evidence for sleep or falls effects is lacking
  • C. Exercise suits mild dementia, but strength and balance training should wait until later stages
  • D. Exercise is mainly useful for slowing memory decline, so mobility goals come second now

The correct answer is A (Regular supervised physical activity supports mobility, mood, sleep and falls prevention in dementia): Exercise cannot reverse neuronal loss or restore memory, but it improves function, mood, sleep, strength and balance and can reduce falls. People with mild to moderate dementia can safely take part in aerobic, strength and balance training with supervision and adaptations. Waiting for later stages loses the benefit, since falls risk and decline in mobility are best addressed early, and memory is not the main target.

Question 235

Neurological

A 6-year-old walks indoors and outdoors without a mobility aid and climbs stairs holding a railing, but can barely manage a few running steps or small jumps and avoids the gravel and busy hallways at recess. Which Gross Motor Function Classification System level fits best? He attends school in Lethbridge and his parents want to plan therapy.

  • A. Level I, with walking without limitations and mild reduced running speed
  • B. Level II, with walking in most settings but limits on uneven ground and in crowds
  • C. Level III, with walking using a hand held device and a wheelchair outdoors
  • D. Level IV, with short distance walking using a walker and powered mobility

The correct answer is B (Level II, with walking in most settings but limits on uneven ground and in crowds): This child walks in most settings without an aid, uses a rail on stairs and can barely run or jump, which fits Level II. Level I children run and jump with only mild reductions in speed and balance. Level III requires a hand held device for walking, and Level IV depends on wheeled mobility in most settings.

Question 236

Neurological

A 9-year-old boy with Down syndrome joining a school gymnastics program in Mississauga complains of neck pain and has new clumsiness in his hands and an unsteady gait. His parents ask about tumbling activities. Which concern should the physiotherapist prioritize?

  • A. Cervical muscle strain from repeated tumbling, managed with rest, heat and gradual progression back to training
  • B. Hip instability or dysplasia explaining the unsteady gait, managed with imaging before further tumbling activities
  • C. Peripheral nerve entrapment at the wrist from gripping the bars, managed with a splint
  • D. Possible atlantoaxial instability, needing medical review and no neck loading before more activity

The correct answer is D (Possible atlantoaxial instability, needing medical review and no neck loading before more activity): Children with Down syndrome have increased ligamentous laxity, and atlantoaxial instability can compress the spinal cord. Neck pain with new hand clumsiness and gait change together point to the cord, so medical assessment is needed and activities that load the cervical spine are paused. Muscle strain, hip instability and wrist entrapment each explain only part of the picture and miss the cord signs.

Question 237

Neurological

A 7-year-old girl in Quebec City has marked difficulty tying shoes, catching a ball and handwriting. Her intelligence and vision are normal. Examination shows no weakness, spasticity or sensory loss. Which diagnosis best fits? Her teacher has noticed the problems for two years.

  • A. Mild hemiplegic cerebral palsy, a nonprogressive motor disorder affecting one side
  • B. Specific learning disorder in writing, a difficulty with spelling and composition unrelated to movement
  • C. Developmental coordination disorder, a motor difficulty not explained by another condition
  • D. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, where inattention fully explains the clumsiness and poor ball skills

The correct answer is C (Developmental coordination disorder, a motor difficulty not explained by another condition): Developmental coordination disorder involves motor skills well below expectation for age that affect daily tasks, in the absence of another neurological, intellectual or visual explanation. Normal tone, strength and sensation make cerebral palsy unlikely, and difficulty with catching and tying shoes goes beyond a writing or attention problem.

Question 238

Neurological

A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because he falls often and rises from the floor by pushing his hands up his thighs. His calves look enlarged. Which finding best supports Duchenne muscular dystrophy? His speech is delayed, and his family has no similar history.

  • A. Proximal weakness shown by the Gowers maneuver, with calf pseudohypertrophy
  • B. Floppy proximal weakness with tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes, as in spinal muscular atrophy
  • C. Distal weakness first with high arched feet and absent ankle reflexes, as in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
  • D. Proximal weakness with an eyelid rash, as in juvenile dermatomyositis

The correct answer is A (Proximal weakness shown by the Gowers maneuver, with calf pseudohypertrophy): The Gowers maneuver shows weak proximal hip muscles, and enlarged calves from fatty replacement of muscle (pseudohypertrophy) are classic for Duchenne. Spinal muscular atrophy and dermatomyositis can also cause proximal weakness, but neither enlarges the calves, and a distal pattern with high arches points to a hereditary neuropathy. Creatine kinase is markedly raised in Duchenne.

Question 239

Neurological

A first-time parent at a well baby clinic in Fredericton asks the physiotherapist when her healthy, full term infant should be able to sit independently without support. The infant is currently four months old and rolls from front to back. When is independent sitting expected in typical development?

  • A. About six to eight months, with most infants sitting steadily by nine months
  • B. About ten to eleven months, after crawling on hands and knees has become fluent
  • C. About twelve months, usually just before the first independent steps appear
  • D. About four months, once rolling from front to back is established and head control is good

The correct answer is A (About six to eight months, with most infants sitting steadily by nine months): Most infants sit without support around six to eight months, and absence of independent sitting by nine months merits review. Rolling is expected earlier and does not mean sitting is due yet. Sitting comes before fluent crawling, and independent walking is typically around twelve to fifteen months.

Question 240

Neurological

A 10-week-old infant has a head tilt to the right with the chin rotated left, and a small firm lump in the right sternocleidomastoid. Hip screening is already booked. A physiotherapist plans an approach. Which intervention is most appropriate? He was born at term after a breech presentation.

  • A. Gentle stretching of the right sternocleidomastoid, positioning and tummy time
  • B. Referral for surgical release of the right sternocleidomastoid before three months of age
  • C. Hip ultrasound before stretching begins, since breech presentation raises the risk of dysplasia
  • D. Gentle stretching of the left sternocleidomastoid with positioning and supervised tummy time

The correct answer is A (Gentle stretching of the right sternocleidomastoid, positioning and tummy time): Congenital muscular torticollis responds well to early, gentle stretching of the tight side, here the right sternocleidomastoid, with positioning and tummy time to build neck strength. Stretching the left side does not lengthen the shortened muscle. Surgery is reserved for cases that fail conservative care. Hip screening after breech birth is reasonable, but it is already arranged and need not delay therapy.

Question 241

Neurological

A physiotherapist in a Saskatoon stroke unit tests balance in a 72-year-old man two months after a left middle cerebral artery stroke. He walks with a cane and reports two near falls at home. His Berg Balance Scale score is 38 out of 56. How is this score best interpreted?

  • A. A score that predicts safe independent walking without his cane on level surfaces in his home
  • B. A score above the cutoff of 45, indicating low fall risk despite his repeated near falls
  • C. A score below 45, suggesting elevated fall risk and the need for balance intervention
  • D. A score within the range that suggests low fall risk once his cane is used

The correct answer is C (A score below 45, suggesting elevated fall risk and the need for balance intervention): Scores under 45 on the Berg Balance Scale are associated with increased fall risk, and lower scores indicate greater impairment. A score of 38 calls for balance intervention and review of the walking aid and home environment. It sits below the cutoff, so it cannot indicate low risk, and the cane use does not remove the risk the score reflects.

Question 242

Neurological

A physiotherapist in a Calgary movement disorders clinic times a 78-year-old woman with Parkinson disease on the Timed Up and Go test using her usual cane. She completes it in 16 seconds with a short shuffling turn and reports one fall last month. Which interpretation and action is most appropriate?

  • A. A time above the 13.5 second fall risk cutoff, so a fall prevention plan is warranted
  • B. A time reflecting slowed turning alone, so turning practice suffices and her fall risk is minor
  • C. A time within expected range for her age, so balance work and home review are unneeded
  • D. A time that cannot be interpreted because assistive device use invalidates the test result entirely

The correct answer is A (A time above the 13.5 second fall risk cutoff, so a fall prevention plan is warranted): A time over about 13.5 seconds on the TUG is linked with elevated fall risk in community dwelling older adults. Her 16 seconds, shuffling turn and recent fall together should prompt balance, strength and gait training plus home safety review. The test is performed with the person's usual walking aid, and it is widely used in neurological populations including Parkinson disease.

Question 243

Neurological

A physiotherapist moves a patient's elbow passively through range and feels a catch in the middle of the movement, followed by minimal resistance for the remainder. Which Modified Ashworth Scale grade fits? The patient is a 58-year-old man with chronic stroke affecting his right arm.

  • A. Grade 1+, a catch followed by minimal resistance through under half the range
  • B. Grade 2, a more marked increase in tone through most of the range, with easy movement
  • C. Grade 1, a slight catch and release at the end of the range of motion
  • D. Grade 3, a considerable increase in tone that makes passive movement difficult throughout

The correct answer is A (Grade 1+, a catch followed by minimal resistance through under half the range): Grade 1+ on the Modified Ashworth Scale is a slight increase in tone shown by a catch in the middle of the range, followed by minimal resistance through the remainder. A catch and release at the very end of the range is grade 1, tone through most of the range is grade 2, and difficult passive movement is grade 3.

Question 244

Neurological

A 69-year-old retired nurse in Ottawa has a hand tremor. It appears when her hands rest in her lap and eases when she reaches for a cup. She also has a stooped posture, reduced facial expression and slowed rising from a chair. Which condition best explains her findings?

  • A. Essential tremor, with an action tremor that worsens when holding a posture or reaching
  • B. Cerebellar disease, with an intention tremor that grows as the hand nears a target
  • C. Parkinson disease, with a resting tremor, bradykinesia, reduced expression and postural change
  • D. Physiologic tremor from caffeine, which is fine, fast and present in both hands

The correct answer is C (Parkinson disease, with a resting tremor, bradykinesia, reduced expression and postural change): A tremor at rest that lessens with purposeful movement, plus slowness, reduced expression and stooped posture, fits Parkinson disease. Essential tremor increases with sustained posture or action, and cerebellar tremor increases near the target. A physiologic tremor would not explain the slowing and posture.

Question 245

Neurological

A 66-year-old man with hypertension has sudden severe vertigo, vomiting and inability to sit unsupported. Spontaneous nystagmus changes direction depending on gaze, and the head impulse test is normal. Hearing is intact. Which conclusion should guide the physiotherapist? He is on a blood thinner.

  • A. Meniere disease is likely, so advise salt reduction and routine follow up next month
  • B. Vestibular neuritis is likely, so begin gaze stabilization exercises at today's session
  • C. Posterior canal BPPV is likely, so perform the Epley maneuver during this visit
  • D. A central cause such as a cerebellar stroke, needing urgent medical referral

The correct answer is D (A central cause such as a cerebellar stroke, needing urgent medical referral): Direction changing gaze evoked nystagmus, a normal head impulse test and severe truncal ataxia in a patient with vascular risk factors are central signs. This needs emergency assessment, not vestibular rehabilitation. Neuritis would show an abnormal head impulse test and unidirectional nystagmus.

Question 246

Neurological

A 47-year-old electrician has numbness of the ring and little fingers with weak finger abduction. Sensation over the medial forearm is normal, and the problem worsens when the elbow is flexed. Neck movement does not change his symptoms. Which lesion site is most likely?

  • A. The ulnar nerve at the elbow, with sparing of the medial forearm skin
  • B. The C8 nerve root, which would also reduce sensation over the medial forearm
  • C. The median nerve at the wrist, which would weaken thumb opposition
  • D. The radial nerve in the arm, which would cause weak wrist extension

The correct answer is A (The ulnar nerve at the elbow, with sparing of the medial forearm skin): The medial forearm is supplied by the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, which arises from the C8 and T1 roots and is spared in an ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow. Elbow flexion provocation and a normal response to neck movement favour a peripheral site over a root lesion.

Question 247

Neurological

A 31-year-old man collapses in a Toronto gym after standing quickly from a bench press. He is pale and sweaty before falling, recovers within a minute with no confusion, and has brief limb jerks after he is on the floor. Which diagnosis is most likely?

  • A. A focal aware seizure, which typically has no color change or sweating
  • B. Generalized tonic-clonic epilepsy, which usually involves prolonged confusion afterward
  • C. Convulsive syncope, a faint with brief jerking from reduced brain blood flow
  • D. A transient ischemic attack, which causes sustained weakness lasting at least an hour

The correct answer is C (Convulsive syncope, a faint with brief jerking from reduced brain blood flow): A prodrome of pallor and sweating, a clear trigger, rapid recovery without postictal confusion and brief jerks after falling are typical of convulsive syncope. Epileptic seizures usually lead to several minutes of confusion. Medical follow up for cardiac causes is still advised after exertional collapse.

Question 248

Neurological

A 74-year-old man has vivid visual hallucinations of small children, daily fluctuations in alertness and mild parkinsonian rigidity. Memory is relatively preserved early on. Which diagnosis best fits this pattern? His wife in Moncton reports that these episodes began six months ago and have been worsening.

  • A. Alzheimer disease, characterized by early prominent loss of recent memory
  • B. Dementia with Lewy bodies, characterized by fluctuations, hallucinations and parkinsonism
  • C. Normal pressure hydrocephalus, characterized by gait change and incontinence
  • D. Vascular dementia, characterized by stepwise decline after strokes

The correct answer is B (Dementia with Lewy bodies, characterized by fluctuations, hallucinations and parkinsonism): Recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism are core features of dementia with Lewy bodies. Alzheimer disease usually begins with memory loss, and vascular dementia follows a stepwise course. Normal pressure hydrocephalus features gait disturbance with incontinence.

Question 249

Neurological

A 5-month-old infant in Winnipeg lies like a frog with limbs flat on the surface, has a weak cry and little spontaneous movement, and cannot lift the head in prone. Reflexes are absent. Which assessment finding would most strongly suggest a lower motor neuron cause, such as spinal muscular atrophy?

  • A. Generalized hypotonia with poor eye contact, seizures and brisk reflexes, suggesting a central cause
  • B. Weakness of face and shoulders with preserved reflexes and a normal tongue, as in congenital myopathy
  • C. Hypotonia with a large tongue, dry skin and prolonged jaundice, suggesting congenital hypothyroidism
  • D. Alert social smiling with weakness, absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations

The correct answer is D (Alert social smiling with weakness, absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations): Infants with spinal muscular atrophy are typically bright and alert yet weak, with absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations from anterior horn cell loss. Poor interaction with seizures and brisk reflexes suggests a central cause, a large tongue with prolonged jaundice suggests hypothyroidism, and preserved reflexes with a normal tongue point away from a lower motor neuron disease.

Question 250

Neurological

A 3-year-old born at 28 weeks has stiff legs that cross in a scissoring pattern when held upright, with toe walking. Arm function is mildly affected and cognition is age appropriate. Which type of cerebral palsy best matches this presentation?

  • A. Athetoid cerebral palsy, with involuntary writhing movements and fluctuating tone
  • B. Ataxic cerebral palsy, with intention tremor and wide based gait
  • C. Spastic diplegia, with legs more affected than arms, common after preterm birth
  • D. Spastic quadriplegia, with all four limbs equally and severely affected

The correct answer is C (Spastic diplegia, with legs more affected than arms, common after preterm birth): Scissoring, toe walking and legs more affected than arms after preterm birth is the classic pattern of spastic diplegia, often linked with periventricular white matter injury. Dyskinetic forms show writhing movements and ataxic forms show cerebellar signs.

Question 251

Neurological

A 34-year-old teacher in a Halifax clinic becomes breathless, dizzy and tingly in both hands during a balance assessment, saying she feels she is dying. Vital signs are stable and she has no chest pain. Which immediate response by the physiotherapist is most appropriate?

  • A. Have her breathe into a paper bag while you stay beside her
  • B. Guide slow diaphragmatic breathing while seated, using a calm and steady voice
  • C. Lay her flat with the legs raised and monitor until symptoms settle
  • D. Call emergency services and start oxygen by mask while she waits

The correct answer is B (Guide slow diaphragmatic breathing while seated, using a calm and steady voice): Overbreathing during a panic attack lowers carbon dioxide and produces the tingling and dizziness described, and her vital signs are stable with no chest pain. Calm presence and slow diaphragmatic breathing restore comfort and give her control. Emergency transfer with oxygen is tempting because she says she is dying, but nothing in her findings supports it. Lying flat suits fainting, and a paper bag is no longer recommended.

Question 252

Neurological

A 41-year-old man has had ascending leg weakness and absent ankle reflexes for ten days after a gastrointestinal illness. His heart rate swings between 48 and 120 beats per minute during bed mobility. Which approach for his acute-phase physiotherapy is best?

  • A. Provide passive range of motion with vital sign checks and begin resisted work once reflexes return
  • B. Use short low-intensity sessions with close vital sign monitoring, avoiding fatiguing exercise
  • C. Defer physiotherapy until heart rate variation settles, then begin graded strengthening
  • D. Start moderate walking and strengthening three times weekly to limit disuse weakness

The correct answer is B (Use short low-intensity sessions with close vital sign monitoring, avoiding fatiguing exercise): Autonomic instability and fatigable weakness mark the acute phase of this inflammatory polyneuropathy. Brief low-load sessions with vital sign monitoring limit complications without overworking weak muscle. Passive movement with later strengthening is tempting because it sounds cautious, but resisted work should wait until fatigue and autonomic swings are settling, not simply until reflexes return. Delaying all care allows contracture and skin problems.

Question 253

Neurological

A 38-year-old woman with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis reports that her vision blurs and legs weaken during warm showers and summer walks, then settle within an hour of cooling. No new symptoms persist at rest. Which explanation and plan fit best?

  • A. A heat-related transient conduction change, managed by cooling and shorter exercise bouts in a cool setting
  • B. Pseudo-relapse caused by infection, requiring urine culture screening and medical review before exercise resumes
  • C. A new relapse, managed by medical review for steroid treatment and a pause in exercise
  • D. Fatigue-related weakness, managed by pacing, scheduled rests and lower-intensity exercise

The correct answer is A (A heat-related transient conduction change, managed by cooling and shorter exercise bouts in a cool setting): Symptoms that appear with raised body temperature and resolve within an hour of cooling describe a transient conduction block, not a relapse. Pre-cooling, cool clothing, fans and shorter exercise periods reduce the effect. Infection can also cause a temporary worsening, which is tempting, but her symptoms track heat exposure and no other illness is described. Fatigue pacing does not address the temperature trigger.

Question 254

Neurological

A 62-year-old man who had paralytic poliomyelitis in childhood reports new fatigue and weakness in the legs he used heavily for decades. Strength testing shows no new deficit. He walks with a cane and wants to keep gardening. Which exercise advice is best for him?

  • A. Increase high-repetition resistance training to the point of muscle burning each session to rebuild strength
  • B. Stop all physical activity so the remaining motor neurons are protected
  • C. Commence maximal-effort intervals three times weekly to rebuild lost strength
  • D. Pace activity with rest breaks and use submaximal exercise, avoiding overuse of already weak muscles

The correct answer is D (Pace activity with rest breaks and use submaximal exercise, avoiding overuse of already weak muscles): New fatigue in a polio survivor reflects strain on surviving motor units that have enlarged over many years. Pacing, energy conservation and gentle non-fatiguing exercise protect them while keeping fitness. Heavy resistance or maximal intervals drive further decline. Total rest is also unhelpful because deconditioning adds to fatigue.

Question 255

Neurological

An 82-year-old woman recovering from hip fracture surgery on a Saskatoon ward was alert yesterday. Today she is drowsy, loses track of your instructions, picks at her blanket and calls you by her daughter's name. Her family says this is new. What is the best action?

  • A. Stop therapy, reorient her gently and let the family stay with her through the afternoon
  • B. Continue gentle mobilization with calm reorientation, and mention the change at the next scheduled team rounds
  • C. Check vital signs and pain, then document the findings for the physician's routine review
  • D. Pause therapy and promptly report the sudden change to the nurse and physician as possible delirium

The correct answer is D (Pause therapy and promptly report the sudden change to the nurse and physician as possible delirium): Acute onset, fluctuating attention and disorganized thinking over hours to days indicate delirium, a medical emergency often driven by infection, pain, medications or metabolic change. Prompt reporting lets the team look for the cause. Calm reorientation and family presence are helpful and tempting, but they do not replace telling the nurse and physician now. Dementia develops gradually and would not explain a change from yesterday.

Question 256

Neurological

A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia, newly started on an antipsychotic, feels light-headed when he stands from the plinth at the start of each session. Seated blood pressure is normal. Which instruction best reduces his risk of falling? He walks independently and needs a position-change technique he can apply at every session.

  • A. Use compression stockings and encourage generous fluids before each session to expand circulating blood volume
  • B. Move in stages with a seated pause before standing, and measure standing pressure if symptoms persist
  • C. Stand quickly and begin walking so the leg muscle pump can restore his pressure
  • D. Ask his prescriber to move the dose timing so sessions fall late in the day

The correct answer is B (Move in stages with a seated pause before standing, and measure standing pressure if symptoms persist): Many antipsychotics block receptors that help the vessels tighten on standing, causing postural hypotension. Gradual staged changes of position give the circulation time to adapt, and measuring standing pressure documents the problem for the prescriber. Compression stockings and fluids can help orthostatic hypotension in general, but they are not a technique he can apply at every position change. Dose timing is the prescriber's decision.

Question 257

Neurological

A 19-year-old university student with restrictive anorexia nervosa is referred for a stress fracture of the tibia. Her body mass index is 15.5 and resting heart rate is 44 beats per minute with dizziness on standing. What is the most appropriate approach?

  • A. Continue weight-bearing rehabilitation with heart rate monitoring, and refer her to a dietitian later
  • B. Offer non-weight-bearing cycling under a heart rate ceiling and review in two weeks
  • C. Limit exercise to what the medical team clears, share findings with them, and agree a plan
  • D. Discuss her low weight and refer her to a counsellor, then continue the tibial program

The correct answer is C (Limit exercise to what the medical team clears, share findings with them, and agree a plan): Low body mass, bradycardia and orthostatic symptoms signal medical instability, and low energy availability also delays bone healing. Exercise should be set with the medical team, who decide the safe limits, and sharing the findings protects her. Non-weight-bearing cycling sounds protective for the tibia, but any exercise needs medical clearance first. Counselling and dietitian referrals matter later and do not replace urgent medical communication.

Question 258

Neurological

A 45-year-old accountant with multiple sclerosis says that by mid-afternoon she is too exhausted for family time after working a full day. Which strategy should the physiotherapist teach first? Her neurologist reports no relapse, and her symptoms do not worsen with heat.

  • A. Plan the day with scheduled rests, shared tasks, and demanding activities placed in good hours
  • B. Take a long afternoon nap on most days and avoid physical activity until fatigue improves
  • C. Start a graded aerobic program with weekly increases to build her stamina
  • D. Use pre-cooling before exertion and cooling vests at work, and plan a nap whenever drowsiness builds

The correct answer is A (Plan the day with scheduled rests, shared tasks, and demanding activities placed in good hours): Energy conservation is the core first approach to disease-related fatigue. Planning, prioritizing and pacing tasks lets her spend limited energy on what matters to her. Cooling strategies help people whose symptoms worsen with heat, which is tempting in multiple sclerosis, but she reports no heat sensitivity. Long daytime rest reduces fitness, and a graded program without pacing risks a crash.

Question 259

Neurological

A 20-year-old university student comes to your clinic for neck pain that began yesterday. She reports a severe headache, light hurting her eyes, a temperature of 39.2 degrees Celsius and difficulty touching her chin to her chest. What should you do?

  • A. Refer for same-day medical review to assess for viral illness, and advise rest and fluids meanwhile
  • B. Arrange emergency medical assessment because the findings suggest possible bacterial meningitis
  • C. Treat as acute neck strain with heat, gentle range of motion and posture advice
  • D. Apply a collar and arrange urgent radiographs to exclude fracture or ligament instability

The correct answer is B (Arrange emergency medical assessment because the findings suggest possible bacterial meningitis): Fever, severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness are classic signs of meningitis, which can progress within hours. She needs emergency medical assessment, not manual therapy. A same-day review sounds responsible and fits a viral illness, but the pattern calls for emergency care now rather than hours later. A collar and radiographs address injury, not infection.

Question 260

Neurological

A 36-year-old woman with a history of sexual assault is referred for pelvic girdle pain. She stiffens when you move toward the plinth to examine her hip. Which approach best reflects trauma-informed practice? She says she wants the pain treated but is anxious about being touched.

  • A. Arrange a chaperone for the session and then continue the planned examination in the usual order
  • B. Explain each step first, ask permission before touching, and let her pause or stop anytime
  • C. Begin by asking her to describe the assault so you can plan which areas to avoid
  • D. Limit the visit to observation and questions, and defer hands-on work to another day

The correct answer is B (Explain each step first, ask permission before touching, and let her pause or stop anytime): Trauma-informed care emphasizes safety, choice, transparency and control. Describing each step, requesting permission, and honouring her right to pause lower the chance of distress. A chaperone can help some patients and is tempting, but it does not give her control over the examination. She asked for treatment, and disclosure of the assault should not be required.

Question 261

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 58-year-old man is in the supervised outpatient program six weeks after an uncomplicated myocardial infarction. He is on stable medication and cleared for moderate aerobic training. Which rating on the Borg 6 to 20 scale best describes an appropriate moderate training intensity?

  • A. A rating of 15 to 17, described as hard to very hard
  • B. A rating of 12 to 14, described as somewhat hard
  • C. A rating of 9 to 10, described as very light
  • D. A rating of 10 to 11, described as light

The correct answer is B (A rating of 12 to 14, described as somewhat hard): On the Borg 6 to 20 scale, a rating of 12 to 14 is the usual moderate training target in cardiac rehabilitation. Ratings of 15 and above approach vigorous effort and are not the starting target six weeks after a heart attack. Ratings of 9 to 11 are tempting for a cautious start but give little training effect and suit warm-up.

Question 262

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 72-year-old woman with chronic heart failure weighs herself every morning at home. She asks what change in weight should make her call her care team before her next scheduled visit. Which advice is the best? She has been stable on her medication for months.

  • A. Report a gain of about two kilograms over one month of daily weighing
  • B. Report a loss of about one kilogram over one week
  • C. Report a gain of about two kilograms over two to three days
  • D. Report a gain of about 500 grams over a single day

The correct answer is C (Report a gain of about two kilograms over two to three days): A gain of about two kilograms over two to three days suggests fluid retention and worsening heart failure, so she should call her care team early. A slow gain over a month is more likely a change in body tissue than in fluid. Small day-to-day swings of a few hundred grams are normal and would cause needless calls, and a loss is a lesser concern.

Question 263

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 76-year-old man with heart failure arrives for his usual session reporting two nights of needing three pillows to sleep. You hear bibasilar crackles and see new ankle swelling. His blood pressure and heart rate are near baseline. What is the most appropriate decision?

  • A. Add a longer warm-up and proceed since vital signs match his usual values
  • B. Continue the planned program but reduce the number of repetitions slightly and monitor his breathing
  • C. Hold exercise and contact the physician the same day about worsening fluid overload
  • D. Increase his fluid intake to help the kidneys clear the extra swelling

The correct answer is C (Hold exercise and contact the physician the same day about worsening fluid overload): Orthopnea, crackles and new edema indicate decompensation even when blood pressure and heart rate look normal. Exercise should be held and the physician informed promptly so treatment can be adjusted. Doing the usual program ignores the findings. Extra fluid would add to the overload.

Question 264

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 55-year-old man with hypertension arrives for a supervised exercise session. After five minutes of seated rest, his blood pressure is 212 over 108 millimetres of mercury on two readings. Which action is most consistent with established exercise screening guidance?

  • A. Defer the session and advise him to see his physician about the readings
  • B. Take another reading with a larger cuff and proceed if diastolic pressure is under 110
  • C. Switch to isometric exercises, which avoid the sustained pressure rise seen with aerobic work
  • D. Proceed at light intensity because his diastolic pressure is within range

The correct answer is A (Defer the session and advise him to see his physician about the readings): Commonly used screening guidance treats resting systolic pressure above 200 or diastolic pressure above 110 millimetres of mercury as a reason to postpone exercise. A systolic value over that limit applies even if the diastolic value is acceptable. A larger cuff is tempting, but two readings already agree. Isometric work raises pressure sharply, so it does not make the session safe.

Question 265

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

During a graded exercise test for a 60-year-old man, his systolic blood pressure rises to 170 and then falls to 150 millimetres of mercury while the workload keeps increasing. He reports mild fatigue only. What should the supervising clinician do? He is on no medications and has no known heart disease.

  • A. Reduce workload to a lower stage, recheck pressure after one minute, then resume if it recovers
  • B. Stop the test once he reports chest discomfort or the ECG shows ST depression
  • C. Stop the test, since a falling pressure with rising workload may signal serious disease
  • D. Continue to peak exertion since a plateau of systolic pressure is expected at high workloads

The correct answer is C (Stop the test, since a falling pressure with rising workload may signal serious disease): A fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 millimetres of mercury as workload increases is a standard termination criterion because it can indicate left ventricular dysfunction or extensive ischemia. A plateau is normal at high workload, which makes continuing tempting, but a true fall is different. Waiting for chest discomfort or ST change, or resuming after a pause, leaves him exposed.

Question 266

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 67-year-old retired farmer has intermittent claudication in both calves after walking about 200 metres. His ankle brachial index is 0.72. Which walking prescription is best supported for improving his walking distance? He takes his medication and wants a home-based plan.

  • A. Walk to moderate calf pain, rest until it settles, then repeat for thirty minutes
  • B. Walk only until calf discomfort begins, rest briefly, then restart walking
  • C. Walk as far as possible without stopping through severe pain
  • D. Use short rests every minute so that no calf pain develops

The correct answer is A (Walk to moderate calf pain, rest until it settles, then repeat for thirty minutes): Supervised walking to moderate claudication pain, with rests until it resolves, repeated across the session, improves collateral flow and walking capacity. Avoiding discomfort gives too little stimulus, while pushing through severe pain is unnecessary and unsafe. Frequent rests that prevent symptoms defeat the purpose of the program.

Question 267

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 71-year-old diabetic smoker has had burning foot pain at night for several months that eases when he hangs the leg over the bed edge. The foot is cool, pale on elevation, hairless, and pedal pulses are absent. What is the most likely cause?

  • A. Painful diabetic neuropathy causing burning night-time foot pain, with reduced sensation in a stocking distribution
  • B. Severe arterial insufficiency from peripheral arterial disease with ischemic rest pain
  • C. Chronic venous insufficiency with stasis changes and aching heaviness that improves on leg elevation
  • D. Acute arterial embolus causing sudden limb ischemia that needs emergency surgery

The correct answer is B (Severe arterial insufficiency from peripheral arterial disease with ischemic rest pain): Rest pain that eases when the leg hangs down, with a cool, pale, hairless foot and absent pulses, indicates severe arterial insufficiency from peripheral arterial disease. Diabetic neuropathy is tempting because he has diabetes and night burning, but it does not cause absent pulses or relief by dependency. Venous disease improves with elevation, and an embolus causes sudden rather than months-long symptoms.

Question 268

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 64-year-old woman, five days after knee replacement, has a swollen, warm left calf. The calf is 3.5 centimetres larger than the right with pitting edema, and she reports a dull ache. What is the most appropriate action? She has no known cancer.

  • A. Apply a compression stocking and elevate the leg, then reassess the calf measurement in the morning
  • B. Encourage ankle pumps and brief walks, then report it if swelling spreads
  • C. Avoid massage and exercise to that leg and arrange urgent medical assessment
  • D. Apply ice and elevation to the calf and reassess at the next visit

The correct answer is C (Avoid massage and exercise to that leg and arrange urgent medical assessment): A warm, swollen calf with pitting edema and a side-to-side difference of 3.5 centimetres five days after knee replacement raises a strong suspicion of deep vein thrombosis. Movement or manual pressure risks dislodging a clot, so she needs urgent medical assessment. Elevation and compression are standard for ordinary swelling, which is tempting, but they delay the assessment.

Question 269

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 59-year-old man being treated for a calf deep vein thrombosis stands from the plinth and suddenly reports sharp chest pain on inspiration and breathlessness. His heart rate is 118 beats per minute and oxygen saturation is 89 percent. What is the best response?

  • A. Lie him flat with legs raised and monitor his vital signs for twenty minutes
  • B. Give oxygen if available and book a same-day physician visit
  • C. Stop activity, keep him seated and calm, and call emergency services immediately
  • D. Have him sit, breathe slowly and call emergency services if saturation falls
