The correct answer is C (Stop activity, keep him seated and calm, and call emergency services immediately): Sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia and low saturation in a patient with known thrombosis strongly suggest pulmonary embolism. This is life threatening and needs emergency services immediately, with rest and monitoring while waiting. Oxygen is a sensible measure, which makes the same-day visit tempting, but the visit is far too slow. Lying him flat or waiting for a lower saturation also delays treatment.

Question 270

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 63-year-old woman takes a beta blocker after a heart attack and starts outpatient aerobic training. Her heart rate reaches only 98 beats per minute even when she feels the work is hard. Which method best guides her exercise intensity?

  • A. Apply an age-predicted maximum heart rate formula with a fixed percentage reduction for her beta blocker
  • B. Set intensity from her blood pressure response and raise it at each session
  • C. Use the rating of perceived exertion with the talk test instead of a heart rate target
  • D. Use a fixed walking speed that she tolerated at her first session each week

The correct answer is C (Use the rating of perceived exertion with the talk test instead of a heart rate target): A beta blocker blunts the heart rate response, so a heart rate target is unreliable for her. Rating of perceived exertion with the talk test reflects how hard she is actually working. Reducing an age-predicted formula by a fixed percentage seems to account for the drug, but the individual response varies too much. A fixed speed ignores how she feels on a given day.

Question 271

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

An 80-year-old man reports dizziness when getting out of bed. You measure blood pressure supine and again after three minutes of standing. Which change in measurements confirms orthostatic hypotension? He takes a diuretic and an antihypertensive and lives alone in a small town.

  • A. A fall of 30 millimetres of mercury systolic or 15 diastolic, within one minute of standing
  • B. A fall of 20 millimetres of mercury systolic or 10 diastolic
  • C. A fall of 10 millimetres of mercury in systolic pressure
  • D. A drop of 10 millimetres of mercury systolic or 5 diastolic after one minute of standing

The correct answer is B (A fall of 20 millimetres of mercury systolic or 10 diastolic): Orthostatic hypotension is confirmed by a fall of at least 20 millimetres of mercury systolic or 10 diastolic within three minutes of standing. A threshold of 10 millimetres systolic is a common normal variation and would label many people wrongly. Raising the thresholds to 30 and 15 is tempting because it sounds more certain, but it would miss many patients who need action.

Question 272

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 66-year-old man with stable angina develops central chest tightness while climbing stairs in your clinic. He carries nitroglycerin spray. After you stop him and he rests, the tightness continues. What is the best next step? He is in his usual health otherwise.

  • A. Wait twenty minutes to see whether the pain settles on its own before taking any action
  • B. Ask him to climb the stairs again slowly to see if the pain fades
  • C. Help with one nitroglycerin dose, then call emergency services if pain persists
  • D. Give him two further doses straight away before calling anyone

The correct answer is C (Help with one nitroglycerin dose, then call emergency services if pain persists): Stopping activity is the first step, and if rest does not relieve the pain, one dose of nitroglycerin should be taken. Pain that remains five minutes after that dose requires a call to emergency services. Climbing again or waiting twenty minutes adds risk. Repeating doses repeatedly without calling delays definitive care.

Question 273

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 70-year-old retired nurse is two weeks after coronary bypass surgery through a median sternotomy. She asks how to get out of a chair at home. Which advice best protects her sternum? She lives alone in a two-storey home in Moncton.

  • A. Push firmly through both arms on the armrests to unload her tired legs
  • B. Rock her body forward and back with hands clasped behind her neck
  • C. Lean forward with arms stretched ahead and pull on the table in front
  • D. Use her legs to rise while hugging a pillow, avoiding pushing through her hands

The correct answer is D (Use her legs to rise while hugging a pillow, avoiding pushing through her hands): After sternotomy, bilateral arm pushing and pulling places shear and traction on the healing bone. Standing from a chair with the legs, with a pillow held against the chest for support, avoids that stress. Pulling on a table or clasping hands behind the head also strain the sternum. Precautions usually last about six to twelve weeks.

Question 274

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 52-year-old woman with controlled hypertension begins a walking program and has no heart rate monitor. You teach her the talk test. At what point does the talk test indicate an appropriate moderate intensity? She walks three mornings a week in her neighbourhood.

  • A. She can say a few words between breaths and needs frequent pauses
  • B. She can sing along with a song at a steady pace while she walks
  • C. She must stop walking to speak because her breathing is too hard
  • D. She can speak in full sentences but cannot sing comfortably while walking

The correct answer is D (She can speak in full sentences but cannot sing comfortably while walking): At moderate intensity she can speak in full sentences but cannot sing comfortably. Being able to sing indicates light intensity and too little challenge. Saying a few words between breaths marks vigorous effort, which is tempting for someone motivated to improve, but it exceeds a moderate target. Stopping to talk indicates near maximal effort.

Question 275

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 48-year-old man with hypertension begins resistance training for the first time. He tends to hold his breath during each lift. Which instruction is best for managing his blood pressure response? He is otherwise healthy and trains at a community gym.

  • A. Breathe in during the effort phase and breathe out slowly as the weight is lowered
  • B. Breathe out during the effort phase of each lift and keep breathing steadily
  • C. Take a deep breath and hold it briefly at the hardest point of the lift
  • D. Use lighter loads with more repetitions and rest between sets

The correct answer is B (Breathe out during the effort phase of each lift and keep breathing steadily): Breath holding during effort produces a Valsalva response that sharply raises blood pressure. Breathing out during the effort phase and breathing steadily keeps the pressure response lower. Lighter loads with more repetitions are sensible in hypertension and tempting, but they do not correct his breath holding. Reversing the pattern, breathing in on effort, still encourages straining.

Question 276

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 69-year-old man has leg pain after 150 metres of walking. It settles within two minutes of standing still without sitting, and cycling reproduces the same pain. Pedal pulses are weak and his skin is shiny and hairless. Which source is most likely?

  • A. Neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis, with pain that eases when he sits or bends forward
  • B. Hip osteoarthritis with referred pain into the thigh during weight bearing
  • C. Peripheral neuropathy causing burning pain in both lower legs while walking
  • D. Vascular claudication from arterial narrowing that reduces blood flow to the leg muscles

The correct answer is D (Vascular claudication from arterial narrowing that reduces blood flow to the leg muscles): Pain that starts at a consistent distance, settles within minutes of standing still, and recurs with cycling, together with weak pulses and shiny hairless skin, points to vascular claudication. Neurogenic claudication is the classic look-alike, but it usually needs sitting or bending forward for relief and cycling is often well tolerated. Hip arthritis and neuropathy do not explain the vascular signs.

Question 277

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 55-year-old man starts a treadmill program after a heart attack. At the second session he reports new central chest pressure and light-headedness at a speed he tolerated last week, with a pale, clammy appearance. What is the best action?

  • A. Stop exercise, seat him, check vital signs, and activate emergency response
  • B. Stop exercise, seat him, recheck symptoms after five minutes, and call for help if they persist
  • C. Lower the speed and monitor his symptoms for another five minutes
  • D. Stop exercise and let him walk slowly to cool down before reassessing

The correct answer is A (Stop exercise, seat him, check vital signs, and activate emergency response): New central chest pressure, light-headedness and pallor at a workload he tolerated last week suggest cardiac ischemia. Exercise stops at once, he is seated, vital signs are checked, and emergency response is activated. Waiting five minutes to see whether symptoms persist is tempting because it seems measured, but it delays treatment. Continued walking, even slow, adds cardiac load.

Question 278

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 68-year-old man with heart failure is comfortable at rest. Walking one level block, or climbing half a flight of stairs, brings on fatigue and breathlessness, though ordinary slow household tasks are manageable. Which New York Heart Association class describes him?

  • A. Class III, with marked limitation from less than ordinary activity
  • B. Class II, with slight limitation of physical activity during ordinary daily tasks
  • C. Class IV, with symptoms present even at complete rest
  • D. Class I, with no limitation during ordinary physical activity

The correct answer is A (Class III, with marked limitation from less than ordinary activity): The functional classification rests on how much activity causes symptoms. Comfort at rest but symptoms with less than ordinary effort, such as a single level block, defines class III. Class II involves symptoms with ordinary activity only, and class IV requires symptoms at rest.

Question 279

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 74-year-old woman had a pacemaker implanted in her left upper chest ten days ago. She asks about exercising the left shoulder. Which instruction is most appropriate? She feels well, has normal heart rhythm on monitoring, and enjoys swimming and gardening at her cottage.

  • A. Avoid raising the left arm above the shoulder and heavy lifting until cleared
  • B. Keep the left arm in a sling for six weeks and move the wrist and hand
  • C. Begin pendulum exercises and full active range, keeping lifts light
  • D. Resume swimming and gardening this week with a lighter effort than before

The correct answer is A (Avoid raising the left arm above the shoulder and heavy lifting until cleared): After a pacemaker implant the leads are not yet secured by scar tissue, so lifting the arm above the shoulder and heavy lifting are avoided until the surgeon or device clinic clears her, with gentle movement below shoulder height encouraged. A sling for weeks is tempting as extra protection, but it raises the risk of a stiff shoulder. Early full range and swimming risk lead displacement.

Question 280

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 73-year-old woman has a leg ulcer with swelling and a history of smoking. Her ankle brachial index is 0.4 on the affected side. A colleague suggests high-strength compression bandaging. What is the best response? She walks with a cane and has diabetes.

  • A. Apply reduced compression at 20 millimetres of mercury and monitor the toes each visit
  • B. Hold compression and refer for vascular assessment because the arterial disease is severe
  • C. Start a moist wound dressing and reassess compression after two weeks of healing
  • D. Use intermittent pneumatic compression and elevate the leg to reduce the swelling

The correct answer is B (Hold compression and refer for vascular assessment because the arterial disease is severe): An ankle brachial index of 0.4 indicates severe arterial disease, and compression could further reduce perfusion and cause tissue loss. Compression is held and she is referred for vascular assessment. Lower pressures are tempting because the swelling is real, but they do not make compression safe at this level. A moist dressing treats the wound without addressing the circulation.

Question 281

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A physiotherapist measures ankle and arm systolic pressures in a 65-year-old patient with leg pain on walking. Which ankle brachial index value is generally taken as diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease? She has smoked for thirty years and has weak foot pulses.

  • A. A value between 0.91 and 0.99, considered borderline for arterial disease
  • B. A value above 1.4, which suggests stiff calcified vessels and a falsely high reading
  • C. A value of 0.90 or lower, calculated by dividing the arm pressure by the ankle pressure
  • D. A value of 0.90 or lower, measured as ankle pressure divided by arm pressure

The correct answer is D (A value of 0.90 or lower, measured as ankle pressure divided by arm pressure): An ankle brachial index of 0.90 or lower, calculated as ankle systolic pressure divided by arm systolic pressure, is generally diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease. Values from 0.91 to 0.99 are borderline and tempting in a symptomatic smoker, but they do not meet the cutoff. Values above 1.4 reflect stiff vessels, and inverting the ratio gives a meaningless number.

Question 282

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 61-year-old man with ischemic heart disease finishes a brisk treadmill session and sits down heavily. He becomes pale and faint within a minute. What should have been part of his program to reduce this risk? His blood pressure was normal before the session.

  • A. A warm-up of low-intensity exercise for five to ten minutes before the main session
  • B. Compression stockings worn during exercise to support venous return
  • C. A gradual cool-down of lower-intensity walking for five to ten minutes
  • D. Seated recovery with the legs raised after the session

The correct answer is C (A gradual cool-down of lower-intensity walking for five to ten minutes): Stopping brisk exercise suddenly lets blood pool in the legs and can cause faintness. A gradual cool-down of lower-intensity walking for five to ten minutes lets heart rate and blood pressure settle. A warm-up is a good practice and tempting, but it comes before exercise and does not prevent post-exercise pooling. Sitting down at once is the behaviour that caused the problem.

Question 283

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 77-year-old man with atrial fibrillation takes warfarin and has a stable international normalized ratio. He presents with a tight calf muscle and asks for deep friction massage. Which approach is most appropriate? He walks daily and has no history of falls.

  • A. Use heat and ultrasound to relax the calf muscle and avoid hands-on pressure
  • B. Use moderate pressure deep friction massage and ask him to report any bruising or soreness afterward
  • C. Use gentle soft tissue techniques with light pressure and check the skin for bruising
  • D. Treat as usual once his international normalized ratio is confirmed in range

The correct answer is C (Use gentle soft tissue techniques with light pressure and check the skin for bruising): Warfarin increases the risk of bruising and hematoma even when the international normalized ratio is stable. Gentle soft tissue techniques with light pressure, along with a skin check, keep the risk low. A stable ratio is reassuring and tempting, but it does not remove the bleeding risk from deep friction. Asking him to report bruising afterward detects harm that has already happened.

Question 284

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 70-year-old man has chronic lung disease and is being assessed for heart failure complications. Which finding is most characteristic of right-sided heart failure rather than left-sided failure? He is on oxygen at night and has noticed his shoes feel tight by evening.

  • A. Raised jugular venous pressure with peripheral edema and an enlarged tender liver
  • B. Pink frothy sputum with sudden severe breathlessness and anxiety at night
  • C. Orthopnea with fine crackles at both lung bases and a dry cough lying flat
  • D. Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea with an audible third heart sound

The correct answer is A (Raised jugular venous pressure with peripheral edema and an enlarged tender liver): Right ventricular failure causes systemic venous congestion, producing raised jugular pressure, dependent edema and hepatic enlargement. Orthopnea, crackles, night-time breathlessness and pulmonary edema arise from backward pressure into the lungs in left-sided failure. Recognizing the pattern directs the referral.

Question 285

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 28-year-old recreational distance runner with no symptoms has a resting heart rate of 48 beats per minute and blood pressure of 112 over 68. He takes no medications and has no dizziness, chest pain or fainting, and no family cardiac history. What is the best interpretation?

  • A. Likely a normal training adaptation, so he can continue activity and watch for symptoms
  • B. Sinus bradycardia that needs a 12-lead ECG and cardiology review before he resumes training
  • C. Early hypothyroidism, so he needs thyroid blood tests and should limit exercise until results return
  • D. Overtraining syndrome, so he should reduce training volume for several weeks

The correct answer is A (Likely a normal training adaptation, so he can continue activity and watch for symptoms): A resting heart rate of 48 in a fit, symptom-free distance runner with normal blood pressure and no family history is a typical training adaptation. He can continue activity and report symptoms such as dizziness, chest pain or fainting. An ECG and cardiology review are tempting because the rate is low, but they are reserved for symptoms or risk factors. He reports no fatigue to suggest overtraining.

Question 286

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 45-year-old woman completes a graded treadmill test. You are asked to describe the expected blood pressure response in a healthy adult as workload increases. Which description is correct? Her resting blood pressure was normal and she has no cardiac symptoms.

  • A. Systolic pressure rises steadily while diastolic pressure also rises by a similar amount with workload
  • B. Systolic pressure rises steadily while diastolic pressure stays similar or changes slightly
  • C. Systolic pressure plateaus early while diastolic pressure falls sharply below rest
  • D. Systolic pressure rises, then falls at moderate workload, with a stable diastolic

The correct answer is B (Systolic pressure rises steadily while diastolic pressure stays similar or changes slightly): During graded dynamic exercise systolic pressure rises steadily and diastolic stays similar or changes slightly. A matching rise in both pressures is tempting because it sounds proportional, but it is typical of static or strength effort and not of treadmill work. A systolic plateau or fall during the test is abnormal and is a reason to stop and review.

Question 287

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 69-year-old woman has a shallow, irregular, moist ulcer above her medial malleolus with surrounding brown staining and swelling that improves overnight. Pedal pulses are strong, and the ulcer is only mildly painful. Which type is most likely? She takes no blood thinners.

  • A. An arterial ulcer from peripheral arterial disease with poor perfusion of the distal foot and toes
  • B. A venous ulcer from chronic venous insufficiency with edema and pigment change
  • C. A neuropathic ulcer from diabetes under a pressure point on the sole
  • D. A pressure injury over a bony prominence from prolonged lying

The correct answer is B (A venous ulcer from chronic venous insufficiency with edema and pigment change): A shallow, irregular, moist ulcer above the medial malleolus with brown staining, swelling that improves overnight and strong pulses is a venous ulcer from chronic venous insufficiency. An arterial ulcer is tempting because of the age and location near the foot, but it is typically deep, punched out and painful with weak pulses. Neuropathic ulcers sit on the sole.

Question 288

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 33-year-old woman reports her fingers turning white, then blue, then red when she handles frozen food or is in cold weather. Examination shows normal pulses and no ulcers. Which advice is most useful? She is a non-smoker and works in a grocery store.

  • A. Keep hands and core warm, wear gloves early, and avoid nicotine, caffeine and sudden cold exposure
  • B. Run hot water over her fingers when colour changes, then dry and massage them
  • C. Practise daily hot and cold contrast baths to train the finger vessels
  • D. Refer urgently for vascular imaging, since the colour changes mean arterial occlusion

The correct answer is A (Keep hands and core warm, wear gloves early, and avoid nicotine, caffeine and sudden cold exposure): Vasospastic episodes follow cold or stress, so the aim is to prevent triggers: keep the whole body warm, wear gloves early, and avoid vasoconstrictors such as nicotine and caffeine. Urgent imaging is tempting because of the dramatic colour changes, but normal pulses and no ulcers point to a benign vasospastic pattern. Hot water, firm rubbing and contrast baths stress fragile skin or provoke more spasm.

Question 289

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 58-year-old man is on day one after total hip replacement and is restricted to bed rest for most of the day. Which intervention should the physiotherapist include to help reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis? He is nervous about moving the leg.

  • A. Massage the calves firmly twice daily to keep blood flowing
  • B. Teach ankle pumps and arrange early mobilization once his surgeon permits it
  • C. Elevate the legs on pillows and delay active movement until day three
  • D. Encourage deep breathing and arm exercises while he rests the legs

The correct answer is B (Teach ankle pumps and arrange early mobilization once his surgeon permits it): Early mobilization and ankle pumps promote venous return and lower the risk of clots after hip replacement, once the surgeon permits movement. Elevating the legs is tempting because it eases swelling, but delaying movement removes the benefit. Firm calf massage could dislodge a clot, and arm exercises do not affect leg circulation.

Question 290

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A physiotherapist in a primary care clinic wants a structured way to estimate the probability that a patient with a swollen leg has a deep vein thrombosis before sending the patient for imaging. Which tool is designed for this purpose?

  • A. The PERC rule, used to exclude pulmonary embolism in patients with low pretest probability
  • B. The Homans sign performed at the bedside to confirm or exclude a deep vein thrombosis
  • C. The ankle-brachial index used to grade the severity of arterial supply to the lower limb
  • D. The Wells clinical prediction rule for deep vein thrombosis

The correct answer is D (The Wells clinical prediction rule for deep vein thrombosis): The Wells rule scores features such as calf swelling, pitting edema, active cancer and recent surgery to place a patient in a low, moderate or high probability group. It guides whether imaging or blood tests are needed. The PERC rule belongs to suspected pulmonary embolism, the Homans sign is too unreliable to rule thrombosis in or out, and the ankle-brachial index assesses arteries.

Question 291

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 57-year-old man in a community clinic has a resting blood pressure of 210 over 128 millimetres of mercury on repeat readings. He reports a severe new headache, blurred vision and confusion that began this morning. What is the best action?

  • A. Have him rest quietly in a dark room for thirty minutes and recheck the pressure
  • B. Treat as a hypertensive emergency and activate emergency services at once
  • C. Arrange urgent physician review within twenty-four hours for medication adjustment of his blood pressure
  • D. Complete a full neurological examination first and decide about referral once findings are documented

The correct answer is B (Treat as a hypertensive emergency and activate emergency services at once): A very high blood pressure with headache, visual change and confusion suggests acute end-organ involvement such as hypertensive encephalopathy, which needs emergency care. Review within a day would suit a high reading without symptoms, which makes it tempting, but these symptoms change the urgency. Resting and rechecking or finishing a long examination first delays treatment.

Question 292

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 74-year-old man fainted twice while climbing stairs and now reports chest tightness and breathlessness with effort. Examination reveals a harsh systolic murmur heard at the right upper sternal border radiating to the neck. What is the most appropriate decision?

  • A. Stop exertional activity and arrange prompt cardiology referral for suspected valve disease
  • B. Continue supervised walking with heart rate monitoring and recheck symptoms next week
  • C. Arrange an orthostatic blood pressure check and review his medications for dizziness
  • D. Refer to his family physician for routine assessment of the murmur within a month

The correct answer is A (Stop exertional activity and arrange prompt cardiology referral for suspected valve disease): Exertional syncope, chest tightness and a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the neck suggest severe aortic stenosis, which carries a risk of sudden death with exertion. Exertional activity stops and he is referred promptly to cardiology. Orthostatic measurements are tempting because he has fainted, but his faints occur with effort and the murmur points to the valve.

Question 293

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 50-year-old woman with heart disease prepares for her first group aerobic class. She asks why the instructor insists on a ten-minute warm-up with low-intensity movement first. Which reason is most accurate? She has been sedentary for years and is nervous about overdoing it.

  • A. It gradually raises heart rate and coronary blood flow, limiting the risk of ischemia
  • B. It raises muscle temperature and tissue elasticity, reducing strain and tear risk
  • C. It drops heart rate below resting values so the main session feels easier
  • D. It increases her resting metabolic rate for the day, helping weight control

The correct answer is A (It gradually raises heart rate and coronary blood flow, limiting the risk of ischemia): Starting gently increases blood flow to the heart and muscles gradually and prepares the cardiovascular system for work. In people with heart disease, sudden hard exertion can provoke ischemia or arrhythmia. Warmer, more elastic muscle is a real effect and makes the injury option tempting, but it is not the key reason for her. Warm-up raises, not lowers, heart rate, and it does not replace cool-down.

Question 294

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 62-year-old man began a statin four weeks ago. He now has diffuse thigh and shoulder aching, weakness climbing stairs, and dark urine since yesterday. He attributes it to the new exercise program. What should you do? He is otherwise well.

  • A. Halve exercise intensity and recommend extra fluids, then reassess symptoms at the next visit
  • B. Suggest he stop the statin himself and continue the exercise program as planned
  • C. Advise rest for two days and a gentle stretching routine, then resume training
  • D. Stop exercise and arrange urgent medical review with blood tests for muscle injury

The correct answer is D (Stop exercise and arrange urgent medical review with blood tests for muscle injury): Diffuse muscle pain and weakness a few weeks after starting a statin, with dark urine, suggest rhabdomyolysis, which can injure the kidneys. Exercise stops and he needs urgent medical review with blood tests. Reducing intensity and drinking more fluids is tempting, but it delays diagnosis. Stopping the statin is a prescriber's decision.

Question 295

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A new physiotherapy graduate asks a senior colleague about the main purpose of an outpatient cardiac rehabilitation program for a patient after a heart attack. Which description is most accurate? The graduate wants to explain it clearly to patients and families.

  • A. Lowering future event risk through supervised exercise, education and risk factor control
  • B. Monitoring heart rhythm and symptoms during activity to detect new cardiac events
  • C. Providing education on medication and diet when he leaves the hospital
  • D. Rebuilding aerobic fitness to the level before the heart attack through a graded walking progression

The correct answer is A (Lowering future event risk through supervised exercise, education and risk factor control): Cardiac rehabilitation combines supervised exercise, education and risk factor control to lower the chance of future cardiac events. Improving fitness is a real benefit and tempting as the answer, but it is one component rather than the main purpose. Monitoring during sessions and discharge education are parts of the program, not its aim.

Question 296

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 56-year-old man with peripheral arterial disease smokes a pack a day. The physiotherapist wishes to use a brief structured framework to raise tobacco cessation during the visit. Which sequence matches the widely used five-step approach? He is willing to discuss it.

  • A. Ask about use, advise quitting, prescribe nicotine replacement, arrange a counselling referral, then discharge
  • B. Assess lung function, advise quitting, treat withdrawal symptoms, review progress monthly, then refer to a specialist
  • C. Assess readiness, advise quitting, assist with a plan, and then ask about use
  • D. Ask about use, advise quitting, assess readiness, assist with a plan, arrange follow-up

The correct answer is D (Ask about use, advise quitting, assess readiness, assist with a plan, arrange follow-up): The widely used five-step approach is ask, advise, assess, assist and arrange follow-up. The first option is tempting because it begins correctly and offers help, but it skips readiness and follow-up and goes beyond physiotherapy scope with prescribing. Assessing readiness before asking about use puts the steps in the wrong order.

Question 297

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 68-year-old male smoker comes for low back pain. It is deep, constant and unaffected by position. Palpation of the abdomen reveals a pulsatile mass just left of the midline, and he feels light-headed. What is the most appropriate response?

  • A. Stop palpating, monitor his blood pressure for thirty minutes, and refer if symptoms worsen
  • B. Stop palpating the abdomen and arrange emergency medical care at once
  • C. Document the mass and arrange an outpatient ultrasound this week
  • D. Use positional relief for the pain and reassess at the next visit

The correct answer is B (Stop palpating the abdomen and arrange emergency medical care at once): Deep constant back pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass and light-headedness in a male smoker suggest an abdominal aortic aneurysm that may be expanding or leaking. Palpation stops and emergency care is arranged at once. Monitoring first is cautious but delays rescue, and an outpatient ultrasound is too slow for a possibly unstable aneurysm.

Question 298

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and peripheral arterial disease has a dry, cool right foot with reduced sensation and a small callus under the first metatarsal head. He asks how to protect his feet between visits. Which instruction best lowers his risk of tissue breakdown?

  • A. Apply daily moisturizer between the toes and trim the callus with a nail clipper at home
  • B. Wear soft slippers or go barefoot indoors to avoid pressure from shoes
  • C. Keep the feet warm with a heating pad set to low each evening
  • D. Inspect both feet daily, wear well-fitting shoes, and report any skin break early

The correct answer is D (Inspect both feet daily, wear well-fitting shoes, and report any skin break early): In diabetes with arterial disease and reduced sensation, daily inspection, well-fitting shoes and early reporting of any skin break prevent tissue breakdown. Moisturizing the feet is advised, but not between the toes where moisture causes skin breakdown, and callus trimming is left to a trained clinician. A heating pad can burn a foot that cannot sense heat.

Question 299

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 19-year-old basketball player faints suddenly while sprinting during a university training session and recovers within a minute. His father died unexpectedly at age 41. He asks to rejoin practice tomorrow because he feels fine. What is the most appropriate advice?

  • A. Allow non-contact drills with a heart rate monitor and arrange outpatient cardiology review within a month
  • B. Ask his family physician to check blood pressure and glucose before any return
  • C. Arrange an exercise stress test next week and allow light training until the result is known
  • D. Stop all sport participation and arrange urgent cardiology assessment before any return

The correct answer is D (Stop all sport participation and arrange urgent cardiology assessment before any return): Sudden fainting during exertion with a father who died unexpectedly at 41 raises concern for an inherited cardiac condition such as cardiomyopathy or a channel disorder. All sport stops and urgent cardiology assessment is arranged before any return. Light training pending a test is tempting because he feels well, but exertion is the trigger for sudden cardiac events.

Question 300

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 66-year-old woman reports sudden palpitations and mild breathlessness at the start of a rehabilitation session. Her pulse is irregularly irregular at 138 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 70, oxygen saturation 96 percent, and she has no chest pain or faintness. What is the best decision?

  • A. Continue the session at light intensity because her blood pressure and saturation are acceptable now
  • B. Hold exercise, monitor her at rest, and arrange same-day medical assessment
  • C. Use the rate of 138 as her target and increase the treadmill speed gradually
  • D. Reassure her that palpitations are common with activity and review her pulse next week

The correct answer is B (Hold exercise, monitor her at rest, and arrange same-day medical assessment): A newly rapid, irregularly irregular pulse suggests atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response, which needs medical assessment the same day even when blood pressure is acceptable. She should rest and be observed for chest pain, faintness or falling pressure, which would require emergency care. Exercising at this rate is unsafe, and waiting a week delays treatment of a rhythm that raises stroke risk.

Question 301

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 68-year-old retired miner from Sudbury has severe COPD and becomes frightened when stair climbing makes him gasp. His physiotherapist wants a strategy that reduces air trapping and slows his rate during exertion, timed with each step. Which technique should be taught?

  • A. Diaphragmatic breathing with a hand on the abdomen, taking a slow deep nasal breath before climbing
  • B. Inspiratory muscle training with a threshold device, doing ten resisted maximal breaths at the stairs base
  • C. Pursed-lip exhalation timed with each step, lengthening expiration to keep small airways open
  • D. Forward lean standing with arms braced on the rail, pausing after every flight until breathing settles

The correct answer is C (Pursed-lip exhalation timed with each step, lengthening expiration to keep small airways open): Pursed-lip breathing creates a small back pressure that holds weakened airways open so more air leaves the lungs. Lengthening exhalation reduces dynamic hyperinflation and lets each step be matched to one controlled breath. Diaphragmatic breathing is useful at rest, but in severe COPD with a flattened diaphragm it is hard to coordinate with stair climbing. Resisted breath training builds strength over weeks and is not a technique used during the climb, and resting in a forward lean helps recovery but does not control breathing step by step.

Question 302

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 72-year-old woman with known COPD and chronic carbon dioxide retention is brought to the emergency department on 6 L/min by mask. She is drowsy and hard to rouse, her pulse oximeter reads 99 percent, and her respiratory rate is 10. The physiotherapist notices the reading while helping with positioning. What is the best action?

  • A. Reduce to nasal prongs at 2 litres per minute and recheck at the next round
  • B. Ask the nurse to titrate oxygen down toward 88 to 92 percent and monitor drowsiness closely
  • C. Sit her upright and give a bronchodilator nebulizer driven by oxygen at 6 L/min
  • D. Coach deep breathing and coughing to raise her respiratory rate and clear secretions

The correct answer is B (Ask the nurse to titrate oxygen down toward 88 to 92 percent and monitor drowsiness closely): Patients who retain carbon dioxide can lose their drive to breathe when oxygen is excessive, so the target is 88 to 92 percent, and 99 percent with drowsiness and a rate of 10 points to over-oxygenation. Dropping to prongs at a lower flow sounds sensible, but without a defined target and close watch on her alertness she may keep sliding. Secretion clearance and oxygen-driven nebulizers do not address the over-oxygenation.

Question 303

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 15-year-old hockey player in Saskatoon coughs and wheezes about ten minutes into cold-weather practice, and the symptoms settle with rest. He has a prescribed reliever inhaler and a diagnosis of asthma. The physiotherapist is advising on preparation before the next practice. Which plan fits best?

  • A. Cover the nose and mouth with a scarf during practice and use the reliever if needed
  • B. Take his regular controller inhaler thirty minutes before practice in place of the reliever
  • C. Do a short high-intensity sprint warm-up and use the reliever once symptoms begin
  • D. Warm up gradually for about ten minutes and take the prescribed reliever shortly before training starts

The correct answer is D (Warm up gradually for about ten minutes and take the prescribed reliever shortly before training starts): A gradual warm-up reduces exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, and a short-acting reliever taken shortly before activity is the standard preventive step when prescribed. Covering the face warms the air and is a useful extra, but it leaves out the pre-exercise dose and the warm-up that prevent the episode. A controller works over days and does not substitute for the reliever, and a sprint warm-up can trigger symptoms.

Question 304

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

During a session, a 34-year-old teacher with asthma becomes wheezy and chest tight while walking on the treadmill. Her saturation is 94 percent, she can speak in full sentences, and her peak flow is 65 percent of her personal best. She has her reliever inhaler with her. What should the physiotherapist do next?

  • A. Have her lie flat and breathe slowly for twenty minutes before deciding whether medication is needed
  • B. Reduce the treadmill speed and continue the session while watching for any further drop in saturation
  • C. Stop exercise, help her sit upright and use the reliever, then recheck symptoms and peak flow
  • D. Call emergency services at once because a peak flow below 80 percent signals imminent respiratory failure

The correct answer is C (Stop exercise, help her sit upright and use the reliever, then recheck symptoms and peak flow): She has a moderate asthma flare, shown by wheeze, tightness and a reduced peak flow, but she is speaking in full sentences with a safe saturation. The expected response is to stop activity, sit upright, use the reliever and recheck. Continuing exercise ignores the trigger, while an emergency call becomes appropriate if she fails to improve or her speech and saturation worsen.

Question 305

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 58-year-old woman with pulmonary fibrosis is sent for spirometry and full lung volume testing before beginning a rehabilitation program. The physiotherapist reviews the report to understand the pattern of impairment. Which result pattern is expected in this type of disease?

  • A. Normal total lung capacity with prolonged expiratory time and marked air trapping on volume testing
  • B. Reduced total lung capacity with a normal or raised ratio of FEV1 to FVC
  • C. Increased residual volume with a reduced ratio of forced expiratory volume to forced vital capacity
  • D. Increased total lung capacity with flattened diaphragms and widened intercostal spaces on the radiograph

The correct answer is B (Reduced total lung capacity with a normal or raised ratio of FEV1 to FVC): Restrictive disease limits how far the lungs can expand, so volumes such as total lung capacity and forced vital capacity fall. Because airways are not narrowed, the ratio of expired volume in one second to forced vital capacity stays normal or rises. Increased residual volume, air trapping and hyperinflation all point to obstructive disease.

Question 306

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 63-year-old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis walks in the corridor, and his saturation falls from 94 to 85 percent by the third minute. He rates breathlessness 6 out of 10 and looks distressed. He has a physician-prescribed oxygen target. What is the most appropriate response?

  • A. Pause and use pursed-lip breathing, then resume at the same pace without oxygen
  • B. Stop, rest in a supported position, then resume with oxygen titrated to the target
  • C. Slow the pace and keep walking while coaching breathing, rechecking saturation at the end
  • D. Stop and lean forward to rest until recovered, then end the session and reassess tomorrow

The correct answer is B (Stop, rest in a supported position, then resume with oxygen titrated to the target): Desaturation to 85 percent with distress in pulmonary fibrosis calls for stopping, recovering in a supported position and then continuing with oxygen titrated to the prescribed target so training can go on safely. Pursed-lip breathing helps breathlessness but does not correct the saturation without oxygen, and ending the session loses a training opportunity. Slowing the pace while walking on leaves him at a low saturation for longer.

Question 307

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

On the second day after an upper abdominal operation, a 61-year-old man has diminished air entry at both bases, a saturation of 91 percent on room air, and a temperature of 37.9 degrees Celsius. He guards his incision, takes only small breaths and has no sputum. What is the best first intervention?

  • A. Perform percussion and vibration over the incision to mobilize secretions at both lung bases
  • B. Arrange analgesia, then sit him upright for deep breaths with holds, splinting the incision
  • C. Repeat forced expiration techniques until a productive cough is obtained from the lower airways
  • D. Keep him supine in bed and increase oxygen until the breath sounds at the bases improve

The correct answer is B (Arrange analgesia, then sit him upright for deep breaths with holds, splinting the incision): The picture is shallow breathing from pain with basal atelectasis, not secretion retention. Adequate analgesia, an upright position, deep breaths with a hold and wound splinting expand the bases. Percussion over a fresh incision is painful and has no sputum to move, and lying flat further reduces lung volume.

Question 308

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A hospital physiotherapist plans preoperative education and must decide which patients on a surgical list are most likely to develop pulmonary complications and so need priority teaching. All four patients are adults of similar age with no previous lung disease. Which planned procedure carries the highest risk?

  • A. Open lower abdominal surgery under general anesthesia lasting about two and a half hours
  • B. Laparoscopic gallbladder removal under general anesthesia lasting about ninety minutes
  • C. Open upper abdominal surgery under general anesthesia lasting over three hours
  • D. Total knee replacement under general anesthesia lasting about two hours with early mobilization

The correct answer is C (Open upper abdominal surgery under general anesthesia lasting over three hours): Incisions near the diaphragm, long general anesthetics and open techniques impair diaphragm function and reduce lung volumes, raising the chance of atelectasis and pneumonia. Open lower abdominal surgery carries real risk, but the incision is farther from the diaphragm and the anesthetic is shorter. The laparoscopic and joint procedures involve smaller or distant incisions, shorter exposure and early mobilization.

Question 309

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 70-year-old man has right lower lobe pneumonia, a saturation of 90 percent on room air and a productive cough. He is sitting in bed and the team asks the physiotherapist to choose a lying position that will improve oxygenation. Which position is best?

  • A. Left side-lying with the unaffected lung dependent so it receives more blood flow
  • B. Supine and flat to maximize diaphragm excursion during the next several hours of rest
  • C. Right side-lying with the affected lung dependent to encourage drainage of the secretions
  • D. Prone with the head below the hips to use gravity for drainage of the lower lobe

The correct answer is A (Left side-lying with the unaffected lung dependent so it receives more blood flow): In unilateral lung disease, placing the healthy lung down directs more blood flow to the better ventilated lung and improves the ventilation and perfusion match. Lying with the affected side down sends blood to consolidated tissue. Flat supine and head-down positions reduce lung volume and add to the work of breathing.

Question 310

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 45-year-old man with mild community-acquired pneumonia is admitted overnight. He coughs up a small amount of sputum on his own, his saturation is 95 percent on room air, and he walked to the washroom unaided. The resident requests chest physiotherapy. What is the best plan?

  • A. Start manual percussion and postural drainage twice daily to speed resolution of the consolidation
  • B. Begin positive expiratory pressure therapy four times daily to prevent mucus plugging
  • C. Start high flow nasal oxygen to prevent progression despite a normal saturation on room air
  • D. Encourage early walking and fluids, and hold airway clearance since he clears sputum himself

The correct answer is D (Encourage early walking and fluids, and hold airway clearance since he clears sputum himself): Routine chest physiotherapy does not shorten recovery in uncomplicated pneumonia, and it is reserved for patients who cannot clear secretions. This man clears sputum independently and is mobile, so early activity and hydration are most useful. Devices and percussion add cost and effort without a matching problem, and oxygen is not needed at a saturation of 95 percent.

Question 311

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 19-year-old university student in Halifax has cystic fibrosis with thick sputum and an FEV1 of 55 percent of predicted. She uses a bronchodilator, an airway clearance technique and an inhaled antibiotic each morning, and asks in what order they should be done so the medication works best.

  • A. Bronchodilator, then airway clearance, then the inhaled antibiotic so it reaches cleared airways
  • B. Airway clearance first, then the bronchodilator once the secretions have been brought up
  • C. Airway clearance, then the inhaled antibiotic, with the bronchodilator last to ease breathing after
  • D. Inhaled antibiotic first, then airway clearance to push the medication deeper through the loosened mucus

The correct answer is A (Bronchodilator, then airway clearance, then the inhaled antibiotic so it reaches cleared airways): The bronchodilator opens the airways so mobilized mucus can move and clearance works better. Clearing mucus before the inhaled antibiotic lets the drug deposit on the airway wall instead of in plugged secretions. Reversing these steps either wastes the antibiotic or makes clearance harder.

Question 312

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 16-year-old with cystic fibrosis plans a full afternoon of outdoor activity at a summer camp in northern Ontario. Sweat on her skin dries to a visible white salt film. Her physiotherapist is advising on preparation for the heat and exertion. Which advice is most appropriate?

  • A. Drink plain water often during activity and eat salty food that evening
  • B. Start with a sports drink before activity and let thirst guide further fluid and salt
  • C. Increase fluid and salt intake before and during prolonged exercise in the heat
  • D. Drink large amounts of plain water before the activity and avoid salty snacks during it

The correct answer is C (Increase fluid and salt intake before and during prolonged exercise in the heat): People with cystic fibrosis lose large amounts of sodium and chloride in sweat, as the white film shows, so they need extra fluid and salt before and during prolonged heat exposure. Taking salt afterward comes too late to prevent dehydration and cramps. Starting with a sports drink is reasonable, but thirst lags behind real losses, and plain water without salt can dilute sodium further.

Question 313

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A physiotherapist is teaching a hospitalized adult with bronchiectasis an airway clearance method made of repeated breathing phases. The patient asks what one full cycle contains and in what order, so she can practise it independently on the ward. Which sequence describes one cycle?

  • A. Thoracic expansion, forced expiration technique, thoracic expansion, forced expiration technique, with coughing between cycles
  • B. Forced expiration technique, breathing control, forced expiration technique, thoracic expansion, then a long rest
  • C. Breathing control, forced expiration technique, thoracic expansion, forced expiration technique, then breathing control
  • D. Breathing control, thoracic expansion, breathing control, forced expiration technique, then breathing control again

The correct answer is D (Breathing control, thoracic expansion, breathing control, forced expiration technique, then breathing control again): One cycle starts with relaxed breathing control, moves to thoracic expansion to loosen secretions, returns to breathing control, uses the forced expiration technique to move mucus, and ends with breathing control. The rest phases prevent bronchospasm and fatigue. The other sequences drop or reorder these phases.

Question 314

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 78-year-old man with COPD is admitted with an exacerbation. The physician orders a fixed, precisely controlled oxygen concentration of 24 percent because his inspired fraction must not vary with his breathing pattern. The physiotherapist is asked to set up the correct device. Which device should be used?

  • A. A nasal cannula at 1 litre per minute, which delivers roughly 24 percent oxygen
  • B. A partial rebreathing mask with the reservoir bag and flow set at 6 litres per minute
  • C. A simple face mask at 5 litres per minute to deliver about 40 percent oxygen
  • D. An air-entrainment mask set to a fixed 24 percent oxygen concentration

The correct answer is D (An air-entrainment mask set to a fixed 24 percent oxygen concentration): An air-entrainment mask draws in room air through a calibrated port, giving a steady concentration that does not change with the breathing pattern, which is what this order requires. A cannula at a low flow gives roughly the same number on paper, but the true inspired fraction shifts with his rate and depth. Reservoir and simple masks also give variable and higher concentrations.

Question 315

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 55-year-old woman in a rehabilitation unit is sitting comfortably with a respiratory rate of 16 and a heart rate of 72. The finger probe reads 84 percent. Her hands feel cold and she is wearing dark nail polish. The reading has not changed in a normal trace. What should the physiotherapist do first?

  • A. Raise the oxygen flow by 2 litres per minute and recheck the reading in five minutes
  • B. Warm the hand, remove the polish, then re-measure before changing any treatment
  • C. Ask the nurse to take an arterial blood gas sample now and recheck the probe afterward
  • D. Pause the session and report the low reading to the nurse, then monitor her closely

The correct answer is B (Warm the hand, remove the polish, then re-measure before changing any treatment): A comfortable patient with a normal rate and pulse and an unexpectedly low reading points to a measurement problem, since cold fingers and dark nail polish both degrade the signal. Warming the hand and removing the polish is quick and low risk. Reporting the number is reasonable if it persists, but it is premature before the technique is corrected, and changing oxygen or sampling blood acts on a doubtful value.

Question 316

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A pulmonary rehabilitation physiotherapist sets exercise intensity for a group of patients with chronic lung disease using the modified 0 to 10 Borg breathlessness scale. A new participant asks what level of breathlessness she should aim for during endurance training. What is the best target?

  • A. Slight breathlessness, rated one to two, kept steady across the whole endurance session
  • B. Marked breathlessness, rated seven, tolerated in short bursts during the second half
  • C. Breathlessness rated three to four on the 6 to 20 Borg exertion scale
  • D. Moderate breathlessness, rated about three to four on the scale

The correct answer is D (Moderate breathlessness, rated about three to four on the scale): Moderate breathlessness, around 3 to 4 on the modified 0 to 10 scale, is intense enough to improve endurance while remaining tolerable. A rating of 3 to 4 on the 6 to 20 exertion scale is a different, much lighter effort and does not match this scale. Very low ratings give a small training stimulus, and ratings of 7 and above are hard to sustain regularly in chronic lung disease.

Question 317

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 66-year-old woman with COPD becomes acutely breathless after a bed bath on a medical ward. She is anxious, her saturation is 90 percent, and she is lying nearly flat. The physiotherapist is called to help relieve her breathlessness immediately. Which action is most appropriate?

  • A. Sit her upright, arms hanging, and coach pursed-lip breathing
  • B. Keep her lying flat with knees bent and coach slow nasal breathing
  • C. Sit her upright against the raised bed and coach deep belly breathing with her hands
  • D. Sit her forward with forearms resting on a table and coach pursed-lip breathing

The correct answer is D (Sit her forward with forearms resting on a table and coach pursed-lip breathing): Leaning forward with the forearms supported fixes the shoulder girdle so accessory muscles can work on the chest and the diaphragm works at a better length, and pursed-lip breathing slows the rate. Sitting upright with the arms hanging gives up that support, and deep belly breathing tends to increase effort when the lungs are hyperinflated. Lying flat worsens breathlessness.

Question 318

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

During a COPD rehabilitation visit one week after discharge, a 71-year-old man reports a sudden sharp chest pain on inspiration. His heart rate is 118, his saturation has fallen by six points from baseline, and his right calf is swollen and tender. He had a long hospital stay. What is the best response?

  • A. Stop the session, keep him resting and urgently report suspected pulmonary embolism
  • B. Have him sit and use his reliever, then reassess the pain after a few minutes
  • C. Apply gentle airway clearance and reassess his chest pain and saturation before deciding on referral
  • D. Check calf circumference and apply light compression stockings, then continue seated exercise gently

The correct answer is A (Stop the session, keep him resting and urgently report suspected pulmonary embolism): Recent immobility, a swollen tender calf, pleuritic pain, tachycardia and a falling saturation form a high-risk picture for pulmonary embolism, which is an emergency. Reassessing after airway clearance or a reliever wastes time and may be harmful. Measuring the calf and adding compression with continued exercise does not address a possible clot, so stopping and notifying the physician promptly is the safe action.

Question 319

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

An 8-year-old girl with asthma presses her pressurized metered dose inhaler while starting to breathe in and often misses the timing. Her mother in Regina asks how to make the medication reach the lungs reliably. The physiotherapist reviews her technique. What is the best recommendation?

  • A. Shake the canister less and fire it into the open mouth held about ten centimetres away
  • B. Use a saline nebuliser before each dose to improve deposition of the inhaled medication
  • C. Attach a valved holding chamber and teach a slow breath in with a short hold
  • D. Press the inhaler twice during one rapid deep breath so one dose gets in

The correct answer is C (Attach a valved holding chamber and teach a slow breath in with a short hold): A valved holding chamber removes the need to coordinate actuation and inhalation and reduces deposition in the throat. A slow breath with a brief hold lets particles settle in the airways. Firing twice into a fast breath or into an open mouth still loses much of the dose.

Question 320

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 47-year-old man with Guillain-Barre syndrome is on a neurology ward. His vital capacity fell from 2.8 litres to 1.6 litres overnight, he now speaks in short phrases, and he has a weak cough. His saturation is still 96 percent. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Teach him supervised assisted cough techniques and recheck vital capacity at the next scheduled visit
  • B. Start incentive spirometry every hour and recheck vital capacity before the afternoon visit today
  • C. Provide gentle active-assisted range of motion and defer respiratory review to the morning rounds
  • D. Report the falling vital capacity urgently and monitor closely for impending ventilatory failure overnight

The correct answer is D (Report the falling vital capacity urgently and monitor closely for impending ventilatory failure overnight): A rapid fall in vital capacity with a weak cough and short phrases signals respiratory muscle failure, and saturation stays normal until late. Urgent medical notification and close monitoring are needed. Cough assistance is a useful skill in this condition, but rechecking at the next visit leaves the decline unreported, and repeated breathing exercise or waiting for rounds risks fatigue or a missed window to support ventilation.

Question 321

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A physiotherapist teaches a post-operative patient how to use a volume-oriented incentive spirometer to reduce the risk of atelectasis. The patient asks what the correct breathing pattern is when using the device, since she is unsure whether to inhale or exhale into it. What is the correct technique?

  • A. Inhale slowly and deeply through the nose, then exhale through the mouthpiece to raise the indicator
  • B. Inhale slowly and deeply, then exhale hard to clear the airways of secretions
  • C. Take rapid deep breaths through the mouthpiece in quick succession until the indicator reaches the goal
  • D. Inhale slowly and deeply through the mouthpiece, hold briefly, then exhale normally

The correct answer is D (Inhale slowly and deeply through the mouthpiece, hold briefly, then exhale normally): A volume-oriented incentive spirometer rewards a slow, sustained maximal inspiration through the mouthpiece, followed by a brief hold and a normal exhalation, which expands the lung and helps prevent atelectasis. Adding a hard exhale to clear secretions mixes in a different technique, and rapid breaths reward flow rather than volume. Nasal inhalation does not move air through the device, and blowing into it does nothing.

Question 322

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 69-year-old man in a community COPD program has completed four weeks of exercise. Today he reports increased breathlessness, a fever of 38.1 degrees Celsius, and green sputum that is double his usual amount. His walking distance is down 30 percent. The therapist is deciding how to proceed.

  • A. Pause progression and notify the physician about the change in sputum and breathlessness
  • B. Continue exercising at reduced intensity and ask him to document sputum colour and temperature
  • C. Hold exercise today and encourage fluids and rest, then reassess at the next visit
  • D. Teach active cycle of breathing for sputum clearance and review his symptoms at the next visit

The correct answer is A (Pause progression and notify the physician about the change in sputum and breathlessness): Increased sputum volume and purulence with worse breathlessness, fever and a 30 percent drop in walking distance suggest an infective exacerbation, which needs prompt medical assessment. Holding exercise is correct, but waiting for the next visit leaves the change unreported. Airway clearance is a useful supportive tool, yet it does not replace the medical review, and carrying on at lower intensity risks deterioration.

Question 323

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A physiotherapist auscultates the lungs of a 66-year-old woman with a confirmed diagnosis of pulmonary fibrosis before her first rehabilitation session at the outpatient clinic this week. She wants to document the abnormal breath sound most characteristic of this condition. Which finding best fits?

  • A. Coarse crackles early in inspiration that change or clear after coughing
  • B. Low-pitched continuous wheeze heard mainly during the expiratory phase of breathing
  • C. Fine crackles heard late in inspiration, mainly over the lung bases
  • D. Absent breath sounds with a dull percussion note over one lung base

The correct answer is C (Fine crackles heard late in inspiration, mainly over the lung bases): Fibrosis stiffens the lungs, and sudden popping open of small airways at the end of inspiration produces fine late crackles at the bases. Wheeze signals narrowed airways, coarse crackles that clear with coughing suggest secretions, and absent sounds with dullness point toward effusion or collapse.

Question 324

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 74-year-old man in Winnipeg is starting home oxygen delivered by a concentrator. He heats his house with a wood stove and sometimes vapes. His physiotherapist is reviewing home safety before discharge and must prioritize one key message. Which advice is the most important?

  • A. Store spare cylinders lying flat in the warm sunroom, away from the stove
  • B. Keep oxygen equipment well away from the wood stove and ban smoking or vaping nearby
  • C. Use petroleum-based lip balm to counter nasal drying from the oxygen flow
  • D. Turn the concentrator off while sleeping to remove any risk of overheating

The correct answer is B (Keep oxygen equipment well away from the wood stove and ban smoking or vaping nearby): Oxygen supports combustion, so equipment must be kept away from open flames and heat sources and nobody should smoke or vape near it. Petroleum products are flammable in oxygen-enriched air, and unsecured cylinders are a hazard. Switching the concentrator off at night removes prescribed therapy without addressing the fire risk.

Question 325

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A tall, thin 22-year-old man develops sudden sharp right-sided chest pain and breathlessness after a coughing fit during an outpatient visit. Breath sounds are reduced on the right, percussion is hyperresonant, and his saturation is 92 percent. He is anxious but alert. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Position him comfortably and give oxygen, then monitor saturation for fifteen minutes
  • B. Stop treatment and have him lie down while arranging a routine chest imaging appointment this week
  • C. Assess for pulmonary embolism by checking his calves and heart rate before deciding on referral
  • D. Stop treatment, keep him seated and call urgently for assessment of suspected pneumothorax

The correct answer is D (Stop treatment, keep him seated and call urgently for assessment of suspected pneumothorax): Sudden one-sided pleuritic pain with reduced breath sounds and hyperresonance in a tall young man strongly suggests a spontaneous pneumothorax, which needs urgent imaging and medical care. Pulmonary embolism is a fair differential for sudden chest pain, but the percussion and breath sound findings point to the pleural space, and either way the response is urgent referral, not observation. A routine appointment is far too slow.

Question 326

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 64-year-old woman with severe COPD cannot sustain more than two minutes of cycling at her target intensity because breathlessness stops her. She wants to improve her endurance. The physiotherapist is writing her exercise program for the next eight weeks. Which approach is most suitable?

  • A. Interval training with brief work bouts and rests, allowing higher intensity with less breathlessness
  • B. Continuous moderate cycling for thirty minutes at a steady pace to build endurance gradually
  • C. Upper limb resistance training with light weights to lower the ventilatory demand of daily tasks
  • D. Inspiratory muscle training at low load as the main program, postponing cycling until stronger

The correct answer is A (Interval training with brief work bouts and rests, allowing higher intensity with less breathlessness): Interval training lets people with severe airflow limitation reach a meaningful training load through short efforts with recovery, so total work is higher with less breathlessness. A continuous thirty-minute bout is the usual goal, but she cannot sustain two minutes at her target. Upper limb and inspiratory muscle training help as adjuncts, yet neither builds cycling endurance, which is her stated aim.

Question 327

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

One day after abdominal surgery, a 58-year-old man is alert and cooperative with controlled pain. His chest radiograph shows left lower lobe collapse, air entry is reduced there, and he has no sputum and is not intubated. His saturation is 92 percent on room air. What is the best treatment?

  • A. Manual hyperinflation with a bag to blow open the collapsed left lower lobe
  • B. Percussion and head-down postural drainage positioning for the left lower lobe each shift
  • C. Upright positioning, mobilization and deep breaths with an inspiratory hold
  • D. Nasopharyngeal suction to remove the mucus plug thought to be blocking the left lower lobe

The correct answer is C (Upright positioning, mobilization and deep breaths with an inspiratory hold): Atelectasis in a cooperative, sputum-free patient is a volume problem, so the aim is to raise lung volume through position change, activity and deep breathing with a hold. Bag hyperinflation is for intubated patients, suction and drainage target secretions he does not have, and percussion would only add pain.

Question 328

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 28-year-old woman with asthma has a written action plan based on her personal best peak flow. This week her readings have fallen to about 60 percent of her best, and she is waking at night coughing. She reports this to her physiotherapist. What guidance fits her plan?

  • A. Use her reliever and recheck peak flow in one hour
  • B. Double her controller dose for a week on her own and recheck the peak flow daily
  • C. Follow the emergency zone steps and go straight to the nearest emergency department now
  • D. Follow the caution zone steps in the plan and contact her clinician promptly

The correct answer is D (Follow the caution zone steps in the plan and contact her clinician promptly): A reading near 60 percent of personal best with night waking indicates poor control and falls in the caution zone, where the plan directs reliever use and prompt clinician contact. Using the reliever and rechecking is only part of those steps. Emergency zone steps apply when readings fall below about half of her best, and changing the controller dose without her clinician steps outside the written plan.

Question 329

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A physiotherapist in a primary care clinic reviews post-bronchodilator spirometry for a 59-year-old smoker with chronic cough and breathlessness. She wants to confirm that the result demonstrates fixed airflow obstruction in keeping with COPD, not another condition. Which finding confirms this?

  • A. Diffusing capacity above 120 percent of the predicted value on gas transfer testing
  • B. Total lung capacity below 80 percent of the predicted value on volume testing
  • C. A post-bronchodilator FEV1 to forced vital capacity ratio persistently below 0.70 on spirometry
  • D. Forced vital capacity below 80 percent with a ratio of expired volume above 0.80

The correct answer is C (A post-bronchodilator FEV1 to forced vital capacity ratio persistently below 0.70 on spirometry): Fixed airflow obstruction is shown by a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70, meaning less of the vital capacity leaves the lungs in the first second. Reduced total lung capacity, or low forced vital capacity with a high ratio, signals restriction, and a raised diffusing capacity does not define obstruction.

Question 330

Cardiovascular-Respiratory

A 26-year-old woman becomes distressed during a gym assessment and reports tingling around her lips and fingers. Her respiratory rate is 28 with frequent sighing, her saturation is 99 percent, her chest is clear, and she has no wheeze. She has no chest pain, leg swelling or lung disease history. What is the best response?

  • A. Check for chest pain and a calf clot, then arrange urgent assessment for pulmonary embolism
  • B. Have her rebreathe slowly into a paper bag until the tingling stops
  • C. Give a short-acting bronchodilator through a spacer and recheck her breath sounds in ten minutes
  • D. Guide relaxed diaphragmatic breathing at a slower rate while reassuring her

The correct answer is D (Guide relaxed diaphragmatic breathing at a slower rate while reassuring her): Fast breathing with sighing, tingling around the mouth and fingers, normal oxygen and a clear chest suggest overbreathing with low carbon dioxide. Slow diaphragmatic breathing with reassurance corrects the pattern. Paper bag rebreathing is outdated and can lower oxygen, a bronchodilator treats obstruction she does not have, and an embolism is unlikely without chest pain or leg swelling.

Question 331

Other Systems

A physiotherapist examines a bed-bound patient and finds a sacral wound that is a shallow open ulcer with a pink-red wound bed. No fat or deeper tissue is visible, and the surrounding skin is intact. The team asks for the correct pressure injury stage. Which description matches this wound?

  • A. Partial-thickness skin loss with an open shallow wound and a pink wound bed
  • B. Intact skin with non-blanchable redness over a bony prominence
  • C. Full-thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat but no exposed bone or tendon
  • D. Persistent deep red or purple discolouration of intact skin over a bony prominence

The correct answer is A (Partial-thickness skin loss with an open shallow wound and a pink wound bed): A shallow open ulcer with a pink-red bed and no visible fat is a partial-thickness injury, classified as stage 2. Intact reddened skin is stage 1, visible fat marks stage 3, and deep purple intact skin suggests deep tissue injury.

Question 332

Other Systems

A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends for debridement of a plantar forefoot ulcer. Today the ulcer is more painful than last week with purulent drainage, spreading redness extending 3 centimetres from the edge, and warmth. His temperature is 38.2 degrees Celsius. What is the best action?

  • A. Stop debridement and arrange urgent medical assessment for suspected spreading infection
  • B. Apply a total contact cast for offloading and schedule a comprehensive reassessment next week
  • C. Send a wound swab for culture and continue gentle debridement while awaiting the laboratory result
  • D. Cleanse and debride gently, then apply a silver dressing and review in two days

The correct answer is A (Stop debridement and arrange urgent medical assessment for suspected spreading infection): Purulence, spreading redness, warmth, increased pain and fever indicate a moderate to severe diabetic foot infection, which threatens the limb and needs urgent medical assessment, imaging and antibiotics. A silver dressing or a swab with gentle debridement is wound care for a local problem, not the response to systemic signs. A total contact cast is used for offloading clean ulcers and is unsafe over an infection.

Question 333

Other Systems

A 52-year-old man with type 1 diabetes arrives for an aerobic class. He injected rapid-acting insulin earlier, his glucose meter reads 3.6 mmol/L, and he is sweaty and shaky. The physiotherapist has fast-acting carbohydrate available. What is the most appropriate step?

  • A. Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck glucose after 15 minutes before any exercise
  • B. Give a chocolate bar with nuts, since the fat will sustain his glucose through the class
  • C. Give 15 grams of carbohydrate and start the class right away since symptoms usually settle quickly
  • D. Begin low intensity exercise because activity will raise glucose through stress hormones

The correct answer is A (Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck glucose after 15 minutes before any exercise): A glucose below 4.0 mmol/L with symptoms needs prompt treatment with 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate and a recheck after 15 minutes. Foods with fat absorb too slowly, exercise tends to lower glucose, and starting before confirming recovery risks a repeat low.

Question 334

Other Systems

A 29-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes arrives for a supervised walking program. Her glucose is 17.5 mmol/L, her urine ketones are negative, and she feels well with no nausea or abdominal pain. She asks if she can exercise today. What is the best advice?

  • A. Delay exercise until her glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, then walk at light intensity
  • B. Proceed with moderate exercise and skip the usual rapid-acting insulin at her next meal
  • C. Proceed with light to moderate exercise, hydrate well, and check glucose more often during activity
  • D. Cancel exercise today and recheck her glucose and ketones in two hours before deciding

The correct answer is C (Proceed with light to moderate exercise, hydrate well, and check glucose more often during activity): With a high glucose but negative ketones and no symptoms, light to moderate exercise is acceptable with good hydration and closer glucose monitoring. Waiting for a lower number sounds cautious, but it is not required when she feels well and ketones are negative. Adjusting insulin without direction from her care team adds risk, and postponing the session withholds a safe benefit.

Question 335

Other Systems

A physiotherapist at a community foot clinic wants to screen a 66-year-old man with long-standing diabetes for loss of protective sensation in his feet. She chooses the standard simple bedside test used in diabetes foot assessment. Which test should she use?

  • A. Palpation of the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses graded on both feet
  • B. A 10 gram monofilament pressed on several plantar sites
  • C. Ankle-brachial index measured with a Doppler at the posterior tibial artery at rest
  • D. Passive range of motion of the first metatarsophalangeal joint measured with a goniometer

The correct answer is B (A 10 gram monofilament pressed on several plantar sites): Inability to feel a 10 gram monofilament at plantar sites identifies loss of protective sensation and predicts ulceration, so it is the standard simple bedside screen. Pulse palpation, the ankle-brachial index and first joint mobility are all parts of a full diabetic foot assessment, but they examine circulation and mobility, not sensation.

Question 336

Other Systems

A 60-year-old man with diabetic neuropathy has a plantar forefoot ulcer under the first metatarsal head. The ulcer is clean, shows no infection, and his ankle-brachial index is normal. He walks on it daily without pain. Which treatment best promotes healing?

  • A. A rigid orthotic with a metatarsal bar worn in regular shoes during sport
  • B. A compression bandage from toes to knee to reduce edema
  • C. A removable cushioned sandal with advice to limit walking when pain increases
  • D. A total contact cast or other non-removable offloading device

The correct answer is D (A total contact cast or other non-removable offloading device): Neuropathic plantar ulcers heal when pressure is removed, and a non-removable total contact cast is the best option because it ensures adherence. Patients without pain cannot use pain as a guide, compression addresses edema in a different ulcer type, and continued sport loads the wound.

Question 337

Other Systems

A 67-year-old woman has a shallow, irregular, moist ulcer above the medial malleolus with surrounding brown staining and leg swelling. The leg feels heavy by day, relief comes with elevation, pedal pulses are strong, and her ankle-brachial index is 1.0. What is the best treatment?

  • A. Graded compression with elevation after arterial supply is confirmed
  • B. Leg elevation with a non-stick dressing, no compression wrap
  • C. Calf muscle pump exercises with an occlusive dressing and the leg left uncompressed
  • D. Sharp debridement of the wound edges followed by a topical antibiotic and regular dressing change

The correct answer is A (Graded compression with elevation after arterial supply is confirmed): A moist shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus with brown staining and swelling, relieved by elevation, indicates venous disease, and graded compression is the cornerstone of treatment once the ankle-brachial index confirms normal arterial supply. Elevation, calf pump exercises and wound care all help, yet none corrects the venous hypertension driving the ulcer, so they fall short as the main treatment.

Question 338

Other Systems

A 74-year-old smoker has a punched-out, pale ulcer on the tip of the second toe. The foot is cool and hairless, capillary refill is slow, pedal pulses are absent, and rest pain at night eases when he hangs the leg over the bed. His ankle-brachial index is 0.4. What is the best plan?

  • A. Start progressive walking exercise and review in two weeks
  • B. Apply a non-adherent dressing and light compression to protect the toe while it heals
