  • C. Withhold compression and refer urgently for vascular assessment
  • D. Advise dependent leg positioning at night and continue weekly dressing changes

The correct answer is C (Withhold compression and refer urgently for vascular assessment): A pale punched-out toe ulcer, cool hairless foot, absent pulses, rest pain eased by dependency and an ankle-brachial index of 0.4 indicate critical limb ischemia. Dependent positioning does relieve night pain, but it only masks the problem while the limb remains at risk. Walking programs and compression reduce or strain flow, so compression is withheld and urgent vascular referral is needed.

Question 339

Other Systems

A 58-year-old woman has a shallow venous ulcer producing heavy exudate. The wound bed is red and granulating, but the surrounding skin is white, soft and macerated, and the current dressing is saturated within a day. Which dressing plan is most suitable?

  • A. A hydrogel dressing covered by a film to keep the wound bed moist
  • B. A hydrocolloid dressing with a border applied over the wound and the surrounding skin
  • C. A non-adherent contact layer with a thin cotton pad, changed once daily
  • D. An absorbent foam or alginate dressing with a barrier on the macerated skin

The correct answer is D (An absorbent foam or alginate dressing with a barrier on the macerated skin): Heavy exudate with maceration calls for a dressing with high absorbency and a barrier to protect the surrounding skin. A hydrocolloid is better for light to moderate drainage and can add to maceration, and a thin contact layer with a pad would saturate within hours. Hydrogels and films add or trap moisture where the wound already has too much.

Question 340

Other Systems

A student physiotherapist is reviewing normal soft tissue repair before observing wound care clinics during her placement this month. She is asked to name the stages of healing in the order in which they occur after a skin injury. Which sequence is correct?

  • A. Hemostasis first, then proliferation, then inflammation, and finally remodelling
  • B. Hemostasis first, then inflammation, then proliferation, and finally remodelling of the tissue
  • C. Inflammation first, then hemostasis, then proliferation, and finally remodelling
  • D. Hemostasis first, then inflammation, then remodelling, and finally proliferation

The correct answer is B (Hemostasis first, then inflammation, then proliferation, and finally remodelling of the tissue): Healing begins with hemostasis to stop bleeding, then inflammation clears debris and bacteria, then proliferation brings granulation and re-epithelialization, and finally remodelling reorganizes collagen. Putting inflammation first or proliferation before it reverses the early phases, and placing remodelling before proliferation reverses the last two, which are the most tempting errors because they keep most of the sequence intact.

Question 341

Other Systems

A 30-year-old man is two weeks after a deep partial-thickness burn involving the front of his neck and right axilla. He holds his neck bent forward and his arm against his side because it hurts less. The therapist is planning positioning and splinting to prevent contracture. What is best?

  • A. Keep the neck flexed on pillows for comfort and the arm adducted to protect the graft
  • B. Fit a soft collar with the neck slightly turned and rest the arm across the trunk
  • C. Place the arm in a sling with the elbow bent to protect the healing skin
  • D. Keep the neck extended and the axilla abducted to about 90 degrees with splinting

The correct answer is D (Keep the neck extended and the axilla abducted to about 90 degrees with splinting): Burn scars shorten along the line of tension, so the neck and axilla should be held in the lengthened position of extension and abduction with splints between exercises. The comfortable flexed and adducted positions encourage contracture, and slings or collars fix the joints in shortened postures.

Question 342

Other Systems

A 57-year-old man with long-standing diabetes and neuropathy has a warm, swollen right foot with no wound. He denies pain, the skin temperature is 4 degrees Celsius higher than the left, and the first radiograph looks normal. He insists on walking in his usual shoes. What is the best plan?

  • A. Begin offloading with a walking boot and recheck the foot in six weeks
  • B. Immobilize non-weight-bearing and request urgent review for suspected Charcot foot
  • C. Order a repeat radiograph in two weeks and allow walking in a cushioned shoe meanwhile
  • D. Treat as cellulitis and request urgent antibiotics while he continues normal walking in shoes

The correct answer is B (Immobilize non-weight-bearing and request urgent review for suspected Charcot foot): A warm, swollen, painless neuropathic foot with a temperature difference above 2 degrees Celsius suggests acute Charcot neuroarthropathy even when early radiographs are normal. Immobilization with offloading prevents collapse and deformity. Cellulitis is a fair differential for a warm foot, but there is no wound and no redness, and a removable boot, delayed imaging or walking in shoes allow continued loading.

Question 343

Other Systems

A 80-year-old woman is on bed rest after a hip fracture. She has non-blanchable redness over the sacrum and heels, and the nursing team asks the physiotherapist to advise on positioning to prevent skin breakdown. Which plan is most appropriate?

  • A. Reposition using a 30 degree side-lying tilt and keep the heels off the mattress
  • B. Massage the reddened bony areas firmly at each turn to stimulate local circulation
  • C. Turn her into a 90 degree side-lying position on the hip bone to unload the sacrum
  • D. Raise the head of the bed to 60 degrees for most of the day for breathing

The correct answer is A (Reposition using a 30 degree side-lying tilt and keep the heels off the mattress): A 30 degree tilt moves the load onto muscle and fat rather than bone, and floating the heels protects them. Full side-lying loads the trochanter, a steeply raised head of bed adds sacral shear, and massaging reddened skin can injure tissue already at risk.

Question 344

Other Systems

A 77-year-old man with urinary and faecal incontinence has shiny, red, weeping skin in the gluteal cleft with diffuse, irregular edges. The damage is shallow with no slough or necrosis, the sacral bone is not under the area, and the skin elsewhere is intact. What is the most likely cause and approach?

  • A. A stage 2 pressure injury requiring foam dressing and strict offloading of the sacrum
  • B. Moisture-associated skin damage, managed with continence care and a barrier product
  • C. A deep tissue injury requiring protection of the limb and imaging of the tissue
  • D. A stage 3 pressure injury needing debridement of slough and a deeper dressing

The correct answer is B (Moisture-associated skin damage, managed with continence care and a barrier product): Diffuse shallow damage in the gluteal cleft with irregular edges in an incontinent patient points to moisture-associated skin damage, not pressure over bone. Treatment focuses on managing the moisture source and protecting skin. Pressure injury stages and deep tissue injury involve different locations and appearance.

Question 345

Other Systems

A physiotherapist runs an exercise class for adults with diabetes who use insulin. A participant asks whether low blood sugar is only a risk during the session itself. The physiotherapist explains the risk after exercise to the whole group. Which statement is correct?

  • A. Exercise taken in the evening carries lower overnight hypoglycemia risk than morning exercise
  • B. Low glucose risk peaks during the session and fades soon afterward
  • C. Cutting the pre-exercise insulin dose by half makes delayed lows later that night unlikely
  • D. Delayed hypoglycemia can occur many hours after exercise, including overnight

The correct answer is D (Delayed hypoglycemia can occur many hours after exercise, including overnight): Exercise increases insulin sensitivity and muscle glucose uptake for hours, and glycogen replacement continues afterward, so low glucose can occur late or overnight. Reducing the pre-exercise insulin dose helps lower the immediate risk but does not remove the later one. Evening sessions actually raise the chance of overnight lows, and the risk does not end when the session does.

Question 346

Other Systems

A 68-year-old man with long-standing diabetes and renal disease has a non-healing toe ulcer and absent pedal pulses. His ankle-brachial index is 1.35, and the ankle arteries are not compressible with the cuff. The physiotherapist must interpret the result. What is the best next step?

  • A. Request a venous duplex scan to look for reflux in the leg veins
  • B. Repeat the index after ten minutes of rest with the leg at heart level
  • C. Request a toe-brachial index because calcified vessels falsely raise ankle readings
  • D. Remeasure ankle pressure using a wider cuff, accepting the resulting value if it falls below 1.0

The correct answer is C (Request a toe-brachial index because calcified vessels falsely raise ankle readings): Values above about 1.3 suggest stiff, calcified vessels, common in diabetes and renal disease, so the ankle index is unreliable and toe pressures or a toe-brachial index assess perfusion better. Repeating with rest or a wider cuff addresses technique, but calcification is the cause here and it persists. A venous scan looks at the wrong system when pulses are absent and the ulcer is on the toe.

Question 347

Other Systems

A 35-year-old woman in Edmonton with a T6 spinal cord injury uses a manual wheelchair all day at work. She has a good gel cushion but asks the physiotherapist how often she needs to relieve pressure from her buttocks while sitting. What is the best advice?

  • A. Perform a weight shift once each hour at a break because the gel cushion lowers risk
  • B. Perform a pressure relief weight shift every 15 to 30 minutes for one to two minutes
  • C. Rely on the gel cushion and change position when she notices discomfort
  • D. Shift position every two to three hours, matching her meal and washroom breaks

The correct answer is B (Perform a pressure relief weight shift every 15 to 30 minutes for one to two minutes): People without sensation need scheduled pressure relief, commonly every 15 to 30 minutes for one to two minutes, because they cannot feel the discomfort that prompts others to move. A good cushion helps but does not replace relief, and hourly or two to three hour intervals leave tissue loaded too long.

Question 348

Other Systems

During a group session, a 61-year-old woman with diabetes becomes pale, sweaty and shaky, and she is confused about where she is. She is awake, can follow simple commands and can swallow safely. Her glucose meter is in her bag across the room. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Ask a colleague to fetch the meter and treat once the reading confirms a low
  • B. Give her a glass of orange juice slowly over thirty minutes and recheck her symptoms
  • C. Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate at once without waiting for a glucose reading to confirm
  • D. Call emergency services and place her in the recovery position, giving nothing by mouth

The correct answer is C (Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate at once without waiting for a glucose reading to confirm): Sweating, shakiness, pallor and confusion in a person with diabetes should be treated as hypoglycemia, and a conscious patient who can swallow should receive fast-acting oral carbohydrate at once. Confirming with the meter is good practice when it is at hand, but fetching it delays treatment. Juice is a suitable sugar only when taken promptly, and she can swallow, so withholding anything by mouth is not needed.

Question 349

Other Systems

A 62-year-old man with diabetic neuropathy and loss of protective sensation has no wounds at present. He works on his feet all day as a cook and asks the physiotherapist what he can do at home to protect them. Which advice is the most appropriate?

  • A. Inspect both feet daily and wear well-fitted closed shoes with seamless socks
  • B. Moisturize between the toes nightly and wear soft slippers indoors
  • C. Soak his feet in warm water daily and then smooth any calluses with a pumice stone
  • D. Choose flexible open-toed sandals for work to let the feet breathe and avoid friction

The correct answer is A (Inspect both feet daily and wear well-fitted closed shoes with seamless socks): With loss of protective sensation, injury goes unnoticed, so daily inspection and well-fitted protective footwear with seamless socks are the core prevention for someone on his feet all day. Moisturizing is a reasonable habit, but not between the toes, and soft slippers give little protection. Warm soaks can scald numb skin, pumice use risks abrasion, and open-toed sandals leave the foot exposed.

Question 350

Other Systems

A 59-year-old man has a plantar diabetic foot ulcer that has decreased in area by less than 20 percent over four weeks despite offloading and routine dressings. It has no infection, no edema, and his last HbA1c was 11 percent. He eats little protein. What is the best next step?

  • A. Review glycemic control, nutrition and perfusion before changing local wound care plans
  • B. Add stronger compression to speed edema reduction around the ulcer
  • C. Increase debridement to daily sessions to force the wound into proliferation
  • D. Switch to a costlier advanced dressing and reassess in another four weeks

The correct answer is A (Review glycemic control, nutrition and perfusion before changing local wound care plans): A wound that has not reduced by about half in four weeks is stalled, and the first step is to look for causes. Poor glycaemic control, inadequate protein intake and reduced perfusion all impair healing and need attention. A new dressing, daily debridement or compression do not target them.

Question 351

Other Systems

A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on insulin arrives for a supervised treadmill session in Halifax. He feels slightly shaky. His capillary glucose is 3.6 mmol/L. He ate lunch four hours ago. He is keen to start because he has a work trip next week. What is the most appropriate next step?

  • A. Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and begin the session at low intensity with symptom checks
  • B. Give 30 g of slow-release carbohydrate with protein, then start the session once the shakiness settles
  • C. Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes before exercising
  • D. Repeat the glucose reading on a second meter and start if unchanged

The correct answer is C (Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes before exercising): A glucose below 4.0 mmol/L with symptoms is hypoglycemia, and the standard response is 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate with a recheck after 15 minutes. Starting at low intensity feels cautious, but exercise lowers glucose further before recovery is confirmed. Slower carbohydrate and protein act too late for a symptomatic low. He can start once the reading is back in a safe range.

Question 352

Other Systems

A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes attends outpatient physiotherapy in Winnipeg for a running program. She feels nauseated and thirsty today. Her glucose is 15.2 mmol/L and her blood ketone reading is 2.0 mmol/L. She says a short run usually brings her glucose down. What is the best decision?

  • A. Hold the exercise, follow her sick-day ketone plan, and contact her diabetes care team promptly
  • B. Allow a low-intensity walk to lower her glucose and recheck ketones afterward at the clinic
  • C. Treat the high glucose with a correction insulin dose and begin a gentle run
  • D. Give oral fluids and rest for an hour, then repeat ketones before deciding on running

The correct answer is A (Hold the exercise, follow her sick-day ketone plan, and contact her diabetes care team promptly): Raised blood ketones with nausea and thirst suggest insulin deficiency and a risk of ketoacidosis, and exercise can push glucose and ketones higher in that state. A correction dose or a gentle walk tries to treat the number while still training an unwell client. Fluids and rest do not clear ketones. She needs her sick-day ketone plan and her diabetes team before training resumes.

Question 353

Other Systems

A 66-year-old retired bus driver in Regina has type 2 diabetes with loss of protective sensation in both feet. Skin is intact, with no ulcer or deformity. He wants to begin a walking program for glycemic control. Which plan is the most appropriate for him?

  • A. Start a progressive walking program in well-fitted shoes with daily foot checks for blisters or redness
  • B. Start with non-weight-bearing cycling and add walking after a podiatry assessment of his feet
  • C. Start a walking program in cushioned sandals with his feet inspected at each weekly visit
  • D. Start a treadmill walking program at a brisk pace with a podiatrist reviewing his feet monthly

The correct answer is A (Start a progressive walking program in well-fitted shoes with daily foot checks for blisters or redness): With intact skin and no deformity, weight-bearing aerobic exercise is encouraged because its benefits outweigh the risk when the feet are protected. Fitted footwear and daily inspection catch early skin damage. Delaying walking for cycling is tempting, but loss of protective sensation alone does not require it. Sandals, a brisk start and infrequent reviews leave injuries unnoticed for too long.

Question 354

Other Systems

A 28-year-old woman at 14 weeks of an uncomplicated pregnancy asks a physiotherapist in Calgary how much physical activity she should aim for each week. She was not active before pregnancy. Her midwife has raised no concerns. According to Canadian guidance for pregnancy, what weekly target is recommended?

  • A. About 75 minutes of moderate-intensity activity weekly in the first trimester, then more as pregnancy advances
  • B. At least 150 minutes of vigorous activity weekly in three long sessions, starting at full intensity
  • C. At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity spread over several days, starting gradually
  • D. Up to 60 minutes of light activity weekly, avoiding any rise in her breathing rate

The correct answer is C (At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity spread over several days, starting gradually): The Canadian guideline for pregnancy recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, spread over several days, when there are no contraindications. Women who were inactive before pregnancy build gradually toward the same goal. A 75 minute figure is tempting because it matches the vigorous-activity equivalent, but it does not apply to moderate effort. Vigorous work started quickly and a very light target both miss the recommendation.

Question 355

Other Systems

A 32-week pregnant teacher is seen in a Toronto clinic for low back pain. She mentions a headache since yesterday that paracetamol does not ease, and she sees flashing spots. Clinic blood pressure is 148/96 mmHg with new ankle puffiness. She wants to continue her usual exercises. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Advise her to phone her midwife later this week and avoid further exercise until then
  • B. Treat the back pain with gentle mobilization first and recheck her blood pressure afterward
  • C. Stop treatment and arrange same-day medical assessment for possible pre-eclampsia
  • D. Stop treatment, advise rest and fluids at home, and ask her to rebook within two days

The correct answer is C (Stop treatment and arrange same-day medical assessment for possible pre-eclampsia): A persistent headache that paracetamol does not ease, visual spots, raised blood pressure and new swelling at 32 weeks are red flags for pre-eclampsia, which can progress to seizures. This needs medical assessment the same day. Telling her to call later this week or to rest and rebook feels cautious but still delays care. Treating the back first reverses the priorities.

Question 356

Other Systems

At 31 weeks of pregnancy, a 35-year-old cashier in Vancouver feels light-headed, sweaty and nauseated about two minutes after lying flat on her back for a pelvic floor exercise. Symptoms ease when she rolls onto her side. Her pulse is 96 beats per minute. What explanation and advice fit best?

  • A. Vasovagal response to exertion; reduce the effort and keep her lying flat for the exercise
  • B. Pregnancy-related low blood sugar; give a carbohydrate snack and resume the exercise on her back
  • C. Early pre-eclampsia; check her blood pressure and sit her upright while the symptoms settle
  • D. Caval compression by the uterus; choose side-lying or semi-reclined positions

The correct answer is D (Caval compression by the uterus; choose side-lying or semi-reclined positions): After about 20 weeks, the uterus can compress the vena cava when she lies supine, which reduces venous return and blood pressure. Symptoms that begin soon after lying flat and ease on rolling to the side point to this. Low blood sugar and pre-eclampsia are possible in pregnancy but do not change with position. Side-lying or semi-reclined positions solve the problem.

Question 357

Other Systems

A 29-year-old woman at 26 weeks of pregnancy has deep buttock pain when turning in bed and climbing stairs. On the active straight leg raise test, she reports heaviness that lessens when the physiotherapist compresses her pelvis. There are no neurological signs. Which plan is the most appropriate?

  • A. Trial a pelvic support belt with stabilizing exercises and modified aggravating activities such as stairs
  • B. Advise relative rest until delivery with a gradual return to walking afterward
  • C. Start sacroiliac manipulation with deep hip stretching to restore pelvic mobility
  • D. Refer for lumbar imaging to look for a disc herniation before any treatment begins

The correct answer is A (Trial a pelvic support belt with stabilizing exercises and modified aggravating activities such as stairs): Relief with manual pelvic compression during the active straight leg raise suggests pelvic girdle pain from reduced load transfer. A support belt, stabilizing exercise and activity modification are standard care. Imaging is tempting for deep buttock pain but there are no neurological signs. Rest deconditions her, and stretching or manipulating a pelvis that is already too mobile can aggravate the problem.

Question 358

Other Systems

A 31-year-old woman, eight weeks after a vaginal birth in Ottawa, notices a ridge doming along her midline when she curls up. The inter-rectus gap measures about three finger widths at the navel. She has no pain. Which advice should the physiotherapist give?

  • A. Add progressive curl-ups with a binder for support and increase them as the ridge fades
  • B. Refer for a surgical opinion at this stage and avoid all abdominal exercise until a repair
  • C. Practise deep abdominal activation on exhaling and limit tasks that dome the midline
  • D. Begin walking and pelvic floor training and delay abdominal work for now

The correct answer is C (Practise deep abdominal activation on exhaling and limit tasks that dome the midline): Many women have a wide gap early postpartum and it often narrows. The aim is good deep abdominal control with exhalation and managing load so the midline does not dome under pressure. Curl-ups with a binder do the opposite by raising intra-abdominal pressure. Surgery is considered later if function remains poor, and delaying all abdominal work until twelve weeks misses the early benefit of deep activation.

Question 359

Other Systems

A breastfeeding woman, three weeks postpartum, books a pelvic health visit in Edmonton for a tender lump. The breast shows a red, hot wedge-shaped area. Her temperature is 38.6 C and she feels achy and chilled. A colleague suggests therapeutic ultrasound to the lump. What is the best next step?

  • A. Advise gentle lymphatic massage toward the armpit and review in a few days
  • B. Advise frequent feeding with warm compresses and a review visit in two days
  • C. Apply low-dose pulsed ultrasound to the lump and refer if the fever persists
  • D. Refer same day for possible mastitis and withhold the ultrasound treatment over the breast

The correct answer is D (Refer same day for possible mastitis and withhold the ultrasound treatment over the breast): Fever, flu-like symptoms and a hot red wedge suggest mastitis that may need antibiotics, so medical assessment comes first. Frequent feeding and warmth are reasonable for a simple blocked duct, which is why that option is tempting, but systemic signs change the priority. Gentle massage and ultrasound do not treat infection and may worsen inflammation, so physiotherapy modalities are withheld.

Question 360

Other Systems

A 27-year-old woman, ten days after a caesarean birth in Montreal, reports a sore right calf. The calf is swollen compared with the left, warm, and tender along the deep veins. She walked normally yesterday and thinks she pulled a muscle. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Treat as a muscle strain with gentle active ankle movements and review at her next appointment
  • B. Apply compression stockings and elevation, then arrange a calf ultrasound if swelling persists next week
  • C. Advise ice and elevation at home and recheck the calf at her next scheduled postpartum visit
  • D. Avoid massage and arrange urgent assessment for deep vein thrombosis

The correct answer is D (Avoid massage and arrange urgent assessment for deep vein thrombosis): The postpartum period raises clot risk, and a swollen, warm, tender unilateral calf is a classic sign of deep vein thrombosis. Massage or vigorous activity could dislodge a clot, so the priority is urgent imaging and medical care. Elevation, stockings or waiting for the next visit feel conservative but postpone diagnosis. A simple strain would not explain warmth and swelling together.

Question 361

Other Systems

A 34-year-old woman, twelve weeks after birth in Saskatoon, wants to return to running. She leaks urine when she jogs and feels heaviness in her pelvis by evening. She has no pain. She is breastfeeding and sleeping poorly. Which plan is the most suitable?

  • A. Begin pelvic floor strengthening and delay all exercise until she finishes breastfeeding
  • B. Refer her for surgical repair, as symptoms at twelve weeks mean permanent pelvic floor damage
  • C. Assess pelvic floor function and begin graded strengthening before adding running impact
  • D. Return to running with a supportive belt and empty her bladder before each run

The correct answer is C (Assess pelvic floor function and begin graded strengthening before adding running impact): Leakage and heaviness with impact show that her pelvic floor and load management are not ready for running yet. Assessment and graded strengthening improve outcomes, and impact is added as symptoms settle. Pelvic floor work alone is partly right but delays all exercise for no reason, since breastfeeding does not limit it. Surgery at twelve weeks is premature, and a belt or bladder routine only hides the problem.

Question 362

Other Systems

A 63-year-old man is on the first day after an elective colorectal resection in Kelowna under an enhanced recovery pathway. He is alert, pain is controlled with an epidural, and his vital signs are stable. The surgeon has ordered mobilization as tolerated. What is the best physiotherapy approach?

  • A. Defer walking until his bowel function has returned
  • B. Start with sitting at the bed edge today and standing after the epidural is removed
  • C. Limit him to bed exercises and chair sitting for two days before walking in the corridor
  • D. Assist him to stand and walk short distances, increasing as tolerated

The correct answer is D (Assist him to stand and walk short distances, increasing as tolerated): Enhanced recovery pathways encourage mobilizing on the day of surgery or the first day, which lowers pulmonary and thrombotic complications and shortens stay. He is alert with stable vital signs and the surgeon has ordered mobilization. Sitting only, a staged delay or waiting for bowel function all feel cautious but lose the benefit. Walking does not endanger the anastomosis, and an epidural does not rule it out when strength and monitoring allow.

Question 363

Other Systems

A 55-year-old woman in Winnipeg is two days after an open cholecystectomy with a right subcostal incision. She is reluctant to cough because of incisional pain and has quiet breath sounds at the bases. Which technique best helps her clear secretions while protecting the wound?

  • A. Use forced expiratory huffs in sitting with the arms raised overhead to open the lower chest
  • B. Cough in a side-lying position with the knees straightened, keeping the abdominal muscles relaxed
  • C. Cough with a pillow held firmly against the incision after deep breaths, with knees bent
  • D. Use an incentive spirometer hourly and cough when she sees sputum rising

The correct answer is C (Cough with a pillow held firmly against the incision after deep breaths, with knees bent): Holding a pillow firmly against the incision reduces pain and wound strain so she can cough effectively after deep breaths, and bent knees relax the abdominal wall. An incentive spirometer helps lung expansion and is tempting, but it does not clear secretions without a cough. Straightened knees and raised arms increase tension on a subcostal incision and make coughing more painful.

Question 364

Other Systems

A 38-year-old office worker in Moncton has irritable bowel syndrome with constipation and bloating. She is inactive and asks whether exercise helps or could make her symptoms worse. Her bowel assessment shows no red flag features. What advice reflects current evidence?

  • A. Gentle yoga and stretching help bowel symptoms, while aerobic work should wait until constipation settles
  • B. Moderate walking helps, but vigorous interval training twice weekly gives faster relief and should start now
  • C. Regular moderate aerobic activity such as walking is helpful and can be increased gradually
  • D. Core strengthening and abdominal exercises several times daily improve bowel motility more than aerobic activity does

The correct answer is C (Regular moderate aerobic activity such as walking is helpful and can be increased gradually): Regular physical activity improves symptoms in irritable bowel syndrome and general health, and moderate walking is a sensible starting point that can progress gradually. Yoga is reasonable, but delaying aerobic work is not supported. Very vigorous exertion in an inactive person can aggravate gut symptoms, and abdominal strengthening has no advantage over walking.

Question 365

Other Systems

A 42-year-old man with Crohn disease in Victoria has taken prednisone for eight months. His recent bone density report shows low bone mass at the hip. He asks what exercise suits him. He has no abdominal pain currently and his disease is in remission. What should the physiotherapist advise?

  • A. Progressive resistance and weight-bearing exercise with attention to fall risk
  • B. Daily swimming and cycling to protect the joints, adding weight-bearing work after the next scan
  • C. Low-impact walking at a gentle pace with no resistance work until the steroid course ends
  • D. Gentle stretching and balance exercise without added loading

The correct answer is A (Progressive resistance and weight-bearing exercise with attention to fall risk): Long-term corticosteroids reduce bone mass, and mechanical loading from resistance and weight-bearing exercise helps preserve it, with technique and fall prevention reducing fracture risk. Swimming and cycling are comfortable but place little load on the hip. Walking alone at a gentle pace and waiting for the steroid course to end postpone useful protection. Stretching and balance training are good additions but do not load bone.

Question 366

Other Systems

A 52-year-old nurse in London, Ontario has rheumatoid arthritis. Both hands show hot, swollen knuckle joints with morning stiffness over an hour and a raised inflammatory marker from last week. She asks whether to stop moving her hands entirely. What is the most suitable advice?

  • A. Apply daily heavy stretching to the swollen joints to prevent contractures
  • B. Gentle comfortable range-of-motion with joint protection, avoiding resisted loading
  • C. Immobilize both hands in rigid splints for several weeks until the swelling has gone
  • D. Perform firm resisted grip exercises to build strength through the pain

The correct answer is B (Gentle comfortable range-of-motion with joint protection, avoiding resisted loading): During a flare, gentle active movement preserves range and function while joint protection reduces stress. Resisted or forceful loading of inflamed joints can aggravate damage. Prolonged rigid immobilization leads to stiffness and weakness. Rest splints may be used at night, not as a replacement for movement.

Question 367

Other Systems

A 64-year-old man with a 25-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents to a physiotherapist in Quebec City with new upper neck pain, brief tingling in both hands on neck flexion, and a sense of head heaviness. He asks for neck manipulation as before. What is the safest action?

  • A. Use gentle mid-range mobilization and a soft collar, then review his symptoms at the next visit
  • B. Avoid end-range neck techniques and refer promptly for assessment of cervical instability
  • C. Perform low-force traction with the neck in neutral and recheck his hand symptoms later today
  • D. Treat with deep neck flexor stretching and review his hand symptoms next week

The correct answer is B (Avoid end-range neck techniques and refer promptly for assessment of cervical instability): Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis can weaken ligaments at the upper cervical spine, and neck flexion symptoms with hand paraesthesia suggest possible cord involvement. Gentle mobilization, low-force traction and flexion stretching feel less risky than manipulation, but each still loads a possibly unstable segment. The priority is protection and prompt medical assessment.

Question 368

Other Systems

A 30-year-old woman in Brampton has systemic lupus erythematosus and reports exhaustion and a facial rash after midday outdoor runs. Her disease is currently quiescent according to her rheumatologist. She wants to keep exercising. She has no joint pain. What advice is best?

  • A. Exercise indoors at midday in a warm gymnasium with frequent pacing breaks and fluids
  • B. Continue her outdoor midday runs in long sleeves and rest the next day after each run
  • C. Exercise at cooler, shaded times or indoors, pace activity, and use sun protection
  • D. Switch to outdoor midday swimming with a rash guard and limit sessions to twenty minutes

The correct answer is C (Exercise at cooler, shaded times or indoors, pace activity, and use sun protection): Exercise is safe and helpful in quiescent lupus, but ultraviolet light can provoke rash and flares, so timing, shade and sunscreen matter, and pacing manages fatigue. Long sleeves help but still leave her running at midday sun levels. Swimming outdoors at midday is tempting because it cools her, but water does not block ultraviolet exposure. A warm room does not reduce fatigue.

Question 369

Other Systems

A 45-year-old woman with fibromyalgia in Thunder Bay reports widespread pain and poor sleep. She stopped exercising because pain increased the day after a hard workout. She sleeps poorly and has tried yoga before. Which exercise approach has the best evidence for her?

  • A. Short daily bouts of stretching and yoga, with aerobic work added after pain has settled
  • B. Low-intensity aerobic exercise started at a tolerable level and progressed slowly
  • C. Moderate-intensity circuit training twice weekly from the first visit, with rest days between sessions
  • D. Pacing and gentle relaxation exercise with no aerobic work yet

The correct answer is B (Low-intensity aerobic exercise started at a tolerable level and progressed slowly): Graded aerobic exercise that starts low and progresses slowly reduces pain and improves function in fibromyalgia. Yoga and pacing are reasonable and have some support, but aerobic exercise has the strongest evidence. Starting at moderate intensity produces the post-exercise flares that reinforced her avoidance in the first place.

Question 370

Other Systems

A 41-year-old paramedic in Fredericton, five months after COVID-19, feels profound fatigue and brain fog that start a day after even a short walk and last two days. Her heart and lung work-up is normal. A program advises increasing walking time by ten percent weekly. What approach is most appropriate?

  • A. Hold walking at the current level for a month, then resume the ten percent weekly increases
  • B. Add a daily heart rate target at moderate intensity and raise it weekly
  • C. Pace activity within her energy limits instead of fixed graded progression, tracking symptom flare-ups
  • D. Reduce to short daily walks and cognitive rest, then resume graded increases

The correct answer is C (Pace activity within her energy limits instead of fixed graded progression, tracking symptom flare-ups): Symptoms that worsen a day or more after even short exertion fit post-exertional malaise, where pushing through can set her back. Pacing activity within her energy limits and monitoring responses is the recommended approach. Pausing and then resuming fixed increases, or adding a heart rate target, are graded exercise approaches that ignore this pattern and risk repeated relapses.

Question 371

Other Systems

A 70-year-old woman with chronic leg lymphedema in Sudbury attends for her compression bandaging. Today her lower leg is hot, red and tender with a spreading edge, and her temperature is 38.2 C. She says the redness appeared overnight. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Keep compression on, elevate the leg, and book a medical review this week
  • B. Do gentle proximal drainage first and refer if the redness spreads
  • C. Elevate the leg with a cool pack and recheck her temperature tomorrow
  • D. Hold bandaging and drainage and arrange urgent assessment for possible cellulitis

The correct answer is D (Hold bandaging and drainage and arrange urgent assessment for possible cellulitis): A hot, red, spreading and tender limb with fever suggests acute cellulitis, which requires prompt antibiotics. Compression and lymphatic drainage are delayed until the infection is treated. Elevation and cooling are comfort measures that feel reasonable, but waiting a day or a week risks sepsis.

Question 372

Other Systems

A 56-year-old woman in Charlottetown has mild arm lymphedema after breast cancer surgery with axillary node dissection. She asks to lift weights at a gym. Her oncologist has cleared her for exercise. She trains twice weekly. What recommendation best fits the evidence?

  • A. Cardiovascular exercise with very light hand weights and no progression of load
  • B. Resistance training without a sleeve, stopping when the arm feels heavy or tight
  • C. Resistance training with heavy loads from the start to build strength quickly
  • D. Supervised progressive resistance training with compression sleeve and close arm monitoring

The correct answer is D (Supervised progressive resistance training with compression sleeve and close arm monitoring): Slowly progressed, supervised resistance training does not increase the risk of lymphedema and may improve symptoms and strength. A compression garment and monitoring of arm size guide progression. Avoiding load progression is outdated, heavy loading from the start risks a flare, and training without a sleeve or monitoring leaves swelling to be noticed late.

Question 373

Other Systems

A 69-year-old man in Saint John with prostate cancer reports a month of deep right thigh pain that wakes him at night and is worse when walking. He denies trauma. X-ray from last year showed no abnormality. He asks for strengthening exercises. What is the most appropriate response?

  • A. Limit weight bearing and arrange urgent imaging and oncology review today
  • B. Apply heat, advise rest and a short course of anti-inflammatories, and review him in one week
  • C. Prescribe gentle hamstring stretching and recheck in two weeks
  • D. Start gentle quadriceps strengthening without weight bearing and arrange imaging at his next oncology visit

The correct answer is A (Limit weight bearing and arrange urgent imaging and oncology review today): Night pain and load-related thigh pain in a person with prostate cancer raise concern for bone metastasis and impending fracture. Loading a weakened femur could cause a complete fracture, so protection and prompt imaging come first. Strengthening, rest and stretching all assume a benign muscle problem. A normal film from last year does not exclude new disease.

Question 374

Other Systems

A 47-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for lymphoma in Hamilton is midway through a supervised walking session. He says he feels shivery. His temperature is 38.4 C. His last blood count, nine days ago, showed a low neutrophil count. What should happen next?

  • A. Stop exercise and arrange immediate medical assessment for febrile neutropenia
  • B. Stop exercise, take his temperature again in ten minutes, and arrange assessment if above 38 C
  • C. Stop exercise and phone his oncology clinic for advice once the session has ended
  • D. Stop exercise and recheck his temperature after fifteen minutes of rest

The correct answer is A (Stop exercise and arrange immediate medical assessment for febrile neutropenia): A temperature of 38.0 C or higher during chemotherapy-related neutropenia can signal overwhelming infection and needs urgent assessment. Each of the other plans correctly stops exercise but waits, rechecks or defers the call, and delay of even hours can be dangerous. He needs immediate medical assessment.

Question 375

Other Systems

A 60-year-old woman in Red Deer has finished chemotherapy for colon cancer and reports persistent fatigue that rest does not relieve. Her blood counts and thyroid tests are normal. She walks daily. Which intervention has the strongest evidence for reducing cancer-related fatigue?

  • A. Energy conservation pacing with scheduled rest periods and gradual reduction of daily activity
  • B. Weekly manual therapy and massage sessions with heat to the large muscle groups of the back
  • C. Therapeutic ultrasound to the quadriceps and spinal muscles three times weekly
  • D. A structured aerobic exercise program, ideally with resistance training two days weekly

The correct answer is D (A structured aerobic exercise program, ideally with resistance training two days weekly): Regular exercise is the best-supported approach for cancer-related fatigue, improving energy and function during and after treatment. Pacing with rest is tempting because it sounds protective, but reducing activity deepens deconditioning. Massage, heat and ultrasound are passive and do not address the underlying fatigue.

Question 376

Other Systems

A 58-year-old man in Brandon finished oxaliplatin chemotherapy and has numb, tingling feet. He sways when standing with eyes closed and stumbled twice at home. Strength is normal. He lives alone in a rural area. Which component should be central to his plan?

  • A. Strengthening of the calf and thigh muscles with progressive leg press loading
  • B. Sensory retraining with textured surfaces and a walking aid for outdoor mobility
  • C. Balance and gait training with attention to footwear, household safety and fall prevention
  • D. Aerobic cycling to improve circulation to the feet, with rest when numbness increases

The correct answer is C (Balance and gait training with attention to footwear, household safety and fall prevention): Sensory loss from chemotherapy neuropathy impairs balance, and balance and gait training with attention to footwear and household safety reduces falls. Strengthening supports function but does not replace sensory feedback. Sensory retraining and cycling are reasonable additions but do not address his instability and the stumbles at home.

Question 377

Other Systems

A 66-year-old man with lung cancer in Windsor reports two weeks of mid-back pain that is worse lying down, now with band-like chest tightness. Today both legs feel heavy and he has difficulty passing urine. Plantar responses are upgoing. What action is most appropriate?

  • A. Arrange emergency transfer for urgent imaging of suspected metastatic spinal cord compression
  • B. Contact his oncologist and arrange an MRI within the next 24 hours
  • C. Refer him to his family physician for same-day assessment of the urinary symptoms
  • D. Stop treatment and advise him to attend the emergency department if weakness worsens

The correct answer is A (Arrange emergency transfer for urgent imaging of suspected metastatic spinal cord compression): Cancer with escalating spinal pain, band-like tightness, leg weakness, urinary difficulty and upgoing plantar responses indicates probable metastatic cord compression. Outcome depends on treatment within hours. Calling his oncologist and arranging an MRI within a day is reasonable in a stable patient but is too slow here. Waiting for worse weakness or routine physician review risks permanent loss of function.

Question 378

Other Systems

A 61-year-old woman in Ottawa has been in intensive care for ten days with septic shock and mechanical ventilation. She is now awake and follows commands. A physiotherapist tests six muscle groups on each side with the Medical Research Council scale and obtains a sum score of 42 out of 60. What does this indicate?

  • A. Mild weakness that falls short of diagnosis, because the threshold is a sum score below 36
  • B. Clinically significant ICU-acquired weakness, as scores below 48 meet the threshold
  • C. Polyneuropathy rather than myopathy, because sum scores below 48 identify the nerve pathology
  • D. Residual sedation effect, so the test should be repeated after sedatives clear before interpreting

The correct answer is B (Clinically significant ICU-acquired weakness, as scores below 48 meet the threshold): A Medical Research Council sum score under 48 of 60 in an awake, cooperative patient is the accepted criterion for ICU-acquired weakness, so 42 is clinically significant. A score under 36 marks severe weakness, not the diagnostic threshold. The score does not separate neuropathy from myopathy, and she is awake and following commands, so sedation does not explain it.

Question 379

Other Systems

A mechanically ventilated 55-year-old man in an intensive care unit in Calgary is on day four of septic shock. He is awake and ready for sitting out of bed. In the past hour, his norepinephrine dose has doubled and his mean arterial pressure has fallen to 58 mmHg. What is the best decision?

  • A. Proceed with sitting at the edge of the bed with monitoring, since early activity lowers delirium
  • B. Defer mobilization, continue passive range, and recheck when hemodynamics are stable
  • C. Transfer him to the chair with a second therapist monitoring his blood pressure throughout the movement
  • D. Stand him briefly at the bedside to test his tolerance

The correct answer is B (Defer mobilization, continue passive range, and recheck when hemodynamics are stable): Worsening hemodynamic instability on escalating vasopressors is a reason to postpone active mobilization, because the cardiovascular reserve to tolerate it is lacking. Passive movement and positioning maintain function meanwhile. Early mobilization is the goal and monitoring is good practice, but neither makes a sitting, transfer or brief stand safe at a pressure of 58 mmHg.

Question 380

Other Systems

A 48-year-old man in an intensive care unit in Montreal is intubated, with a Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale score of minus four after abdominal surgery. His circulation and oxygen levels are stable. He does not respond to voice. Which intervention is the most appropriate now?

  • A. Active-assisted exercises with verbal coaching and sitting at the bedside, since early activity lightens sedation
  • B. Passive range of motion, regular repositioning and splinting while sedation lightens
  • C. Chest physiotherapy techniques and cough stimulation each hour
  • D. Sitting him upright in bed with the head elevated and monitoring his response

The correct answer is B (Passive range of motion, regular repositioning and splinting while sedation lightens): A patient at minus four on the scale does not respond to voice and cannot participate, so passive movement, positioning and splinting to prevent contracture are suitable. Active-assisted work needs cooperation. Airway clearance and upright positioning have a place but do not protect joints and skin. Withholding care until he is awake misses these chances.

Question 381

Other Systems

A critical care team in Edmonton wants to identify patients at highest risk of developing ICU-acquired weakness. They review a list of exposures during intensive care. One patient is awake and weaning off the ventilator. Which combination is most strongly associated with developing this condition?

  • A. Older age, hypertension, high-dose opioid use and prolonged ward bed rest after discharge
  • B. Sepsis, deep sedation, mild hypoxia and early mobilization during the first week
  • C. Sepsis, prolonged ventilation, high glucose levels and prolonged immobility
  • D. Pneumonia, inhaled bronchodilators, daily physiotherapy and a long stay on supplemental oxygen

The correct answer is C (Sepsis, prolonged ventilation, high glucose levels and prolonged immobility): Sepsis, prolonged ventilation, hyperglycemia, corticosteroids, neuromuscular blockers and immobility are well documented contributors. The closest alternatives mix real exposures with protective ones such as early mobilization, or list common factors that are not strongly linked. Early mobility, glucose control and sedation holidays are linked to lower risk and guide prevention.

Question 382

Other Systems

A 79-year-old woman in Truro has fallen twice this year and scores 16 seconds on the Timed Up and Go. She lives alone, is cognitively intact and takes four medications. She enjoys group activity. Which exercise approach has the strongest evidence for reducing her falls?

  • A. A supervised walking group with progressive distance, twice weekly, without balance tasks
  • B. A strength program on seated machines, three times weekly, avoiding standing tasks
  • C. A progressive balance and strength program such as Otago, three times weekly, in a small group
  • D. A home program of upper body resistance bands and stretching, done five times weekly

The correct answer is C (A progressive balance and strength program such as Otago, three times weekly, in a small group): Falls are reduced by exercise that challenges balance and builds leg strength with progression and sufficient dose, such as the Otago program. Walking groups and seated strength work are valuable for fitness but lack the balance challenge needed to cut falls. Upper body bands and stretching do not train the systems that prevent falls.

Question 383

Other Systems

A 81-year-old man in Sherbrooke feels dizzy when he stands from the bed and nearly fell yesterday. In supine his blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg. After three minutes standing it is 112/70 mmHg and he feels faint. He recently started a new antihypertensive. What is the most appropriate response?

  • A. Teach staged position changes and advise increased fluid and salt intake to restore his pressure
  • B. Report the postural drop to his physician and teach staged position changes
  • C. Apply compression stockings to both legs and continue the planned mobility session as scheduled today
  • D. Advise him to skip tomorrow's dose of the new antihypertensive until his next routine physician review

The correct answer is B (Report the postural drop to his physician and teach staged position changes): A systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more on standing meets the definition of orthostatic hypotension, and a new antihypertensive is a likely contributor. The physician should review the medication, and staged position changes reduce symptoms and fall risk. Fluids, stockings or advising a missed dose are plausible measures, but each acts without the medical review his medication needs.

Question 384

Other Systems

A 72-year-old retired teacher in Nanaimo asks what the Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines recommend for adults aged 65 years and older. She is generally healthy and walks daily. She lives alone. Which recommendation is part of the guideline for her age group?

  • A. 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity weekly plus strengthening and balance work
  • B. 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity weekly plus strengthening, with balance work added after a first fall
  • C. At least 300 minutes of moderate activity weekly, with strengthening and balance work for frail adults
  • D. 75 minutes of vigorous activity weekly in place of moderate activity, with strengthening on one day

The correct answer is A (150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity weekly plus strengthening and balance work): For adults 65 and older, the guidelines recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity weekly, muscle strengthening on at least two days, several hours of light activity and balance work. Balance work is advised before a fall happens, not after. Doubling the aerobic target or cutting strengthening to one day does not match the guideline.

Question 385

Other Systems

A 40-year-old accountant in Mississauga sits for most of his day and asks a physiotherapist about the minimum activity needed for health benefit. He has no medical conditions. According to the Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for adults aged 18 to 64, what is recommended?

  • A. At least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity weekly, with strengthening needed on three or more days
  • B. At least 75 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity weekly plus two strengthening days
  • C. At least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity weekly plus two strengthening days
  • D. At least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity weekly, completed in bouts of ten minutes or longer

The correct answer is C (At least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity weekly plus two strengthening days): The guideline for adults 18 to 64 is at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic activity plus muscle strengthening on at least two days, with limited sedentary time and good sleep. Halving the aerobic amount or demanding three strengthening days misstates it, and the older ten minute bout rule is no longer required.

Question 386

Other Systems

A mother in Iqaluit brings her healthy 11-year-old son, who plays video games for hours daily, to a physiotherapist. She asks how much activity he needs. Which recommendation matches the Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for children aged 5 to 17?

  • A. At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, strengthening on one day
  • B. At least 90 minutes of light activity daily with strengthening on three days weekly
  • C. At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, strengthening on three days weekly
  • D. At least 30 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, strengthening on three days

The correct answer is C (At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, strengthening on three days weekly): Children and youth aged 5 to 17 should accumulate an average of at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, including vigorous aerobic and muscle and bone strengthening activities on at least three days. Strengthening on one day falls short. Thirty minutes is the adult style amount, and light activity does not count toward the target.

Question 387

Other Systems

A 45-year-old sales manager in Moncton currently walks about 60 minutes weekly and wants to lower his cardiovascular disease risk. He has no symptoms and no medical conditions. He has two free evenings each week. What plan best fits current guidance?

  • A. Jump to two 75 minute vigorous sessions on his free evenings, then add strengthening work afterward
  • B. Add two strengthening days now and keep walking at 60 minutes until his next check-up
  • C. Raise walking to 90 minutes weekly and hold it before adding strengthening later
  • D. Progress gradually toward 150 minutes of moderate weekly activity plus two strengthening days

The correct answer is D (Progress gradually toward 150 minutes of moderate weekly activity plus two strengthening days): The target is at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week plus strengthening on two days, reached progressively to protect against injury and drop-out. Adding strengthening is tempting, but his aerobic volume stays well below target. Jumping to long vigorous sessions skips progression and strengthening, and holding at 90 minutes leaves both targets unmet.

Question 388

Other Systems

A 50-year-old man in Gatineau wants to start a fitness program. On the PAR-Q+ he answers yes to chest pain during activity and to a heart condition diagnosed last year. He feels well at the moment and is eager to begin. What is the right next step?

  • A. Begin supervised light exercise with heart rate monitoring while the follow-up questions are completed
  • B. Complete the follow-up questions and obtain clearance from a qualified provider before starting any exercise
  • C. Refer him for a maximal exercise stress test before the screening form is fully reviewed
  • D. Start low-intensity walking with a heart rate ceiling and complete the follow-up questions next week

The correct answer is B (Complete the follow-up questions and obtain clearance from a qualified provider before starting any exercise): Positive answers to key PAR-Q+ questions mean the follow-up section and review by a qualified provider are needed before an exercise plan, especially with known heart disease and exertional chest pain. Supervised light exercise or a low-intensity walk still begins before clearance, and a maximal test is not the next step.

Question 389

Other Systems

A 67-year-old woman in Winnipeg receives hemodialysis through a left forearm arteriovenous fistula. She joins an outpatient program and the physiotherapist plans resistance exercises and a blood pressure check. She also has hypertension and wants to track her pressure. Which precaution is most appropriate?

  • A. Avoid blood pressure measurement and heavy resistance exercise on the fistula arm
  • B. Allow blood pressure measurement on the fistula arm, but avoid heavy resistance exercise with that arm
  • C. Avoid blood pressure measurement on the fistula arm, but encourage heavy gripping to enlarge the vessel
  • D. Measure blood pressure on the fistula arm with a wide cuff set at low inflation pressure

The correct answer is A (Avoid blood pressure measurement and heavy resistance exercise on the fistula arm): The fistula arm should not be used for blood pressure measurement, venepuncture or heavy load bearing, because compression or strain can damage or clot the access. A low-pressure cuff or a post-dialysis reading feels safer but still compresses the access. Heavy gripping to enlarge the vessel strains an established fistula.

Question 390

Other Systems

A 54-year-old woman in Kingston reports six months of tiredness, constipation, cold intolerance and difficulty rising from a chair. She has proximal thigh weakness, slowly relaxing ankle reflexes and a puffy face. A colleague suggests a progressive leg strengthening plan. What is the best action?

  • A. Begin light resistance training with a review in a month, and refer if weakness persists
  • B. Suggest an aerobic program and a sleep review before testing her strength
  • C. Refer for a vitamin D and iron review and delay the exercise program
  • D. Recommend medical assessment for possible thyroid dysfunction before strengthening

The correct answer is D (Recommend medical assessment for possible thyroid dysfunction before strengthening): Proximal weakness with cold intolerance, constipation, slow reflex relaxation and facial puffiness suggests hypothyroidism, which is diagnosed with blood tests and treated medically. Light resistance training or other lifestyle measures treat weakness without addressing the cause. Referring for the wrong tests or waiting a month prolongs symptoms and risks complications.

Question 391

Other Systems

A 30-year-old man with type 1 diabetes in Moncton completes a two-hour hiking session with a physiotherapy group and feels fine afterward. He ate a normal dinner and took his usual insulin dose. He asks about overnight risk. What should the physiotherapist tell him?

  • A. Glucose may fall for about an hour afterward, so a bedtime check is a reasonable safeguard
  • B. Glucose can drop overnight, so he should lower his evening insulin without asking his team
  • C. Glucose can drop for many hours afterward, so he should monitor overnight
  • D. Glucose tends to rise after prolonged hiking from stress hormones, so a bedtime check is enough

The correct answer is C (Glucose can drop for many hours afterward, so he should monitor overnight): Muscle glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity stay raised for up to 24 hours after prolonged or vigorous exercise, causing delayed and nocturnal hypoglycemia. A bedtime check misses the overnight window. Reducing insulin without his team is outside the physiotherapist's role, and a short-lived rise from stress hormones does not remove the later drop.

Question 392

Other Systems

A 33-year-old woman at 29 weeks of pregnancy in Barrie has been diagnosed with gestational diabetes managed by diet. Her obstetrician has cleared her for activity. She asks how exercise can help her glucose control. What is the best advice?

  • A. Complete one long morning walk of about an hour, which lowers glucose levels across the day
  • B. Do moderate resistance exercises with light weights after the largest meal each day
  • C. Walk briskly for thirty minutes after the largest meal at a vigorous intensity
  • D. Walk about fifteen minutes after meals to blunt the glucose rise

The correct answer is D (Walk about fifteen minutes after meals to blunt the glucose rise): Light activity of about fifteen minutes after meals improves post-meal glucose in gestational diabetes and is safe when the obstetrician agrees. A single morning walk does not blunt later meal rises, and resistance work after one meal or a vigorous effort covers fewer meals or exceeds what is suitable at 29 weeks.

Question 393

Other Systems

An 82-year-old man in London, Ontario with heart failure, chronic kidney disease and diabetes is attending a multicomponent exercise class. Today he has gained 2.5 kg in three days, has more breathlessness lying flat, and swollen ankles. His resting heart rate is 104 beats per minute. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Withhold exercise today and report these signs to his physician promptly
  • B. Continue light exercise with close monitoring and mention the weight gain at his next appointment
  • C. Reduce today's class to gentle stretching and ask him to weigh himself again next week
  • D. Withhold exercise today and advise him to book a routine appointment with his family doctor

The correct answer is A (Withhold exercise today and report these signs to his physician promptly): Rapid weight gain, orthopnea, edema and tachycardia suggest decompensated heart failure that needs medical review, not exercise. Gentle stretching or light monitored exercise still treats him as fit to train. Stopping exercise but booking a routine appointment feels close, yet the signs call for prompt reporting to his physician.

Question 394

Other Systems

A 45-year-old man in Peterborough has a hot, swollen right knee with sudden onset over two days, shaking chills, and a temperature of 38.9 C. He cannot bear weight, resists all knee motion, and has not had an injury. He has diabetes. What is the appropriate action?

  • A. Suspect acute gout, apply cold packs, and arrange rheumatology review
  • B. Arrange urgent emergency department assessment for suspected septic arthritis
  • C. Suspect a ligament sprain, begin protected range of motion, and review his progress in three days
  • D. Request a knee x-ray and a physician referral next week, resting the joint in the meantime

The correct answer is B (Arrange urgent emergency department assessment for suspected septic arthritis): A hot swollen joint with fever, severe loss of motion, no trauma and diabetes raises strong concern for septic arthritis, which can destroy a joint within days and needs urgent aspiration and antibiotics. Gout can look similar but fever with chills and diabetes make infection the priority. A sprain label or a referral next week delays care.

Question 395

Other Systems

A physiotherapist in a Halifax hospital is about to treat a patient with confirmed Clostridioides difficile infection and watery diarrhea. The room has a sink, and alcohol-based hand rub is at the door. How should she manage hand hygiene and equipment?

  • A. Wear gloves, clean hands with alcohol-based rub, and wipe equipment with a quaternary cleaner
  • B. Wear a gown and gloves, use alcohol-based hand rub, and dedicate one stethoscope to the room
  • C. Wear gown and gloves, wash hands with soap and water, use sporicidal cleaner on patient equipment
  • D. Wear gloves, wash hands with soap and water, and wipe equipment with alcohol swabs afterward

The correct answer is C (Wear gown and gloves, wash hands with soap and water, use sporicidal cleaner on patient equipment): Clostridioides difficile spreads by spores on hands and surfaces, and alcohol rub or alcohol swabs do not kill the spores, so soap and water and a sporicidal clean are needed. Gown and gloves complete contact precautions. A dedicated stethoscope is helpful, but hand rub and standard cleaners leave spores behind. It is not an airborne infection.

Question 396

Other Systems

A 68-year-old woman in Oshawa has had burning pain along her left lower ribs for two days. This morning small clustered blisters appeared on a red base in the same band. She asks about thoracic mobilization for presumed muscle strain. What is the best approach?

  • A. Treat the thoracic segments above and below the rash with gloves and refer if pain worsens
  • B. Refer her for zoster assessment but continue thoracic mobilization at the rash margin using gloves
  • C. Avoid treating over the rash, use contact precautions and refer for zoster assessment
  • D. Apply light massage over the blisters to desensitize the nerve, wearing gloves, then refer if painful

The correct answer is C (Avoid treating over the rash, use contact precautions and refer for zoster assessment): Dermatomal pain followed by grouped vesicles points to herpes zoster. Antiviral medication works best when started within 72 hours of rash onset, so same-day referral matters. Fluid in lesions can spread the virus, so precautions and avoiding the area are needed. Gloves while treating nearby segments or the margin do not justify mobilizing or massaging an infectious region.

Question 397

Other Systems

A 30-year-old woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy in Fort McMurray attends an exercise class. She reports persistent vaginal bleeding since yesterday and her ultrasound shows a placenta lying over the cervix. She feels well otherwise. Which statement about exercise is correct?

  • A. Continue walking and pelvic floor work at a low intensity and stop if the bleeding increases
  • B. Stop exercise, since persistent bleeding with placenta previa contraindicates activity
  • C. Switch to gentle aquatic exercise, keeping her heart rate under 140 beats per minute throughout
  • D. Reduce the class to seated upper-body exercise and avoid any lower-body or impact movement for now

The correct answer is B (Stop exercise, since persistent bleeding with placenta previa contraindicates activity): Persistent second or third trimester bleeding and placenta previa are listed contraindications to exercise in pregnancy. Low-intensity walking, water exercise, a heart rate ceiling or seated upper-body work make the session feel safer, but none removes the underlying risk. She needs medical follow-up before any return to activity.

Question 398

Other Systems

A 76-year-old woman in Cornwall fell at home last month and lay on the floor for forty minutes before a neighbour found her. She was not injured. She now fears falling again and avoids going out. What is a useful component of her plan?

  • A. Fit a personal alarm pendant and arrange a home safety review
  • B. Limit outings to accompanied trips until confidence returns, and begin balance training after several weeks
  • C. Arrange a grab bar and a cane, and begin balance training after her fear resolves
  • D. Practise floor recovery technique and a plan to summon help, alongside balance training

The correct answer is D (Practise floor recovery technique and a plan to summon help, alongside balance training): Practising how to get up from the floor and having a plan to call for help reduce the harm of a long lie and build confidence. Balance and strength training address the underlying risk and fear of falling. A personal alarm, accompanied outings or aids are helpful supports, but waiting for confidence delays the exercise that builds it.

Question 399

Other Systems

A therapist in Vancouver is explaining treatment for chronic lymphedema of the leg to a student. The patient has had swelling for three years. The student lists the usual components of complex decongestive therapy. Which set of components is correct?

  • A. Manual lymphatic drainage, compression bandaging, diuretic medication and fluid restriction
  • B. Deep tissue massage, intermittent pneumatic compression, skin care and prolonged limb elevation
  • C. Compression bandaging, therapeutic ultrasound, skin care and high-load resistance exercise
  • D. Manual lymphatic drainage, compression bandaging, skin care and exercise

The correct answer is D (Manual lymphatic drainage, compression bandaging, skin care and exercise): Complex decongestive therapy combines manual lymphatic drainage, compression bandaging or garments, skin and nail care, and decongestive exercise, with education for self-management. The first alternative shares two real components, but diuretics and fluid restriction are not part of it. The others replace core elements with deep massage, pneumatic devices, ultrasound or heavy loading.

Question 400

Other Systems

A 52-year-old mechanic in Lethbridge has type 2 diabetes and an HbA1c of 8.4 percent. He has time for about four sessions weekly and asks which mix of exercise would improve his glucose control most. He has no complications and his physician has cleared him for activity. What do you recommend?

  • A. Choose moderate aerobic training on four days weekly, adding resistance work after his HbA1c improves
  • B. Choose resistance training on four days weekly, adding aerobic work after his strength has improved
  • C. Choose interval training on most days, adding strength work later
  • D. Combine aerobic and resistance training across the week, as together they help most

The correct answer is D (Combine aerobic and resistance training across the week, as together they help most): Combined aerobic and resistance training lowers HbA1c more than either alone in type 2 diabetes, and both are recommended. Starting with one type and adding the other later feels like sensible progression, but it delays the larger benefit of combining them. Interval training is useful but is not shown to beat the combined approach.

Question 401

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 68-year-old retired teacher in Manitoba attends her first visit for knee osteoarthritis. Before starting joint mobilization, the physiotherapist explains the technique, expected benefits, common temporary soreness and alternatives, and answers her questions. She agrees to proceed. The physiotherapist now wants the record to show that the consent was informed. What is the best action?

  • A. Record the information discussed, her questions, and her decision in the chart, with the date.
  • B. Note that she attended and cooperated, which shows her consent was implied.
  • C. Have her sign a general form covering all treatment she may receive at this clinic.
  • D. Record that verbal consent was obtained, with the date and the name of the technique.

The correct answer is A (Record the information discussed, her questions, and her decision in the chart, with the date.): Informed consent is shown by what was disclosed, what the patient asked and what she decided. A form covering all future treatment is tempting, but it does not reflect a decision about this technique. A bare note that consent was obtained proves nothing about the information given.

Question 402

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 79-year-old man in Nova Scotia is recovering from hip fracture surgery and refuses to transfer to a chair. He repeats that he is going home tomorrow to a farm he sold last year and cannot describe what could happen if he stands alone. His surgeon documented that he consented to the operation. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Contact his family to give consent for the transfer before any capacity review.
  • B. Ask the surgeon to confirm that the operative consent also covers his rehabilitation decisions.
  • C. Offer a trial transfer with a nurse present and note his verbal agreement in the chart.
  • D. Request a capacity assessment for mobility decisions, since capacity is decision specific.

The correct answer is D (Request a capacity assessment for mobility decisions, since capacity is decision specific.): Capacity is assessed for a particular decision at a particular time, so consent to the operation does not settle this one. Involving family sounds careful, but a substitute decision-maker is only sought once he is found to lack capacity for this decision. Agreement from a man who cannot describe the risks of standing is not informed consent.

Question 403

Professional Practice and Ethics

During a lumbar traction session, a 45-year-old welder in Alberta says the pulling feels uncomfortable and asks the physiotherapist to stop. The physiotherapist believes the treatment is helping and that one more minute would finish the planned dose. The patient had agreed to traction at the start of the visit. What is the appropriate response?

  • A. Stop the treatment right away and discuss his concerns and alternatives.
  • B. Lower the traction force by half and finish the minute, since his earlier consent still applies.
  • C. Complete the planned minute, then stop and record that he asked to end the session early.
  • D. Pause traction briefly, explain the intended benefit, and resume once he sounds reassured about it.

The correct answer is A (Stop the treatment right away and discuss his concerns and alternatives.): Consent can be withdrawn at any moment, even after earlier agreement. Lowering the force or finishing the minute is tempting because the dose is nearly complete, but each continues treatment after he asked to stop. Stopping first allows an honest discussion of his discomfort and other options.

Question 404

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 15-year-old hockey player in Ontario arrives alone for a first visit after a shoulder injury. She explains the problem clearly, repeats back the risks and benefits of the proposed exercises, and asks that her parents not be told about a related sleep and anxiety concern. The clinic has no age rule. What is the best approach?

  • A. Seek a parent's consent as well, since a guardian should confirm decisions made by a minor.
  • B. Use the provincial age of majority as a firm cutoff and require guardian consent.
  • C. Assess her understanding of the treatment and decision instead of relying on age.
  • D. Accept her consent for the shoulder but tell her parents about the sleep concern for safety.

The correct answer is C (Assess her understanding of the treatment and decision instead of relying on age.): Capacity to consent depends on understanding the information and its consequences, not on a birthday. Phoning her parents is tempting because she is 15, but it overrides a decision she can already explain. Confirming understanding supports both her consent and her request for privacy.

Question 405

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 72-year-old woman in British Columbia has a severe stroke and cannot understand or communicate treatment choices. She has no written directive. Her estranged son and her long-term partner both want to direct her rehabilitation plan. The physiotherapist needs to know whose consent to seek. Which source should the physiotherapist consult?

  • A. Provincial legislation and facility policy ranking who may decide for her.
  • B. The patient's family physician, who knows which relative she would most likely have chosen.
  • C. The relative with the closest day-to-day involvement in her life during the past year.
  • D. The hospital ethics committee, which can appoint a decision-maker whenever relatives disagree about her care.

The correct answer is A (Provincial legislation and facility policy ranking who may decide for her.): Provincial health care consent legislation sets an order of who may decide for an incapable adult, and facility policy applies it. An ethics committee can help when a dispute remains, and the physician or a relative may offer useful background, but none of them replaces the ranking itself.

Question 406

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 58-year-old man collapses in a clinic gym in Saskatchewan, is unresponsive and not breathing normally, and has no identification or known relatives present. A physiotherapist starts CPR and calls emergency services. A bystander says treatment without permission is unlawful. How is the physiotherapist's action best described?

  • A. Acceptable if the emergency policy lists CPR as covered by the consent form signed at registration.
  • B. Justified once the clinic has tried to reach next of kin through its registration records.
  • C. Unlawful without the consent of a substitute decision-maker, who must be located before compressions begin.
  • D. Justified, since emergency care may proceed when delay risks life.

The correct answer is D (Justified, since emergency care may proceed when delay risks life.): When a person is unresponsive and delay risks life, consent is implied and emergency care may proceed. Searching for relatives is reasonable once the emergency is managed, but it cannot hold up compressions. A signed form is not needed because the emergency exception stands on its own.

Question 407

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 34-year-old woman in Quebec is treated for pelvic floor dysfunction. Her husband phones the clinic and asks the physiotherapist for details about her diagnosis and progress, saying he pays for the sessions. She has not authorized any disclosure. What should the physiotherapist do?
