  • A. Share a general summary because he funds the treatment and is her spouse.
  • B. Tell him whether she attended, since attendance is not considered health information.
  • C. Confirm her diagnosis, since the details of progress are the sensitive part.
  • D. Decline to share information and offer to pass his request to her.

The correct answer is D (Decline to share information and offer to pass his request to her.): Health information belongs to the patient, and a spouse or payer has no automatic right to it. Even a partial disclosure, including confirming attendance, can breach privacy. Offering to relay the request respects her control over her own information.

Question 408

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Newfoundland and Labrador realizes she emailed a patient's exercise handout and treatment summary to the wrong address because of an autocomplete error. The recipient is unknown. She feels embarrassed and considers saying nothing, since the handout seems harmless. What is the best course of action?

  • A. Wait to see whether anyone responds, then decide whether reporting is really needed.
  • B. Report it to the privacy officer, try to retrieve it, and notify her.
  • C. Resend the handout to the correct address and delete the original sent message today.
  • D. Record the error in her own private notes to avoid worrying the patient needlessly.

The correct answer is B (Report it to the privacy officer, try to retrieve it, and notify her.): A known breach should be reported promptly so containment can start and the affected person can be told. Quietly deleting the message or keeping private notes hides the incident and denies the patient information she is owed. Prompt reporting also lets the organization meet any legal notification duty.

Question 409

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a hospital rehabilitation unit in Ontario needs to share a patient's mobility status with the nurse and occupational therapist caring for him on the same unit. The patient has not objected to team sharing. Which principle best supports this disclosure?

  • A. Information may be shared with his employer's health and safety lead once the plan is finalized.
  • B. Information may be shared within the circle of care when needed.
  • C. Information may be shared with a relative listed as his emergency contact.
  • D. Information may be shared with the hospital quality team after names have been removed.

The correct answer is B (Information may be shared within the circle of care when needed.): Custodians may rely on implied consent to share information among the providers directly involved in a patient's care, known as the circle of care. De-identified data can be used for quality work and an emergency contact may be told some things, but neither is the basis for sharing mobility status with the nurse and occupational therapist.

Question 410

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Alberta posts a short video of a patient walking with a new prosthesis on her clinic's social media page. The patient's face is blurred and no name is given, but a distinctive tattoo and the clinic's small-town location are visible. The patient was never asked. What is the main problem?

  • A. The clinic did not seek the prosthesis manufacturer's approval.
  • B. The post should have been reviewed by the clinic owner before it went online.
  • C. The clinic should have posted a still image, since video carries more identifying detail.
  • D. The patient could still be identified, and no consent was obtained.

The correct answer is D (The patient could still be identified, and no consent was obtained.): A blurred face and no name do not make a person unidentifiable when a distinctive tattoo and a small-town setting remain visible. Any recording used for promotion needs the patient's informed consent, which was never sought. Owner review or format choices do not replace it.

Question 411

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Nunavut delivers a telehealth session to a patient at his shared family home. During the video call, the patient is in the kitchen while relatives move behind him and can hear the exchange. The patient is discussing a sensitive bladder issue. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Move the camera so the relatives are out of view, then continue the assessment as planned.
  • B. Continue but avoid naming the bladder concern, using general terms instead.
  • C. Pause the session and ask whether he can move somewhere private before continuing.
  • D. Tell the relatives to leave the kitchen immediately and resume the session without asking him.

The correct answer is C (Pause the session and ask whether he can move somewhere private before continuing.): Virtual care must protect privacy as much as an in-person room, and the patient decides who hears his information. Hiding relatives from the camera or using vague language is tempting but they can still overhear. Pausing and asking lets him choose a private space.

Question 412

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a busy Ontario outpatient clinic wants to delegate ultrasound to a newly hired rehabilitation assistant who has no formal training in that modality. The caseload is heavy and the assistant says she has watched it done many times. What must be true before delegating?

  • A. The assistant has a written job description listing ultrasound as an eligible task at this clinic.
  • B. The assistant must be competent for the task and supervised appropriately.
  • C. The physiotherapist has watched the assistant perform ultrasound once and signed her off for the day.
  • D. The clinic's liability insurance covers the assistant for ultrasound before the task is delegated to her.

The correct answer is B (The assistant must be competent for the task and supervised appropriately.): Delegation depends on the assistant being competent for the specific task and on appropriate supervision. A job description or insurance cover is tempting because it is documented, but neither shows she can apply ultrasound safely. Watching others informally is not training.

Question 413

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a province where the regulator requires added authorization for a specific advanced procedure is asked by a patient's employer to perform it, though the physiotherapist has completed a weekend course and has not applied for the authorization. The employer says the course was sufficient. What is the best response?

  • A. Decline until the regulator's authorization requirements have been met.
  • B. Perform it under an authorized colleague's supervision, naming that colleague in the record.
  • C. Perform it once the course provider confirms in writing that it meets the regulator's standard.
  • D. Perform it after informing the regulator in writing that an application for authorization is in progress.

The correct answer is A (Decline until the regulator's authorization requirements have been met.): Authorization to perform a restricted procedure is granted to the individual by the regulator, so supervision, a provider's letter or a pending application does not allow practice. The employer's view of the course is not the regulator's standard. She should decline until the requirements are met.

Question 414

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Newfoundland sees a 52-year-old man with low back pain who now reports new numbness in the saddle region, difficulty starting urination, and bilateral leg weakness developing over the past day. His next appointment is in three days. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Phone his family physician for an appointment within the next two days.
  • B. Book an outpatient MRI for next week and continue treatment while he waits for the scan.
  • C. Arrange urgent emergency assessment today and hand over the findings to the team.
  • D. Teach positions of relief and nerve glides, with a recheck in the clinic tomorrow morning.

The correct answer is C (Arrange urgent emergency assessment today and hand over the findings to the team.): Saddle numbness, urinary difficulty and bilateral weakness suggest possible cauda equina syndrome, which needs surgical assessment within hours. A booked MRI or a next-day recheck feels measured, but delay risks permanent loss of bladder and leg function. Same-day emergency referral is the safe step.

Question 415

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Saskatchewan with a general musculoskeletal background is asked to take over a patient with complex post-stroke spasticity and botulinum toxin follow-up. She has little neurological experience and no local mentor. The clinic is short-staffed. What is the most appropriate step?

  • A. Accept him and book extra sessions to study the evidence before each visit.
  • B. Refer him back to the physician managing his botulinum toxin injections.
  • C. Accept him but limit treatment to the musculoskeletal problems she knows well.
  • D. Seek mentorship or transfer care to a more experienced colleague, ensuring continuity.

The correct answer is D (Seek mentorship or transfer care to a more experienced colleague, ensuring continuity.): Practice within competence means getting guidance or passing care to someone better placed while keeping care continuous. Self-study between visits and partial treatment both leave a complex neurological patient with an inexperienced therapist, and sending him back to the physician leaves his rehabilitation without a plan.

Question 416

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Manitoba treating a 7-year-old for a wrist injury notices bruising in several stages of healing on the child's back and upper arms. The child avoids eye contact and the parent's explanations change between questions. The physiotherapist is unsure and wonders whether to gather more proof first. What is the correct action?

  • A. Document the findings and phone the parent to offer support resources before deciding on a report.
  • B. Ask the clinic's lead physiotherapist to review the findings, and report if she judges them sufficient.
  • C. Refer the family to the child's physician to assess the bruising and leave reporting to her.
  • D. Report the reasonable concern to child protection authorities without waiting for confirmation.

The correct answer is D (Report the reasonable concern to child protection authorities without waiting for confirmation.): The duty to report arises from a reasonable suspicion, not proof, and it cannot be handed to another person. Referring to the physician or reviewing with a colleague feels responsible but postpones a report only she is obliged to make. Child protection decides whether the suspicion is substantiated.

Question 417

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Ontario notices that a respected colleague has smelled of alcohol at work on several mornings and recently made two charting errors in dosing of therapeutic ultrasound. The colleague is a friend and says it is a temporary rough patch. Patients are being treated daily. What should she do?

  • A. Speak privately with the colleague, offer support, and report only if errors recur.
  • B. Raise it with the professional association, which can counsel members confidentially.
  • C. Report the concern to the regulator or employer, since continued practice puts patients at risk.
  • D. Submit an anonymous peer review form to the quality committee and await its response.

The correct answer is C (Report the concern to the regulator or employer, since continued practice puts patients at risk.): A physiotherapist who believes a colleague's impairment puts patients at risk must report to the regulator or employer. Supporting a friend or using internal quality channels feels kind but leaves patients exposed while it plays out. Associations do not hold the authority to protect the public.

Question 418

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Alberta treats a 40-year-old man for chronic pain. During a session he says, calmly, that he plans to hurt his ex-partner tonight and names the place where he will find her. He asks that this stay private. What principle applies?

  • A. Confidentiality may be breached to prevent a clear, serious and imminent risk of harm to someone.
  • B. Confidentiality may be breached to inform his employer when threats are made in clinic.
  • C. Confidentiality may be breached after the clinic manager approves it on the next business day.
  • D. Confidentiality may be breached after he is warned and refuses help.

The correct answer is A (Confidentiality may be breached to prevent a clear, serious and imminent risk of harm to someone.): The duty of confidentiality gives way when there is a clear, serious and imminent risk of harm to an identifiable person, and disclosure goes to those who can prevent it, such as police. Here a named person and a specific time create that risk, so a warning step or a next-day approval would leave her exposed tonight.

Question 419

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a small Newfoundland community is asked to treat the owner of the local hardware store, who is also her landlord and a close friend of her family. The nearest other clinic is two hours away. The man needs care for a rotator cuff tear. What is the best approach?

  • A. Discuss the dual relationship openly, manage it transparently, and document safeguards.
  • B. Treat him without mention, since small communities make overlap unavoidable and common.
  • C. Refuse to treat him because of the overlap, despite the lack of other clinics.
  • D. Treat him after accepting a month of free rent as a thank-you.

The correct answer is A (Discuss the dual relationship openly, manage it transparently, and document safeguards.): In small communities, dual relationships cannot always be avoided, so the duty is to identify the risk, discuss it, protect the patient's interests and keep records. Silence leaves the risk unmanaged, while a flat refusal may leave him without care. A benefit from the patient would create a conflict.

Question 420

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Ontario discharged a patient after treatment for neck pain two weeks ago. The patient, an adult, now sends friendly messages and suggests dinner. The physiotherapist has found the patient attractive. Treatment ended well and no further visits are planned. What is the best response?

  • A. Reply politely and meet once as friends, keeping the clinic out of it.
  • B. Refer her to a colleague first so that she is formally no longer a patient.
  • C. Consult a trusted colleague, then accept if they see no conflict.
  • D. Decline the relationship, because the duty of boundaries continues after discharge.

The correct answer is D (Decline the relationship, because the duty of boundaries continues after discharge.): Duties about boundaries and sexual relationships do not end on the day of discharge, and a patient seen two weeks ago is still within the period regulators protect. A referral or a colleague's approval does not change that, so the right response is to decline.

Question 421

Professional Practice and Ethics

A grateful patient in Nova Scotia offers his physiotherapist a gift card worth two hundred dollars after a successful rehabilitation from a knee replacement. He insists, saying it is not tied to any future treatment. The clinic has no gift policy, but her regulator advises declining gifts of significant value. How should the physiotherapist respond?

  • A. Politely decline the large gift, explaining the boundary, and suggest a thank-you note instead.
  • B. Accept it on behalf of the clinic and place the card in the staff social fund.
  • C. Accept it because he offered it freely after treatment finished.
  • D. Accept it with thanks and disclose it to the clinic manager so it is on record.

The correct answer is A (Politely decline the large gift, explaining the boundary, and suggest a thank-you note instead.): A gift of significant value can create the appearance of influence, even after treatment ends. Accepting and disclosing it is tempting, but the concern is the gift itself. Declining kindly and suggesting a note keeps the relationship professional and still honours his gratitude.

Question 422

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in British Columbia sells a branded knee brace from her clinic and earns a commission on each sale. A patient with mild patellofemoral pain would likely recover with exercise alone, but she believes the brace might help and recommends it. What is the key ethical duty?

  • A. Disclose the commission in a notice posted at reception and then recommend the brace.
  • B. Disclose the commission and offer the brace as the first line of treatment.
  • C. Disclose her financial interest and recommend it if it serves the patient's needs.
  • D. Disclose her commission and recommend the brace because the patient is likely to value the support.

The correct answer is C (Disclose her financial interest and recommend it if it serves the patient's needs.): A conflict of interest is managed by telling the patient directly about the financial interest and by recommending a product only when it serves that patient. Disclosure alone is not enough, because the stem shows exercise would likely be sufficient for her mild pain.

Question 423

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Alberta is offered a payment by a private imaging clinic for every patient she refers there. The clinic's quality is good and its wait times are short. A colleague says the payment is simply a thank-you for helping patients. What should she do?

  • A. Accept payment if she discloses the arrangement to every patient she refers to the clinic.
  • B. Accept the payment if her employer approves the arrangement in writing and quality is confirmed.
  • C. Accept a flat monthly payment instead of a per-patient fee, which keeps referrals independent.
  • D. Decline payment tied to referrals and refer based on patient need.

The correct answer is D (Decline payment tied to referrals and refer based on patient need.): Payment tied to referrals creates a conflict between her interests and the patient's. Disclosure or a different payment structure is tempting because it looks transparent, but the incentive remains. Referring according to patient need and declining the payment protects trust.

Question 424

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist employed at a Quebec private clinic is told by management to book every patient for twelve visits, whatever the assessment shows. A patient with a simple ankle sprain is already improving after three. The physiotherapist feels pressure to follow the policy. What should guide her decision?

  • A. The insurer's approved number of visits for an ankle sprain, which sets the standard of care.
  • B. The clinic's written policy, which she accepted at hiring, until a regulator rules it unsafe.
  • C. A compromise number of visits set by management and adjusted to the patient's reported satisfaction.
  • D. Her professional duty to provide care based on the patient's needs.

The correct answer is D (Her professional duty to provide care based on the patient's needs.): A physiotherapist's duty is to the patient's needs, and an employer cannot direct a fixed number of visits regardless of assessment. Policy, funding limits and satisfaction are tempting influences, but none shows this sprain needs twelve visits. Clinical judgment based on his progress must lead.

Question 425

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a community clinic in Saskatchewan sees eight patients on a busy day and plans to write all the notes over the weekend from memory. Her regulator expects records to be accurate. Which statement best reflects the standard for timing of clinical notes?

  • A. Notes should be recorded as soon as practical after the encounter.
  • B. Notes should be written when the insurer or billing office requests them for payment.
  • C. Notes should be completed by the end of the working week in which care was provided.
  • D. Notes should be pre-written before the visit from the plan, then edited if something differs.

The correct answer is A (Notes should be recorded as soon as practical after the encounter.): Records should be made as soon as practical after care, while the details are fresh and accurate. Writing everything over the weekend or at the week's end is tempting on a busy day, but memory fades and the record becomes less reliable. Pre-written notes do not capture what actually happened.

Question 426

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in New Brunswick finds she recorded the wrong side for a patient's knee swelling in a note written the day before. The patient's care has not yet been affected. A colleague suggests erasing the entry or using correction fluid so the chart looks clean. What is the proper action?

  • A. Cross out the wrong side and write the right side without a date or initials.
  • B. Write the correct side in tomorrow's note and mark yesterday's entry as under review.
  • C. Add a dated, signed correction while leaving the original entry readable.
  • D. Notify the patient and the clinic manager of the error but leave the original entry unchanged.

The correct answer is C (Add a dated, signed correction while leaving the original entry readable.): Records must stay accurate and traceable, so an error is corrected by a dated, signed addition while the original remains readable. Crossing out without a date or initials leaves no trace of who changed it, and telling others without amending the entry leaves a wrong side in the record.

Question 427

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Prince Edward Island realizes the next morning that she forgot to document a patient's reported dizziness during exercise, and the patient later fainted at home. A hospital asks to review her notes. She is tempted to insert the dizziness into yesterday's note as if written then. What is correct?

  • A. Add the dizziness to yesterday's note and mark the addition with a small asterisk.
  • B. Inform the hospital orally of the dizziness and leave the chart unchanged to protect its integrity.
  • C. Write a new note dated for the original session, adding the dizziness and omitting the time.
  • D. Add a clearly labelled late entry with the current date and time.

The correct answer is D (Add a clearly labelled late entry with the current date and time.): A late entry is dated and timed when it is written and says it refers to the earlier session. Inserting the information into yesterday's note or backdating it falsifies the record. Telling the hospital by phone is honest, but the chart must still be completed.

Question 428

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Ontario plans to close her private practice and move to another city. She has hundreds of patient files stored in the clinic and wonders what to do with them, since she will no longer have premises or staff. Which statement best describes her responsibility for these records?

  • A. She must mail each patient a notice and shred any files not collected after one month.
  • B. She must keep them secure for the required retention period and give patients access on request.
  • C. She must keep files for patients seen in the past year and shred the rest.
  • D. She may leave the files with the building landlord, who then becomes responsible for them.

The correct answer is B (She must keep them secure for the required retention period and give patients access on request.): Custodial duty continues after a practice closes, so she must keep the records secure for the full retention period and give patients access on request. Destroying files early or abandoning them with a landlord who has no custodial standing leaves patients without access.

Question 429

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 29-year-old woman in Alberta asks her former physiotherapist for a copy of her complete treatment notes for an insurance claim. The physiotherapist is concerned the notes include candid comments about her mood. The request is in writing and she has identified herself. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Provide access under privacy legislation unless a defined exception applies.
  • B. Provide a summary prepared by the physiotherapist, because the full notes contain clinical opinions.
  • C. Release the notes directly to the insurer, since the claim is the reason for the request.
  • D. Provide access once she confirms in writing that she will not share the notes further.

The correct answer is A (Provide access under privacy legislation unless a defined exception applies.): Patients have a right of access to their own records under privacy legislation, and the custodian may withhold information only under a defined exception, such as a risk of serious harm. Candid comments about mood are part of the record and do not by themselves meet an exception.

Question 430

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Saskatchewan is treating a First Nations elder with chronic hip pain. The elder prefers to include a family member and a traditional healer in the care discussion, and the clinic's usual process treats this as a delay. The physiotherapist feels rushed. What approach reflects cultural safety?

  • A. Allow both guests but limit their time in the room to keep the visit within schedule.
  • B. Let the patient guide who is involved and adapt the process.
  • C. Invite the family member and book a separate longer session for the traditional healer's input.
  • D. Offer to share the plan by phone with the family member and healer after each visit.

The correct answer is B (Let the patient guide who is involved and adapt the process.): Cultural safety means the patient defines what safe care looks like, so she directs who participates and the process adapts. Limiting or separating guests is tempting because it saves time, but it replaces her preference with the clinic's. Efficiency does not outweigh respect.

Question 431

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Winnipeg is about to explain home exercises to a 63-year-old man who speaks little English. His teenage grandson offers to translate, and the patient seems comfortable with that. The exercises include a precaution about chest pain that must be understood. What is the best approach?

  • A. Use a qualified interpreter, confirming understanding, especially for safety information.
  • B. Translate the key instructions with a phone app and print them in his language.
  • C. Book an interpreter for the next visit and give verbal instructions today.
  • D. Let the grandson interpret, then confirm understanding with teach-back.

The correct answer is A (Use a qualified interpreter, confirming understanding, especially for safety information.): Safety information such as a chest pain precaution should be conveyed through a qualified interpreter, with understanding confirmed. Family members may lack medical vocabulary or soften messages, and a teach-back with an untrained interpreter, an app or a later visit does not remove the risk today.

Question 432

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Vancouver is preparing to assess a 26-year-old patient who has introduced themself with a name and pronouns that differ from those on the health card. The front desk used the card name loudly in the waiting room. The patient looks uncomfortable. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Use the stated name and pronouns aloud, and keep the card name in the chart.
  • B. Ask the patient to bring documents showing the name change before using it in the clinic.
  • C. Use the patient's stated name and pronouns, and ask how to record them.
  • D. Use the card name on forms and confirm the patient's pronouns at the next visit instead.

The correct answer is C (Use the patient's stated name and pronouns, and ask how to record them.): Respectful care uses the name and pronouns the patient states and lets them guide how these are recorded. Keeping the card name in the chart seems consistent with the official record, but it makes a decision that belongs to the patient. Asking also repairs the discomfort caused at reception.

Question 433

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Ontario is about to begin pelvic floor assessment on a 31-year-old woman who disclosed a past sexual assault at the intake. She appears tense and gives short answers when the gown and internal exam are described. She has consented on paper. What approach best fits trauma-informed care?

  • A. Ask her to describe the assault in detail so that the exam can be adapted safely.
  • B. Complete the assessment efficiently in one visit, because prolonged anticipation raises distress for survivors.
  • C. Offer choices, explain each step, and pause when she signals discomfort.
  • D. Replace the internal assessment with external techniques and avoid discussing her history again.

The correct answer is C (Offer choices, explain each step, and pause when she signals discomfort.): Trauma-informed care restores control through choice, explanation at each step and a pause when she signals discomfort. Written consent at intake does not mean she agrees to each moment. Asking for details or removing the exam on her behalf takes decisions away from her.

Question 434

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Nova Scotia applies a hot pack to a patient's lower back and, on checking after ten minutes, finds a blistered burn because the towel layer was too thin. The patient had not noticed. The physiotherapist considers saying nothing so as not to alarm him. What should she do?

  • A. Provide first aid, disclose openly, apologize, and report the incident internally.
  • B. Provide first aid, disclose to the patient, and wait for him to ask before reporting internally.
  • C. Provide first aid, chart the burn, and let his physician explain it to him.
  • D. Provide first aid, explain the burn as a recognized heat therapy risk, and record the event.

The correct answer is A (Provide first aid, disclose openly, apologize, and report the incident internally.): After harm, the physiotherapist treats the injury, discloses honestly, apologizes and reports internally so the system can learn. Calling the burn a known risk is tempting but is not honest about the thin towel layer. Delegating disclosure leaves the patient without a direct explanation.

Question 435

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Ontario gave a patient the wrong home exercise sheet, which led to a minor flare-up of his shoulder pain. She worries that saying sorry will be treated as an admission of legal liability. The patient is upset and wants an explanation. What is accurate?

  • A. An apology is encouraged, but it should be offered by the clinic manager.
  • B. A sincere apology is encouraged, and many provinces protect apologies from use as admissions.
  • C. A sincere apology is encouraged, and provincial protection covers statements to the insurer and regulator.
  • D. An apology is expected after harmful errors, and its legal protection is uniform in all provinces.

The correct answer is B (A sincere apology is encouraged, and many provinces protect apologies from use as admissions.): Disclosure and a sincere apology are encouraged after an error, and many provinces have legislation that stops an apology being used as an admission of liability. Protection varies by province and is aimed at apologies made to the patient, so it cannot be assumed to be identical everywhere.

Question 436

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a Calgary hospital notices that two patients with the same surname were nearly given each other's gait aids before she caught the error. No harm occurred. A colleague says reporting is pointless since nothing happened. Why is reporting a near miss valuable?

  • A. It creates a record that she caught the error, protecting her from complaints.
  • B. It meets a duty to report to the regulator, which treats near misses like harmful events.
  • C. It lets the unit track how often each staff member errs so supervisors can coach them.
  • D. It reveals system weaknesses so changes can prevent future harm.

The correct answer is D (It reveals system weaknesses so changes can prevent future harm.): Near-miss reporting is valuable because it reveals system weaknesses, such as look-alike surnames, so that changes can prevent harm before it happens. A personal record or a legal duty may follow in some settings, but they are not the main reason.

Question 437

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Ontario treats a patient for 20 minutes but the clinic's billing software defaults to 45 minutes of direct treatment, and the insurer pays for the longer time. The patient has no idea of the length billed. The clinic manager says this is the usual practice. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Bill 20 minutes of treatment plus a 25 minute education line to reach the default.
  • B. Bill the default time and tell the patient afterward, since the insurer already approved it.
  • C. Bill for the services and time provided and raise the default with management.
  • D. Ask the insurer whether the longer default may be billed, then bill it if they agree.

The correct answer is C (Bill for the services and time provided and raise the default with management.): Billing must reflect the services and time actually provided. An insurer's payment or approval does not make time that was not delivered legitimate, so she should bill 20 minutes and ask management to correct the default setting.

Question 438

Professional Practice and Ethics

A new patient in Saskatchewan asks a physiotherapist about the cost of a first visit and whether her extended health plan will cover it. The clinic has a different rate for insured and uninsured patients. The front desk is busy. What is the best practice?

  • A. Quote the insured-patient rate and advise her to check coverage details with her insurer.
  • B. Give her the full fee schedule at the end of the first visit.
  • C. Direct her to the website fee list and begin the first assessment.
  • D. Tell the patient the fees before treatment starts and explain what her coverage may not pay.

The correct answer is D (Tell the patient the fees before treatment starts and explain what her coverage may not pay.): Patients should know fees, and what their plan may not cover, before treatment begins so they can make an informed choice. Giving the schedule afterward, pointing to a website or quoting a rate that may not apply to her does not meet that standard.

Question 439

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Alberta has treated a 55-year-old woman for plantar fasciitis for ten visits. Her symptoms and function have plateaued for the last four visits, but the insurer still approves sessions and she enjoys the attention. The physiotherapist could keep treating without objection. What is the ethical response?

  • A. Reduce visits to every second week while the insurer approves, tapering care.
  • B. Discuss discharge or a change of plan, since no benefit has been shown after four visits.
  • C. Refer her to another physiotherapist for a fresh opinion before discussing discharge.
  • D. Request more approval from the insurer and extend the plan with a new set of goals.

The correct answer is B (Discuss discharge or a change of plan, since no benefit has been shown after four visits.): Care should continue only while the patient is likely to benefit, and four visits without change show it has stopped. Insurer approval and patient enjoyment are tempting reasons to continue, but they are not clinical justification. Discussing discharge or a new plan serves her interests.

Question 440

Professional Practice and Ethics

A patient in Quebec asks his physiotherapist to issue receipts for twelve visits when only eight took place, because his plan reimburses him for twelve and he says everyone does it. He offers to pay a small extra fee for the favour. How should the physiotherapist respond?

  • A. Issue twelve receipts if he signs a statement accepting responsibility for any insurer inquiry.
  • B. Issue receipts for the eight visits and one for a prepayment toward four future visits.
  • C. Refuse, because issuing false receipts is fraud and a breach of integrity.
  • D. Refuse the extra payment but issue twelve receipts, as the plan terms involve the insurer.

The correct answer is C (Refuse, because issuing false receipts is fraud and a breach of integrity.): Receipts must show only services actually provided, so issuing twelve for eight visits is fraud and a breach of integrity whatever waiver or fee is offered. Even a prepayment receipt designed to let him claim for visits that did not occur misleads the insurer.

Question 441

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Manitoba is designing a clinic brochure and wants to say, 'Guaranteed relief from chronic back pain or your money back.' She also wants to quote a patient testimonial without naming the patient. Which approach meets professional advertising standards?

  • A. Keep the guarantee but add a note listing the conditions that apply.
  • B. Describe services accurately without guarantees, using consented testimonials where permitted.
  • C. Use the testimonial but remove any details that could identify the patient.
  • D. Replace the guarantee with a promise of the clinic's typical outcomes for back pain.

The correct answer is B (Describe services accurately without guarantees, using consented testimonials where permitted.): Advertising must be accurate and must not promise outcomes, and testimonials are used only where the regulator permits and the patient has consented. Removing the name or adding conditions to a guarantee still leaves the same problems.

Question 442

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a rural Ontario clinic has been sleeping three hours a night after a family crisis, and today nearly applied the wrong electrode settings to a patient. The clinic has only one other therapist, who is away. Patients are booked all day. What is the most appropriate action?

  • A. Cancel the highest-risk treatments such as electrical modalities and keep the rest of the day's patients.
  • B. Tell the clinic owner about the lost sleep and continue treating while the owner finds support.
  • C. Continue treating while a nurse checks the first and last treatments of each patient.
  • D. Recognize reduced fitness to practise, adjust the schedule, and seek coverage.

The correct answer is D (Recognize reduced fitness to practise, adjust the schedule, and seek coverage.): A practitioner must stop or limit practice when fatigue or personal crisis compromises safe care. A near error with electrode settings shows the risk is real. Trimming only the riskiest treatments or adding partial checks is tempting, but safe practice requires adjusting the schedule and arranging coverage.

Question 443

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapy student on placement in a Halifax clinic asks to perform a joint manipulation on a patient she has seen once. The supervising physiotherapist is behind schedule and thinks the student is capable. The patient has not been told a student is involved. What should the supervisor do?

  • A. Tell the patient a student will observe, then allow the manipulation with the supervisor present.
  • B. Obtain the patient's consent to student involvement and supervise closely.
  • C. Let the student perform a gentler mobilization instead without disclosing her student status.
  • D. Allow the student to attempt it after she demonstrates the technique on the supervisor first.

The correct answer is B (Obtain the patient's consent to student involvement and supervise closely.): Patients must agree to a student's involvement, and a supervisor must be close enough to intervene. Telling the patient about observation seems adequate, but consent to hands-on care by a student is a separate matter. Supervision protects the patient while the student learns.

Question 444

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a private clinic in British Columbia wants to assign gait training to a kinesiologist employed at the clinic. The kinesiologist is skilled but is not part of her regulatory college. Who remains accountable for the care the physiotherapist assigns?

  • A. The physiotherapist remains accountable for the plan, for the choice of delegate, and for supervision.
  • B. The clinic owner, who employs the kinesiologist and sets delegation policy.
  • C. The kinesiologist, who accepted the delegation in writing and performs the task.
  • D. The physiotherapist for the plan, and the kinesiologist for how the task is carried out.

The correct answer is A (The physiotherapist remains accountable for the plan, for the choice of delegate, and for supervision.): A regulated professional who delegates remains accountable for the plan, for choosing a competent delegate and for supervision. The delegate carries responsibility for their own conduct, but that does not take away her accountability for the care she assigns.

Question 445

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Ontario needs to assess a 47-year-old woman's thoracic spine and shoulder, which requires exposing her back. She seems uneasy and the clinic room has a curtain but no gown. The physiotherapist usually treats alone. What is the best practice?

  • A. Explain why exposure is needed and offer draping, then proceed alone.
  • B. Explain why exposure is needed, offer draping, offer a chaperone, and respect her answer.
  • C. Offer a chaperone, and begin the exposed assessment once she nods.
  • D. Explain why exposure is needed, obtain her signature on a form, and proceed alone.

The correct answer is B (Explain why exposure is needed, offer draping, offer a chaperone, and respect her answer.): Exposing the body requires a clear reason, appropriate draping and an offer of a chaperone, each of which she can accept or refuse. Offering draping alone, or a chaperone alone, is tempting but leaves part of her comfort unaddressed. A signed form cannot replace a continuing conversation.

Question 446

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a Toronto hospital invites a 60-year-old patient to join a research study testing a new balance program. The patient is hesitant, and the physiotherapist who also treats him is the study's lead. The patient asks whether declining will affect his care. What is the correct answer?

  • A. Declining is permitted, but his care would then move to another therapist.
  • B. Declining will not affect his usual care, but his spouse should countersign the written consent form.
  • C. Declining will not affect his usual care, and verbal consent to the lead investigator is enough.
  • D. Declining will not affect his usual care, and participation must be voluntary and informed.

The correct answer is D (Declining will not affect his usual care, and participation must be voluntary and informed.): Research participation must be voluntary and informed, and refusal cannot change a patient's usual care. Because the lead investigator is also his treating therapist, that assurance matters more. Verbal consent and consent from a spouse do not meet research ethics standards for a capable adult.

Question 447

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a Quebec hospital disagrees with the orthopedic surgeon's weight-bearing orders for a 70-year-old after fracture fixation, believing the instructions are too restrictive and delaying recovery. The surgeon is busy and sometimes dismissive. What is the most appropriate response?

  • A. Follow the order for now and wait for the surgeon's next scheduled review before raising concerns.
  • B. Respectfully share her clinical reasoning with the surgeon and seek clarification.
  • C. Modify the order slightly within her own judgment and document the reasons in the physiotherapy notes.
  • D. Ask the nurse manager to request that the surgeon change the order on her behalf.

The correct answer is B (Respectfully share her clinical reasoning with the surgeon and seek clarification.): A physiotherapist who disagrees with an order raises it directly and respectfully with the prescriber, with her reasoning, and seeks clarification. Waiting, going through a manager or adjusting the order herself avoids the conversation that could resolve it. Documentation does not make a unilateral change acceptable.

Question 448

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist registered in Ontario is asked to provide a series of video sessions to a patient who lives in another province and is visiting family there for several weeks. She wonders about her authority to practise in that place. Which principle is most accurate?

  • A. Her Ontario registration is enough, because the patient is an Ontario resident visiting family.
  • B. Follow the requirements of the province where the patient normally lives and holds a health card.
  • C. Confirm the regulatory requirements of the province where the patient is located.
  • D. Follow the rules of the province where the video platform's servers are hosted.

The correct answer is C (Confirm the regulatory requirements of the province where the patient is located.): Regulators generally treat care as occurring where the patient is located, so she must confirm that province's requirements. Her home registration and the patient's residency are tempting, but they do not create authority elsewhere. Platform servers have no bearing on the matter.

Question 449

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in Alberta decides to end care for a patient who has repeatedly yelled at reception staff and missed several appointments. The patient still needs rehabilitation after a rotator cuff repair. How should she end the relationship in a professionally acceptable way?

  • A. Give reasonable notice, explain why, offer referral options, and document it.
  • B. Give notice and reasons, then pass the patient to a colleague without documenting the discontinuation.
  • C. Send a written discharge letter stating the reasons and end care that day without notice.
  • D. Warn him in writing and agree to continue care on conditions, with no mention of alternatives.

The correct answer is A (Give reasonable notice, explain why, offer referral options, and document it.): Ending care properly requires reasonable notice, an explanation, help finding other care and a record of the decision. He still needs rehabilitation after surgery, so abrupt discharge risks his recovery. Written warnings alone do not meet that standard.

Question 450

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in British Columbia has been charged with an offence unrelated to her practice and is awaiting a court date. She believes it will be resolved and thinks mentioning it to her regulator is unnecessary because it is outside work. What should she consider?

  • A. Her regulator expects reports of practice-related charges, so she should wait for the court outcome.
  • B. She should report once the court date is set, as it is public.
  • C. Her regulator may require prompt reporting of certain charges, so she should check.
  • D. She should tell her employer first, and the employer will inform the regulator.

The correct answer is C (Her regulator may require prompt reporting of certain charges, so she should check.): Many regulators require members to report certain charges promptly, including some that are unrelated to practice, and waiting for an outcome may breach that duty. She should read her regulator's rules and not leave reporting to her employer or to public records.

Question 451

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist phones a physician about an inpatient whose oxygen saturation fell during a mobility session on a medical ward. She plans to structure the call with SBAR. Which element of SBAR is the correct place to state the specific action she wants, such as an urgent bedside review?

  • A. Recommendation: the specific action or review the clinician is asking the physician to provide.
  • B. Assessment: her interpretation of the problem, its likely cause and its seriousness.
  • C. Situation: the current problem, who the patient is and why the call is being made.
  • D. Background: the admission diagnosis, relevant history, medications and recent changes in the patient's condition.

The correct answer is A (Recommendation: the specific action or review the clinician is asking the physician to provide.): SBAR ends with the step in which the caller states exactly what she needs and by when, here an urgent bedside review. The assessment step is tempting because it conveys seriousness, but it gives her reading of the problem and leaves the request itself unspoken.

Question 452

Professional Practice and Ethics

At shift change, a physiotherapist hands over a client recovering from hip fracture surgery. She reports the diagnosis and weight-bearing status but omits that the client became dizzy on standing yesterday and needed two staff. The next clinician plans an independent walking trial. Which handoff quality problem does this best illustrate?

  • A. Giving the report away from the bedside, so the client could not confirm details
  • B. Describing the surgical procedure in detail while current function stays vague
  • C. Omitting a recent safety change that affects the next clinician's plan
  • D. Leaving out the client's goals for the coming week

The correct answer is C (Omitting a recent safety change that affects the next clinician's plan): The dizziness and the need for two staff are a recent change in safety status, and leaving them out directly threatens the planned independent walking trial. A handoff that skips the client's goals or the bedside location is weaker, but neither one changes what the next clinician does safely today.

Question 453

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist in a Canadian outpatient clinic has assessed a client after knee arthroplasty and written a progressive exercise plan. Her physiotherapist assistant has completed the clinic's competency training for these exercises. The client is stable and the plan is clear. Which delegation decision is most appropriate?

  • A. Delegate the first two sessions, then transfer the plan to the assistant once tolerance is confirmed
  • B. Delegate the sessions and allow the assistant to progress them, with a physiotherapist review at discharge
  • C. Delegate the sessions with a defined plan, monitoring and scheduled physiotherapist reassessment
  • D. Keep the sessions with the physiotherapist until the client reaches full range of motion

The correct answer is C (Delegate the sessions with a defined plan, monitoring and scheduled physiotherapist reassessment): A stable client, a clear plan and a trained assistant fit delegation, provided the physiotherapist keeps the plan, monitors and reassesses on a schedule. Handing over progression decisions or the whole plan fails that oversight, and keeping every session herself ignores a delegation the stem supports.

Question 454

Professional Practice and Ethics

A clinic owner asks a new physiotherapist who remains accountable for the care of a client when part of the treatment plan has been delegated to a physiotherapist assistant. The physiotherapist wants the correct professional principle before she signs the clinic's delegation policy. Which statement is correct?

  • A. Accountability passes to the assistant for the delegated task once competency has been documented and accepted
  • B. Accountability is shared between the physiotherapist and the clinic owner according to the signed delegation policy
  • C. The physiotherapist is accountable for the plan, while the assistant answers for each delegated task
  • D. The delegating physiotherapist remains accountable for the client's overall care.

The correct answer is D (The delegating physiotherapist remains accountable for the client's overall care.): Delegation passes the task but not the professional accountability, which stays with the physiotherapist for the client's overall care. The split-by-task idea sounds reasonable, but it still moves part of the accountability to the assistant, and a clinic policy cannot move a regulated professional's own duty.

Question 455

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist assistant is supervising a delegated walking program for a man three days after abdominal surgery. Midway through the session he reports new chest tightness and looks pale. His plan said to progress distance daily. The supervising physiotherapist is on site in another room. What should the assistant do first?

  • A. Stop the activity, seat the client safely and alert the supervising physiotherapist immediately
  • B. Stop the activity, seat the client and record the chest symptoms for the next review
  • C. Stop the activity, seat the client and check vital signs before telling anyone
  • D. Stop the activity and ask the unit nurse to decide whether the program can resume

The correct answer is A (Stop the activity, seat the client safely and alert the supervising physiotherapist immediately): New chest tightness with pallor falls outside the delegated plan, so the assistant makes the client safe and brings in the physiotherapist who holds clinical responsibility straight away. Stopping and recording is a sound first half, but waiting for a later review leaves a possibly serious problem with no clinical decision-maker involved.

Question 456

Professional Practice and Ethics

A client who speaks Punjabi and limited English attends for a shoulder assessment. Her adult son offers to interpret and the clinic has a telephone interpreter service available at no cost. The assessment includes sensitive questions about falls at home and medication use. What is the best approach?

  • A. Use the son as interpreter for medical content and the telephone service for consent
  • B. Ask the son to interpret the history, then confirm key points later through the telephone interpreter
  • C. Use the professional interpreter and invite the son to stay as support
  • D. Reschedule with a Punjabi-speaking clinician and postpone the assessment until one is available next month

The correct answer is C (Use the professional interpreter and invite the son to stay as support): A trained interpreter protects accuracy and privacy, and the son can stay for support. Sensitive questions about falls and medications are the situation where a family interpreter may filter or soften answers, and postponing care is unnecessary when a free telephone service is available now.

Question 457

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist is working with an in-person interpreter for the first time during an initial assessment. She wants to follow good practice for the conversation itself and avoid common errors that reduce accuracy. Which behaviour best supports accurate communication during the session?

  • A. Speaking to the interpreter and asking the interpreter to relay each question
  • B. Speaking in long, complete passages so the interpreter can translate the full meaning
  • C. Using exact medical terminology so the interpreter can translate each term precisely
  • D. Speaking directly to the client in short segments and pausing after each for the interpreter

The correct answer is D (Speaking directly to the client in short segments and pausing after each for the interpreter): Addressing the client directly in short segments, with pauses for the interpreter, keeps the relationship with the client and lets the interpreter render each point accurately. Long passages seem efficient but strain recall, and exact jargon often has no direct equivalent, so both reduce accuracy.

Question 458

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist has just taught a client with osteoarthritis a home program of four exercises and a pacing plan. The client nods and says it all makes sense. The physiotherapist wants to confirm that her teaching, not the client's memory, is the thing being checked. Which action fits best?

  • A. Ask whether she has any questions and wait quietly for a response before ending
  • B. Ask her to describe or show the exercises in her own words
  • C. Hand her a printed copy and ask her to read it aloud twice at home
  • D. Repeat the full explanation more slowly so the instructions are heard a second time

The correct answer is B (Ask her to describe or show the exercises in her own words): Teach-back checks understanding by having the client restate or show the content, and any gap is treated as a flaw in the explanation. A nod or an absence of questions does not show the plan was understood.

Question 459

Professional Practice and Ethics

A clinic is revising its handouts on back pain self-management for the general adult population in Canada. The manager asks which design choice best supports readers with limited health literacy. The physiotherapist must pick one principle for the revision team. Which is most appropriate?

  • A. Short sentences, with every technical term defined in a glossary at the handout's end
  • B. Plain language, short sentences, key actions first and relevant pictures placed beside the text
  • C. Bullet points with every picture removed, so the page looks clean and uncluttered
  • D. Key points placed in a summary box at the end after the detailed explanation

The correct answer is B (Plain language, short sentences, key actions first and relevant pictures placed beside the text): Readers with limited health literacy act on what they see first, so plain words, key actions at the front and pictures beside the text work best. A glossary at the end defines terms, which is tempting, but the reader must search for meaning instead of having it in the sentence.

Question 460

Professional Practice and Ethics

A capable 68-year-old man with a stroke consents to treatment but tells his physiotherapist not to share his prognosis with his daughter. The daughter arrives, says she is the family decision-maker and asks for details of his expected recovery. What is the most appropriate response?

  • A. Respect his instruction, explain the limit and invite him to reconsider
  • B. Share the general recovery outlook with her but withhold specific details and test results
  • C. Ask the daughter for her authority documents, then share if she is his substitute decision-maker
  • D. Defer to the treating physician to decide what the daughter should be told about his recovery

The correct answer is A (Respect his instruction, explain the limit and invite him to reconsider): A capable adult controls who receives his health information, so the physiotherapist respects his instruction, explains what that means to the daughter and invites him to reconsider. A substitute decision-maker only acts for someone who lacks capacity, and a partial summary still breaches his stated wish.

Question 461

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 44-year-old warehouse worker reports low back pain for two weeks, now with new numbness in the groin area, difficulty starting urination and bilateral leg weakness that began this morning. He wants to continue with his booked treatment. What should the physiotherapist do?

  • A. Arrange emergency medical assessment today and pass findings to the receiving team
  • B. Advise emergency department attendance if his symptoms worsen overnight
  • C. Do a neurological screen first, then refer to a spine clinic if abnormal
  • D. Stop treatment and request an urgent MRI through the family physician

The correct answer is A (Arrange emergency medical assessment today and pass findings to the receiving team): Saddle numbness, urinary difficulty and bilateral weakness with sudden onset suggest cauda equina compression, so the client goes to emergency care today with a handoff of findings. An urgent MRI request through a family physician sounds proactive, but it takes days and the nerve damage can become permanent in that time.

Question 462

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist treating a woman after a hip fracture notes that she struggles with bathing, dressing and meal preparation despite good progress in walking. She and her husband want her to relearn these tasks and adapt the home. Which referral best addresses the barrier her physiotherapy goals do not cover?

  • A. Referral to home care services for personal support with bathing, dressing and meal preparation
  • B. Referral to a community balance and fall prevention exercise program
  • C. Referral to social work for caregiver support and home modification funding
  • D. Referral to occupational therapy for assessment of daily tasks and home equipment

The correct answer is D (Referral to occupational therapy for assessment of daily tasks and home equipment): The gap is in daily tasks and home adaptation, which is the focus of occupational therapy assessment and retraining. Home care would supply help, but this couple wants her to relearn the tasks, and exercise or funding referrals do not assess how she performs bathing, dressing or cooking.

Question 463

Professional Practice and Ethics

In a rehabilitation team meeting, a physiotherapist wants a client discharged home with support, while the nurse believes a short stay in a rehabilitation unit is safer. The tone is becoming tense and the client has not been asked. What is the best next step in collaborative practice?

  • A. Agree with the nurse to restore calm and raise her concern later
  • B. Clarify each member's reasons and the client's goals, then agree on a plan
  • C. Present evidence for discharge home until the nurse accepts the plan
  • D. Ask the manager to choose between the two plans and announce the final decision

The correct answer is B (Clarify each member's reasons and the client's goals, then agree on a plan): Collaborative practice means understanding each discipline's reasons and bringing the client's own goals into the decision before agreeing on a plan. Presenting evidence is useful, which makes it tempting, but pushing until the nurse accepts it treats the meeting as a contest and still leaves the client unheard.

Question 464

Professional Practice and Ethics

A busy outpatient physiotherapist has a client arrive 20 minutes late for a 45-minute follow-up. The next client is already waiting and the late client is in moderate pain after an ankle sprain. The clinic policy allows shortened sessions. Which response best balances fairness and safety?

  • A. Run the full 45 minutes and shorten the next client's session so both are treated
  • B. Treat the late client fully, then move the waiting client to a later slot
  • C. Offer a shortened, focused session and rebook the remaining items
  • D. Cancel the visit and offer the next available appointment

The correct answer is C (Offer a shortened, focused session and rebook the remaining items): A shortened, focused session meets the late client's pain and respects the waiting client's booking, and the remaining items can be rebooked under clinic policy. Giving the late client the full time or bumping the waiting client is unfair, and cancelling leaves a client in moderate pain untreated.

Question 465

Professional Practice and Ethics

A clinic is retraining staff on the four moments for hand hygiene used in Canadian health care. A physiotherapist has just finished palpating a client's joint, with no body fluid exposure, and is about to leave the treatment space to prepare supplies for the next client. Which hand hygiene moment applies right now?

  • A. Before the next client is touched, at the start of that client's treatment
  • B. Before an aseptic procedure on the client, such as handling an open wound or dressing
  • C. After contact with the client or their surroundings, before moving to the next task
  • D. After the session ends and before the visit is documented

The correct answer is C (After contact with the client or their surroundings, before moving to the next task): The fourth moment is after contact with the client or anything in the client's immediate surroundings, before moving on to another task. Before an aseptic procedure applies only when a sterile or open site will be handled, and before touching the next client is a real moment that comes later. Finishing documentation is not a defined moment.

Question 466

Professional Practice and Ethics

A client on an inpatient unit has a diagnosis of Clostridioides difficile infection and is under contact precautions. A physiotherapist plans gait training. Her unit stocks both alcohol-based hand rub and soap with running water at the room entrance. Which hand hygiene action is best after leaving the room?

  • A. Use alcohol-based hand rub because it is quicker and kills the organism
  • B. Wash with soap and running water, since alcohol rub does not reliably remove spores
  • C. Use alcohol-based hand rub and then put on fresh gloves before the next client
  • D. Wear gloves throughout the visit and skip hand hygiene after removing them

The correct answer is B (Wash with soap and running water, since alcohol rub does not reliably remove spores): Spores of this organism resist alcohol, so mechanical washing with soap and water is preferred. Gloves reduce contamination but do not replace hand hygiene after removal.

Question 467

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist is about to treat a client on droplet and contact precautions who needs help with transfers. The unit protocol requires a gown, a procedure mask, eye protection and gloves. Which order for putting on this equipment matches standard infection prevention practice?

  • A. Mask, eye protection, gown, then gloves pulled over the cuffs of the gown
  • B. Gown, mask, eye protection, then gloves pulled over the gown cuffs
  • C. Gown, gloves, mask, then eye protection fitted over the mask's upper straps
  • D. Mask, gown, gloves, then eye protection fitted last

The correct answer is B (Gown, mask, eye protection, then gloves pulled over the gown cuffs): The standard order is gown, mask, eye protection and then gloves, with the gloves covering the gown cuffs so skin is sealed. The other sequences use the same items but put gloves on too early, which risks contaminating the face equipment while it is adjusted.

Question 468

Professional Practice and Ethics

Between clients in a busy gym, a physiotherapist notices that a shared exercise bike handle and a plinth have visible sweat and skin contact. The clinic stocks a hospital-grade disinfectant wipe with a stated contact time. What is the best practice for this noncritical equipment?

  • A. Remove soil, wipe with disinfectant and keep it wet for the contact time
  • B. Wipe with disinfectant and dry the surface at once with a clean towel to prevent residue
  • C. Spray disinfectant over visible soil and leave it to air dry for the stated contact time
  • D. Clean with soap and water, then leave the surface to air dry

The correct answer is A (Remove soil, wipe with disinfectant and keep it wet for the contact time): Visible soil must be removed first because it shields microbes from the disinfectant, and the surface must stay wet for the full labelled contact time. Cleaning alone is sensible for some surfaces, but shared equipment with skin contact needs disinfection, and wiping it dry early cuts the contact time short.

Question 469

Professional Practice and Ethics

While setting up a therapeutic ultrasound unit, a physiotherapist notices that the power cord has a frayed section with exposed wire near the plug. A client is waiting and there is no other unit available. The device still powers on. What is the most appropriate action?

  • A. Use the unit on a ground fault interrupter circuit and report the frayed cord after treatment
  • B. Insulate the frayed section with electrical tape and report the cord later
  • C. Remove the unit from service, label it as faulty and report it for repair or replacement
  • D. Switch to another modality for this client and record the frayed cord in the chart

The correct answer is C (Remove the unit from service, label it as faulty and report it for repair or replacement): A cord with exposed wire is an electrical hazard, so the unit is removed from service, labelled as faulty and reported for repair or replacement. A ground fault interrupter reduces shock risk but does not make a damaged cord safe, and tape or a chart note leaves the unit available to the next user.

Question 470

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist prepares to use a gait belt and a height-adjustable walker with a client who is a fall risk. The walker's rubber tip on one leg is worn smooth, and one height-adjustment pin will not lock securely despite repeated attempts. What should she do before the session?

  • A. Re-seat the pin and test the height with body weight before proceeding
  • B. Fit a spare rubber tip and continue, as the tip is the main hazard
  • C. Replace the walker with a safe one and report the faulty walker for repair
  • D. Limit the session to hallway walking and lower the walker height

The correct answer is C (Replace the walker with a safe one and report the faulty walker for repair): A walker with a pin that will not lock and a worn tip can collapse or slip, so it is replaced with a safe one and the faulty walker is reported for repair. Fitting a new tip fixes the slip hazard and seems practical, but the unlocked height pin can still let the frame give way under load.

Question 471

Professional Practice and Ethics

A new physiotherapist joins a private clinic that owns an electrotherapy unit, a hydrocollator and a treadmill. She asks the manager how the clinic ensures these remain safe. Which practice best reflects accepted equipment management in a regulated Canadian clinic?

  • A. Yearly servicing of electrical devices, with records kept of repairs made
  • B. Pre-use visual checks by each clinician, with notes made when a fault is found
  • C. Manufacturer inspection at purchase and replacement of each device every five years
  • D. Scheduled preventive maintenance and safety checks, with records kept for each electrical device

The correct answer is D (Scheduled preventive maintenance and safety checks, with records kept for each electrical device): Safe equipment depends on planned preventive maintenance and safety checks, documented for each device. Pre-use visual checks by clinicians are worth doing and sound thorough, but they cannot detect internal electrical or calibration faults that develop gradually.

Question 472

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 37-year-old forklift operator injured his shoulder at work and has an accepted claim with the provincial workers' compensation board. He asks his physiotherapist who is paying for treatment. The clinic is registered with the board. What should the physiotherapist explain?

  • A. The board usually funds approved treatment under its reporting rules
  • B. The employer pays the clinic and then claims the cost back
  • C. His extended health plan covers the visits before the board
  • D. Provincial health insurance covers the visits first, and the board reimburses the plan for approved claims

The correct answer is A (The board usually funds approved treatment under its reporting rules): For an accepted workplace claim, the board usually funds approved treatment from a registered clinic under its reporting and approval rules. Provincial plans and extended health benefits are the usual payers for non-work conditions, and the employer is not the payer of treatment in this process.

Question 473

Professional Practice and Ethics

A woman has neck pain after a rear-end collision and has opened a claim with her auto insurer. She also has extended health benefits through her job and asks the physiotherapist how to bill. The treatment plan has not been approved by the insurer yet. What is the best approach?

  • A. Bill the extended health plan first to avoid delaying her treatment
  • B. Start treatment now and send the invoice to the auto insurer afterward
  • C. Clarify which insurer pays, follow its preapproval process and explain possible costs
  • D. Wait for the insurer's approval before booking any assessment visit at the clinic

The correct answer is C (Clarify which insurer pays, follow its preapproval process and explain possible costs): With a collision claim open, the auto insurer is the expected payer, so the clinician clarifies this, follows its preapproval process and explains costs that may fall to the client. Billing the work benefits first or starting unapproved care risks denied claims and surprise bills for her.

Question 474

Professional Practice and Ethics

A client asks why some physiotherapy is free through a hospital program while the clinic charges a fee for similar exercise sessions. The physiotherapist wants an accurate, simple explanation of funding in her province that does not mislead him. Which statement is most accurate?

  • A. Hospital programs are publicly funded and clinics are privately funded, with the same rules everywhere
  • B. Funding varies with setting, eligibility and province, and some services are privately paid
  • C. Federal rules set the same physiotherapy coverage in every province and territory
  • D. Public programs cover chronic conditions while clinics treat acute injuries for a fee

The correct answer is B (Funding varies with setting, eligibility and province, and some services are privately paid): Physiotherapy funding is mostly provincial, so coverage depends on the setting, who is eligible and where the client lives, and some services are paid privately. The setting-based split is partly true but leaves out eligibility and provincial differences, which is why it would mislead him.

Question 475

Professional Practice and Ethics

A client calls a private clinic to book a first visit and asks what the initial assessment and follow-ups will cost. The administrator is unsure, and the physiotherapist knows the clinic fee schedule. What does good practice require regarding fees?

  • A. Give the fee schedule at the first session, after the assessment and plan are fully explained
  • B. Give an approximate fee by phone and confirm the final amount at the last visit
  • C. Post the fee schedule at reception where clients can read it
  • D. Give clear fee information before treatment begins and confirm the client understands

The correct answer is D (Give clear fee information before treatment begins and confirm the client understands): Clients need clear, accurate fee information before treatment starts so they can consent knowing the cost, and the clinician checks that they understood. Disclosure after the assessment, a posted sheet or a rough estimate each leaves the client committed or unsure before the actual fees are known.

Question 476

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapy department wants to reduce missed appointments using a quality improvement approach. The lead proposes a small test of text reminders with one team for two weeks, followed by review of the results and a decision to adopt, adapt or drop the change. Which model does this describe?

  • A. DMAIC, a five-phase method for reducing variation in established, high-volume processes
  • B. Plan, do, study, act (PDSA), a cycle for testing and learning from changes
  • C. Root cause analysis, a review that traces an event to its causes
  • D. Audit and feedback, a review that compares practice against a standard

The correct answer is B (Plan, do, study, act (PDSA), a cycle for testing and learning from changes): A small test on one team over two weeks, followed by study of the result and a decision to adopt, adapt or drop, is the plan, do, study, act cycle. DMAIC is a quality method too, but it suits large, stable processes rather than a quick pilot, and the audit and cause-analysis tools do not test a change.

Question 477

Professional Practice and Ethics

A clinic manager reviews outcome data and sees that clients with chronic low back pain improved less on a validated functional measure than expected. She wants to use this finding for quality improvement and has the support of the clinical team. What is the most useful next step?

  • A. Review how care is delivered, identify likely causes with the team and test a targeted change
  • B. Repeat the measure on every client for another quarter to confirm the trend
  • C. Compare the clinic's results with published benchmarks and change the program to match the best performers
  • D. Adopt a new exercise protocol from a recent trial across the whole clinic at once

The correct answer is A (Review how care is delivered, identify likely causes with the team and test a targeted change): The useful next step is to examine how care is delivered, find likely causes with the team and test a targeted change on a small scale. Benchmarking and more data may add context, but they do not identify local causes, and a clinic-wide protocol switch skips testing.

Question 478

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist almost gave a client the wrong home exercise sheet, which listed restricted movements for a different surgery, but noticed the error before handing it over. No harm occurred. A colleague says reporting is pointless because nothing happened. What is the best response?

  • A. Fix the sheet template and keep a personal note of what happened
  • B. Discuss it at the next team meeting and note it in the minutes rather than reporting
  • C. Report it through the clinic's system, since it reveals process weaknesses to fix
  • D. Report it to the regulatory college as a practice concern

The correct answer is C (Report it through the clinic's system, since it reveals process weaknesses to fix): A near miss shows where the process can fail, so it goes into the clinic's reporting system, where patterns across events can be seen and fixed. Quiet fixes and meeting talk help one person, and a regulator report is meant for conduct or serious concerns, not an error caught before any harm.

Question 479

Professional Practice and Ethics

During an exercise session, a client fell from a stool and fractured her wrist because the stool had a loose leg the physiotherapist had not checked. She is being sent for imaging. What should the physiotherapist do after ensuring she receives appropriate care?

  • A. Tell her she fell and record the loose leg in the internal report
  • B. Apologize sincerely and keep the chart entry brief and neutral to avoid legal exposure
  • C. Wait for the clinic manager to decide what the client should be told
  • D. Tell her honestly what happened, express concern, and report and document it

The correct answer is D (Tell her honestly what happened, express concern, and report and document it): Clients are entitled to prompt, honest disclosure of harm, including how it happened, and the clinician then reports and documents the event. Telling her only that she fell and noting the cause internally is tempting, but it holds back what she is entitled to know.

Question 480

Professional Practice and Ethics
