A frustrated client shouting about wait times follows a physiotherapist into the treatment room, stands close and raises his voice, clenching his fists. She has a call button and a colleague nearby. Which action best protects her safety while following professional standards?

  • A. Move him to a seat and remain between him and the door
  • B. Tell him she will call security unless he calms down at once
  • C. Offer an earlier appointment to settle him and continue with the session
  • D. Stay calm, keep an exit open, set a clear limit and call for help if needed

The correct answer is D (Stay calm, keep an exit open, set a clear limit and call for help if needed): Her safety and professionalism are best served by staying calm, keeping her exit open, setting a clear limit and calling for help if needed. Threats escalate, an earlier appointment rewards the behaviour, and standing between herself and the door leaves her trapped if he becomes violent.

Question 481

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist is scheduled for her first visit to a client's home in an unfamiliar neighbourhood, late in the afternoon. The client has a history of aggressive behaviour noted in the referral. The clinic has a lone worker policy. What is the most appropriate preparation?

  • A. Ask the client's family to remain present throughout the visit and proceed as scheduled
  • B. Book an earlier time of day and notify the clinic after the visit
  • C. Convert the first visit to a phone assessment and plan in-person care later
  • D. Share the visit details with the clinic, arrange check-ins and review the risk

The correct answer is D (Share the visit details with the clinic, arrange check-ins and review the risk): The lone worker policy exists for a visit like this, so she shares the visit details, arranges check-ins and reviews the documented risk beforehand. Family presence or an earlier time may help, but without notice to the clinic nobody knows whether she is safe during the visit.

Question 482

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist must help a 120 kg client move from bed to a chair. She has had low back pain from prior transfers. The unit has a ceiling lift and a second staff member available. Which approach best protects the clinician while keeping the transfer safe?

  • A. Perform a manual transfer with the second staff member, a gait belt and good body mechanics
  • B. Use the ceiling lift with the second staff member and the unit's procedure
  • C. Use a sliding board with the second staff member and let the client help as able
  • D. Ask the second staff member to complete the transfer with a gait belt

The correct answer is B (Use the ceiling lift with the second staff member and the unit's procedure): A ceiling lift is on the unit and she already has back pain, so the lift with a second staff member and the unit's procedure best protects both people. Manual handling, even with a belt or board, still places heavy load on the back of whoever is moving a 120 kg client.

Question 483

Professional Practice and Ethics

During a hands-on session, a client makes repeated sexual comments toward his physiotherapist and asks her to meet outside the clinic. She has already asked him to stop once. He says it is only a joke. What should she do next?

  • A. State that the behaviour is unacceptable, end the session if it continues and document it
  • B. Give a second warning, continue treatment and document it if it happens again
  • C. Transfer his care to a male colleague and explain the reason to him calmly
  • D. Report the client to the police immediately and stop all physiotherapy care for him

The correct answer is A (State that the behaviour is unacceptable, end the session if it continues and document it): She has already asked him to stop, so the next step is a clear statement that the behaviour is unacceptable, ending the session if it continues, and documenting it. Giving a second warning seems fair, but continuing treatment while waiting for a repeat leaves her exposed.

Question 484

Professional Practice and Ethics

A new physiotherapist asks a senior colleague when entries should be written in the client record. Several clients were treated in one afternoon and she is tempted to complete the notes after the weekend from memory. Which standard best describes appropriate documentation practice?

  • A. Record care as soon as practical after the visit so the entry is accurate
  • B. Write notes within a week of the visit, dating each entry
  • C. Complete notes at the end of each week from the day's schedule and the appointment log
  • D. Write a full note when the plan changes and a brief one otherwise

The correct answer is A (Record care as soon as practical after the visit so the entry is accurate): Records are written as soon as practical after care so they are accurate and complete. A one-week window or weekly summaries rely on memory, and notes limited to visits with a problem leave routine care undocumented.

Question 485

Professional Practice and Ethics

A 79-year-old woman with early dementia is assessed for her ability to make a decision about discharge home. The physiotherapist judges that she understands the choices and risks. Her son demands that she go to a care home. What is the most appropriate response?

  • A. Treat the son as the substitute decision-maker because her diagnosis may limit her judgment later
  • B. Request a formal capacity assessment from a physician before accepting her decision to go home
  • C. Support her decision as a capable adult and involve her son with her agreement
  • D. Delay discharge until the family agrees on a plan

The correct answer is C (Support her decision as a capable adult and involve her son with her agreement): Capacity is decision-specific, and a diagnosis of early dementia does not remove it. Having judged that she understands the choices and risks, the physiotherapist supports her decision and involves her son only with her agreement; a further assessment or a substitute is unnecessary.

Question 486

Professional Practice and Ethics

A man with a severe brain injury cannot understand or weigh the options for a proposed change to his rehabilitation plan. No advance directive exists and several relatives disagree about what to do. How should the physiotherapist proceed in accordance with provincial consent rules?

  • A. Identify the legal substitute decision-maker by the provincial order and seek consent
  • B. Seek consent from the relative who knew him longest and attends most often
  • C. Proceed under the emergency exception because the change benefits his recovery
  • D. Ask the relatives to agree on one spokesperson and follow that person's instructions for the plan

The correct answer is A (Identify the legal substitute decision-maker by the provincial order and seek consent): When a client lacks capacity and has no directive, provincial law sets an order of substitute decision-makers, and the physiotherapist identifies who ranks highest and seeks consent from that person. Family agreement, closeness or perceived benefit do not replace that legal order.

Question 487

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist wants a client with mixed feelings about exercise to explore her own reasons for change. She uses motivational interviewing and is about to ask the first question of the conversation. Which type of question best supports this aim at the start of the conversation?

  • A. Would you agree that regular exercise would help your pain and your daily function?
  • B. What stops you from doing the exercises you were given at your last visit?
  • C. What are the main reasons your doctor has recommended that you become more active?
  • D. What would being more active allow you to do that matters to you?

The correct answer is D (What would being more active allow you to do that matters to you?): Motivational interviewing starts with an open question that draws out her own reasons for change, such as what being more active would allow her to do. Closed or leading questions invite a yes, and asking about the doctor's reasons or her barriers shifts the focus away from her motivation.

Question 488

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist needs to explain to a client that her persistent nerve injury may not fully recover. The client appears anxious and has not said what she expects. Which approach to sharing this information best supports a respectful, honest conversation about her outlook?

  • A. Ask what she understands, share in small pieces, then check her understanding
  • B. Avoid the subject until she asks, so she is not distressed by premature news
  • C. Describe the best case outcome to protect her hope while treatment continues
  • D. Give the full prognosis immediately so that she hears the facts without being misled

The correct answer is A (Ask what she understands, share in small pieces, then check her understanding): Checking what the client already knows, sharing in chunks and responding to her reaction respects her need for honest information. Hiding or sugarcoating the prognosis undermines trust and informed decision making.

Question 489

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist is about to teach a client who is hard of hearing a new exercise sequence. The client uses a hearing aid and lip-reads. The clinic room has a noisy fan nearby and the physiotherapist usually wears a mask. What is the best way to improve communication?

  • A. Reduce the background noise, face the client and use a clear mask when giving instructions
  • B. Speak slowly with the mask on and repeat each instruction twice
  • C. Stand beside the hearing aid side and speak louder when giving instructions
  • D. Provide written instructions and demonstrate each movement while giving no verbal cues

The correct answer is A (Reduce the background noise, face the client and use a clear mask when giving instructions): Lowering the background noise, facing him and using a clear mask supports both his hearing aid and his lip-reading. Louder speech or repetition through an opaque mask leaves the main barriers in place, and removing speech discards a channel he can still use.

Question 490

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist is working with a man who has expressive aphasia after a stroke. He understands most of what is said but struggles to find words and becomes frustrated during longer exchanges. Which communication strategy is most helpful in this session?

  • A. Practise naming drills at the start of each session until his word finding recovers
  • B. Ask open-ended questions and wait for him to find each word without offering any prompts
  • C. Ask short yes or no questions and allow extra time, gestures or pictures
  • D. Speak slowly using simple words suited to reduced understanding

The correct answer is C (Ask short yes or no questions and allow extra time, gestures or pictures): Because he understands most of what is said, short yes or no questions with extra time, gestures or pictures lower the word-finding demand and ease his frustration. Open questions raise that demand, drills belong to speech-language pathology, and simplified speech wrongly assumes his comprehension is reduced.

Question 491

Professional Practice and Ethics

A woman on a medical unit is nearing discharge after a hospital stay. The physiotherapist thinks she needs a walker at home, and the occupational therapist is concerned about stairs and bathing. Nursing wants a date confirmed. How can the team best plan the discharge?

  • A. Hold a team conference with the client and family to agree on supports and timing
  • B. Follow the standard pathway for her diagnosis and adjust supports at home
  • C. Have nursing set the date and let each discipline arrange its own supports
  • D. Circulate a shared written plan for sign-off by each discipline before the discharge date is confirmed

The correct answer is A (Hold a team conference with the client and family to agree on supports and timing): Different disciplines have raised different concerns, so a team conference with the client and family lets everyone agree on supports and timing together. A written sign-off or separate planning misses the chance to resolve conflicts, and a generic pathway ignores her stairs and bathing needs.

Question 492

Professional Practice and Ethics

A client with chronic knee pain asks his physiotherapist to review an unexplained unintentional weight loss of 8 kg and night sweats over the past two months. These symptoms are not explained by his knee condition. What is the most appropriate action?

  • A. Complete a systems review first and refer if findings persist after two visits
  • B. Recommend prompt medical assessment and document the findings and advice given to him
  • C. Advise him to mention the weight loss at his next routine physician visit
  • D. Refer him to a dietitian for assessment of the weight loss and sweats

The correct answer is B (Recommend prompt medical assessment and document the findings and advice given to him): Unexplained weight loss with night sweats is a systemic red flag outside the knee condition, so he needs prompt medical assessment with the advice documented. A systems review is part of good practice, which is tempting, but waiting two more visits delays a possibly serious diagnosis.

Question 493

Professional Practice and Ethics

A clinic is drafting an internal policy that sets out which tasks may be delegated to physiotherapist assistants. A manager suggests that assistants should complete new client assessments to increase capacity. Which task should remain with the physiotherapist under accepted practice?

  • A. Instructing a stable client in a home program the physiotherapist has already prescribed and demonstrated
  • B. Leading a supervised group exercise class from a designed program
  • C. Applying a hot pack for ten minutes under written directions
  • D. Performing the initial assessment, forming the diagnosis and developing the treatment plan

The correct answer is D (Performing the initial assessment, forming the diagnosis and developing the treatment plan): Initial assessment, diagnosis and treatment planning require the physiotherapist's clinical judgment and cannot be delegated. The other tasks follow a plan the physiotherapist has already made and can be delegated with supervision, so they do not answer the question.

Question 494

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapy student on placement asks to carry out a manual technique on a client with recent spinal surgery. The clinical instructor has seen the student perform this technique only once on a classmate. The client has consented to student involvement. What should the instructor do?

  • A. Allow the student to try the technique with the instructor observing from across the room
  • B. Ask the student to repeat the technique once more on a classmate, then proceed unsupervised
  • C. Directly supervise the student or perform the technique herself
  • D. Let the student perform a modified version at lower intensity while the instructor reviews the chart

The correct answer is C (Directly supervise the student or perform the technique herself): The student has shown the technique only once, and the client has recent spinal surgery, so the instructor supervises directly or performs it. Consent to student involvement does not replace supervision, and distant observation or reduced intensity leaves a high-risk technique unsupervised.

Question 495

Professional Practice and Ethics

A physiotherapist is going on leave and transferring a client with chronic pain to a colleague. She plans to leave a brief note saying only that treatment is going well. The client has a history of a past adverse reaction to manual therapy. Which transfer approach is best?

  • A. Give a verbal update on progress and remind the colleague to review the chart
  • B. Provide a structured summary of findings, goals, precautions and the prior reaction
  • C. Write a summary of goals and current treatment, since precautions are already in the chart
  • D. Send the full chart and ask the colleague to read it before the first visit

The correct answer is B (Provide a structured summary of findings, goals, precautions and the prior reaction): A structured summary of findings, goals, precautions and the prior reaction puts the safety information where the colleague will see it. Sending the full chart seems complete, but the past adverse reaction can be buried in a long record that the colleague may not read closely.

Question 496

Professional Practice and Ethics

An insurance adjuster phones a physiotherapist and asks for the full treatment record of a client who has a disability claim. The adjuster says the client signed up for benefits, but the physiotherapist has no consent on file for the release. What should she do?

  • A. Decline until she has the client's valid consent, then share what is relevant
  • B. Release the attendance dates and diagnosis, since these are minimal information
  • C. Verify the adjuster's identity by callback, then release the full record
  • D. Ask the adjuster to send a written request, then release the record on receipt

The correct answer is A (Decline until she has the client's valid consent, then share what is relevant): Without valid consent on file, the physiotherapist declines and shares only what is relevant once consent is obtained. Verifying the adjuster by callback is careful and tempting, but confirming who is asking does not replace the client's permission.

Question 497

Professional Practice and Ethics

On a busy acute care morning, a physiotherapist has four referrals: a stable post-operative hip client, a client with new neurological symptoms awaiting a plan, a client whose discharge this morning depends on equipment, and a routine mobility check. Time allows two assessments before noon. Which pair should she prioritize?

  • A. The client with new neurological symptoms and the stable post-operative hip client
  • B. The routine mobility check and the client with new neurological symptoms this morning
  • C. The discharge equipment client and the stable post-operative hip client
  • D. The client with new neurological symptoms and the discharge equipment client

The correct answer is D (The client with new neurological symptoms and the discharge equipment client): New neurological symptoms need early assessment, and the client whose discharge this morning depends on equipment is next because delay holds a bed and the discharge. The stable hip client and routine check can wait, which is why pairing the neurological client with either is a lower-value choice.

Question 498

Professional Practice and Ethics

A client with a new cough and fever arrives at a physiotherapy clinic waiting room. The receptionist notices that other clients are seated close by. The clinic has masks and hand rub at the front desk. Which action best reduces transmission risk?

  • A. Give him a mask and hand rub, seat him apart and notify the physiotherapist
  • B. Give him a mask and ask him to complete the intake forms at the desk
  • C. Cancel his visit and send him home without further advice
  • D. Move other clients to another seating area and leave him where he is

The correct answer is A (Give him a mask and hand rub, seat him apart and notify the physiotherapist): Source control means a mask, hand hygiene and distance from others, and the physiotherapist is told so suitable precautions can be used. Masking him at the desk is tempting, but standing there close to seated clients does not separate him from them.

Question 499

Professional Practice and Ethics

A client with private extended health coverage asks the physiotherapist for a receipt so that she can claim her physiotherapy costs. The insurer requires the clinician's registration details and itemized services on the receipt, and the client has attended six sessions this month. What should the physiotherapist provide?

  • A. A receipt with dates and services that shows the plan's covered rate, not the clinic's fee
  • B. An accurate itemized receipt with dates, services, fees and registration details
  • C. A receipt that lists services in general terms with the dates
  • D. A receipt listing the month's total with the registration number

The correct answer is B (An accurate itemized receipt with dates, services, fees and registration details): The insurer requires itemized services, dates, actual fees and registration details, so an accurate itemized receipt supports a valid claim. Receipts with a monthly total, vague services or an altered fee are incomplete or inaccurate and can be rejected or misrepresent what was charged.

Question 500

Professional Practice and Ethics

A clinic collects patient experience surveys and finds that many clients say they were unsure about their home program. Clinicians believe their teaching is clear, and the manager wants to improve the results over the coming year. Which response best reflects quality improvement thinking?

  • A. Retrain every clinician on a new teaching script and move on
  • B. Audit a sample of charts to check that home programs were documented as they were taught
  • C. Change teaching to match what the few most dissatisfied clients requested
  • D. Treat the feedback as data, test changes like teach-back and measure the results

The correct answer is D (Treat the feedback as data, test changes like teach-back and measure the results): Quality improvement treats feedback as data, tests a change such as teach-back and measures the effect. A chart audit seems like measurement, which makes it tempting, but it shows what was written down and says nothing about whether clients understood the program.
